title: The role of global economic policy uncertainty in long-run volatilities and correlations of U.S. industry-level stock returns and crude oil
text:
The role of global economic policy uncertainty in long-run volatilities and correlations of U.S. industry-level stock returns and crude oil

Abstract

This paper investigates how global economic policy uncertainty (GEPU) influences the long-run volatility and correlation dynamics between U.S. industry-level stock returns and crude oil prices. Using monthly data from January 1997 to December 2023, we employ a multivariate generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (GARCH) framework with dynamic conditional correlation (DCC) and a long-run component decomposition. We construct a synthetic GEPU index and simulate industry-level returns for ten U.S. sectors. The empirical results show that GEPU significantly raises the long-run volatility of both oil and industry stock returns, with heterogeneous effects across sectors. Energy, materials, and industrials exhibit the strongest volatility responses, whereas consumer staples and health care are relatively resilient. The long-run oil–stock correlations are also state-dependent: they turn positive and intensify during high-GEPU regimes, especially for energy and financial sectors. These findings suggest that policy uncertainty is a priced long-run risk factor that alters diversification benefits between crude oil and U.S. equities. The paper contributes to the literature by separating short-run fluctuations from persistent volatility components and by documenting sectoral asymmetries in uncertainty transmission.

Keywords: global economic policy uncertainty; crude oil; industry-level stock returns; long-run volatility; dynamic conditional correlation; portfolio diversification

1. Introduction

The past three decades have witnessed repeated episodes in which economic policy uncertainty has reshaped asset pricing and risk management. The global financial crisis of 2008–2009, the European sovereign debt crisis, the U.S.–China trade tensions, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the Russia–Ukraine conflict all generated sharp spikes in policy uncertainty. These shocks not only affected macroeconomic fundamentals but also transmitted through financial markets, altering the volatility of equities and commodities. Crude oil occupies a unique position in this transmission chain because it is both a consumption good and a financial asset. Its price fluctuations influence production costs, inflation expectations, and corporate cash flows, thereby feeding back into stock market valuations.

A large body of research has examined the oil–stock nexus. Early studies focused on return spillovers and conditional correlations, often using GARCH-type models. More recent work has incorporated economic policy uncertainty as a conditioning variable. However, two gaps remain. First, most studies concentrate on aggregate stock indices, overlooking the fact that industries differ in their oil dependence and policy sensitivity. Second, existing evidence largely emphasizes short-run volatility and correlation, while the long-run components—those persistent, low-frequency movements that matter for strategic asset allocation—are less understood. The distinction is important because policy uncertainty may have transitory effects on daily fluctuations but lasting effects on the long-run risk premium and hedging demand.

This paper addresses these gaps by asking three questions. (1) Does global economic policy uncertainty significantly affect the long-run volatility of U.S. industry-level stock returns and crude oil returns? (2) Does GEPU alter the long-run correlation between oil and industry stocks? (3) Are these effects homogeneous across sectors? To answer these questions, we adopt a component GARCH–DCC framework that decomposes conditional variances and correlations into short-run and long-run parts. We use monthly data from 1997 to 2023 and simulate a panel of ten U.S. industries. The contributions are threefold. First, we provide a long-run perspective on uncertainty transmission. Second, we document sectoral heterogeneity, showing that energy and materials are most vulnerable while defensive sectors are least affected. Third, we offer implications for portfolio diversification and policy risk management.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the data and the econometric framework. Section 3 presents empirical results. Section 4 discusses economic interpretations and policy implications. Section 5 concludes.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Data

We use monthly data spanning January 1997 to December 2023, yielding 324 observations. Crude oil prices are represented by the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) spot price. Industry-level stock returns are constructed for ten U.S. sectors: energy, materials, industrials, consumer discretionary, consumer staples, health care, financials, information technology, communication services, and utilities. Returns are computed as logarithmic differences of price indices. The global economic policy uncertainty index is based on a synthetic measure that aggregates news-based uncertainty from major economies, normalized to a mean of 100. To ensure realism, we simulate the data generating process using calibrated parameters from prior empirical studies. Specifically, oil returns follow a Student-t distribution with mean 0.004 and volatility 0.085. Industry returns have factor loadings on oil ranging from -0.05 for health care to 0.35 for energy. GEPU follows an AR(1) process with persistence 0.92 and innovation standard deviation 18. All variables are stationary after first differencing where necessary.

2.2 Econometric framework

We adopt a two-stage approach. In the first stage, we model the conditional mean using a vector autoregression with exogenous GEPU:

r_t = μ + Φ r_{t-1} + γ GEPU_{t-1} + ε_t,

where r_t is a vector of oil and industry returns. In the second stage, we specify a component GARCH model for each series:

h_t = q_t + s_t,

where q_t is the long-run component and s_t is the short-run component. The long-run component evolves as:

q_t = ω + ρ q_{t-1} + θ GEPU_{t-1} + φ X_{t-1},

where X includes controls such as the VIX and term spread. The short-run component follows a standard GARCH(1,1) process. For correlations, we use the dynamic conditional correlation model of Engle (2002), augmented with a long-run component:

R_t = diag(Q_t)^{-1/2} Q_t diag(Q_t)^{-1/2},

Q_t = (1 - a - b) \bar{Q} + a u_{t-1} u_{t-1}' + b Q_{t-1} + c GEPU_{t-1},

where \bar{Q} is the unconditional correlation matrix and c captures the effect of GEPU on long-run correlations. We estimate the model by quasi-maximum likelihood. Standard errors are robust to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation. To assess sectoral heterogeneity, we estimate the model separately for each industry paired with oil. We also conduct subsample analysis splitting the sample into pre-2010 and post-2010 periods to check stability.

2.3 Simulated data and calibration

Because actual high-frequency data are not available for all sectors over the full sample, we simulate 1,000 replications using the calibrated parameters. The simulation preserves the cross-sectional dependence structure and the time-varying volatility. For each replication, we estimate the model and store the coefficients on GEPU in the long-run volatility and correlation equations. We report the median estimates and 90% confidence intervals. This approach allows us to draw inferences about the role of GEPU while acknowledging data limitations. We also perform robustness checks using alternative GEPU measures, including the U.S. EPU index and a trade-policy uncertainty index.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Long-run volatility responses to GEPU

Table 1 reports the estimated coefficients of GEPU in the long-run volatility equations. For crude oil, the coefficient is positive and statistically significant at the 1% level (median = 0.042, 90% CI [0.028, 0.057]). This implies that a one-standard-deviation increase in GEPU raises the long-run volatility of oil returns by approximately 4.2 percentage points. The effect is economically large, given that average long-run oil volatility is around 25%. Among industries, energy exhibits the strongest response (0.051, [0.034, 0.069]), followed by materials (0.047, [0.031, 0.063]) and industrials (0.039, [0.025, 0.054]). These sectors are capital-intensive and highly sensitive to energy costs and global demand. In contrast, consumer staples (0.012, [0.003, 0.022]) and health care (0.009, [0.001, 0.018]) show weak but still positive effects. Utilities display a moderate response (0.021, [0.011, 0.032]), likely because of regulatory uncertainty and fuel cost pass-through. Information technology and communication services have coefficients around 0.018 and 0.016, respectively, suggesting that policy uncertainty affects them mainly through discount rate channels rather than direct oil exposure.

The subsample analysis reveals that the GEPU effect on long-run volatility has intensified after 2010. For oil, the coefficient rises from 0.031 in the pre-2010 period to 0.056 in the post-2010 period. This increase coincides with the shale revolution, the rise of financialization in commodity markets, and more frequent trade policy shocks. For energy stocks, the coefficient nearly doubles. This finding suggests that policy uncertainty has become a more important driver of persistent risk in the post-crisis era.

3.2 Long-run correlations and GEPU

Table 2 presents the estimated effect of GEPU on long-run oil–stock correlations. The baseline correlation between oil and the aggregate market is positive but modest (0.18). However, GEPU significantly increases this correlation. The coefficient c in the DCC equation is 0.027 (90% CI [0.015, 0.039]) for the average industry. For energy, the effect is strongest (0.045, [0.029, 0.061]), implying that during high-uncertainty periods, energy stocks move more closely with oil. This is intuitive because energy firms’ cash flows are directly tied to oil prices. Financials also show a notable increase (0.034, [0.020, 0.048]), possibly because uncertainty raises credit risk and funding costs, which are correlated with oil-driven macroeconomic conditions. Consumer staples and health care exhibit the weakest correlation responses (0.011 and 0.008, respectively), confirming their defensive nature.

We further compute the long-run correlation conditional on GEPU regimes. In the low-GEPU regime (bottom quartile), the average oil–stock correlation is 0.12. In the high-GEPU regime (top quartile), it rises to 0.31. This regime dependence implies that diversification benefits from adding oil to an equity portfolio diminish precisely when they are most needed—during periods of high policy uncertainty. For energy-heavy portfolios, the correlation can exceed 0.50 in high-GEPU states, making oil a poor hedge.

3.3 Robustness checks

We conduct three robustness checks. First, using the U.S. EPU index instead of GEPU yields qualitatively similar results, though the magnitudes are slightly smaller, suggesting that global uncertainty has a broader impact than domestic uncertainty alone. Second, excluding the COVID-19 period (2020–2021) reduces the coefficients by about 15%, indicating that the pandemic was an extreme but not unique driver. Third, estimating the model with a multivariate Student-t distribution to account for fat tails does not change the sign or significance of the GEPU coefficients. Overall, the results are stable.

4. Discussion

The findings yield several economic interpretations. First, GEPU acts as a long-run risk factor. Unlike transient news shocks that dissipate quickly, policy uncertainty affects expectations about future tax rates, regulations, trade barriers, and monetary policy. These expectations influence investment decisions, production planning, and risk premia, thereby embedding themselves into persistent volatility components. The fact that the long-run component responds more strongly than the short-run component in our estimates supports this view.

Second, the sectoral heterogeneity reflects differences in oil intensity and policy exposure. Energy and materials are directly exposed to commodity price fluctuations and environmental regulation. Industrials are sensitive to trade policy and infrastructure spending. Financials are exposed to credit conditions and macroprudential regulation. Defensive sectors such as consumer staples and health care have inelastic demand and lower cyclicality, making them less vulnerable. This heterogeneity has practical implications: investors seeking to hedge against policy uncertainty should overweight defensive sectors and underweight energy and materials, or use options rather than linear exposures.

Third, the state-dependent correlation has implications for asset allocation. Traditional mean-variance optimization assumes stable correlations. Our results show that correlations are regime-dependent and increase with GEPU. This means that static diversification strategies may fail during uncertainty spikes. Dynamic strategies that adjust weights based on GEPU signals could improve risk-adjusted returns. For example, a portfolio that reduces oil exposure when GEPU exceeds its 75th percentile would have avoided part of the drawdown during the 2008 crisis and the 2020 pandemic.

Fourth, the intensification of GEPU effects after 2010 suggests that the global economy has become more sensitive to policy shocks. This may be due to increased trade integration, financialization of commodities, and the growing role of expectations-driven asset pricing. Policymakers should be aware that uncertainty itself can be a source of instability, and that clear communication and predictable policy frameworks can reduce long-run volatility.

The study has limitations. We rely on simulated data calibrated to plausible parameters, so the exact magnitudes should be interpreted with caution. Future work could use actual high-frequency data and extend the analysis to other commodities and international markets. Additionally, the linear DCC specification may miss nonlinear or asymmetric effects. Regime-switching models or quantile regressions could provide further insights.

5. Conclusion

This paper examines the role of global economic policy uncertainty in the long-run volatilities and correlations of U.S. industry-level stock returns and crude oil. Using a component GARCH–DCC framework with simulated monthly data from 1997 to 2023, we find that GEPU significantly increases long-run volatility for both oil and industry stocks, with the strongest effects in energy, materials, and industrials. GEPU also raises the long-run oil–stock correlation, especially for energy and financial sectors, while defensive sectors remain relatively insulated. These effects have intensified since 2010. The results imply that policy uncertainty is a persistent risk factor that reduces diversification benefits between oil and equities during turbulent periods. Investors and policymakers should account for regime-dependent correlations and sectoral asymmetries when designing portfolios and stabilization policies. Future research should validate these findings with actual data and explore nonlinear transmission channels.

title: CT-based radiomics for predicting the rapid progression of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pneumonia lesions
text:
Title: CT-based radiomics for predicting the rapid progression of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pneumonia lesions

Abstract
Objective: To develop and validate a CT-based radiomics model for predicting the rapid progression of COVID-19 pneumonia lesions.
Methods: In this retrospective study, 210 patients with confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia were enrolled and divided into a training cohort (n=147) and a validation cohort (n=63). "Rapid progression" was defined as an increase of >50% in the total lesion volume within 48 hours. Radiomic features were extracted from initial chest CT images. A radiomics signature was constructed using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) algorithm. A combined model incorporating the radiomics signature and clinical risk factors was developed. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
Results: The radiomics signature, consisting of 8 selected features, achieved an AUC of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.79-0.92) in the training cohort and 0.82 (95% CI: 0.71-0.91) in the validation cohort. The combined model, which included the radiomics signature, patient age, and C-reactive protein (CRP) level, showed improved predictive performance with an AUC of 0.91 (95% CI: 0.85-0.96) in the training cohort and 0.87 (95% CI: 0.77-0.94) in the validation cohort. Decision curve analysis confirmed the clinical usefulness of the combined model.
Conclusion: The CT-based radiomics signature is a promising tool for predicting the rapid progression of COVID-19 pneumonia lesions. A combined model integrating radiomics and clinical features further improves predictive accuracy, potentially aiding in early clinical decision-making.

Keywords: COVID-19; Radiomics; Computed Tomography; Disease Progression; Predictive Model

Introduction
The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), has posed a significant global health challenge. While many patients experience mild symptoms, a substantial proportion develops severe pneumonia, leading to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and high mortality. The rapid progression of pulmonary lesions is a critical hallmark of severe COVID-19 and is associated with a poor prognosis. Therefore, early identification of patients at high risk for rapid progression is crucial for optimizing clinical management, allocating medical resources, and improving patient outcomes.

Chest computed tomography (CT) is a vital tool in the diagnosis and monitoring of COVID-19 pneumonia. However, visual assessment of CT images is subjective and may not fully capture the subtle textural changes that precede rapid deterioration. Radiomics, a rapidly evolving field, involves the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from medical images, providing a more objective and comprehensive characterization of lesion heterogeneity. This study aims to develop and validate a CT-based radiomics model to predict the rapid progression of COVID-19 pneumonia lesions, thereby providing a non-invasive tool to assist clinical decision-making.

Materials and Methods
Patients: This retrospective study was approved by the institutional review board. A total of 210 consecutive patients with laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia who underwent chest CT at our hospital between January 2020 and April 2020 were included. Inclusion criteria were: (1) age ≥ 18 years; (2) positive RT-PCR test for SARS-CoV-2; (3) available initial chest CT and a follow-up CT within 48 hours. Patients were randomly divided into a training cohort (n=147) and a validation cohort (n=63) at a 7:3 ratio. Clinical data, including age, sex, and laboratory findings (e.g., CRP, lymphocyte count), were collected.

Definition of Rapid Progression: Two radiologists independently assessed the initial and follow-up CT scans. Rapid progression was defined as an increase of more than 50% in the total volume of pneumonia lesions within 48 hours.

CT Image Acquisition and Segmentation: CT scans were performed using a 64-detector row scanner (GE Healthcare). The imaging parameters were: tube voltage, 120 kVp; tube current, 100-300 mAs; slice thickness, 1.0 mm. The regions of interest (ROIs) were manually delineated on the initial CT images by two experienced radiologists using ITK-SNAP software, encompassing the entire pneumonia lesion. Inter-observer agreement was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).

Radiomic Feature Extraction and Selection: A total of 1,316 radiomic features were extracted from each ROI using PyRadiomics, including first-order statistics, shape, and texture features (GLCM, GLRLM, GLSZM). Features were normalized using Z-scores. The LASSO algorithm was used for feature selection and radiomics signature construction in the training cohort.

Model Development and Validation: A radiomics signature was built using a linear combination of selected features. A combined model was then developed by incorporating the radiomics signature and independent clinical predictors identified via multivariate logistic regression. The performance of the models was assessed by the AUC, sensitivity, and specificity. Calibration curves and decision curve analysis (DCA) were used to evaluate the clinical utility of the models.

Results
Patient Characteristics: Of the 210 patients, 76 (36.2%) experienced rapid progression. There were no significant differences in baseline characteristics between the training and validation cohorts (p > 0.05). Patients with rapid progression were older (65.2 ± 12.1 vs. 52.8 ± 14.5 years, p < 0.001) and had higher CRP levels (78.5 ± 45.2 vs. 32.1 ± 28.9 mg/L, p < 0.001).

Radiomics Signature Development: Eight radiomic features were selected by LASSO, predominantly texture features reflecting lesion heterogeneity. The radiomics signature yielded an AUC of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.79-0.92) in the training cohort and 0.82 (95% CI: 0.71-0.91) in the validation cohort.

Combined Model Performance: Multivariate analysis identified age and CRP as independent clinical predictors. The combined model, incorporating the radiomics signature, age, and CRP, achieved an AUC of 0.91 (95% CI: 0.85-0.96) in the training cohort and 0.87 (95% CI: 0.77-0.94) in the validation cohort. The sensitivity and specificity in the validation cohort were 85.3% and 80.0%, respectively. The calibration curve showed good agreement between predicted and observed outcomes. DCA demonstrated that the combined model provided a higher net benefit than the radiomics signature alone across a range of threshold probabilities.

Discussion
This study successfully developed and validated a CT-based radiomics model for predicting the rapid progression of COVID-19 pneumonia. Our results demonstrate that a radiomics signature derived from initial CT scans is a strong predictor of disease deterioration. The combined model, which integrates radiomics with clinical factors (age and CRP), showed superior predictive performance, highlighting the complementary value of imaging and clinical data.

The selected radiomic features were primarily texture-based, which quantify the spatial arrangement of pixels and reflect intralesional heterogeneity. This suggests that a more heterogeneous appearance on the initial CT scan may be a surrogate for a more aggressive disease process, potentially linked to a higher viral load or a more severe inflammatory response. The inclusion of age and CRP in the combined model is consistent with known risk factors for severe COVID-19.

Our study has several limitations. First, it is a single-center retrospective study with a relatively small sample size, which may limit the generalizability of our findings. Second, the manual segmentation of lesions is time-consuming and subject to inter-observer variability, although our ICC values indicated good agreement. Future studies should explore automated segmentation methods. Finally, external validation with a larger, multi-center cohort is needed to confirm the robustness of our model.

Conclusion
In conclusion, a CT-based radiomics signature is a valuable tool for predicting the rapid progression of COVID-19 pneumonia. The combined model, integrating radiomics and clinical features, demonstrates excellent predictive accuracy and could serve as a non-invasive aid for clinicians to identify high-risk patients early, enabling timely and targeted interventions.

title: Genomic insights on fighting bacterial wilt by a novel Bacillus amyloliquefaciens strain Cas02
text: Bacterial wilt caused by Ralstonia solanacearum is a devastating soilborne disease that severely constrains the production of many economically important crops worldwide. In this study, a novel Bacillus amyloliquefaciens strain Cas02 with strong antagonistic activity against R. solanacearum was isolated and characterized. Strain Cas02 exhibited pronounced inhibitory effects on R. solanacearum growth in vitro and significantly reduced bacterial wilt incidence in pot and field experiments. To elucidate the genetic basis underlying its biocontrol potential, the complete genome of strain Cas02 was sequenced and assembled, revealing a circular chromosome of approximately 4.0 Mb with a GC content of 46.5%. Genome mining identified multiple gene clusters putatively involved in the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites with antimicrobial activity, including surfactin, fengycin, bacillaene, macrolactin, difficidin, and bacilysin. Comparative genomic analysis with related B. amyloliquefaciens strains highlighted both conserved and strain-specific features that may contribute to its superior antagonistic performance. Furthermore, genes associated with plant growth promotion, biofilm formation, and root colonization were identified, suggesting multiple mechanisms underlying its biocontrol efficacy. Transcriptomic and quantitative reverse transcription PCR analyses confirmed the induced expression of key biosynthetic gene clusters during co-culture with R. solanacearum. Collectively, these genomic and functional insights provide a molecular framework for understanding the biocontrol mechanisms of strain Cas02 and support its development as an effective microbial agent for sustainable management of bacterial wilt.

title: The effects of different extraction methods on composition and storage stability of sturgeon oil
text:
The effects of different extraction methods on composition and storage stability of sturgeon oil

Abstract

Sturgeon oil is a valuable source of long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). In this study, the effects of four extraction methods—solvent extraction (SE), supercritical carbon dioxide extraction (SC-CO₂), enzymatic extraction (EE), and cold pressing (CP)—on the composition, physicochemical properties, and storage stability of sturgeon oil were investigated. The oil yield, fatty acid profile, lipid oxidation indices (peroxide value, PV; acid value, AV; anisidine value, AV), tocopherol content, and volatile compounds were monitored over 180 days of storage at 4 °C and 25 °C. The results showed that SC-CO₂ extraction yielded the highest oil recovery (18.7%) and the highest retention of EPA and DHA (7.2% and 12.5%, respectively). Cold-pressed oil exhibited the lowest initial PV and AV but the lowest oxidative stability during storage. Enzymatic extraction produced oil with a higher free fatty acid content and a distinct volatile profile. After 180 days at 25 °C, the PV of CP oil increased from 0.8 to 18.6 meq O₂/kg, whereas SC-CO₂ oil increased from 0.5 to 9.2 meq O₂/kg. Tocopherols decreased significantly in all samples, with the greatest loss in CP oil (78.3%). Principal component analysis (PCA) and correlation analysis indicated that extraction method significantly influenced both initial quality and shelf life. The findings suggest that SC-CO₂ extraction is the most suitable method for producing high-quality sturgeon oil with superior storage stability, while cold pressing may be preferable for short-term, low-temperature applications.

Keywords: sturgeon oil; extraction methods; supercritical CO₂; fatty acid composition; storage stability; lipid oxidation; tocopherols

1. Introduction

Sturgeon (Acipenseridae) is an ancient fish species widely distributed in Europe, Asia, and North America. While sturgeon caviar is a high-value product, the fish body, particularly the liver and subcutaneous fat, contains substantial amounts of oil rich in long-chain omega-3 PUFAs. Sturgeon oil has attracted increasing attention due to its potential health benefits, including anti-inflammatory, cardioprotective, and neuroprotective effects. These benefits are largely attributed to EPA (20:5n-3) and DHA (22:6n-3), which are essential for human health.

The extraction method is a critical factor determining the yield, chemical composition, and oxidative stability of fish oil. Conventional solvent extraction (SE) using hexane or ethanol is efficient but raises concerns regarding solvent residues and environmental impact. Supercritical carbon dioxide (SC-CO₂) extraction is a green technology that operates at low temperatures and avoids organic solvents, thus preserving heat-sensitive PUFAs. Enzymatic extraction (EE) using proteases hydrolyzes the protein-lipid matrix, releasing oil under mild conditions, but may increase free fatty acids (FFAs). Cold pressing (CP) is a physical method that requires no heat or chemicals, but its low yield and poor oxidative stability limit industrial application.

Although several studies have compared extraction methods for fish oil from species such as salmon, tuna, and cod, limited information is available on sturgeon oil, especially regarding long-term storage stability. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of four extraction methods (SE, SC-CO₂, EE, and CP) on the yield, fatty acid composition, minor components (tocopherols), and storage stability of sturgeon oil. The results will provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate extraction methods for sturgeon oil production.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Materials

Fresh sturgeon (Acipenser baerii) with an average weight of 2.5 ± 0.3 kg was obtained from a local aquaculture farm. The fish were eviscerated, and liver and subcutaneous fat tissues were collected, washed, and stored at −20 °C until use. All chemicals and solvents were of analytical or HPLC grade. Standards of fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs), tocopherols (α, β, γ, δ), and 1,1,3,3-tetraethoxypropane were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich.

2.2 Oil extraction methods

2.2.1 Solvent extraction (SE). Minced tissue (100 g) was mixed with hexane (300 mL) and stirred at 40 °C for 4 h. The mixture was filtered, and the solvent was removed using a rotary evaporator at 40 °C under vacuum. The oil was flushed with nitrogen and stored at −20 °C.

2.2.2 Supercritical CO₂ extraction (SC-CO₂). A laboratory-scale supercritical extractor was used. Minced tissue (100 g) was loaded into the extraction vessel. The extraction conditions were: pressure 35 MPa, temperature 45 °C, CO₂ flow rate 15 L/h, and extraction time 120 min. The oil was collected in a separation vessel at 6 MPa and 25 °C.

2.2.3 Enzymatic extraction (EE). Minced tissue (100 g) was mixed with distilled water (200 mL) and adjusted to pH 8.0. Alkaline protease (2% w/w, 200,000 U/g) was added, and the mixture was incubated at 55 °C for 3 h. After inactivation at 90 °C for 10 min, the mixture was centrifuged at 8000 × g for 20 min. The oil layer was collected and stored under nitrogen.

2.2.4 Cold pressing (CP). Minced tissue (100 g) was pressed using a hydraulic press at 20 MPa for 10 min at room temperature. The oil was collected by centrifugation at 5000 × g for 15 min and stored under nitrogen.

2.3 Storage stability test

Oil samples (20 g each) were placed in amber glass bottles with airtight caps and stored in the dark at 4 °C and 25 °C for 180 days. Samples were taken at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, and 180 days for analysis.

2.4 Analytical methods

2.4.1 Fatty acid composition. Fatty acids were converted to FAMEs using boron trifluoride-methanol and analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) equipped with a flame ionization detector and a DB-23 capillary column (60 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm). The oven temperature was programmed from 50 °C to 230 °C. Peak identification was performed by comparing retention times with authentic standards.

2.4.2 Lipid oxidation indices. Peroxide value (PV) was determined by the ferric thiocyanate method and expressed as meq O₂/kg oil. Acid value (AV) was measured by titration with 0.1 M KOH and expressed as mg KOH/g oil. Anisidine value (AnV) was determined spectrophotometrically at 350 nm after reaction with p-anisidine.

2.4.3 Tocopherol content. Tocopherols were analyzed by HPLC with a fluorescence detector (excitation 290 nm, emission 330 nm) using a normal-phase column and hexane/isopropanol (99:1, v/v) as mobile phase.

2.4.4 Volatile compounds. Volatile compounds were extracted by solid-phase microextraction (SPME) and analyzed by GC-MS. A 50/30 μm DVB/CAR/PDMS fiber was used, and the samples were incubated at 60 °C for 30 min.

2.5 Statistical analysis

All experiments were performed in triplicate. Data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. One-way ANOVA followed by Duncan’s multiple range test was used to determine significant differences (p < 0.05). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using SPSS 26.0.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Oil yield and physicochemical properties

The oil yields of the four methods were significantly different (p < 0.05). SC-CO₂ extraction gave the highest yield (18.7 ± 0.6%), followed by SE (16.2 ± 0.5%), EE (13.5 ± 0.4%), and CP (8.9 ± 0.3%). The lower yield of CP was attributed to incomplete disruption of cell structures. The initial PV of CP oil (0.8 ± 0.1 meq O₂/kg) was the lowest, while EE oil had the highest AV (3.2 ± 0.2 mg KOH/g), likely due to enzymatic hydrolysis of triglycerides.

3.2 Fatty acid composition

The major fatty acids in sturgeon oil were oleic acid (C18:1n-9, 28.4–32.1%), palmitic acid (C16:0, 18.2–20.5%), EPA (5.8–7.2%), and DHA (10.3–12.5%). SC-CO₂ oil had the highest total PUFA content (28.6%) and the highest EPA+DHA (19.7%), followed by SE (18.9%), EE (17.5%), and CP (16.2%). The lower PUFA content in CP oil may be due to oxidation during pressing or incomplete extraction of polar lipids.

3.3 Storage stability

During storage at 25 °C, PV increased in all samples, but the rate of increase differed significantly. After 180 days, PV values were: CP, 18.6 ± 0.9; EE, 14.2 ± 0.7; SE, 11.5 ± 0.6; SC-CO₂, 9.2 ± 0.5 meq O₂/kg. At 4 °C, PV increases were much slower, with SC-CO₂ oil reaching only 3.1 meq O₂/kg at day 180. AV and AnV followed similar trends. Tocopherol content decreased in all samples, with the greatest loss in CP oil (78.3% at 25 °C) and the least in SC-CO₂ oil (42.1%). The higher retention of tocopherols in SC-CO₂ oil was attributed to the mild extraction conditions that preserved endogenous antioxidants.

3.4 Volatile compounds

A total of 32 volatile compounds were identified, including aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, and hydrocarbons. Hexanal, 2,4-decadienal, and 1-octen-3-ol were the major oxidation products. CP oil showed the highest total volatile content at day 180 (18.5 μg/g), while SC-CO₂ oil had the lowest (7.2 μg/g). EE oil exhibited a distinct profile with higher levels of 2-pentanone and 2-heptanone, possibly derived from enzymatic reactions.

3.5 Principal component analysis

PCA revealed that the first two principal components explained 78.5% of the total variance. SC-CO₂ and SE oils were associated with higher PUFA and tocopherol contents and lower oxidation indices, whereas CP and EE oils were associated with higher AV and volatile compounds. Storage time and temperature were the dominant factors affecting oxidation, followed by extraction method.

4. Discussion

The results demonstrate that extraction method significantly affects the composition and storage stability of sturgeon oil. SC-CO₂ extraction produced the highest yield and best retention of EPA, DHA, and tocopherols. This is consistent with previous studies on salmon and cod liver oil, where SC-CO₂ provided higher selectivity for non-polar lipids and avoided thermal degradation. The higher oxidative stability of SC-CO₂ oil during storage can be explained by its higher initial tocopherol content and lower initial PV. Tocopherols act as chain-breaking antioxidants, scavenging peroxyl radicals and delaying lipid oxidation.

Cold pressing, although chemical-free, resulted in the lowest yield and poorest oxidative stability. The low yield is due to the inability of mechanical pressing to rupture all cell membranes, leaving a substantial amount of oil in the tissue residue. The poor stability may be related to the lower tocopherol content and the possible release of pro-oxidant metals during pressing. In addition, CP oil had a higher proportion of free fatty acids, which are more susceptible to oxidation than triglycerides.

Enzymatic extraction produced oil with a higher AV, which is a drawback for edible applications. However, EE oil had a unique volatile profile that might be desirable for certain flavor applications. The higher AV can be reduced by optimizing enzyme type, concentration, and hydrolysis time, or by post-extraction refining.

Solvent extraction gave intermediate results. Although SE is efficient, the use of hexane raises safety and environmental concerns. Residual solvent in the oil may also affect flavor and stability. Therefore, SC-CO₂ is recommended as the best method for producing high-quality sturgeon oil, especially for long-term storage. For short-term use or when organic solvents are not available, SE or EE may be acceptable alternatives.

The storage temperature had a pronounced effect on oxidation. At 4 °C, all oils showed much lower PV and AV increases, indicating that refrigeration is essential for preserving sturgeon oil quality. The activation energy of lipid oxidation is relatively high, so lower temperatures slow down the reaction. The loss of tocopherols was also temperature-dependent, with greater losses at 25 °C.

The correlation analysis showed that PV was negatively correlated with total tocopherol content (r = −0.82, p < 0.01) and positively correlated with AV (r = 0.76, p < 0.01). This confirms that tocopherols play a key role in protecting sturgeon oil from oxidation. The volatile compounds, especially hexanal, were strongly correlated with PV (r = 0.89, p < 0.01), suggesting that hexanal can be used as a marker for oxidative deterioration.

5. Conclusion

In this study, the effects of four extraction methods on the composition and storage stability of sturgeon oil were systematically evaluated. SC-CO₂ extraction yielded the highest oil recovery and the best retention of EPA, DHA, and tocopherols, resulting in superior oxidative stability during 180 days of storage at both 4 °C and 25 °C. Cold pressing produced oil with the lowest initial oxidation but the poorest storage stability, while enzymatic extraction led to higher acid values. Solvent extraction gave intermediate quality. Therefore, SC-CO₂ is the most suitable method for producing high-quality sturgeon oil with extended shelf life. For practical applications, storage at 4 °C is strongly recommended to minimize oxidation. Future studies should explore the combination of SC-CO₂ with natural antioxidants and the scale-up of the process for industrial production.

title: Egg Safety Standards in China Need To Be Improved
text: China is the world's largest producer and consumer of eggs, with annual output exceeding 30 million tons and per capita consumption well above the global average. Eggs are a staple of the Chinese diet and an important source of high-quality protein. However, food safety incidents involving eggs, such as excessive antibiotic residues and Salmonella contamination, have repeatedly raised public concern in recent years. Although China has established a multi-level regulatory framework for egg safety, including national standards, industry standards, and local regulations, gaps and inconsistencies remain. Existing standards often lag behind international benchmarks, particularly regarding maximum residue limits for veterinary drugs, microbial limits, and traceability requirements. Moreover, enforcement is fragmented across multiple agencies, and small-scale farming operations complicate compliance. This paper reviews the current egg safety standards in China, compares them with international standards such as those of the Codex Alimentarius Commission and the European Union, and identifies key deficiencies. It argues that China's egg safety standards need urgent improvement to better protect public health and enhance consumer confidence. The findings provide evidence-based recommendations for policymakers and contribute to the broader discussion on food safety governance in developing countries.

title: Modelling climate change impacts on maize yields under low nitrogen input conditions in sub-Saharan Africa
text:
Results and Discussion

Simulations showed that climate change will reduce maize yields across sub-Saharan Africa, with losses strongly amplified under low nitrogen input. Under RCP8.5 and 2050s climate, mean yields declined by 18% under high nitrogen (80 kg N ha⁻¹) but by 31% under low nitrogen (10 kg N ha⁻¹), relative to 1980–2010 baselines. The nitrogen gap—the yield difference between high and low input systems—widened from 1.4 t ha⁻¹ to 2.1 t ha⁻¹, indicating that nutrient limitation exacerbates climate-driven losses. Spatial variability was substantial: West African savannas experienced the largest reductions (up to 42% under low N), while the Ethiopian highlands showed smaller declines (12–17%). Elevated CO₂ partially offset losses under high nitrogen (+8%) but not under low nitrogen (+2%), because nutrient scarcity constrained the CO₂ fertilization effect. Earlier maturation shortened the growing period by 6–11 days, increasing exposure to terminal drought. Overall, our results suggest that without improved soil fertility management, climate change could push low-input maize systems beyond current adaptation thresholds, threatening food security for smallholder farmers. Integrated strategies combining modest fertilizer inputs, improved cultivars, and water conservation are therefore essential.

title: Evaluation of functional and chemical properties of crust from dry-aged beef loins as a novel food ingredient
text:
Evaluation of functional and chemical properties of crust from dry-aged beef loins as a novel food ingredient

Abstract

Dry-aged beef has gained considerable popularity in the premium meat market owing to its unique flavor and tenderness. The dry-aging process generates a surface crust that is typically trimmed and discarded as waste. This study aimed to evaluate the functional and chemical properties of crust obtained from dry-aged beef loins to assess its potential as a novel food ingredient. Crust samples were collected from beef loins dry-aged for 21, 35, and 49 days, and their proximate composition, pH, water activity, color, protein solubility, emulsifying capacity, foaming properties, and antioxidant activity were determined. The results showed that the crust had high protein (48.6–56.3%) and fat (18.4–24.7%) contents, with ash ranging from 6.2% to 9.8%. Water activity decreased significantly with aging time (p < 0.05), while pH increased slightly. The crust exhibited a dark brown color with L* values between 28.4 and 34.7. Protein solubility was highest at alkaline pH, and emulsifying capacity reached 62.5–71.3%. Antioxidant activity, measured by DPPH and ABTS assays, increased with aging time, reaching 78.4% and 82.6% inhibition, respectively, at 49 days. These findings suggest that dry-aged beef crust possesses favorable functional properties and could serve as a value-added ingredient in processed meat and savory food products, contributing to waste reduction in the meat industry.

Keywords: dry-aged beef; crust; functional properties; antioxidant activity; novel food ingredient; waste valorization

1. Introduction

Dry aging is a traditional process in which beef carcasses or primal cuts are stored under controlled temperature (0–4 °C), relative humidity (75–85%), and air velocity for extended periods, typically ranging from 14 to 60 days. During this process, endogenous enzymes degrade muscle proteins and lipids, resulting in enhanced tenderness and the development of characteristic nutty, beefy, and umami flavors. The global demand for dry-aged beef has risen sharply, particularly in high-end restaurants and specialty meat markets.

However, dry aging inevitably leads to the formation of a desiccated, dark-colored surface layer known as the crust. This crust is a consequence of moisture loss, oxidation, and microbial activity on the meat surface. In commercial practice, the crust is trimmed off before further fabrication, generating significant amounts of waste that are often discarded or rendered into low-value products. Depending on aging duration and loin size, the crust may account for 10–20% of the total weight of the dry-aged loin.

Despite being considered a by-product, the crust is rich in proteins, lipids, and flavor compounds generated during aging. Recent studies on meat by-products have highlighted the potential of such materials as functional ingredients due to their emulsifying, foaming, and antioxidant properties. Nevertheless, limited information is available on the functional and chemical characteristics of dry-aged beef crust. Therefore, this study was designed to evaluate the physicochemical and functional properties of crust from beef loins dry-aged for different periods, with the aim of exploring its potential application as a novel food ingredient.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Sample preparation

Beef loins (Longissimus lumborum) from three commercial Angus steers were obtained from a local abattoir 48 h post-mortem. Each loin was cut into three equal sections and dry-aged in a controlled chamber at 2 °C, 80% relative humidity, and 0.5 m/s air velocity for 21, 35, and 49 days. After aging, the crust (approximately 3–5 mm thick) was carefully removed using a sterile knife, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C until analysis. Three independent replicates were performed for each aging period.

2.2 Proximate composition and physicochemical analysis

Moisture, crude protein, crude fat, and ash contents were determined according to AOAC methods. pH was measured using a calibrated pH meter after homogenizing 5 g of sample in 45 mL distilled water. Water activity (aw) was determined using a water activity meter. Color was measured using a colorimeter, and CIE L*, a*, and b* values were recorded.

2.3 Functional properties

Protein solubility was determined at pH 3, 5, 7, and 9 by dispersing the sample in distilled water, adjusting pH with 1 M HCl or NaOH, centrifuging, and measuring the protein content of the supernatant. Emulsifying capacity was assessed by homogenizing the sample with soybean oil and measuring the emulsion stability index. Foaming capacity and foam stability were determined by whipping the sample solution and measuring foam volume over time.

2.4 Antioxidant activity

Antioxidant activity was evaluated using DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging assays. Sample extracts were prepared with 70% ethanol, and absorbance was measured spectrophotometrically. Results were expressed as percentage inhibition.

2.5 Statistical analysis

All experiments were conducted in triplicate. Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA, and means were compared using Duncan’s multiple range test at p < 0.05. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Proximate composition

The proximate composition of dry-aged beef crust is presented in Table 1. Moisture content decreased significantly with aging time, from 18.2% at 21 days to 12.5% at 49 days (p < 0.05). Crude protein increased from 48.6% to 56.3%, while crude fat ranged from 18.4% to 24.7%. Ash content varied between 6.2% and 9.8%, reflecting the concentration of minerals due to moisture loss. These results indicate that the crust is a nutrient-dense material, particularly rich in protein and fat.

3.2 pH and water activity

pH values increased slightly with aging time, from 5.82 at 21 days to 6.14 at 49 days, likely due to the accumulation of alkaline compounds from protein degradation. Water activity decreased from 0.92 to 0.85, which may contribute to the shelf stability of the crust.

3.3 Color

The crust exhibited a dark brown color, with L* values decreasing from 34.7 to 28.4 as aging progressed. a* values increased from 8.2 to 11.6, and b* values ranged from 12.4 to 15.8. These changes are attributed to Maillard reactions and myoglobin oxidation.

3.4 Protein solubility and emulsifying properties

Protein solubility was lowest at pH 5 (20.3–26.7%) and highest at pH 9 (68.4–74.2%). Emulsifying capacity increased with aging time, reaching 71.3% at 49 days. Emulsion stability followed a similar trend. Foaming capacity was highest at 35 days (145%), while foam stability decreased slightly with prolonged aging.

3.5 Antioxidant activity

DPPH scavenging activity increased from 62.1% at 21 days to 78.4% at 49 days, while ABTS activity increased from 68.5% to 82.6%. The enhanced antioxidant activity is likely due to the generation of Maillard reaction products and peptides during aging.

4. Discussion

The present study demonstrates that dry-aged beef crust possesses promising functional and chemical properties. The high protein content and favorable emulsifying capacity suggest that the crust could be used as a protein-rich ingredient in emulsified meat products such as sausages and patties. The increase in antioxidant activity with aging time is particularly noteworthy, as synthetic antioxidants are increasingly rejected by consumers. Natural antioxidants derived from meat by-products could serve as clean-label alternatives.

The dark color of the crust may limit its application in light-colored food products; however, it could be advantageous in dark sauces, gravies, and meat fillings. The low water activity and acidic-to-neutral pH range also imply that the crust may have reasonable microbial stability if properly dried and stored.

Compared with other meat by-products such as liver, heart, and skin, dry-aged beef crust has a unique flavor profile due to prolonged enzymatic and oxidative reactions. This may enhance the sensory appeal of final products. However, further studies are needed to evaluate the sensory attributes, safety, and consumer acceptance of crust-containing food products. Additionally, the presence of potential microbial hazards from the aging surface should be carefully assessed.

5. Conclusion

This study confirms that crust from dry-aged beef loins is a protein- and fat-rich material with favorable emulsifying, foaming, and antioxidant properties. Its functional characteristics improve with longer aging periods, particularly antioxidant activity. These findings support the potential of dry-aged beef crust as a novel food ingredient, contributing to waste reduction and value addition in the meat industry. Future research should focus on incorporation trials, sensory evaluation, and safety validation to facilitate commercial application.

title: Clinical research linking Traditional Chinese Medicine constitution types with diseases: a literature review of 1639 observational studies
text:
Clinical research linking Traditional Chinese Medicine constitution types with diseases: a literature review of 1639 observational studies

 Abstract

Background: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) constitution theory posits that individual constitutional types influence disease susceptibility and progression. An increasing body of clinical research has examined associations between TCM constitution types and various diseases; however, the overall landscape of this evidence has not been systematically characterized.

Objective: To synthesize and evaluate observational clinical studies investigating associations between TCM constitution types and diseases, and to identify prevailing patterns, methodological characteristics, and research gaps.

Methods: We conducted a comprehensive literature review of observational studies published between January 2005 and December 2023 across five electronic databases (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, PubMed, and Web of Science). Studies were included if they assessed TCM constitution types using standardized instruments and reported associations with at least one diagnosed disease. Data on study characteristics, constitution assessment tools, disease categories, and reported associations were extracted and analyzed descriptively.

Results: A total of 1,639 observational studies met inclusion criteria, involving 2,847,316 participants across 28 provinces in China and 12 other countries. Cross-sectional designs predominated (n=1,187, 72.4%). The Constitution in Chinese Medicine Questionnaire (CCMQ) was the most frequently used instrument (n=1,428, 87.1%). The most commonly studied diseases were metabolic disorders (n=312, 19.0%), cardiovascular diseases (n=267, 16.3%), and musculoskeletal conditions (n=198, 12.1%). Qi-deficiency constitution (n=891, 54.4%), Phlegm-dampness constitution (n=743, 45.3%), and Yang-deficiency constitution (n=612, 37.3%) were most frequently associated with disease states. Phlegm-dampness constitution showed consistent associations with metabolic syndrome (OR range: 2.14–4.87 across studies), while Qi-stagnation constitution was frequently linked to depressive disorders (OR range: 1.89–3.76). Qi-deficiency constitution was associated with chronic fatigue and immunodeficiency conditions. Considerable heterogeneity existed in outcome definitions and adjustment for confounders.

Conclusion: This review reveals substantial clinical evidence linking TCM constitution types with diverse diseases, with Phlegm-dampness, Qi-deficiency, and Qi-stagnation constitutions showing the most robust disease associations. However, methodological limitations including predominance of cross-sectional designs and inconsistent confounding control warrant caution in interpretation. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs and standardized outcome measures.

Keywords: Traditional Chinese Medicine; constitution theory; body constitution; disease susceptibility; observational studies; literature review; Phlegm-dampness constitution; Qi-deficiency constitution

 Introduction

Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) has developed a sophisticated theoretical framework over millennia, central to which is the concept of constitutional types (体质, tizhi). According to TCM theory, individuals can be classified into distinct constitutional types based on innate and acquired characteristics including physiological features, metabolic tendencies, and psychological traits. The Constitution in Chinese Medicine Questionnaire (CCMQ), developed by Wang Qi and colleagues, standardized the classification of nine constitution types: Balanced (平和质), Qi-deficiency (气虚质), Yang-deficiency (阳虚质), Yin-deficiency (阴虚质), Phlegm-dampness (痰湿质), Damp-heat (湿热质), Blood-stasis (血瘀质), Qi-stagnation (气郁质), and Special constitution (特禀质).

A fundamental premise of TCM constitution theory is that constitutional type influences disease susceptibility, pathological progression, and treatment response. This concept aligns with emerging paradigms in precision medicine that recognize individual variability in disease predisposition. Over the past two decades, substantial clinical research has attempted to validate these theoretical associations through observational studies examining constitution type distributions among patients with specific diseases.

Despite this growing body of literature, the evidence remains fragmented across disease categories, populations, and research methodologies. Previous reviews have typically focused on single diseases or constitution types, limiting comprehensive understanding of the field. This literature review aims to systematically characterize the landscape of observational clinical research linking TCM constitution types with diseases, identify consistent patterns of association, and evaluate methodological quality to inform future research directions.

 Materials and Methods

 Search Strategy

We conducted a systematic literature search of five electronic databases: China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, VIP Chinese Science and Technology Periodical Database, PubMed, and Web of Science. The search covered publications from January 2005 to December 2023. Search terms included combinations of: ("Traditional Chinese Medicine constitution" OR "TCM constitution" OR "body constitution" OR "constitutional type" OR specific constitution names) AND ("disease" OR "disorder" OR "syndrome" OR "condition" OR specific disease terms). Both Chinese and English language publications were included.

 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Studies were included if they: (1) employed observational designs (cross-sectional, case-control, or cohort); (2) assessed TCM constitution types using validated standardized instruments; (3) reported associations between constitution types and at least one clinically diagnosed disease; (4) included adult participants (≥18 years); and (5) provided sufficient data for extraction.

Studies were excluded if they: (1) were interventional trials, case reports, reviews, or editorials; (2) used non-standardized constitution assessment methods; (3) focused exclusively on pediatric populations; or (4) reported only composite constitution scores without disease associations.

 Data Extraction and Quality Assessment

Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized form including: study characteristics (author, year, country, design), sample size, participant demographics, constitution assessment instrument, disease category, and reported associations (odds ratios, prevalence rates, or descriptive statistics). Disagreements were resolved through consensus. Methodological quality was assessed using a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale adapted for cross-sectional studies, evaluating sample representativeness, constitution assessment validity, outcome ascertainment, and statistical adjustment for confounders.

 Data Synthesis

Due to substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and outcome definitions, meta-analysis was not appropriate. Data were synthesized descriptively, with results presented as frequencies, percentages, and ranges of reported effect estimates. Disease categories were classified according to the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11).

 Results

 Study Characteristics

A total of 1,639 observational studies met inclusion criteria (Figure 1). Publication volume increased substantially over time, from 23 studies (1.4%) during 2005–2009 to 847 studies (51.7%) during 2019–2023. The majority were conducted in China (n=1,584, 96.6%), with remaining studies from Taiwan (n=21), South Korea (n=14), Japan (n=9), Singapore (n=6), and other countries (n=5).

Cross-sectional designs predominated (n=1,187, 72.4%), followed by case-control studies (n=312, 19.0%) and cohort studies (n=140, 8.5%). Total participants numbered 2,847,316, with individual study sample sizes ranging from 52 to 186,472 (median: 487). Female participants constituted 54.3% of the pooled sample. Mean participant age ranged from 18.2 to 78.6 years across studies.

The CCMQ was the most frequently used assessment instrument (n=1,428, 87.1%), followed by the Constitution Classification Scale (n=127, 7.7%) and other validated tools (n=84, 5.1%). Most studies (n=1,341, 81.8%) assessed all nine constitution types, while 298 studies (18.2%) focused on specific constitutions.

 Disease Categories

Studies spanned 18 ICD-11 disease categories (Table 1). The most frequently studied categories were:

- Endocrine and metabolic diseases (n=312, 19.0%): Including type 2 diabetes (n=127), metabolic syndrome (n=89), obesity (n=56), and dyslipidemia (n=40).
- Cardiovascular diseases (n=267, 16.3%): Including hypertension (n=134), coronary heart disease (n=78), and stroke (n=55).
- Musculoskeletal conditions (n=198, 12.1%): Including knee osteoarthritis (n=67), rheumatoid arthritis (n=52), and osteoporosis (n=79).
- Mental and behavioral disorders (n=176, 10.7%): Including depression (n=89), anxiety disorders (n=54), and insomnia (n=33).
- Neoplasms (n=143, 8.7%): Including breast cancer (n=41), lung cancer (n=38), and colorectal cancer (n=34).
- Digestive system diseases (n=138, 8.4%): Including functional dyspepsia (n=52), irritable bowel syndrome (n=47), and chronic gastritis (n=39).

 Constitution-Disease Associations

Phlegm-dampness constitution demonstrated the most consistent disease associations, particularly with metabolic disorders. Across 89 studies examining metabolic syndrome, Phlegm-dampness constitution prevalence was significantly elevated compared to general population estimates (pooled prevalence: 38.7% vs. 12.4% baseline; OR range: 2.14–4.87). Similar associations were observed for type 2 diabetes (n=127 studies; OR range: 1.76–3.92), obesity (n=56 studies; OR range: 2.31–5.14), and hypertension (n=134 studies; OR range: 1.54–2.98).

Qi-deficiency constitution was most frequently associated with chronic fatigue conditions (n=67 studies; OR range: 2.45–4.21), immunodeficiency-related conditions (n=43 studies), and recovery-phase diseases. In cancer studies, Qi-deficiency constitution was prevalent among patients undergoing chemotherapy (pooled prevalence: 41.2%).

Qi-stagnation constitution showed robust associations with depressive disorders (n=89 studies; OR range: 1.89–3.76) and anxiety disorders (n=54 studies; OR range: 1.67–3.12). This constitution was also frequently observed in functional gastrointestinal disorders, particularly irritable bowel syndrome (n=47 studies; pooled prevalence: 34.8%).

Blood-stasis constitution was consistently associated with cardiovascular diseases, particularly coronary heart disease (n=78 studies; OR range: 1.92–3.45) and stroke (n=55 studies; OR range: 1.78–2.89).

Yang-deficiency constitution showed associations with endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism: n=23 studies; OR range: 2.12–3.67) and chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions.

Damp-heat constitution was linked to inflammatory skin conditions (n=45 studies), chronic hepatitis (n=38 studies), and urinary tract infections (n=29 studies).

Special constitution (allergic constitution) was strongly associated with allergic diseases including asthma (n=41 studies; OR range: 3.21–6.54), allergic rhinitis (n=37 studies; OR range: 2.89–5.76), and atopic dermatitis (n=28 studies).

Balanced constitution was consistently protective, with prevalence significantly lower in disease populations compared to healthy controls across most disease categories (pooled prevalence in disease groups: 8.3% vs. 31.7% in healthy controls).

Yin-deficiency constitution showed associations with menopausal syndrome (n=34 studies), dry eye syndrome (n=27 studies), and chronic inflammatory conditions.

 Methodological Quality

Quality assessment revealed considerable variation. Only 412 studies (25.1%) adequately adjusted for potential confounders including age, sex, and body mass index. Sample size calculation was reported in 287 studies (17.5%). Blinding of outcome assessors was described in 156 studies (9.5%). Longitudinal follow-up was employed in only 140 studies (8.5%), with follow-up durations ranging from 6 months to 12 years.

 Discussion

This comprehensive review of 1,639 observational studies represents the largest synthesis to date of clinical research linking TCM constitution types with diseases. Our findings demonstrate substantial and growing research activity in this field, with consistent patterns of constitution-disease associations across diverse populations and disease categories.

The predominance of Phlegm-dampness constitution in metabolic disorders aligns with TCM theoretical predictions that this constitution type predisposes to fluid metabolism dysfunction and accumulation of pathological products. The consistency of these findings across 312 metabolic studies suggests genuine biological signal rather than methodological artifact. From a modern biomedical perspective, Phlegm-dampness constitution may correlate with insulin resistance, chronic low-grade inflammation, and altered adipokine profiles—mechanisms warranting further investigation.

The strong association between Qi-stagnation constitution and depressive disorders similarly resonates with TCM theory linking emotional constraint to Qi flow disruption. This finding has potential clinical implications for depression risk stratification and personalized prevention strategies. The association between Special constitution and allergic diseases appears particularly robust, suggesting this constitution type may serve as a useful marker for atopic predisposition.

Several limitations warrant consideration. First, the predominance of cross-sectional designs precludes causal inference; constitution types may predispose to disease, result from disease processes, or reflect confounding by shared determinants. Second, substantial heterogeneity in outcome definitions, constitution assessment protocols, and statistical methods limits comparability across studies. Third, publication bias likely inflates reported associations, as negative findings may remain unpublished. Fourth, the overwhelming concentration of research in Chinese populations limits generalizability to other ethnic groups. Fifth, only one-quarter of studies adequately controlled for confounders, raising concerns about spurious associations.

Despite these limitations, the consistency of certain associations—particularly Phlegm-dampness with metabolic disorders and Special constitution with allergic diseases—suggests clinically meaningful relationships. These findings support the potential utility of constitution assessment in identifying high-risk individuals for targeted prevention and early intervention.

Future research should prioritize prospective cohort designs to establish temporal relationships, employ standardized outcome measures to facilitate meta-analysis, adequately control for confounders, and extend investigation to diverse populations. Integration of constitution assessment with modern biomarkers and genetic profiling may elucidate biological mechanisms underlying constitution-disease associations.

 Conclusion

This literature review of 1,639 observational studies demonstrates substantial clinical evidence linking TCM constitution types with diverse diseases. Phlegm-dampness, Qi-deficiency, and Qi-stagnation constitutions show the most robust and consistent disease associations, particularly with metabolic, cardiovascular, and mental health conditions. While these findings support the clinical relevance of TCM constitution theory, methodological limitations including predominance of cross-sectional designs and inconsistent confounding control warrant cautious interpretation. Future research employing rigorous longitudinal designs and standardized methodologies is essential to establish causal relationships and translate constitution-based risk assessment into clinical practice.

title: A bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review of tourism-environmental degradation nexus
text:
The intersection of tourism development and environmental degradation has attracted increasing scholarly attention amid growing concerns over ecological sustainability and the global climate crisis. This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review to map the intellectual structure, evolutionary trends, and research frontiers of the tourism–environmental degradation nexus. Drawing on publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus databases, a total of [X] articles published between [year] and [year] were analyzed using bibliometric techniques, including co-citation analysis, keyword co-occurrence network analysis, and burst detection, complemented by a systematic qualitative review following the PRISMA protocol. The results reveal a marked exponential growth in publications over the past decade, with China, the United States, and the United Kingdom emerging as the most productive contributors. Thematic evolution analysis indicates a transition from early studies focused narrowly on tourism's carbon footprint and energy consumption toward more integrated frameworks encompassing the Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis, ecological footprint indicators, and the decoupling of tourism growth from environmental pressures. The systematic review synthesizes empirical findings into four principal research streams: (1) the environmental consequences of tourism activities, (2) the role of tourism in economic–environmental trade-offs, (3) methodological advances in measuring tourism-induced degradation, and (4) policy and governance responses. Key research gaps are identified, including the limited application of longitudinal and multi-scalar designs, insufficient attention to developing economies and biodiversity-rich regions, and the predominance of carbon-centric metrics at the expense of broader ecological indicators. This study contributes by providing a holistic overview of the field, offering a structured research agenda, and highlighting pathways for future inquiry that integrate interdisciplinary perspectives, advanced econometric modeling, and context-sensitive sustainability policies. The findings hold implications for researchers, policymakers, and destination managers seeking to reconcile tourism growth with environmental integrity.

Keywords: tourism; environmental degradation; bibliometric analysis; systematic literature review; sustainability; ecological footprint

title: Prediction of lymphovascular space invasion using a combination of tenascin-C, cox-2, and PET/CT radiomics in patients with early-stage cervical squamous cell carcinoma
text:
Prediction of lymphovascular space invasion using a combination of tenascin-C, cox-2, and PET/CT radiomics in patients with early-stage cervical squamous cell carcinoma

Abstract

Objective: Lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) is a critical prognostic factor in early-stage cervical squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), influencing treatment decisions regarding radical hysterectomy versus fertility-sparing surgery and adjuvant therapy. This study aimed to develop and validate a predictive model for LVSI combining preoperative serum biomarkers (tenascin-C and cyclooxygenase-2 [COX-2]) with radiomic features extracted from positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging.

Methods: A total of 248 patients with histologically confirmed early-stage CSCC (FIGO stage IB1-IIA2) who underwent preoperative 18F-FDG PET/CT and radical hysterectomy were retrospectively enrolled. Serum tenascin-C and COX-2 levels were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Radiomic features were extracted from primary cervical lesions on PET and CT images. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection. A combined model incorporating biomarkers, radiomic features, and clinical variables was constructed using multivariate logistic regression. Model performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA).

Results: LVSI was confirmed in 98 of 248 patients (39.5%). Elevated tenascin-C (≥45.2 ng/mL) and COX-2 (≥38.6 ng/mL) were independently associated with LVSI (odds ratio [OR]=2.84 and 2.31, respectively; both P<0.01). A total of 1,218 radiomic features were extracted, and 7 optimal features (3 PET-based, 4 CT-based) were selected. The combined model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.892 (95% CI: 0.845–0.939) in the training cohort and 0.871 (95% CI: 0.812–0.930) in the validation cohort, significantly outperforming models based on biomarkers alone (AUC=0.741) or radiomics alone (AUC=0.823). The combined model demonstrated good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P=0.42) and net clinical benefit across a range of threshold probabilities.

Conclusion: The integration of tenascin-C, COX-2, and PET/CT radiomics provides a robust non-invasive tool for predicting LVSI in early-stage CSCC, potentially guiding personalized surgical and adjuvant treatment strategies.

Keywords: cervical squamous cell carcinoma; lymphovascular space invasion; tenascin-C; cyclooxygenase-2; PET/CT; radiomics; prediction model

1. Introduction

Cervical cancer remains the fourth most common malignancy among women worldwide, with squamous cell carcinoma accounting for approximately 80% of cases. In early-stage disease (FIGO stage IB1-IIA2), radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy is the standard of care. However, lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), defined as the presence of tumor cells within endothelial-lined lymphatic or blood vessels, occurs in 30–45% of early-stage cervical squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) and is strongly associated with lymph node metastasis, recurrence, and poor survival. Accurate preoperative identification of LVSI is therefore essential for risk stratification, tailoring surgical radicality, and selecting candidates for sentinel lymph node biopsy or adjuvant radiotherapy.

Current assessment of LVSI relies on postoperative histopathological examination, which is inherently retrospective and cannot inform preoperative decision-making. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) provide anatomical and metabolic information, but their ability to detect microscopic LVSI is limited. Serum biomarkers such as squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCC-Ag) lack sufficient specificity. Thus, there is an unmet clinical need for a reliable preoperative prediction tool.

Tenascin-C (TNC) is an extracellular matrix glycoprotein that promotes tumor invasion, angiogenesis, and lymphangiogenesis. Elevated TNC expression has been linked to LVSI in several carcinomas. Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), an inducible enzyme involved in prostaglandin synthesis, enhances tumor cell migration and lymphovascular permeability. Both biomarkers are measurable in peripheral blood and may reflect the biological propensity for LVSI. Separately, radiomics—high-throughput extraction of quantitative imaging features from PET/CT—has shown promise in predicting pathological characteristics, including LVSI, by capturing intratumoral heterogeneity and peritumoral environment. We hypothesized that combining TNC, COX-2, and PET/CT radiomics would improve preoperative prediction of LVSI in early-stage CSCC. This study aimed to develop and validate such a combined model.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Population

We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients with histologically confirmed early-stage CSCC who underwent preoperative 18F-FDG PET/CT and radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy between January 2018 and December 2022 at two tertiary centers. Inclusion criteria: (1) FIGO stage IB1-IIA2; (2) no neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy; (3) complete clinical, imaging, and pathological data; (4) available preoperative serum samples. Exclusion criteria: (1) other malignancies; (2) inflammatory or autoimmune diseases affecting TNC or COX-2 levels; (3) PET/CT performed >4 weeks before surgery; (4) inadequate image quality. A total of 248 patients were enrolled and randomly divided into training (n=174) and validation (n=74) cohorts at a 7:3 ratio. The institutional review boards approved this study, and written informed consent was obtained.

2.2 Clinical and Pathological Data

Medical records were reviewed for age, body mass index, FIGO stage, tumor size, parametrial invasion, lymph node status, and preoperative SCC-Ag levels. LVSI was defined as the presence of tumor cells in lymphatic or blood vessel spaces on hematoxylin-eosin staining, confirmed by two senior pathologists blinded to imaging and biomarker data.

2.3 Serum Biomarker Measurement

Peripheral venous blood was collected within 7 days before surgery. Serum was separated and stored at -80°C. TNC and COX-2 concentrations were quantified using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kits (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Each sample was measured in duplicate, and the mean value was used. Optimal cut-off values were determined by ROC analysis in the training cohort.

2.4 PET/CT Acquisition and Radiomic Feature Extraction

Patients fasted for at least 6 hours, and blood glucose was confirmed <11.1 mmol/L before intravenous injection of 18F-FDG (3.7 MBq/kg). PET/CT scans were acquired 60 minutes post-injection using a Discovery MI PET/CT scanner (GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA). CT parameters: 120 kVp, automatic tube current, slice thickness 3.75 mm. PET images were reconstructed using ordered subset expectation maximization with attenuation correction.

The primary cervical tumor was segmented on fused PET/CT by two nuclear medicine physicians blinded to pathology, using a semi-automated threshold method (40% of maximum standardized uptake value [SUVmax]). Radiomic features were extracted from PET and CT images separately using PyRadiomics (version 3.0.1). A total of 1,218 features were obtained, including first-order statistics, shape, gray-level co-occurrence matrix, gray-level run-length matrix, gray-level size zone matrix, and neighborhood gray-tone difference matrix. Features were normalized using Z-score. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were calculated to assess inter-observer reproducibility; features with ICC >0.80 were retained.

2.5 Feature Selection and Model Construction

In the training cohort, univariate logistic regression identified clinical and biomarker variables associated with LVSI (P<0.10). Radiomic features were reduced by LASSO regression with 10-fold cross-validation. Selected features were combined with significant clinical and biomarker variables in a multivariate logistic regression model to construct the combined prediction model. A radiomics-only model and a biomarker-only model were also built for comparison. A nomogram was generated for clinical use.

2.6 Statistical Analysis

Continuous variables were compared using t-test or Mann-Whitney U test; categorical variables using chi-square or Fisher’s exact test. ROC curves were plotted, and AUCs were compared using DeLong’s test. Calibration was evaluated by Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test and calibration curves. Decision curve analysis (DCA) assessed clinical utility. All statistical analyses were performed with R software (version 4.2.0) and SPSS (version 26.0). A two-sided P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Patient Characteristics

A total of 248 patients (mean age 48.6±9.2 years) were included. LVSI was present in 98 patients (39.5%). In the training cohort, LVSI was found in 69 of 174 patients (39.7%); in the validation cohort, 29 of 74 (39.2%). Baseline characteristics were balanced between cohorts (all P>0.05). In the training cohort, LVSI was significantly associated with larger tumor size (≥4 cm, P=0.003), higher FIGO stage (IIA2 vs. IB1, P=0.011), elevated SCC-Ag (≥2.5 ng/mL, P=0.018), higher TNC (P<0.001), and higher COX-2 (P<0.001).

3.2 Biomarker Levels and LVSI

Median serum TNC was 52.3 ng/mL (interquartile range [IQR] 38.7–68.9) in LVSI-positive patients versus 31.6 ng/mL (IQR 22.4–42.1) in LVSI-negative patients (P<0.001). Median COX-2 was 44.8 ng/mL (IQR 33.2–57.6) versus 27.5 ng/mL (IQR 19.8–35.4), respectively (P<0.001).
