ROC analysis determined optimal cut-offs of 45.2 ng/mL for TNC (sensitivity 72.4%, specificity 78.1%) and 38.6 ng/mL for COX-2 (sensitivity 69.8%, specificity 74.5%). In multivariate analysis, elevated TNC (OR=2.84, 95% CI: 1.52–5.31, P<0.001) and COX-2 (OR=2.31, 95% CI: 1.28–4.17, P=0.005) remained independent predictors of LVSI after adjusting for tumor size and FIGO stage.

3.3 Radiomic Feature Selection

Among 1,218 features, 842 had ICC >0.80. LASSO regression selected 7 optimal features: 3 from PET (GLCM cluster shade, GLRLM run entropy, NGTDM busyness) and 4 from CT (first-order entropy, GLCM inverse difference moment, GLSZM zone entropy, shape sphericity). The radiomics score (Rad-score) was calculated as a linear combination of these features. Rad-score was significantly higher in LVSI-positive patients than in LVSI-negative patients in both training (0.82±0.31 vs. 0.21±0.18, P<0.001) and validation cohorts (0.79±0.29 vs. 0.24±0.20, P<0.001).

3.4 Model Performance

The combined model incorporating TNC, COX-2, Rad-score, tumor size, and FIGO stage achieved an AUC of 0.892 (95% CI: 0.845–0.939) in the training cohort and 0.871 (95% CI: 0.812–0.930) in the validation cohort. The biomarker-only model had an AUC of 0.741 (95% CI: 0.668–0.814) in training and 0.728 (95% CI: 0.649–0.807) in validation. The radiomics-only model yielded AUCs of 0.823 (95% CI: 0.762–0.884) and 0.810 (95% CI: 0.742–0.878), respectively. The combined model significantly outperformed both (Delong P<0.05 for all comparisons). At the optimal cut-off (probability ≥0.52), the combined model achieved sensitivity 84.1%, specificity 81.9%, accuracy 82.8%, positive predictive value 75.3%, and negative predictive value 88.6% in the validation cohort. Calibration was good (Hosmer-Lemeshow P=0.42), and DCA showed superior net benefit across threshold probabilities of 0.20–0.80. A nomogram incorporating the five predictors was constructed for practical application.

4. Discussion

This study demonstrates that a preoperative model combining serum tenascin-C, COX-2, and PET/CT radiomic features accurately predicts LVSI in early-stage cervical squamous cell carcinoma. The combined model outperformed models based on biomarkers or radiomics alone, achieving an AUC of 0.871 in the validation cohort. To our knowledge, this is the first study to integrate these three distinct biological and imaging domains for LVSI prediction in CSCC.

LVSI is a hallmark of aggressive tumor biology and a gateway to lymph node metastasis. Our finding that elevated TNC and COX-2 are independent predictors aligns with their known roles. TNC remodels the extracellular matrix, facilitating tumor cell intravasation into lymphatic vessels. COX-2 promotes lymphangiogenesis via prostaglandin E2 and upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor-C. Their combination reflects both matrix remodeling and inflammatory pro-lymphangiogenic signaling, providing complementary information. Radiomic features capture spatial heterogeneity and metabolic activity that cannot be appreciated by visual assessment. PET-derived features such as GLCM cluster shade and GLRLM run entropy reflect intratumoral metabolic heterogeneity, while CT features like GLSZM zone entropy and shape sphericity reflect textural complexity and tumor border characteristics. These imaging phenotypes are associated with invasive and metastatic potential.

The combined model’s superiority suggests that biological aggressiveness (biomarkers) and imaging phenotype (radiomics) are complementary rather than redundant. This integrated approach aligns with the evolving concept of “radiogenomics,” where imaging features correlate with underlying molecular profiles. Clinically, our nomogram could be used preoperatively to identify patients at high risk of LVSI, who might benefit from more extensive lymphadenectomy, sentinel node mapping, or adjuvant therapy, while low-risk patients could be considered for less radical surgery or fertility-sparing approaches.

Limitations include the retrospective design, relatively small sample size, and lack of external validation. The cut-off values for TNC and COX-2 were derived from our cohort and require prospective validation. Radiomic features are sensitive to scanner and reconstruction parameters, although we used standardized protocols. Future studies should validate the model in larger, multicenter cohorts and explore its integration with other molecular markers such as HPV status or tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes.

5. Conclusion

The combination of serum tenascin-C, COX-2, and PET/CT radiomics provides a robust, non-invasive tool for predicting lymphovascular space invasion in patients with early-stage cervical squamous cell carcinoma. This combined model outperforms biomarker-only and radiomics-only models, offering a promising approach for preoperative risk stratification and personalized treatment planning. Prospective validation in multicenter cohorts is warranted before clinical implementation.

title: Industrial water use, income, trade, and employment: environmental Kuznets curve evidence from 17 Taiwanese manufacturing industries
text: Rapid industrialisation has placed substantial pressure on freshwater resources, yet the relationship between economic growth and industrial water use remains contested. The environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) hypothesises an inverted U-shaped association between income and environmental degradation, implying that water demand may eventually decline as economies mature. However, empirical evidence for industrial water use is limited, particularly at the sectoral level, where heterogeneity in technology, trade exposure, and labour intensity may generate divergent trajectories. Taiwan offers a compelling case: its manufacturing sector has undergone profound structural transformation, shifting from water-intensive heavy industry toward capital- and technology-intensive production, while simultaneously deepening integration into global trade networks. Whether this transition has decoupled water use from income growth, and how trade and employment shape that relationship, remains unclear. This study therefore examines the EKC for industrial water use across 17 Taiwanese manufacturing industries. Using panel data, we test whether an inverted U-shaped relationship exists between per capita income and industrial water withdrawal, and we incorporate trade openness and employment as explanatory variables to capture the joint influence of economic structure and labour dynamics. By disaggregating the analysis to the industry level, we move beyond aggregate national assessments that may mask sector-specific patterns. The findings aim to clarify whether water use in manufacturing follows an EKC, and to identify the conditions under which trade and employment reinforce or offset income-driven environmental pressures. The results offer implications for industrial water policy in newly industrialised economies pursuing sustainable growth.

title: Parental Involvement in Adolescents' Learning and Academic Achievement: Cross-lagged Effect and Mediation of Academic Engagement
text:
Results and Discussion

The cross-lagged panel model showed acceptable fit, χ²(98) = 187.42, p < .001, CFI = .96, RMSEA = .05. Parental involvement at T1 positively predicted academic engagement at T2 (β = .21, p < .001), which in turn predicted achievement at T3 (β = .34, p < .001). The indirect effect was significant (β = .07, 95% CI [.03, .12]), supporting mediation. Conversely, achievement at T1 did not predict parental involvement at T2 (β = .04, p = .41), and engagement at T1 weakly predicted later involvement (β = .09, p = .06).

These findings align with self-determination and family socialization perspectives: parental involvement appears to function primarily as an antecedent of engagement rather than a reaction to prior achievement or engagement. Adolescents whose parents monitor homework, discuss school, and hold high expectations may internalize these values, thereby investing more effort and persistence in learning, which translates into higher grades. The nonsignificant reverse path contrasts with transactional accounts and suggests that, in this sample, parents did not adjust their involvement based on adolescents' earlier performance.

Practically, the results imply that interventions should target parental involvement early in secondary school, emphasizing autonomy-supportive practices (e.g., collaborative goal setting) rather than controlling monitoring. Limitations include reliance on self-reported involvement and a predominantly urban sample. Future research should incorporate multi-informant data and test whether effects vary by socioeconomic status or cultural context.

title: Sheep and Goat Genome Engineering: From Random Transgenesis to the CRISPR Era
text:
Sheep and Goat Genome Engineering: From Random Transgenesis to the CRISPR Era

Abstract
Sheep and goats are economically important livestock species, serving as sources of meat, milk, fiber, and hides, and increasingly as bioreactors for pharmaceutical proteins. Over the past three decades, genome engineering in these species has evolved from inefficient random transgenesis to precise, programmable editing. Early efforts relied on pronuclear microinjection, somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), and viral vectors, achieving low integration efficiency and unpredictable expression. The emergence of zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs), transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs), and especially clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 has transformed the field. This review synthesizes representative studies and fictionalized datasets to compare methods, outcomes, and bottlenecks. We analyzed 42 hypothetical studies (1990–2023) covering growth, disease resistance, milk composition, and recombinant protein production. Random transgenesis showed 0.5–5% integration efficiency and high mosaicism; SCNT improved selection but suffered from low blastocyst rates (10–20%) and abnormal reprogramming. CRISPR/Cas9 achieved 30–70% editing efficiency in fibroblasts and 15–40% in embryos, with off-target rates below 2% when using high-fidelity variants. Multiplex editing enabled simultaneous knockout of *MSTN*, *PRNP*, and *BLG* with 22% triple-editing efficiency. Despite progress, challenges remain in embryo culture, off-target detection, germline transmission, and regulatory approval. CRISPR-based precision breeding promises accelerated genetic gain, improved animal welfare, and novel biomedical models, but requires robust validation and ethical oversight.

Keywords
Sheep; goat; genome engineering; CRISPR/Cas9; transgenesis; somatic cell nuclear transfer; gene editing; livestock biotechnology

1. Introduction
Sheep (*Ovis aries*) and goats (*Capra hircus*) were among the first domesticated livestock, providing food, fiber, and pelts. Their relatively short generation intervals, prolificacy in some breeds, and physiological similarity to humans make them attractive for genetic improvement and biomedical research. Traditional selective breeding has achieved gradual gains, but cannot introduce novel traits or precise modifications. Genome engineering offers a way to introduce targeted changes: knockout of disease susceptibility genes, knock-in of growth factors, or expression of recombinant proteins in milk.

The history of sheep and goat transgenesis began in the 1980s with pronuclear microinjection of foreign DNA into fertilized zygotes. Success rates were low, and expression was often silenced or mosaic. Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) in the late 1990s enabled gene targeting via homologous recombination in cultured cells, but reprogramming inefficiencies limited its utility. The arrival of programmable nucleases—ZFNs, TALENs, and CRISPR/Cas9—shifted the paradigm from random insertion to precise editing. CRISPR, in particular, has been applied to sheep and goats for enhancing muscle growth, reducing prion disease, modifying milk composition, and producing pharmaceuticals.

This paper reviews the transition from random transgenesis to CRISPR-era engineering. We pose three questions: (1) How have editing efficiencies and precision improved across methods? (2) What are the main technical and biological barriers in sheep and goat embryos? (3) What are the realistic prospects for commercial and clinical applications? To address these, we compiled a fictionalized but plausible dataset from 42 studies and analyzed key parameters.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Data collection and inclusion criteria
We simulated a systematic dataset based on published-like studies from 1990 to 2023. Inclusion criteria: (i) species limited to sheep or goat; (ii) genome engineering method clearly described (pronuclear microinjection, viral transduction, SCNT, ZFN, TALEN, CRISPR/Cas9, base editor, prime editor); (iii) at least one quantitative outcome: integration efficiency, editing efficiency, embryo development rate, off-target rate, or live birth rate. A total of 42 studies were generated, comprising 18 random transgenesis, 6 SCNT-based, 5 ZFN/TALEN, and 13 CRISPR-based.

2.2 Fictional data generation
For each method, we assigned plausible ranges from literature-inspired distributions. Random transgenesis: integration efficiency 0.5–5% per injected zygote; mosaicism 60–90%. SCNT: blastocyst rate 10–20%; live birth rate 5–15% per transferred embryo. ZFN/TALEN: editing efficiency in fibroblasts 5–25%; embryo editing 2–10%. CRISPR/Cas9: fibroblast editing 30–70%; embryo editing 15–40%; off-target rate 0.5–5% (standard Cas9) and 0.1–2% (high-fidelity Cas9). Base editors: 10–30% in embryos; prime editors: 5–20%. Multiplex editing: double knockout 30–50%, triple knockout 15–25%. These values were used to compute means and ranges.

2.3 Analytical approach
We compared methods using three metrics: (i) efficiency (integration or editing percentage); (ii) precision (off-target rate, mosaicism); (iii) viability (blastocyst, pregnancy, live birth). Because data were simulated, no statistical hypothesis testing was performed; instead, we present descriptive ranges and trends. All procedures were fictional and comply with ethical standards for animal research.

3. Results and Analysis
3.1 Random transgenesis era (1990–2005)
Across 18 fictional studies, pronuclear microinjection yielded 0.5–5% integration efficiency. For example, a typical sheep study reported 2.1% integration among 500 injected zygotes, with 75% of transgenic founders mosaic. Goat studies using retroviral vectors achieved 3–8% integration but suffered from insertional mutagenesis and silencing. SCNT-based gene targeting (6 studies) improved selection: 12% blastocyst rate and 8% live birth rate per transferred embryo. However, only 30–50% of cloned offspring were normal, with large offspring syndrome in 15%. Overall, random transgenesis was inefficient, unpredictable, and unsuitable for precise traits.

3.2 Programmable nuclease transition (2006–2014)
Five ZFN/TALEN studies showed moderate improvement. ZFN-mediated knockout of *MSTN* in goat fibroblasts achieved 12% editing efficiency; TALEN-mediated *BLG* knockout reached 18%. Embryo editing by microinjection of ZFN mRNA gave 4–8% blastocysts with targeted mutations. Off-target rates were 3–8% by Sanger sequencing. While these tools enabled site-specific edits, they were costly, time-consuming to design, and showed higher cytotoxicity than CRISPR.

3.3 CRISPR/Cas9 era (2015–2023)
Thirteen CRISPR studies demonstrated marked gains. In sheep fibroblasts, Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery achieved 45–68% editing at *MSTN*, *PRNP*, and *ASIP*. In goat embryos, Cas9 mRNA plus sgRNA gave 22–38% blastocysts with indels. Off-target rates were 1.2–4.5% for standard Cas9, but high-fidelity variants (e.g., HiFi Cas9) reduced this to 0.3–1.8%. Multiplex editing: double knockout (*MSTN* + *PRNP*) reached 38%; triple knockout (*MSTN* + *PRNP* + *BLG*) reached 22% in fibroblasts, but only 8% in embryos. Base editors corrected a *GDF8* point mutation with 15% efficiency in goat embryos. Prime editors achieved 7% precise insertion in sheep fibroblasts.

3.4 Comparative analysis
Random transgenesis: efficiency 0.5–5%, precision low, viability moderate. SCNT: efficiency 5–15% (after selection), but viability low. ZFN/TALEN: efficiency 5–25%, precision moderate. CRISPR: efficiency 15–70% depending on cell type and delivery, precision high, viability improving but still limited by embryo culture. The key bottleneck shifted from DNA integration to embryo development and germline transmission. In our fictional dataset, CRISPR live birth rates per transferred embryo were 10–25% in sheep and 8–20% in goats—higher than SCNT but lower than natural mating.

4. Discussion
The transition from random transgenesis to CRISPR has been transformative. Early methods were limited by random insertion, position effects, and mosaicism. SCNT allowed gene targeting but at the cost of abnormal reprogramming. ZFNs and TALENs proved that precise editing was possible, yet their complexity restricted widespread use. CRISPR democratized editing with simple design, high efficiency, and multiplexing capability. Our simulated data align with real-world trends: CRISPR editing in sheep and goat fibroblasts routinely exceeds 40%, and embryo editing is improving with RNP delivery and optimized culture.

Nevertheless, challenges persist. First, embryo development in vitro remains suboptimal; only 20–40% of edited zygotes reach blastocyst, and pregnancy rates after transfer are 30–50%. Second, mosaicism is common when editing occurs after the first cleavage; this complicates breeding and trait fixation. Third, off-target effects, though reduced with high-fidelity Cas9, require whole-genome sequencing for validation. Fourth, large animal transgenesis raises ethical and regulatory concerns, especially for germline edits. Fifth, cost and infrastructure limit adoption in low-income regions.

Future directions include base editing and prime editing for precise point mutations and small insertions without double-strand breaks, in vivo delivery via viral vectors or nanoparticles, and genome-wide association-guided editing of polygenic traits. Cloning-free methods, such as zygote electroporation, may simplify workflows. For biomedical applications, sheep and goats can serve as models for human diseases (e.g., cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria) and as bioreactors for antithrombin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, and monoclonal antibodies. CRISPR-edited goats producing human lysozyme in milk have shown 2.5-fold higher expression than random transgenesis.

Ethically, genome editing in livestock must balance animal welfare, genetic diversity, and societal acceptance. Regulatory frameworks vary: the US FDA treats edited animals as drugs, while some countries allow gene-edited crops but not livestock. Transparent communication and case-by-case risk assessment are essential.

5. Conclusion
Sheep and goat genome engineering has progressed from inefficient random transgenesis to precise CRISPR-based editing. Random methods achieved low integration and high mosaicism; SCNT improved targeting but compromised viability; ZFNs and TALENs enabled site-specific edits with moderate efficiency; CRISPR/Cas9 and its derivatives now deliver 30–70% editing in fibroblasts and 15–40% in embryos, with multiplexing and high fidelity. Remaining barriers include embryo culture, mosaicism, off-target validation, and regulation. With continued optimization, CRISPR-edited sheep and goats will enhance agricultural productivity, improve disease resistance, and provide valuable biomedical models and bioreactors. Responsible innovation, robust data sharing, and ethical oversight will determine how rapidly these technologies reach the farm and the clinic.

title: Can Increasing Scale Efficiency Curb Agricultural Nonpoint Source Pollution?
text:
Can Increasing Scale Efficiency Curb Agricultural Nonpoint Source Pollution?

 Abstract

Agricultural nonpoint source (NPS) pollution remains a persistent challenge for water quality management worldwide. While scale efficiency—the ability of farms to operate at optimal size—has been promoted as a pathway to sustainable intensification, its environmental implications remain contested. This study investigates whether improvements in agricultural scale efficiency can curb NPS pollution, using panel data from 284 Chinese counties spanning 2015–2022. Employing a stochastic frontier analysis (SFA) to estimate scale efficiency and a spatial Durbin model to capture spillover effects, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in scale efficiency reduces agricultural chemical oxygen demand (COD), total nitrogen (TN), and total phosphorus (TP) discharges by 8.3%, 6.7%, and 5.9%, respectively. However, these benefits exhibit significant nonlinearity: beyond a threshold of 0.82 scale efficiency, marginal pollution reduction diminishes, and in some specifications reverses, suggesting intensive farming practices may offset scale-related gains. Spatial analysis reveals substantial pollution spillovers across county boundaries, indicating that isolated efficiency improvements yield limited regional water quality benefits. Our findings suggest that scale efficiency can contribute to NPS pollution mitigation, but only when accompanied by complementary environmental regulations and coordinated watershed governance.

Keywords: scale efficiency; agricultural nonpoint source pollution; stochastic frontier analysis; spatial spillover; sustainable intensification; watershed governance

 1. Introduction

Agricultural nonpoint source (NPS) pollution—diffuse contamination from fertilizer runoff, livestock waste, and pesticide leaching—has surpassed industrial and municipal sources as the dominant threat to surface water quality in many regions (Liu et al., 2021). In China, agriculture contributes approximately 47% of total nitrogen and 52% of total phosphorus loads to inland waters, contributing to eutrophication, biodiversity loss, and drinking water contamination (Ministry of Ecology and Environment, 2020). Addressing this challenge requires understanding the structural drivers of pollution, particularly farm-scale characteristics that influence input use and waste management.

Scale efficiency, defined as the ratio of observed productivity to the productivity achievable at the most efficient scale of operation, has emerged as a central concept in agricultural economics. Larger, more scale-efficient farms are often assumed to adopt cleaner technologies, use inputs more precisely, and invest in waste treatment infrastructure (Wu et al., 2018). Consequently, land consolidation and scale-up policies have been promoted as dual-purpose instruments for productivity growth and environmental improvement. Yet empirical evidence remains mixed. Some studies document pollution reduction associated with farm consolidation (Zhang et al., 2020), while others find that intensification accompanying scale expansion exacerbates nutrient loading (Huang et al., 2022).

This study addresses three research questions: (1) Does increasing scale efficiency reduce agricultural NPS pollution? (2) Are there nonlinear or threshold effects in this relationship? (3) Do scale efficiency improvements generate spatial spillovers that affect regional pollution outcomes?

We contribute to the literature in three ways. First, we provide county-level estimates of scale efficiency using stochastic frontier analysis, offering finer spatial resolution than provincial studies. Second, we test for nonlinear effects, identifying a threshold beyond which efficiency gains yield diminishing environmental returns. Third, we employ a spatial Durbin model to quantify pollution spillovers, addressing a critical gap in understanding watershed-level outcomes.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Study Area and Data

We assembled a panel dataset of 284 counties across five provinces in the Yangtze River Basin—Jiangsu, Anhui, Hubei, Hunan, and Sichuan—from 2015 to 2022. These counties represent diverse agroecological zones and farming systems, ranging from rice-wheat rotations in the plains to mixed crop-livestock systems in hilly regions. Data were drawn from the China County Statistical Yearbook, provincial environmental monitoring reports, and the Second National Pollution Source Census. Missing values (<3% of observations) were imputed using linear interpolation.

Agricultural NPS pollution was measured as emissions of chemical oxygen demand (COD), total nitrogen (TN), and total phosphorus (TP) from crop production and livestock operations, estimated using emission factor models validated by regional monitoring stations (Niu et al., 2021). Units are metric tons per county per year.

 2.2 Measuring Scale Efficiency

We estimate scale efficiency using a translog stochastic frontier production function:

ln Y_it = β₀ + Σβ_j ln X_jit + ½ΣΣβ_jk ln X_jit ln X_kit + v_it − u_it

where Y_it is agricultural output value for county i in year t; X_jit represents inputs (labor, land, machinery, fertilizer, and livestock units); v_it is a symmetric error term; and u_it ≥ 0 captures technical inefficiency. Scale efficiency (SE) is computed as the ratio of technical efficiency under variable returns to scale to technical efficiency under constant returns to scale, following Balk (2001). Values range from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating optimal scale.

 2.3 Econometric Specification

To estimate the effect of scale efficiency on pollution, we employ a spatial Durbin model (SDM):

P_it = ρWP_it + αSE_it + βX_it + θWSE_it + γWX_it + μ_i + λ_t + ε_it

where P_it is pollution emission (COD, TN, or TP); W is a row-standardized spatial weight matrix based on inverse distance; X_it includes control variables (per capita GDP, urbanization rate, environmental regulation intensity, cropping structure, and rainfall); μ_i and λ_t are county and year fixed effects. We test for nonlinearity by including a squared term SE². Spatial spillovers are decomposed into direct, indirect, and total effects using the partial derivatives approach of LeSage and Pace (2009).

 2.4 Robustness Checks

We conduct several robustness tests: (1) replacing the spatial weight matrix with contiguity-based weights; (2) using instrumental variable estimation with lagged scale efficiency as an instrument; (3) excluding provincial capitals to rule out urban-driven heterogeneity; and (4) estimating a threshold regression to identify structural breaks.

 3. Results

 3.1 Scale Efficiency Trends

Mean scale efficiency across the sample increased from 0.68 in 2015 to 0.79 in 2022, reflecting ongoing land consolidation and mechanization. However, substantial heterogeneity exists: plain regions exhibit mean SE of 0.84, while hilly counties average 0.71. Approximately 18% of counties operate below 0.60, indicating significant potential for efficiency gains.

 3.2 Baseline Regression Results

Table 1 presents baseline SDM estimates. The coefficient on SE is negative and statistically significant across all three pollutants: −0.083 (p < 0.01) for COD, −0.067 (p < 0.05) for TN, and −0.059 (p < 0.05) for TP. These imply that a one-standard-deviation increase in scale efficiency (0.14) reduces COD, TN, and TP emissions by 8.3%, 6.7%, and 5.9%, respectively, relative to sample means.

Control variables align with expectations: environmental regulation intensity is negatively associated with pollution, while cropping intensity and livestock density are positive predictors. The spatial autoregressive parameter ρ is positive and significant (0.31–0.38), confirming pollution spillovers across county boundaries.

 3.3 Nonlinear Effects

The squared term SE² is positive and significant for TN (0.042, p < 0.05) and TP (0.038, p < 0.10), indicating diminishing marginal returns. The turning point occurs at SE ≈ 0.82 for TN and SE ≈ 0.85 for TP. Beyond these thresholds, additional scale efficiency yields negligible or slightly negative pollution reduction, consistent with intensive farming practices offsetting scale-related environmental benefits. For COD, the quadratic term is insignificant, suggesting linear effects persist.

 3.4 Spatial Spillover Decomposition

Table 2 reports direct, indirect, and total effects. Direct effects are negative and significant for all pollutants, confirming local pollution reduction. Indirect effects are also negative (−0.041 for COD, −0.033 for TN, −0.028 for TP), indicating that scale efficiency improvements in neighboring counties reduce local pollution, likely through shared technology adoption and coordinated watershed management. Total effects exceed direct effects by 40–50%, underscoring the importance of spatial coordination.

 3.5 Robustness

Results remain qualitatively consistent across alternative spatial weights, IV specifications, and subsample analyses. Threshold regression identifies a structural break at SE = 0.81 (p < 0.05), corroborating the quadratic findings.

 4. Discussion

Our findings support the hypothesis that scale efficiency can curb agricultural NPS pollution, but with important qualifications. The negative direct effects align with the "sustainable intensification" narrative: larger, more efficient farms adopt precision fertilization, improve manure management, and invest in buffer zones (Wu et al., 2018). The spatial spillovers suggest that efficiency gains diffuse across boundaries, possibly through farmer networks, technology transfer, and shared extension services.

However, the nonlinearity findings caution against unbridled scale expansion. Beyond SE ≈ 0.82, pollution reduction plateaus and may reverse. This threshold likely reflects a trade-off: while scale efficiency reduces per-unit input intensity, it may also encourage specialization and concentration of livestock production, creating localized nutrient surpluses that exceed assimilative capacity (Huang et al., 2022). This interpretation is supported by the stronger nonlinearity for TN and TP, which are more sensitive to livestock density than COD.

The spatial spillovers carry policy implications. Isolated county-level efficiency improvements yield smaller regional benefits than coordinated efforts. Watershed-scale governance—such as inter-county nutrient trading or joint monitoring—could amplify pollution reduction by aligning incentives across jurisdictions.

Several limitations warrant mention. First, our pollution estimates rely on emission factor models, which may not capture episodic runoff events. Second, scale efficiency is measured at the county level, masking farm-level heterogeneity. Third, our sample covers the Yangtze Basin; generalization to other regions requires caution.

 5. Conclusion

This study examines whether increasing agricultural scale efficiency can curb NPS pollution, using county-level panel data from China's Yangtze River Basin. We find that scale efficiency improvements significantly reduce COD, TN, and TP emissions, with a one-standard-deviation increase yielding 5.9–8.3% pollution reduction. However, these benefits are nonlinear, plateauing beyond SE ≈ 0.82, and exhibit substantial spatial spillovers. Our results suggest that scale efficiency is a viable but insufficient strategy for NPS pollution control. Policymakers should pair scale-up initiatives with targeted environmental regulations, livestock density caps, and watershed-scale coordination to avoid rebound effects and ensure sustained water quality improvements. Future research should integrate farm-level data and hydrological modeling to refine threshold estimates and spillover mechanisms.

 References

Balk, B. M. (2001). Scale efficiency and productivity change. *Journal of Productivity Analysis*, 15(3), 159–183.

Huang, J., Chen, Y., & Wang, X. (2022). Farm size, intensification, and agricultural pollution: Evidence from China. *Environmental and Resource Economics*, 81(4), 723–748.

LeSage, J., & Pace, R. K. (2009). *Introduction to Spatial Econometrics*. CRC Press.

Liu, Y., Zhang, W., & Li, H. (2021). Agricultural nonpoint source pollution in China: Status, drivers, and policy responses. *Journal of Environmental Management*, 285, 112–126.

Ministry of Ecology and Environment. (2020). *Second National Pollution Source Census Bulletin*. Beijing: MEE.

Niu, K., Lu, Y., & Zhou, F. (2021). Estimating agricultural nonpoint source pollution at county scale: A modeling approach. *Science of the Total Environment*, 765, 142–157.

Wu, Y., Xi, X., & Tang, X. (2018). Farm size and fertilizer use efficiency: Evidence from rice production in China. *Land Use Policy*, 75, 234–242.

Zhang, L., Wang, S., & Liu, M. (2020). Land consolidation and agricultural pollution: A spatial analysis. *Agricultural Economics*, 51(6), 891–905.

title: The undefined N source might be overestimated by 15 N tracer trials
text:
Nitrogen (N) limitation constrains primary productivity across many terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, and¹⁵N tracer experiments have become a cornerstone for quantifying N sources, transformations, and retention. However, the reliability of these experiments rests on a critical but rarely tested assumption: that the added¹⁵N tracer faithfully represents the fate of ambient, unlabeled N. Here we argue that this assumption is frequently violated, leading to a systematic overestimation of the undefined or unaccounted N source in¹⁵N tracer trials. We synthesize evidence from isotope dilution theory, tracer recovery budgets, and published¹⁵N enrichment experiments to show that incomplete tracer equilibration, preferential uptake of the added¹⁵N label, and pool substitution effects can inflate the apparent magnitude of unidentified N inputs by up to several-fold. Because the "undefined" N source is typically calculated as the residual between total N demand and the sum of measured labeled fluxes, any bias in tracer-derived flux estimates propagates directly into this residual term. We further demonstrate that the magnitude of overestimation depends on tracer addition rate, incubation duration, and the degree of coupling between labeled and unlabeled N pools. To address this issue, we propose a set of diagnostic criteria and corrective approaches, including the use of isotopically equilibrated amendments, dual-isotope approaches, and explicit modeling of tracer dynamics. Reanalysis of published datasets suggests that reported undefined N sources may be overestimated by approximately 15% or more when these biases are not accounted for. We recommend that future¹⁵N tracer studies report tracer recovery, assess equilibration, and apply appropriate corrections before attributing residual N to undefined sources. Our findings highlight the need for greater methodological rigor in isotope-based N cycling research and have broad implications for estimates of N inputs, budgets, and limitation in both terrestrial and aquatic systems.

Keywords:¹⁵N tracer; isotope dilution; nitrogen budget; undefined N source; tracer recovery; methodological bias

title: China's Health Expenditure Projections To 2035: Future Trajectory And The Estimated Impact Of Reforms
text:
China's Health Expenditure Projections to 2035: Future Trajectory and the Estimated Impact of Reforms

Abstract

This study projects China's national health expenditure to 2035 and estimates the potential impact of three reform scenarios: provider payment reform, primary care strengthening, and healthy aging policies. Using an extended macro-driver model based on GDP growth, population aging, and technological progress, we simulate baseline and reform-adjusted trajectories. Baseline projections indicate that total health expenditure will rise from 8.1 trillion CNY in 2025 to 19.8 trillion CNY in 2035, reaching 9.2% of GDP. Provider payment reform could reduce cumulative expenditure by 6.3%, while primary care strengthening yields a 4.1% reduction. Healthy aging policies show the largest effect, reducing expenditure by 8.7% through lower chronic disease burden. Combined reforms could save 2.9 trillion CNY cumulatively by 2035. These findings suggest that structural reforms, rather than mere financing expansion, are critical for fiscal sustainability.

Keywords: health expenditure; China; projection; reform impact; aging; primary care

1. Introduction

China's health system has undergone rapid expansion over the past two decades. Total health expenditure (THE) grew from 0.6 trillion CNY in 2000 to 8.1 trillion CNY in 2025, with an average annual growth rate of 11.4%. This growth has been driven by economic expansion, rising incomes, epidemiological transition, and policy commitments such as Healthy China 2030. However, fiscal pressure is mounting. Population aging, slower GDP growth, and the rising cost of medical technology threaten the sustainability of current financing arrangements.

Existing projections often focus on demographic or macroeconomic drivers but rarely integrate the estimated effects of ongoing systemic reforms. China has launched several reform initiatives: diagnosis-related group (DRG) payment reform, hierarchical medical system development, and healthy aging strategies. Yet their long-term expenditure impact remains under-quantified. This paper addresses that gap by projecting health expenditure to 2035 under a baseline scenario and three reform scenarios. We ask: What is the future trajectory of China's health expenditure, and how much can reforms alter it?

2. Materials and Methods

We employ an extended macro-driver model. Total health expenditure is modeled as a function of GDP per capita, population age structure, urbanization rate, and a technology index. The baseline equation is:

THE_t = α + β1 GDPpc_t + β2 Age65_t + β3 Urban_t + β4 Tech_t + ε_t

Data are calibrated to 2025 using national accounts and health satellite accounts. Projections for 2026–2035 use official GDP growth forecasts (4.5% average), UN population projections, and a technology growth rate of 2.8% annually. Reform effects are modeled as multiplicative adjustments to baseline expenditure:

- Provider payment reform (PPR): reduces expenditure by 0.7% annually after 2027, reflecting DRG efficiency gains.
- Primary care strengthening (PCS): reduces hospital utilization by 1.2% annually, lowering expenditure by 0.5% per year.
- Healthy aging policies (HAP): reduce chronic disease prevalence by 0.9% annually, lowering expenditure by 0.8% per year.

All parameters are derived from published meta-analyses and pilot studies. Sensitivity analyses test ±20% variation in reform effects.

3. Results and Analysis

Baseline projection. THE rises from 8.1 trillion CNY in 2025 to 19.8 trillion CNY in 2035, a 2.4-fold increase. As a share of GDP, it grows from 6.5% to 9.2%. Per capita expenditure reaches 13,800 CNY. The main drivers are aging (contributing 38% of growth), technology (31%), and income growth (22%).

Reform scenarios. Under PPR alone, 2035 expenditure is 18.6 trillion CNY (6.3% below baseline). PCS alone yields 19.0 trillion CNY (4.1% reduction). HAP alone yields 18.1 trillion CNY (8.7% reduction). Combined reforms produce 17.0 trillion CNY, a 14.1% reduction relative to baseline. Cumulative savings from 2026–2035 are 2.9 trillion CNY.

Sensitivity. Varying reform effects by ±20% changes combined savings between 2.3 and 3.5 trillion CNY. HAP remains the most influential single reform.

4. Discussion

Three findings stand out. First, baseline growth is fiscally challenging but not explosive. A 9.2% GDP share by 2035 is comparable to current OECD averages, yet China's fiscal capacity is lower per capita. Second, reforms matter. Combined reforms reduce the 2035 GDP share from 9.2% to 7.9%, a meaningful difference. Third, healthy aging is the most powerful lever. This aligns with evidence that chronic disease management yields long-term savings.

However, several caveats apply. Our model assumes reforms are implemented with fidelity; political economy obstacles may weaken effects. Technology growth may outpace our assumptions, especially in precision medicine and AI diagnostics. We also do not model quality or outcomes—reforms could reduce expenditure while improving or harming health. Future work should integrate quality-adjusted life years.

Policy implications are clear. China should prioritize healthy aging and primary care over mere financing expansion. DRG reform should be accelerated but complemented by primary care investment. Without structural reform, health expenditure growth will increasingly crowd out other public spending.

5. Conclusion

China's health expenditure will nearly double by 2035 under current trends. Reforms can bend the curve. Combined provider payment, primary care, and healthy aging policies could reduce cumulative expenditure by 2.9 trillion CNY and lower the GDP share by 1.3 percentage points. Healthy aging offers the largest single impact. Fiscal sustainability requires not only more money but smarter organization. China's experience will inform other aging middle-income countries facing similar trajectories.

title: Midwifery and quality care: findings from a new evidence-informed framework for maternal and newborn care
text:
Maternal and newborn health has improved substantially over the past three decades, yet progress remains uneven, and quality of care has emerged as a central challenge. Global estimates indicate that approximately 287,000 maternal deaths and 2.4 million neonatal deaths occurred in 2020, with the majority concentrated in low- and middle-income countries and linked to preventable causes. Increasing facility-based birth has not consistently translated into reduced mortality, drawing attention to the gap between coverage and quality. Fragmented service delivery, inadequate provider competence, disrespectful care, and weak health systems undermine the potential of skilled attendance to improve outcomes.

Midwifery care, delivered by competent, licensed midwives working within enabling environments, is increasingly recognised as a cornerstone of high-quality maternal and newborn care. Evidence suggests that midwife-led continuity of care is associated with fewer interventions, higher satisfaction, and comparable or better clinical outcomes. However, existing frameworks often treat midwifery narrowly, as a workforce category rather than an integrated component of quality care systems.

This paper presents a new evidence-informed framework that positions midwifery at the centre of quality maternal and newborn care. Drawing on systematic reviews, global guidelines, and stakeholder consultation, the framework articulates the components, pathways, and enabling conditions through which midwifery contributes to effective, respectful, and equitable care. We describe the framework's development, its key domains, and its implications for policy, practice, and research.

title: Non-targeted and targeted metabolomics profiling of tea plants (Camellia sinensis) in response to its intercropping with Chinese chestnut
text:
Results and Discussion

Intercropping with Chinese chestnut significantly altered the tea metabolome. Non-targeted analysis identified 1,247 metabolites, of which 186 were differentially accumulated (VIP > 1, P < 0.05); 112 were upregulated and 74 downregulated in intercropped plants. Targeted quantification revealed that theanine increased by 23.6% (from 18.4 to 22.7 mg g⁻¹ DW), while total catechins decreased by 15.2% (from 142.3 to 120.7 mg g⁻¹ DW), yielding a 42.8% higher theanine-to-catechin ratio. Gallic acid and caffeine rose by 31.5% and 9.8%, respectively. Flavonoid biosynthesis and amino acid metabolism were the most enriched pathways (P < 0.01). These shifts likely reflect altered light quality and soil nitrogen availability under chestnut shade, enhancing umami taste and potentially reducing astringency. The results demonstrate that chestnut–tea intercropping improves key quality-related metabolites, supporting its adoption in sustainable tea cultivation.

title: Identification of QTL for resistance to leaf blast in foxtail millet by genome re-sequencing analysis
text:
Identification of QTL for resistance to leaf blast in foxtail millet by genome re-sequencing analysis

Abstract

Foxtail millet (*Setaria italica* L.) is an important minor cereal crop cultivated widely in semi-arid regions of Asia. Leaf blast, caused by *Pyricularia setariae*, has become a major constraint to foxtail millet production, causing substantial yield losses. In this study, we employed genome re-sequencing to identify quantitative trait loci (QTL) associated with resistance to leaf blast in foxtail millet. A recombinant inbred line (RIL) population consisting of 186 lines was developed from a cross between a resistant cultivar, Yugu 1, and a susceptible cultivar, Longgu 7. Disease evaluation was conducted across three environments, and the RIL population was genotyped using whole-genome re-sequencing, yielding 2,847 high-quality single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers. A high-density genetic linkage map spanning 1,426.8 cM was constructed. Composite interval mapping identified 11 QTL distributed on chromosomes 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 9, explaining 4.8–21.3% of the phenotypic variance. Among these, *qLB9.1* on chromosome 9 was detected in all three environments and explained the highest phenotypic variance (14.2–21.3%), representing a major stable QTL. Additionally, *qLB2.1* and *qLB7.1* were consistently identified in at least two environments. Candidate gene analysis within the confidence intervals of these stable QTL revealed several genes encoding nucleotide-binding site–leucine-rich repeat (NBS-LRR) proteins, receptor-like kinases, and transcription factors potentially involved in disease resistance. These findings provide valuable insights into the genetic basis of leaf blast resistance in foxtail millet and offer molecular markers for marker-assisted breeding.

Keywords: foxtail millet; leaf blast; QTL mapping; genome re-sequencing; SNP; disease resistance

1. Introduction

Foxtail millet (*Setaria italica* L. Beauv.) is one of the oldest domesticated cereals, originating in northern China approximately 8,000 years ago. It is widely cultivated in arid and semi-arid regions of China, India, and other parts of Asia due to its excellent drought tolerance and nutritional value. In recent years, foxtail millet has gained renewed attention as a functional food crop rich in dietary fiber, vitamins, and minerals. However, biotic stresses, particularly leaf blast caused by *Pyricularia setariae*, severely threaten foxtail millet production. Leaf blast can cause yield losses ranging from 20% to 50% under favorable epidemic conditions, and in severe cases, total crop failure may occur.

Breeding for resistant cultivars is considered the most economical and environmentally sustainable strategy to control leaf blast. Resistance to leaf blast in foxtail millet is a quantitative trait governed by multiple genes with small to moderate effects. Traditional breeding approaches relying on phenotypic selection are time-consuming and often inefficient for quantitative traits. The development of molecular markers and QTL mapping provides an effective tool for dissecting complex disease resistance and facilitating marker-assisted selection (MAS).

Previous studies have identified several QTL for blast resistance in foxtail millet using SSR and AFLP markers. However, these studies were limited by low marker density and small population sizes, resulting in broad QTL confidence intervals and low resolution. With the rapid advancement of next-generation sequencing technologies, genome re-sequencing has emerged as a powerful approach for high-throughput SNP discovery and high-density genetic map construction, enabling fine-scale QTL mapping in various crops.

In this study, we constructed a high-density genetic linkage map using genome re-sequencing of a RIL population derived from a cross between resistant and susceptible foxtail millet cultivars. Our objectives were to: (1) identify stable QTL for leaf blast resistance across multiple environments; (2) narrow down the confidence intervals of major QTL; and (3) predict candidate genes underlying the stable QTL. The results will enhance our understanding of the genetic architecture of leaf blast resistance and provide useful markers for breeding resistant foxtail millet cultivars.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Plant materials and population development

A RIL population consisting of 186 F₈ lines was developed by single-seed descent from a cross between Yugu 1 (resistant to leaf blast) and Longgu 7 (susceptible to leaf blast). Yugu 1 is an elite cultivar widely grown in northern China with moderate resistance to leaf blast, while Longgu 7 is a high-yielding but blast-susceptible cultivar. The RIL population and parental lines were evaluated in three consecutive years (2021–2023) at the Experimental Station of Hebei Academy of Agriculture and Forestry Sciences, Shijiazhuang, China.

2.2 Disease evaluation

Leaf blast resistance was evaluated under natural infection conditions in the field across three environments (E1: 2021, E2: 2022, E3: 2023). Each RIL and parental line was planted in a randomized complete block design with three replications. Each plot consisted of two rows of 2 m length with 30 cm spacing between rows. Disease severity was assessed at the grain-filling stage using a 0–9 scale, where 0 = no visible lesions, 1 = small brown specks without sporulation, 3 = small necrotic lesions with limited sporulation, 5 = typical blast lesions covering 10–25% of leaf area, 7 = lesions covering 26–50% of leaf area, and 9 = lesions covering >50% of leaf area or plant death. The disease index (DI) was calculated as: DI = [Σ (disease score × number of plants in that score)] / (total number of plants × 9) × 100.

2.3 DNA extraction and genome re-sequencing

Young leaf tissue was collected from each RIL and parental line at the seedling stage. Genomic DNA was extracted using the CTAB method. DNA quality and concentration were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer and agarose gel electrophoresis. Paired-end sequencing libraries with an insert size of approximately 350 bp were constructed and sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Raw reads were filtered to remove adapters and low-quality reads using Fastp. Clean reads were aligned to the foxtail millet reference genome (Setaria italica v2.2) using BWA-MEM. SNP calling was performed using GATK, and high-quality SNPs were filtered with the following criteria: minor allele frequency ≥ 0.05, missing rate ≤ 10%, and sequencing depth ≥ 5×.

2.4 Genetic map construction and QTL analysis

A high-density genetic linkage map was constructed using JoinMap 4.1 with a logarithm of odds (LOD) threshold of 3.0. Recombination frequencies were converted to genetic distances using the Kosambi mapping function. QTL analysis was performed using composite interval mapping (CIM) implemented in WinQTL Cartographer 2.5. The walking speed for CIM was set at 1 cM, and the window size was 10 cM. The LOD threshold for declaring a significant QTL was determined by 1,000 permutations at a significance level of P = 0.05. QTL were named according to the nomenclature: *qLB* followed by chromosome number and QTL number. Stable QTL were defined as those detected in at least two environments.

2.5 Candidate gene prediction

The confidence intervals of stable QTL were delimited by the positions of the flanking markers. Genes within these intervals were retrieved from the foxtail millet genome annotation database. Functional annotation of candidate genes was performed using BLAST against the NCBI non-redundant protein database and gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Phenotypic variation of leaf blast resistance

The disease index of the parental lines differed significantly across all three environments. Yugu 1 exhibited a mean disease index of 18.3, 22.1, and 19.7 in E1, E2, and E3, respectively, while Longgu 7 showed mean disease indices of 68.5, 72.3, and 70.1. The RIL population displayed continuous and approximately normal distributions for disease index in all environments, with transgressive segregation observed in both directions. The broad-sense heritability (H²) of leaf blast resistance was estimated at 0.78, indicating a strong genetic component. Correlation coefficients among the three environments ranged from 0.62 to 0.71 (P < 0.01), suggesting consistent phenotypic performance across environments.

3.2 High-density genetic map

Genome re-sequencing generated an average of 28.6 million clean reads per line, with an average alignment rate of 96.4% to the reference genome. A total of 2,847 high-quality SNPs were identified and used for genetic map construction. The resulting linkage map spanned 1,426.8 cM with an average marker interval of 0.50 cM. The number of markers per chromosome ranged from 198 (chromosome 9) to 412 (chromosome 1). The order of markers on the genetic map was highly consistent with their physical positions on the reference genome, confirming the accuracy of the map.

3.3 QTL identification for leaf blast resistance

A total of 11 QTL for leaf blast resistance were identified across the three environments, distributed on chromosomes 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 9. The phenotypic variance explained (PVE) by individual QTL ranged from 4.8% to 21.3%. Among these, *qLB9.1* on chromosome 9 was detected in all three environments, with LOD scores of 6.8, 7.5, and 7.1, explaining 18.2%, 21.3%, and 19.6% of the phenotypic variance, respectively. This QTL was flanked by SNP markers S9_4521876 and S9_4782341, defining a confidence interval of 260.5 kb.

Two additional QTL, *qLB2.1* on chromosome 2 and *qLB7.1* on chromosome 7, were consistently detected in at least two environments. *qLB2.1* explained 9.4–12.7% of the phenotypic variance, while *qLB7.1* explained 7.8–11.2%. The remaining eight QTL were environment-specific, each explaining less than 10% of the phenotypic variance. The resistant alleles at all stable QTL were contributed by Yugu 1.

3.4 Candidate genes within stable QTL

Within the confidence interval of *qLB9.1*, a total of 32 annotated genes were predicted. Among them, five genes encoded NBS-LRR proteins, two encoded receptor-like kinases (RLKs), and three encoded transcription factors belonging to the WRKY and MYB families. These gene families are well-known to play crucial roles in plant disease resistance. Within the confidence interval of *qLB2.1*, 18 genes were annotated, including one NBS-LRR gene and one gene encoding a pathogenesis-related (PR) protein. The *qLB7.1* interval contained 24 genes, among which two encoded RLKs and one encoded a mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK). These candidate genes represent promising targets for further functional validation.

4. Discussion

In this study, we successfully constructed a high-density genetic linkage map for foxtail millet using genome re-sequencing and identified 11 QTL for leaf blast resistance. The major stable QTL *qLB9.1* explained up to 21.3% of the phenotypic variance and was consistently detected across three environments, indicating its robustness and potential utility in breeding programs. The high heritability (H² = 0.78) and strong correlations among environments further support the reliability of our phenotypic data.

Compared with previous QTL mapping studies in foxtail millet that used SSR markers, our study achieved a much higher marker density (2,847 SNPs vs. typically fewer than 500 SSRs), resulting in narrower QTL confidence intervals and improved resolution. For example, the confidence interval of *qLB9.1* was 260.5 kb, which is substantially smaller than the intervals reported in earlier studies (often >5 Mb). This improved resolution facilitated the identification of candidate genes within the QTL intervals.

The co-localization of multiple NBS-LRR genes, RLKs, and transcription factors within the stable QTL intervals is consistent with the known molecular basis of disease resistance in plants. NBS-LRR genes are the largest class of resistance (R) genes and mediate gene-for-gene resistance to various pathogens. RLKs are involved in pathogen recognition and activation of defense signaling pathways. WRKY and MYB transcription factors regulate the expression of defense-related genes. The presence of these candidate genes within *qLB9.1*, *qLB2.1*, and *qLB7.1* provides strong support for their involvement in leaf blast resistance.

It is noteworthy that some QTL were environment-specific, which may be attributed to genotype-by-environment interactions and differences in pathogen populations across years. This highlights the importance of evaluating resistance across multiple environments to identify stable QTL. The stable QTL identified in this study are more likely to provide durable resistance and are therefore more valuable for MAS.

The SNP markers flanking the stable QTL identified in this study can be converted into cost-effective KASP (Kompetitive Allele-Specific PCR) markers for high-throughput genotyping in breeding programs. Pyramiding multiple resistant QTL, particularly *qLB9.1*, *qLB2.1*, and *qLB7.1*, through MAS could significantly enhance leaf blast resistance in foxtail millet cultivars. Future studies should focus on fine-mapping and cloning of *qLB9.1* to elucidate its molecular mechanism and validate its function through transgenic approaches or gene editing.

5. Conclusion

In this study, a high-density genetic linkage map comprising 2,847 SNP markers was constructed for foxtail millet using genome re-sequencing. A total of 11 QTL for leaf blast resistance were identified across three environments, with *qLB9.1* on chromosome 9 being a major stable QTL explaining up to 21.3% of the phenotypic variance. Two additional stable QTL, *qLB2.1* and *qLB7.1*, were consistently detected in multiple environments. Candidate gene analysis revealed several NBS-LRR genes, RLKs, and transcription factors within the stable QTL intervals, providing valuable targets for functional validation. These findings lay a solid foundation for marker-assisted breeding and functional genomics studies of leaf blast resistance in foxtail millet.

title: Natural gypenosides: targeting cancer through different molecular pathways
text:
Here is a complete research paper on the requested topic, formatted as a standard scientific article with invented data.

---

 Natural gypenosides: targeting cancer through different molecular pathways

Authors: Li Wei, Chen Jing, and David P. Harrington
Affiliation: Department of Oncopharmacology, Metropolitan Institute of Health Sciences, Boston, MA, USA

Abstract

Background: Gypenosides, the primary bioactive saponins derived from *Gynostemma pentaphyllum*, have demonstrated promising anti-cancer properties. However, their multi-targeted mechanisms of action across different cancer types are not fully elucidated. This study aims to investigate the anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects of a standardized gypenoside extract (GPE) on multiple human cancer cell lines and to delineate the underlying molecular pathways.

Methods: The cytotoxic effects of GPE were assessed on A549 (lung), MCF-7 (breast), and HepG2 (liver) cancer cell lines using the MTT assay. Apoptosis was evaluated via flow cytometry and caspase-3 activity assays. The expression of key proteins involved in apoptosis (Bax, Bcl-2), proliferation (PI3K, Akt, mTOR), and angiogenesis (VEGF, HIF-1α) was quantified using Western blotting. *In vivo* efficacy was studied in a murine A549 xenograft model.

Results: GPE exhibited significant dose- and time-dependent cytotoxicity against all three cancer cell lines, with IC50 values of 85.2 µg/mL (A549), 92.7 µg/mL (MCF-7), and 78.9 µg/mL (HepG2) at 48 hours. GPE treatment significantly induced apoptosis (p < 0.01) and increased caspase-3 activity in a dose-dependent manner. Western blot analysis revealed a significant upregulation of pro-apoptotic Bax and a downregulation of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2. Furthermore, GPE treatment markedly inhibited the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway and reduced the expression of VEGF and HIF-1α. In the *in vivo* study, GPE administration (50 mg/kg and 100 mg/kg) significantly reduced tumor volume and weight compared to the control group (p < 0.05), with no observable systemic toxicity.

Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that natural gypenosides exert potent anti-cancer effects by simultaneously targeting multiple molecular pathways, including the induction of intrinsic apoptosis, inhibition of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR proliferation pathway, and suppression of angiogenesis. These results position gypenosides as promising multi-targeted agents for cancer therapy.

Keywords: Gypenosides, *Gynostemma pentaphyllum*, Apoptosis, PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, Angiogenesis, Natural compounds, Cancer therapy.

---

 1. Introduction

Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide, characterized by uncontrolled cell proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, and the ability to induce angiogenesis and metastasis. Despite significant advances in targeted therapies and immunotherapy, the high rate of adverse effects and the emergence of drug resistance necessitate the discovery of novel, multi-targeted therapeutic agents with better safety profiles [1]. In this context, natural products, particularly those from traditional medicinal plants, have gained considerable attention as a rich source of anti-cancer compounds [2].

*Gynostemma pentaphyllum* (Thunb.) Makino, a perennial creeping herb of the Cucurbitaceae family, is widely used in traditional Chinese medicine. Its primary bioactive components are a group of dammarane-type saponins known as gypenosides [3]. Gypenosides have been reported to possess a wide range of pharmacological activities, including anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic, neuroprotective, and notably, anti-cancer properties [4]. Previous studies have shown that gypenosides can inhibit the proliferation of various cancer cells, such as hepatocellular carcinoma, lung cancer, and colorectal cancer [5, 6]. However, the precise molecular mechanisms by which gypenosides exert their broad-spectrum anti-cancer effects are still an area of active investigation.

The PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway is a critical intracellular cascade that regulates cell growth, proliferation, and survival, and is frequently hyperactivated in human cancers [7]. Concurrently, the induction of apoptosis, particularly the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway regulated by Bcl-2 family proteins, is a key strategy for eliminating cancer cells [8]. Furthermore, tumor angiogenesis, driven by factors like Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) and Hypoxia-Inducible Factor-1α (HIF-1α), is essential for tumor growth and metastasis [9].

We hypothesized that gypenosides exert their anti-cancer effects by concurrently modulating these key pathways. To test this, we investigated the effects of a standardized gypenoside extract (GPE) on three different human cancer cell lines (lung, breast, and liver) and in a murine xenograft model. Our study aimed to systematically evaluate its anti-proliferative, pro-apoptotic, and anti-angiogenic activities and to delineate the underlying molecular mechanisms.

 2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Preparation of Gypenoside Extract (GPE)
A standardized extract of *Gynostemma pentaphyllum* was purchased from a commercial supplier. The extract was standardized to contain ≥98% total gypenosides, as determined by HPLC analysis, with gypenoside XLIX as the primary marker compound. A stock solution was prepared in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and stored at -20°C.

2.2. Cell Culture
Human lung adenocarcinoma (A549), breast adenocarcinoma (MCF-7), and hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2) cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Cells were cultured in DMEM (A549, HepG2) or RPMI-1640 (MCF-7) medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37°C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere.

2.3. Cell Viability Assay
Cell viability was measured using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay. Cells were seeded in 96-well plates (5×10³ cells/well) and treated with various concentrations of GPE (0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150 µg/mL) for 24, 48, and 72 hours. Absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader. The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) was calculated using GraphPad Prism software.

2.4. Apoptosis Assay
Apoptosis was assessed using the Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, cells were treated with GPE (0, 50, 100 µg/mL) for 48 hours, harvested, and stained with Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide (PI). The percentage of apoptotic cells was analyzed by flow cytometry (BD FACSCanto II).

2.5. Caspase-3 Activity Assay
Caspase-3 activity was measured using a colorimetric assay kit. Cells were lysed after treatment, and the lysate was incubated with a caspase-3 specific substrate. The absorbance was read at 405 nm.

2.6. Western Blot Analysis
Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined using a BCA protein assay kit. Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. Membranes were blocked and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against Bax, Bcl-2, PI3K, p-Akt, Akt, p-mTOR, mTOR, VEGF, HIF-1α, and β-actin. After incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies, protein bands were visualized using an ECL detection system.

2.7. *In Vivo* Xenograft Model
All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. A549 cells (5×10⁶) were subcutaneously injected into the right flank of 6-week-old male BALB/c nude mice. When tumors reached a volume of ~100 mm³, mice were randomly divided into three groups (n=6 per group): control (vehicle), GPE-low dose (50 mg/kg), and GPE-high dose (100 mg/kg). GPE was administered via oral gavage daily for 21 days. Tumor volume was measured every three days. At the end of the study, mice were sacrificed, and tumors were excised and weighed.

2.8. Statistical Analysis
All experiments were performed in triplicate. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance was determined using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

 3. Results

3.1. GPE Inhibits Proliferation of Cancer Cells
Treatment with GPE resulted in a significant dose- and time-dependent inhibition of cell viability in all three cancer cell lines (A549, MCF-7, and HepG2). The calculated IC50 values at 48 hours were 85.2 µg/mL for A549, 92.7 µg/mL for MCF-7, and 78.9 µg/mL for HepG2 cells (Table 1). The A549 cell line was selected for subsequent mechanistic and *in vivo* studies due to its high sensitivity.

Table 1: IC50 values of GPE on different cancer cell lines at 48h.
| Cell Line | IC50 (µg/mL) |
| :--- | :--- |
| A549 (Lung) | 85.2 ± 3.1 |
| MCF-7 (Breast) | 92.7 ± 4.5 |
| HepG2 (Liver) | 78.9 ± 2.8 |

3.2. GPE Induces Apoptosis in A549 Cells
Flow cytometry analysis showed that GPE significantly increased the percentage of apoptotic cells in a dose-dependent manner. The total apoptosis rate (early + late) increased from 5.2% in the control group to 28.1% and 45.9% in the 50 µg/mL and 100 µg/mL GPE-treated groups, respectively (p < 0.01 vs. control). This was accompanied by a significant increase in caspase-3 activity, a key executioner of apoptosis, in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 1A, B).

3.3. GPE Modulates Apoptosis-Related Proteins
Western blot analysis revealed that GPE treatment significantly upregulated the expression of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax and downregulated the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 in A549 cells. This resulted in a significant increase in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, a key indicator of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway activation (Figure 1C).

3.4. GPE Inhibits the PI3K/Akt/mTOR Pathway
To investigate the effect of GPE on proliferative signaling, we examined the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway. GPE treatment markedly decreased the protein levels of PI3K and the phosphorylation of both Akt (p-Akt) and mTOR (p-mTOR) in a dose-dependent manner, while total Akt and mTOR levels remained largely unchanged. This indicates that GPE suppresses the activation of this critical pro-survival pathway (Figure 2A).

3.5. GPE Downregulates Angiogenic Factors
The expression of key angiogenic proteins, VEGF and HIF-1α, was significantly reduced in A549 cells following GPE treatment compared to the control group (Figure 2B). This suggests that GPE possesses anti-angiogenic potential.

3.6. GPE Suppresses Tumor Growth *In Vivo*
In the A549 xenograft mouse model, oral administration of GPE significantly inhibited tumor growth. After 21 days of treatment, the mean tumor volume in the high-dose GPE group (100 mg/kg) was 412.5 ± 55.3 mm³, which was significantly smaller than the control group's volume of 985.6 ± 110.2 mm³ (p < 0.05). The low-dose group (50 mg/kg) also showed significant tumor reduction (675.4 ± 82.1 mm³, p < 0.05 vs. control). The final tumor weights showed a consistent trend. No significant differences in body weight or signs of toxicity were observed between the groups.

 4. Discussion

The present study provides comprehensive evidence that gypenosides, a natural compound from *Gynostemma pentaphyllum*, exert potent anti-cancer effects through a multi-pronged approach. Our findings demonstrate that GPE inhibits cancer cell proliferation, induces intrinsic apoptosis, suppresses the PI3K/Akt/mTOR survival pathway, and downregulates key angiogenic factors, culminating in significant tumor growth inhibition *in vivo*.

The cytotoxicity of GPE was confirmed across three distinct cancer cell lines—lung, breast, and liver—highlighting its broad-spectrum potential. The observed IC50 values are consistent with previous reports on the anti-proliferative effects of gypenosides [5]. A key mechanism of its anti-cancer activity is the induction of apoptosis. Our data show that GPE treatment led to a significant increase in the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, a critical event that permeabilizes the mitochondrial membrane and triggers the intrinsic apoptotic cascade, leading to caspase-3 activation [8]. This is a well-established mechanism for many chemotherapeutic agents, and our results confirm that gypenosides utilize this pathway.

Dysregulation of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway is a hallmark of many cancers, driving uncontrolled proliferation and survival [7]. Our study found that GPE effectively inhibited this pathway by reducing the expression of PI3K and the phosphorylation of its downstream effectors, Akt and mTOR. This finding is significant as it suggests that gypenosides can directly interfere with a central hub of oncogenic signaling. This inhibition of pro-survival signaling, coupled with the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins, creates a synergistic effect that pushes cancer cells towards death.

Angiogenesis is essential for tumors to grow beyond a few millimeters and to metastasize. The hypoxic tumor microenvironment stabilizes HIF-1α, which in turn drives the expression of VEGF, a potent angiogenic factor [9]. Our results demonstrate that GPE significantly downregulated both HIF-1α and VEGF expression. This indicates that gypenosides can disrupt the tumor's blood supply, a crucial strategy in cancer therapy. This anti-angiogenic effect, combined with its direct cytotoxic and pro-apoptotic activities, likely contributes to the robust tumor growth inhibition observed in our *in vivo* study. The lack of significant toxicity in the mouse model is particularly encouraging and aligns with the known safety profile of *Gynostemma pentaphyllum* as a dietary supplement and traditional medicine [3].

The primary limitation of this study is the use of a standardized extract rather than a single purified gypenoside compound. The extract contains a mixture of gypenosides, and it is possible that the observed effects are due to the synergistic action of multiple components. Future studies will aim to isolate and test individual gypenosides to identify the most potent molecules and their specific targets. Furthermore, while our *in vivo* model is a good starting point, more complex models, such as orthotopic or genetically engineered mouse models, would provide a more physiologically relevant assessment of efficacy.

 5. Conclusion

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that natural gypenosides are effective multi-targeted anti-cancer agents. They simultaneously induce intrinsic apoptosis, inhibit the PI3K/Akt/mTOR proliferative pathway, and suppress angiogenesis. These combined actions lead to significant inhibition of tumor growth *in vitro* and *in vivo* with a favorable safety profile. Our findings provide a strong mechanistic rationale for the further development of gypenosides as a novel adjunctive or standalone therapy for the treatment of various cancers.

title: Deficit irrigation and sustainable water-resource strategies in agriculture for China's food security
text: China’s food security depends on irrigated agriculture, yet freshwater scarcity and competing demands increasingly constrain crop production. Deficit irrigation (DI) has emerged as a viable strategy to sustain yields while reducing water use, but its large-scale applicability and integration with sustainable water-resource strategies remain insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews the principles, agronomic responses, and limitations of DI, and evaluates complementary measures including improved irrigation scheduling, soil moisture conservation, water-saving technologies, and policy instruments. Evidence indicates that regulated deficit irrigation can maintain or slightly reduce yields while substantially enhancing water productivity, particularly for drought-tolerant crops and in water-scarce regions. However, outcomes are highly context-specific, depending on crop species, growth stage, soil conditions, and climate variability. We argue that DI should be embedded within an integrated framework combining precision irrigation, groundwater management, recycled water use, and institutional incentives. Such a framework can reconcile agricultural water conservation with China’s food-security goals, but requires site-specific validation, farmer adoption, and supportive policies.

title: Traditional Chinese medicine in cancer care: a review of controlled clinical studies published in chinese
text:
Traditional Chinese medicine in cancer care: a review of controlled clinical studies published in Chinese

Abstract

Objective: To systematically review controlled clinical studies published in Chinese on the use of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in cancer care, and to summarize evidence regarding efficacy, safety, and methodological quality. Methods: We searched the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, and VIP databases for controlled clinical studies published in Chinese between January 2005 and December 2023. Studies were included if they evaluated TCM as an adjunct to conventional cancer treatment in adults with histologically confirmed malignancy. Data on study design, sample size, intervention, outcomes, and adverse events were extracted. Results: A total of 126 studies involving 11,842 patients met the inclusion criteria. The most common cancers were lung (32.5%), gastric (21.4%), and breast (15.1%). TCM interventions included decoctions (58.7%), patent medicines (27.0%), and injections (14.3%). Compared with conventional treatment alone, TCM plus conventional treatment was associated with improved objective response rate (RR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.21–1.44), enhanced quality of life (RR = 1.45, 95% CI: 1.30–1.62), and reduced chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (RR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.57–0.81). However, only 18.3% of studies reported randomization methods adequately, and 9.5% used blinding. Conclusion: TCM as an adjunct to conventional cancer treatment may improve clinical outcomes and reduce adverse effects, but the evidence is limited by methodological weaknesses. Rigorously designed trials are needed.

Keywords: traditional Chinese medicine; cancer; controlled clinical study; systematic review; Chinese literature

1. Introduction

Cancer remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. In China, approximately 4.8 million new cancer cases and 3.2 million cancer-related deaths were estimated in 2022. Conventional treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy, have improved survival but are often accompanied by significant adverse effects and impaired quality of life. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has been used in cancer care in China for centuries, with a focus on restoring balance, enhancing immunity, and alleviating symptoms. In recent decades, a large number of controlled clinical studies on TCM in oncology have been published in Chinese-language journals. However, these studies are often overlooked in international reviews due to language barriers. This review aims to synthesize controlled clinical studies published in Chinese, evaluating the role of TCM in cancer care, and to assess the methodological quality of this body of evidence.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Search strategy

We searched CNKI, Wanfang Data, and VIP databases from January 2005 to December 2023. Search terms included “traditional Chinese medicine,” “cancer,” “tumor,” “controlled clinical study,” and their Chinese equivalents. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were also screened.

2.2 Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Inclusion criteria: (1) controlled clinical studies, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized controlled trials (non-RCTs); (2) adults (≥18 years) with histologically or cytologically confirmed malignancy; (3) TCM intervention combined with conventional treatment versus conventional treatment alone or placebo; (4) reported at least one clinical outcome. Exclusion criteria: case reports, animal studies, reviews, and studies without a control group.

2.3 Data extraction and quality assessment

Two reviewers independently extracted data on study characteristics, participants, interventions, outcomes, and adverse events. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Methodological quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for RCTs and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for non-RCTs.

2.4 Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed using Review Manager 5.4. Dichotomous outcomes were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity was assessed using I² statistics. A random-effects model was used when I² > 50%.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Study characteristics

A total of 126 studies involving 11,842 patients were included. Of these, 78 (61.9%) were RCTs and 48 (38.1%) were non-RCTs. The mean sample size was 94 (range 40–320). The most common cancer types were lung (32.5%), gastric (21.4%), breast (15.1%), colorectal (12.7%), and liver (9.5%). TCM interventions included oral decoctions (58.7%), patent medicines (27.0%), and injections (14.3%). The most frequently used herbs were Astragalus membranaceus, Panax ginseng, and Atractylodes macrocephala. Treatment duration ranged from 4 to 24 weeks.

3.2 Efficacy outcomes
