Objective response rate (ORR): 72 studies reported ORR. TCM plus conventional treatment significantly improved ORR compared with conventional treatment alone (RR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.21–1.44, p < 0.001, I² = 42%).

Quality of life (QoL): 58 studies assessed QoL using the Karnofsky Performance Scale or EORTC QLQ-C30. TCM combined with conventional treatment improved QoL (RR = 1.45, 95% CI: 1.30–1.62, p < 0.001, I² = 38%).

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV): 44 studies reported CINV. TCM significantly reduced the incidence of CINV (RR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.57–0.81, p < 0.001, I² = 51%).

Immune function: 36 studies reported immune parameters. TCM increased CD4+ T cell counts and CD4+/CD8+ ratio (standardized mean difference = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.51–0.93, p < 0.001).

3.3 Safety

Adverse events were reported in 62 studies. The most common TCM-related adverse events were mild gastrointestinal discomfort (4.2%), elevated liver enzymes (1.8%), and skin rash (1.1%). No severe TCM-related adverse events were reported. The incidence of adverse events was not significantly different between TCM plus conventional treatment and conventional treatment alone (RR = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.82–1.10, p = 0.49).

3.4 Methodological quality

Among the 78 RCTs, only 18.3% described adequate randomization methods, 9.5% used blinding, and 12.8% reported allocation concealment. Dropout rates were reported in 41.2% of studies. Among non-RCTs, selection bias and confounding were common. Publication bias was suggested by funnel plot asymmetry for ORR.

4. Discussion

This review of 126 controlled clinical studies published in Chinese suggests that TCM as an adjunct to conventional cancer treatment may improve objective response rates, enhance quality of life, reduce chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, and improve immune function. These findings are consistent with previous systematic reviews, including those published in English. However, the methodological quality of the included studies was generally low. Most lacked adequate randomization, blinding, and allocation concealment, which may overestimate treatment effects. Heterogeneity in TCM interventions, including variations in herbal formulas, doses, and durations, limits comparability. Safety data were inconsistently reported, and long-term toxicity was rarely assessed. Publication bias is likely, as negative studies may be underrepresented in Chinese-language journals. Despite these limitations, the consistency of findings across multiple studies and cancer types supports the potential adjunctive role of TCM. Future research should prioritize large, multicenter, double-blind RCTs with standardized TCM interventions and comprehensive safety monitoring.

5. Conclusion

TCM combined with conventional cancer treatment may improve clinical outcomes and reduce adverse effects in Chinese patients. However, the current evidence is limited by methodological weaknesses and heterogeneity. Rigorously designed clinical trials are needed to confirm these findings and to integrate TCM into evidence-based oncology care.

title: Symptom trajectories for palliative care inpatients with and without hyperactive delirium in the last week of life
text: Hyperactive delirium is highly prevalent among palliative care inpatients and often intensifies in the last week of life, yet its impact on symptom trajectories near death remains poorly characterised. Existing studies have largely examined delirium as a cross-sectional diagnosis or focused on single symptoms, rather than modelling how physical and psychological symptoms evolve day by day in the terminal phase. Whether patients with hyperactive delirium experience distinct trajectories of pain, dyspnoea, agitation, and other burdensome symptoms compared with those without delirium is unclear. Such knowledge is essential for anticipatory prescribing, prognostication, and family communication. This study therefore aimed to compare symptom trajectories during the last seven days of life between palliative care inpatients with and without hyperactive delirium, using repeated daily assessments. We hypothesised that patients with hyperactive delirium would show steeper symptom escalation and greater overall symptom burden as death approached.

title: Effectiveness of electroacupuncture for pain after osteosarcoma post surgery: A study protocol of systematic review of randomized controlled trial
text:
Results and Discussion

It is anticipated that this systematic review will identify approximately 12 randomized controlled trials involving 960 participants (mean sample size 80, range 40–160). The pooled analysis is expected to show that electroacupuncture significantly reduces postoperative pain compared with routine care, with a mean difference in visual analogue scale scores of −1.42 cm (95% CI −1.85 to −0.99, P < 0.001, I² = 46%). Responder analysis is expected to yield a risk ratio of 1.38 (95% CI 1.15–1.66) for achieving ≥50% pain relief, with a number needed to treat of 6. Secondary outcomes are projected to favor electroacupuncture for opioid consumption (mean difference −9.6 mg morphine equivalents/24 h, 95% CI −14.2 to −5.0) and time to first ambulation (mean difference −0.8 days, 95% CI −1.3 to −0.3), while adverse events are expected to be mild and comparable between groups (risk ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.84–1.49).

These findings would suggest that electroacupuncture is a promising adjunct for post-osteosarcoma pain, plausibly through segmental modulation of nociceptive transmission and endogenous opioid release. However, heterogeneity in stimulation parameters (2–100 Hz), acupoint selection, and concurrent chemotherapy may limit comparability. Because all included trials are anticipated to originate from China, language and publication bias, small sample sizes, and absent blinding of assessors are likely to reduce certainty of evidence. Consequently, conclusions should be interpreted cautiously, and large, multicenter, sham-controlled trials with standardized protocols and long-term follow-up are warranted.

title: Parental material and cultivation determine soil bacterial community structure and fertility
text:
Parental material and cultivation determine soil bacterial community structure and fertility

Abstract

Soil formation and fertility are jointly governed by geological and anthropogenic factors, yet the relative importance of parent material versus long-term cultivation in shaping soil bacterial communities remains contested. Here we examined 36 surface soils developed from three contrasting parent materials (granite, limestone, and alluvial deposits) under two land-use types (paired cultivated and adjacent uncultivated plots) in a subtropical region. Soil physicochemical properties, enzyme activities, and bacterial community structure (16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing) were measured. Cultivated soils showed significantly higher available phosphorus (AP), soil organic carbon (SOC), and urease activity but lower bacterial alpha diversity than uncultivated soils. Parent material explained 31.4% of the variation in bacterial community composition, while cultivation explained 22.7%; their interaction accounted for a further 11.2%. Limestone-derived soils harbored the highest proportion of Actinobacteria and the highest pH, whereas granite-derived soils were dominated by Acidobacteria. Co-occurrence network analysis revealed that cultivated soils had more compact networks but fewer keystone taxa. Structural equation modeling indicated that parent material influenced fertility mainly indirectly through pH and texture, while cultivation affected fertility directly via fertilization and indirectly by simplifying the bacterial network. Our results demonstrate that parent material sets the geochemical template for bacterial communities, whereas cultivation reshapes community structure and enhances short-term fertility at the cost of diversity and network stability. These findings highlight the need to integrate geological background into soil health assessment and sustainable management.

Keywords: parent material; long-term cultivation; bacterial community; soil fertility; 16S rRNA; co-occurrence network

1. Introduction

Soil microorganisms mediate nutrient cycling, organic matter decomposition, and plant productivity, and are therefore central to soil fertility. Bacterial communities are structured by a hierarchy of factors operating at different spatial and temporal scales, including climate, parent material, topography, vegetation, and land management. Parent material provides the initial mineralogical and geochemical template, controlling pH, texture, and base saturation, which in turn filter bacterial taxa. Cultivation, by contrast, imposes rapid changes through tillage, fertilization, irrigation, and crop rotation, often increasing nutrient availability while reducing biodiversity.

Whether geological legacy or anthropogenic management dominates bacterial community assembly is still debated, partly because most studies confound the two by comparing distant sites with different climates. Paired sampling of cultivated and uncultivated plots on the same parent material offers a way to disentangle these effects. We hypothesized that (i) parent material determines the baseline composition and diversity of bacterial communities, (ii) cultivation homogenizes communities and reduces diversity while increasing fertility indices, and (iii) the interaction between parent material and cultivation explains a significant, non-additive portion of community variation. To test these hypotheses, we sampled soils from three parent materials under paired land uses and integrated physicochemical, enzymatic, and molecular data.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Site description and sampling

The study area is located in a subtropical hilly region (28°32′–28°47′N, 115°12′–115°36′E). Mean annual temperature is 17.2 °C and mean annual precipitation is 1,620 mm. Three parent materials were selected: granite (GR), limestone (LS), and alluvial deposit (AL). At each parent material, three replicate sites were chosen, each containing a cultivated plot (CT, >50 years of continuous cropping with mineral fertilization) and an adjacent uncultivated plot (UC, natural grassland or shrubland) within 100 m. Surface soil (0–20 cm) was collected from five points per plot and composited. In total, 36 samples (3 parent materials × 2 land uses × 3 sites × 2 composite replicates) were analyzed.

2.2 Physicochemical and enzymatic analyses

Soil pH was measured in a 1:2.5 soil:water suspension. SOC was determined by dichromate oxidation. Total nitrogen (TN) was measured by Kjeldahl digestion, and AP by the Olsen method. Soil texture was determined by the hydrometer method. Urease, acid phosphatase, and β-glucosidase activities were assayed colorimetrically following standard protocols.

2.3 DNA extraction, sequencing, and bioinformatics

DNA was extracted using a PowerSoil kit. The V3–V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified and sequenced on an Illumina platform. Sequences were processed in QIIME2; amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were taxonomically assigned against the SILVA database. Alpha diversity (Shannon, Chao1) and beta diversity (Bray–Curtis) were calculated. Co-occurrence networks were constructed using Spearman correlations (|r| > 0.6, P < 0.01).

2.4 Statistical analysis

Two-way ANOVA tested the effects of parent material and land use. Variation partitioning and structural equation modeling (SEM) were performed in R. All tests used α = 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Soil properties and enzyme activities

Parent material significantly affected pH, texture, and exchangeable bases (P < 0.01). Limestone soils had the highest pH (7.6–7.9), followed by alluvial (6.8–7.1) and granite (5.2–5.6). Cultivation significantly increased SOC (by 18.6%), TN (by 12.4%), and AP (by 63.2%) across all parent materials (P < 0.05), with the largest AP increase in granite soils. Urease and phosphatase activities were 24–41% higher in cultivated plots, whereas β-glucosidase showed no consistent trend.

3.2 Bacterial diversity and composition

A total of 8,742 ASVs were obtained. Shannon diversity was highest in uncultivated limestone soils (6.42 ± 0.11) and lowest in cultivated granite soils (5.31 ± 0.14). Two-way ANOVA showed that both parent material (F = 12.8, P < 0.001) and land use (F = 9.4, P < 0.01) significantly influenced diversity, with no significant interaction for Shannon index but a significant interaction for Chao1 (P < 0.05). At phylum level, Proteobacteria dominated all soils (32–41%). Actinobacteria were enriched in limestone (24.7%) and Acidobacteria in granite (21.3%). Cultivation increased the relative abundance of Firmicutes and Actinobacteria but decreased Acidobacteria and Verrucomicrobia.

3.3 Community structure and variation partitioning

Principal coordinates analysis showed clear separation by parent material along PC1 (28.6%) and by land use along PC2 (16.9%). Variation partitioning revealed that parent material alone explained 31.4% of community variation, cultivation alone 22.7%, and their shared fraction 11.2%, leaving 34.7% unexplained. Mantel tests indicated that pH (r = 0.61) and SOC (r = 0.44) were the strongest correlates of community structure.

3.4 Co-occurrence networks and SEM

Uncultivated networks had more nodes (1,142 vs. 806) and higher modularity, whereas cultivated networks had higher average connectivity and a lower ratio of positive to negative edges. Keystone taxa in uncultivated soils included Acidobacteria and Verrucomicrobia; cultivated soils were dominated by Bacillus and Streptomyces. SEM showed that parent material had a strong indirect effect on fertility (standardized total effect = 0.58) via pH and texture, while cultivation had a direct positive effect (0.47) and a negative indirect effect (−0.19) through reduced network complexity.

4. Discussion

Our results support the view that parent material and cultivation operate as hierarchical filters on soil bacterial communities. Parent material explained more community variation than cultivation, consistent with its role in setting pH and mineralogy, which are strong determinants of bacterial taxa at broad scales. Limestone soils, with near-neutral pH and high calcium availability, favored Actinobacteria, whereas acidic granite soils favored Acidobacteria, a pattern widely reported.

Cultivation increased short-term fertility, as indicated by higher AP, SOC, and enzyme activities, but reduced diversity and network complexity. This is likely due to repeated fertilization and tillage, which select for copiotrophic taxa and disrupt microhabitats. The significant interaction between parent material and cultivation for Chao1 suggests that the magnitude of diversity loss depends on the initial geochemical template, with granite soils being most sensitive.

The negative indirect pathway from cultivation to fertility via network simplification implies a potential trade-off: management that boosts nutrients may erode the microbial infrastructure supporting long-term nutrient supply. The high unexplained variation (34.7%) indicates that unmeasured factors such as crop type, fertilization history, and microclimate also matter.

5. Conclusion

Parent material determines the baseline composition and diversity of soil bacterial communities, whereas long-term cultivation enhances short-term fertility at the expense of diversity and network stability. The two factors interact, with the strongest cultivation effects on nutrient-poor, acidic parent materials. Sustainable soil management should therefore consider geological background and preserve microbial network complexity alongside nutrient inputs.

title: Synergistic Antifungal Activity of Graphene Oxide and Fungicides against Fusarium Head Blight In Vitro and In Vivo
text:
Synergistic Antifungal Activity of Graphene Oxide and Fungicides against Fusarium Head Blight In Vitro and In Vivo

 Abstract

Fusarium head blight (FHB), caused predominantly by *Fusarium graminearum*, represents one of the most devastating diseases affecting wheat production worldwide, resulting in substantial yield losses and mycotoxin contamination. The emergence of fungicide-resistant *Fusarium* populations necessitates the development of novel control strategies. This study investigated the synergistic antifungal potential of graphene oxide (GO) combined with commercial fungicides (tebuconazole and metconazole) against *F. graminearum* both in vitro and in vivo. In vitro assays demonstrated that GO alone exhibited moderate antifungal activity with a half-maximal effective concentration (EC₅₀) of 287.4 μg/mL. However, combinations of GO (50-100 μg/mL) with fungicides at sub-inhibitory concentrations (0.1-0.5 μg/mL) produced significant synergistic effects, with fractional inhibitory concentration indices (FICI) ranging from 0.31 to 0.48. The most effective combination (GO 75 μg/mL + tebuconazole 0.2 μg/mL) reduced mycelial growth by 89.3% and conidial germination by 94.7%. In vivo greenhouse experiments demonstrated that GO-fungicide combinations reduced disease severity by 76.8% compared to untreated controls and by 42.3% compared to fungicide-alone treatments. Additionally, deoxynivalenol (DON) production was reduced by 81.2% in plants treated with combination formulations. Mechanistic studies revealed that GO disrupted fungal cell membrane integrity, increased reactive oxygen species accumulation, and downregulated trichothecene biosynthesis genes. These findings suggest that GO-fungicide combinations represent a promising sustainable approach for FHB management, potentially reducing fungicide application rates while maintaining efficacy.

Keywords: graphene oxide, *Fusarium graminearum*, fusarium head blight, synergistic antifungal activity, tebuconazole, deoxynivalenol, wheat

 1. Introduction

Fusarium head blight (FHB), primarily caused by *Fusarium graminearum* Schwabe (teleomorph: *Gibberella zeae*), poses a persistent threat to global wheat and barley production (Dean et al., 2012). Beyond direct yield losses that can reach 50% during epidemic years, FHB contamination with trichothecene mycotoxins, particularly deoxynivalenol (DON), renders harvested grain unsuitable for human and animal consumption (Pestka, 2010). The economic impact of FHB in the United States alone has been estimated at $2.7 billion over the past two decades.

Current FHB management relies heavily on fungicide applications during anthesis, with demethylation inhibitor (DMI) fungicides such as tebuconazole and metconazole serving as the primary chemical control options (McMullen et al., 2012). However, the widespread and repeated use of these compounds has led to the emergence of reduced sensitivity in *F. graminearum* populations, raising concerns about long-term efficacy. Furthermore, stringent maximum residue limits for fungicides in grain commodities necessitate the development of strategies that maintain disease control while reducing chemical inputs.

Nanomaterials have emerged as promising alternatives in agricultural disease management due to their unique physicochemical properties and multiple modes of action that may circumvent resistance development (Servin et al., 2015). Graphene oxide (GO), a two-dimensional carbon nanomaterial, has demonstrated broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against bacteria and fungi (Chen et al., 2014). The proposed mechanisms of GO toxicity include physical disruption of cell membranes through sharp edge interactions, oxidative stress induction via reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and nucleic acid damage.

Despite growing evidence of GO's antimicrobial properties, its application in crop protection remains largely unexplored, particularly regarding potential synergistic interactions with conventional fungicides. We hypothesized that combining GO with sub-inhibitory concentrations of DMI fungicides would produce synergistic antifungal effects against *F. graminearum*, enabling reduced fungicide usage while maintaining or enhancing disease control efficacy.

This study aimed to: (1) evaluate the in vitro antifungal activity of GO against *F. graminearum*; (2) assess synergistic interactions between GO and commercial fungicides; (3) investigate the mechanisms underlying observed antifungal effects; and (4) validate efficacy under greenhouse conditions while monitoring mycotoxin production.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Materials

Graphene oxide (single-layer, 99% purity, lateral size 100-500 nm) was purchased from Graphene Supermarket (Calverton, NY, USA). Tebuconazole (97% purity) and metconazole (98% purity) analytical standards were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Commercial fungicide formulations (Folicur 3.6F and Caramba 90SL) were purchased from local agricultural suppliers. Potato dextrose agar (PDA) and potato dextrose broth (PDB) were obtained from Difco Laboratories (Detroit, MI, USA).

 2.2 Fungal Isolates and Culture Conditions

Three *F. graminearum* isolates (PH-1, GZ-3639, and a field isolate designated Fg-2021) were maintained on PDA at 25°C under continuous darkness. For conidial production, cultures were grown in carboxymethylcellulose medium as previously described (Cappellini and Peterson, 1965). Conidia were harvested by filtration through sterile cheesecloth and adjusted to 1 × 10⁵ conidia/mL using a hemocytometer.

 2.3 In Vitro Antifungal Activity

The antifungal activity of GO was assessed using mycelial growth inhibition assays in 96-well microplates. GO suspensions (0-500 μg/mL) were prepared in PDB via probe sonication (30% amplitude, 10 min). Each well received 100 μL of GO suspension and 100 μL of conidial suspension (final concentration 5 × 10⁴ conidia/mL). Plates were incubated at 25°C for 72 h, and optical density (OD₆₀₀) was measured using a microplate reader. EC₅₀ values were calculated using probit analysis.

For checkerboard assays, serial two-fold dilutions of GO (0-400 μg/mL) were combined with fungicide concentrations (0-10 μg/mL for tebuconazole, 0-5 μg/mL for metconazole). The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was calculated as: FICI = (FIC_GO) + (FIC_fungicide), where FIC represents the ratio of the concentration in combination to the concentration alone that produces the same effect. Synergy was defined as FICI ≤ 0.5, additivity as 0.5 < FICI ≤ 4.0, and antagonism as FICI > 4.0.

 2.4 Conidial Germination Inhibition

Conidial germination assays were performed in PDB with varying GO and fungicide concentrations. After 8 h incubation at 25°C, germination was assessed microscopically (>200 conidia per treatment). Germination was defined as germ tube emergence exceeding half the conidial diameter.

 2.5 Membrane Integrity Assessment

Fungal membrane integrity was evaluated using propidium iodide (PI) staining and electrolyte leakage measurements. Mycelia treated with GO (100 μg/mL), tebuconazole (1 μg/mL), or combinations for 12 h were stained with PI (10 μg/mL) for 15 min and examined using fluorescence microscopy. Electrolyte leakage was measured by determining relative conductivity of fungal suspensions using a conductivity meter.

 2.6 Reactive Oxygen Species Detection

Intracellular ROS levels were quantified using 2',7'-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA). Treated mycelia were incubated with DCFH-DA (10 μM) for 30 min, and fluorescence intensity was measured at excitation/emission wavelengths of 488/525 nm.

 2.7 Gene Expression Analysis

Total RNA was extracted from treated mycelia using TRIzol reagent. Quantitative RT-PCR was performed to assess expression of trichothecene biosynthesis genes (*TRI5*, *TRI6*, *TRI10*) and oxidative stress response genes (*CAT*, *SOD1*). The β-tubulin gene served as an internal reference.

 2.8 Greenhouse Experiments

Wheat cultivar 'Norm' (moderately susceptible to FHB) was grown in pots under greenhouse conditions (22/18°C day/night, 16 h photoperiod). At mid-anthesis, plants were spray-inoculated with *F. graminearum* conidial suspension (1 × 10⁵ conidia/mL). Treatments included: (1) untreated control; (2) GO alone (100 μg/mL); (3) tebuconazole alone (recommended field rate); (4) GO + tebuconazole (75 μg/mL + 0.2 μg/mL); and (5) GO + metconazole (75 μg/mL + 0.15 μg/mL). Disease severity was assessed 21 days post-inoculation using a 0-100% scale. DON content in harvested grain was quantified by ELISA.

 2.9 Statistical Analysis

All experiments were performed in triplicate and repeated at least twice. Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's HSD test (P < 0.05) using SPSS software version 26.0.

 3. Results

 3.1 In Vitro Antifungal Activity of GO

Graphene oxide exhibited concentration-dependent inhibition of *F. graminearum* mycelial growth (Table 1). The EC₅₀ values for the three isolates ranged from 267.3 to 312.8 μg/mL, with a mean of 287.4 μg/mL. Complete growth inhibition was observed at concentrations ≥400 μg/mL. Conidial germination was more sensitive to GO, with an EC₅₀ of 156.2 μg/mL.

Table 1. Antifungal activity of graphene oxide against *Fusarium graminearum* isolates

| Isolate | EC₅₀ Mycelial Growth (μg/mL) | EC₅₀ Conidial Germination (μg/mL) |
|---------|------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| PH-1 | 267.3 ± 12.4 | 148.7 ± 9.2 |
| GZ-3639 | 282.1 ± 15.8 | 162.4 ± 11.3 |
| Fg-2021 | 312.8 ± 18.2 | 157.5 ± 10.8 |

 3.2 Synergistic Interactions with Fungicides

Checkerboard assays revealed strong synergistic interactions between GO and both DMI fungicides (Table 2). The FICI values for GO-tebuconazole combinations ranged from 0.31 to 0.48, while GO-metconazole combinations yielded FICI values of 0.35 to 0.50. The most effective combination (GO 75 μg/mL + tebuconazole 0.2 μg/mL) reduced mycelial growth by 89.3% and conidial germination by 94.7%, despite tebuconazole concentration being 25-fold below its individual EC₅₀.

Table 2. Synergistic interactions between GO and fungicides

| Combination | FICI Range | Interpretation |
|-------------|------------|----------------|
| GO + Tebuconazole | 0.31-0.48 | Synergistic |
| GO + Metconazole | 0.35-0.50 | Synergistic |

 3.3 Membrane Integrity and ROS Production

Propidium iodide staining revealed that GO-treated hyphae exhibited 67.4% membrane permeability compared to 12.3% in controls. Combination treatments increased membrane damage to 84.2%. Electrolyte leakage followed similar patterns, with combination treatments causing 3.2-fold higher conductivity than controls.

ROS accumulation increased 4.7-fold in GO-treated mycelia and 6.8-fold in combination-treated samples compared to untreated controls (Figure 1). The addition of the antioxidant ascorbic acid (5 mM) partially rescued growth inhibition, confirming oxidative stress as a contributing mechanism.

 3.4 Gene Expression Modulation

Quantitative RT-PCR analysis demonstrated significant downregulation of trichothecene biosynthesis genes in combination-treated samples. *TRI5* expression decreased by 78.3%, *TRI6* by 71.5%, and *TRI10* by 69.2% compared to untreated controls. Conversely, oxidative stress response genes (*CAT* and *SOD1*) were upregulated 3.4-fold and 2.8-fold, respectively, indicating cellular response to GO-induced oxidative stress.

 3.5 Greenhouse Efficacy

Under greenhouse conditions, GO-fungicide combinations provided superior disease control compared to individual treatments (Table 3). The GO + tebuconazole combination reduced FHB severity by 76.8% compared to untreated controls and by 42.3% compared to tebuconazole alone. Similar results were observed with GO + metconazole combinations.

Table 3. Greenhouse efficacy against Fusarium head blight

| Treatment | Disease Severity (%) | DON Content (ppm) |
|-----------|---------------------|-------------------|
| Untreated control | 68.4 ± 5.2 a | 12.7 ± 1.8 a |
| GO alone | 52.1 ± 4.8 b | 9.4 ± 1.2 b |
| Tebuconazole alone | 27.6 ± 3.1 c | 4.2 ± 0.6 c |
| GO + Tebuconazole | 15.9 ± 2.4 d | 2.4 ± 0.4 d |
| GO + Metconazole | 17.3 ± 2.7 d | 2.7 ± 0.5 d |

Values followed by different letters are significantly different (P < 0.05).

DON contamination was reduced by 81.2% in combination-treated plants compared to controls, significantly lower than the 66.9% reduction achieved with fungicide alone.

 4. Discussion

This study demonstrates for the first time that graphene oxide exhibits synergistic antifungal activity with DMI fungicides against *F. graminearum*, both in vitro and in planta. The observed synergy allows for substantial reductions in fungicide concentrations while maintaining or improving disease control efficacy.

The antifungal mechanism of GO appears to involve multiple complementary pathways. Physical membrane disruption, evidenced by increased PI permeability and electrolyte leakage, likely facilitates enhanced fungicide uptake into fungal cells. This mechanical disruption may explain the synergistic interactions observed, as DMI fungicides require intracellular accumulation to reach their target (CYP51, sterol 14α-demethylase). The increased membrane permeability induced by GO may therefore amplify fungicide efficacy by promoting cellular entry.

Oxidative stress represents another key mechanism contributing to GO toxicity. The 4.7-fold increase in ROS accumulation following GO treatment exceeds typical cellular antioxidant capacity, leading to lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, and DNA damage. The upregulation of *CAT* and *SOD1* indicates that fungal cells attempt to counteract this oxidative challenge but ultimately fail at higher GO concentrations. The partial rescue by ascorbic acid confirms the importance of oxidative stress in GO-mediated growth inhibition.

The downregulation of trichothecene biosynthesis genes in combination-treated samples has significant implications for food safety. DON contamination remains a primary concern in FHB management, as even moderate disease levels can result in unacceptable mycotoxin concentrations. The 81.2% reduction in DON content achieved with combination treatments suggests that GO not only enhances disease control but also directly impacts mycotoxin production. This effect may result from both reduced fungal biomass and specific inhibition of trichothecene biosynthesis pathways.

The practical implications of this research are substantial. Current FHB management relies on multiple fungicide applications at or near maximum label rates, contributing to selection pressure for resistant populations and raising concerns about environmental contamination and residue accumulation. The demonstrated synergy enables reductions in fungicide application rates of 75-90% while maintaining efficacy, potentially extending the useful lifespan of existing fungicides and reducing environmental impact.

However, several considerations warrant attention before field implementation. The long-term fate and environmental impact of GO in agricultural systems remain incom

title: The Toxicity and Attenuation Methods of Toxic Chinese Materia Medica for its Reasonable Application: A Review
text: Abstract: Toxic Chinese materia medica (TCMM) constitutes a unique category of medicinal substances that have demonstrated remarkable therapeutic efficacy in treating intractable and severe diseases since ancient times. However, their clinical application is frequently constrained by potential toxicity, which may lead to adverse reactions and organ damage when improperly used. This review systematically summarizes the toxicity characteristics of TCMM, including hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and reproductive toxicity, as well as the underlying toxic mechanisms involving oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis, and metabolic activation. Furthermore, traditional and modern attenuation methods are comprehensively discussed, encompassing processing (paozhi), compatibility (peiwu), dosage control, decoction optimization, and structural modification of toxic components. Recent advances in toxicological evaluation, such as network toxicology, metabonomics, and transcriptomics, provide novel insights into the mechanistic understanding and safety assessment of TCMM. Notably, the principle of "toxicity-attenuation-efficacy preservation" should be adhered to during detoxification, ensuring that therapeutic benefits are maintained while toxicity is minimized. This review aims to provide a scientific basis for the rational and safe clinical application of TCMM, and to offer perspectives for future research on toxicity attenuation and quality control of toxic traditional Chinese medicines.

title: COVID-19: Analysis of Factors Affecting the Economy of Hunan Province Based on the Spatial Econometric Model
text:
COVID-19: Analysis of Factors Affecting the Economy of Hunan Province Based on the Spatial Econometric Model

Abstract

The COVID-19 pandemic has exerted heterogeneous shocks on regional economies, yet the spatial spillover mechanisms of these shocks at the prefectural level remain underexplored. This study investigates the factors influencing the economic performance of 14 prefecture-level cities in Hunan Province during 2020–2022 using a spatial econometric approach. A spatial Durbin model (SDM) is specified with GDP growth rate as the dependent variable, and epidemic intensity, industrial structure, fiscal expenditure, population mobility, and digital infrastructure as explanatory variables. Moran's I tests confirm significant positive spatial autocorrelation in economic performance. Estimation results reveal that epidemic intensity suppresses local economic growth but generates a positive spillover to neighboring cities, while digital infrastructure and fiscal support exhibit strong local and neighboring positive effects. The findings suggest that coordinated regional policies and digital economy development can mitigate pandemic-induced economic losses.

Keywords: COVID-19; Hunan Province; spatial econometric model; economic impact; spatial spillover

1. Introduction

The outbreak of COVID-19 in late 2019 triggered unprecedented global economic disruption. In China, strict containment measures such as city lockdowns, travel restrictions, and business closures effectively curbed virus transmission but simultaneously depressed production, consumption, and investment. Hunan Province, a major agricultural and manufacturing hub in central China with a population exceeding 66 million, experienced pronounced economic fluctuations during the pandemic. Its 14 prefecture-level cities display substantial heterogeneity in industrial structure, fiscal capacity, and digital readiness, making the province an ideal case for examining spatial economic dynamics.

Existing studies on pandemic economic impacts often rely on non-spatial models, overlooking interdependence among neighboring regions. Economic activities across cities are inherently connected through labor migration, supply chains, and trade, producing spatial spillovers. Ignoring such effects may yield biased estimates. This paper therefore employs a spatial econometric model to analyze factors affecting Hunan's economy during the pandemic, addressing two questions: (1) Is there spatial autocorrelation in economic performance across Hunan's cities? (2) How do epidemic intensity and socioeconomic factors influence local and neighboring economies?

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Area and Data

The study covers all 14 prefecture-level cities of Hunan Province: Changsha, Zhuzhou, Xiangtan, Hengyang, Shaoyang, Yueyang, Changde, Zhangjiajie, Yiyang, Chenzhou, Yongzhou, Huaihua, Loudi, and Xiangxi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture. Panel data for 2020–2022 were compiled. The dependent variable is the annual GDP growth rate (%). Explanatory variables include: epidemic intensity (confirmed cases per 10,000 population), industrial structure (share of tertiary industry, %), fiscal expenditure (government spending on health and social security as % of GDP), population mobility (passenger turnover per capita), and digital infrastructure (internet broadband subscribers per 100 people). Data were obtained from Hunan Statistical Yearbooks and provincial health commission reports; some values were interpolated and reasonably simulated where official records were incomplete.

2.2 Spatial Weight Matrix

A row-standardized first-order contiguity matrix W was constructed, where wij = 1 if cities i and j share a border, and 0 otherwise. This specification captures geographic proximity effects.

2.3 Model Specification

The spatial Durbin model (SDM) is specified as:

Y = ρWY + Xβ + WXθ + ε

where Y is the vector of GDP growth rates, X is the matrix of explanatory variables, ρ is the spatial autoregressive coefficient, β and θ are parameter vectors, and ε is the error term. The SDM nests spatial lag and spatial error models and allows for both endogenous and exogenous spatial interactions. Moran's I was used to test spatial autocorrelation. Estimation was performed via maximum likelihood. Direct, indirect (spillover), and total effects were decomposed following LeSage and Pace (2009).

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Spatial Autocorrelation

Moran's I values for GDP growth were positive and significant in all three years (2020: 0.312, p<0.05; 2021: 0.287, p<0.05; 2022: 0.341, p<0.01), indicating that cities with similar economic performance cluster spatially. High-growth cities such as Changsha, Zhuzhou, and Xiangtan form a core agglomeration in eastern Hunan, while western cities like Huaihua and Xiangxi exhibit lower growth, confirming a core-periphery pattern.

3.2 SDM Estimation Results

The spatial autoregressive coefficient ρ is 0.276 (p<0.01), confirming strong spatial dependence. Key findings are as follows. Epidemic intensity has a negative direct effect (−0.184, p<0.05), meaning higher case rates reduce local GDP growth. However, its indirect effect is positive (0.097, p<0.10), suggesting that when a city suffers severe outbreaks, neighboring cities may benefit from diverted production and consumption. Industrial structure (tertiary share) shows a positive direct effect (0.213, p<0.01) but a negative indirect effect (−0.121, p<0.05), implying that service-oriented cities grow faster locally but may drain demand from neighbors. Fiscal expenditure yields positive direct (0.165, p<0.05) and indirect (0.134, p<0.05) effects, highlighting the stabilizing role of government spending. Population mobility has a positive direct effect (0.142, p<0.05) but insignificant spillovers. Digital infrastructure exhibits the strongest total effect (direct: 0.238, p<0.01; indirect: 0.187, p<0.01), underscoring the pandemic-era importance of internet access for remote work, e-commerce, and service delivery.

3.3 Robustness Checks

Alternative weight matrices (inverse distance and economic proximity) yield consistent signs and significance, confirming result stability.

4. Discussion

This study provides three key insights. First, the significant spatial autocorrelation implies that pandemic economic shocks are not confined to administrative boundaries. A city's growth depends on both its own epidemic situation and that of its neighbors, validating the use of spatial models. The positive spillover of epidemic intensity may reflect substitution effects: when one city locks down, nearby cities absorb its production orders and labor force.

Second, digital infrastructure emerges as the most potent mitigator of pandemic economic damage. Cities with better broadband coverage sustained higher growth, as digital platforms enabled telework, online education, and contactless commerce. This finding aligns with the "digital resilience" hypothesis and suggests that investing in digital networks is a long-term buffer against future shocks.

Third, fiscal expenditure generates positive externalities, indicating that coordinated fiscal policies across neighboring cities amplify regional stability. In contrast, the negative spillover of tertiary industry share warns that service-driven growth can be fragile and competitive during crises.

The results carry policy implications. Hunan should promote inter-city coordination in epidemic control to avoid beggar-thy-neighbor lockdowns, accelerate digital infrastructure in western underdeveloped areas, and design joint fiscal stimulus packages that account for spatial spillovers.

5. Conclusion

This paper applied a spatial Durbin model to analyze factors affecting Hunan Province's economy during COVID-19. Using panel data for 14 cities from 2020 to 2022, we found significant positive spatial autocorrelation in GDP growth. Epidemic intensity harms local growth but benefits neighbors; digital infrastructure and fiscal expenditure exert robust positive direct and spillover effects; industrial structure and population mobility show mixed effects. The study demonstrates that spatial econometric models offer superior explanatory power over non-spatial approaches. Policymakers should adopt regionally coordinated strategies that leverage digital economy development and fiscal transfers to build economic resilience against pandemics. Future research could incorporate finer-grained monthly data and inter-city migration flows to refine spillover mechanisms.

title: Compositional and gastrointestinal prokinetic studies of Pugionium (L.)
text:
Gastrointestinal motility disorders, including functional dyspepsia, gastroparesis, and irritable bowel syndrome, represent a substantial global health burden and significantly impair patients’ quality of life. Current prokinetic agents, such as metoclopramide, domperidone, and mosapride, are widely prescribed but are frequently associated with limited efficacy and adverse effects, including extrapyramidal symptoms, cardiac arrhythmias, and drug tolerance. Consequently, there is growing interest in identifying novel prokinetic candidates from natural sources with favourable safety profiles.

*Pugionium* (L.), a genus belonging to the family Brassicaceae, comprises several halophytic species distributed mainly in the arid and semi-arid regions of northwestern China, Mongolia, and Central Asia. Species such as *Pugionium cornutum* (L.) Gaertn. and *Pugionium dolabratum* Maxim. have long been consumed as traditional vegetables and folk medicines by local populations, and are reputed to relieve indigestion, abdominal distension, and constipation. Despite these ethnomedicinal claims, the chemical composition and pharmacological basis of *Pugionium* remain poorly characterised, and no systematic evaluation of its gastrointestinal prokinetic activity has been reported.

Preliminary phytochemical investigations indicate that *Pugionium* species are rich in glucosinolates, isothiocyanates, flavonoids, phenolic acids, and polysaccharides. Several of these constituents, particularly isothiocyanates and flavonoids, have been documented to modulate gut motility, exert anti-inflammatory effects, and regulate the enteric nervous system. These findings suggest that *Pugionium* may contain bioactive compounds worthy of further development as gastrointestinal prokinetic agents.

In the present study, we therefore aimed to (i) characterise the chemical composition of *Pugionium* (L.) extracts using chromatographic and spectroscopic techniques, and (ii) evaluate their gastrointestinal prokinetic effects in vitro and in vivo, with a focus on gastric emptying, small intestinal transit, and possible underlying mechanisms. Our results are expected to provide a scientific rationale for the traditional use of *Pugionium* and to support its potential development as a functional food or therapeutic agent for gastrointestinal motility disorders.

title: Efficacy and safety of traditional Chinese herbal medicine in the treatment of threatened abortion: A protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Results and Discussion

A total of 1,247 records were identified through the initial search, of which 38 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Ultimately, 12 randomized controlled trials involving 1,586 participants were included in the quantitative synthesis. The mean participant age was 28.4 ± 4.2 years, and the mean gestational age at enrollment was 7.3 ± 1.5 weeks. All included trials compared traditional Chinese herbal medicine (TCHM) plus conventional treatment (e.g., dydrogesterone or progesterone) versus conventional treatment alone, with treatment durations ranging from 2 to 8 weeks.

The meta-analysis demonstrated that adjunctive TCHM significantly improved the total effective rate (risk ratio [RR] = 1.18, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.11–1.26, P < 0.001; I² = 32%). TCHM was also associated with a lower incidence of miscarriage (RR = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.38–0.71, P < 0.001; I² = 0%) and a higher proportion of participants achieving continued pregnancy beyond 12 weeks (RR = 1.15, 95% CI: 1.07–1.23, P < 0.001). Regarding safety, the incidence of adverse events did not differ significantly between groups (RR = 0.89, 95% CI: 0.61–1.30, P = 0.55; I² = 18%), with the most commonly reported events being mild gastrointestinal discomfort and dizziness.

Subgroup analyses suggested that trials using individualized TCHM formulations showed a greater effect on total effective rate (RR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.14–1.35) than those using fixed patent medicines (RR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.01–1.20). Sensitivity analyses excluding trials with high risk of bias did not materially alter the pooled estimates. However, heterogeneity in outcome definitions and TCHM composition, along with generally small sample sizes, limits definitive conclusions. These findings suggest that TCHM may be a beneficial adjunct for threatened abortion, but large-scale, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials are warranted to confirm efficacy and long-term safety.

title: The effect of shower time, electrolyte treatment, and electrical stimulation on meat quality of cattle longissimus thoracis muscle in cold weather
text:
The effect of shower time, electrolyte treatment, and electrical stimulation on meat quality of cattle longissimus thoracis muscle in cold weather

Abstract

Cold weather is known to accelerate pre-rigor muscle chilling, which can induce cold shortening and negatively affect beef tenderness and water-holding capacity. This study investigated the combined effects of shower time (0, 5, 10, and 15 min), electrolyte treatment (0.9% NaCl + 0.3% KCl spray vs. no treatment), and electrical stimulation (ES: 0, 60, and 120 s at 45 V) on the quality of cattle longissimus thoracis muscle under cold environmental conditions (ambient temperature 2 ± 1°C). A total of 48 cattle were randomly assigned to a 4 × 2 × 3 factorial design. Meat quality parameters including pH decline, Warner-Bratzler shear force (WBSF), drip loss, cooking loss, color (L*, a*, b*), and sarcomere length were measured at 24 h post-mortem. Results showed that shower time significantly affected pH decline and sarcomere length (P < 0.05), with 10 min showering maintaining higher pH and longer sarcomeres. Electrolyte treatment reduced drip loss and improved tenderness (P < 0.05). Electrical stimulation at 120 s significantly accelerated pH decline but decreased WBSF and increased sarcomere length (P < 0.01). The optimal combination was 10 min showering + electrolyte treatment + 120 s ES, which yielded the lowest WBSF (32.4 N) and drip loss (1.82%) compared with the control (48.7 N and 3.15%, respectively). These findings suggest that integrated pre-rigor interventions can effectively mitigate cold-induced meat quality deterioration in cattle.

Keywords: cold weather; shower time; electrolyte treatment; electrical stimulation; longissimus thoracis; meat quality; cold shortening

1. Introduction

Beef quality is influenced by numerous pre- and post-mortem factors, among which temperature management during the early post-mortem period is critical. In cold weather conditions, the rapid decline in muscle temperature before rigor mortis can lead to cold shortening, a phenomenon characterized by excessive muscle contraction, resulting in tough meat and poor water-holding capacity (Locker and Hagyard, 1963). This is particularly problematic in regions with harsh winters or in abattoirs where chilling rates are difficult to control.

Several interventions have been proposed to counteract cold shortening. Showering carcasses with water before chilling is a common practice to maintain muscle temperature and delay pH decline. However, the optimal duration of showering under cold conditions remains unclear. Electrolyte treatment, such as spraying with saline solutions, has been shown to influence osmotic balance and improve water retention in meat. Electrical stimulation (ES) is widely used to accelerate glycolysis and prevent cold shortening by inducing rapid pH decline while muscle temperature is still relatively high. However, the interactive effects of these three factors under cold weather have not been systematically evaluated.

The longissimus thoracis muscle is a commercially important cut, and its quality is highly sensitive to chilling rate. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the individual and combined effects of shower time, electrolyte treatment, and electrical stimulation on the meat quality of cattle longissimus thoracis muscle in cold weather. We hypothesized that a combination of moderate showering, electrolyte treatment, and ES would synergistically improve meat tenderness and water-holding capacity by mitigating cold shortening.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Animals and experimental design

A total of 48 healthy crossbred steers (Simmental × local yellow cattle, 18–24 months old, body weight 450 ± 30 kg) were used. All animals were slaughtered following standard commercial procedures in a licensed abattoir during winter (ambient temperature 2 ± 1°C, relative humidity 65 ± 5%). Immediately after exsanguination, carcasses were randomly assigned to a 4 × 2 × 3 factorial design: shower time (0, 5, 10, or 15 min), electrolyte treatment (with or without), and electrical stimulation (0, 60, or 120 s). Each treatment combination was applied to two carcasses (n = 2), and the experiment was replicated twice on separate slaughter days (total n = 4 per combination).

2.2 Shower and electrolyte treatments

Showering was performed using a perforated stainless-steel pipe system delivering potable water at 10 ± 1°C at a flow rate of 2 L/min per carcass. Electrolyte treatment consisted of spraying the longissimus thoracis surface with 500 mL of a chilled solution containing 0.9% NaCl and 0.3% KCl (w/v) immediately after showering. Control carcasses received no spray.

2.3 Electrical stimulation

ES was applied within 30 min post-mortem using a commercial stimulator (Model ES-24, Germany). Parameters were 45 V, 50 Hz, and pulse duration of 2 ms, delivered for 0, 60, or 120 s via rectal and nasal electrodes.

2.4 Sampling and meat quality measurements

At 24 h post-mortem, the longissimus thoracis muscle was excised from the 12th–13th rib region. Muscle pH was measured at 1, 6, and 24 h using a calibrated portable pH meter (HI 99163, Hanna Instruments). Color (L*, a*, b*) was determined using a Minolta CR-400 chromameter. Drip loss was measured by suspending 2.5 cm cubes in plastic bags at 4°C for 24 h. Cooking loss was assessed by cooking samples in a water bath at 75°C until an internal temperature of 70°C was reached. Warner-Bratzler shear force (WBSF) was measured on cooked samples using a TA.XT Plus texture analyzer. Sarcomere length was determined by laser diffraction microscopy.

2.5 Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0 (IBM, USA). Three-way ANOVA was performed to evaluate the main effects and interactions. Duncan’s multiple range test was used for post-hoc comparisons. Significance was set at P < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 pH decline

Shower time significantly influenced pH at 6 h post-mortem (P < 0.05). Carcasses showered for 10 min had the highest pH (6.12 ± 0.08), while the 0 min group had the lowest (5.78 ± 0.09). Electrolyte treatment alone did not affect pH (P > 0.05). ES significantly accelerated pH decline at 6 h (P < 0.01), with 120 s ES resulting in pH 5.85 ± 0.07 compared with 6.05 ± 0.10 for non-ES controls. However, the interaction between shower time and ES was significant (P < 0.05): the combination of 10 min showering and 120 s ES maintained pH at 6.02 ± 0.06, higher than 120 s ES alone.

3.2 Water-holding capacity

Drip loss was significantly reduced by electrolyte treatment (P < 0.05), from 2.94 ± 0.21% to 2.11 ± 0.18%. Shower time also affected drip loss, with 10 min showing the lowest value (2.05 ± 0.15%) and 0 min the highest (3.12 ± 0.24%). ES at 120 s further reduced drip loss to 1.82 ± 0.12% when combined with 10 min showering and electrolyte treatment. Cooking loss followed a similar trend, with the optimal combination yielding 18.4 ± 0.9% versus 24.7 ± 1.2% in controls (P < 0.01).

3.3 Tenderness and sarcomere length

WBSF was significantly affected by all three factors (P < 0.01). The lowest WBSF (32.4 ± 2.1 N) was observed in the 10 min shower + electrolyte + 120 s ES group, while the control group had 48.7 ± 3.5 N. Sarcomere length showed a negative correlation with WBSF (r = -0.78, P < 0.01). The optimal combination resulted in sarcomere length of 1.92 ± 0.05 μm, compared with 1.58 ± 0.06 μm in controls. ES alone increased sarcomere length to 1.78 ± 0.04 μm (120 s), but the effect was more pronounced when combined with showering and electrolyte treatment.

3.4 Color

No significant differences were found in L* or b* values among treatments (P > 0.05). However, a* values were slightly higher in ES groups (P < 0.05), indicating improved redness, possibly due to faster pH decline and reduced oxidation.

4. Discussion

The present study demonstrates that cold weather exacerbates cold shortening, as evidenced by the high WBSF and short sarcomere length in control carcasses. Showering for 10 min was effective in maintaining muscle temperature and delaying pH decline, which is consistent with previous findings that pre-chilling showering can mitigate cold-induced toughening (Hwang et al., 2003). However, excessive showering (15 min) did not further improve quality, possibly due to surface water accumulation and increased microbial risk.

Electrolyte treatment improved water-holding capacity, likely through osmotic retention of water within muscle fibers. The combination of NaCl and KCl may also enhance ionic strength, reducing protein denaturation. This is in agreement with studies on brine injection improving tenderness (Offer and Trinick, 1983).

Electrical stimulation accelerated glycolysis and pH decline, which is crucial in cold environments to prevent cold shortening by ensuring that rigor mortis occurs while muscle temperature is still above 10°C. The 120 s ES was more effective than 60 s, likely due to more complete depletion of ATP. The synergistic effect of ES with showering and electrolyte treatment suggests that multiple interventions targeting different mechanisms (temperature maintenance, osmotic balance, and rapid pH decline) can collectively improve meat quality.

The reduction in WBSF and increase in sarcomere length in the optimal group indicate that cold shortening was effectively prevented. The lack of significant color differences suggests that these treatments do not adversely affect appearance. Future studies should evaluate microbial safety and consumer acceptance of these combined interventions.

5. Conclusion

Under cold weather conditions (2 ± 1°C), the combination of 10 min showering, electrolyte treatment (0.9% NaCl + 0.3% KCl), and 120 s electrical stimulation (45 V, 50 Hz) significantly improved the quality of cattle longissimus thoracis muscle by reducing drip loss, cooking loss, and Warner-Bratzler shear force, while increasing sarcomere length. This integrated approach effectively mitigates cold shortening and offers a practical strategy for abattoirs operating in cold environments.

title: RNAi-mediated SMV P3 cistron silencing confers significantly enhanced resistance to multiple Potyvirus strains and isolates in transgenic soybean
text:
RNAi-mediated SMV P3 cistron silencing confers significantly enhanced resistance to multiple Potyvirus strains and isolates in transgenic soybean

 Abstract

Soybean mosaic virus (SMV) is one of the most devastating pathogens of soybean (*Glycine max* (L.) Merr.), causing substantial yield losses and seed quality deterioration worldwide. The P3 cistron of potyviruses encodes a multifunctional protein involved in viral replication, movement, and pathogenicity determination. In this study, we developed transgenic soybean lines expressing an intron-hairpin RNA (ihpRNA) construct targeting the P3 cistron of SMV. A 312-bp conserved fragment of the P3 gene from SMV strain SC3 was cloned into the pCAMBIA3301-derived binary vector in sense and antisense orientations separated by the soybean intron 1 of the *GmFAD2-1B* gene. Stable transgenic lines were generated via *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*-mediated cotyledonary node transformation of cultivar Jack. Molecular characterization of T₃ homozygous lines revealed single-copy transgene insertions with stable inheritance and high-level accumulation of P3-specific small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). Challenge inoculation with six SMV strains (SC3, SC7, SC15, SC18, SMV-N, and SMV-G7H) and three isolates (HeN1, JS1, and ZJ1) showed that transgenic lines exhibited significantly enhanced resistance, with disease indices reduced by 68.4–92.7% compared to wild-type plants across all tested strains and isolates. Virus accumulation, quantified by double antibody sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (DAS-ELISA) and reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), was suppressed by 74.3–97.1% in transgenic lines. Furthermore, no yield penalty was observed under field conditions across two growing seasons. These results demonstrate that RNAi-mediated silencing of the SMV P3 cistron provides broad-spectrum, durable resistance to multiple potyvirus strains and isolates, offering a promising strategy for soybean breeding programs.

Keywords: Soybean mosaic virus; RNA interference; P3 cistron; transgenic soybean; broad-spectrum resistance; potyvirus

 Introduction

Soybean (*Glycine max* (L.) Merr.) is a globally important oilseed and protein crop, with worldwide production exceeding 350 million metric tons annually. However, soybean production is constantly threatened by viral diseases, among which soybean mosaic virus (SMV) is the most widespread and economically significant. SMV belongs to the genus *Potyvirus* within the family *Potyviridae* and is transmitted by more than 30 aphid species in a non-persistent manner, as well as through infected seeds. Infection typically results in mosaic mottling, leaf distortion, stunting, and reduced pod set, with yield losses ranging from 10% to 100% depending on cultivar susceptibility, virus strain, and environmental conditions.

The SMV genome consists of a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA of approximately 9.6 kb that encodes a single polyprotein subsequently cleaved into ten mature proteins: P1, HC-Pro, P3, P3N-PIPO, CI, 6K1, 6K2, NIa-VPg, NIa-Pro, NIb, and CP. Among these, the P3 cistron has emerged as a critical determinant of viral pathogenicity, host range, and symptom severity. P3 participates in viral replication complex formation, cell-to-cell movement, and suppression of host RNA silencing. Notably, P3 is one of the most variable regions among potyvirus strains, yet it contains conserved domains essential for viral function, making it an attractive target for RNA interference (RNAi)-based resistance strategies.

Conventional breeding for SMV resistance has relied primarily on the deployment of resistance genes such as *Rsv1*, *Rsv3*, and *Rsv4*. However, the rapid emergence of resistance-breaking strains, coupled with the narrow strain specificity of these genes, has limited their long-term effectiveness. RNAi, a conserved eukaryotic post-transcriptional gene silencing mechanism, offers an alternative approach by targeting conserved viral sequences, thereby conferring broad-spectrum resistance. Previous studies have demonstrated RNAi-mediated resistance against SMV by targeting the CP, HC-Pro, or NIb genes; however, the P3 cistron has received comparatively less attention despite its functional importance.

In this study, we generated transgenic soybean lines expressing an intron-hairpin RNA construct targeting a conserved region of the SMV P3 cistron. We evaluated the resistance spectrum of these lines against six SMV strains and three field isolates, quantified virus accumulation, and assessed agronomic performance under field conditions. Our results demonstrate that P3-targeted RNAi confers significantly enhanced, broad-spectrum resistance to multiple potyvirus strains and isolates without yield penalty.

 Materials and Methods

 Plant materials and virus strains

Soybean cultivar Jack (susceptible to SMV) was used for transformation. Seeds of six SMV strains (SC3, SC7, SC15, SC18, SMV-N, and SMV-G7H) and three isolates (HeN1, JS1, and ZJ1) were obtained from the National Soybean Improvement Center. Viruses were maintained in soybean cultivar Williams 82 and propagated by mechanical inoculation.

 Construction of the RNAi vector

Total RNA was extracted from SMV-SC3-infected soybean leaves using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen). A 312-bp fragment corresponding to nucleotides 2,431–2,742 of the SMV P3 cistron was amplified by RT-PCR using primers P3-F (5′-CGGGATCCATGGCAGATTCAGAAGTT-3′) and P3-R (5′-CGAGCTCTTACTTGTTCCTGCTGC-3′). The fragment was cloned into the pCAMBIA3301-derived binary vector pRNAi-3301 in sense and antisense orientations, separated by the 512-bp intron 1 of the soybean *GmFAD2-1B* gene, under the control of the cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter. The resulting construct, designated pRNAi-P3, was introduced into *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* strain EHA105 by electroporation.

 Soybean transformation

Cotyledonary node explants of cultivar Jack were transformed as described previously with minor modifications. Putative transgenic shoots were selected on medium containing 5 mg L⁻¹ glufosinate. Regenerated T₀ plants were acclimatized and grown in a greenhouse. T₁ and T₂ generations were screened by PCR and herbicide tolerance assays to identify homozygous lines.

 Molecular characterization

Genomic DNA was extracted from leaf tissues using the CTAB method. PCR was performed to detect the *bar* selectable marker and the P3 hairpin cassette. Southern blot analysis was conducted using a digoxigenin-labeled *bar* probe to determine transgene copy number. Small RNA was extracted using the mirVana miRNA Isolation Kit (Ambion), and siRNA accumulation was detected by Northern blot using a ³²P-labeled P3-specific probe.

 Virus inoculation and disease evaluation

T₃ homozygous transgenic lines (L1, L4, and L7) and wild-type Jack plants were mechanically inoculated with each SMV strain or isolate at the V2 stage. Inoculated plants were maintained in a growth chamber at 25°C with a 16-h photoperiod. Disease symptoms were scored at 14, 21, and 28 days post-inoculation (dpi) using a 0–4 scale: 0 = no symptoms; 1 = mild mosaic; 2 = moderate mosaic with slight leaf distortion; 3 = severe mosaic with leaf distortion and stunting; 4 = severe symptoms with necrosis or plant death. Disease index (DI) was calculated as: DI = [Σ (disease rating × number of plants in that rating) / (4 × total number of plants)] × 100.

 Virus quantification

Virus accumulation was quantified at 21 dpi by DAS-ELISA using a polyclonal antibody against SMV CP, following the manufacturer's instructions. Absorbance was measured at 405 nm. RT-qPCR was performed using primers targeting the SMV CP gene, with *GmActin* as the internal reference. Relative virus accumulation was calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCt method.

 Field trials

Field trials were conducted over two consecutive growing seasons (2022 and 2023) at the Experimental Station of the National Soybean Improvement Center. A randomized complete block design with three replications was used. Each plot consisted of four rows of 3 m length with 0.5 m spacing. Agronomic traits including plant height, pod number per plant, seed number per pod, 100-seed weight, and seed yield were recorded.

 Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0 software. Means were compared using one-way ANOVA followed by Duncan's multiple range test at *P* < 0.05.

 Results

 Generation and molecular characterization of transgenic lines

A total of 18 independent T₀ transgenic events were generated, of which 12 survived to maturity. PCR analysis confirmed the presence of the *bar* gene and the P3 hairpin cassette in all 12 events. Southern blot analysis revealed that three events (L1, L4, and L7) harbored single-copy transgene insertions, while the remaining events had two or more copies. The three single-copy lines were advanced to T₃ homozygosity and used for subsequent analyses. Northern blot analysis detected abundant P3-specific siRNAs of 21–24 nt in all three transgenic lines, with line L4 showing the highest accumulation (approximately 2.3-fold higher than L1 and L7).

 Resistance evaluation against multiple SMV strains and isolates

Wild-type Jack plants exhibited severe mosaic symptoms, leaf distortion, and stunting by 14 dpi following inoculation with all tested SMV strains and isolates, with disease indices ranging from 72.5 to 91.3 at 28 dpi. In contrast, transgenic lines showed significantly reduced symptoms. Line L4 exhibited the strongest resistance, with disease indices ranging from 6.7 to 18.9 across all strains and isolates, representing reductions of 78.9–92.7% compared to wild-type plants. Lines L1 and L7 showed intermediate resistance, with disease indices ranging from 12.4 to 28.7 and 14.2 to 31.5, respectively (reductions of 68.4–84.6% and 65.2–82.1%, respectively). Notably, no symptoms were observed in line L4 following inoculation with strains SC7, SC15, and isolate JS1 at 28 dpi.

 Virus accumulation in transgenic lines

DAS-ELISA results showed that SMV CP accumulation in transgenic lines was significantly lower than in wild-type plants at 21 dpi. In line L4, virus accumulation was suppressed by 84.6–97.1% across all strains and isolates. Lines L1 and L7 showed suppression levels of 74.3–89.2% and 71.8–87.5%, respectively. RT-qPCR analysis of SMV CP gene expression corroborated these findings, with relative virus accumulation in line L4 reduced by 89.3–98.2% compared to wild-type plants. There was a strong negative correlation between siRNA accumulation and virus titer (r = −0.87, *P* < 0.01), suggesting that RNAi-mediated silencing was the primary mechanism of resistance.

 Agronomic performance under field conditions

Field trials across two growing seasons revealed no significant differences in plant height, pod number per plant, seed number per pod, or 100-seed weight between transgenic lines and wild-type Jack under virus-free conditions. Under natural SMV infection pressure, transgenic lines exhibited significantly higher seed yield than wild-type plants. In 2022, seed yield of line L4 was 2,847 kg ha⁻¹ compared to 1,623 kg ha⁻¹ for wild-type Jack, representing a 75.4% increase. Similar results were observed in 2023, with line L4 yielding 2,912 kg ha⁻¹ compared to 1,584 kg ha⁻¹ for wild-type Jack (83.8% increase). No yield penalty associated with the transgene was observed in any line.

 Discussion

Our results demonstrate that RNAi-mediated silencing of the SMV P3 cistron confers significantly enhanced resistance to multiple potyvirus strains and isolates in transgenic soybean. The P3 protein is a multifunctional virulence determinant involved in viral replication, movement, and suppression of host defenses, making it an excellent target for RNAi-based resistance. The broad-spectrum resistance observed in our study is likely attributable to the high degree of sequence conservation within the targeted 312-bp P3 fragment across the tested strains and isolates. Sequence analysis revealed 91.3–98.7% identity among the nine virus variants within this region, explaining the effectiveness of the P3-targeted construct against all of them.

The correlation between siRNA accumulation and resistance level observed in our study is consistent with previous reports that RNAi efficacy is dose-dependent. Line L4, which exhibited the highest siRNA accumulation, also showed the strongest resistance and lowest virus titers. This suggests that selection of transgenic events with high siRNA expression should be a priority in breeding programs utilizing RNAi technology.

The absence of yield penalty under virus-free conditions is an important finding, as constitutive overexpression of transgenes can sometimes impose metabolic burdens. The 35S promoter-driven expression of the P3 hairpin did not adversely affect agronomic traits, likely because the resulting siRNAs are processed and incorporated into the RNA-induced silencing complex without interfering with endogenous gene expression.

Compared to previous studies targeting the SMV CP or HC-Pro genes, our P3-targeted approach offers several advantages. First, the P3 cistron contains conserved domains essential for viral function, reducing the likelihood of escape mutants. Second, P3 is less prone to recombination than CP, which is frequently exchanged among potyviruses. Third, targeting P3 may simultaneously disrupt multiple viral functions, including replication and movement, thereby enhancing resistance durability.

One limitation of our study is that resistance was evaluated under controlled conditions and in field trials with natural infection pressure. Long-term field monitoring across diverse geographic locations will be necessary to confirm durability. Additionally, the potential for RNAi-based resistance to be overcome by viruses with mutations in the target region cannot be excluded, although the conserved nature of the P3 fragment reduces this risk.

 Conclusion

In conclusion, we have demonstrated that RNAi-mediated silencing of the SMV P3 cistron confers significantly enhanced, broad-spectrum resistance to multiple potyvirus strains and isolates in transgenic soybean. The resistance was stable across generations, correlated with siRNA accumulation, and effective against all nine tested virus variants. Importantly, no yield penalty was observed under field conditions. These findings establish P3-targeted RNAi as a promising strategy for developing soybean cultivars with durable resistance to SMV and potentially other potyviruses. Future work should focus on pyramiding P3-targeted RNAi with natural resistance genes to achieve synergistic and durable protection, as well as evaluating the long-term stability of resistance under diverse field conditions.

title: Foliage application of selenium and silicon nanoparticles alleviates Cd and Pb toxicity in rice (Oryza sativa L.)
text: Cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) contamination in paddy soils poses a serious threat to rice production and food safety. Nanoparticle-based foliar interventions offer a promising strategy to mitigate heavy metal toxicity in crops, yet the comparative efficacy and underlying mechanisms of selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) and silicon nanoparticles (SiNPs) remain poorly understood. In this study, a pot experiment was conducted to investigate the effects of foliar application of SeNPs and SiNPs, applied individually and in combination, on the growth, physiological responses, Cd and Pb accumulation, and grain yield of rice (*Oryza sativa* L.) grown in soil co-contaminated with Cd and Pb. Results showed that Cd and Pb stress markedly inhibited rice growth, disrupted photosynthetic pigment synthesis, induced oxidative stress, and enhanced metal translocation to grains. Foliar spraying of SeNPs and SiNPs significantly alleviated these adverse effects, with the combined treatment (SeNPs + SiNPs) exhibiting the greatest mitigation efficacy. Compared with the control, the combined application increased shoot and root biomass by 38.6% and 31.2%, respectively, and elevated grain yield by 42.3%. The combined treatment reduced root Cd and Pb concentrations by 44.7% and 39.5%, and grain Cd and Pb concentrations by 56.8% and 51.3%, respectively. These reductions were accompanied by decreased metal translocation factors and enhanced sequestration of Cd and Pb in root cell walls. Moreover, SeNPs and SiNPs synergistically enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD, POD, and CAT), reduced malondialdehyde and reactive oxygen species accumulation, and improved chlorophyll content and photosynthetic performance. The combined treatment also upregulated the expression of genes related to metal detoxification and antioxidant defense. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that foliar co-application of SeNPs and SiNPs effectively mitigates Cd and Pb toxicity in rice by restricting metal uptake and translocation, alleviating oxidative damage, and promoting growth, providing a feasible and sustainable approach for producing safe rice in heavy metal-contaminated paddy fields.

title: Soil protist communities form a dynamic hub in the soil microbiome
text:
Soil protist communities form a dynamic hub in the soil microbiome

Abstract

Soil protists are increasingly recognized as key consumers of bacteria and fungi, yet their functional position within the broader soil microbiome remains poorly resolved. Here we combined high-throughput 18S rRNA gene sequencing, metagenomics, and network analysis across 48 agricultural and forest soils to test whether protist communities act as a dynamic hub linking bacterial, fungal, and archaeal assemblages. Protist richness averaged 412 OTUs per gram of soil and was strongly correlated with bacterial (r = 0.71) and fungal (r = 0.68) diversity. Network analysis revealed that protist taxa had the highest betweenness centrality (mean = 18.4) among all microbial groups, exceeding that of bacteria (6.2) and fungi (9.1). Structural equation modeling indicated that protist grazing explained 34% of bacterial community turnover and 21% of fungal community variation, while environmental variables explained only 18% and 12%, respectively. When protist communities were experimentally reduced by 70% via selective inhibitors, bacterial evenness declined by 26% and fungal biomass increased by 41% within 14 days. These results demonstrate that soil protists function as a dynamic hub, coupling multiple microbial compartments and stabilizing microbiome structure through selective predation.

Keywords: soil protists; microbiome network; predation; microbial hub; community dynamics

1. Introduction

Soil harbors one of the most diverse microbial communities on Earth, with bacteria, fungi, archaea, and protists coexisting in complex spatial and trophic networks. While bacteria and fungi have received most attention, protists—single-celled eukaryotes—are now recognized as dominant consumers in the soil food web. They regulate bacterial abundance, shape community composition, and accelerate nutrient cycling by releasing immobilized nitrogen and phosphorus. Despite this ecological importance, protists are rarely integrated into conceptual models of the soil microbiome. Most studies treat them as passive grazers rather than active organizers of microbial structure. The hub hypothesis, originally developed for macroecological networks, predicts that taxa with high connectivity and centrality disproportionately influence community stability. Whether soil protists satisfy this criterion remains untested at the microbiome scale. We hypothesized that (i) protist diversity covaries with bacterial and fungal diversity across contrasting soils, (ii) protists occupy central positions in cross-domain co-occurrence networks, and (iii) experimental reduction of protists destabilizes bacterial and fungal communities. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a combined observational and manipulative study across 48 soils.

2. Materials and Methods

*2.1 Site description and sampling.* Soils were collected from 24 agricultural and 24 forest sites in eastern China (30°N–42°N). Each site was sampled in triplicate (0–15 cm depth), yielding 144 composite samples. Physicochemical properties (pH, organic carbon, total nitrogen, moisture) were measured using standard protocols.

*2.2 DNA extraction and sequencing.* Soil DNA was extracted using the PowerSoil kit. Bacterial 16S rRNA (V3–V4), fungal ITS1, archaeal 16S rRNA, and protist 18S rRNA (V4) genes were amplified and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq platform. Reads were processed in QIIME2; OTUs were clustered at 97% similarity.

*2.3 Network construction.* Cross-domain co-occurrence networks were built using SparCC on rarefied OTU tables. Nodes with >5 connections were retained. Betweenness centrality, degree, and modularity were calculated in igraph.

*2.4 Structural equation modeling.* SEM was performed in lavaan to partition direct and indirect effects of environment, protist grazing pressure (estimated from predator-prey ratios), and microbial diversity on community turnover.

*2.5 Protist reduction experiment.* Six soils were treated with cycloheximide (200 mg kg⁻¹) to suppress protists, with controls receiving distilled water. Bacterial evenness, fungal biomass (ergosterol), and protist abundance (qPCR) were measured at 0, 7, and 14 days.

3. Results and Analysis

Protist richness ranged from 287 to 563 OTUs per sample (mean = 412). Bacterial and fungal richness averaged 2,841 and 689 OTUs, respectively. Protist richness was positively correlated with bacterial (r = 0.71, P < 0.001) and fungal richness (r = 0.68, P < 0.001), and with soil organic carbon (r = 0.52, P = 0.003). Network analysis produced a cross-domain network with 1,842 nodes and 9,317 edges. Protist nodes represented only 6.8% of all nodes but had the highest mean betweenness centrality (18.4 ± 3.2), compared with bacteria (6.2 ± 1.1), fungi (9.1 ± 1.8), and archaea (4.7 ± 0.9). Removal of protist nodes increased network fragmentation by 43%, whereas removal of an equivalent number of bacterial nodes increased fragmentation by only 11%. SEM explained 62% of bacterial and 54% of fungal community turnover. Protist grazing had a direct effect on bacteria (β = −0.58, P < 0.001) and fungi (β = −0.41, P = 0.002), exceeding the effects of pH (β = 0.22) and moisture (β = 0.19). In the reduction experiment, protist abundance declined by 70% within 7 days. By day 14, bacterial evenness decreased by 26% (P = 0.004), fungal biomass increased by 41% (P = 0.001), and the bacterial/fungal ratio shifted from 8.3 to 5.1. Network stability, measured as the inverse of fragmentation, declined by 37% in treated soils.

4. Discussion

Our results support the hypothesis that soil protists function as a dynamic hub in the soil microbiome. The strong correlations between protist and bacterial/fungal diversity confirm that protists are not randomly distributed but track their prey. The network analysis provides more direct evidence: despite low relative abundance, protists exhibited the highest betweenness centrality, indicating that they connect otherwise separate bacterial and fungal modules. This topological position explains why removing protist nodes caused disproportionate fragmentation. The SEM results further show that protist grazing is a stronger driver of bacterial and fungal turnover than major abiotic factors.
