This is consistent with the “killing the winner” hypothesis, where selective predation prevents competitive exclusion and maintains coexistence. The reduction experiment provides causal support: suppressing protists reduced bacterial evenness, likely because relaxed predation allowed dominant taxa to proliferate. The simultaneous increase in fungal biomass suggests that protists also graze on fungi, and that fungal release from predation can alter bacterial-fungal balance. These findings position protists as regulators rather than passive consumers. However, our study has limitations. The inhibitor approach is not fully taxon-specific, and we did not distinguish between different protist functional groups (e.g., bacterivores vs. fungivores). Future work should combine single-cell sequencing and stable isotope probing to resolve trophic links at finer resolution.

5. Conclusion

Soil protist communities form a dynamic hub that links bacterial, fungal, and archaeal compartments. Their high network centrality and strong predatory effects on microbial turnover indicate that protists stabilize soil microbiome structure. Incorporating protists into predictive models of soil health and nutrient cycling is therefore essential. Management practices that preserve protist diversity may enhance microbiome resilience under environmental change.

title: Evaluation of genetic diversity and population structure of Fragaria nilgerrensis using EST-SSR markers
text: Fragaria nilgerrensis, a wild diploid strawberry species native to Southwest China, is valued for its exceptional stress tolerance, disease resistance, and characteristic peach-like aroma. These traits make it a promising genetic resource for cultivated strawberry improvement. However, natural populations of F. nilgerrensis have been increasingly threatened by habitat fragmentation and anthropogenic disturbance, raising concerns about the loss of genetic diversity. Understanding the extent and distribution of genetic variation within and among populations is therefore essential for effective conservation and utilization. Although previous studies have examined genetic diversity in this species using morphological, cytological, and a limited number of molecular markers, the resolution has often been insufficient to reveal fine-scale population structure. Expressed sequence tag-derived simple sequence repeat (EST-SSR) markers offer advantages such as high polymorphism, codominant inheritance, reproducibility, and close linkage to functional genes. In this study, we developed and applied EST-SSR markers to evaluate the genetic diversity and population structure of F. nilgerrensis accessions collected from its major distribution range. Our objectives were to quantify genetic variation within and among populations, clarify population differentiation and relationships, and provide a scientific basis for the conservation and sustainable exploitation of this wild strawberry resource.

title: Effect of economic policies on the stock and bond market under the impact of COVID-19
text:
Results and Discussion

The event study reveals a sharp divergence between market segments. In the 30-day window following the WHO pandemic declaration (March 11, 2020), the stock index posted a cumulative abnormal return (CAR) of −28.4% (t = −6.12, p < 0.01), while the bond market CAR was only −3.1% (t = −2.04, p < 0.05), confirming equities' greater vulnerability to pandemic shocks. Policy responses, however, altered these trajectories asymmetrically. A 100-basis-point policy rate cut was associated with a +6.8% rebound in stock returns within 15 trading days (β = 0.068, p < 0.01), whereas quantitative easing (QE) announcements produced a stronger effect on bonds, raising daily bond returns by 0.42% (β = 0.0042, p < 0.01) and compressing the 10-year yield by 54 basis points. Fiscal stimulus showed the largest equity impact: each 1% of GDP in announced spending generated a +2.3% stock market response (p < 0.05) but only +0.3% for bonds.

These findings suggest that monetary easing primarily stabilized fixed-income markets, while fiscal expansion drove equity recovery—consistent with the view that QE addresses liquidity and duration risk, whereas fiscal transfers support corporate earnings expectations. The muted bond reaction to fiscal news likely reflects offsetting inflation and default-risk channels. Overall, the results indicate that policy mix, not policy volume alone, determined cross-market outcomes during the COVID-19 crisis.

title: Real-Time Estimation of Population Exposure to PM2.5 Using Mobile- and Station-Based Big Data
text:
Real-Time Estimation of Population Exposure to PM2.5 Using Mobile- and Station-Based Big Data

Abstract

Accurate estimation of population exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is essential for assessing public health risks and formulating targeted mitigation policies. Traditional exposure assessments often rely on static residential locations and sparse monitoring stations, which fail to capture the dynamic spatiotemporal interactions between human mobility and air pollution. This study proposes a real-time framework that integrates mobile phone signaling data and station-based air quality observations to estimate population exposure to PM2.5 at high spatiotemporal resolution. Using a case study in a major metropolitan area, we combine anonymized mobile phone records from 2.1 million users with hourly PM2.5 measurements from 45 monitoring stations. A land-use regression model is employed to interpolate PM2.5 concentrations at 500 m × 500 m grid cells, while mobile data are used to derive hourly population density distributions. Exposure is then calculated by overlaying dynamic population surfaces with pollution surfaces. Results show that static residential-based exposure estimates differ substantially from dynamic estimates, with an average absolute deviation of 18.7 μg/m³ during daytime hours. The proposed method reveals that commuting flows significantly alter exposure patterns, particularly in urban core and suburban areas. This framework offers a scalable and transferable approach for real-time exposure assessment in other cities with similar data availability.

Keywords: PM2.5; population exposure; mobile phone data; air quality monitoring; real-time estimation; urban mobility

1. Introduction

Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is a leading environmental risk factor for premature mortality and cardiovascular and respiratory diseases worldwide (Cohen et al., 2017). Accurate quantification of population exposure—defined as the concentration of PM2.5 to which people are actually exposed—is critical for epidemiological studies and evidence-based policy making. However, conventional exposure assessments often assume that individuals remain at their residential locations throughout the day, using static census data and interpolated pollution surfaces (Jerrett et al., 2005). This assumption introduces substantial bias because people move across urban spaces for work, education, and leisure, encountering highly variable pollution levels.

The emergence of big data offers new opportunities to capture human mobility at unprecedented scales. Mobile phone signaling data, which record anonymous location updates as users move through the network, provide a dynamic representation of population distribution (Song et al., 2010). Simultaneously, dense air quality monitoring networks and advanced spatial models enable high-resolution PM2.5 estimation. Yet few studies have integrated these two data streams for real-time exposure assessment.

This study aims to fill this gap by developing a real-time estimation framework that combines mobile- and station-based big data. We address three research questions: (1) How do dynamic population distributions differ from static residential distributions? (2) To what extent does incorporating mobility alter PM2.5 exposure estimates? (3) What are the spatiotemporal patterns of exposure across different urban zones? We apply the framework to a synthetic metropolitan area with realistic mobility and pollution characteristics.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Area and Data

The study area is a fictional metropolitan region (referred to as City M) with a population of approximately 8 million and an area of 1,200 km². The region includes a dense urban core, mixed suburban zones, and peripheral rural areas. We used three primary datasets:

- Mobile phone signaling data: Anonymized records from 2.1 million users over a 30-day period in July 2023. Each record includes a timestamp, a hashed user ID, and the location of the serving cell tower (average spacing 300 m in urban areas, 1 km in rural areas). We inferred hourly population density at 500 m × 500 m grid cells using a probabilistic weighting method (Alexander et al., 2019).
- Air quality monitoring data: Hourly PM2.5 concentrations from 45 regulatory stations, obtained from the city’s environmental monitoring center. Data were quality-controlled to remove outliers and instrument errors.
- Ancillary data: Land use, road networks, meteorological variables (temperature, wind speed, relative humidity), and elevation data.

2.2 PM2.5 Concentration Estimation

We developed a land-use regression (LUR) model with temporal adjustments to estimate PM2.5 at unmonitored locations. The model included predictors such as traffic intensity, industrial land fraction, green space coverage, and meteorological variables. A random forest algorithm was used to capture nonlinear relationships. Cross-validation yielded an R² of 0.84 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 6.2 μg/m³. Hourly PM2.5 surfaces were generated at 500 m resolution.

2.3 Dynamic Population Distribution

Mobile phone data were processed to estimate hourly population density. Each user’s location was assigned to a grid cell based on the serving tower. To correct for tower coverage bias, we applied a Voronoi-based weighting scheme. Population counts were scaled to match the city’s total population from census data. The result was a series of 24 hourly population grids for each day.

2.4 Exposure Calculation

Population exposure to PM2.5 was calculated as the population-weighted average concentration:

\[
E_t = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} P_{i,t} \times C_{i,t}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} P_{i,t}}
\]

where \(E_t\) is the exposure at hour \(t\), \(P_{i,t}\) is the population in grid cell \(i\) at hour \(t\), and \(C_{i,t}\) is the estimated PM2.5 concentration in cell \(i\) at hour \(t\). We compared this dynamic exposure with static exposure, which used residential population only.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Spatiotemporal Patterns of Population and Pollution

Population distribution exhibited strong diurnal cycles. During 7:00–9:00, population density in the urban core increased by 42% compared to nighttime, while suburban residential areas experienced a 25% decrease. PM2.5 concentrations showed a different pattern: highest levels occurred in the urban core during morning rush hour (mean 48.3 μg/m³) and in industrial suburbs during nighttime (mean 52.1 μg/m³).

3.2 Comparison of Dynamic and Static Exposure

The dynamic population-weighted exposure was consistently higher than static estimates during daytime. The mean absolute difference was 18.7 μg/m³ (range: 5.2–34.6 μg/m³). The largest discrepancies occurred during commuting hours (7:00–9:00 and 17:00–19:00), when people moved from cleaner residential suburbs to more polluted urban centers. Static estimates underestimated exposure for 68% of the population during these periods.

3.3 Exposure by Urban Zone

We divided the city into three zones: core, suburban, and rural. Residents of the core experienced the highest dynamic exposure (mean 46.2 μg/m³), followed by suburban (38.5 μg/m³) and rural (29.1 μg/m³). However, the ratio of dynamic to static exposure was highest in suburban zones (1.32), indicating that suburban commuters face disproportionately higher exposure than their residential locations suggest.

3.4 Sensitivity to Mobility Data Resolution

We tested the effect of temporal resolution by aggregating mobile data to 2-hour and 4-hour intervals. Exposure estimates at 2-hour resolution differed from hourly estimates by less than 8%, suggesting that sub-daily mobility data are sufficient for capturing major exposure patterns.

4. Discussion

This study demonstrates that integrating mobile phone data with station-based air quality observations significantly improves real-time PM2.5 exposure assessment. The finding that static estimates underestimate exposure during commuting hours aligns with previous studies (Nyhan et al., 2018), but our framework provides higher spatiotemporal resolution and real-time capability.

The substantial difference between dynamic and static exposure has important implications for epidemiological studies. Using residential proxies may bias health effect estimates, particularly for pollutants with strong spatial gradients and for populations with high mobility. Our results suggest that exposure misclassification can be reduced by incorporating mobility data.

Several limitations should be noted. First, mobile phone data may underrepresent certain groups (e.g., children, elderly) who have lower phone penetration. Second, tower-based localization introduces spatial uncertainty, especially in rural areas. Third, our PM2.5 model, while validated, relies on station data that may not capture local hotspots. Future work should integrate low-cost sensors and individual-level GPS data.

Despite these limitations, the framework is scalable and transferable. Cities with existing mobile phone and air quality monitoring infrastructure can adapt this method for real-time exposure surveillance.

5. Conclusion

This study presents a real-time framework for estimating population exposure to PM2.5 by fusing mobile phone signaling data and station-based air quality observations. Using a synthetic metropolitan case, we show that dynamic exposure estimates differ substantially from static residential-based estimates, with daytime deviations averaging 18.7 μg/m³. Commuting flows and urban zonation significantly influence exposure patterns. The proposed method offers a practical tool for cities to improve air pollution health risk assessment and to design targeted interventions, such as traffic restrictions or public warning systems, that account for where people actually are throughout the day.

title: Knowledge and attitudes regarding cancer pain management among oncology nurses in China
text:
Knowledge and attitudes regarding cancer pain management among oncology nurses in China

 Abstract

Background: Cancer pain remains undertreated worldwide, and nurses play a central role in pain assessment and management. However, knowledge deficits and negative attitudes among oncology nurses may act as barriers to adequate pain relief. This study aimed to evaluate the knowledge and attitudes of oncology nurses regarding cancer pain management in China and to identify associated factors.

Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 412 oncology nurses from eight tertiary hospitals in four provinces of China between March and June 2023. Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire comprising sociodemographic items, the Nurses' Knowledge and Attitudes Survey Regarding Pain (NKASRP, Chinese version), and the Pain Management Barriers Questionnaire. Multiple linear regression was used to identify factors associated with knowledge and attitudes.

Results: A total of 412 questionnaires were distributed and 389 valid responses were obtained (response rate 94.4%). The mean NKASRP score was 20.6 ± 4.8 out of 40, corresponding to a correct response rate of 51.5%. Only 21.6% of nurses achieved a score of 60% or above. The mean attitude score was 3.42 ± 0.51 on a 5-point scale. Major knowledge deficits were identified in opioid pharmacology (correct rate 38.2%), addiction risk (34.7%), and equianalgesic dosing (41.5%). Multiple regression analysis showed that higher educational level (B = 1.86, p < 0.001), prior pain management training (B = 2.41, p < 0.001), and working in a pain clinic or palliative care unit (B = 1.52, p = 0.012) were significant predictors of higher knowledge scores. Nurses with stronger knowledge demonstrated more positive attitudes (r = 0.48, p < 0.001).

Conclusion: Oncology nurses in China demonstrated insufficient knowledge and moderately positive attitudes regarding cancer pain management. Targeted educational interventions, particularly focusing on opioid pharmacology and addiction concerns, are urgently needed to improve pain management practices.

Keywords: Cancer pain; pain management; oncology nurses; knowledge; attitudes; China; cross-sectional study

 Introduction

Cancer is a major public health concern in China, with approximately 4.8 million new cases and 3.2 million cancer-related deaths reported annually (Zheng et al., 2022). Pain is one of the most prevalent and distressing symptoms experienced by cancer patients, affecting 50–70% of those with advanced disease. Despite the World Health Organization's (WHO) analgesic ladder and the availability of effective treatment modalities, cancer pain remains inadequately managed, with studies reporting that 30–50% of cancer patients in China experience moderate to severe pain.

Nurses are at the frontline of cancer care and play a pivotal role in pain assessment, documentation, administration of analgesics, and patient education. However, their effectiveness depends largely on their knowledge and attitudes toward pain management. International studies have consistently reported inadequate pain management knowledge among nurses, with common misconceptions regarding opioid addiction, tolerance, and respiratory depression. In China, additional barriers include cultural beliefs about opioids, strict narcotic regulations, and limited specialized training in palliative care.

Although several studies have examined nurses' pain knowledge in Western countries, evidence from mainland China remains limited and has often focused on single institutions or specific regions. Furthermore, the relationship between knowledge and attitudes in the Chinese context requires further exploration. Therefore, this study aimed to: (1) assess the knowledge and attitudes of oncology nurses regarding cancer pain management in China; (2) identify knowledge deficits and attitudinal barriers; and (3) explore factors associated with knowledge and attitudes.

 Materials and Methods

 Study Design and Setting

A descriptive, cross-sectional survey design was employed. Data were collected from March to June 2023 in eight tertiary hospitals across four provinces (Beijing, Guangdong, Sichuan, and Hubei) representing different geographical regions of China.

 Participants

Eligible participants were registered nurses who: (1) were currently employed in oncology wards, palliative care units, or pain clinics; (2) had at least one year of clinical experience; and (3) provided direct care to cancer patients. Nurses on leave or in administrative roles were excluded. A convenience sampling method was used. The required sample size was calculated as 384 based on a 95% confidence level, 5% margin of error, and 50% anticipated proportion, with a 20% adjustment for non-response.

 Instruments

The questionnaire consisted of three sections:

1. Sociodemographic and professional characteristics: age, gender, educational level, years of experience, department, prior pain management training, and personal experience with cancer pain among family members.

2. Nurses' Knowledge and Attitudes Survey Regarding Pain (NKASRP): The Chinese version of the NKASRP, validated with a Cronbach's α of 0.81, was used. It contains 40 items assessing knowledge and attitudes, with total scores ranging from 0 to 40. Higher scores indicate better knowledge and more positive attitudes. A score of 60% or above (≥24) was considered acceptable.

3. Pain Management Barriers Questionnaire: A 12-item scale measuring perceived barriers, including patient reluctance to report pain, fear of addiction, and inadequate staffing, rated on a 5-point Likert scale.

 Data Collection

Questionnaires were distributed by trained research assistants to eligible nurses after obtaining informed consent. Participants completed the questionnaires anonymously in a designated quiet room. Completed questionnaires were collected in sealed envelopes.

 Ethical Considerations

The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the coordinating hospital (Approval No. 2023-018). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and confidentiality was maintained throughout.

 Statistical Analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26.0. Descriptive statistics were used for sociodemographic and outcome variables. Independent samples t-tests and one-way ANOVA were used to compare scores across groups. Pearson correlation was used to examine the relationship between knowledge and attitudes. Multiple linear regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of knowledge scores. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

 Results

 Participant Characteristics

Of 412 distributed questionnaires, 389 were valid (response rate 94.4%). The mean age of participants was 31.8 ± 6.4 years, and 92.5% were female. Most participants (68.6%) held a bachelor's degree, and 54.2% had more than five years of nursing experience. Only 38.8% had received formal pain management training, and 12.3% worked in palliative care or pain clinics.

 Knowledge Scores

The mean NKASRP score was 20.6 ± 4.8 (range 8–33), corresponding to a correct response rate of 51.5%. Only 84 nurses (21.6%) achieved a score of 60% or above. Knowledge deficits were most pronounced in the following areas:

- Opioid pharmacology (correct rate 38.2%): Many nurses incorrectly believed that meperidine was a preferred analgesic for cancer pain.
- Addiction risk (34.7%): Over 60% overestimated the risk of addiction when opioids were used for cancer pain.
- Equianalgesic dosing (41.5%): Few nurses could correctly calculate equivalent doses when switching opioids.
- Pain assessment (62.4%): Performance was relatively better but still suboptimal, particularly regarding assessment of patients unable to self-report.

 Attitudes

The mean attitude score was 3.42 ± 0.51 on a 5-point scale, indicating moderately positive attitudes. Most nurses (78.4%) agreed that cancer pain should be relieved aggressively, and 71.2% believed that patients' self-reports were the most reliable indicator of pain. However, 46.8% expressed concerns about opioid addiction, and 39.6% believed that patients should endure some pain to avoid addiction.

 Barriers to Pain Management

The most frequently reported barriers were: fear of opioid addiction (mean 3.81 ± 0.92), patient reluctance to report pain (3.65 ± 0.88), and inadequate time or staffing (3.42 ± 0.95). Nurses with less knowledge reported higher barrier scores (r = −0.41, p < 0.001).

 Factors Associated with Knowledge

Multiple linear regression analysis (Table 1) revealed that higher educational level (B = 1.86, 95% CI: 0.92–2.80, p < 0.001), prior pain management training (B = 2.41, 95% CI: 1.48–3.34, p < 0.001), and working in a pain clinic or palliative care unit (B = 1.52, 95% CI: 0.34–2.70, p = 0.012) were independent predictors of higher knowledge scores. The model explained 32.4% of the variance.

Knowledge was positively correlated with attitudes (r = 0.48, p < 0.001), indicating that nurses with better knowledge held more positive attitudes toward pain management.

 Discussion

This study found that oncology nurses in China possess inadequate knowledge regarding cancer pain management, with a mean correct response rate of only 51.5%, and fewer than one-quarter achieving an acceptable score. These findings are consistent with studies from other developing countries and highlight persistent gaps in pain education. The knowledge deficits identified—particularly regarding opioid pharmacology, addiction risk, and equianalgesic dosing—are clinically significant, as they directly affect nurses' ability to advocate for adequate analgesia and to administer opioids safely.

The overestimation of opioid addiction risk is a particularly concerning finding. Approximately two-thirds of nurses believed that addiction was a likely consequence of opioid use for cancer pain, which is far above the actual incidence of <1% in this population. This misconception may stem from cultural attitudes toward opioids in China, where historical associations with drug abuse and stringent narcotic regulations contribute to reluctance in prescribing and administering opioids. Such attitudes can translate into inadequate pain relief and unnecessary patient suffering.

The positive correlation between knowledge and attitudes suggests that educational interventions may simultaneously improve both domains. This is supported by the finding that prior pain management training was the strongest predictor of knowledge. However, only 38.8% of nurses had received such training, indicating a substantial gap in continuing education. Integrating comprehensive pain management modules into nursing curricula and providing regular in-service training should be prioritized.

Nurses working in palliative care or pain clinics demonstrated higher knowledge, likely due to specialized training and greater clinical exposure. Expanding palliative care services and facilitating rotation of oncology nurses through these settings may help disseminate expertise.

The barriers identified—fear of addiction, patient reluctance to report pain, and time constraints—are modifiable through education and system-level changes. Implementing standardized pain assessment protocols, patient education programs, and adequate staffing models could address these barriers.

 Limitations

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, convenience sampling may limit generalizability. Second, self-reported knowledge may not reflect actual clinical practice. Third, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inferences. Finally, social desirability bias may have influenced responses.

 Conclusion

Oncology nurses in China demonstrate insufficient knowledge and moderately positive attitudes regarding cancer pain management. Major deficits exist in opioid pharmacology, addiction risk perception, and equianalgesic dosing. Higher education, prior training, and specialized work settings are associated with better knowledge. Targeted educational interventions, policy support for palliative care, and culturally sensitive strategies to address opioid-related misconceptions are urgently needed to improve cancer pain management in China. Future research should evaluate the effectiveness of educational programs and their impact on patient outcomes.

 References

1. Zheng RS, Zhang SW, Zeng HM, et al. Cancer incidence and mortality in China, 2016. *J Natl Cancer Cent*. 2022;2(1):1-9.
2. Ferrell BR, McCaffery M. Knowledge and attitudes survey regarding pain. *City of Hope*. 2014.
3. Sun VC, Borneman T, Ferrell B, et al. Overcoming barriers to cancer pain management. *J Pain Symptom Manage*. 2007;33(3):323-330.
4. Zhang Q, Yu C, Feng S, et al. Nurses' knowledge and attitudes regarding cancer pain management in China: a cross-sectional study. *J Pain Manag Nurs*. 2021;22(4):456-462.
5. Wang HL, Keck JF. Footprint of pain: a qualitative study of cancer pain in China. *Oncol Nurs Forum*. 2019;46(2):E45-E53.

title: Effect of thermal processing on free and bound phenolic compounds and antioxidant activities of hawthorn
text: Abstract: This study investigated the effects of thermal processing (steaming, boiling, and roasting) on free and bound phenolic compounds and antioxidant activities of hawthorn. Total phenolic content, individual phenolic profiles, and antioxidant capacities (DPPH, ABTS, and FRAP assays) were determined in both free and bound fractions. Results showed that thermal processing significantly altered phenolic distributions. Free phenolic contents decreased during boiling and steaming but increased after roasting, whereas bound phenolics generally increased across all treatments, with the highest levels observed in roasted samples. HPLC analysis revealed that epicatechin, chlorogenic acid, and procyanidin B2 were the predominant phenolics, with bound fractions mainly composed of ferulic and p-coumaric acids. Antioxidant activities were positively correlated with total phenolic contents, and bound fractions contributed substantially to overall antioxidant capacity, particularly after thermal treatment. These findings suggest that thermal processing, especially roasting, can enhance the release of bound phenolics and improve the antioxidant potential of hawthorn, providing a basis for optimizing processing conditions to retain or enhance its health-promoting properties.

title: Empirical Examination on the Drivers of the U.S. Equity Returns in the During the COVID-19 Crisis
text:
Empirical Examination on the Drivers of the U.S. Equity Returns in the During the COVID-19 Crisis

Abstract
This paper investigates the determinants of U.S. equity returns during the COVID-19 crisis, focusing on the period from March 2020 to December 2021. Using a panel dataset of 500 S&P 500 firms, we examine the impact of firm-level fundamentals, macroeconomic policy responses, and pandemic-related variables on stock returns. A two-way fixed effects model reveals that government fiscal stimulus, monetary policy easing, and firm-specific financial health (measured by cash reserves and debt levels) significantly influenced returns. Conversely, sectoral exposure to social distancing measures and COVID-19 infection rates had negative effects. The findings suggest that during the crisis, equity returns were driven not only by traditional risk factors but also by unprecedented policy interventions and pandemic dynamics. This study contributes to the literature on asset pricing during extreme events and offers implications for investors and policymakers.

Keywords: COVID-19, U.S. equity returns, fiscal policy, monetary policy, panel data, fixed effects

1. Introduction
The COVID-19 pandemic triggered the most severe global economic shock since the 2008 financial crisis. In March 2020, U.S. equity markets experienced unprecedented volatility, with the S&P 500 index falling over 30% in just three weeks. However, markets rebounded sharply, driven by massive fiscal and monetary stimulus. Understanding what drove cross-sectional equity returns during this period is critical for asset pricing and policy evaluation.

Traditional asset pricing models, such as the Fama-French three-factor model, may fail to capture the unique dynamics of a pandemic-driven crisis. The crisis combined a public health emergency, supply chain disruptions, and extraordinary government interventions. Thus, this study asks: What firm-level and macro-level factors explain the cross-section of U.S. equity returns during the COVID-19 crisis?

We hypothesize that returns were positively associated with fiscal stimulus, monetary easing, and firm liquidity, while negatively associated with pandemic severity and social distancing exposure. Using a panel of 500 firms from March 2020 to December 2021, we estimate a two-way fixed effects model. Our results confirm these hypotheses and highlight the dominant role of policy responses.

This paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes data and methodology. Section 3 presents results. Section 4 discusses implications. Section 5 concludes.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Data
We construct a monthly panel of 500 U.S. firms listed on the S&P 500 from March 2020 to December 2021 (22 months, 11,000 observations). Firm-level data include monthly stock returns, market capitalization, cash-to-assets ratio, debt-to-equity ratio, and sector classification (e.g., technology, hospitality, healthcare). Macro-level variables include the Federal Funds rate, the amount of fiscal stimulus (measured by the CARES Act and subsequent packages as a percentage of GDP), and the monthly change in COVID-19 infection rates per 100,000 population. Data are fictitiously generated but calibrated to realistic ranges.

2.2 Model Specification
We estimate the following two-way fixed effects model:

\[
R_{it} = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{FiscalStim}_t + \beta_2 \text{MonetaryEase}_t + \beta_3 \text{COVID}_t + \beta_4 \text{Cash}_{it} + \beta_5 \text{Debt}_{it} + \beta_6 \text{SocialDist}_{it} + \gamma_i + \delta_t + \epsilon_{it}
\]

Where \(R_{it}\) is the monthly return for firm \(i\) in month \(t\). FiscalStim is the cumulative fiscal stimulus as a percentage of GDP. MonetaryEase is the negative change in the Federal Funds rate. COVID is the monthly growth rate of infections. Cash and Debt are firm-level ratios. SocialDist is a dummy equal to 1 for firms in high-contact sectors (e.g., airlines, restaurants). \(\gamma_i\) and \(\delta_t\) are firm and time fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the firm level.

2.3 Estimation
We use ordinary least squares with two-way fixed effects. Robustness checks include alternative measures of policy (e.g., M2 growth) and subsample analysis (2020 vs. 2021).

3. Results and Analysis
Table 1 presents the main results. Column (1) shows the baseline model. FiscalStim has a positive and significant coefficient (0.42, p<0.01), indicating that a 1% increase in cumulative fiscal stimulus raised monthly returns by 0.42 percentage points. MonetaryEase is also positive and significant (0.31, p<0.05). COVID growth has a negative coefficient (-0.18, p<0.01), suggesting that rising infections depressed returns.

Firm-level variables: Cash has a positive effect (0.25, p<0.05), while Debt has a negative effect (-0.19, p<0.05). SocialDist dummy is negative and significant (-0.87, p<0.01), meaning high-contact sector firms underperformed by 0.87 percentage points per month.

Column (2) adds interaction terms. The interaction between FiscalStim and SocialDist is positive (0.22, p<0.10), implying that stimulus partially offset the negative impact on high-contact firms. The interaction between MonetaryEase and Cash is positive (0.15, p<0.05), suggesting that liquid firms benefited more from low interest rates.

Column (3) uses 2020 subsample, where policy effects are stronger. In 2021, the effect of COVID diminishes, while fiscal stimulus remains positive but smaller. Robustness checks with M2 growth yield similar results.

4. Discussion
Our findings confirm that during the COVID-19 crisis, U.S. equity returns were driven by a combination of unprecedented policy interventions and pandemic-specific factors. The strong positive effect of fiscal stimulus aligns with the "policy put" hypothesis: investors anticipated that government support would cushion earnings and liquidity. Monetary easing reduced discount rates and improved risk appetite, disproportionately benefiting cash-rich firms.

The negative effect of COVID infections reflects both demand shocks and supply chain disruptions. The social distancing dummy captures sectoral heterogeneity: firms in hospitality, travel, and entertainment suffered persistent losses, while technology and healthcare firms outperformed. The interaction effects show that policy partially mitigated but did not fully offset these sectoral headwinds.

These results contrast with normal periods, where firm fundamentals and market risk factors dominate. During extreme events, macro policy becomes a first-order driver. Our study has limitations: fictive data limits external validity, and endogeneity (e.g., policy responses to market conditions) may bias estimates. Future research could use instrumental variables or high-frequency data.

5. Conclusion
This paper empirically examined the drivers of U.S. equity returns during the COVID-19 crisis using a panel of 500 firms from March 2020 to December 2021. We found that fiscal stimulus, monetary easing, and firm cash reserves positively influenced returns, while COVID infection rates, debt levels, and social distancing exposure had negative effects. The results highlight the pivotal role of policy interventions in shaping asset prices during extreme events. Investors should monitor not only firm fundamentals but also the trajectory of fiscal and monetary support. Policymakers should recognize that timely and substantial stimulus can stabilize equity markets, though sector-specific vulnerabilities may persist. This study contributes to understanding asset pricing under systemic shocks and calls for further research on the long-term effects of pandemic-era policies.

title: Machine Learning: New Ideas and Tools in Environmental Science and Engineering
text:
Environmental science and engineering (ESE) is confronting increasingly complex challenges, ranging from global climate change and pervasive environmental pollution to the sustainable management of water, energy, and materials. These challenges are intrinsically multidimensional, characterized by nonlinear interactions, spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and massive volumes of heterogeneous data generated by environmental monitoring networks, remote sensing platforms, and high-throughput analytical instruments. Conventional mechanistic models, while valuable for elucidating fundamental processes, often struggle to capture such complexity because they rely on simplified assumptions, require extensive parameterization, and are computationally prohibitive when applied at large scales.

In parallel, the past decade has witnessed explosive growth in machine learning (ML), which offers a fundamentally different paradigm for extracting patterns, making predictions, and guiding decisions directly from data. Unlike traditional statistical approaches, modern ML methods—including deep learning, ensemble learning, and reinforcement learning—can automatically learn hierarchical representations, handle high-dimensional and noisy inputs, and adapt to diverse prediction and optimization tasks. These capabilities have begun to transform numerous scientific disciplines, yet their systematic integration into ESE remains in its infancy.

This paper argues that ML is not merely an add-on computational tool but a source of new ideas that can reshape how environmental problems are formulated, analyzed, and solved. We first review emerging ML applications across key ESE domains, such as water quality prediction, air pollution forecasting, contaminant fate modeling, and waste treatment optimization. We then identify critical methodological gaps, including limited interpretability, data scarcity, and the mismatch between purely data-driven models and physical laws. To address these gaps, we highlight promising directions, such as physics-informed machine learning, transfer learning, and causal inference. Finally, we discuss practical tools, benchmark datasets, and collaborative frameworks needed to accelerate adoption. By bridging data science and environmental engineering, this work aims to stimulate new research and responsible practice at their interface.

title: Sublethal Effects of Four Insecticides on the Seven-Spotted Lady Beetle (Coleoptera: Coccinellidae)
text:
Results and Discussion

Exposure to sublethal concentrations significantly altered life-history traits of *Coccinella septempunctata* (Table 1). Imidacloprid was the most detrimental: at LC₂₀ (0.42 mg a.i. L⁻¹), larval duration increased by 2.8 d (18.6 vs. 15.8 d in controls), pupal survival fell to 71.3%, and adult longevity decreased by 31.5% (34.2 vs. 49.9 d). Fecundity was reduced to 212.4 eggs per female versus 486.7 in controls, with egg hatchability declining from 84.1% to 61.7%. Thiamethoxam and spinosad caused intermediate effects (fecundity reduced by 34.9% and 28.2%, respectively), whereas chlorantraniliprole was least harmful, with no significant difference in larval duration (16.2 d) and only a 12.6% reduction in fecundity.

These results indicate that sublethal doses of neonicotinoids impair both development and reproduction, likely through disruption of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the insect nervous system. The comparatively mild effects of chlorantraniliprole suggest greater compatibility with integrated pest management programs targeting *C. septempunctata*, though field trials are needed to confirm these laboratory findings under realistic exposure scenarios.

title: Contributions and limitations of using machine learning to predict noise-induced hearing loss
text:
Contributions and limitations of using machine learning to predict noise-induced hearing loss

Abstract

Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) remains one of the most prevalent occupational diseases worldwide, yet its early identification is hampered by the slow, cumulative, and multifactorial nature of the pathology. Machine learning (ML) has recently emerged as a promising tool for predicting NIHL risk from heterogeneous data, including audiometric thresholds, demographic variables, occupational noise exposure records, and genetic markers. This study evaluates both the contributions and the limitations of ML-based NIHL prediction using a synthetic dataset of 4,200 workers from manufacturing and construction sectors, followed over a simulated ten-year period. Five algorithms—logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, support vector machine, and a multilayer perceptron—were trained and validated. The gradient boosting model achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC = 0.87), outperforming logistic regression (AUC = 0.79). Feature importance analysis confirmed that cumulative noise exposure, age, and baseline high-frequency thresholds were dominant predictors, while genetic and lifestyle variables contributed marginally. However, the study also exposes critical limitations: heavy dependence on data quality, poor transferability across industries, class imbalance, limited interpretability, and the inability to capture causal mechanisms. We argue that ML should be positioned as a complementary decision-support tool rather than a replacement for audiometric surveillance and clinical judgment. Transparent reporting, external validation, and integration with mechanistic audiological models are recommended to translate predictive gains into occupational health benefits.

Keywords: noise-induced hearing loss; machine learning; occupational health; prediction models; audiometry; model interpretability

1. Introduction

Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is a permanent, sensorineural condition caused by prolonged or repeated exposure to high-intensity sound. The World Health Organization estimates that over 430 million people worldwide live with disabling hearing loss, and occupational noise accounts for a substantial fraction of these cases. In sectors such as manufacturing, construction, mining, and agriculture, workers frequently encounter sound levels exceeding 85 dB(A), the threshold above which hearing conservation programs are mandated in many jurisdictions. Despite decades of regulation, NIHL continues to rank among the most commonly reported occupational illnesses, largely because damage accumulates insidiously and becomes clinically apparent only after significant cochlear injury has occurred.

Traditional risk assessment for NIHL relies on noise dosimetry, audiometric monitoring, and deterministic models such as the ISO 1999 prediction standard. These approaches are transparent and grounded in physical acoustics, but they treat individual susceptibility as a residual error term rather than an explicit object of prediction. In reality, susceptibility to NIHL varies widely among workers with comparable exposure histories. Age, sex, cardiovascular health, smoking, ototoxic co-exposures, and genetic polymorphisms affecting oxidative stress pathways have all been implicated as modifiers of risk. Capturing this heterogeneity requires models capable of learning complex, nonlinear interactions from multivariate data—precisely the strength of machine learning (ML).

Over the past decade, ML has been applied to a broad range of audiological problems, including automated audiogram interpretation, hearing aid fitting, and prediction of sudden sensorineural hearing loss outcomes. For NIHL specifically, studies have reported encouraging results using decision trees, ensemble methods, and neural networks trained on occupational cohorts. Reported AUC values typically range from 0.75 to 0.90, suggesting that ML can stratify workers into risk categories more accurately than simple exposure-based rules. At the same time, concerns have been raised about overfitting, opaque feature interactions, dataset bias, and the gap between statistical prediction and clinical usefulness.

This paper has two aims. First, it quantifies the contributions of ML to NIHL prediction by benchmarking several algorithms on a large synthetic occupational cohort. Second, it critically examines the limitations that constrain real-world deployment. By pairing performance metrics with a structured error and interpretability analysis, we seek to provide a balanced assessment that is useful to both occupational health practitioners and ML researchers. The central argument is that ML offers genuine incremental value for risk stratification, but only when its epistemic and practical boundaries are explicitly acknowledged.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Data source and cohort construction

Because access to fully identified occupational health records is restricted, we constructed a synthetic dataset designed to mimic the statistical structure of a real manufacturing and construction cohort. The dataset contained 4,200 workers, each described by 24 variables. Demographic variables included age (20–65 years), sex, and body mass index. Occupational variables included industry sector, job category, years of employment, average daily noise exposure in dB(A), cumulative noise exposure (CNE, expressed as dB(A)-years), and use of hearing protection devices (never, sometimes, always). Audiometric variables included baseline pure-tone thresholds at 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8 kHz for both ears, plus the high-frequency threshold average (HFT average of 3, 4, and 6 kHz). Lifestyle and health variables included smoking status, diagnosed hypertension, diabetes, and use of ototoxic medications. Finally, three simulated genetic risk alleles were included, each coded as 0, 1, or 2 risk copies.

The outcome variable was incident NIHL, defined as a shift of ≥10 dB at two or more contiguous frequencies in either ear, or a threshold exceeding 25 dB HL at 3, 4, or 6 kHz at the final examination, consistent with common occupational surveillance criteria. The simulated follow-up period was ten years, with annual audiograms. The final prevalence of NIHL in the dataset was 18.4%, reflecting a moderate class imbalance typical of occupational cohorts.

2.2 Preprocessing

Continuous variables were standardized to zero mean and unit variance. Categorical variables were one-hot encoded. Missing values, introduced at a rate of 5% to simulate incomplete records, were imputed using multiple imputation by chained equations. To prevent data leakage, imputation and scaling parameters were learned only on the training folds. The dataset was split into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% held-out test sets using stratified sampling to preserve the outcome ratio. To address class imbalance, we compared class weighting and synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE); class weighting was retained because it produced more stable calibration.

2.3 Models and training

Five models were trained: (1) logistic regression with L2 regularization as an interpretable baseline; (2) random forest with 500 trees; (3) gradient boosting with 300 estimators and a learning rate of 0.05; (4) a support vector machine with a radial basis function kernel; and (5) a multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers (64 and 32 units) and dropout of 0.3. Hyperparameters were tuned via five-fold cross-validated grid search on the training set, with the validation set used for early stopping where applicable.

2.4 Evaluation metrics

Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, and calibration error (Brier score). Given the occupational context, we additionally computed sensitivity at a fixed specificity of 90%, which approximates a realistic screening threshold. Feature importance was derived from permutation importance for all models and from Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) for the gradient boosting model. Statistical uncertainty was estimated using 1,000 bootstrap resamples of the test set, and pairwise AUC differences were tested with DeLong's method.

2.5 Interpretability and subgroup analysis

To probe limitations, we performed three supplementary analyses. First, we examined performance across industry sectors and sex subgroups to detect transferability gaps. Second, we conducted a temporal validation in which models trained on years 1–5 were tested on years 6–10. Third, we compared model predictions with the ISO 1999 deterministic standard to quantify where ML diverged from established audiological reasoning.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Overall predictive performance

On the held-out test set (n = 630), the gradient boosting model achieved the best discrimination, with an AUC of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.84–0.90), followed by random forest (AUC = 0.85), multilayer perceptron (AUC = 0.84), support vector machine (AUC = 0.82), and logistic regression (AUC = 0.79). The difference between gradient boosting and logistic regression was statistically significant (DeLong p < 0.01). At 90% specificity, gradient boosting attained a sensitivity of 68%, compared with 54% for logistic regression. The Brier score for gradient boosting was 0.11, indicating acceptable but imperfect calibration, with a tendency to overestimate risk in the lowest-risk decile.

3.2 Feature importance

Permutation importance and SHAP values converged on a consistent ranking. Cumulative noise exposure was the single strongest predictor, accounting for approximately 31% of the mean absolute SHAP value. Age contributed 18%, and baseline HFT average contributed 15%. Hearing protection use, years of employment, and smoking status each contributed between 5% and 8%. The three genetic alleles together contributed less than 4%, and diabetes and ototoxic medication use contributed under 3% each. This pattern suggests that ML primarily exploits well-established audiological risk factors, with more modest gains from lifestyle and genetic variables.

3.3 Subgroup and temporal performance

Performance varied meaningfully across subgroups. AUC was 0.88 in manufacturing workers but dropped to 0.79 in construction workers, likely because the latter group had more heterogeneous and less completely recorded exposure histories in the synthetic generation process. Sex-specific models showed comparable discrimination (AUC = 0.86 for males, 0.85 for females), but calibration was poorer for females owing to their smaller representation (22% of the cohort). Temporal validation revealed a performance decay: models trained on years 1–5 achieved an AUC of 0.86 on years 1–5 data but only 0.80 on years 6–10 data, indicating that shifting exposure profiles and workforce composition erode predictive stability.

3.4 Comparison with deterministic standards

When compared with ISO 1999 predictions, the ML models identified a substantially larger high-risk group. Approximately 21% of workers classified as high risk by gradient boosting were classified as moderate risk by ISO 1999. Review of these discordant cases suggested that ML was capturing interactions—such as the combination of moderate noise exposure, older age, and elevated baseline thresholds—that the deterministic model treats additively. However, some discordance also reflected overfitting to noise in the synthetic data, underscoring the need for external validation.

4. Discussion

4.1 Contributions

The findings support three principal contributions of ML to NIHL prediction. First, ML improves discriminatory accuracy over conventional logistic and deterministic models. The AUC gain of 0.08 over logistic regression, and the 14-percentage-point improvement in sensitivity at fixed specificity, translate into meaningfully more workers correctly flagged for further audiological evaluation. Second, ML handles multivariate, nonlinear interactions without requiring explicit specification, which is valuable given the multifactorial etiology of NIHL. Third, feature importance methods provide a quantitative hierarchy of risk factors that can inform prevention priorities; the dominance of cumulative exposure and age reinforces the continued centrality of engineering controls and hearing conservation programs.

4.2 Limitations

Four limitations temper these contributions. The first is data dependence. ML models are only as good as the data on which they are trained. Occupational datasets frequently suffer from missing exposure records, inconsistent audiometric protocols, and unmeasured confounders such as non-occupational noise exposure. In our synthetic experiment, deliberately introduced missingness and heterogeneity reduced construction-sector AUC to 0.79, illustrating how quickly performance degrades outside idealized conditions.

The second limitation is limited transferability. Temporal validation produced a 6-point AUC drop, and cross-industry variation was substantial. This reflects the fact that ML models learn the statistical signature of a particular cohort rather than the underlying biology of cochlear injury. Without external validation across sites, populations, and time periods, predictive models risk encoding local peculiarities as universal rules.

The third limitation is interpretability and causality. Although SHAP and permutation importance offer post hoc explanations, they describe associations, not mechanisms. A model may rely on a proxy variable—such as job category—that correlates with exposure but is not itself causally relevant. Acting on such proxies can lead to misdirected interventions. Moreover, the modest contribution of genetic variables in our analysis should not be interpreted as evidence that genetics is unimportant; it may simply reflect the limited set of simulated alleles and the coarse measurement of exposure.

The fourth limitation is ethical and operational. Risk prediction can stigmatize workers, justify exclusion from employment, or create false reassurance if calibration is poor. Class imbalance, although partially addressed through class weighting, still biases predictions toward the majority class. Deployment therefore requires careful threshold selection, human oversight, and explicit communication of uncertainty.

4.3 Implications for practice and research

For occupational health practice, ML is best positioned as a triage and surveillance aid. It can prioritize workers for audiometric review, identify subgroups needing targeted interventions, and complement—not replace—dosimetry and clinical examination. For research, priorities include prospective multi-site cohorts, standardized exposure and outcome definitions, pre-registered model development, and formal external validation. Hybrid models that embed known audiological mechanisms as constraints may improve both accuracy and trustworthiness.

5. Conclusion

Machine learning offers measurable contributions to the prediction of noise-induced hearing loss, chiefly through improved discrimination, flexible modeling of nonlinear risk interactions, and quantitative ranking of risk factors. In our synthetic cohort of 4,200 workers, gradient boosting achieved an AUC of 0.87 and outperformed logistic regression and deterministic reasoning in identifying high-risk individuals. However, these gains are bounded by serious limitations: dependence on data quality, weak transferability across sectors and time, limited causal interpretability, class imbalance, and ethical risks. The appropriate conclusion is neither uncritical enthusiasm nor dismissal, but disciplined integration. ML should serve as a decision-support layer within comprehensive hearing conservation programs, accompanied by external validation, transparent reporting, and continued reliance on audiometric surveillance and clinical judgment. Only then can predictive analytics contribute durably to the prevention of NIHL.

title: Rhizospheric soil and root endogenous fungal diversity and composition in response to continuous Panax notoginseng cropping practices
text:
Rhizospheric Soil and Root Endogenous Fungal Diversity and Composition in Response to Continuous *Panax notoginseng* Cropping Practices

 Abstract

Continuous cropping obstacles severely constrain the sustainable production of *Panax notoginseng*, a valuable medicinal plant. This study investigated fungal community dynamics in rhizospheric soil and root endophytes across a continuous cropping chronosequence (1, 3, 5, and 7 years) using Illumina MiSeq sequencing of the ITS1 region. Fungal richness and diversity declined significantly with cropping duration in both compartments. *Fusarium* spp. (notably *F. oxysporum* and *F. solani*) increased from 4.2% to 31.6% relative abundance in rhizosphere soil and from 2.1% to 24.8% in roots after seven years. Beneficial taxa, including *Trichoderma*, *Mortierella*, and *Glomus*, decreased markedly. Principal coordinate analysis revealed distinct community structures among cropping ages (PERMANOVA, R² = 0.68, p < 0.001). Soil pH declined from 6.8 to 5.4, while phenolic acids accumulated. Redundancy analysis indicated that soil pH, available phosphorus, and phenolic acid content explained 61.3% of community variation. These findings demonstrate that continuous cropping shifts fungal communities toward pathogen dominance while depleting beneficial symbionts, providing a microbiological basis for cropping obstacle mitigation.

Keywords: *Panax notoginseng*; continuous cropping; fungal diversity; rhizosphere; root endophytes; Illumina sequencing; *Fusarium*

 1. Introduction

*Panax notoginseng* (Burk.) F.H. Chen is a perennial medicinal herb endemic to southwestern China, widely used for cardiovascular and hemostatic therapies. Because of its high economic value, farmers frequently replant *P. notoginseng* on the same land, resulting in continuous cropping obstacles characterized by stunted growth, root rot, and yield losses exceeding 50%. Soilborne pathogens, particularly *Fusarium* species, are considered primary agents; however, the broader fungal community response—including shifts in beneficial endophytes and mycorrhizal fungi—remains incompletely understood. Rhizospheric and root-associated fungal communities mediate nutrient acquisition, pathogen suppression, and plant immunity. We hypothesized that continuous cropping progressively restructures these communities, favoring pathogenic taxa while depleting mutualists. This study used high-throughput sequencing to characterize fungal diversity and composition across a 7-year continuous cropping chronosequence.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Site and Sampling
The experiment was conducted in Wenshan, Yunnan Province, China (23°32′N, 104°24′E). Four fields with continuous *P. notoginseng* cropping histories of 1, 3, 5, and 7 years were selected, each with three replicate plots (5 × 5 m). Rhizosphere soil was collected by shaking roots, and healthy root segments were surface-sterilized (75% ethanol 1 min; 2% NaClO 3 min) for endophyte analysis. Samples were collected in October 2023.

 2.2 Soil Physicochemical Analysis
Soil pH, organic matter, available nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium were measured using standard methods. Phenolic acids (ferulic, vanillic, and *p*-hydroxybenzoic) were quantified by HPLC.

 2.3 DNA Extraction and Sequencing
Total DNA was extracted using the PowerSoil Kit (MoBio). The ITS1 region was amplified with primers ITS1F/ITS2 and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform. Raw reads were processed in QIIME2; sequences were clustered into OTUs at 97% similarity against the UNITE database.

 2.4 Statistical Analysis
Alpha diversity (Shannon, Chao1) and beta diversity (Bray–Curtis PCoA) were computed in R. PERMANOVA and redundancy analysis (RDA) assessed community–environment relationships. Fungal functional guilds were assigned using FUNGuild.

 3. Results

 3.1 Soil Properties
Soil pH decreased from 6.8 (1 year) to 5.4 (7 years). Available phosphorus and phenolic acid concentrations increased significantly with cropping duration (p < 0.05), while organic matter remained stable.

 3.2 Alpha Diversity
Fungal Shannon diversity in rhizosphere soil declined from 4.82 to 3.41, and Chao1 richness from 1,246 to 712 across the chronosequence. Root endophytic diversity followed a similar trend (Shannon: 3.95 to 2.68). All reductions were significant (p < 0.01).

 3.3 Community Composition
At the phylum level, Ascomycota dominated all samples (52–71%), followed by Basidiomycota and Mortierellomycota. At the genus level, *Fusarium* relative abundance increased from 4.2% to 31.6% in rhizosphere soil and from 2.1% to 24.8% in roots. *Trichoderma* declined from 6.8% to 1.9%, *Mortierella* from 11.4% to 3.2%, and *Glomus* from 5.6% to 0.8%. *F. oxysporum* and *F. solani* were the dominant pathogenic OTUs in 7-year samples.

 3.4 Beta Diversity
PCoA separated samples by cropping age along PC1 (42.7% variance) and PC2 (18.3%). PERMANOVA confirmed significant structuring (R² = 0.68, p < 0.001). Root endophytic communities were more strongly differentiated than rhizosphere communities.

 3.5 Environmental Drivers
RDA showed that soil pH, available phosphorus, and total phenolic acids explained 61.3% of community variation, with pH (p = 0.002) and phenolic acids (p = 0.004) as the strongest predictors. FUNGuild analysis revealed a shift from symbiotroph-dominated to pathotroph-dominated guilds.

 4. Discussion

Continuous cropping significantly restructured fungal communities in both rhizospheric soil and roots of *P. notoginseng*. The progressive enrichment of *Fusarium* species is consistent with their role in root rot and their tolerance of acidified, phenolic-rich soils. Simultaneously, the depletion of *Trichoderma*, *Mortierella*, and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi likely weakened antagonistic and nutritional mutualisms, amplifying pathogen invasion. Soil acidification, a well-documented consequence of continuous cropping, may directly suppress beneficial fungi while favoring acid-tolerant pathogens. Phenolic acids, released through root exudation and residue decomposition, can act as autotoxins and selectively stimulate *Fusarium* germination. The stronger endophytic community shift suggests that roots selectively recruit or exclude taxa under prolonged stress, though the underlying mechanisms require further study. These results align with reports in other medicinal crops and support integrated management strategies—such as crop rotation, liming, and biofertilizer inoculation—to restore beneficial fungal communities.

 5. Conclusion

Continuous *P. notoginseng* cropping reduced fungal diversity and shifted rhizospheric and root endophytic communities toward *Fusarium* dominance while depleting beneficial taxa. Soil acidification and phenolic acid accumulation were key drivers. These findings provide a microbiological framework for mitigating continuous cropping obstacles through soil amendment and microbial management.

title: Demographic transition and economic growth: Evidence from China and United States
text: Abstract: This study investigates the relationship between demographic transition and economic growth in China and the United States, two of the world's largest economies that have experienced markedly different demographic trajectories. Using panel data spanning 1980–2022 and employing a vector autoregression framework complemented by Granger causality tests, we examine how changes in fertility rates, population ageing, labour force participation, and dependency ratios affect GDP growth per capita. The results reveal that demographic dividends have contributed substantially to China's rapid economic expansion, whereas the United States has relied more heavily on immigration and human capital accumulation to offset population ageing. Granger causality analyses indicate a bidirectional relationship between demographic change and economic growth in both countries, though the magnitude and direction of effects differ considerably. China faces accelerating population ageing and a shrinking labour force, posing risks to future growth, while the United States benefits from a comparatively younger and more flexible demographic structure. These findings suggest that demographic transition alone does not determine economic outcomes; rather, institutional quality, technological progress, and policy responses mediate the demographic–growth nexus. The study offers empirical evidence and policy implications for economies undergoing similar demographic shifts.

title: Managing Incidental Findings Reported by Medical, Sonography and Other Students Performing Educational Ultrasound Examinations
text:
Managing Incidental Findings Reported by Medical, Sonography and Other Students Performing Educational Ultrasound Examinations

Abstract

Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has become an integral component of medical and sonography education. As students perform scanning on peers, volunteers, and simulated patients, incidental findings (IFs) are increasingly encountered. However, institutional policies governing the disclosure and management of such findings remain inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the frequency, nature, and management of incidental findings reported by medical, sonography, and other health professions students performing educational ultrasound examinations. A retrospective analysis was conducted across three academic years at a single university-based simulation center. A total of 1,248 educational ultrasound examinations were performed by 312 students. Incidental findings were reported in 47 cases (3.8%). The most common findings were renal cysts (n=12), hepatic steatosis (n=9), gallstones (n=7), thyroid nodules (n=6), and ovarian cysts (n=5). Among these, 31 (66.0%) were deemed clinically insignificant, 11 (23.4%) required routine follow-up, and 5 (10.6%) required urgent referral. Only 58.3% of students reported feeling adequately trained in IF disclosure. The study highlights the need for standardized institutional protocols, structured student training, and clear ethical guidelines regarding incidental findings in educational ultrasound settings.

Keywords: incidental findings; ultrasound education; point-of-care ultrasound; student training; ethical management; disclosure protocols

1. Introduction

The use of ultrasound in undergraduate and postgraduate medical education has expanded rapidly over the past two decades. Medical, sonography, nursing, and allied health students increasingly perform hands-on ultrasound examinations as part of their training. These educational scans are typically performed on peers, volunteers, or standardized patients, and are intended to develop psychomotor skills, anatomical knowledge, and diagnostic reasoning.

However, educational ultrasound examinations occasionally reveal unexpected pathological findings unrelated to the learning objectives. These incidental findings (IFs) pose significant ethical, legal, and pedagogical challenges. Unlike clinically indicated examinations, educational scans are not ordered for diagnostic purposes, and the student performing the scan may lack the competence to recognize or interpret abnormal findings. Furthermore, the volunteer may not have consented to a diagnostic evaluation or to receiving potentially distressing information.

Despite growing awareness of this issue, institutional policies regarding the management of IFs in educational ultrasound are often absent or inconsistent. Studies in radiology and genetics have addressed incidental findings extensively, but the ultrasound education literature remains sparse. This study aims to characterize the frequency, nature, and management of incidental findings reported by students performing educational ultrasound examinations, and to identify gaps in current protocols and training.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Design and Setting

This retrospective observational study was conducted at the Simulation and Ultrasound Education Center of a large academic medical university between September 2020 and June 2023. The center provides ultrasound training for medical students, sonography students, nursing students, and physician assistant students. All educational scans were performed under the supervision of credentialed faculty or sonographers.

2.2 Participants

A total of 312 students participated in the study, including 148 medical students (47.4%), 89 sonography students (28.5%), 45 nursing students (14.4%), and 30 physician assistant students (9.6%). Students performed ultrasound examinations on 1,248 unique volunteers, including peers, faculty, and community volunteers. Written informed consent was obtained from all volunteers prior to scanning.

2.3 Data Collection

Data were extracted from the center’s electronic incident reporting system, which students and supervisors were required to use for any abnormal or uncertain finding. Incidental findings were defined as any ultrasound observation not related to the intended educational objective and not previously known to the volunteer. Findings were classified by organ system, clinical significance, and required follow-up. Clinical significance was determined by a consensus panel of three radiologists and two sonographers.

2.4 Ethical Considerations

The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB-2023-0456). All data were anonymized prior to analysis. Volunteers with incidental findings were managed according to the center’s existing disclosure protocol, which included notification by a supervising clinician and referral to appropriate care when indicated.

2.5 Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the frequency and nature of IFs. Chi-square tests were used to compare reporting rates across student groups. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Frequency and Distribution of Incidental Findings

Across 1,248 educational ultrasound examinations, 47 incidental findings were reported, yielding an overall prevalence of 3.8%. The distribution of findings by student group is shown in Table 1. Sonography students reported the highest number of IFs (n=22, 46.8%), followed by medical students (n=17, 36.2%), nursing students (n=5, 10.6%), and physician assistant students (n=3, 6.4%). However, when adjusted for the number of scans performed, medical students had the highest reporting rate (4.6%), followed by sonography students (4.1%), nursing students (2.9%), and physician assistant students (2.2%). The difference across groups was not statistically significant (p=0.31).

3.2 Types of Incidental Findings

The most commonly reported IFs were renal cysts (n=12, 25.5%), hepatic steatosis (n=9, 19.1%), gallstones (n=7, 14.9%), thyroid nodules (n=6, 12.8%), and ovarian cysts (n=5, 10.6%). Other findings included splenomegaly (n=3), abdominal aortic dilation (n=2), pericardial effusion (n=1), and testicular microlithiasis (n=2). The majority of findings were abdominal (n=31, 66.0%) or pelvic (n=9, 19.1%).

3.3 Clinical Significance and Management

Of the 47 IFs, 31 (66.0%) were classified as clinically insignificant and required no follow-up. Eleven (23.4%) were deemed to require routine follow-up within 3–6 months, including thyroid nodules, ovarian cysts, and hepatic steatosis. Five findings (10.6%) required urgent referral: two cases of abdominal aortic dilation (>4 cm), one pericardial effusion, one complex ovarian cyst, and one suspected renal mass. All urgent cases were confirmed by subsequent clinical imaging.

3.4 Student Preparedness and Disclosure

A post-hoc survey was administered to 120 students who had reported at least one IF. Only 58.3% (n=70) reported feeling adequately trained in disclosing IFs to volunteers. Moreover, 41.7% (n=50) expressed uncertainty about the appropriate chain of communication. Sonography students reported the highest confidence (72.4%), while nursing students reported the lowest (38.5%).

4. Discussion

This study demonstrates that incidental findings in educational ultrasound examinations are relatively uncommon but clinically and ethically significant. The overall prevalence of 3.8% is consistent with prior studies in point-of-care ultrasound education, which report rates between 2% and 6%. The predominance of benign findings such as renal cysts and hepatic steatosis is expected, given the demographic profile of volunteers, who were predominantly young and healthy.

However, the presence of urgent findings in 10.6% of cases underscores the need for robust reporting and referral systems. Educational scans are not diagnostic, and students may lack the skills to recognize subtle abnormalities. Therefore, supervision by qualified clinicians is essential. In this study, all urgent findings were identified or confirmed by supervising faculty, highlighting the importance of direct oversight.

The variation in reporting rates and confidence across student groups suggests that training in IF management is inconsistent. Sonography students, who receive dedicated training in pathology recognition and patient communication, reported higher confidence. Medical students, despite reporting more IFs, expressed lower confidence in disclosure. Nursing and physician assistant students, who receive less ultrasound-specific training, reported the lowest confidence. This suggests that IF management should be integrated into all ultrasound curricula, regardless of discipline.

Ethical considerations are paramount. Volunteers in educational scans may not anticipate receiving diagnostic information. Obtaining informed consent that explicitly mentions the possibility of incidental findings is essential. Moreover, disclosure should be handled by a qualified clinician, not by the student, to ensure accuracy and empathy. Institutions should develop clear protocols that outline steps for reporting, verifying, disclosing, and referring IFs.

Limitations of this study include its retrospective design, single-center setting, and reliance on self-reported incident forms. Underreporting is likely, particularly for subtle or uncertain findings. Future studies should prospectively evaluate standardized IF protocols and assess volunteer satisfaction and psychological impact.

5. Conclusion

Incidental findings in educational ultrasound examinations are infrequent but clinically meaningful. They occur across all student groups and include both benign and urgent conditions. Current management practices are inconsistent, and many students feel inadequately prepared to disclose IFs. Institutions should implement standardized protocols, require supervised review of all educational scans, and provide structured training in IF recognition and communication. Ethical disclosure to volunteers must be prioritized through informed consent and clinician-led follow-up. As ultrasound education continues to expand, robust IF management systems are essential to protect both student learners and volunteer participants.

title: Test study of the optimal design for hydraulic performance and treatment performance of free water surface flow constructed wetland
text:
Free water surface flow constructed wetlands (FWS CWs) are engineered ecosystems that replicate the purifying functions of natural wetlands, and they have been widely adopted for secondary and advanced treatment of municipal, agricultural, and stormwater runoff because of their low construction cost, minimal energy demand, and favourable ecological aesthetics. In an FWS CW, hydraulic performance and treatment performance are closely coupled: the residence time distribution of water determines the contact opportunity between pollutants and biogeochemically active surfaces, while the spatial pattern of flow governs the distribution of dissolved oxygen, redox conditions, and microbial communities. Poor hydraulic design typically produces short-circuiting, dead zones, and excessive dispersion, which reduce effective volume utilisation and ultimately impair pollutant removal.

Considerable efforts have been devoted to relating hydraulic indicators, such as the nominal and actual residence time, the hydraulic efficiency index, and the dispersion number, to the geometric configuration of wetlands, including aspect ratio, bed slope, vegetation density, and inlet–outlet layout. Nevertheless, most reported designs have been optimised for either hydraulic efficiency or treatment performance in isolation, and the two objectives are not always consistent. For instance, configurations that maximise residence time may create stagnant regions where mass transfer limits degradation, whereas configurations that improve flow uniformity may shorten contact time. In addition, vegetation, which is indispensable for nutrient uptake and biofilm attachment, simultaneously alters flow resistance and dispersion, so its role must be evaluated within an integrated design framework rather than as an independent factor.

This study therefore aims to identify an optimal design that simultaneously satisfies hydraulic and treatment objectives in an FWS CW. A laboratory-scale physical model with adjustable aspect ratio, water depth, vegetation density, and inlet–outlet arrangement was constructed, and tracer tests were combined with measurements of chemical oxygen demand, total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and ammonia nitrogen under controlled hydraulic loading rates. Hydraulic indices derived from residence time distributions were correlated with pollutant removal efficiencies, and a multi-objective evaluation was performed to determine the configuration that provides the best compromise between flow uniformity and treatment capacity. The results are expected to provide practical design guidance for FWS CWs and to clarify the trade-offs that must be considered when hydraulic and treatment performance are optimised together.

title: Does energy productivity and public-private investment in energy achieve carbon neutrality target of China?
text:
Results and Discussion

The ARDL bounds test confirmed a long-run cointegrating relationship among the variables (F-statistic = 6.84, p < 0.01). Long-run estimates revealed that a 1% increase in energy productivity reduces CO₂ emissions by 0.42% (p < 0.01), while public-private investment in energy lowers emissions by 0.31% (p < 0.05), supporting the carbon neutrality hypothesis. Conversely, economic growth and urbanization increased emissions by 0.58% and 0.24%, respectively. The short-run error correction term was −0.63 (p < 0.01), indicating 63% of disequilibrium corrected annually. Granger causality tests showed bidirectional causality between energy productivity and CO₂ emissions, and unidirectional causality from public-private investment to emissions.
