These findings suggest that scaling energy productivity and private capital mobilization could cut China's emissions by an estimated 18.7% by 2035, underscoring their pivotal role in achieving the carbon neutrality target.

title: Heavy Metal Pollution in a Soil-Rice System in the Yangtze River Region of China
text:
Heavy Metal Pollution in a Soil-Rice System in the Yangtze River Region of China

Abstract

Heavy metal contamination in agricultural soils poses a serious threat to food security and human health. The Yangtze River region is one of China's most important rice-producing areas, yet it has experienced rapid industrialization and urbanization, leading to potential heavy metal accumulation in soil-rice systems. In this study, 120 paired soil and rice grain samples were collected from five representative rice-growing areas in the Yangtze River region. The concentrations of cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), chromium (Cr), arsenic (As), and copper (Cu) were determined using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). The results showed that the mean concentrations of Cd, Pb, Cr, As, and Cu in soils were 0.42, 38.6, 72.3, 12.5, and 35.8 mg kg⁻¹, respectively. Among these, Cd exceeded the national soil environmental quality standard (GB 15618–2018) in 28.3% of the samples. Rice grain concentrations of Cd, Pb, Cr, As, and Cu averaged 0.12, 0.08, 0.15, 0.09, and 3.21 mg kg⁻¹, respectively, with 15.8% of rice samples exceeding the maximum permissible limit for Cd (0.2 mg kg⁻¹). The transfer factors from soil to rice grain followed the order of Cd > Cu > As > Cr > Pb. Spatial distribution analysis revealed that the highest contamination levels occurred in areas with intensive industrial activities and long-term wastewater irrigation. Health risk assessment indicated that the target hazard quotient (THQ) for Cd through rice consumption exceeded 1.0 for children in contaminated areas, suggesting a potential non-carcinogenic risk. These findings highlight the urgent need for targeted remediation and sustainable agricultural practices in the Yangtze River region.

Keywords: heavy metals; soil-rice system; Yangtze River region; cadmium; health risk assessment; transfer factor

1. Introduction

Heavy metal pollution in agricultural ecosystems has become a global environmental concern due to its toxicity, persistence, and bioaccumulation potential (Alloway, 2013). In China, rapid industrialization and urbanization over the past four decades have resulted in the release of large quantities of heavy metals into the environment, particularly into agricultural soils (Zhao et al., 2015). The Yangtze River region, covering approximately 20% of China's land area and supporting over 40% of the national population, is a critical agricultural zone. It accounts for more than 50% of the country's rice production (NBSC, 2021). However, intensive industrial activities, mining, and the application of agrochemicals have led to elevated levels of heavy metals such as cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), chromium (Cr), arsenic (As), and copper (Cu) in the soil-rice system (Hu et al., 2020).

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is the staple food for more than half of the world's population, and its safety is directly linked to human health (Meharg et al., 2013). Heavy metals in paddy soils can be taken up by rice roots and translocated to grains, entering the food chain and posing risks to consumers (Williams et al., 2009). Among heavy metals, Cd is of particular concern because of its high mobility in soil-plant systems and its nephrotoxic and carcinogenic effects (Järup & Åkesson, 2009). The transfer factor (TF) of heavy metals from soil to rice grain is a key indicator for assessing the potential risk of contamination.

Previous studies have investigated heavy metal pollution in soils and rice in various regions of China (Chen et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019). However, comprehensive assessments of soil-rice systems in the Yangtze River region, particularly those integrating spatial distribution, transfer characteristics, and health risk assessment, remain limited. Therefore, this study aims to: (1) determine the concentrations of Cd, Pb, Cr, As, and Cu in paired soil and rice grain samples from the Yangtze River region; (2) evaluate the transfer factors of these metals from soil to rice grain; (3) assess the potential health risks associated with rice consumption; and (4) provide scientific basis for pollution control and agricultural management in the region.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Area and Sampling

The study was conducted in five representative rice-growing areas in the Yangtze River region: Area A (Jiangsu Province), Area B (Anhui Province), Area C (Hubei Province), Area D (Hunan Province), and Area E (Jiangxi Province). These areas were selected based on their industrial development levels and agricultural importance. A total of 120 paired soil and rice grain samples were collected during the rice harvest season in 2022. At each sampling site, surface soil (0–20 cm) was collected using a stainless steel auger, and corresponding rice grain samples were obtained from the same location. All samples were stored in polyethylene bags and transported to the laboratory for analysis.

2.2 Sample Preparation and Analysis

Soil samples were air-dried, ground, and passed through a 2-mm sieve. For heavy metal analysis, 0.5 g of soil was digested with a mixture of HNO₃-HClO₄-HF (5:1:1, v/v/v) at 180°C. Rice grain samples were oven-dried at 70°C, ground, and digested with HNO₃-H₂O₂ (3:1, v/v). The concentrations of Cd, Pb, Cr, As, and Cu were determined using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS, Agilent 7900, USA). Certified reference materials (GBW07401 for soil and GBW10010 for rice) were used for quality control. The recovery rates ranged from 92% to 106%.

2.3 Data Analysis

The transfer factor (TF) was calculated as the ratio of heavy metal concentration in rice grain to that in soil. The geo-accumulation index (Igeo) was used to assess soil contamination levels. Health risk assessment was conducted using the target hazard quotient (THQ) and hazard index (HI) according to USEPA guidelines. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 26.0, and spatial distribution maps were generated using ArcGIS 10.8.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Heavy Metal Concentrations in Soils

The mean concentrations of Cd, Pb, Cr, As, and Cu in soils were 0.42, 38.6, 72.3, 12.5, and 35.8 mg kg⁻¹, respectively (Table 1). The corresponding background values for the Yangtze River region are 0.15, 26.0, 65.0, 10.0, and 25.0 mg kg⁻¹. The mean Cd concentration was 2.8 times the background value, and 28.3% of soil samples exceeded the risk screening value of 0.3 mg kg⁻¹ (GB 15618–2018). Pb, Cr, As, and Cu concentrations were generally below the national standards, although localized hotspots were observed. The geo-accumulation index indicated that Cd was the primary contaminant, with Igeo values ranging from 0.5 to 2.1, classifying the soils as moderately to strongly contaminated in Areas A and D.

3.2 Heavy Metal Concentrations in Rice Grains

The mean concentrations of Cd, Pb, Cr, As, and Cu in rice grains were 0.12, 0.08, 0.15, 0.09, and 3.21 mg kg⁻¹, respectively (Table 2). The maximum permissible limit for Cd in rice (0.2 mg kg⁻¹) was exceeded in 15.8% of the samples, particularly in Areas A and D. Pb and As concentrations were below the national limits (0.2 mg kg⁻¹ for Pb and 0.2 mg kg⁻¹ for inorganic As). Cr and Cu concentrations were within safe limits. The spatial distribution of rice grain Cd showed a similar pattern to that of soil Cd, with the highest values in areas affected by industrial emissions and wastewater irrigation.

3.3 Transfer Factors from Soil to Rice Grain

The transfer factors of heavy metals from soil to rice grain followed the order: Cd (0.29) > Cu (0.09) > As (0.007) > Cr (0.002) > Pb (0.002). Cd exhibited the highest mobility, indicating its greater potential for accumulation in rice grains. The TF of Cd was significantly positively correlated with soil Cd concentration (r = 0.72, p < 0.01) and negatively correlated with soil pH (r = -0.45, p < 0.05). These results suggest that soil acidification may enhance Cd uptake by rice.

3.4 Health Risk Assessment

The THQ values for individual heavy metals through rice consumption were calculated for adults and children. For adults, the THQ values were all below 1.0, indicating no significant non-carcinogenic risk. However, for children, the THQ for Cd exceeded 1.0 in Areas A and D, with values of 1.32 and 1.18, respectively. The HI values for children in these areas were 1.56 and 1.41, suggesting a potential health risk from combined heavy metal exposure. The carcinogenic risk (CR) for Cd and As through rice consumption was within the acceptable range (1×10⁻⁶ to 1×10⁻⁴) for adults but slightly exceeded the threshold for children in contaminated areas.

4. Discussion

The results of this study demonstrate that the soil-rice system in the Yangtze River region is contaminated with heavy metals, particularly Cd. The elevated Cd levels in soils can be attributed to both geogenic and anthropogenic sources. The Yangtze River region is underlain by rocks with relatively high Cd background levels, and intensive industrial activities such as mining, smelting, and electroplating have further enriched Cd in agricultural soils (Zhao et al., 2015). Additionally, the long-term application of phosphate fertilizers and wastewater irrigation has contributed to Cd accumulation (Hu et al., 2020).

The high transfer factor of Cd from soil to rice grain is consistent with previous studies (Williams et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2018). Cd is readily taken up by rice roots through transporters for essential elements such as zinc and manganese (Uraguchi & Fujiwara, 2012). Soil pH plays a critical role in Cd bioavailability; acidic conditions increase Cd solubility and uptake. In this study, soil pH ranged from 5.2 to 6.8, with lower pH values observed in Areas A and D, which may explain the higher Cd accumulation in rice grains.

The health risk assessment revealed that children are more vulnerable to heavy metal exposure through rice consumption than adults. This is due to their lower body weight and higher metabolic rate, resulting in higher THQ values. The exceedance of THQ for Cd in children in contaminated areas highlights the need for immediate intervention. Previous studies have also reported elevated health risks associated with rice consumption in polluted regions of China (Yang et al., 2019).

To mitigate heavy metal pollution in the soil-rice system, several strategies can be implemented. First, source control is essential to reduce industrial emissions and wastewater discharge. Second, soil remediation techniques such as immobilization, phytoremediation, and electrokinetic remediation can be applied to contaminated soils. Third, agricultural practices such as liming, organic matter amendment, and water management can reduce Cd bioavailability and uptake by rice. Finally, regular monitoring and risk assessment should be conducted to ensure food safety.

5. Conclusion

This study investigated heavy metal pollution in the soil-rice system of the Yangtze River region. The results showed that Cd was the most concerning contaminant, with 28.3% of soil samples and 15.8% of rice grain samples exceeding national standards. The transfer factor of Cd from soil to rice grain was the highest among the studied metals, indicating its high mobility and accumulation potential. Health risk assessment revealed that children in contaminated areas face potential non-carcinogenic risks from Cd exposure through rice consumption. These findings underscore the urgent need for integrated pollution control and sustainable agricultural practices in the Yangtze River region. Future research should focus on long-term monitoring, source apportionment, and the development of cost-effective remediation technologies to ensure the safety of rice production and human health.

title: TCM-Blast for traditional Chinese medicine genome alignment with integrated resources
text:
TCM-Blast for traditional Chinese medicine genome alignment with integrated resources

 Abstract

Motivation: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) genomics research increasingly requires alignment of herb, pathogen, and human sequences against heterogeneous reference databases. Existing BLAST wrappers lack TCM-specific reference curation, batch annotation, and reproducible reporting.

Results: We present TCM-Blast, an integrated alignment platform combining a BLAST+ core with three curated TCM resources: TCMHerbDB (1,284 medicinal plant genomes, 3.9 Gb), TCMTargetDB (46,712 human genes with 8,905 TCM–target associations), and TCMCompoundDB (62,340 phytochemical records). TCM-Blast supports nucleotide/protein searches, batch processing, and automatic functional annotation. Benchmarking on 500 randomly selected *Salvia miltiorrhiza* transcripts achieved 98.4% alignment rate with a mean runtime of 42.7 s per 1,000 queries, 3.1-fold faster than a naïve sequential BLAST pipeline. In a case study of 120 *Danshen* unigenes, 87 (72.5%) were annotated to terpenoid biosynthesis pathways (FDR < 0.01), and 34 mapped to TCMTargetDB entries. TCM-Blast provides a reproducible, TCM-oriented alignment workflow for herb genomics and pharmacological target discovery.

Availability: Freely available for academic use at https://tcmblast.example.org.

Keywords: traditional Chinese medicine; genome alignment; BLAST; medicinal plant genomics; functional annotation; database integration

 1. Introduction

Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has been used for millennia, but its molecular basis remains incompletely characterized. Next-generation sequencing now enables genome and transcriptome analysis of medicinal herbs such as *Salvia miltiorrhiza*, *Panax ginseng*, and *Artemisia annua*, generating large volumes of sequences requiring alignment against reference data (Chen et al., 2019). Standard BLAST (Altschul et al., 1990) remains the most widely used alignment tool, yet TCM researchers face three obstacles: (i) reference sequences are scattered across NCBI, herbal genome portals, and pharmacopoeia databases; (ii) annotation of hits requires manual cross-referencing with TCM-specific target and compound resources; and (iii) batch workflows are difficult to reproduce.

Several integrated platforms exist, including Blast2GO (Conesa et al., 2005) and KEGG-based annotation pipelines, but none integrate TCM-specific reference genomes, human target associations, and phytochemical records in a single alignment environment. To address this gap, we developed TCM-Blast, which couples a BLAST+ engine with three curated TCM resources and an automated annotation layer.

Our contributions are: (1) a curated TCM reference collection spanning 1,284 plant genomes; (2) integration of 8,905 TCM–target associations; (3) a batch alignment engine with reproducible reporting; and (4) benchmarking and a case study demonstrating utility for *Danshen* transcript annotation.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 System architecture

TCM-Blast consists of four modules: (i) the Alignment Core, wrapping NCBI BLAST+ 2.14.0 (`blastn`, `blastp`, `blastx`, `tblastn`); (ii) the Resource Layer, hosting TCMHerbDB, TCMTargetDB, and TCMCompoundDB; (iii) the Annotation Engine, mapping hits to Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathways; and (iv) the Report Generator, producing HTML/TSV outputs with provenance metadata. The system runs on Linux (Ubuntu 22.04), requires 32 GB RAM and 500 GB storage for full database indexing, and is implemented in Python 3.11 with a Flask web interface.

 2.2 Database construction

TCMHerbDB. We collected 1,284 medicinal plant genome assemblies (3.9 Gb total) from public repositories and internal sequencing, covering 412 species listed in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia. Sequences were deduplicated at 95% identity using CD-HIT (Li and Godzik, 2006), yielding 28.6 million non-redundant sequences.

TCMTargetDB. We integrated 46,712 human protein-coding genes with 8,905 experimentally supported or predicted TCM–target associations curated from literature and docking studies. Each entry includes gene symbol, UniProt ID, associated herb, and evidence level (A–D).

TCMCompoundDB. A total of 62,340 phytochemical records were compiled, each linked to source herbs, molecular formula, and, where available, known targets.

 2.3 Alignment workflow

Users submit FASTA files (≤ 500 MB) and select a program, database, and E-value threshold (default 1e-5). Queries are split into chunks of 1,000 sequences and processed in parallel (default 8 threads). Hits are filtered by identity ≥ 70% and coverage ≥ 50% for annotation. The Annotation Engine assigns GO terms and KEGG orthologs via best-hit transfer and computes enrichment using Fisher's exact test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction.

 2.4 Benchmarking

We randomly selected 500 transcripts from a *S. miltiorrhiza* transcriptome (average length 1,142 bp). Three pipelines were compared: (a) TCM-Blast; (b) sequential BLAST+ against the same databases; and (c) BLAST+ against NCBI nt only. Runtime, alignment rate, and annotation completeness were recorded on a server with 2 × Intel Xeon Gold 6338 CPUs and 256 GB RAM. Each pipeline was run three times; means are reported.

 2.5 Case study

A set of 120 *Danshen* unigenes from a tanshinone biosynthesis study was aligned against TCMHerbDB and TCMTargetDB. Enriched KEGG pathways were identified at FDR < 0.01.

 3. Results

 3.1 Database statistics

TCMHerbDB contained 28.6 million non-redundant sequences from 1,284 genomes (Table 1). TCMTargetDB comprised 46,712 genes and 8,905 herb–target associations, of which 2,317 (26.0%) were evidence level A. TCMCompoundDB included 62,340 compounds, with 41,208 (66.1%) linked to at least one target.

Table 1. Summary of integrated TCM resources.

| Resource | Entries | Size | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| TCMHerbDB | 28.6 M sequences | 3.9 Gb | 1,284 genomes / 412 species |
| TCMTargetDB | 46,712 genes | 210 Mb | 8,905 associations |
| TCMCompoundDB | 62,340 compounds | 95 Mb | 41,208 target-linked |

 3.2 Benchmarking performance

TCM-Blast aligned 492/500 (98.4%) transcripts, versus 489/500 (97.8%) for sequential BLAST+ and 461/500 (92.2%) for NCBI nt BLAST. Mean runtime per 1,000 queries was 42.7 s for TCM-Blast, 132.4 s for sequential BLAST+, and 68.9 s for NCBI nt BLAST, corresponding to a 3.1-fold speedup over the sequential pipeline. Annotation completeness (queries receiving GO and KEGG assignments) was 91.6% for TCM-Blast versus 63.2% for sequential BLAST+ with manual annotation.

 3.3 Case study: *Danshen* unigenes

Of 120 unigenes, 87 (72.5%) were annotated. KEGG enrichment identified diterpenoid biosynthesis (ko00904, 23 genes, FDR = 3.2e-9), terpenoid backbone biosynthesis (ko00900, 19 genes, FDR = 1.1e-6), and plant hormone signal transduction (ko04075, 11 genes, FDR = 4.7e-3). Thirty-four unigenes mapped to TCMTargetDB entries, including *CYP76AH1* and *CYP76AH3*, consistent with prior reports on tanshinone biosynthesis. Compound cross-referencing linked 41 unigenes to 76 phytochemical records, predominantly tanshinones and salvianolic acids.

 4. Discussion

TCM-Blast addresses a practical bottleneck in TCM genomics by unifying alignment and TCM-specific annotation. Its 98.4% alignment rate and 3.1-fold speedup over sequential BLAST+ stem from chunked parallelization and pre-indexed, deduplicated databases. The case study reproduced known tanshinone pathway genes, supporting validity.

Compared with Blast2GO, TCM-Blast offers TCM-specific resources (herb genomes, herb–target associations, phytochemicals) absent from general platforms. However, limitations remain. First, TCMTargetDB associations are partly computational (evidence levels C–D, 48.3%), which may introduce false positives; users should filter by evidence level. Second, TCMHerbDB is biased toward well-studied species, with 412 Pharmacopoeia species but thousands of traditionally used herbs unrepresented. Third, annotation transfer by best-hit can misassign paralogous genes.

Future work will expand genome coverage, incorporate experimental validation scores, and add variant-level alignment for pharmacogenomic applications.

 5. Conclusion

TCM-Blast integrates BLAST+ with curated TCM genomic, target, and compound resources, enabling fast, reproducible alignment and annotation for medicinal plant research. Benchmarking and a *Danshen* case study demonstrate high alignment rates, substantial speedup, and biologically coherent annotations. TCM-Blast is freely available for academic use and provides a foundation for TCM-oriented comparative and functional genomics.

 References

Altschul, S.F., Gish, W., Miller, W., Myers, E.W., Lipman, D.J. (1990) Basic local alignment search tool. *J. Mol. Biol.*, 215, 403–410.

Chen, S. et al. (2019) Genome sequencing of medicinal plants. *Nat. Plants*, 5, 1–8.

Conesa, A. et al. (2005) Blast2GO: a universal tool for annotation, visualization and analysis in functional genomics research. *Bioinformatics*, 21, 3674–3676.

Li, W., Godzik, A. (2006) Cd-hit: a fast program for clustering and comparing large sets of protein or nucleotide sequences. *Bioinformatics*, 22, 1658–1659.

title: Electrical stimulation on adverse events caused by chemotherapy in patients with cervical cancer: A protocol for a systematic review of randomized controlled trial
text:
Background: Chemotherapy for cervical cancer frequently causes adverse events that impair quality of life and may compromise treatment adherence. Electrical stimulation, a non-invasive neuromodulatory intervention, has been proposed as a potential strategy to alleviate these chemotherapy-related adverse events, but evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remains inconclusive.

Methods: This systematic review protocol follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines. A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Chinese databases from inception to the present. RCTs evaluating electrical stimulation for chemotherapy-induced adverse events in cervical cancer patients will be included. Primary outcomes will encompass chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, nausea and vomiting, fatigue, and quality of life. Two reviewers will independently perform study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment using the Cochrane tool. Meta-analysis will be conducted using RevMan 5.4 where heterogeneity permits; otherwise, a narrative synthesis will be presented.

Results: This review will synthesize current evidence on the efficacy and safety of electrical stimulation for chemotherapy-related adverse events in cervical cancer.

Conclusion: Findings may inform clinical decision-making and guide future research.

title: Soil acidification in Chinese tea plantations
text:
Soil acidification in Chinese tea plantations

Abstract

Soil acidification is a major threat to the sustainability of tea production in China. This study investigated the status, spatial pattern, and driving factors of soil acidification in major tea-producing regions of China. A total of 360 topsoil samples (0–20 cm) were collected from 12 provinces between 2021 and 2023, and soil pH, exchangeable acidity, base cations, soil organic carbon, and nitrogen forms were measured. The results showed that mean soil pH in Chinese tea plantations was 4.52, with 67.8% of samples below pH 4.5 and 31.4% below pH 4.0. Soil acidification was more severe in the eastern and southern tea regions than in the southwestern and central regions. Exchangeable Al³⁺ and H⁺ accounted for 58.3% and 24.7% of exchangeable acidity, respectively. Long-term tea cultivation, high nitrogen fertilization, and low return of organic matter were the main drivers of acidification. Soil pH decreased by 0.28 units per decade under continuous tea planting. The findings suggest that integrated management practices, including optimized fertilization, liming, and organic amendment, are urgently needed to mitigate soil acidification and maintain tea productivity.

Keywords: soil acidification; tea plantation; pH; exchangeable aluminum; nitrogen fertilization; China

1. Introduction

Tea (*Camellia sinensis* L.) is one of the most important cash crops in China, with a planting area exceeding 3.3 million hectares and production accounting for nearly half of the world's total. Tea plants are naturally adapted to acidic soils, typically with pH 4.5–5.5, and moderate acidity enhances the availability of certain nutrients and the synthesis of tea polyphenols and amino acids. However, excessive acidification below pH 4.0 can cause aluminum toxicity, nutrient imbalance, reduced microbial diversity, and decline in tea yield and quality. In recent decades, soil acidification has become increasingly severe in Chinese tea plantations due to intensive management, high nitrogen input, and monoculture. Understanding the current status and drivers of soil acidification is essential for sustainable tea production.

Previous studies have reported pH declines in tea soils across several provinces, but most were limited to local scales or single regions. A national-scale assessment integrating soil pH, exchangeable acidity, and management factors is still lacking. Moreover, the relative contribution of natural and anthropogenic factors to acidification remains debated. Therefore, this study aimed to (1) quantify the current status and spatial variation of soil pH in Chinese tea plantations, (2) identify the main forms of exchangeable acidity, and (3) evaluate the effects of tea cultivation age, fertilization, and organic matter management on soil acidification. The results are expected to provide a scientific basis for soil improvement and sustainable tea plantation management.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study area and sampling

The study covered 12 major tea-producing provinces in China: Zhejiang, Fujian, Anhui, Jiangsu, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Guangdong, Guangxi, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou. These regions represent more than 85% of the national tea planting area. A total of 360 topsoil samples (0–20 cm) were collected from 120 tea plantations between 2021 and 2023, with three composite samples per plantation. Each composite sample consisted of 10–15 random cores. Samples were air-dried, sieved through 2 mm and 0.15 mm screens, and stored for analysis.

2.2 Soil analysis

Soil pH was measured in a 1:2.5 soil:water suspension using a glass electrode. Exchangeable acidity (H⁺ and Al³⁺) was determined by titration with NaOH after extraction with 1 M KCl. Exchangeable base cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺, Na⁺) were extracted with 1 M NH₄OAc and measured by atomic absorption spectrophotometry. Soil organic carbon (SOC) was determined by the dichromate oxidation method. Total nitrogen (TN) was measured by the Kjeldahl method, and available nitrogen (AN) by the alkaline hydrolysis diffusion method. Available phosphorus (AP) was extracted with 0.5 M NaHCO₃ and measured by the molybdenum blue method. Available potassium (AK) was extracted with 1 M NH₄OAc and measured by flame photometry.

2.3 Management survey

A questionnaire survey was conducted with plantation owners to collect information on tea planting age, fertilization regime (annual N input), organic amendment application, and liming history. Plantations were grouped into three cultivation age classes: <10 years, 10–30 years, and >30 years. Nitrogen input was classified as low (<200 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), medium (200–400 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), and high (>400 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹).

2.4 Data analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0 and R 4.2.1. One-way ANOVA and Duncan's multiple range test were used to compare means among groups. Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression were used to identify relationships between soil pH and explanatory variables. Spatial distribution maps were generated using ArcGIS 10.8 with inverse distance weighting interpolation. A significance level of P < 0.05 was applied.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Overall soil pH status

The mean soil pH across all tea plantation samples was 4.52, with a range of 3.21–6.18. The frequency distribution showed that 67.8% of samples had pH below 4.5, and 31.4% were below 4.0, indicating severe acidification. Only 12.5% of samples fell within the optimal range for tea growth (pH 4.5–5.5). The coefficient of variation was 14.6%, suggesting moderate spatial heterogeneity.

3.2 Spatial variation

Soil pH varied significantly among regions. The lowest mean pH was observed in Fujian (4.18), followed by Zhejiang (4.26), Jiangxi (4.31), and Hunan (4.37). In contrast, Yunnan (4.89), Guizhou (4.82), and Sichuan (4.76) had relatively higher pH values. Eastern and southern tea regions were more acidic than southwestern and central regions. This pattern was consistent with the intensity of tea cultivation and nitrogen fertilization.

3.3 Exchangeable acidity and base cations

Exchangeable acidity ranged from 0.82 to 6.45 cmol kg⁻¹, with a mean of 3.12 cmol kg⁻¹. Exchangeable Al³⁺ was the dominant form, accounting for 58.3% of total exchangeable acidity, followed by H⁺ (24.7%) and other forms (17.0%). Exchangeable Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ were generally low, with means of 2.45 and 0.86 cmol kg⁻¹, respectively. The ratio of exchangeable Al³⁺ to base cations increased significantly as pH decreased below 4.5.

3.4 Relationships with cultivation age and fertilization

Soil pH decreased significantly with tea cultivation age. Mean pH was 4.91 in plantations <10 years, 4.48 in 10–30 years, and 4.12 in >30 years. The average decline rate was 0.28 pH units per decade. Nitrogen input showed a negative correlation with pH (r = –0.62, P < 0.01). High-N plantations (>400 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹) had a mean pH of 4.21, significantly lower than low-N plantations (4.78). Organic amendment application was positively correlated with pH (r = 0.48, P < 0.01). Plantations that applied organic fertilizer annually had pH 0.35 units higher than those without organic amendment.

3.5 Soil organic carbon and nutrients

Mean SOC was 12.4 g kg⁻¹, with a range of 5.2–24.8 g kg⁻¹. SOC was positively correlated with pH (r = 0.41, P < 0.01). TN averaged 1.32 g kg⁻¹, and AN averaged 98.6 mg kg⁻¹. AP and AK averaged 28.4 mg kg⁻¹ and 112.5 mg kg⁻¹, respectively. High-N plantations had higher TN and AN but lower pH and exchangeable Ca²⁺, indicating that nitrogen fertilization accelerated acidification and base cation leaching.

4. Discussion

4.1 Severe acidification in Chinese tea plantations

The mean pH of 4.52 and the high proportion of samples below pH 4.0 indicate that soil acidification is a widespread problem in Chinese tea plantations. This is consistent with previous regional reports and suggests that acidification has intensified over the past two decades. The optimal pH range for tea growth is generally considered to be 4.5–5.5; therefore, more than two-thirds of the sampled soils were below the optimal range. Severe acidification can reduce tea yield and quality by inducing aluminum toxicity, inhibiting root growth, and decreasing nutrient availability.

4.2 Role of exchangeable aluminum

Exchangeable Al³⁺ was the dominant component of exchangeable acidity, accounting for nearly 60%. As pH decreases, Al³⁺ becomes more soluble and can replace base cations on the exchange complex, leading to nutrient loss and root damage. The high proportion of Al³⁺ in acidic tea soils highlights the need for liming and organic amendment to reduce Al toxicity. The low levels of exchangeable Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ further indicate base cation depletion, which may limit tea growth.

4.3 Drivers of acidification

Long-term tea cultivation was a major driver of acidification. The decline rate of 0.28 pH units per decade is comparable to or higher than that reported for other perennial cropping systems. Several mechanisms contribute to this process. First, tea plants absorb more cations than anions, leading to H⁺ release from roots. Second, high nitrogen fertilization, especially ammonium-based fertilizers, generates H⁺ through nitrification. Third, removal of tea leaves and pruning litter reduces the return of base cations to the soil. Fourth, organic matter depletion reduces buffering capacity. The negative correlation between nitrogen input and pH confirms the important role of fertilization in acidification.

4.4 Implications for management

The results suggest that integrated management practices are needed to mitigate soil acidification. Optimized nitrogen fertilization, including reduced application rates and use of controlled-release or organic fertilizers, can slow acidification. Liming with calcium carbonate or dolomite can raise pH and reduce exchangeable Al³⁺. Organic amendment, such as compost or biochar, can increase soil organic matter, improve buffering capacity, and enhance base cation retention. In addition, planting green manure and returning pruning litter to the soil can help maintain nutrient balance. Regular soil monitoring is essential to track pH changes and adjust management practices.

4.5 Limitations and future research

This study has some limitations. The sampling was limited to 120 plantations, which may not fully represent all tea-growing regions. The questionnaire survey relied on farmer recall, which may introduce uncertainty. Future research should include long-term field experiments to quantify the effects of different management practices on soil pH and tea productivity. Moreover, the interactions among soil acidification, microbial communities, and tea quality deserve further investigation.

5. Conclusion

This study provides a national-scale assessment of soil acidification in Chinese tea plantations. The mean soil pH was 4.52, and 67.8% of samples were below pH 4.5, indicating severe acidification. Exchangeable Al³⁺ was the dominant form of exchangeable acidity, accounting for 58.3%. Soil pH decreased with tea cultivation age at a rate of 0.28 units per decade. High nitrogen fertilization and low organic amendment were major drivers of acidification. Eastern and southern tea regions were more acidic than southwestern and central regions. Integrated management practices, including optimized fertilization, liming, and organic amendment, are urgently needed to mitigate soil acidification and ensure the sustainability of tea production in China.

title: MiR319-targeted OsTCP21 and OsGAmyb regulate tillering and grain yield in rice
text:
Rice tillering is a key determinant of panicle number and grain yield, and its genetic improvement has long been a major goal in rice breeding. Tillering is regulated by a complex network of transcription factors, phytohormones, and small RNAs, among which microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as critical post-transcriptional regulators of plant architecture. MiR319 is a conserved plant miRNA that primarily targets TEOSINTE BRANCHED1/CYCLOIDEA/PCF (TCP) transcription factors and has been implicated in leaf development, senescence, and branching in several species. However, whether miR319 functions in rice tillering and how it coordinates downstream targets to influence yield remain largely unclear.

TCP transcription factors are known to modulate axillary bud outgrowth, but the specific rice TCP members acting downstream of miR319 and their interacting partners have not been fully characterized. Moreover, the gibberellin (GA) pathway is well established in promoting tiller bud elongation, yet the molecular link between miR319-targeted TCPs and GA-related regulators in rice is poorly understood. OsGAmyb, a GA-responsive MYB transcription factor, represents a potential node connecting these pathways, but its functional relationship with miR319 and TCPs has not been explored.

Here, we report that miR319-targeted OsTCP21 and OsGAmyb act as key regulators of rice tillering and grain yield. We show that OsTCP21 is directly repressed by miR319 and that manipulating its expression alters tiller number and panicle productivity. Furthermore, OsGAmyb interacts with OsTCP21 to modulate downstream GA signaling and tiller bud outgrowth. Our findings define a miR319–OsTCP21–OsGAmyb module that integrates miRNA and hormonal signals to control tillering, providing new targets for improving rice architecture and yield potential.

title: Behavioral thermoregulation in a small herbivore avoids direct UVB damage
text:
Results and Discussion

Over 42 observation days, animals selected significantly warmer microhabitats during UVB peaks (11:00–15:00) than at other times (mean ± SE: 31.4 ± 0.6 °C vs. 24.8 ± 0.5 °C; LMM, χ² = 47.2, df = 1, P < 0.001), while surface UVB irradiance in occupied patches averaged 38% lower than in randomly paired available patches (0.42 ± 0.03 vs. 0.68 ± 0.04 W m⁻²; paired t = 6.81, df = 41, P < 0.001). Shuttling frequency increased from 1.2 ± 0.2 bouts h⁻¹ in the morning to 4.7 ± 0.4 bouts h⁻¹ at midday (χ² = 31.5, df = 2, P < 0.001), and individuals spent 71 ± 3% of midday time in shade or burrows despite operative temperatures there falling below preferred body temperature (T_pref = 32 °C). This apparent trade-off indicates that thermoregulation was constrained by UVB avoidance rather than by thermal optima alone.

To test whether this behavior prevents direct UVB damage, we measured dorsal skin cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs). Shaded animals accumulated 2.1 ± 0.3 CPDs per 10⁶ bases over six hours, compared with 9.8 ± 1.1 in animals experimentally prevented from shading (Mann–Whitney U = 12, P < 0.001), and 4.3 ± 0.5 in a control group given access to shade but no thermal gradient. CPD load correlated strongly with cumulative UVB exposure (r² = 0.79, P < 0.001) but not with mean body temperature (r² = 0.04, P = 0.41). Together, these results show that behavioral shifts toward shade at midday are primarily driven by UVB avoidance and reduce direct DNA damage by roughly 78%, even at a modest cost to thermal gain. We suggest that UVB, not heat, may be the principal selective pressure shaping diurnal microhabitat use in small, thinly furred herbivores.

title: Prevalence and treatment gap of active convulsive epilepsy: a large community-based survey in rural West China
text:
Prevalence and treatment gap of active convulsive epilepsy: a large community-based survey in rural West China

Abstract

Objective: To estimate the prevalence of active convulsive epilepsy (ACE) and the magnitude of its treatment gap in rural areas of West China, and to identify factors associated with untreated epilepsy. Methods: A door-to-door community-based survey was conducted in 12 villages of a rural county in West China between March and October 2023. A two-stage screening strategy was used: trained village health workers administered a validated seizure screening questionnaire, and positive responders were evaluated by neurologists using standardized diagnostic criteria. Active convulsive epilepsy was defined as at least one unprovoked convulsive seizure in the previous 12 months. The treatment gap was defined as the proportion of individuals with ACE who had not received any appropriate antiseizure medication during the preceding 12 months. Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine factors associated with the treatment gap. Results: Among 48,762 residents screened, 312 individuals met the criteria for ACE, yielding a crude prevalence of 6.40 per 1,000 population (95% CI: 5.71–7.14). The prevalence was slightly higher in males (6.78/1,000) than in females (6.01/1,000). Of the 312 patients with ACE, 214 (68.6%, 95% CI: 63.2–73.6) had not received appropriate antiseizure treatment in the past 12 months. The treatment gap was greater among patients aged ≥60 years (adjusted OR = 2.14, 95% CI: 1.21–3.78), those with no formal education (adjusted OR = 2.86, 95% CI: 1.54–5.31), those living more than 10 km from a township hospital (adjusted OR = 2.37, 95% CI: 1.36–4.13), and those from households in the lowest income quartile (adjusted OR = 3.02, 95% CI: 1.67–5.46). Conclusions: Active convulsive epilepsy is a substantial public health problem in rural West China, and the treatment gap remains very high. Targeted interventions are urgently needed to improve access to diagnosis and affordable antiseizure medication in remote rural settings.

Keywords: active convulsive epilepsy; prevalence; treatment gap; rural health; West China; community-based survey

1. Introduction

Epilepsy is one of the most common serious neurological disorders worldwide, affecting approximately 50 million people. It is estimated that nearly 80% of people with epilepsy live in low- and middle-income countries, where the burden is disproportionately high because of limited healthcare resources, stigma, and inadequate access to treatment. Active convulsive epilepsy (ACE), defined as the occurrence of at least one unprovoked convulsive seizure within the previous 12 months, represents the most visible and clinically significant subgroup of epilepsy and is associated with increased risks of injury, cognitive impairment, and premature death.

China accounts for a large proportion of the global epilepsy burden. Although national estimates suggest a prevalence of approximately 4 to 7 per 1,000, marked regional heterogeneity exists. Rural areas in West China are characterized by mountainous terrain, sparse health facilities, low household income, and limited neurological services. These conditions may contribute to both a higher prevalence of untreated epilepsy and a wider treatment gap. The treatment gap, defined as the proportion of people with epilepsy who require treatment but do not receive it, is a key indicator of health system performance. Previous studies in China have reported treatment gaps ranging from 40% to more than 70%, with the highest values in remote rural regions. However, large community-based surveys focusing specifically on ACE in rural West China remain scarce.

Accurate local estimates are essential for planning epilepsy services, allocating resources, and designing culturally appropriate interventions. Therefore, we conducted a large door-to-door community-based survey in a rural county in West China. The objectives were to estimate the prevalence of ACE, quantify the treatment gap, and identify sociodemographic and geographic factors associated with untreated epilepsy.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study setting and population

The survey was conducted in 12 villages of a rural county in West China between March and October 2023. The county is located in a mountainous area, with a total population of approximately 260,000, of whom more than 70% reside in rural villages. The study population included all permanent residents of the selected villages, regardless of age or sex. Temporary residents and individuals who had lived in the area for less than six months were excluded.

2.2 Sampling strategy

A two-stage sampling procedure was used. First, 12 villages were randomly selected from a list of 86 villages in the county, stratified by distance from the township hospital. Second, all households in the selected villages were visited. Village health workers, who had received standardized training, administered a validated seizure screening questionnaire to the head of each household or another adult informant. The questionnaire included questions about episodes of loss of consciousness, convulsions, tongue biting, urinary incontinence, and postictal confusion.

2.3 Diagnostic assessment

All individuals who screened positive were invited to a temporary clinic established in the village. Neurologists from a tertiary hospital reviewed the history, performed a structured interview, and conducted a general and neurological examination. The diagnosis of ACE was based on the definition of the International League Against Epilepsy: at least one unprovoked convulsive seizure in the previous 12 months, excluding acute symptomatic seizures due to fever, trauma, infection, metabolic disturbance, or alcohol withdrawal. When necessary, witnesses were interviewed to confirm seizure semiology. Electroencephalography was available at the county hospital, but because of logistical constraints, it was not required for diagnosis.

2.4 Treatment gap definition

The treatment gap was defined as the proportion of individuals with ACE who had not received any appropriate antiseizure medication during the 12 months preceding the survey. Appropriate treatment included continuous use of at least one standard antiseizure medication, such as phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine, or valproate, at an adequate dose. Traditional herbal remedies and intermittent use of sedatives were not considered appropriate treatment.

2.5 Data collection and quality control

Data were collected using a structured questionnaire that included sociodemographic characteristics, seizure history, treatment history, distance to the nearest health facility, and household income. Household income was categorized into quartiles based on self-reported annual income. Training workshops were held for all field workers, and 10% of the questionnaires were rechecked by supervisors. Diagnostic consistency was assessed by independent review of 50 randomly selected cases by two neurologists, with a kappa value of 0.86.

2.6 Statistical analysis

Data were entered into EpiData 3.1 and analyzed using SPSS 26.0. Prevalence was calculated as the number of ACE cases per 1,000 population, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The treatment gap was expressed as a proportion with 95% CI. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with the treatment gap. Variables with a p-value < 0.10 in univariable analysis were included in the multivariable model. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs were reported. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

2.7 Ethical considerations

The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the participating institution. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal guardians. For individuals diagnosed with ACE but not receiving treatment, referral letters were provided, and assistance was offered to facilitate access to care.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Study population and prevalence

A total of 48,762 residents from 12 villages were screened, representing 92.4% of the eligible population. The mean age was 41.3 years (standard deviation: 18.7), and 51.2% were female. Among them, 1,146 individuals screened positive, and 312 were confirmed to have ACE. The crude prevalence of ACE was 6.40 per 1,000 population (95% CI: 5.71–7.14). The prevalence was 6.78 per 1,000 in males and 6.01 per 1,000 in females. Prevalence increased with age, from 3.12 per 1,000 in children aged 0–14 years to 9.86 per 1,000 in adults aged 60 years and older.

3.2 Treatment gap

Of the 312 patients with ACE, 214 (68.6%, 95% CI: 63.2–73.6) had not received appropriate antiseizure medication in the previous 12 months. Among the 98 treated patients, 61 were receiving phenobarbital, 22 phenytoin, 11 carbamazepine, and 4 valproate. Only 37 patients reported uninterrupted medication use during the previous year. The most commonly reported reasons for not seeking treatment were financial difficulty (42.1%), lack of awareness that the condition was treatable (28.5%), distance to health facilities (15.4%), and fear of stigma (9.8%).

3.3 Factors associated with the treatment gap

In multivariable logistic regression, older age, lower educational level, greater distance from a township hospital, and lower household income were independently associated with a higher odds of being untreated. Patients aged 60 years and older had more than twice the odds of being untreated compared with those aged 18–39 years (adjusted OR = 2.14, 95% CI: 1.21–3.78). Individuals with no formal education had nearly three times the odds of being untreated compared with those with at least primary education (adjusted OR = 2.86, 95% CI: 1.54–5.31). Living more than 10 km from a township hospital was associated with a higher treatment gap (adjusted OR = 2.37, 95% CI: 1.36–4.13). Compared with the highest income quartile, the lowest income quartile had the strongest association with being untreated (adjusted OR = 3.02, 95% CI: 1.67–5.46). Sex was not significantly associated with the treatment gap after adjustment.

4. Discussion

This large community-based survey found a crude prevalence of ACE of 6.40 per 1,000 in rural West China, which is consistent with previous estimates from other rural areas of China but higher than estimates from many high-income countries. The high prevalence may reflect a combination of genetic susceptibility, high rates of perinatal complications, head trauma, central nervous system infections, and limited access to preventive care. The increasing prevalence with age is also consistent with the accumulation of cerebrovascular disease and other acquired causes of epilepsy in older adults.

The most striking finding was the very high treatment gap of 68.6%. This figure is higher than the global average and exceeds estimates from many urban areas in China. Several factors may explain this gap. First, financial constraints remain a major barrier. Although antiseizure medications such as phenobarbital are inexpensive, indirect costs related to transportation, lost work time, and repeated clinic visits can be prohibitive for poor rural households. Second, limited health literacy and widespread misconceptions about epilepsy contribute to delayed diagnosis and treatment. Many participants believed that epilepsy was a spiritual or incurable condition. Third, the shortage of neurologists and trained primary care physicians in rural areas means that many patients never receive an accurate diagnosis or a prescription for appropriate medication. Fourth, stigma continues to discourage help-seeking, particularly among women and older adults.

The association between the treatment gap and distance from a township hospital highlights the importance of geographic accessibility. In mountainous regions, travel to a health facility may take several hours, and public transportation is limited. Community-based delivery models, such as mobile epilepsy clinics and training of village doctors to diagnose and manage uncomplicated cases, may help reduce this barrier. The strong association with low income and low education suggests that interventions must address both affordability and knowledge. Free or subsidized antiseizure medication, combined with community health education, could substantially improve treatment coverage.

This study has several strengths. It was a large, door-to-door survey with a high response rate, and diagnoses were confirmed by neurologists using standardized criteria. However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the diagnosis relied on clinical history and witness accounts rather than routine electroencephalography, which may have led to some misclassification. Second, the cross-sectional design cannot establish causality. Third, self-reported income and treatment history may be subject to recall bias. Fourth, the findings may not be generalizable to all rural areas of West China, given the heterogeneity of the region.

5. Conclusion

Active convulsive epilepsy is a significant public health problem in rural West China, with a prevalence of 6.40 per 1,000 and a treatment gap of 68.6%. Older age, low educational level, long distance from a township hospital, and low household income are independently associated with untreated epilepsy. Reducing this treatment gap will require a multifaceted approach that includes free or subsidized antiseizure medication, training and support of village doctors, mobile epilepsy clinics, and community education to reduce stigma and improve health literacy. Policymakers should prioritize epilepsy care in rural health system strengthening efforts to ensure equitable access to effective treatment.

title: Global mapping of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 and H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4 viruses with spatial cross-validation
text:
Global mapping of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 and H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4 viruses with spatial cross-validation

 Abstract

Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) viruses of the H5Nx subtype belonging to clade 2.3.4.4 have spread intercontinentally since 2014, causing substantial mortality in wild birds and poultry and sporadic human infections. Robust spatial estimates of outbreak risk are needed to guide surveillance, but naïve occurrence models are prone to spatial autocorrelation and overfitting. We compiled a global database of 6,842 georeferenced HPAI H5N1 and H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4 outbreak records in wild birds and poultry from 2014 to 2024, together with 38 environmental, anthropogenic, and host-related covariates. Using an ensemble of boosted regression trees and random forests, we produced 5-km resolution global suitability maps under a spatially blocked cross-validation framework (200-km blocks) to obtain honest performance estimates. The ensemble achieved a spatially cross-validated AUC of 0.86 (95% CI 0.84–0.88) and a true skill statistic of 0.61, substantially lower than under random cross-validation (AUC 0.96), confirming that conventional validation inflates accuracy. Highest suitability occurred in temperate and boreal wetlands of Europe, East Asia, and North America, the Nile Delta, and parts of South America and sub-Saharan Africa. Key predictors included minimum winter temperature, wetland extent, poultry density, and migratory waterfowl richness. Approximately 41% of global poultry production occurred within the top suitability decile. Our maps provide a validated, spatially honest baseline for risk-based surveillance of clade 2.3.4.4 HPAI viruses.

Keywords: highly pathogenic avian influenza; H5N1; clade 2.3.4.4; species distribution modelling; spatial cross-validation; boosted regression trees; risk mapping; wild birds; poultry

 Introduction

Since the emergence of the Goose/Guangdong lineage H5N1 virus in 1996, highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) has evolved into a recurring panzootic threat. A pivotal development was the appearance of clade 2.3.4.4 viruses, first recognized in 2013–2014, which reassorted into multiple H5Nx subtypes (H5N1, H5N2, H5N5, H5N6, H5N8) and spread rapidly along migratory flyways. Unlike earlier HPAI waves, clade 2.3.4.4 viruses have caused extensive wild-bird mortality, including in previously unaffected taxa, and have reached every continent except Antarctica. The 2021–2024 H5N1 wave produced unprecedented outbreaks in seabird colonies, raptors, and mammals, raising concerns about pandemic potential.

Effective surveillance is constrained by the sheer spatial extent of at-risk areas. Statistical species distribution models (SDMs) can identify environmental correlates of outbreaks and extrapolate risk to unsampled regions. However, outbreak data are strongly spatially biased: surveillance intensity follows poultry industry density, reporting infrastructure, and wild-bird monitoring programmes, generating spatial autocorrelation that violates the independence assumptions of standard cross-validation. Random k-fold cross-validation therefore yields optimistically biased performance metrics and can select overfitted models.

Spatial cross-validation, in which training and testing folds are separated by geographic blocks, provides more realistic estimates of transferability. Here we assemble a global, georeferenced database of HPAI H5N1 and H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4 events and fit an ensemble SDM with spatial block cross-validation, producing 5-km resolution global suitability maps and identifying priority regions for surveillance.

 Materials and Methods

 Outbreak data

We compiled 6,842 unique outbreak records (2014–2024) from WOAH, FAO EMPRES-i, national veterinary services, and wild-bird mortality databases. Records were retained if they met at least one criterion: (i) laboratory confirmation of HPAI H5N1 or H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4 by HA/NA sequencing or clade-specific RT-qPCR; (ii) official notification; or (iii) documented mass mortality with virological confirmation. Records were deduplicated to a 5-km grid, yielding 4,317 presence cells. Poultry outbreaks comprised 58% of records, wild-bird events 35%, and mixed events 7%. Europe (31%), East Asia (24%), and North America (19%) dominated the sample; Africa (9%), South America (7%), South Asia (6%), and Oceania (4%) were underrepresented.

 Environmental covariates

We assembled 38 predictors in five groups: (1) climate (mean, minimum and maximum temperature, precipitation seasonality, frost days; CHELSA, 1979–2013 normals); (2) hydrology and land cover (wetland fraction, open water, cropland, urban extent); (3) host proxies (modelled richness of Anatidae and Charadriiformes from expert range maps); (4) anthropogenic factors (poultry density, human population, road density, live-bird market density); and (5) topography (elevation, ruggedness). All layers were resampled to a 5-km equal-area grid (EPSG:6933). Collinearity was reduced by removing variables with |r| > 0.85, retaining 26 predictors.

 Modelling framework

We fitted an ensemble of boosted regression trees (BRT; learning rate 0.005, tree complexity 5, 3,000 trees) and random forests (RF; 1,000 trees, mtry = 6) using the `dismo` and `randomForest` implementations in R 4.3.2. Pseudo-absences (n = 20,000) were drawn with a target-group background weighting to reduce sampling bias. Ensemble weights were proportional to spatially cross-validated TSS.

 Spatial cross-validation

We partitioned the globe into 200-km × 200-km blocks and assigned blocks randomly to five folds, ensuring no spatial overlap between training and testing data. This block size approximates the mean dispersal and reporting radius of outbreak clusters. For comparison, we also ran standard random 5-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed with AUC, TSS, sensitivity, and Boyce index (presence-only calibration). Variable importance was computed by permutation, and response curves were inspected for ecological plausibility.

 Results

 Model performance

Under random cross-validation, the ensemble appeared near-perfect (AUC = 0.96, TSS = 0.89). Under spatial block cross-validation, performance declined markedly but remained useful: AUC = 0.86 (95% CI 0.84–0.88), TSS = 0.61, sensitivity = 0.79, specificity = 0.82, Boyce index = 0.84. The gap between validation schemes (ΔAUC = 0.10) was largest for models dominated by poultry-density predictors, indicating that spatially clustered poultry signal inflates random-fold accuracy. BRT and RF performed similarly (spatial AUC 0.87 and 0.85), and the weighted ensemble (0.6 BRT, 0.4 RF) outperformed either alone.

 Variable importance

The four most important predictors were minimum temperature of the coldest month (18.4% permutation importance), wetland fraction (15.1%), poultry density (13.7%), and Anatidae richness (11.2%). Precipitation seasonality (8.0%), cropland fraction (6.5%), and human population density (5.9%) followed. Response curves were unimodal for winter temperature, with suitability peaking between −8 °C and 6 °C, consistent with the freezing threshold limiting waterbird aggregation and virus persistence. Wetland suitability increased monotonically up to ~40% cover. Poultry density showed a saturating relationship, with risk plateauing above ~2,000 birds km⁻².

 Global suitability patterns

High-suitability areas (top decile) covered 6.8% of the terrestrial surface but contained 41% of global poultry production and 37% of modelled waterfowl richness. Hotspots included: (i) northern and central Europe, particularly the North Sea and Baltic coasts; (ii) the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, including the Yellow Sea coast, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula; (iii) the Mississippi and Central Flyways of North America; (iv) the Nile Delta and Rift Valley lakes; (v) the Pantanal and La Plata basin; and (vi) scattered highland wetlands of East Africa. Oceania, central Amazonia, and the Sahara showed low suitability. Under a 2 °C warming scenario, suitability shifted poleward by a mean of 3.1° latitude and contracted in southern Europe and the southern United States.

 Discussion

Our analysis provides the first spatially cross-validated global risk map for HPAI H5N1 and H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4 viruses. The central methodological finding is quantitative: random cross-validation overestimated discrimination by 0.10 AUC points. This inflation arises because outbreak records cluster in space, so random folds share near-neighbours between training and testing sets. Spatial blocking removes this leakage and yields performance estimates that better reflect prediction into new regions—precisely the use case for surveillance planning. We therefore recommend that spatial cross-validation become standard practice in avian influenza SDMs, as it is becoming in ecology more broadly.

Ecologically, the results align with the known epidemiology of clade 2.3.4.4 viruses. The unimodal winter-temperature response reflects the role of cold snaps in concentrating waterfowl on unfrozen water bodies and enhancing environmental persistence of influenza A viruses. The prominence of wetland extent and Anatidae richness supports the wild-bird pathway, while the independent contribution of poultry density confirms the importance of poultry trade and production networks in amplification and spread. Regions where all three factors coincide—northern Europe, the Yellow Sea coast, the Nile Delta—emerge as the highest-risk interfaces.

The maps have practical implications. First, the top suitability decile captures a disproportionate share of poultry production, so targeted surveillance there could be highly efficient. Second, several high-suitability regions in Africa and South America have sparse outbreak records, likely reflecting surveillance gaps rather than true absence; these are priority areas for capacity building. Third, the projected poleward shift under warming suggests that currently low-risk boreal and Arctic regions may require new monitoring, particularly as wild-bird breeding grounds shift.

Several limitations apply. Outbreak data are opportunistic and biased toward regions with strong veterinary infrastructure; target-group background weighting mitigates but does not eliminate this bias. Host richness layers are expert-derived and coarse. We modelled suitability, not transmission probability, and did not explicitly incorporate viral phylogenetics or trade flows. Finally, our 200-km blocks, while justified, represent one choice among many; sensitivity analyses with 100-km and 300-km blocks changed AUC by less than 0.02 (data not shown), suggesting robustness.

 Conclusion

We produced global, 5-km resolution suitability maps for HPAI H5N1 and H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4 viruses using an ensemble SDM validated with spatial block cross-validation. Spatially honest validation reduced apparent accuracy relative to random cross-validation but yielded a model that transfers across regions (AUC 0.86, TSS 0.61). Risk is concentrated in temperate and boreal wetlands with cold winters, abundant waterfowl, and dense poultry production, and is projected to shift poleward with warming. These maps offer a defensible, openly reproducible baseline for risk-based surveillance and for prioritizing regions where current data are too sparse to distinguish low risk from low detection.

 Data availability

All outbreak records, covariate layers, model code, and spatial fold assignments are available in the accompanying repository (synthetic demonstration dataset).

title: Survivorship Care Practices and Confidence of Oncology Nurses in Singapore: A Cross-Sectional Study
text:
Background: As cancer survival rates improve, survivorship care has become an integral component of oncology nursing. However, little is known about the survivorship care practices and perceived confidence of oncology nurses in Singapore.

Aim: To examine the survivorship care practices and confidence of oncology nurses in Singapore and to identify associated factors.

Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among oncology nurses recruited from two tertiary cancer centres in Singapore between January and April 2023. Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire comprising sociodemographic and professional characteristics, the Survivorship Care Practices Scale, and the Survivorship Care Confidence Scale. Descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, one-way analysis of variance, and multiple linear regression were used for analysis.

Results: A total of 218 oncology nurses completed the survey (response rate 78.4%). The mean score for survivorship care practices was 3.42 ± 0.68 (range 1–5), indicating moderate engagement, with the lowest scores in the domains of health promotion and care coordination. The mean confidence score was 3.18 ± 0.74, reflecting moderate confidence, with the lowest confidence reported in managing late and long-term effects. Higher educational level (B = 0.21, p = 0.008), prior survivorship care training (B = 0.34, p < 0.001), and greater years of oncology nursing experience (B = 0.02, p = 0.013) were significantly associated with higher confidence. Prior training was also the strongest predictor of survivorship care practices (B = 0.29, p < 0.001).

Conclusion: Oncology nurses in Singapore demonstrated moderate levels of survivorship care practices and confidence, with notable gaps in health promotion, care coordination, and management of late effects. Targeted education and training programmes are needed to strengthen survivorship care delivery.

Keywords: cancer survivorship; survivorship care; oncology nursing; confidence; cross-sectional study; Singapore

title: The 2021 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: code red for a healthy future
text:
The 2021 Report of the Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change: Code Red for a Healthy Future

Abstract

The 2021 Lancet Countdown report represents the most comprehensive assessment to date of the links between climate change and human health. Drawing on 44 indicators across five working groups, this study synthesizes global data on climate hazards, exposure pathways, vulnerability, adaptation, and economic costs. Our analysis reveals that no country is immune to the health impacts of climate change, yet the burden falls disproportionately on low- and middle-income nations. We find that global heat-related mortality among adults over 65 has increased by 68% since the early 2000s, while climate suitability for infectious disease transmission has risen significantly across multiple regions. Simultaneously, only 0.3% of global climate finance has been allocated to health-specific adaptation, and 69% of national adaptation plans fail to mention health. These findings constitute a code red for a healthy future. We argue that the window for equitable, health-centered climate action is narrowing rapidly, and that recovery from COVID-19 must be aligned with the Paris Agreement to prevent catastrophic health outcomes.

Keywords: climate change; public health; adaptation; heat-related mortality; infectious diseases; climate finance; Lancet Countdown

1. Introduction

The relationship between climate change and human health has moved from the periphery of scientific inquiry to the center of global policy debate. While early research framed climate change primarily as an environmental and economic challenge, a growing body of evidence demonstrates that it is fundamentally a health crisis—one that amplifies existing inequalities and threatens to reverse decades of public health progress (Watts et al., 2015). The Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change was established in 2015 to provide an independent, multidisciplinary monitoring mechanism that tracks the evolving health profile of climate change and evaluates the world's response.

The 2021 report arrives at a critical juncture. The COVID-19 pandemic has exposed the fragility of global health systems, while record-breaking heatwaves, wildfires, floods, and droughts have simultaneously demonstrated the accelerating pace of climate disruption. The sixth assessment report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2021) declared that human-induced warming has already reached approximately 1.1°C above pre-industrial levels and that some changes are now irreversible. Against this backdrop, the Lancet Countdown's 2021 assessment aims to answer three questions: How is climate change currently affecting human health? How are countries and health systems responding? And what are the implications for equitable climate action?

This paper presents the key findings of the 2021 report, organized around the Countdown's five working groups: climate hazards, exposures, and vulnerabilities; adaptation, planning, and resilience for health; mitigation actions and health co-benefits; economics and finance; and public and political engagement. We synthesize data from 44 indicators, drawing on peer-reviewed literature, global datasets, and national policy documents. Our analysis reveals a stark gap between the scale of the health threat and the adequacy of the response—a gap we characterize as a "code red" for a healthy future.

2. Materials and Methods

The 2021 Lancet Countdown report employed a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative indicator tracking with qualitative policy analysis. The methodology was developed by five working groups comprising over 100 experts from 38 academic institutions and UN agencies.

Quantitative indicators were constructed using publicly available global datasets. For climate hazards and exposure, we used ERA5 reanalysis data from the Copernicus Climate Change Service to calculate heatwave exposure, wildfire risk, and drought indices. Health impact estimates—including heat-related mortality, infectious disease suitability, and air pollution mortality—were derived from epidemiological models and meta-analyses. For example, heat-related mortality was estimated using temperature-mortality relationships from 750 locations worldwide, applied to population-weighted temperature data.

Adaptation and resilience indicators were based on a systematic review of national adaptation plans, health sector strategies, and urban planning documents. We assessed 192 UN member states for the inclusion of health considerations in their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and National Adaptation Plans (NAPs). Mitigation indicators tracked energy system transitions, including coal phase-out commitments, renewable energy share, and the health co-benefits of reduced air pollution.

Economic indicators used data from the Climate Policy Initiative, the World Bank, and national budget documents to assess climate finance flows and the extent to which health adaptation is funded. Public and political engagement was measured through media analysis, academic publication counts, and UN General Assembly debate records.

All indicators were normalized and aggregated where appropriate, with uncertainty ranges reported. The report underwent peer review by external experts and was published in The Lancet on October 20, 2021. Limitations include data gaps in low-income countries, lag times in health surveillance, and the inherent difficulty of attributing specific health outcomes to climate change. Nevertheless, the convergent evidence across multiple independent indicators strengthens confidence in the overall findings.

3. Results and Analysis

Our analysis reveals accelerating health impacts across all five working groups, with the most severe effects concentrated in vulnerable populations.

3.1 Climate Hazards, Exposures, and Vulnerabilities

Global mean surface temperature in 2020 was 1.2°C above the 1850–1900 baseline. The number of people exposed to extreme heat increased by 125 million between 2000–2004 and 2016–2020. Heat-related mortality among adults over 65 rose by 68% over the same period, reaching an estimated 345,000 deaths in 2019. The highest burdens were observed in India, China, and sub-Saharan Africa.

Climate suitability for Vibrio cholerae and dengue virus transmission increased by 12% and 15%, respectively, compared with the 1950s. The transmission season for malaria in highland areas of Africa lengthened by 39% since 1950. Wildfire exposure increased in 134 countries, with the western United States, Australia, and the Mediterranean basin experiencing the most dramatic rises.

3.2 Adaptation, Planning, and Resilience

Despite these escalating risks, adaptation remains grossly inadequate. Of 192 countries, only 45 (23%) had a national health and climate change plan. Sixty-nine percent of NAPs failed to mention health at all. Urban green space—a critical buffer against heat and pollution—decreased in 78% of surveyed cities. Only 0.3% of global climate finance was allocated to health-specific adaptation, amounting to approximately $5 billion annually—a fraction of the estimated $100 billion needed.

3.3 Mitigation Actions and Health Co-Benefits

Progress on mitigation remains insufficient. Fossil fuel combustion accounted for 65% of global CO₂ emissions in 2020. However, renewable energy capacity grew by 45% between 2015 and 2020. The health co-benefits of a rapid energy transition are substantial: phasing out coal would prevent an estimated 1.2 million premature deaths annually from air pollution. Yet only 18% of NDCs included health co-benefit quantification.

3.4 Economics and Finance

The economic costs of climate-related health impacts are rising. Heat-related labor productivity losses reached 295 billion hours in 2020, equivalent to $800 billion in potential income. Climate-related disasters caused $210 billion in damages, with health systems bearing a significant share. Meanwhile, fossil fuel subsidies totaled $5.9 trillion in 2020—more than 1,000 times the amount allocated to health adaptation.

3.5 Public and Political Engagement

Media coverage of health and climate change increased by 96% between 2018 and 2020, largely driven by the COVID-19 pandemic and extreme weather events. However, engagement remains uneven: 80% of coverage originated in high-income countries. UN General Assembly debates mentioned health and climate change in only 12% of speeches.

4. Discussion

The 2021 Lancet Countdown findings constitute an unambiguous code red for a healthy future. Three overarching conclusions emerge.

First, the health impacts of climate change are accelerating and are already being felt on every continent. The 68% increase in heat-related mortality among older adults is particularly alarming, as aging populations in tropical and subtropical regions face compounding vulnerabilities. Our estimates are likely conservative, given that heat-related deaths are systematically underreported, especially in low-resource settings.

Second, adaptation efforts are dangerously insufficient. The finding that 69% of national adaptation plans omit health is a profound policy failure. Health systems must be at the center of adaptation planning, not an afterthought. The disparity between fossil fuel subsidies ($5.9 trillion) and health adaptation finance ($5 billion) reveals a fundamental misalignment of global priorities. Governments are effectively subsidizing the causes of climate change while underfunding the solutions.

Third, the health co-benefits of mitigation provide a powerful argument for accelerated action. The 1.2 million premature deaths that could be prevented annually through coal phase-out represent a tangible, near-term return on climate investment. Framing climate action as a health intervention may mobilize constituencies—especially health professionals—that have historically been peripheral to climate politics.

Our findings are consistent with other major assessments, including the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2021) and the WHO's 2021 COP26 report. However, the Lancet Countdown's unique contribution is its annual, indicator-based tracking, which allows for accountability and trend analysis. Limitations include reliance on modeled estimates, data gaps in low-income countries, and the challenge of capturing indirect health effects such as mental health impacts, food insecurity, and displacement.

The policy implications are clear. First, health must be integrated into all climate policies, including NDCs, NAPs, and recovery packages. Second, climate finance must be redirected toward health adaptation, with a target of at least 10% of total climate finance. Third, fossil fuel subsidies must be phased out and replaced with investments in renewable energy, public transportation, and active travel. Fourth, health systems must be strengthened to withstand climate shocks, including heat action plans, early warning systems, and climate-resilient infrastructure.

5. Conclusion

The 2021 Lancet Countdown report delivers a sobering verdict: climate change is already harming human health at a scale that demands urgent, transformative action. The code red is not a metaphor—it is a call to action. Every indicator we track points in the same direction: the window for equitable, health-centered climate action is closing rapidly.

Yet there is cause for cautious optimism. The rapid development of COVID-19 vaccines demonstrated that science, policy, and public will can converge to address global health emergencies. The same mobilization is needed for climate change. Health professionals, policymakers, and citizens must demand that climate action be treated as a health imperative. The health co-benefits of mitigation—clean air, active lifestyles, nutritious food—offer a compelling vision of a healthier, more equitable future.

The 2021 report is the most comprehensive assessment of its kind, but its true value will be measured by the actions it inspires. As the world recovers from COVID-19 and prepares for COP26 and beyond, the choice is stark: continue on a path of escalating climate health harms, or pivot toward a healthy, sustainable, and just future. The code red is flashing. The time to act is now.

title: Antibacterial activities against rice bacterial leaf blight and tomato bacterial wilt of 2-mercapto-5-substituted-1,3,4-oxadiazole/thiadiazole derivatives
text: Rice bacterial leaf blight and tomato bacterial wilt, caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae and Ralstonia solanacearum, respectively, are among the most devastating bacterial diseases threatening global rice and tomato production. Chemical control remains a primary strategy; however, the widespread use of conventional bactericides has led to resistant strains and environmental concerns, creating an urgent need for novel antibacterial agents. 1,3,4-Oxadiazole and 1,3,4-thiadiazole derivatives represent privileged scaffolds in medicinal and agrochemical chemistry, exhibiting diverse biological activities including antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral effects. Introduction of a mercapto group at the 2-position and various substituents at the 5-position of these heterocycles may modulate their physicochemical properties and enhance bioactivity. Nevertheless, systematic studies on 2-mercapto-5-substituted-1,3,4-oxadiazole/thiadiazole derivatives against these two phytopathogens remain limited.
