In this study, a series of such derivatives was synthesized and evaluated for their antibacterial activities, aiming to provide promising lead compounds for the development of novel bactericides.

title: Aeromonas shuberti as a cause of multi-organ necrosis in internal organs of Nile tilapia, Oreochromis niloticus
text:
Results and Discussion

Experimentally infected Nile tilapia exhibited 80% cumulative mortality within 7 days post-injection (dpi) at a dose of 1×10⁷ CFU/fish, compared to 0% in PBS-injected controls (p < 0.001). Gross pathology revealed marked splenomegaly (spleen index 2.4 ± 0.3 vs. 0.9 ± 0.1 in controls) and pale, friable livers with multifocal hemorrhagic foci. Histopathology showed extensive coagulative necrosis in the liver (65 ± 8% of examined fields), kidney (48 ± 6%), and spleen (57 ± 9%), accompanied by macrophage infiltration and melanomacrophage center hyperplasia. *A. shuberti* was re-isolated from all necrotic organs, fulfilling Koch's postulates, with mean bacterial loads of 3.2×10⁶ CFU/g in liver and 1.8×10⁶ CFU/g in kidney at 5 dpi. Hemato-biochemical analysis showed elevated AST (312 ± 24 U/L), ALT (198 ± 17 U/L), and creatinine (2.1 ± 0.2 mg/dL) relative to controls (p < 0.01), indicating hepatic and renal dysfunction. These findings establish *A. shuberti* as a highly virulent pathogen for *O. niloticus*, causing systemic multi-organ necrosis. The severity and reproducibility of the model support its use for future vaccine and antimicrobial trials.

title: Bank systemic risk around COVID-19: A cross-country analysis
text:
Bank systemic risk around COVID-19: A cross-country analysis

Abstract

This paper investigates the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on bank systemic risk across 42 countries over the period from January 2019 to December 2021. Using a panel dataset of 1,260 listed banks and employing the conditional value-at-risk (CoVaR) and marginal expected shortfall (MES) as measures of systemic risk, we examine how pandemic severity, government policy responses, and bank-specific characteristics influence the contribution of individual banks to systemic distress. Our results show that systemic risk increased sharply during the first wave of COVID-19, particularly in countries with higher infection rates and stricter containment measures. Banks with lower capital adequacy, higher loan-to-deposit ratios, and greater reliance on short-term wholesale funding exhibited larger increases in systemic risk contributions. Government fiscal and monetary interventions mitigated but did not fully offset these effects. The findings underscore the importance of macroprudential buffers and international coordination in managing systemic risk during global health crises.

Keywords: COVID-19; systemic risk; CoVaR; MES; bank regulation; cross-country analysis

1. Introduction

The COVID-19 pandemic triggered an unprecedented global economic shock. Unlike the 2008 financial crisis, which originated within the financial sector, the pandemic was an exogenous health shock that rapidly transmitted to the real economy and then to banking systems worldwide. Governments responded with a combination of lockdowns, fiscal stimulus, and monetary easing. While these measures supported households and firms, they also altered bank risk profiles through increased credit demand, deteriorating asset quality, and compressed interest margins.

Systemic risk—the risk that the failure of one or more banks triggers widespread instability in the financial system—became a central concern. Prior research has examined systemic risk during the global financial crisis and the European sovereign debt crisis. However, evidence on how a global pandemic affects bank systemic risk across countries remains limited. This paper addresses that gap by asking three questions: (1) Did bank systemic risk increase during COVID-19? (2) Which bank-level and country-level factors explain cross-sectional variation in systemic risk changes? (3) Did government policy responses attenuate or amplify systemic risk?

We contribute to the literature in two ways. First, we provide cross-country evidence using a consistent systemic risk measure. Second, we link pandemic severity and policy responses to bank-level systemic risk contributions, offering policy implications for macroprudential regulation.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Data

We construct a panel of 1,260 publicly listed banks from 42 countries covering January 2019 to December 2021. Bank financial data are obtained from a hypothetical global banking database. Country-level pandemic data (daily confirmed cases and deaths per million) are simulated based on a plausible epidemiological pattern. Policy response stringency is measured using a containment and health index, and fiscal stimulus is measured as a percentage of GDP. After removing observations with missing values, the final sample contains 38,640 bank-month observations.

2.2 Measures of Systemic Risk

We use two market-based measures. First, conditional value-at-risk (CoVaR) captures the value-at-risk of the banking system conditional on a bank being in distress. We estimate CoVaR using quantile regressions of system returns on bank returns and state variables. The contribution of bank *i* to systemic risk is ΔCoVaR = CoVaR_{system|i in distress} − CoVaR_{system|i in median state}. Second, marginal expected shortfall (MES) measures the expected loss of a bank when the system is in its worst 5% of outcomes. Both measures are estimated monthly using daily stock returns.

2.3 Empirical Model

We estimate the following panel regression:

ΔCoVaR_{i,c,t} = α + β1 PandemicSeverity_{c,t} + β2 PolicyResponse_{c,t} + γ X_{i,t-1} + δ Z_{c,t-1} + μ_i + λ_t + ε_{i,c,t}

where *i* indexes banks, *c* countries, and *t* months. PandemicSeverity is the log of new cases per million. PolicyResponse includes containment stringency and fiscal stimulus. X is a vector of bank characteristics (size, capital adequacy, loan-to-deposit ratio, wholesale funding ratio, profitability). Z includes country macroeconomic controls (GDP growth, unemployment, inflation). μ_i and λ_t are bank and month fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered at the bank and country levels.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Baseline Results

Table 1 reports baseline estimates. Pandemic severity is positively and significantly associated with ΔCoVaR. A one-standard-deviation increase in log new cases per million raises a bank’s systemic risk contribution by 0.18 standard deviations (p < 0.01). The effect on MES is similar (0.14, p < 0.05). Containment stringency also has a positive coefficient, suggesting that stricter lockdowns initially increased systemic risk, likely through heightened uncertainty and liquidity hoarding. Fiscal stimulus, by contrast, is negatively associated with systemic risk, consistent with its role in stabilizing borrower balance sheets.

3.2 Bank Characteristics

Banks with lower Tier 1 capital ratios exhibit larger increases in ΔCoVaR. A one-percentage-point lower capital ratio is associated with a 0.06 standard deviation higher ΔCoVaR. Higher loan-to-deposit ratios and greater short-term wholesale funding reliance also amplify systemic risk. Bank size is positively but weakly significant, indicating that larger banks contribute more to systemic risk during crises. Profitability (return on assets) is negatively associated with systemic risk, though the effect is modest.

3.3 Country Heterogeneity

We split countries by income level and pandemic severity. The effect of pandemic severity on systemic risk is stronger in emerging markets than in advanced economies. This may reflect weaker fiscal capacity, less credible monetary policy, and thinner capital buffers. Among advanced economies, countries with higher pre-pandemic household debt experienced larger systemic risk increases.

3.4 Dynamic Effects

Event-study estimates show that systemic risk rose sharply in March 2020, peaked in April 2020, and declined gradually thereafter. By December 2021, ΔCoVaR remained slightly above pre-pandemic levels in most countries, suggesting persistent fragility. Policy responses had lagged effects: fiscal stimulus reduced systemic risk with a two-month delay, while containment stringency’s positive effect faded after three months.

4. Discussion

Our findings confirm that COVID-19 significantly increased bank systemic risk worldwide. The results are consistent with the “real economy channel” of systemic risk: a health shock reduces corporate cash flows, raises loan defaults, and weakens bank balance sheets, which in turn amplifies system-wide distress. The finding that lower-capitalized and wholesale-funding-dependent banks contributed more to systemic risk supports the Basel III emphasis on capital and liquidity buffers.

The positive coefficient on containment stringency may appear counterintuitive. However, lockdowns initially increased economic uncertainty and market volatility, which are direct inputs to CoVaR and MES. Over time, as infections fell and policy support took effect, this effect reversed. Fiscal stimulus was more effective in reducing systemic risk than monetary policy alone, highlighting the importance of coordinated fiscal-monetary responses.

Cross-country heterogeneity suggests that emerging markets face greater systemic risk during global health crises. International financial institutions should therefore tailor macroprudential support to country-specific conditions. Our results also imply that pre-pandemic capital and liquidity buffers were insufficient for a shock of this magnitude, arguing for a countercyclical buffer that is built up during good times and released during crises.

Several limitations apply. First, our systemic risk measures rely on market data, which may overstate risk for banks with limited trading activity. Second, the pandemic severity variable may suffer from reporting biases. Third, we cannot fully rule out omitted variable bias, although bank and month fixed effects mitigate this concern.

5. Conclusion

This paper provides cross-country evidence that COVID-19 significantly increased bank systemic risk, with effects varying by bank capital, funding structure, and country income level. Government fiscal stimulus attenuated systemic risk, while containment measures had short-term amplifying effects. The findings support the use of macroprudential buffers and coordinated policy responses to manage systemic risk during global shocks. Future research should examine the long-term effects of pandemic-era credit guarantees and loan moratoria on bank risk-taking and financial stability.

title: Acupuncture for hearing loss after traumatic brain injury: A protocol for systematic review of randomized controlled trial
text:
Acupuncture for hearing loss after traumatic brain injury: A protocol for systematic review of randomized controlled trials

 Abstract

Background: Hearing loss is a common yet frequently overlooked sequela of traumatic brain injury (TBI), affecting an estimated 20–40% of patients with moderate-to-severe injury. Conventional management, including hearing aids and cochlear implantation, is limited by cost, invasiveness, and variable outcomes. Acupuncture has been increasingly applied in China and elsewhere for sensorineural hearing loss, but its efficacy specifically in post-TBI hearing loss remains uncertain. No systematic review has yet addressed this population.

Objective: This protocol describes the design of a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for hearing loss following TBI.

Methods: We will search PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and SinoMed from inception to December 2025, without language restrictions. Randomized controlled trials comparing acupuncture (manual, electroacupuncture, or auricular acupuncture), alone or as an adjunct to conventional therapy, versus sham acupuncture, no treatment, or conventional therapy alone in adults and children with TBI-related hearing loss will be included. The primary outcome will be mean change in pure-tone average (PTA) at 0.5–4 kHz. Secondary outcomes include speech discrimination score, tinnitus handicap inventory, auditory brainstem response (ABR) wave V latency, quality of life, and adverse events. Two reviewers will independently screen records, extract data, and assess risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Data synthesis will use RevMan 5.4; continuous outcomes will be pooled as mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity will be assessed with the I² statistic, and publication bias with funnel plots and Egger's test where ≥10 studies are available. Subgroup analyses will explore acupuncture modality, TBI severity, and timing of intervention. The certainty of evidence will be graded using GRADE.

Discussion: This review will provide the first synthesis of evidence on acupuncture for post-TBI hearing loss and will inform both clinical practice and future trial design.

Trial registration: PROSPERO CRD42025123456 (invented for illustrative purposes).

Keywords: Acupuncture; traumatic brain injury; hearing loss; sensorineural hearing loss; systematic review; protocol; randomized controlled trial; meta-analysis

 1. Introduction

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of disability worldwide, with an estimated global incidence of 69 million cases annually. While motor and cognitive deficits dominate clinical attention, sensory impairments—particularly hearing loss—are increasingly recognized as important determinants of long-term outcome. Post-traumatic hearing loss may arise from temporal bone fracture, labyrinthine concussion, shearing injury to the cochlear nerve, or secondary inflammatory and ischemic damage to the cochlea. Cohort studies suggest that 20–40% of patients with moderate-to-severe TBI experience persistent hearing impairment, and even mild TBI has been associated with auditory processing difficulties.

Current management options include corticosteroid therapy in the acute phase, hearing aids, assistive listening devices, and cochlear implantation for severe-to-profound loss. However, corticosteroids have uncertain benefit in trauma-related cochlear injury, hearing aids provide only symptomatic amplification, and implantation is invasive and costly. Consequently, many patients seek complementary therapies, including acupuncture.

Acupuncture has been used for auditory disorders in East Asia for centuries, and modern studies have explored its effects on sensorineural hearing loss of various etiologies. Proposed mechanisms include increased cochlear blood flow, modulation of neurotrophic factors such as BDNF, anti-inflammatory effects, and modulation of central auditory processing via somatosensory-auditory interactions. Several small RCTs have reported improvements in pure-tone thresholds and tinnitus severity after acupuncture in patients with sudden sensorineural hearing loss and noise-induced hearing loss. However, evidence specific to TBI-related hearing loss is sparse, heterogeneous in design, and has not been systematically appraised.

To our knowledge, no systematic review has specifically evaluated acupuncture for hearing loss after TBI. We therefore designed this protocol to outline a rigorous systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, aiming to determine whether acupuncture, compared with sham acupuncture, no treatment, or conventional therapy alone, improves auditory outcomes in this population, and to characterize its safety profile.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Study registration and reporting

This protocol will be conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (version 6.5) and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) 2015 statement. The final review will be reported according to PRISMA 2020. The protocol has been registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025123456, invented).

 2.2 Eligibility criteria

Types of studies: Randomized controlled trials, including parallel-group, crossover (first phase only), and cluster-randomized trials. Quasi-randomized trials will be excluded.

Types of participants: Adults and children (≥6 years) with hearing loss attributed to TBI of any severity, diagnosed by a physician according to accepted criteria (e.g., Glasgow Coma Scale at injury, neuroimaging, or clinical history). Hearing loss will be confirmed by pure-tone audiometry (PTA > 25 dB HL at any frequency 0.5–4 kHz) or auditory brainstem response. Participants with pre-existing hearing loss unrelated to TBI will be excluded.

Types of interventions: Acupuncture modalities including manual acupuncture, electroacupuncture, auricular acupuncture, scalp acupuncture, and laser acupuncture. Interventions may be used alone or as an adjunct to conventional treatment (e.g., corticosteroids, vasodilators, neurotrophic agents, hearing aids). Trials will be excluded if acupuncture is combined with another complementary therapy in a way that prevents isolation of its effects.

Types of comparators: Sham acupuncture (non-penetrating or off-point needling), no treatment/waiting list, or conventional therapy alone.

Types of outcomes: 
- *Primary:* Mean change in pure-tone average (PTA) at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 kHz, measured in dB HL.
- *Secondary:* Speech discrimination score (%), tinnitus handicap inventory (THI), auditory brainstem response (ABR) wave V latency, quality of life (e.g., SF-36, WHOQOL-BREF), and adverse events.

 2.3 Search strategy

We will search PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and SinoMed from database inception to December 2025. The search will combine MeSH terms and free-text words: ("acupuncture" OR "electroacupuncture" OR "auricular acupuncture" OR "scalp acupuncture") AND ("traumatic brain injury" OR "TBI" OR "head injury" OR "craniocerebral trauma") AND ("hearing loss" OR "hearing impairment" OR "sensorineural hearing loss" OR "deafness" OR "tinnitus"). Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews will be hand-searched. Clinical trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov, ChiCTR) will be searched for ongoing or unpublished trials.

 2.4 Study selection and data extraction

Two reviewers (invented initials: L.W. and Y.C.) will independently screen titles and abstracts, then full texts, using EndNote 21. Disagreements will be resolved by a third reviewer (H.Z.). A standardized Excel form will be used to extract: study characteristics (author, year, country, design, sample size), participant characteristics (age, sex, TBI severity, duration of hearing loss), intervention details (acupuncture type, acupoints, sessions, duration), comparator, outcomes, and adverse events. Authors will be contacted for missing data.

 2.5 Risk of bias and certainty assessment

Risk of bias will be assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool across five domains: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Certainty of evidence will be evaluated using GRADE, considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias.

 2.6 Data synthesis and analysis

Statistical analysis will be performed in RevMan 5.4 and Stata 17. Continuous outcomes will be pooled as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) when the same scale is used, or standardized mean differences (SMD) when scales differ. Dichotomous outcomes (e.g., adverse events) will be pooled as risk ratios (RR). Heterogeneity will be quantified with the I² statistic; I² > 50% will be considered substantial, and a random-effects model will be used in such cases. If ≥10 studies are included, funnel plots and Egger's test will assess publication bias. Subgroup analyses will examine acupuncture modality, TBI severity (mild vs. moderate-to-severe), and timing of intervention (acute vs. chronic). Sensitivity analyses will exclude studies with high risk of bias.

 3. Results

As this is a protocol, no results are available. Based on a preliminary scoping search conducted in November 2025, we anticipate identifying approximately 320 records, of which an estimated 12–18 RCTs (total N ≈ 1,100–1,500 participants) will meet eligibility criteria. We expect most trials to originate from China, with a smaller number from South Korea, Germany, and the United States. Anticipated participant mean age will be 35–50 years, with a male predominance consistent with TBI epidemiology. Intervention durations are expected to range from 2 to 12 weeks, with 10–30 sessions of manual or electroacupuncture. We hypothesize that acupuncture, compared with control, may be associated with a mean improvement in PTA of approximately 5–10 dB HL and a reduction in THI of 8–15 points, though these estimates are speculative and will be replaced by pooled effect estimates in the completed review. Adverse events are expected to be minor (transient pain, minor bleeding, dizziness), with an anticipated incidence of 5–10%.

 4. Discussion

This protocol outlines the first systematic review specifically targeting acupuncture for hearing loss after TBI. The rationale is grounded in the unmet need for non-invasive, accessible therapies in this population and in preliminary evidence suggesting auditory benefits of acupuncture in other forms of sensorineural hearing loss.

Several methodological challenges are anticipated. First, heterogeneity in acupuncture protocols—point selection (e.g., SJ5, SJ17, GB2, LI4, local scalp points), needling depth, stimulation frequency, and session number—may limit pooling. Second, blinding is difficult in acupuncture trials; while sham needling can mitigate this, the adequacy of blinding will be assessed carefully. Third, outcome measurement varies widely, with some trials reporting only categorical improvement ("effective" vs. "ineffective") rather than continuous audiometric data; we will attempt to convert or exclude such data as appropriate. Fourth, TBI severity and time since injury may modify treatment response, and subgroup analyses may be underpowered.

Strengths of this review include a comprehensive search without language restrictions, independent duplicate screening, use of RoB 2 and GRADE, and inclusion of safety outcomes. Limitations include the anticipated predominance of small, single-center trials with possible publication bias, and the likelihood that most evidence will be of low or very low certainty.

The findings will have implications for clinicians counseling patients with post-TBI hearing loss, for researchers designing future RCTs (including recommendations on outcome standardization and sham design), and for guideline developers. We will also identify research gaps, such as the need for trials in pediatric populations and in patients with blast-related TBI.

 5. Conclusion

This systematic review will provide the first comprehensive appraisal of acupuncture for hearing loss following traumatic brain injury. By synthesizing available RCT evidence and grading its certainty, the review will clarify whether acupuncture offers meaningful auditory benefit and will inform clinical decision-making and future trial design. We anticipate that the results will highlight both the potential of acupuncture as an adjunctive therapy and the urgent need for larger, methodologically rigorous trials in this understudied population.

title: Dissemination of blaNDM-5 via IncX3 plasmids in carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae among humans and in the environment in an intensive vegetable cultivation area in eastern China
text: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) pose a serious threat to public health, yet the transmission dynamics of carbapenem resistance genes in vegetable cultivation areas remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the prevalence and dissemination of blaNDM-5 in CRE recovered from humans and the environment in an intensive vegetable cultivation area in eastern China. A total of 23 blaNDM-5-positive CRE isolates were obtained from clinical, vegetable, soil, and water samples. Whole-genome sequencing and conjugation experiments revealed that blaNDM-5 was predominantly carried by IncX3 plasmids, which were highly conjugative and structurally conserved. Phylogenetic analysis indicated close genetic relatedness among isolates from different sources, suggesting cross-species and cross-environment transmission. Our findings demonstrate that IncX3 plasmids serve as key vectors for the dissemination of blaNDM-5 among humans and the environment in vegetable cultivation areas, highlighting the need for integrated surveillance under the One Health framework.

title: Effect of income and energy efficiency on natural capital demand
text:
Effect of income and energy efficiency on natural capital demand

Abstract

This study investigates how income levels and energy efficiency jointly influence natural capital demand across 42 economies over the period 2005–2022. Using a panel dataset of constructed indicators for natural capital demand, GDP per capita, energy intensity, renewable energy share, and urbanization, we employ fixed-effects and threshold regression models. Results indicate an inverted U-shaped relationship between income and natural capital demand, consistent with the environmental Kuznets curve hypothesis, with the turning point at approximately USD 28,500 per capita. Energy efficiency improvements significantly reduce natural capital demand, and the marginal effect is stronger in high-income economies. A 10% reduction in energy intensity is associated with a 2.7% decline in the natural capital demand index. The interaction term between income and energy efficiency is negative, suggesting that efficiency gains amplify the dematerialization effect of income growth. Policy implications emphasize coupling efficiency standards with income-sensitive resource governance.

Keywords: natural capital demand; income; energy efficiency; environmental Kuznets curve; panel analysis

1. Introduction

Natural capital—forests, fisheries, minerals, water, and atmospheric services—underpins economic activity but is increasingly stressed by rising consumption. A central question is whether economic growth inevitably raises natural capital demand or whether decoupling is possible through efficiency gains. The environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) literature suggests that resource pressure first rises with income and later declines (Grossman & Krueger, 1995). However, evidence remains mixed, and the role of energy efficiency as a moderating mechanism is underexplored.

Energy efficiency lowers the energy and material inputs required per unit of output, potentially reducing the ecological footprint of growth. Yet rebound effects may offset savings, particularly in lower-income economies where efficiency improvements lower effective costs and stimulate demand. This paper addresses two questions: (1) Does income exhibit an inverted U-shaped effect on natural capital demand? (2) Does energy efficiency reduce natural capital demand, and does its effect vary by income level?

We contribute by constructing a composite Natural Capital Demand Index (NCDI) and estimating panel models with interaction and threshold specifications. The findings inform policies aiming at resource decoupling.

2. Materials and Methods

*2.1 Data and variables*

We assemble a balanced panel of 42 countries from 2005 to 2022 (756 observations). The dependent variable, NCDI, is a composite index (0–100) derived from per capita ecological footprint, freshwater withdrawal, and timber harvest, normalized and weighted equally. Data are constructed from publicly available national accounts and environmental statistics, with missing values imputed by linear interpolation.

Independent variables:
- Income: GDP per capita (constant 2015 USD, logged).
- Energy efficiency: inverse of energy intensity (GDP per unit of primary energy), logged.
- Renewable share: percentage of renewable energy in total final consumption.
- Urbanization: urban population share.
- Trade openness: exports plus imports as share of GDP.

*2.2 Model specification*

We estimate:
NCDI_it = α + β1 lnIncome_it + β2 (lnIncome_it)^2 + β3 lnEE_it + β4 (lnIncome × lnEE)_it + γX_it + μ_i + λ_t + ε_it
where μ_i and λ_t are country and year fixed effects, and X is a vector of controls. A threshold model tests whether the energy efficiency coefficient differs above and below median income.

*2.3 Estimation*

Fixed-effects OLS with cluster-robust standard errors is used. Endogeneity of income is addressed via lagged instruments (two-step GMM) as robustness. Threshold significance is tested via bootstrap (1,000 replications).

3. Results and Analysis

*3.1 Baseline results*

The linear income term is positive (β1 = 4.82, p < 0.01) and the squared term negative (β2 = −0.29, p < 0.01), confirming an inverted U-shape. The turning point is USD 28,500 (2015 constant). Energy efficiency has a negative coefficient (β3 = −0.61, p < 0.01): a 10% improvement in efficiency reduces NCDI by 2.7%. The interaction term is negative (β4 = −0.14, p < 0.05), implying that efficiency reinforces the dematerialization effect at higher incomes.

*3.2 Threshold and robustness*

The threshold model identifies a break at USD 12,000. Below it, efficiency elasticity is −0.21; above it, −0.48. GMM results remain consistent, though the interaction term weakens slightly (β4 = −0.11, p < 0.10). Renewable share and urbanization are negative and positive respectively, both significant.

4. Discussion

The inverted U-shape supports the EKC for natural capital, but the turning point is high, implying that many middle-income economies remain on the rising segment. Energy efficiency emerges as a robust lever: its negative coefficient is consistent with dematerialization, and the stronger effect in high-income economies suggests that efficiency policies work best when institutional and infrastructural conditions are mature.

The negative interaction implies that income growth and efficiency improvements are complements, not substitutes. In low-income economies, efficiency gains may be offset by rebound effects and scale expansion, explaining the weaker elasticity. This nuances the optimistic decoupling narrative: efficiency alone may not suffice before income thresholds are reached.

Limitations include the composite nature of NCDI and potential omitted variables such as governance quality. Future work should disaggregate natural capital types and test nonlinear efficiency effects.

5. Conclusion

Income and energy efficiency jointly shape natural capital demand. The relationship between income and demand is inverted U-shaped, while energy efficiency consistently reduces demand, especially at higher income levels. Policies should therefore combine stringent efficiency standards with income-sensitive resource pricing and protection measures. For lower-income economies, complementary instruments—renewable deployment, urban planning, and trade governance—are needed to avoid lock-in to resource-intensive growth. Decoupling natural capital demand from income is feasible but conditional on efficiency and institutional thresholds.

title: Defining compassionate nursing care
text:
Compassionate nursing care is widely regarded as a cornerstone of high-quality healthcare and a core professional value in nursing. It is associated with improved patient satisfaction, enhanced emotional well-being, greater adherence to treatment, and stronger nurse–patient relationships. Despite its centrality, compassion remains a contested and ambiguously defined concept in nursing research and practice. Existing definitions often overlap with related constructs such as empathy, sympathy, caring, and person-centred care, which creates conceptual confusion and limits the development of clear educational and assessment strategies.

This ambiguity has practical consequences. In clinical settings, compassion is frequently assumed to be an innate disposition rather than a teachable competence, and it is often measured through patient satisfaction surveys that capture only partial dimensions of the concept. Moreover, cultural, organisational, and relational factors shape how compassion is expressed and perceived, yet these contextual influences are rarely integrated into definitional frameworks. As a result, nurses, educators, and policymakers lack a shared understanding of what compassionate nursing care actually entails and how it can be recognised, taught, and evaluated.

The aim of this paper is to develop a conceptually robust definition of compassionate nursing care that distinguishes it from adjacent concepts and captures its multidimensional nature. Drawing on a critical synthesis of existing theoretical and empirical literature, the paper examines the core attributes, antecedents, and consequences of compassionate care in nursing. By clarifying the concept, this paper seeks to provide a foundation for future research, curriculum design, and clinical practice, and to support more precise measurement of compassion in nursing care delivery.

title: Effects of Soil Conditions on Root Rot of Soybean Caused by Fusarium graminearum
text:
Results and Discussion

Across two seasons, root rot severity was highest in compacted, poorly drained plots and lowest in well-drained, loamy sand. In 2022, mean disease severity (0–4 scale) reached 3.1 ± 0.3 in compacted clay loam versus 1.2 ± 0.2 in loamy sand (*P* < 0.001). Soil water content above 28% (w/w) for 72 h increased lesion length on taproots by 64% relative to controls (18.7 vs. 11.4 mm; *P* = 0.004). *Fusarium graminearum* recovery from roots averaged 78% in saturated soils compared with 31% in drained soils. Soil pH had a weaker effect: severity declined from 2.8 at pH 5.2 to 1.9 at pH 7.1 (*r* = −0.62, *P* = 0.012), suggesting acidity exacerbates infection. Inoculum density correlated positively with disease incidence (*r* = 0.74, *P* < 0.001), with 42% incidence at 10² CFU g⁻¹ soil rising to 89% at 10⁴ CFU g⁻¹.

These results indicate that soil physical conditions, particularly waterlogging and compaction, are stronger drivers of root rot than pH alone, likely because prolonged saturation reduces oxygen availability, stressing roots and enhancing fungal colonization. The interaction between high moisture and high inoculum density produced the greatest severity (3.6 ± 0.2), implying that management should prioritize drainage and compaction alleviation alongside inoculum reduction. Limitations include the use of a single susceptible cultivar and two seasons; further work should test resistant genotypes and field-scale drainage treatments.

title: Peer-led diabetes self-management programme for community-dwelling older people in China: study protocol for a quasi-experimental design
text:
Peer-led diabetes self-management programme for community-dwelling older people in China: study protocol for a quasi-experimental design

Abstract

Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is highly prevalent among community-dwelling older adults in China, yet access to structured self-management education remains limited. Peer-led interventions may offer a culturally acceptable and cost-effective alternative, but evidence from mainland Chinese community settings is scarce. Objectives: This study protocol aims to evaluate the feasibility and preliminary effectiveness of a peer-led diabetes self-management programme (PD-SMP) for community-dwelling older people in China. Methods: A quasi-experimental, non-equivalent control group design will be adopted in two urban communities in Nanjing. A total of 120 participants aged ≥60 years with T2DM will be recruited: 60 in the intervention community and 60 in the control community. The intervention group will receive a 12-week peer-led programme delivered by trained older peer leaders, comprising weekly group sessions on diet, medication adherence, foot care, physical activity, and emotional coping, plus monthly telephone follow-ups. The control group will receive usual community care. Primary outcomes are glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) and diabetes self-management behaviour. Secondary outcomes include self-efficacy, health-related quality of life, and depressive symptoms. Data will be collected at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months. Results: It is hypothesised that the intervention group will show a mean reduction in HbA1c of 0.6% and a significant improvement in self-management scores compared with controls at 6 months. Conclusion: This protocol provides a culturally tailored, community-based model that may inform scalable diabetes self-management strategies for older Chinese adults.

Keywords: type 2 diabetes; peer education; self-management; older adults; community health; China; quasi-experimental design

1. Introduction

China has the largest population of adults with diabetes worldwide, and more than half are aged 60 years or above. In community settings, older adults with type 2 diabetes often face inadequate disease knowledge, low medication adherence, poor dietary control, and limited physical activity. Although hospital-based education is available, it is usually brief, disease-focused, and difficult to sustain after discharge. Community health service centres are expected to provide chronic disease management, but staffing shortages and heavy administrative workloads constrain individualised support.

Peer-led education has been proposed as a complementary strategy. Peer leaders are non-professional individuals with similar age, culture, and disease experience who are trained to deliver structured support. Systematic reviews suggest that peer-led diabetes self-management education can improve glycaemic control, self-efficacy, and psychosocial outcomes. However, most evidence comes from Western countries, and the few Chinese studies have mainly targeted younger adults, urban employees, or hospital outpatients. Older community dwellers may respond differently because of lower health literacy, stronger family involvement, and preferences for group-based, oral, and practical learning.

This study protocol describes a quasi-experimental trial designed to evaluate a peer-led diabetes self-management programme (PD-SMP) for community-dwelling older people in China. The aims are: (1) to assess the feasibility of recruiting and training older peer leaders; (2) to examine the preliminary effects of PD-SMP on glycaemic control and self-management behaviour; and (3) to explore changes in self-efficacy, quality of life, and depressive symptoms.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study design and setting

A quasi-experimental, non-equivalent control group design will be used in two comparable urban communities in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province. Randomisation at the community level is not feasible because of administrative and ethical considerations. The intervention community will receive PD-SMP plus usual care; the control community will receive usual care alone.

2.2 Participants

Inclusion criteria: age ≥60 years; diagnosed with T2DM for at least one year; residing in the community for ≥6 months; able to communicate in Mandarin; and willing to provide informed consent. Exclusion criteria: severe cognitive impairment; terminal illness; severe hearing or visual impairment; or participation in another diabetes education programme within the previous six months. A sample of 120 participants (60 per group) will be recruited through community health records and health education sessions. This sample size is sufficient to detect a 0.6% between-group difference in HbA1c with 80% power at a two-sided 5% significance level, assuming a standard deviation of 1.1% and 15% attrition.

2.3 Peer leader selection and training

In the intervention community, six older adults with T2DM and good self-management will be nominated by community physicians and health workers. They will complete a 20-hour training programme over four weeks, covering diabetes pathophysiology, nutrition, medication safety, foot care, exercise prescription, communication skills, group facilitation, and ethical boundaries. Two community nurses will supervise and provide monthly refresher sessions.

2.4 Intervention

The PD-SMP is a 12-week manualised programme. Weekly 60-minute group sessions will be held in the community activity room, with 8–10 participants per group. Sessions follow a structured curriculum: weeks 1–2, understanding diabetes and goal setting; weeks 3–4, healthy eating and portion control; weeks 5–6, medication adherence and monitoring; weeks 7–8, physical activity and foot care; weeks 9–10, stress management and emotional coping; weeks 11–12, problem-solving and maintaining behaviour. Peer leaders use pictorial flipcharts, food models, and role-play to accommodate low health literacy. Monthly telephone follow-ups will reinforce goals and identify barriers. Family members are invited to two sessions.

2.5 Control condition

The control group will receive usual community care, including routine blood glucose monitoring, medication prescription, and standard health education leaflets. They will not receive peer-led group sessions or structured follow-up calls.

2.6 Outcome measures

Primary outcomes: HbA1c and diabetes self-management behaviour, measured by the Chinese version of the Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities. Secondary outcomes: self-efficacy (Chinese Diabetes Empowerment Scale), health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L), and depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire-9). Data will be collected at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months by trained research assistants blinded to group allocation.

2.7 Data analysis

Statistical analyses will use SPSS 26.0. Independent t-tests and chi-square tests will compare baseline characteristics. Repeated-measures ANOVA will examine group × time interactions. Missing data will be handled by multiple imputation. A p-value <0.05 will be considered statistically significant. Qualitative interviews with 15 intervention participants and all peer leaders will explore acceptability and implementation barriers, analysed using thematic analysis.

2.8 Ethical considerations

The study will be approved by the Institutional Review Board of Nanjing Medical University. Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants. Peer leaders will receive a modest stipend, and participants will receive a small gift for each assessment.

3. Results and Analysis

As this is a study protocol, no empirical results are yet available. Based on previous peer-led diabetes trials in Chinese and Asian populations, we anticipate the following. At 6 months, the intervention group is expected to show a mean HbA1c reduction of 0.6% from baseline, compared with 0.1% in the control group. The between-group difference is expected to be statistically significant (p < 0.05). Diabetes self-management scores are expected to improve by 1.2 points in the intervention group versus 0.3 points in controls. Self-efficacy and EQ-5D-5L scores are expected to improve modestly, while depressive symptoms may decrease. Process evaluation is expected to show high attendance (≥75%) and high satisfaction among participants. Potential challenges include slower recruitment of male participants and varying literacy levels; these will be addressed through pictorial materials and flexible scheduling.

4. Discussion

This protocol addresses an important gap in community-based diabetes care for older Chinese adults. The peer-led design is culturally congruent: older peer leaders share language, life experience, and social networks with participants, which may reduce stigma and increase trust. The programme also aligns with China’s national policy of strengthening community chronic disease management and promoting healthy ageing.

Several methodological considerations warrant attention. First, the quasi-experimental design limits causal inference because of potential selection bias. However, it is pragmatic in real-world community settings where randomisation is difficult. Second, blinding of participants and peer leaders is impossible, but outcome assessors will be blinded. Third, contamination between communities is possible; the two communities will be geographically separated and served by different health teams. Fourth, the 6-month follow-up may not capture long-term maintenance, so future studies should extend follow-up to 12 months. Finally, the involvement of family members may enhance sustainability, but it also introduces variability that should be measured.

If effective, PD-SMP could be integrated into community health service centres as a low-cost, scalable model. It may also reduce reliance on professional staff and empower older adults as health mentors.

5. Conclusion

This study protocol outlines a quasi-experimental evaluation of a peer-led diabetes self-management programme for community-dwelling older people in China. The programme is culturally tailored, community-based, and potentially sustainable. Findings will inform the design of a future cluster randomised controlled trial and provide practical guidance for community health policy and practice.

title: In-depth secretome analysis of Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici in infected wheat uncovers effector functions
text:
Title: In-depth secretome analysis of *Puccinia striiformis* f. sp. *tritici* in infected wheat uncovers effector functions

Abstract
*Puccinia striiformis* f. sp. *tritici* (Pst) causes wheat stripe rust, a devastating disease threatening global food security. The molecular dialogue between Pst and wheat is mediated by secreted proteins, including effectors that suppress plant immunity. Here, we performed an in-depth secretome analysis of Pst during infection of susceptible wheat cultivar 'Fielder'. Using a combination of transcriptomics, proteomics, and bioinformatics, we identified 1,248 candidate secreted effector proteins (CSEPs). Of these, 87 were highly expressed during early infection stages (12–48 h post-inoculation). Functional characterization of 15 core effectors revealed that four (Pst_Eff1, Pst_Eff4, Pst_Eff9, and Pst_Eff12) significantly suppressed programmed cell death (PCD) triggered by the pro-apoptotic protein BAX in *Nicotiana benthamiana*. Pst_Eff4 and Pst_Eff9 interacted with wheat pathogenesis-related proteins TaPR1 and TaPR5, respectively, inhibiting their antifungal activity. Furthermore, Pst_Eff12 targeted wheat catalase TaCAT1, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. Heterologous expression of Pst_Eff4 in wheat enhanced susceptibility to Pst by 45%. Our findings provide a comprehensive resource of Pst effectors and uncover novel virulence mechanisms, offering potential targets for durable resistance breeding.

Keywords: *Puccinia striiformis* f. sp. *tritici*, secretome, effector, wheat, stripe rust, plant immunity

Introduction
Wheat stripe rust, caused by the obligate biotrophic fungus *Puccinia striiformis* f. sp. *tritici* (Pst), is one of the most destructive diseases of wheat worldwide. Yield losses can reach 70% under favorable conditions. The Pst-wheat interaction involves the secretion of effector proteins that manipulate host cellular processes to facilitate colonization. Despite advances in genomics, the functional repertoire of Pst effectors remains largely unexplored. Here, we conducted an in-depth secretome analysis of Pst during wheat infection, aiming to identify and functionally characterize key effectors involved in virulence.

Materials and Methods
*Plant and fungal materials*: Wheat (*Triticum aestivum* cv. Fielder) was grown at 20°C/18°C (day/night) with 16 h light. Pst race CYR32 was maintained on susceptible wheat. Inoculation was performed on 10-day-old seedlings.

*RNA-seq and secretome prediction*: Total RNA was extracted from infected leaves at 12, 24, 48, 72, and 120 h post-inoculation (hpi). Libraries were sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Transcripts were mapped to the Pst genome (version 2.0). Secreted proteins were predicted using SignalP 5.0, TMHMM 2.0, and TargetP 2.0.

*Proteomics*: Apoplastic fluid was collected from infected leaves at 48 hpi via vacuum infiltration. Proteins were digested and analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Spectra were searched against the Pst predicted secretome.

*Effector cloning and functional assays*: Candidate effectors were cloned into pEarlyGate101 for transient expression in *N. benthamiana*. PCD suppression was assessed by co-expressing with BAX. Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) and bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) were used for protein interaction. ROS was measured by luminol-based assay. Wheat transformation was performed via *Agrobacterium*-mediated immature embryo transformation.

Results
*Identification of Pst secretome*: We identified 1,248 CSEPs, with 87 showing high expression (FPKM > 50) at 12–48 hpi. Proteomics confirmed 214 secreted proteins in the apoplast, including 32 CSEPs. Four effectors (Pst_Eff1, 4, 9, 12) were selected for functional analysis based on high expression and conserved domains.

*Pst_Eff4 and Pst_Eff9 suppress plant immunity*: Transient expression of Pst_Eff4 or Pst_Eff9 in *N. benthamiana* significantly reduced BAX-induced PCD (65% and 58% reduction, respectively). Y2H and BiFC revealed that Pst_Eff4 interacts with wheat TaPR1, and Pst_Eff9 interacts with TaPR5. Recombinant TaPR1 and TaPR5 exhibited antifungal activity against *Fusarium graminearum*, which was inhibited by co-incubation with Pst_Eff4 and Pst_Eff9, respectively.

*Pst_Eff12 targets TaCAT1*: Pst_Eff12 interacted with wheat catalase TaCAT1 in Y2H and co-immunoprecipitation. Transient expression of Pst_Eff12 in wheat protoplasts reduced catalase activity by 40% and increased ROS levels by 2.3-fold. Silencing of TaCAT1 in wheat enhanced Pst infection, confirming its role in defense.

*Pst_Eff4 enhances Pst virulence*: Stable transgenic wheat lines overexpressing Pst_Eff4 showed 45% more fungal biomass (measured by Pst *EF1α* transcript levels) at 14 days post-inoculation compared to wild type. No visible growth penalty was observed.

Discussion
Our study provides a comprehensive secretome atlas of Pst during wheat infection, expanding the known effector repertoire. The identification of Pst_Eff4 and Pst_Eff9 as suppressors of PR protein-mediated immunity highlights a common virulence strategy. Pst_Eff12-mediated ROS scavenging via TaCAT1 inhibition reveals a novel mechanism to counteract oxidative burst. These effectors likely act in concert to establish biotrophy. The lack of sequence similarity to known effectors suggests Pst possesses unique virulence factors. Future work will explore the structural basis of effector-target interactions and their potential as resistance engineering targets.

Conclusion
We identified 1,248 Pst CSEPs and functionally characterized four core effectors. Pst_Eff4, Pst_Eff9, and Pst_Eff12 suppress wheat immunity by targeting PR proteins and catalase. These findings advance our understanding of Pst pathogenesis and provide candidate effectors for breeding resistant wheat.

title: QTL Mapping and Candidate Gene Identification of Swollen Root Formation in Turnip
text: Abstract: Swollen root is the primary edible organ of turnip (*Brassica rapa* ssp. *rapa*), and its formation directly determines yield and commercial quality. However, the genetic basis underlying swollen root development remains poorly understood. In this study, an F₂ population derived from a cross between a swollen-root cultivar and a non-swollen-root line was used to map quantitative trait loci (QTLs) controlling swollen root formation. A total of five QTLs distributed on chromosomes A03, A05, and A09 were identified, with the major QTL *qSR.A05* explaining 23.6% of the phenotypic variation. Combined transcriptome analysis revealed 1,847 differentially expressed genes between swollen and non-swollen roots, and integrative analysis narrowed the candidate region of *qSR.A05* to a 186-kb interval containing 27 annotated genes. Among them, *BrEXPA1*, encoding an expansin-like protein, and *BrWOX4*, a WUSCHEL-related homeobox transcription factor, exhibited significantly higher expression in swollen roots and were co-localized with the major QTL. Subcellular localization assays confirmed that both proteins are localized to the cell wall and nucleus, respectively. These results provide novel insights into the genetic architecture of swollen root formation and identify promising candidate genes for molecular breeding of turnip root traits.

title: Application of DGT/DIFS to assess bioavailable Cd to maize and its release in agricultural soils
text:
Application of DGT/DIFS to assess bioavailable Cd to maize and its release in agricultural soils

Abstract

Cadmium (Cd) contamination in agricultural soils poses a serious threat to crop safety and human health. Conventional total metal analysis often overestimates the risk because it ignores speciation and bioavailability. In this study, the diffusive gradients in thin films (DGT) technique combined with the diffusive flux model (DIFS) was applied to evaluate the bioavailable Cd in maize-cultivated soils and to quantify its release kinetics from the solid phase. Six agricultural soils with a gradient of Cd contamination (0.18–3.42 mg kg⁻¹) were collected, and maize (Zea mays L.) was grown in pot experiments. DGT-labile Cd (C_DGT) ranged from 0.21 to 8.94 μg L⁻¹ and correlated significantly with Cd concentrations in maize roots (r = 0.91, p < 0.01) and shoots (r = 0.87, p < 0.01). DIFS modelling revealed that the response time (T_c) decreased from 38.5 to 4.2 min as contamination increased, indicating a shift from slow desorption to rapid resupply. The labile pool size and desorption rate constant were the key parameters controlling Cd release. These results demonstrate that DGT/DIFS can predict Cd bioavailability to maize more accurately than total Cd and can characterize the dynamic release of Cd from soil solids, providing a robust tool for risk assessment and remediation prioritization.

Keywords: Cadmium; DGT; DIFS; bioavailability; maize; agricultural soil; desorption kinetics

1. Introduction

Cadmium is a non-essential, highly toxic trace metal that enters agricultural soils through atmospheric deposition, irrigation with wastewater, and application of phosphate fertilizers. Unlike organic contaminants, Cd is non-degradable and can accumulate in crops, eventually entering the food chain. Maize is one of the most widely cultivated cereals worldwide, and its uptake of Cd is a critical pathway for human exposure. Therefore, accurate assessment of Cd bioavailability in maize-cultivated soils is essential for food safety and soil management.

Total Cd concentration, commonly used in regulatory frameworks, is a poor predictor of plant uptake because only a fraction of the metal is mobile and bioavailable. Chemical extraction methods (e.g., DTPA, CaCl₂) provide operational estimates but cannot reflect dynamic supply from the solid phase. The diffusive gradients in thin films (DGT) technique measures the labile metal fraction in situ by mimicking the diffusive supply to a sink, and it has shown strong correlations with plant uptake across various soil–crop systems. However, DGT alone gives a time-integrated concentration and does not quantify the kinetics of metal release. The DIFS (DGT-induced fluxes in soils) model, coupling DGT measurement with diffusion theory, can derive kinetic parameters such as the response time (T_c), the labile pool concentration (C_L), and the desorption rate constant (k_d), thereby revealing how rapidly the soil can resupply Cd to the solution.

Despite the increasing use of DGT/DIFS in contaminated soils, its application to assess bioavailable Cd specifically for maize in agricultural soils, particularly with a focus on release kinetics, remains limited. This study aims to: (1) quantify DGT-labile Cd in a range of agricultural soils; (2) relate DGT-labile Cd to maize uptake; and (3) use DIFS to characterize the release of Cd from the solid phase and identify the controlling kinetic parameters.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Soil sampling and characterization

Six surface soils (0–20 cm) were collected from maize fields in a peri-urban agricultural region. Soils were air-dried, sieved (<2 mm), and characterized for pH (1:2.5 soil/water), organic matter (OM) by dichromate oxidation, cation exchange capacity (CEC) by ammonium acetate, and total Cd by digestion with HNO₃–HClO₄ followed by ICP-MS. Selected properties are shown in Table 1 (pH 5.8–7.4; OM 1.6–3.8%; CEC 12.4–24.7 cmol kg⁻¹; total Cd 0.18–3.42 mg kg⁻¹).

2.2 Pot experiment

Maize (Zea mays L., cv. Zhengdan 958) was grown in 2-kg pots with three replicates per soil. Plants were harvested after 45 days, separated into roots and shoots, washed, dried, digested, and analyzed for Cd by ICP-MS. Certified reference material (GBW10012) was used for quality control (recovery 94–106%).

2.3 DGT deployment and analysis

DGT devices with Chelex-100 binding gel and 0.8-mm diffusive gel were deployed in soil slurries (soil:water = 1:2) at 25 °C for 24 h. After retrieval, the binding gel was eluted with 1 M HNO₃ and analyzed by ICP-MS. The DGT-labile concentration (C_DGT) was calculated using the standard equation:

C_DGT = M·Δg / (D·A·t)

where M is the accumulated mass, Δg is the diffusive gel thickness, D is the diffusion coefficient of Cd, A is the exposure area, and t is deployment time.

2.4 DIFS modelling

DIFS (version 2.0) was used to simulate Cd release. Input parameters included C_DGT, soil solution concentration (C_sol) measured by centrifugation, and soil physical properties. The model assumed a labile solid phase and a solution phase, and derived the response time T_c = 1/(k_1 + k_−1), the labile pool concentration C_L, and the desorption rate constant k_d.

2.5 Statistical analysis

Correlations were analyzed with Pearson’s test using SPSS 26.0. Significance was set at p < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Cd in soils and maize

Total Cd in soils increased from 0.18 to 3.42 mg kg⁻¹ (Table 1). Maize root Cd ranged from 0.12 to 4.86 mg kg⁻¹, and shoot Cd from 0.05 to 1.92 mg kg⁻¹. Both root and shoot Cd increased with total Cd, but the relationship was non-linear, suggesting that soil properties modulate bioavailability.

3.2 DGT-labile Cd

C_DGT ranged from 0.21 to 8.94 μg L⁻¹, representing 0.08–0.31% of total Cd. C_DGT was strongly correlated with root Cd (r = 0.91, p < 0.01) and shoot Cd (r = 0.87, p < 0.01), while total Cd showed weaker correlations (r = 0.68 and 0.61, respectively). This confirms that DGT-labile Cd is a better predictor of maize uptake than total Cd.

3.3 DIFS-derived kinetics

DIFS modelling showed that the response time T_c decreased from 38.5 min in the least contaminated soil to 4.2 min in the most contaminated soil (Table 2). The labile pool concentration C_L increased from 0.42 to 6.87 mg kg⁻¹, and k_d increased from 0.014 to 0.21 min⁻¹. These trends indicate that as contamination increases, Cd desorbs more rapidly and the soil can resupply the solution more efficiently. The ratio C_DGT/C_sol (R_dif) also increased, suggesting a higher diffusive supply.

3.4 Relationship between DIFS parameters and plant uptake

Root Cd was significantly correlated with C_L (r = 0.89, p < 0.01) and k_d (r = 0.84, p < 0.05), but not with T_c (r = −0.52, p > 0.05). This implies that the size of the labile pool and the desorption rate, rather than the response time alone, govern Cd bioavailability to maize.

4. Discussion

The strong correlation between C_DGT and maize Cd confirms that DGT mimics the diffusive supply of Cd to plant roots and integrates both intensity and capacity factors. This is consistent with earlier studies on wheat and rice, and extends the applicability to maize in slightly acidic to neutral agricultural soils. The DIFS results provide a mechanistic explanation: in highly contaminated soils, Cd is not only more abundant in the labile pool but also desorbs faster, leading to a higher effective concentration at the root surface. In contrast, in low-contamination soils, slow desorption (long T_c) limits the flux, and plants may take up less Cd than predicted by total concentration.

The decrease in T_c with increasing contamination can be attributed to the saturation of high-affinity binding sites and the presence of more weakly bound Cd fractions. This has important implications for risk assessment: soils with the same total Cd may pose different risks depending on their desorption kinetics. DGT/DIFS therefore offers a dynamic, bioavailable-based metric that can refine soil quality guidelines.

Several limitations should be noted. The pot experiment may not fully represent field conditions, and the DIFS model assumes a single labile pool, whereas real soils may have multiple binding sites. Future work should validate the approach across different soil types and maize cultivars, and integrate it with crop uptake models.

5. Conclusion

This study demonstrates that DGT combined with DIFS is an effective tool for assessing bioavailable Cd to maize in agricultural soils. DGT-labile Cd correlated better with maize root and shoot Cd than total Cd. DIFS modelling revealed that Cd release kinetics shift from slow to fast as contamination increases, with the labile pool size and desorption rate constant being the key controls on bioavailability. These findings support the use of DGT/DIFS for refined risk assessment and for identifying soils where remediation is most urgently needed to reduce Cd transfer to the food chain.

title: Antifungal activity of rapamycin on Botryosphaeria dothidea and its effect against Chinese hickory canker
text:
Chinese hickory (*Carya cathayensis* Sarg.) is an economically important nut crop in China, but its production is increasingly threatened by canker disease caused by *Botryosphaeria dothidea*. This pathogen infects trunks and branches, leading to dieback, reduced yield, and substantial economic losses. Current management relies mainly on cultural practices and repeated fungicide applications, yet effective control remains difficult because of the pathogen's broad host range, prolonged latent infection, and the emergence of fungicide resistance. Therefore, novel antifungal agents with distinct modes of action are urgently needed.

Rapamycin is a macrolide produced by *Streptomyces hygroscopicus* that inhibits the target of rapamycin (TOR) kinase, a central regulator of cell growth, proliferation, and stress responses in eukaryotes. Although rapamycin is well known for its immunosuppressive and antifungal properties, its activity against *B. dothidea* and its potential to control Chinese hickory canker have not been systematically evaluated. In this study, we assessed the in vitro antifungal activity of rapamycin against *B. dothidea*, examined its effects on mycelial growth, spore germination, and cell integrity, and evaluated its efficacy in controlling canker disease on Chinese hickory. Our results provide the first evidence that rapamycin effectively suppresses *B. dothidea* and reduces canker development, suggesting that TOR inhibition may represent a promising strategy for managing this devastating disease.

title: Ammonia Volatilization and Greenhouse Gases Emissions during Vermicomposting with Animal Manures and Biochar to Enhance Sustainability
text:
Results and Discussion

Vermicomposting reduced total mass by 38.4–52.7% across treatments, with the greatest loss in poultry manure (PM). Ammonia (NH₃) volatilization peaked during weeks 2–3 and differed significantly among feedstocks (p < 0.05). Cumulative NH₃ losses were highest in PM (4.82 g N kg⁻¹ initial N), followed by pig manure (3.61 g N kg⁻¹) and cattle manure (2.47 g N kg⁻¹). Biochar addition (10% w/w) reduced NH₃ emissions by 27–41%, likely due to adsorption of NH₄⁺/NH₃ and improved aeration. Similarly, CO₂ fluxes were 18–33% lower in biochar-amended treatments, reflecting slower labile-C mineralization. Methane emissions were negligible (<0.05 g CH₄-C kg⁻¹), consistent with the aerobic conditions maintained in the vermireactors. In contrast, N₂O emissions increased transiently in PM + biochar (0.41 g N₂O-N kg⁻¹) compared with PM alone (0.29 g N₂O-N kg⁻¹), probably because biochar promoted incomplete denitrification in localized anoxic microsites. Earthworm biomass gain was highest in cattle manure + biochar (68.3%), indicating favorable habitat conditions. Overall, biochar co-composting with animal manures reduced NH₃ and CO₂ emissions while maintaining vermicompost quality (C/N 14.2–16.8, germination index >85%). These results suggest that integrating biochar into vermicomposting can enhance environmental sustainability, though N₂O trade-offs warrant site-specific management.

title: Weight status in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: A study protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Weight status in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: A study protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis

Abstract

Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition frequently accompanied by atypical eating behaviours, sensory processing differences, and comorbid medical conditions that may collectively influence body weight. Existing evidence regarding the prevalence of underweight, overweight, and obesity in autistic individuals remains inconsistent, with heterogeneous sample characteristics, diagnostic criteria, and measurement approaches limiting comparability across studies. Objective: This protocol outlines a systematic review and meta-analysis designed to synthesise available evidence on weight status in children, adolescents, and adults with ASD compared with non-autistic controls, and to examine potential moderators of between-study heterogeneity. Methods: We will search PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and CINAHL from inception to December 2025. Observational studies reporting weight status (underweight, normal weight, overweight, obesity) or continuous anthropometric measures (body mass index [BMI], BMI z-scores, waist circumference) in individuals with a formal ASD diagnosis will be eligible. Two reviewers will independently screen records, extract data, and assess risk of bias using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Random-effects models will be used to pool odds ratios and standardised mean differences. Heterogeneity will be quantified using I² and explored through subgroup and meta-regression analyses. Publication bias will be evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's test. Expected outcomes: The review is anticipated to clarify the direction and magnitude of differences in weight status between autistic and non-autistic populations, and to identify methodological and demographic factors contributing to inconsistent findings. Conclusion: This protocol provides a transparent framework for a comprehensive synthesis that may inform screening guidelines and tailored weight-management interventions for autistic individuals.

Keywords: autism spectrum disorder; weight status; obesity; overweight; underweight; body mass index; systematic review; meta-analysis; protocol

1. Introduction

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent differences in social communication and interaction, alongside restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Global estimates suggest that approximately 1–2% of children and adolescents meet diagnostic criteria for ASD, with prevalence continuing to rise owing to improved awareness, broader diagnostic criteria, and enhanced screening practices. As the autistic population ages, attention has increasingly shifted from core diagnostic features toward co-occurring physical health conditions that shape long-term quality of life and mortality risk.

Weight status represents one such health domain of growing interest. Obesity and overweight in the general population are established risk factors for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnoea, and musculoskeletal disorders. Conversely, underweight status may signal nutritional deficiency, feeding difficulties, or underlying gastrointestinal pathology. Both extremes of the weight spectrum carry implications for morbidity and healthcare utilisation, and both have been reported at elevated rates in autistic populations relative to the general population.

Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain atypical weight distributions in ASD. First, selective eating and food neophobia are common in autistic children and may lead to energy-dense, nutrient-poor diets or, alternatively, restricted intake resulting in underweight. Second, sensory sensitivities to food texture, smell, and colour can further narrow dietary variety. Third, psychotropic medications, particularly atypical antipsychotics such as risperidone and aripiprazole, are frequently prescribed for irritability and aggression and are associated with significant weight gain. Fourth, differences in physical activity patterns, motor coordination difficulties, and reduced participation in organised sports may contribute to positive energy balance. Fifth, genetic and neuroendocrine factors, including alterations in leptin and ghrelin signalling, have been hypothesised to influence appetite regulation in ASD. Finally, family-level factors, including parental feeding practices and household food environment, may interact with child characteristics to shape weight trajectories.

Despite this plausible mechanistic basis, empirical findings have been notably inconsistent. Some studies report a two- to three-fold increase in obesity prevalence among autistic children compared with typically developing peers, whereas others find no significant difference after adjusting for confounders such as age, sex, socioeconomic status, and medication use. Discrepancies may arise from differences in sampling frames (clinical versus population-based), diagnostic verification, anthropometric measurement (direct measurement versus parental report), reference standards (CDC versus WHO growth charts), and the age ranges studied. Moreover, relatively few studies have examined weight status in autistic adults, and findings in this subgroup remain sparse and contradictory.

Previous systematic reviews have addressed related questions but are now dated, have focused exclusively on children, or have not quantitatively pooled estimates across weight categories. A comprehensive, up-to-date synthesis that encompasses the full lifespan, distinguishes between underweight and excess weight, and formally investigates sources of heterogeneity is therefore warranted. Such a synthesis can inform clinical screening recommendations, guide the development of tailored nutritional and behavioural interventions, and highlight priority areas for future research.

The objective of this protocol is to describe the planned methodology for a systematic review and meta-analysis that will: (1) estimate the prevalence of underweight, overweight, and obesity in individuals with ASD; (2) compare weight status between autistic individuals and non-autistic controls; and (3) identify demographic, clinical, and methodological moderators of between-study variability.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Protocol registration and reporting

This protocol will be reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement. The completed review will follow the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The protocol will be registered in PROSPERO prior to initiation of formal screening.

2.2 Eligibility criteria

Studies will be eligible if they: (1) include individuals of any age with a diagnosis of ASD, Asperger syndrome, or pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified, based on established diagnostic criteria (DSM-III-R, DSM-IV, DSM-IV-TR, DSM-5, ICD-9, ICD-10, or ICD-11) or validated diagnostic instruments (e.g., ADOS, ADI-R); (2) report at least one measure of weight status, including categorical classifications (underweight, normal weight, overweight, obesity) or continuous anthropometric indices (BMI, BMI z-score, BMI percentile, waist circumference); (3) include a non-autistic comparison group or provide normative reference data permitting comparison; and (4) be published in English in a peer-reviewed journal. Cross-sectional, cohort, and case–control designs will be included. Case reports, narrative reviews, editorials, conference abstracts without full data, and studies with fewer than 30 participants will be excluded to reduce small-study bias. Studies relying exclusively on self-reported height and weight without validation will be excluded in a sensitivity analysis.

2.3 Information sources and search strategy

A systematic search will be conducted in PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science Core Collection, and CINAHL from database inception to 31 December 2025. The search strategy will combine controlled vocabulary and free-text terms across three domains: (a) autism (e.g., "autism spectrum disorder," "autism," "Asperger," "pervasive developmental disorder"); (b) weight status (e.g., "obesity," "overweight," "underweight," "body mass index," "BMI," "waist circumference," "weight"); and (c) study design where appropriate. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews will be hand-searched, and forward citation tracking will be performed using Google Scholar. Grey literature will be sought through ProQuest Dissertations and OpenGrey.

2.4 Study selection and data extraction

Records will be imported into Covidence. After removal of duplicates, two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review. Disagreements will be resolved through discussion or adjudication by a third reviewer. A standardised extraction form will capture: study characteristics (author, year, country, design, setting); participant characteristics (sample size, age, sex, diagnostic criteria, intellectual disability status); weight outcomes (definitions and cut-offs used, prevalence by category, mean BMI and standard deviation); comparison data; and covariates (medication use, socioeconomic status, physical activity). Where multiple publications report overlapping cohorts, the most comprehensive report will be retained.

2.5 Risk of bias assessment

Risk of bias will be assessed independently by two reviewers. The Newcastle–Ottawa Scale will be used for cohort and case–control studies, and an adapted version for cross-sectional studies. The Joanna Briggs Institute Prevalence Critical Appraisal Checklist will be applied to studies reporting prevalence estimates. Discrepancies will be resolved by consensus. A sensitivity analysis restricted to studies judged at low risk of bias will be conducted.

2.6 Statistical analysis

Meta-analyses will be performed using R (version 4.3.0) with the meta and metafor packages. For categorical outcomes, pooled odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals will be calculated comparing autistic individuals with controls for underweight, overweight, and obesity separately. For continuous outcomes, standardised mean differences in BMI or BMI z-scores will be pooled. Given anticipated clinical and methodological diversity, random-effects models will be employed using restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Heterogeneity will be assessed with Cochran's Q and I² statistics, with I² values of 25%, 50%, and 75% interpreted as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively.

Subgroup analyses will examine age group (children <12 years, adolescents 12–18 years, adults >18 years), sex, geographic region, diagnostic criteria, recruitment setting (clinical versus population-based), and medication status. Meta-regression will explore the contribution of mean age, proportion of males, and study quality score. Publication bias will be assessed via funnel plot asymmetry and Egger's regression test when at least ten studies are available per outcome. If substantial heterogeneity persists, a narrative synthesis will supplement quantitative findings.

3. Results and Analysis

As this manuscript reports a study protocol, no empirical results are presented. Nevertheless, based on a preliminary scoping of the literature, we anticipate identifying approximately 90–120 eligible studies, encompassing an estimated 250,000 autistic individuals and 1.8 million controls. We project that roughly 60% of studies will originate from North America, 25% from Europe, and 15% from Asia and Oceania, with limited representation from low- and middle-income countries.

We hypothesise that pooled analyses will indicate a significantly higher prevalence of obesity among autistic children and adolescents compared with controls, with an anticipated pooled odds ratio of approximately 1.6 (95% CI 1.4–1.9) and substantial heterogeneity (I² > 70%). For underweight, we anticipate a smaller but statistically significant elevation, with a pooled odds ratio of approximately 1.3 (95% CI 1.1–1.6). Among adults, we expect fewer eligible studies and wider confidence intervals, potentially precluding definitive conclusions. Continuous analyses of BMI z-scores are expected to show a modest positive standardised mean difference of approximately 0.25 (95% CI 0.15–0.35) in children.

Subgroup analyses are anticipated to reveal stronger associations in clinical samples than in population-based cohorts, and in individuals prescribed atypical antipsychotics compared with medication-naïve participants. Meta-regression is expected to identify study quality and measurement method as significant moderators, with parental-report studies yielding attenuated estimates relative to directly measured anthropometry. Sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk-of-bias studies are expected to preserve the direction of effects while reducing heterogeneity.

4. Discussion

This protocol describes the first comprehensive, lifespan-spanning synthesis of weight status in autistic individuals that will quantitatively pool estimates across underweight, overweight, and obesity categories while systematically interrogating sources of heterogeneity. The anticipated findings carry several implications.

First, from a clinical perspective, confirmation of elevated obesity risk would reinforce the need for routine anthropometric monitoring as part of standard autism healthcare, commencing in early childhood and continuing through adulthood. Given that autistic individuals often experience barriers to accessing preventive services, proactive screening within developmental and psychiatric settings may be particularly valuable. Second, identification of underweight as a co-occurring concern would underscore the importance of assessing feeding difficulties, gastrointestinal symptoms, and nutritional adequacy, rather than focusing exclusively on excess weight. Third, evidence that medication status moderates weight outcomes would support calls for careful metabolic monitoring and consideration of non-pharmacological alternatives when clinically appropriate.

From a research perspective, this review is expected to expose important gaps.
