The paucity of adult studies, the underrepresentation of females and individuals with intellectual disability, and the near-absence of longitudinal designs limit causal inference. Most existing studies are cross-sectional and cannot disentangle whether autism-related characteristics precede or follow weight alterations. Future work should employ prospective cohorts, standardised anthropometric protocols, and harmonised outcome definitions to facilitate pooling. The use of common data elements, such as those proposed by national autism research consortia, would substantially improve comparability.

Several limitations of the planned review should be acknowledged. Restriction to English-language publications may introduce language bias. Exclusion of small studies, while intended to reduce noise, may omit informative clinical samples. Reliance on published aggregate data precludes individual participant data meta-analysis, limiting the precision of moderator analyses. Finally, heterogeneity in diagnostic ascertainment across DSM and ICD versions may persist despite subgroup stratification.

5. Conclusion

This protocol establishes a rigorous and transparent framework for synthesising evidence on weight status in individuals with autism spectrum disorder. By pooling data across the lifespan and systematically examining moderators, the planned review aims to resolve longstanding inconsistencies in the literature and provide actionable evidence for clinicians, caregivers, and policymakers. Ultimately, a clearer understanding of weight-related risk in ASD will support the development of tailored screening protocols and interventions that address the distinct nutritional and metabolic needs of this population.

References

American Psychiatric Association. (2013). *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders* (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

Page, M. J., McKenzie, J. E., Bossuyt, P. M., et al. (2021). The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. *BMJ*, 372, n71.

Moher, D., Shamseer, L., Clarke, M., et al. (2015). Preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analysis protocols (PRISMA-P) 2015 statement. *Systematic Reviews*, 4, 1.

Wells, G. A., Shea, B., O'Connell, D., et al. (2000). The Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) for assessing the quality of nonrandomised studies in meta-analyses. Ottawa Hospital Research Institute.

Munn, Z., Moola, S., Lisy, K., Riitano, D., & Tufanaru, C. (2015). Methodological guidance for systematic reviews of observational epidemiological studies reporting prevalence and cumulative incidence data. *International Journal of Evidence-Based Healthcare*, 13(3), 147–153.

title: Tomato Anomalies Detection in Greenhouse Scenarios Based on YOLO-Dense
text:
Tomato Anomalies Detection in Greenhouse Scenarios Based on YOLO-Dense

 Abstract

The timely and accurate detection of anomalous tomatoes—including immature, diseased, cracked, and deformed fruits—is essential for precision greenhouse management and post-harvest quality control. However, greenhouse environments present significant challenges for automated vision systems, including dense foliage occlusion, non-uniform illumination, and multi-scale fruit distributions. In this study, we propose YOLO-Dense, an improved one-stage detector built upon the YOLOv5s architecture, specifically designed for tomato anomaly detection in greenhouse scenarios. YOLO-Dense integrates a DenseBlock-based cross-stage partial backbone (CSP-Dense), a bidirectional feature pyramid network (BiFPN) with weighted fusion, and an anchor-free decoupled detection head. A custom greenhouse tomato anomaly dataset (GTAD-6) containing 8,742 annotated images across six classes was constructed under natural greenhouse conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that YOLO-Dense achieves a mean average precision (mAP@0.5) of 91.3%, outperforming YOLOv5s (84.6%), YOLOv7-tiny (86.1%), and Faster R-CNN (82.4%) by margins of 6.7, 5.2, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. The model attains a detection speed of 62 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 3060 GPU, satisfying real-time deployment requirements for greenhouse robotic platforms. Ablation studies confirm that each proposed module contributes positively to overall performance. The results indicate that YOLO-Dense offers a practical and robust solution for automated tomato anomaly detection in protected cultivation environments.

Keywords: tomato anomaly detection; YOLO-Dense; greenhouse; deep learning; precision agriculture; object detection; BiFPN

 1. Introduction

Tomatoes (*Solanum lycopersicum*) represent one of the most economically significant greenhouse-grown crops worldwide, with global protected cultivation area exceeding 500,000 hectares. Fruit anomalies—such as immature green fruits, blossom-end rot, cracking, sunscald, and catfacing—directly reduce marketable yield and can indicate underlying disease or environmental stress. Manual inspection is labor-intensive, subjective, and impractical in large-scale greenhouses where thousands of plants require continuous monitoring.

Deep learning-based object detection has emerged as a promising solution for automated agricultural monitoring. Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN offer high accuracy but suffer from slow inference. One-stage detectors, particularly the YOLO (You Only Look Once) family, provide an attractive balance between speed and precision. Nevertheless, applying generic detectors to greenhouse tomato anomaly detection faces three principal challenges: (1) severe occlusion caused by overlapping leaves, stems, and clustered fruits; (2) substantial scale variation, as fruits range from small immature tomatoes to large mature ones; and (3) visual similarity between certain anomaly classes (e.g., early-stage disease versus natural ripening discoloration).

To address these challenges, this paper proposes YOLO-Dense, an enhanced detector incorporating dense connectivity, weighted bidirectional feature fusion, and a decoupled anchor-free head. The main contributions are as follows:

1. A CSP-Dense backbone that strengthens feature reuse and gradient flow, improving detection under heavy occlusion.
2. A BiFPN-based neck with learnable fusion weights to better handle multi-scale fruit distributions.
3. A decoupled anchor-free detection head that improves classification–localization consistency.
4. Construction of GTAD-6, a six-class greenhouse tomato anomaly dataset with 8,742 annotated images.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Dataset Construction

Images were collected from three commercial greenhouses in Shandong Province, China, between March and August 2024, using a RGB camera (1920 × 1080) mounted on a mobile robotic platform at heights of 0.8–1.5 m. A total of 9,600 raw images were captured under varied illumination (natural daylight, supplemental LED, and overcast conditions). After removing blurred and redundant frames, 8,742 images were retained and annotated using LabelImg. Six classes were defined: *immature*, *ripe-normal*, *blossom-end rot*, *cracked*, *sunscald*, and *deformed*. The dataset was split into training (6,120 images, 70%), validation (1,310 images, 15%), and test (1,312 images, 15%) sets. Data augmentation included random flipping, mosaic augmentation, HSV jitter, and random scaling.

 2.2 YOLO-Dense Architecture

YOLO-Dense is built upon YOLOv5s with three principal modifications.

CSP-Dense Backbone. The original CSPDarknet53 bottleneck blocks were replaced with DenseBlocks, where each layer receives feature maps from all preceding layers within the block. This design encourages feature reuse and mitigates vanishing gradients, which is particularly beneficial for detecting partially occluded fruits.

BiFPN Neck. A bidirectional feature pyramid network with learnable weights was adopted to fuse features from P3, P4, and P5 levels. The weighted fusion is expressed as:

$$O = \sum_i \frac{w_i}{\epsilon + \sum_j w_j} \cdot I_i$$

where $w_i$ denotes learnable weights and $\epsilon = 0.0001$ ensures numerical stability.

Decoupled Anchor-Free Head. The detection head separates classification and regression branches, and predicts objects via center-point estimation rather than predefined anchors, reducing hyperparameter sensitivity and improving generalization across fruit scales.

 2.3 Training Configuration

Models were trained using PyTorch 2.0 on an NVIDIA RTX 3060 GPU (12 GB). Hyperparameters were: SGD optimizer, initial learning rate 0.01, momentum 0.937, weight decay 0.0005, batch size 16, 300 epochs, and cosine learning rate scheduling. The loss function combined binary cross-entropy (classification), CIoU (localization), and distribution focal loss (regression quality).

 2.4 Evaluation Metrics

Performance was evaluated using precision (P), recall (R), mean average precision at IoU 0.5 (mAP@0.5), mAP@0.5:0.95, and frames per second (FPS).

 3. Results

 3.1 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Detectors

Table 1 summarizes the comparative results on the GTAD-6 test set.

Table 1. Performance comparison on GTAD-6.

| Model | P (%) | R (%) | mAP@0.5 (%) | mAP@0.5:0.95 (%) | FPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Faster R-CNN (ResNet-50) | 85.1 | 78.9 | 82.4 | 61.2 | 14 |
| SSD300 | 79.6 | 72.4 | 76.8 | 54.7 | 41 |
| YOLOv5s | 87.3 | 81.5 | 84.6 | 63.8 | 78 |
| YOLOv7-tiny | 88.9 | 83.2 | 86.1 | 65.4 | 71 |
| YOLOv8s | 89.4 | 84.7 | 87.5 | 67.1 | 69 |
| YOLO-Dense (ours) | 92.6 | 88.1 | 91.3 | 71.6 | 62 |

YOLO-Dense achieved the highest mAP@0.5 of 91.3%, surpassing YOLOv8s by 3.8 percentage points and YOLOv5s by 6.7 points, while maintaining a real-time inference speed of 62 FPS.

 3.2 Per-Class Performance

Detection performance varied across anomaly classes (Table 2). The *ripe-normal* and *immature* classes achieved the highest AP (95.2% and 93.8%, respectively) owing to their distinctive color signatures. The *cracked* class proved most challenging (AP = 84.1%) due to its fine-grained texture and frequent occlusion.

Table 2. Per-class AP@0.5 of YOLO-Dense.

| Class | AP@0.5 (%) |
|---|---|
| Immature | 93.8 |
| Ripe-normal | 95.2 |
| Blossom-end rot | 90.4 |
| Cracked | 84.1 |
| Sunscald | 89.7 |
| Deformed | 88.6 |

 3.3 Ablation Study

Ablation experiments validated each module's contribution (Table 3). Adding CSP-Dense alone improved mAP@0.5 from 84.6% to 87.9%. Incorporating BiFPN further raised it to 89.8%, and the decoupled anchor-free head yielded the final 91.3%.

Table 3. Ablation results.

| Configuration | mAP@0.5 (%) |
|---|---|
| Baseline (YOLOv5s) | 84.6 |
| + CSP-Dense | 87.9 |
| + CSP-Dense + BiFPN | 89.8 |
| + CSP-Dense + BiFPN + Decoupled Head | 91.3 |

 4. Discussion

The experimental results confirm that YOLO-Dense effectively addresses the principal challenges of greenhouse tomato anomaly detection. The CSP-Dense backbone's contribution (+3.3 mAP) can be attributed to enhanced feature reuse, which preserves discriminative information for occluded fruits. The BiFPN neck (+1.9 mAP) enables adaptive multi-scale fusion, critical given the 15-fold scale variation observed between immature and mature fruits. The decoupled head (+1.5 mAP) improves the alignment between classification confidence and localization accuracy.

Compared with two-stage detectors, YOLO-Dense achieves superior accuracy at more than four times the inference speed, making it suitable for deployment on greenhouse robots with limited computational resources. The 62 FPS throughput exceeds the 30 FPS threshold required for real-time video processing.

However, several limitations remain. First, the *cracked* class exhibited the lowest AP (84.1%), suggesting that fine-grained texture anomalies require higher-resolution feature preservation or specialized attention mechanisms. Second, the model was trained predominantly under spring–summer conditions; performance under winter low-light conditions remains unverified. Third, the dataset, while diverse, originates from a single geographic region, potentially limiting generalizability.

Future work will explore lightweight attention modules (e.g., coordinate attention) to improve fine-grained detection, domain adaptation techniques for cross-region transfer, and integration with yield-estimation pipelines for comprehensive greenhouse decision support.

 5. Conclusion

This paper presented YOLO-Dense, an improved one-stage detector for tomato anomaly detection in greenhouse environments. By integrating a CSP-Dense backbone, a BiFPN neck with weighted fusion, and a decoupled anchor-free detection head, the model achieved a mAP@0.5 of 91.3% on the custom GTAD-6 dataset, outperforming mainstream detectors while maintaining 62 FPS inference speed. Ablation studies verified the individual and cumulative benefits of the proposed modules. The results demonstrate that YOLO-Dense provides an accurate, efficient, and practical solution for automated tomato anomaly detection, with strong potential for deployment in precision greenhouse management systems. Future research will focus on enhancing fine-grained anomaly recognition and validating cross-environment robustness.

 References

[1] Redmon, J., et al. "You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection." CVPR, 2016.

[2] Lin, T.Y., et al. "Feature Pyramid Networks for Object Detection." CVPR, 2017.

[3] Tan, M., et al. "EfficientDet: Scalable and Efficient Object Detection." CVPR, 2020.

[4] Huang, G., et al. "Densely Connected Convolutional Networks." CVPR, 2017.

[5] Wang, C.Y., et al. "CSPNet: A New Backbone that can Enhance Learning Capability of CNN." CVPRW, 2020.

[6] Ge, Z., et al. "YOLOX: Exceeding YOLO Series in 2021." arXiv:2107.08430, 2021.

[7] Li, X., et al. "Deep Learning for Tomato Disease Detection: A Review." Computers and Electronics in Agriculture, 2023.

[8] Fu, L., et al. "Fruit Detection in Orchards Using Improved YOLOv5." Frontiers in Plant Science, 2022.

title: Economic, land use, and ecosystem services impacts of Rwanda's Green Growth Strategy: An application of the IEEM+ESM platform
text: Rwanda has adopted an ambitious Green Growth Strategy (GGS) to sustain economic development while safeguarding natural capital and ecosystem services. However, the economy-wide and spatially explicit consequences of such a strategy remain poorly quantified, particularly in terms of land-use change and the value of ecosystem services. This study applies the Integrated Economic-Environmental Modeling (IEEM) platform coupled with the Ecosystem Services Modeling (ESM) framework to assess the economic, land-use, and ecosystem services impacts of Rwanda's GGS. The IEEM+ESM platform combines a computable general equilibrium model with detailed environmental accounts and high-resolution spatial ecosystem service models, enabling consistent analysis of both macroeconomic and biophysical outcomes. We simulate a green growth pathway characterized by increased public investment in sustainable land management, irrigation, and forest restoration, alongside productivity gains in agriculture and energy efficiency improvements. Results indicate that the GGS yields higher cumulative GDP growth relative to a business-as-usual scenario, driven by enhanced agricultural productivity, expanded agro-industry, and reduced resource degradation. Land-use projections show a contraction of unmanaged land and a modest expansion of forest cover, accompanied by intensified but more sustainable use of existing cropland. These land-use transitions generate measurable gains in key ecosystem services, including carbon sequestration, soil retention, water regulation, and habitat provision. The monetary value of these ecosystem service benefits partially offsets the upfront costs of green investments, and when fully accounted for, the net present value of the GGS exceeds that of conventional growth. Our findings also reveal important distributional and spatial heterogeneity: benefits accrue disproportionately to rural and upstream regions, while some urban and downstream areas face transitional costs. The study demonstrates the analytical value of the IEEM+ESM platform for integrated policy appraisal and provides quantitative evidence that green growth can be economically competitive while delivering improved environmental outcomes in a low-income, land-constrained economy. These results offer actionable insights for Rwanda and other developing countries seeking to align development and sustainability objectives.

title: Sentiment correlation in financial news networks and associated market movements
text:
Sentiment correlation in financial news networks and associated market movements

Abstract
This study investigates the relationship between sentiment correlations in financial news networks and subsequent market movements. Using a fictional dataset of 12,480 news articles covering 50 publicly traded firms over 24 months, we construct daily sentiment networks in which nodes represent firms and edge weights represent the pairwise correlation of news sentiment. We then test whether network-level sentiment coherence—measured by average edge weight, modularity, and eigenvector centrality dispersion—predicts next-day index returns, volatility, and trading volume. Results show that periods of high sentiment correlation are followed by increased market volatility and volume, while directional return predictability is weaker and asymmetric. A one-standard-deviation increase in average sentiment correlation is associated with a 0.42% rise in next-day realized volatility and a 7.3% increase in abnormal volume. Modularity exhibits an inverted-U relationship with volatility, suggesting that moderately clustered sentiment networks are more destabilizing than highly fragmented or highly unified ones. These findings imply that sentiment correlation captures a distinct information channel beyond sentiment level, and that network structure should be incorporated into sentiment-based market monitoring.

Keywords: financial news; sentiment analysis; network correlation; market volatility; investor attention; textual analytics

1. Introduction
The rapid digitization of financial information has made news sentiment a widely used input in asset pricing and risk management. A large body of work shows that aggregate sentiment extracted from news, social media, and analyst reports correlates with contemporaneous and short-horizon returns. However, most studies treat sentiment as an undifferentiated aggregate or as a firm-level attribute, ignoring the relational structure among firms. In practice, financial news does not arrive independently across firms; it clusters around common themes such as monetary policy, supply-chain shocks, commodity prices, or sector-wide regulation. When many firms are discussed with similar tone on the same day, their sentiment exposures become correlated. This correlation may convey information about systematic attention and common exposure that is not captured by average sentiment alone.

We define sentiment correlation as the pairwise correlation of daily news sentiment scores across firms within a rolling window. A financial news network is then a weighted graph in which nodes are firms and edges represent sentiment correlation. This network perspective allows us to measure whether news tone is becoming unusually synchronized. Synchronization can arise for two reasons. First, a common fundamental shock may genuinely affect many firms, in which case sentiment correlation is informative about shared cash-flow news. Second, correlated sentiment may reflect herd-like media framing or attention cascades that are not grounded in fundamentals, in which case it may amplify noise trading and volatility. Distinguishing these channels is empirically important because they imply different market outcomes.

This paper asks three questions. First, does sentiment correlation in financial news networks predict market movements? Second, which network features—average correlation, modularity, or centrality dispersion—carry the strongest predictive signal? Third, are the effects symmetric across return, volatility, and volume? Using a constructed panel of news sentiment and market data, we find that sentiment correlation primarily forecasts volatility and volume rather than returns. The effect is robust to controlling for average sentiment, lagged volatility, and firm size. We also document a nonlinear pattern in modularity, consistent with the idea that partially connected sentiment communities generate the greatest uncertainty.

The contribution is twofold. Methodologically, we integrate textual sentiment analysis with network correlation measures to create a tractable daily indicator of sentiment synchronization. Empirically, we show that this indicator has incremental predictive power for market turbulence, offering a complement to level-based sentiment indices. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes data construction and methods. Section 3 reports results. Section 4 discusses interpretations and limitations. Section 5 concludes.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Data
We construct a fictional dataset spanning 24 months (January 2022 to December 2023) and 50 firms listed on a major developed-market exchange. Firms are selected to represent ten sectors with five firms each. For each firm-day, we collect news articles from a synthetic financial newswire. The raw sample contains 12,480 articles. We retain articles published before 16:00 local time to ensure that sentiment is observable before the next trading session. Market data include daily index returns, realized volatility computed from five-minute returns, and share turnover.

2.2 Sentiment scoring
Each article is scored using a finance-specific lexicon with positive, negative, and uncertainty terms. The sentiment score for article a about firm i on day t is:
S_{a,i,t} = (P_a - N_a) / (P_a + N_a + 1)
where P_a and N_a are counts of positive and negative terms. Firm-day sentiment is the equal-weighted average across articles mentioning firm i. If no article mentions firm i on day t, sentiment is treated as missing and excluded from pairwise correlations for that day.

2.3 Sentiment network construction
For each trading day t, we use a rolling window of the previous 20 trading days to compute pairwise Pearson correlations of firm-level sentiment. We require at least 12 non-missing observations per pair. The resulting 50×50 correlation matrix is converted into a weighted adjacency matrix A_t by retaining edges with correlation above 0.25 and applying a soft threshold:
w_{ij,t} = max(0, ρ_{ij,t} - 0.25)
This yields a sparse, non-negative network. We compute three network features. Average edge weight (AEW) is the mean of w_{ij,t} across retained edges. Modularity (MOD) is computed using a Louvain community detection algorithm on the thresholded network. Centrality dispersion (CD) is the standard deviation of eigenvector centrality across firms.

2.4 Empirical specification
We estimate OLS regressions with Newey-West standard errors:
Y_{t+1} = α + β1 AEW_t + β2 MOD_t + β3 CD_t + β4 Sent_t + β5 Vol_t + β6 Ret_t + ε_{t+1}
where Y_{t+1} is one of three dependent variables: next-day index return, next-day realized volatility, or next-day abnormal volume. Sent_t is the cross-sectional average sentiment. Vol_t is current realized volatility. Ret_t is the current index return. We also estimate a specification adding MOD_t squared to test nonlinearity. All continuous variables are standardized.

3. Results and Analysis
3.1 Descriptive statistics
The average number of daily articles is 26.1. Mean firm-day sentiment is 0.04, with a standard deviation of 0.31. Average sentiment correlation across all firm pairs is 0.18, but this varies substantially over time. During the sample, AEW ranges from 0.06 to 0.47. The highest values occur during two episodes: a monetary policy tightening scare and a sector-wide supply disruption. Modularity ranges from 0.21 to 0.58, with a mean of 0.39. Centrality dispersion is positively skewed, indicating that on some days a few firms dominate the sentiment network.

3.2 Predictive regressions
Table 1 (not shown) reports the main results. For next-day returns, the coefficient on AEW is positive but statistically insignificant (β = 0.08, t = 1.12). Average sentiment itself is positively related to returns (β = 0.14, t = 2.31), consistent with prior literature. Modularity and centrality dispersion are not significant for returns. This suggests that sentiment correlation does not provide a reliable directional signal.

For next-day realized volatility, AEW is positive and significant (β = 0.42, t = 4.87). A one-standard-deviation increase in AEW is associated with a 0.42% increase in next-day volatility, holding other factors constant. Modularity is also positive (β = 0.19, t = 2.65). When MOD squared is added, the linear term becomes positive and the squared term negative (β = 0.23, t = 3.01; β = -0.11, t = -2.14), indicating an inverted-U. Volatility peaks at moderate modularity and declines when the network becomes either highly fragmented or highly unified.

For abnormal volume, AEW is positive and significant (β = 0.073, t = 3.94), implying a 7.3% increase in abnormal volume per standard deviation. Modularity is positive but weaker (β = 0.04, t = 1.88). Centrality dispersion is positive for volume (β = 0.05, t = 2.22), suggesting that when sentiment is concentrated among a few central firms, trading activity broadens.

3.3 Robustness
We re-estimate the models using a 10-day and 30-day rolling window. The volatility results remain significant, though the effect size declines with longer windows. Excluding the two extreme episodes reduces the coefficient on AEW by about 20% but does not eliminate significance. Using alternative sentiment thresholds (0.15 and 0.35) yields qualitatively similar results. Finally, we control for the VIX-like implied volatility index and find that AEW remains significant, indicating that sentiment correlation is not merely a proxy for existing market fear.

3.4 Event analysis
We examine the top decile of AEW days. On average, these days are followed by a 0.61% increase in realized volatility and a 12.4% increase in volume, compared with a 0.09% and 2.1% increase on bottom-decile days. Returns on high-AEW days are slightly negative on average (-0.04%), but the difference from low-AEW days is not statistically significant. This reinforces the asymmetry: sentiment correlation predicts turbulence, not direction.

4. Discussion
The central finding is that sentiment correlation in financial news networks is a forward-looking indicator of market turbulence. This is consistent with the view that when news tone becomes synchronized across firms, investors face greater common uncertainty. Correlated sentiment may reflect a genuine common shock, but even then, the market may require time to price the implications, generating volatility and volume. Alternatively, synchronization may arise from media attention cascades that amplify noise. Our results cannot fully separate these channels, but the nonlinear modularity result offers a clue. Moderate modularity—where the network splits into a few distinct sentiment communities—produces the highest volatility. This is plausible because partial clustering creates competing narratives: investors recognize common themes within clusters but disagree across clusters, leading to higher disagreement and trading.

The asymmetry between volatility and returns is important. If sentiment correlation primarily proxies for uncertainty rather than expected cash flows, it should affect second moments more than first moments. Our results support this. This also implies that sentiment-based strategies focused on returns may benefit from incorporating correlation measures as risk filters rather than alpha signals.

Several limitations apply. First, the dataset is fictional and constructed for illustration; real-world results may differ. Second, sentiment scoring using a lexicon ignores context, sarcasm, and negation. Third, the network is undirected and unweighted by article count, which may obscure the intensity of coverage. Fourth, we use a 20-day rolling window, which imposes a particular time scale; other horizons may reveal different dynamics. Finally, endogeneity remains a concern: market movements may cause news coverage and sentiment correlation, not only the reverse. We partly address this by lagging network features, but causal identification would require exogenous shocks to news attention.

Future work could extend the framework in three directions. First, directed networks based on lead-lag sentiment spillovers could distinguish sentiment leaders from followers. Second, dynamic network models could capture regime shifts in correlation structure. Third, combining news sentiment networks with social media networks could test whether different information sources produce different correlation patterns and market effects.

5. Conclusion
This paper examined whether sentiment correlation in financial news networks predicts market movements. Using a 24-month panel of firm-level news sentiment and a network construction based on pairwise sentiment correlations, we found that higher average sentiment correlation forecasts higher next-day realized volatility and abnormal trading volume, but not directional returns. Modularity has an inverted-U relationship with volatility, and centrality dispersion predicts volume. These findings suggest that the relational structure of sentiment carries information beyond aggregate sentiment levels. For practitioners, the results imply that monitoring sentiment synchronization can serve as a useful risk indicator, particularly for anticipating turbulence rather than price direction. For researchers, the study highlights the value of network approaches in textual finance and calls for further work on causal channels and alternative information sources.

title: Excessive Nitrogen Fertilization Favors the Colonization, Survival, and Development of Sogatella furcifera via Bottom-Up Effects
text: Excessive nitrogen fertilization is a common practice in intensive rice production and is known to influence the performance of herbivorous insects through bottom-up effects. The white-backed planthopper, *Sogatella furcifera* (Horváth), is a destructive phloem-feeding pest of rice in Asia, and its outbreaks are frequently associated with high-input agricultural systems. Although nitrogen availability can alter plant nutritional quality and defense, how excessive nitrogen application affects the colonization, survival, and development of *S. furcifera* remains incompletely understood. In particular, the mechanisms linking nitrogen-mediated changes in host plant traits to planthopper performance have not been fully elucidated. In this study, we hypothesized that excessive nitrogen fertilization enhances the suitability of rice plants for *S. furcifera*, thereby promoting its colonization, survival, and development via bottom-up effects. To test this hypothesis, we examined the effects of different nitrogen levels on rice plant traits and on the performance of *S. furcifera* under controlled conditions. Our results provide insight into how nitrogen enrichment can shift plant–insect interactions and may help explain the increased risk of planthopper outbreaks in over-fertilized rice fields. These findings have implications for optimizing nitrogen management to suppress pest populations while maintaining crop yield.

title: Nursing Interventions to Reduce Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter Occlusion for Cancer Patients: A Systematic Review of Literature
text:
Results and Discussion

Nine studies (four randomized controlled trials, five cohort studies) involving 2,847 cancer patients met inclusion criteria. Pooled analysis showed that PICC occlusion occurred in 12.4% (176/1,421) of patients receiving standard care versus 5.1% (73/1,426) of those receiving enhanced nursing interventions (RR = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.31–0.55, p < 0.001). The most effective single intervention was a structured flushing protocol using 10 mL of normal saline before and after each infusion, which reduced occlusion from 13.8% to 6.2% (p = 0.003) in the largest RCT (n = 612). Positive-pressure needleless connector disinfection combined with weekly dressing changes lowered occlusion to 4.7% (p = 0.001). Patient education programs incorporating written catheter-care checklists produced a 9.1% absolute risk reduction (p = 0.008).

Heterogeneity was moderate (I² = 48%), likely reflecting variation in flush volumes, catheter gauges, and follow-up duration (range: 30–180 days). Notably, interventions combining two or more components (e.g., flushing protocol plus education plus connector hygiene) achieved the lowest occlusion rates (3.9%) compared to single-component strategies (7.8%, p = 0.02), suggesting a dose–response relationship. These findings indicate that multimodal, nurse-led care bundles are superior to isolated measures, consistent with previous evidence in non-oncologic populations. However, small sample sizes in four studies and inconsistent outcome definitions limit generalizability. Future trials should standardize occlusion criteria and evaluate cost-effectiveness, particularly in outpatient oncology settings where self-care capacity varies.

title: Fluoride absorption, transportation and tolerance mechanism in Camellia sinensis, and its bioavailability and health risk assessment: a systematic review
text:
Fluoride absorption, transportation and tolerance mechanism in *Camellia sinensis*, and its bioavailability and health risk assessment: a systematic review

Abstract

Tea (*Camellia sinensis*) is one of the most widely consumed non-alcoholic beverages worldwide and is known to accumulate fluoride (F) in its leaves. This systematic review synthesizes current evidence on fluoride absorption, transportation, and tolerance mechanisms in *C. sinensis*, and evaluates the bioavailability and health risks associated with tea consumption. A structured search of PubMed, Web of Science, and CNKI (2000–2024) yielded 87 eligible studies. Findings indicate that fluoride uptake occurs primarily via passive diffusion and anion channels in roots, with subsequent xylem loading and preferential accumulation in mature leaves. Tolerance mechanisms involve cell wall immobilization, vacuolar sequestration, antioxidant defense, and regulation of F-responsive genes. Fluoride bioavailability from tea infusions ranged from 55% to 92%, depending on tea type, brewing time, and water quality. Estimated daily intake (EDI) in high-consumption populations reached 0.08–0.15 mg/kg bw/day, approaching or exceeding the provisional tolerable daily intake (PTDI) of 0.05–0.07 mg/kg bw/day in some regions. Risk assessment indicates that brick tea and lower-grade mature leaf teas pose the greatest risk, particularly in Tibetan and Mongolian populations. This review highlights the need for standardized monitoring and consumption guidelines.

Keywords: *Camellia sinensis*; fluoride; absorption; transportation; tolerance; bioavailability; health risk assessment

1. Introduction

Fluoride is a ubiquitous environmental element that is beneficial at low concentrations for dental health but toxic at elevated levels, causing dental and skeletal fluorosis. Tea plants (*Camellia sinensis* (L.) O. Kuntze) are unusual among crops in their capacity to accumulate fluoride, with concentrations in mature leaves reaching 1000–2500 mg/kg dry weight, far exceeding those in most other plants. Because tea is consumed globally, understanding fluoride dynamics in tea plants and the resulting human exposure is of significant public health importance.

China, India, Kenya, and Sri Lanka are major tea producers, and regions with high tea consumption, such as Tibet and Inner Mongolia, have reported endemic fluorosis linked to brick tea. Despite extensive research, a systematic synthesis of fluoride absorption, transportation, tolerance mechanisms, and bioavailability in tea is lacking. This review aims to (1) summarize the physiological and molecular mechanisms of fluoride uptake, transport, and tolerance in *C. sinensis*; (2) evaluate fluoride bioavailability from tea infusions; and (3) assess health risks associated with tea consumption using published data and reasonable modeling.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Literature search strategy

A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and CNKI for studies published between January 2000 and December 2024. Search terms included combinations of “fluoride,” “fluorine,” “tea,” “*Camellia sinensis*,” “uptake,” “transport,” “tolerance,” “bioavailability,” and “risk assessment.” Boolean operators (AND, OR) were used.

2.2 Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Inclusion criteria: (i) original research or reviews on fluoride in tea plants or tea products; (ii) studies reporting quantitative data on fluoride concentration, uptake, transport, or health risk; (iii) English or Chinese language. Exclusion criteria: (i) conference abstracts without full data; (ii) studies on non-tea plants; (iii) duplicate publications.

2.3 Data extraction and synthesis

Two reviewers independently extracted data on fluoride concentrations, experimental conditions, bioavailability rates, and risk estimates. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus. A total of 87 studies were included. For risk assessment, estimated daily intake (EDI) was calculated as: EDI = (C × IR × EF × ED) / (BW × AT), where C is fluoride concentration in tea infusion (mg/L), IR is ingestion rate (L/day), EF is exposure frequency, ED is exposure duration, BW is body weight, and AT is averaging time. Hazard quotient (HQ) = EDI / PTDI.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Fluoride absorption in roots

Fluoride uptake by tea roots occurs mainly in the form of free F⁻ ions. Studies using ¹⁸F labeling and electrophysiological techniques indicate that F⁻ enters root cells via two pathways: (i) passive diffusion across the plasma membrane, driven by electrochemical gradient; and (ii) facilitated transport through anion channels, including members of the ALMT (aluminum-activated malate transporter) and CLC (chloride channel) families. Root F concentration in hydroponic experiments reached 320–480 mg/kg after 7 days exposure to 10 mg/L F, with uptake rate following Michaelis–Menten kinetics (Km = 0.42 mM, Vmax = 18.6 mg/kg/h). Low pH (4.5–5.5) enhanced uptake by 35–50%, likely due to increased HF formation.

3.2 Long-distance transportation

Following root uptake, fluoride is loaded into the xylem and transported to shoots. Xylem sap analysis revealed F concentrations of 2.1–4.8 mg/L, with translocation efficiency of 22–38%. Radial transport in roots involves apoplastic and symplastic pathways, with Casparian bands limiting apoplastic flow. In leaves, fluoride is preferentially accumulated in mature leaves rather than young buds, with a basipetal gradient. A study using detached leaf petiole feeding showed that F is phloem-mobile to a limited extent, with export rate <5% of total leaf F.

3.3 Tolerance mechanisms

Tea plants exhibit several tolerance strategies: (i) cell wall immobilization—up to 45% of root F is bound to pectin and hemicellulose; (ii) vacuolar sequestration—F is stored in vacuoles as AlF complexes, reducing cytoplasmic toxicity; (iii) antioxidant defense—SOD, POD, and CAT activities increased by 1.5–2.3 fold under 5 mg/L F stress; (iv) gene regulation—transcriptome analysis identified 126 F-responsive genes, including those encoding transporters (CsALMT1, CsCLC1), transcription factors (CsWRKY, CsMYB), and stress proteins. Overexpression of CsALMT1 in Arabidopsis increased F tolerance by 40%.

3.4 Bioavailability from tea infusions

Fluoride bioavailability from tea infusions varied by tea type: green tea (65–78%), black tea (70–85%), oolong tea (60–75%), and brick tea (80–92%). Brewing time significantly affected release: 5 min released 45–60% of total leaf F, while 30 min released 75–90%. Water quality (hardness, pH) also influenced bioavailability; high Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ reduced F bioavailability by 15–25% due to complexation. In vitro simulated digestion showed that 55–70% of tea F was bioaccessible in the gastric phase and 40–55% in the intestinal phase.

3.5 Health risk assessment

Based on 87 studies, mean fluoride concentration in tea infusions was 0.8–2.5 mg/L for green and black tea, and 3.5–7.8 mg/L for brick tea. For a 60 kg adult consuming 1 L/day of brick tea, EDI = 0.058–0.130 mg/kg bw/day, with HQ = 0.83–1.86 (PTDI = 0.07 mg/kg bw/day). In Tibetan children (30 kg) consuming 0.8 L/day, EDI reached 0.093–0.208 mg/kg bw/day, HQ = 1.33–2.97. Dental fluorosis prevalence in high-brick-tea regions was 35–60%, and skeletal fluorosis 8–15%. In contrast, green tea consumption in urban China (0.5 L/day) gave EDI = 0.007–0.021 mg/kg bw/day, HQ < 0.3, indicating low risk.

4. Discussion

This review confirms that *C. sinensis* possesses efficient fluoride absorption and transport systems, with mature leaves acting as a major sink. The tolerance mechanisms are multifaceted, involving physical barriers, biochemical detoxification, and genetic regulation. Compared with other crops, tea’s unique fluoride accumulation is likely an evolutionary adaptation to acidic soils rich in aluminum and fluoride, where Al–F complexation reduces toxicity.

Bioavailability data indicate that tea infusion is a significant dietary fluoride source, especially for brick tea consumers. The high bioavailability (up to 92%) is attributable to the soluble ionic form of F in infusions. However, the presence of Al, Ca, and polyphenols may reduce net absorption in vivo, suggesting that in vitro data may overestimate risk.

Risk assessment reveals a clear dose–response relationship between brick tea consumption and fluorosis. The HQ values >1 in Tibetan and Mongolian populations are consistent with epidemiological findings. Limitations of this review include heterogeneity in study designs, lack of standardized brewing protocols, and limited human biomarker data. Future research should focus on (i) molecular identification of F transporters; (ii) field-based bioavailability studies; and (iii) development of low-fluoride tea cultivars through breeding or agronomic practices.

5. Conclusion

Fluoride absorption in *C. sinensis* occurs via passive diffusion and anion channels, followed by xylem transport and preferential accumulation in mature leaves. Tolerance is mediated by cell wall binding, vacuolar sequestration, antioxidant defense, and gene regulation. Fluoride bioavailability from tea infusions ranges from 55% to 92%, with brick tea posing the highest risk. In high-consumption regions, EDI and HQ values exceed safe thresholds, particularly for children. Systematic monitoring, consumption advisories, and breeding of low-fluoride tea varieties are recommended to mitigate health risks while preserving tea’s cultural and economic benefits.

title: Drought degree constrains the beneficial effects of a fungal endophyte on Atractylodes lancea
text:
Title: Drought degree constrains the beneficial effects of a fungal endophyte on *Atractylodes lancea*

Abstract
Fungal endophytes often enhance host plant performance under abiotic stress, but whether these benefits persist across a gradient of stress severity remains poorly understood. We investigated the interaction between the root endophyte *Serendipita indica*-like strain AL-7 and *Atractylodes lancea* (Thunb.) DC. under four watering regimes: well-watered (WW, 75% field capacity), mild drought (MD, 55% FC), moderate drought (MoD, 35% FC) and severe drought (SD, 20% FC). Endophyte inoculation significantly increased shoot biomass, root biomass and leaf relative water content under WW, MD and MoD conditions, with the largest relative benefit at MoD (+38.4% shoot biomass). However, under SD, colonised plants showed no biomass advantage and exhibited higher leaf malondialdehyde and lower peroxidase activity than non-colonised controls. Endophyte colonisation rates declined from 68.2% (WW) to 21.5% (SD). Volatile oil yield, the primary medicinal trait, was enhanced by inoculation under MD and MoD (+26.1% and +19.7%, respectively) but not under WW or SD. These results indicate that the beneficial effects of AL-7 on *A. lancea* are unimodal across the drought gradient, peaking at moderate stress and collapsing under severe stress, and that drought degree is a critical modulator of endophyte–host outcomes.

Keywords: *Atractylodes lancea*; drought stress; fungal endophyte; plant growth promotion; secondary metabolites; symbiosis

Introduction
*Atractylodes lancea* is a perennial Asteraceae herb whose rhizomes are widely used in traditional Chinese medicine. Cultivation is increasingly constrained by seasonal drought, which reduces both yield and volatile oil content. Fungal endophytes can mitigate drought stress through osmoregulation, antioxidant enhancement and nutrient acquisition, yet most studies compare only two watering levels (well-watered vs. drought), implicitly assuming a monotonic benefit. Stress-severity thresholds may exist beyond which symbiotic costs outweigh benefits, because the host reduces carbon allocation to the symbiont and the endophyte itself becomes stressed. We hypothesised that the growth-promoting effect of a drought-tolerant endophyte on *A. lancea* follows a unimodal response, peaking at moderate drought and diminishing under severe drought. To test this, we inoculated plants with strain AL-7 and measured growth, physiological and quality traits across four drought intensities.

Materials and Methods
*Plant material and endophyte.* *A. lancea* seeds were surface-sterilised and germinated in sterilised vermiculite. The endophyte AL-7 (closely related to *Serendipita indica*) was isolated from wild *A. lancea* roots, confirmed by ITS sequencing, and cultured on potato dextrose agar. Inoculum consisted of mycelial plugs suspended in sterile water (10⁶ CFU mL⁻¹).

*Experimental design.* Sixty uniform 30-day-old seedlings were transplanted into pots (12 cm diameter) filled with sterilised soil–sand mixture (3:1). Half were inoculated with 10 mL AL-7 suspension; controls received autoclaved suspension. Plants were grown in a greenhouse (25/18 °C, 14 h photoperiod, 60% RH). After 14 days, four watering regimes were imposed: WW (75% FC), MD (55% FC), MoD (35% FC) and SD (20% FC), maintained gravimetrically for 30 days. Each treatment combination had 15 replicates.

*Measurements.* Shoot and root dry mass were recorded. Leaf relative water content (RWC), malondialdehyde (MDA), peroxidase (POD) and proline were measured using standard assays. Colonisation rate was determined by re-isolation from surface-sterilised root segments. Volatile oil was extracted by hydrodistillation and quantified by GC-MS.

*Statistics.* Data were analysed by two-way ANOVA (drought × inoculation) followed by Tukey's HSD test (P < 0.05).

Results
Drought significantly reduced all growth parameters in non-inoculated plants (Table 1). Inoculation increased shoot biomass by 16.8%, 27.5% and 38.4% under WW, MD and MoD, respectively, but by only 2.1% under SD. Root biomass followed a similar pattern. Leaf RWC of inoculated plants was 8.9–14.2% higher than controls under MD and MoD, but did not differ under SD.

Physiologically, inoculated plants under MoD showed 31.6% lower MDA and 42.3% higher POD activity than controls. Under SD, however, inoculated plants had 12.4% higher MDA and 15.8% lower POD activity than non-inoculated plants. Proline accumulation was highest in SD and was not affected by inoculation.

Root colonisation declined with drought severity: 68.2% (WW), 59.4% (MD), 41.7% (MoD) and 21.5% (SD). Volatile oil yield was significantly enhanced by inoculation under MD (+26.1%) and MoD (+19.7%), unchanged under WW, and slightly reduced under SD.

Discussion
Our results support a unimodal model of endophyte benefit along a drought gradient. Moderate drought likely represents an optimal window in which host stress is sufficient to make symbiont-derived water and nutrient uptake valuable, while host carbon supply and endophyte viability remain adequate. Under severe drought, two mechanisms may explain the loss of benefit: reduced colonisation, indicating endophyte sensitivity to low water potential, and increased oxidative damage in colonised plants, suggesting that the symbiont becomes a carbon sink without delivering sufficient protection.

The decline in volatile oil under severe drought in inoculated plants is agronomically important, as it implies that inoculation could reduce medicinal quality precisely where drought is most limiting. The unchanged oil yield under well-watered conditions suggests that AL-7 mainly buffers stress rather than directly stimulating biosynthesis.

A limitation of this study is the use of a single endophyte strain and one soil type; field trials across seasons are needed. Nevertheless, the clear threshold between moderate and severe drought demonstrates that drought degree must be treated as a quantitative variable in endophyte research.

Conclusion
The beneficial effects of AL-7 on *A. lancea* are constrained by drought degree, peaking under moderate drought and disappearing under severe drought. Inoculation programmes should therefore target mildly to moderately drought-prone environments, and severe-drought sites may require complementary irrigation or alternative strains.

title: Restoration of organic-matter-impoverished arable soils through the application of soil conditioner prepared via short-time hydrothermal fermentation
text: Abstract: The degradation of arable soils with low organic matter content poses a serious threat to soil productivity and agricultural sustainability. In this study, a novel soil conditioner was prepared via short-time hydrothermal fermentation (SHF) and applied to restore organic-matter-impoverished arable soils. The physicochemical properties of the conditioner, including organic matter composition, humic-like substances, and nutrient content, were characterized. A field-scale experiment was conducted to evaluate the effects of the conditioner on soil organic carbon (SOC), aggregate stability, microbial biomass, and crop yield. The results showed that SHF significantly accelerated the humification process, yielding a conditioner rich in fulvic- and humic-like substances with a low molecular weight and high aromaticity. Application of the conditioner markedly increased SOC content by 28.6–45.3% compared with the control, and improved the proportion of macro-aggregates (>0.25 mm) by 17.2–31.5%. Soil microbial biomass carbon and activities of urease, invertase, and catalase were also significantly enhanced. Moreover, the conditioner improved soil water-holding capacity and cation exchange capacity, while maintaining a neutral to slightly alkaline pH suitable for crop growth. Crop yields increased by 12.4–19.8% following conditioner application, which was attributed to improved nutrient availability and soil structure. Correlation analysis indicated that the humic-like substances in the conditioner played a key role in stabilizing soil aggregates and enhancing carbon sequestration. These findings demonstrate that the SHF-derived soil conditioner is an effective and sustainable amendment for restoring organic-matter-impoverished arable soils, offering a promising strategy for improving soil quality and ensuring food security.

title: Variations in nutrient and trace element composition of rice in an organic rice-frog coculture system
text:
Variations in nutrient and trace element composition of rice in an organic rice-frog coculture system

Abstract

Organic rice-frog coculture (RFC) is an environmentally friendly farming practice that integrates rice cultivation with frog rearing, potentially influencing the nutritional quality of rice grains. This study investigated the variations in nutrient and trace element composition of rice under an organic rice-frog coculture system compared with a conventional rice monoculture (RM) system. Field experiments were conducted over two consecutive years (2022–2023) in a subtropical region of southern China. Rice grains were analyzed for proximate composition (protein, fat, starch, ash, and crude fiber), mineral nutrients (K, Mg, Ca, P), and trace elements (Fe, Zn, Cu, Mn, Se, Cd, Pb, As). The results showed that RFC significantly increased grain protein, Zn, Fe, and Se contents by 8.6%, 15.3%, 12.7%, and 21.4%, respectively, while reducing Cd and Pb accumulation by 18.2% and 22.5% compared with RM. Starch and fat contents did not differ significantly between the two systems. The improved nutrient and trace element profiles in RFC rice were associated with higher soil organic matter, increased microbial activity, and reduced heavy metal availability. These findings suggest that organic rice-frog coculture can enhance the nutritional quality and safety of rice grains, providing a sustainable approach for producing micronutrient-enriched rice.

Keywords: rice-frog coculture; organic farming; nutrient composition; trace elements; heavy metals; rice quality

1. Introduction

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is the staple food for more than half of the world’s population, particularly in Asia. With increasing consumer awareness of food quality and safety, there is growing interest in rice production systems that not only maintain yield but also improve nutritional value and reduce harmful substance accumulation (Zhang et al., 2020). Conventional rice monoculture relies heavily on chemical fertilizers and pesticides, which can lead to soil degradation, biodiversity loss, and heavy metal contamination in grains (Huang et al., 2019). Therefore, sustainable alternatives such as organic farming and integrated rice-animal coculture systems have attracted considerable attention.

Rice-frog coculture (RFC) is a traditional yet revitalized practice in which frogs are introduced into paddy fields to control pests and provide additional income. Frogs prey on insects, reducing the need for insecticides, and their feces contribute organic matter and nutrients to the soil (Li et al., 2021). Previous studies have reported that RFC can improve soil fertility, increase rice yield, and enhance ecosystem services (Wang et al., 2022). However, the effects of RFC on the nutritional composition and trace element profiles of rice grains remain poorly understood. In particular, whether RFC can simultaneously increase beneficial elements (e.g., Zn, Fe, Se) and decrease toxic heavy metals (e.g., Cd, Pb, As) in rice deserves systematic investigation.

This study aimed to (1) compare the nutrient and trace element composition of rice grains between organic rice-frog coculture and conventional rice monoculture, and (2) explore the potential mechanisms underlying the observed variations. We hypothesized that RFC would improve grain nutritional quality by increasing protein and beneficial trace elements while reducing heavy metal accumulation, due to enhanced soil biological activity and altered element cycling.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Experimental site and design

The field experiment was conducted at an experimental farm in Hunan Province, China (28°12′N, 112°58′E) during the rice growing seasons of 2022 and 2023. The soil was a typical paddy soil with pH 6.2, organic matter 24.5 g kg⁻¹, total N 1.42 g kg⁻¹, available P 18.6 mg kg⁻¹, and available K 95.3 mg kg⁻¹. The region has a subtropical monsoon climate with a mean annual temperature of 17.5°C and precipitation of 1,350 mm.

Two treatments were established in a randomized complete block design with three replications: (1) organic rice-frog coculture (RFC) and (2) conventional rice monoculture (RM). Each plot was 100 m² (10 m × 10 m) and separated by 30-cm-wide ridges covered with plastic film to prevent water and frog movement between plots. Rice cultivar “Huanghuazhan” (a common indica variety) was used in both years. In RFC, rice seedlings were transplanted at a spacing of 30 cm × 20 cm, and 15-day-old froglets (Rana nigromaculata) were released at a density of 0.5 individuals m⁻² 10 days after transplanting. No chemical fertilizers or pesticides were applied in RFC; instead, decomposed farmyard manure (3,000 kg ha⁻¹) was applied as basal fertilizer. In RM, conventional practices were followed: chemical fertilizers (N 150 kg ha⁻¹, P₂O₅ 75 kg ha⁻¹, K₂O 120 kg ha⁻¹) and pesticides were applied according to local recommendations. Water management followed local practices: shallow water (3–5 cm) during tillering, mid-season drainage, and alternate wetting and drying thereafter.

2.2 Sampling and analysis

At maturity, rice grains were harvested from each plot, air-dried, and dehulled. Brown rice was ground into fine powder and stored at 4°C for analysis. Proximate composition (crude protein, crude fat, starch, ash, and crude fiber) was determined according to AOAC (2000) methods. Protein content was calculated as N × 5.95. For mineral and trace element analysis, ground samples were digested with HNO₃-HClO₄ (4:1, v/v) and analyzed by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES, PerkinElmer Optima 8300) for K, Mg, Ca, P, Fe, Zn, Cu, Mn, and by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS, Agilent 7900) for Se, Cd, Pb, and As. Certified reference material (GBW10045 rice flour) was used for quality control.

2.3 Soil analysis

Soil samples (0–20 cm) were collected at rice maturity. Soil organic matter was determined by dichromate oxidation, available N by alkaline hydrolysis diffusion, available P by Olsen method, and available K by ammonium acetate extraction. Soil microbial biomass carbon (MBC) was measured by chloroform fumigation-extraction. DTPA-extractable Cd, Pb, and As were determined by ICP-MS.

2.4 Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS 22.0. Two-way ANOVA was used to test the effects of treatment, year, and their interaction. Means were compared using Duncan’s multiple range test at P < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Proximate composition of rice grains

The protein content of RFC rice was significantly higher than that of RM rice in both years (P < 0.05), with an average increase of 8.6% (Table 1). The fat, starch, ash, and crude fiber contents showed no significant differences between treatments (P > 0.05). Year-to-year variation was insignificant for all parameters except protein, which was slightly higher in 2023 than in 2022.

Table 1 Proximate composition of rice grains under rice-frog coculture (RFC) and rice monoculture (RM) (mean ± SD, n = 3)

| Parameter (g 100 g⁻¹) | RFC | RM |
|----------------------|-----|-----|
| Crude protein        | 8.82 ± 0.21 a | 8.12 ± 0.18 b |
| Crude fat            | 2.45 ± 0.12 a | 2.38 ± 0.15 a |
| Starch               | 76.3 ± 1.2 a | 75.8 ± 1.4 a |
| Ash                  | 1.32 ± 0.05 a | 1.28 ± 0.06 a |
| Crude fiber          | 1.05 ± 0.04 a | 1.02 ± 0.05 a |

Different letters within a row indicate significant differences at P < 0.05.

3.2 Mineral nutrients

The concentrations of K, Mg, Ca, and P in rice grains did not differ significantly between RFC and RM (Table 2). However, RFC rice showed a slight but non-significant increase in Mg (4.2%) and P (3.8%) compared with RM.

Table 2 Mineral nutrient contents of rice grains (mg kg⁻¹, mean ± SD, n = 3)

| Element | RFC | RM |
|---------|-----|-----|
| K       | 2850 ± 120 a | 2790 ± 135 a |
| Mg      | 1250 ± 45 a | 1200 ± 52 a |
| Ca      | 185 ± 12 a | 178 ± 10 a |
| P       | 3120 ± 98 a | 3005 ± 110 a |

3.3 Trace elements

Significant differences were observed in trace element concentrations (Table 3). RFC rice had 15.3% higher Zn, 12.7% higher Fe, and 21.4% higher Se than RM rice (P < 0.05). Cu and Mn contents were slightly higher in RFC but not significantly different. In contrast, the toxic elements Cd and Pb were significantly lower in RFC rice by 18.2% and 22.5%, respectively (P < 0.05). Arsenic content did not differ significantly between the two systems.

Table 3 Trace element contents of rice grains (mg kg⁻¹, mean ± SD, n = 3)

| Element | RFC | RM |
|---------|-----|-----|
| Zn      | 22.6 ± 0.9 a | 19.6 ± 1.1 b |
| Fe      | 10.6 ± 0.5 a | 9.4 ± 0.6 b |
| Cu      | 3.2 ± 0.2 a | 3.0 ± 0.2 a |
| Mn      | 18.5 ± 0.8 a | 17.9 ± 0.9 a |
| Se      | 0.085 ± 0.004 a | 0.070 ± 0.005 b |
| Cd      | 0.045 ± 0.003 b | 0.055 ± 0.004 a |
| Pb      | 0.062 ± 0.005 b | 0.080 ± 0.006 a |
| As      | 0.105 ± 0.008 a | 0.110 ± 0.009 a |

3.4 Soil properties

RFC soil had significantly higher organic matter (28.6 vs. 23.1 g kg⁻¹), available N (125 vs. 105 mg kg⁻¹), and microbial biomass carbon (312 vs. 245 mg kg⁻¹) than RM soil (P < 0.05). DTPA-extractable Cd and Pb were significantly lower in RFC soil (0.021 and 0.035 mg kg⁻¹) than in RM soil (0.032 and 0.052 mg kg⁻¹). Available P and K did not differ significantly.

4. Discussion

The present study demonstrated that organic rice-frog coculture significantly improved the nutritional quality of rice grains, particularly by increasing protein and beneficial trace elements (Zn, Fe, Se) while reducing toxic heavy metals (Cd, Pb). These findings are consistent with previous reports that integrated rice-animal systems can enhance grain nutrient density (Li et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022). The increase in protein content may be attributed to the slow release of organic nitrogen from farmyard manure and frog feces, which promotes sustained nitrogen uptake and grain filling (Huang et al., 2019). In contrast, conventional RM with chemical fertilizers often leads to luxury nitrogen consumption and lower nitrogen use efficiency.

The elevated Zn, Fe, and Se concentrations in RFC rice could result from multiple mechanisms. First, higher soil organic matter in RFC may form stable complexes with micronutrients, increasing their availability to rice roots (Zhang et al., 2020). Second, the presence of frogs may enhance soil microbial activity, as indicated by higher MBC, which can solubilize minerals and facilitate their uptake. Third, the reduced use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides in RFC may alleviate antagonistic interactions between nutrients; for example, high P fertilization in RM can reduce Zn and Fe availability through precipitation (Alloway, 2008). The significant increase in Se is particularly noteworthy, as Se is an essential micronutrient with antioxidant properties. Frogs may accumulate Se from their diet and excrete it in feces, thereby enriching the soil-plant system.

The lower Cd and Pb concentrations in RFC rice are of great importance for food safety. Heavy metal uptake by rice is influenced by soil pH, organic matter, and redox conditions. In this study, RFC soil had higher organic matter and lower DTPA-extractable Cd and Pb, suggesting that organic matter immobilizes these metals through adsorption and complexation (Li et al., 2021). Additionally, the alternating wetting and drying regime in both systems may affect metal mobility, but the higher microbial activity in RFC could promote the formation of metal-sulfide complexes, reducing bioavailability (Huang et al., 2019). The non-significant difference in As may be due to the contrasting effects of organic matter on As mobility, as organic acids can both compete with As for sorption sites and enhance microbial reduction of As(V) to As(III) (Wang et al., 2022).

The lack of significant differences in starch, fat, and most mineral nutrients (K, Mg, Ca, P) suggests that RFC primarily affects protein and trace element accumulation rather than overall carbohydrate and macronutrient deposition. This selective effect may be related to the specific roles of these elements in plant metabolism and the timing of nutrient supply relative to grain filling.

From a practical perspective, RFC offers a dual benefit: improved rice nutritional quality and reduced heavy metal accumulation, without compromising yield (data not shown). This system aligns with the principles of organic agriculture and sustainable development. However, long-term studies are needed to assess the stability of these benefits across different soil types and climatic conditions. Furthermore, the economic viability of RFC depends on frog survival and market demand, which may vary regionally.

5. Conclusion

Organic rice-frog coculture significantly enhanced the nutritional quality of rice grains by increasing protein, Zn, Fe, and Se contents while reducing Cd and Pb accumulation compared with conventional rice monoculture. These improvements were associated with higher soil organic matter, increased microbial biomass, and reduced availability of toxic heavy metals. The coculture system did not affect starch, fat, or major mineral nutrient contents. Our findings suggest that rice-frog coculture is a promising sustainable practice for producing micronutrient-enriched and safer rice. Future research should focus on optimizing frog density and organic amendment regimes to maximize both nutritional benefits and yield stability.

title: Terrestrial biodiversity threatened by increasing global aridity velocity under high-level warming
text: Climate change is intensifying the global water cycle, driving widespread increases in aridity across terrestrial ecosystems. While considerable attention has been devoted to the magnitude of aridity change, the velocity at which arid conditions shift across landscapes—termed aridity velocity—remains poorly quantified, despite its critical role in determining whether species can track suitable climates through dispersal. Rapid aridity velocity may outpace the migration capacity of many plants and animals, leading to local extinctions and biodiversity loss, yet the global patterns and magnitude of future aridity velocity under different warming levels are largely unknown. Here, we quantify global terrestrial aridity velocity under 1.5 °C, 2 °C, and 3 °C warming scenarios and assess the exposure of biodiversity hotspots and protected areas to rapid aridification. Our results show that aridity velocity increases nonlinearly with warming, with high-level warming (3 °C) producing velocities that substantially exceed the dispersal capabilities of most terrestrial species. These findings reveal a pronounced and uneven threat to global biodiversity, highlighting the urgent need to limit warming to avoid widespread, dispersal-limited range shifts in terrestrial ecosystems.

title: An Exploration of Hiking Risk Perception: Dimensions and Antecedent Factors
text:
Results and Discussion

Factor analysis of the 24-item risk perception scale yielded four dimensions, accounting for 68.4% of total variance (KMO = 0.87; Bartlett's χ² = 2143.6, p < .001). The dimensions were labelled *Physical Hazard* (α = 0.89), *Environmental Uncertainty* (α = 0.84), *Competence Deficit* (α = 0.81), and *Social and Managerial Risk* (α = 0.78). Respondents rated Physical Hazard highest (M = 4.12, SD = 0.76), followed by Environmental Uncertainty (M = 3.85, SD = 0.81), Competence Deficit (M = 3.41, SD = 0.92), and Social and Managerial Risk (M = 2.97, SD = 0.88).

Regression analysis showed that hiking experience (β = −0.31, p < .001), self-efficacy (β = −0.27, p < .01), and risk information exposure (β = 0.22, p < .01) significantly predicted overall risk perception, explaining 34% of the variance (R² = 0.34, F(5, 412) = 42.17, p < .001). Gender and age were non-significant.

The four-factor structure suggests hikers distinguish physical, environmental, competence-based, and social-managerial threats, consistent with multidimensional conceptualisations of risk. The dominance of Physical Hazard implies that injury-related concerns anchor hikers' appraisals. Notably, experience and self-efficacy reduced perceived risk, supporting a confidence-buffering mechanism, whereas greater exposure to risk information heightened it—evidence that awareness campaigns can sensitise rather than reassure. These findings suggest that safety interventions should target competence-building and calibrated information provision, particularly for less experienced hikers, rather than assuming that information alone attenuates risk perception.

title: Non-thermal combined treatments in the processing of açai (Euterpe oleracea) juice
text:
Non-thermal combined treatments in the processing of açai (Euterpe oleracea) juice

 Abstract

Açai (Euterpe oleracea) juice is a highly perishable Amazonian product rich in anthocyanins, phenolic acids, and unsaturated fatty acids, but its sensitivity to heat limits the application of conventional pasteurization. This study evaluated the effects of three non-thermal combined treatments—high-intensity ultrasound (HIUS), pulsed electric field (PEF), and ultraviolet-C light (UV-C)—applied individually and in sequence on the physicochemical, microbiological, and bioactive properties of açai juice during 30 days of refrigerated storage (4 °C). A combined sequence of PEF (20 kV/cm, 100 μs) followed by HIUS (20 kHz, 400 W, 10 min) and UV-C (254 nm, 1.2 J/cm²) was compared with conventional thermal pasteurization (90 °C, 60 s). The combined non-thermal treatment reduced total aerobic mesophilic counts by 4.1 log CFU/mL and yeasts and molds by 3.8 log CFU/mL, while preserving 91.2% of total anthocyanins and 88.5% of total phenolic compounds, compared with 68.4% and 72.1%, respectively, in the thermally treated samples. Color parameters (L*, a*, b*) and antioxidant capacity (ORAC and DPPH) were also better retained. The non-thermal combined process increased the shelf life of açai juice to 30 days without detectable microbial growth, whereas the thermally treated juice showed spoilage after 21 days. These findings indicate that sequential non-thermal treatments are a promising alternative for preserving the nutritional and sensory quality of açai juice.

 Keywords

Açai juice; non-thermal processing; ultrasound; pulsed electric field; UV-C; anthocyanins; shelf life

 1. Introduction

Açai (Euterpe oleracea Mart.) is a palm fruit native to the Amazon floodplains, and its juice has gained global popularity because of its high content of anthocyanins, particularly cyanidin-3-O-glucoside and cyanidin-3-O-rutinoside, as well as phenolic acids, flavonoids, and unsaturated fatty acids (Pacheco-Palencia et al., 2008). These compounds are associated with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cardioprotective effects. However, açai juice is highly susceptible to microbial spoilage and enzymatic browning, and its anthocyanins are unstable under thermal stress. Conventional pasteurization, typically performed at 85–95 °C for 15–60 s, ensures microbial safety but causes significant degradation of anthocyanins, color changes, and losses of antioxidant capacity (Del Pozo-Insfran et al., 2006).

Non-thermal technologies such as high-intensity ultrasound (HIUS), pulsed electric field (PEF), and ultraviolet-C light (UV-C) have been proposed as alternatives to thermal pasteurization. HIUS generates cavitation, which disrupts cell membranes and inactivates microorganisms, while PEF induces electroporation of microbial cells. UV-C at 254 nm causes DNA damage in microorganisms. Individually, however, these treatments often achieve limited microbial inactivation in opaque or viscous juices such as açai. Combined or sequential treatments may provide synergistic effects, allowing lower individual intensities and better preservation of bioactive compounds (Cruz et al., 2020; Rios-Romero et al., 2022).

The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of combined non-thermal treatments (PEF + HIUS + UV-C) on the microbiological, physicochemical, and bioactive properties of açai juice during refrigerated storage, compared with conventional thermal pasteurization.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Juice preparation

Frozen açai pulp (Euterpe oleracea) was obtained from a commercial supplier (Belém, Pará, Brazil) and thawed at 4 °C for 12 h. The pulp was diluted with distilled water (1:1, w/w) and homogenized. The initial pH was 4.8 ± 0.1, and soluble solids were 8.2 ± 0.3 °Brix.

 2.2 Non-thermal treatments

PEF treatment was performed using a laboratory-scale continuous system with a co-field flow chamber. The juice was treated at 20 kV/cm, 100 μs total specific energy, and a flow rate of 20 mL/min. HIUS treatment was carried out with a 20 kHz probe system (400 W, 13 mm diameter) at 40% amplitude for 10 min, with the sample maintained at 25 °C using a water bath. UV-C treatment was applied in a annular reactor with a 254 nm low-pressure mercury lamp at a dose of 1.2 J/cm². The combined treatment consisted of PEF followed by HIUS and then UV-C (PEF + HIUS + UV-C). Thermal pasteurization was performed at 90 °C for 60 s in a water bath, followed by immediate cooling. Untreated juice was used as a control.

 2.3 Microbiological analysis

Total aerobic mesophilic bacteria, yeasts and molds, and psychrotrophic bacteria were enumerated using plate count agar (PCA), potato dextrose agar (PDA), and PCA incubated at 7 °C, respectively. Results were expressed as log CFU/mL.

 2.4 Physicochemical and bioactive analyses

pH, titratable acidity, and soluble solids were determined according to AOAC methods. Color was measured using a HunterLab colorimeter (L*, a*, b*). Total anthocyanins were quantified by the pH differential method and expressed as cyanidin-3-O-glucoside equivalents. Total phenolic compounds were determined by the Folin–Ciocalteu method. Antioxidant capacity was assessed by DPPH and ORAC assays. All analyses were performed in triplicate at 0, 7, 14, 21, and 30 days of storage at 4 °C.

 2.5 Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed by ANOVA and Tukey’s test (p < 0.05) using SAS 9.4.

 3. Results and Analysis

 3.1 Microbial inactivation

The initial microbial load of untreated açai juice was 5.6 ± 0.2 log CFU/mL for total aerobic mesophiles, 4.9 ± 0.3 log CFU/mL for yeasts and molds, and 4.2 ± 0.2 log CFU/mL for psychrotrophs. After the combined non-thermal treatment, total aerobic mesophiles were reduced by 4.1 log CFU/mL, yeasts and molds by 3.8 log CFU/mL, and psychrotrophs by 3.5 log CFU/mL. Thermal pasteurization achieved reductions of 4.5, 4.2, and 4.0 log CFU/mL, respectively. During storage, the non-thermal combined treatment maintained microbial counts below the detection limit (1 log CFU/mL) for 30 days, whereas the thermally treated juice exceeded 5 log CFU/mL for mesophiles after 21 days. The control juice spoiled within 7 days.

 3.2 Physicochemical properties

pH and titratable acidity did not differ significantly among treatments (p > 0.05). Soluble solids remained stable at 8.1–8.3 °Brix. Color analysis showed that the non-thermal combined treatment better preserved the typical dark purple color of açai juice. After 30 days, the thermal treatment reduced L* from 12.5 to 9.8 and a* from 8.4 to 5.1, indicating darkening and loss of redness. In contrast, the non-thermal combined treatment maintained L* at 11.9 and a* at 7.8. The b* values remained near 2.0 in all samples.

 3.3 Bioactive compounds and antioxidant capacity

Total anthocyanins in untreated juice were 245.3 ± 8.7 mg cyanidin-3-O-glucoside equivalents/L. After thermal pasteurization, anthocyanin retention was 68.4% immediately after treatment and decreased to 52.1% after 30 days. The non-thermal combined treatment retained 91.2% immediately after treatment and 84.7% after 30 days. Total phenolic compounds followed a similar trend: 88.5% retention after non-thermal treatment versus 72.1% after thermal treatment at day 0, and 79.3% versus 58.6% at day 30. Antioxidant capacity (ORAC) was 1,245 ± 45 μmol TE/L in untreated juice. After 30 days, the non-thermal combined treatment retained 82.4% of ORAC, while the thermal treatment retained 61.2%. DPPH results were consistent with ORAC.

 4. Discussion

The superior microbial inactivation of the combined non-thermal treatment can be attributed to synergistic mechanisms. PEF induces electroporation of cell membranes, increasing permeability and sensitizing microorganisms to subsequent HIUS cavitation and UV-C damage. HIUS generates localized high pressure and temperature gradients that disrupt cell walls, while UV-C causes thymine dimer formation in DNA. The sequence PEF → HIUS → UV-C was more effective than individual treatments (data not shown), likely because PEF and HIUS compromise membrane integrity, allowing UV-C to penetrate more effectively. Similar synergistic effects have been reported for combined PEF and UV treatments in fruit juices (Cruz et al., 2020).

The better retention of anthocyanins and phenolics in the non-thermal combined treatment is explained by the absence of high temperatures, which normally accelerate anthocyanin degradation through hydrolysis, oxidation, and polymerization. Anthocyanins are particularly sensitive to temperatures above 70 °C, and thermal pasteurization at 90 °C for 60 s likely caused substantial degradation. In contrast, the non-thermal treatments, despite generating some heat through cavitation, maintained the juice temperature below 40 °C, minimizing thermal degradation. The slight reduction in bioactive compounds after non-thermal treatment may be due to oxidative reactions induced by cavitation and UV-C, but these effects were much less severe than thermal degradation.

The extended shelf life of 30 days for the non-thermal combined treatment, compared with 21 days for thermal pasteurization, is noteworthy. Thermal pasteurization may have damaged the juice matrix, releasing nutrients that promoted the growth of surviving thermoduric microorganisms. In contrast, the non-thermal combined treatment likely caused sublethal injury to microbial cells, which were unable to recover during refrigerated storage. Additionally, the retention of natural antimicrobial compounds, such as phenolic acids, in the non-thermal treated juice may have contributed to microbial inhibition.

The color results are consistent with anthocyanin retention. The decrease in L* and a* in thermally treated juice reflects anthocyanin degradation and browning reactions, such as Maillard and ascorbic acid oxidation. The non-thermal combined treatment better preserved the original color, which is a critical quality attribute for consumer acceptance of açai juice.

One limitation of this study is the use of a laboratory-scale system, which may not directly translate to industrial-scale continuous processing. Further studies should evaluate the scalability, energy consumption, and cost-effectiveness of the combined non-thermal process. Additionally, the effects on sensory attributes and volatile compounds should be investigated.

 5. Conclusion

The combined non-thermal treatment (PEF + HIUS + UV-C) effectively inactivated spoilage microorganisms in açai juice while preserving anthocyanins, phenolic compounds, antioxidant capacity, and color better than conventional thermal pasteurization. The non-thermal process extended the shelf life of açai juice to 30 days at 4 °C, compared with 21 days for thermally pasteurized juice. These results suggest that sequential non-thermal treatments are a promising alternative for the processing of açai juice and other heat-sensitive fruit juices. Optimization of treatment parameters and pilot-scale validation are recommended before industrial application.

title: Chinese Medicine in Management of Chronic Disease Endometriosis
text:
Chinese Medicine in Management of Chronic Disease Endometriosis

 Abstract
