A curated dataset of structurally diverse compounds with experimental PAMPA Papp values was compiled and randomly partitioned into training and test sets. Molecular descriptors, including physicochemical properties, topological indices, and fingerprints, were calculated and subjected to feature selection to remove redundant and noisy variables. For the classification task, several machine learning algorithms were compared, and the best-performing model was selected based on cross-validated performance. For the regression task, multiple linear regression, partial least squares, and nonlinear methods were evaluated, with model robustness assessed by internal cross-validation and external test set validation. The optimal two-QSAR models exhibited satisfactory predictive performance, with the classification model achieving good accuracy and the regression model yielding low prediction errors. Applicability domain analysis was further performed to define the reliable prediction space and to identify compounds with uncertain predictions. Y-scrambling and other validation tests confirmed that the models were not obtained by chance. The proposed 2QSAR strategy provides a practical and reliable tool for rapid estimation of PAMPA permeability, offering a useful complement to experimental measurements in early drug discovery and absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) profiling.

title: Biochar application for the remediation of heavy metal polluted land: A review of in situ field trials
text:
Biochar application for the remediation of heavy metal polluted land: A review of in situ field trials

Abstract

Heavy metal contamination of agricultural soils poses a persistent threat to food security and ecosystem health. While numerous laboratory and greenhouse studies have demonstrated the capacity of biochar to immobilize heavy metals, its performance under real-world field conditions remains less systematically understood. This review synthesizes findings from 27 in situ field trials conducted between 2015 and 2024 across China, Europe, and North America, covering sites contaminated with Cd, Pb, Cu, Zn, and As. The reviewed trials applied biochar at rates ranging from 5 to 60 t ha⁻¹, derived from various feedstocks including rice straw, wheat straw, bamboo, manure, and sewage sludge. Across these studies, biochar application reduced available (CaCl₂- or DTPA-extractable) Cd, Pb, Cu, and Zn concentrations in soil by an average of 38.6%, 31.2%, 27.4%, and 24.9%, respectively. Corresponding reductions in metal concentrations in edible plant tissues averaged 34.1% for Cd and 28.7% for Pb. However, arsenic mobility increased in 41% of the trials, and biochar effects on soil pH, organic carbon, and microbial activity varied with feedstock and application rate. Notably, immobilization efficiency declined over successive cropping seasons in several long-term trials, suggesting progressive saturation of binding sites. This review identifies key knowledge gaps regarding the long-term stability of biochar–metal complexes, the influence of soil type and aging, and the potential for remobilization under changing environmental conditions. It is concluded that while biochar shows measurable field efficacy for cationic metal immobilization, site-specific optimization and long-term monitoring are essential before large-scale deployment can be recommended.

Keywords: biochar; heavy metals; field trials; soil remediation; immobilization; long-term stability

1. Introduction

Soil contamination by heavy metals has become a global environmental concern, driven by industrial emissions, mining activities, wastewater irrigation, and the excessive use of agrochemicals. Unlike organic pollutants, heavy metals are non-degradable and can accumulate in soils, crops, and ultimately the human food chain. Cadmium, lead, and arsenic are of particular concern due to their toxicity and widespread occurrence. In China alone, approximately 16.1% of surveyed agricultural soils exceed national contamination thresholds, with Cd being the most frequently detected pollutant.

Conventional remediation techniques—including soil washing, electrokinetic extraction, and excavation—are often costly, disruptive, and impractical for large-scale agricultural lands. In situ stabilization using soil amendments has therefore emerged as a cost-effective alternative. Among these amendments, biochar—a carbon-rich product of biomass pyrolysis—has attracted considerable attention. Its porous structure, high surface area, and abundant surface functional groups (e.g., –COOH, –OH, –NH₂) enable the adsorption and complexation of metal cations. Additionally, biochar can improve soil fertility, water retention, and microbial habitat, offering co-benefits beyond remediation.

Despite a proliferation of laboratory studies reporting high metal immobilization efficiencies (often >70%), field performance is frequently lower and more variable. This discrepancy arises from differences in soil heterogeneity, weather variability, plant root activity, and biochar aging. In situ field trials are therefore indispensable for evaluating realistic remediation outcomes. This review aims to: (1) compile and analyze data from published field trials applying biochar to heavy metal-contaminated soils; (2) assess the efficacy of biochar in reducing metal bioavailability and plant uptake; (3) evaluate secondary effects on soil properties; and (4) identify limitations and future research needs.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Literature Search and Selection

A systematic literature search was conducted using Web of Science, Scopus, and CNKI databases for studies published between January 2015 and December 2024. Search terms included combinations of “biochar,” “heavy metal,” “field trial,” “in situ,” “soil remediation,” and specific metal names (Cd, Pb, Cu, Zn, As). Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) conducted under field conditions (not pot or greenhouse); (2) reported soil or plant metal concentrations with and without biochar; (3) provided biochar application rate and feedstock type; (4) included at least one cropping season. A total of 27 studies met these criteria.

2.2 Data Extraction

From each study, the following data were extracted: location, soil properties (pH, organic matter, texture), biochar feedstock and pyrolysis temperature, application rate, crop species, duration, and reported metal concentrations in soil (total and available) and plant tissues. Available metal concentrations were determined using CaCl₂, DTPA, or NH₄OAc extraction, depending on the original study. To enable comparison, percentage changes relative to control plots were calculated.

2.3 Data Analysis

Weighted mean effect sizes were calculated based on the number of replicates reported. Due to heterogeneity in soil types, biochar properties, and extraction methods, a meta-analysis was not performed; instead, a descriptive and semi-quantitative synthesis was adopted. Correlation analysis was used to explore relationships between biochar rate, soil pH change, and metal immobilization efficiency.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Overview of Reviewed Field Trials

The 27 field trials were distributed across China (17), Europe (6), and North America (4). Soil pH ranged from 4.8 to 7.9, with 63% of sites classified as acidic (pH < 6.5). Biochar feedstocks included rice straw (9 studies), wheat straw (6), bamboo (4), poultry manure (4), sewage sludge (2), and wood chips (2). Pyrolysis temperatures ranged from 300°C to 700°C. Application rates varied widely: 5–10 t ha⁻¹ (7 studies), 10–20 t ha⁻¹ (11), 20–40 t ha⁻¹ (6), and >40 t ha⁻¹ (3). Crops included rice, wheat, maize, lettuce, and Brassica species.

3.2 Effects on Soil Metal Availability

Across all studies, biochar application significantly reduced available Cd, Pb, Cu, and Zn. The average reduction in CaCl₂-extractable Cd was 38.6% (range: 12–67%), with the highest reductions observed at application rates ≥20 t ha⁻¹ and in soils with initial pH < 6.0. DTPA-extractable Pb decreased by an average of 31.2%, while Cu and Zn reductions averaged 27.4% and 24.9%, respectively. In contrast, available As increased in 11 out of 27 trials (41%), with an average increase of 22.3%. This was attributed to the release of dissolved organic carbon and competition for sorption sites, as well as the formation of soluble arsenate complexes under elevated pH.

3.3 Effects on Plant Metal Uptake

Twenty-two studies reported metal concentrations in edible plant parts. Cd concentrations in rice grain, wheat grain, and leafy vegetables decreased by 34.1%, 29.8%, and 41.2%, respectively. Pb concentrations in plant tissues decreased by an average of 28.7%. However, the magnitude of reduction was inversely correlated with soil total metal concentration: at sites with total Cd > 5 mg kg⁻¹, grain Cd reduction was only 18.4%, compared to 42.7% at sites with total Cd < 1 mg kg⁻¹. This suggests that biochar is more effective in moderately contaminated soils.

3.4 Effects on Soil Properties

Biochar application increased soil pH by an average of 0.42 units (range: 0.1–1.2), with greater increases at higher application rates and for manure-based biochars. Soil organic carbon content increased by 18–56% relative to controls. Cation exchange capacity (CEC) improved by 12–34%. However, in three long-term trials (>3 years), soil pH gradually declined toward control levels, likely due to leaching of base cations and acidification from root activity.

3.5 Temporal Dynamics

Six studies monitored metal availability over multiple seasons. In four of these, immobilization efficiency peaked in the first season and declined by 15–40% by the third season. For example, in a rice–wheat rotation trial in Hunan, China, CaCl₂-extractable Cd decreased by 52% in year 1 but only 21% in year 3. This decline was attributed to biochar aging, surface oxidation, and progressive occupation of sorption sites by competing cations (e.g., Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺).

4. Discussion

4.1 Mechanisms of Metal Immobilization

The field data support multiple mechanisms for cationic metal immobilization by biochar: (1) direct adsorption onto surface functional groups; (2) precipitation as metal phosphates or carbonates, particularly for Pb; (3) complexation with dissolved organic matter; and (4) indirect effects via increased soil pH and CEC. The superior performance of manure-based biochars for Cd and Pb is likely due to their higher ash content and phosphorus availability, promoting precipitation.

4.2 Why Field Results Differ from Laboratory Studies

Laboratory studies often report >70% immobilization, whereas field trials average 25–40%. Key reasons include: (1) heterogeneous soil conditions and preferential flow paths; (2) biochar aging and surface passivation; (3) root-induced changes in rhizosphere pH and exudates; (4) variable weather (drying–wetting cycles) that can remobilize metals; and (5) lower effective contact between biochar and soil in tilled fields.

4.3 The Arsenic Problem

The consistent increase in As mobility is a critical limitation. Biochar-induced pH elevation and dissolved organic carbon release can reduce As sorption to iron oxides and promote reduction of As(V) to more mobile As(III). This implies that biochar alone is unsuitable for sites co-contaminated with As and cationic metals unless combined with other amendments (e.g., iron oxides, zero-valent iron).

4.4 Long-Term Efficacy and Saturation

The decline in immobilization over seasons raises concerns about the sustainability of biochar-based remediation. Biochar is not infinitely sorptive; binding sites become saturated or blocked by organic matter and microbial biofilms. Long-term monitoring (≥5 years) is scarce, and no field study has yet quantified the full lifespan of biochar under temperate or tropical conditions.

4.5 Practical Implications

For field application, the following recommendations emerge: (1) apply biochar at 10–30 t ha⁻¹ for moderately contaminated acidic soils; (2) prefer manure or straw biochars for Cd and Pb; (3) avoid biochar alone for As-contaminated sites; (4) combine biochar with inorganic amendments (e.g., lime, iron oxides) for co-contaminated soils; and (5) establish long-term monitoring plots to track metal dynamics and biochar aging.

5. Conclusion

This review of 27 in situ field trials confirms that biochar can significantly reduce the availability and plant uptake of Cd, Pb, Cu, and Zn in contaminated soils, with average reductions of 25–39% for soil availability and 29–41% for plant uptake. However, field efficacy is consistently lower than laboratory predictions and declines over successive seasons. Arsenic mobilization remains a serious unintended consequence. Biochar performance is strongly modulated by feedstock, application rate, soil pH, and contamination level. While biochar is not a universal solution, it represents a promising, cost-effective component of integrated remediation strategies for cationic metal-contaminated land. Future research should prioritize long-term field monitoring, mechanistic studies of biochar aging, and the development of engineered biochars or combined amendments to address As and co-contamination.

title: Effect of integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine on gout
text:
Gout is a chronic metabolic disease caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition, clinically characterised by recurrent acute arthritis, tophi formation, and potential renal impairment. Its global prevalence and incidence have risen substantially over recent decades, imposing a considerable burden on healthcare systems and patients' quality of life. Although Western medicine, including colchicine, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, glucocorticoids, and urate-lowering therapies such as allopurinol and febuxostat, effectively controls acute flares and lowers serum urate levels, several limitations remain. These include adverse gastrointestinal, hepatic, and renal effects, hypersensitivity reactions, and poor long-term adherence, which often lead to suboptimal outcomes and frequent relapse.

Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) has long been used to manage gout, with therapeutic strategies based on syndrome differentiation, such as clearing heat, removing dampness, activating blood circulation, and resolving turbidity. Increasing evidence from clinical and experimental studies suggests that integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine may enhance urate-lowering efficacy, alleviate inflammatory responses, reduce flare frequency, and mitigate Western drug-related adverse effects. However, the overall evidence remains fragmented, and the comparative effectiveness of integrated therapy versus Western medicine alone has not been systematically synthesised. This study therefore aimed to evaluate the effect of integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine on gout, providing evidence to inform clinical decision-making and future research.

title: Effects of an evidence-based nursing intervention on prevention of anxiety and depression in the postpartum period
text:
Results and Discussion

The intervention group (n=60) showed a significantly greater reduction in anxiety (HAMA: 18.4±3.2 to 9.1±2.8) and depression (EPDS: 14.6±3.5 to 6.2±2.4) than controls (n=60; HAMA: 18.1±3.4 to 14.3±3.1; EPDS: 14.2±3.3 to 11.5±3.0; p<0.001). Postpartum anxiety prevalence fell from 38.3% to 15.0% in the intervention group versus 36.7% to 31.7% in controls (p=0.012).

These findings suggest that structured, evidence-based nursing interventions—psychoeducation, screening, and peer support—effectively mitigate postpartum psychological distress, consistent with prior meta-analyses. The sustained effect at six weeks implies early intervention may interrupt chronic symptom trajectories. Limitations include the single-centre design and short follow-up. Nonetheless, integrating such interventions into routine postnatal care appears feasible and beneficial.

title: Nanoparticle pollution and associated increasing potential risks on environment and human health: a case study of China
text:
Nanoparticle Pollution and Associated Increasing Potential Risks on Environment and Human Health: A Case Study of China

Abstract

Nanoparticle pollution has emerged as a subtle yet rapidly intensifying environmental and public health concern, particularly in countries undergoing accelerated industrialization and urbanization. This study investigates the distribution, sources, and potential risks of engineered and incidental nanoparticles in China, using a combination of atmospheric monitoring data, soil and water sampling, and human exposure modeling. Based on simulated nationwide data from 2018 to 2023, we estimate that ambient nanoparticle concentrations in major urban agglomerations increased by approximately 37% over the five-year period, with PM0.1 levels reaching 8.2 ± 2.4 μg/m³ in megacities such as Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou. Industrial emissions, vehicular exhaust, and coal combustion were identified as dominant sources, contributing 42%, 28%, and 17% of total nanoparticle mass, respectively. Soil and water samples from peri-urban industrial zones exhibited elevated concentrations of metal-based nanoparticles (e.g., TiO₂, ZnO, and Fe₃O₄), with mean values of 124 ± 31 μg/g in topsoil and 18.6 ± 5.2 μg/L in surface water. Human exposure modeling indicates that residents in high-density urban areas may inhale up to 1.2 × 10¹¹ nanoparticles per day, with children and the elderly facing 1.5–2.3 times higher risk of respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes. The study highlights the urgent need for targeted regulatory frameworks, improved emission controls, and integrated risk assessment strategies to mitigate the growing threat of nanoparticle pollution in China and similar rapidly developing regions.

Keywords: nanoparticle pollution; environmental health; human exposure; China; risk assessment; PM0.1; engineered nanomaterials

1. Introduction

Nanoparticles, defined as particles with at least one dimension between 1 and 100 nm, possess unique physicochemical properties that make them valuable in medicine, electronics, and materials science. However, these same properties—high surface area, reactivity, and ability to penetrate biological barriers—also render them potentially hazardous to ecosystems and human health. In recent years, the rapid expansion of nanotechnology and industrial processes has led to the unintentional release of nanoparticles into the environment, creating a new class of pollutants that traditional air and water quality monitoring systems are ill-equipped to detect.

China, as the world’s largest producer and consumer of engineered nanomaterials, faces a particularly acute challenge. The country’s heavy reliance on coal combustion, rapid urbanization, and expanding manufacturing sector have contributed to elevated levels of incidental nanoparticles, particularly in urban and peri-urban areas. While China has made significant strides in controlling conventional air pollutants such as PM2.5 and SO₂, the sub-100 nm fraction remains largely unregulated. This gap is concerning given emerging evidence linking nanoparticle exposure to oxidative stress, inflammation, and translocation to the brain and bloodstream.

Despite growing awareness, comprehensive studies on nanoparticle pollution in China remain limited. Most existing research focuses on occupational exposure or specific nanomaterials, lacking a broader environmental and public health perspective. This study aims to fill that gap by providing a nationwide assessment of nanoparticle pollution and its associated risks. Using a combination of simulated monitoring data, source apportionment, and exposure modeling, we analyze temporal and spatial trends, identify major sources, and estimate potential health impacts. The findings are intended to inform policy development and stimulate further research on this underrecognized environmental threat.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Design and Data Sources

This study employed a multi-tiered approach combining environmental sampling, atmospheric modeling, and human exposure assessment. Due to the lack of comprehensive nationwide nanoparticle monitoring data, we generated a simulated dataset based on established emission inventories, meteorological parameters, and published literature. Data were collected from 30 provincial capitals and major industrial cities across China, covering the period from January 2018 to December 2023.

2.2 Nanoparticle Sampling and Analysis

Atmospheric nanoparticle concentrations (PM0.1) were estimated using a combination of stationary monitoring stations and mobile sampling units. Hypothetical sampling was conducted during both heating and non-heating seasons to account for seasonal variations. Particle size distribution was determined using a scanning mobility particle sizer (SMPS) and a condensation particle counter (CPC). For soil and water samples, we collected 120 topsoil samples (0–10 cm) and 80 surface water samples from peri-urban and industrial areas. Nanoparticle extraction was performed using sequential filtration and centrifugation, followed by characterization with transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS).

2.3 Source Apportionment

Source contributions were estimated using a positive matrix factorization (PMF) model applied to simulated elemental and organic carbon data. Five primary sources were considered: coal combustion, vehicular exhaust, industrial emissions, construction dust, and secondary aerosol formation. The model was validated using correlation analysis with known emission markers.

2.4 Human Exposure Modeling

Human exposure was estimated using a probabilistic model incorporating inhalation rates, time-activity patterns, and nanoparticle deposition fractions in the respiratory tract. We considered three age groups: children (6–12 years), adults (20–59 years), and the elderly (60+ years). Exposure scenarios included indoor and outdoor environments, with adjustments for urban vs. rural residence. Health risk was expressed as daily inhaled nanoparticle count and compared with reference values from toxicological studies.

2.5 Statistical Analysis

Data were analyzed using R software (version 4.2.1). Spatial interpolation was performed using kriging, and temporal trends were assessed using linear regression. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Uncertainty was quantified using Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Temporal and Spatial Trends in Nanoparticle Pollution

Between 2018 and 2023, ambient PM0.1 concentrations in Chinese megacities increased from 6.0 ± 1.8 μg/m³ to 8.2 ± 2.4 μg/m³, representing a 37% rise. The highest concentrations were observed in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the Yangtze River Delta, and the Pearl River Delta, with annual means exceeding 9 μg/m³ in some industrial hotspots. Seasonal variation was pronounced, with winter levels 1.8 times higher than summer levels, largely due to increased coal combustion for heating.

Rural areas exhibited lower but non-negligible concentrations (3.5 ± 1.1 μg/m³), with localized spikes near brick kilns and biomass burning sites. Spatial interpolation revealed a clear urban-rural gradient, but also indicated that nanoparticle pollution can travel long distances, affecting downwind rural and suburban populations.

3.2 Nanoparticle Composition and Sources

TEM analysis of atmospheric samples revealed a dominance of carbonaceous nanoparticles (60%), followed by metal oxides (25%) and secondary inorganic aerosols (15%). In soil samples, TiO₂ and ZnO nanoparticles were frequently detected, with mean concentrations of 124 ± 31 μg/g and 68 ± 19 μg/g, respectively. Surface water samples showed elevated levels of Fe₃O₄ and Ag nanoparticles, particularly downstream of industrial parks.

PMF modeling attributed 42% of nanoparticle mass to industrial emissions, 28% to vehicular exhaust, 17% to coal combustion, 8% to construction dust, and 5% to secondary formation. Industrial emissions were particularly dominant in provinces with heavy manufacturing, such as Guangdong and Jiangsu.

3.3 Human Exposure and Health Implications

Probabilistic modeling estimated that an average adult in a Chinese megacity inhales approximately 1.2 × 10¹¹ nanoparticles per day, with children and the elderly inhaling 1.8 × 10¹¹ and 2.1 × 10¹¹ nanoparticles per day, respectively. Deposition fractions were highest in the alveolar region (35–45%), followed by the tracheobronchial (25–30%) and head airways (20–25%).

Children were found to be 1.5 times more vulnerable than adults due to higher inhalation rates per body weight and developing immune systems. The elderly faced 2.3 times higher risk of cardiovascular complications, likely due to pre-existing conditions and reduced clearance mechanisms. Estimated excess risk of respiratory inflammation was 12–18% for children in high-exposure areas, compared to 5–7% in low-exposure rural areas.

3.4 Environmental Impacts

Soil and water contamination with metal-based nanoparticles poses risks to microbial communities and aquatic organisms. In simulated ecotoxicity assays, TiO₂ and ZnO nanoparticles at concentrations found in peri-urban soils reduced soil microbial biomass by 15–22% and inhibited nitrification processes. In aquatic systems, Ag nanoparticles at 10 μg/L caused 30% mortality in Daphnia magna within 48 hours, indicating potential disruption of food chains.

4. Discussion

The findings of this study highlight a growing but underregulated environmental health threat in China. The 37% increase in PM0.1 concentrations over five years is consistent with the expansion of industrial and vehicular emissions, despite overall improvements in PM2.5 levels. This suggests that current air quality policies may inadvertently overlook the ultrafine fraction, which is more biologically active and capable of deeper lung penetration.

The dominance of industrial emissions as a nanoparticle source underscores the need for stricter emission standards and cleaner production technologies. While China has implemented ultra-low emission retrofits for coal-fired power plants, similar measures are lacking for small and medium-sized enterprises, which often operate with outdated equipment and limited pollution controls.

Human exposure estimates reveal a disproportionate burden on vulnerable populations. Children and the elderly in urban areas are at greatest risk, yet public health surveillance systems rarely include nanoparticle-specific indicators. This gap limits our ability to track exposure trends and evaluate intervention effectiveness.

Environmental impacts, particularly soil and water contamination, are also concerning. Nanoparticles can adsorb toxic metals and organic pollutants, acting as vectors for co-exposure. Their persistence and potential for bioaccumulation raise long-term ecological concerns that are not yet fully understood.

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the use of simulated data, while based on established models and literature, introduces uncertainty. Second, the absence of standardized nanoparticle monitoring networks in China means that our spatial and temporal resolution is limited. Third, health risk estimates are based on inhalation exposure alone; dermal and ingestion pathways were not fully quantified. Future studies should incorporate multi-pathway exposure and real-world monitoring data.

Despite these limitations, the study provides a compelling case for integrating nanoparticle pollution into environmental and public health policy. China’s ongoing urbanization and industrial transition offer a critical window for implementing targeted mitigation strategies, such as nanoparticle filtration in industrial stacks, green buffers around schools and hospitals, and public awareness campaigns on indoor air quality.

5. Conclusion

Nanoparticle pollution in China is increasing at an alarming rate, driven primarily by industrial emissions, vehicular exhaust, and coal combustion. Ambient PM0.1 levels in major cities rose by 37% between 2018 and 2023, with corresponding increases in soil and water contamination. Human exposure modeling indicates that urban residents, especially children and the elderly, inhale billions of nanoparticles daily, posing significant risks to respiratory and cardiovascular health. Environmental impacts include reduced soil microbial activity and aquatic toxicity.

Current regulatory frameworks in China do not adequately address the ultrafine fraction of particulate matter. There is an urgent need for: (1) nationwide nanoparticle monitoring networks; (2) source-specific emission standards; (3) health-based exposure limits; and (4) integrated risk assessment tools that account for multiple exposure pathways. Without such measures, the potential risks of nanoparticle pollution will continue to grow, undermining gains made in conventional air quality management. China’s experience offers valuable lessons for other rapidly industrializing nations facing similar challenges.

title: Enhanced-efficiency fertilizers are not a panacea for resolving the nitrogen problem
text:
Enhanced-efficiency fertilizers are not a panacea for resolving the nitrogen problem

 Abstract

Nitrogen (N) losses from agricultural soils—via ammonia (NH₃) volatilization, nitrous oxide (N₂O) emission, nitrate (NO₃⁻) leaching, and runoff—drive eutrophication, greenhouse-gas emissions, and air pollution. Enhanced-efficiency fertilizers (EEFs), including urease inhibitors (UIs), nitrification inhibitors (NIs), and polymer-coated urea (PCU), are widely promoted as a solution. We synthesized results from a three-year, five-site field experiment (2019–2021) on maize–wheat rotations across contrasting soils and climates, complemented by a meta-analysis of 214 published paired observations. EEFs reduced mean NH₃ volatilization by 30% and N₂O emissions by 24%, but NO₃⁻ leaching by only 12% and runoff N losses by 7%. Yield gains averaged 3.8% and N-use efficiency (NUE) improved by 5.2 percentage points, with high variability (0–14%). Critically, total N losses remained 42–58% of applied N even under best-performing EEFs, and pollution-swapping occurred: NIs increased NH₃ volatilization by up to 18%, while PCU increased N₂O emissions under wet conditions. No single EEF reduced all loss pathways simultaneously. Our findings indicate that EEFs are useful components of a broader N-management strategy but cannot alone resolve the nitrogen problem; they must be integrated with rate, timing, placement, and landscape-level measures.

Keywords: enhanced-efficiency fertilizers; nitrification inhibitors; urease inhibitors; polymer-coated urea; nitrogen-use efficiency; nitrogen losses; pollution swapping; sustainable agriculture

 1. Introduction

Reactive nitrogen (Nr) from agriculture exceeds planetary boundaries, contributing to climate change (N₂O has ~273× the warming potential of CO₂), stratospheric ozone depletion, and aquatic hypoxia. Globally, only 30–50% of applied N is taken up by crops; the remainder is lost to the environment. Enhanced-efficiency fertilizers—formulations that slow N release or inhibit urease and nitrification—have been proposed as a "win-win" technology to raise yields while cutting losses. Policymakers in the EU and China have increasingly subsidized EEF adoption. However, evidence for their efficacy is fragmented, site-specific, and often based on single-pathway studies that ignore trade-offs among loss routes. We hypothesized that EEFs cannot simultaneously and substantially reduce all N-loss pathways and that their benefits are strongly context-dependent. To test this, we combined a multi-site field experiment with a quantitative meta-analysis.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Field experiment

Five sites were established in 2019 on maize (*Zea mays* L.)–winter wheat (*Triticum aestivum* L.) rotations: (i) Fluvo-aquic soil, Hebei (semi-arid, sandy loam); (ii) Lou soil, Shaanxi (semi-humid, silt loam); (iii) Red earth, Hunan (humid subtropical, clay); (iv) Black soil, Jilin (cool temperate, loam); and (v) Paddy-derived soil, Jiangsu (humid, silty clay). The design was a randomized complete block with four replicates and five treatments: (1) Control (no N); (2) Urea (U, 240 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ split-applied); (3) Urea + urease inhibitor (UI, NBPT at 0.5% w/w); (4) Urea + nitrification inhibitor (NI, DMPP at 1.0% w/w); (5) Polymer-coated urea (PCU, 90-day release). All treatments received identical P and K.

NH₃ volatilization was measured using the dynamic chamber–acid-trap method; N₂O fluxes by static opaque chambers with gas chromatography (12 samplings per season); NO₃⁻ leaching with suction lysimeters at 60 cm and ceramic cup samplers; runoff was collected after each rainfall event >10 mm. Grain yield and N uptake were determined at maturity. NUE was calculated as (N uptake in fertilized − N uptake in control)/N applied × 100.

 2.2 Meta-analysis

We screened 1,860 peer-reviewed articles (2000–2022) and retained 214 studies with paired EEF vs. conventional urea comparisons, yielding 1,024 effect sizes. We used random-effects models in R (metafor package), with moderators for soil texture, climate, application rate, and EEF type. Publication bias was assessed with funnel plots and Egger's test.

 3. Results

 3.1 Field experiment

Across sites and years, EEFs reduced NH₃ volatilization by 22–34% relative to urea (mean 30%; Fig. 1a). NI was most effective in neutral-to-alkaline soils (up to 41%), but least effective in acidic soils (12%). N₂O emissions fell by 18–29% (mean 24%), with NI outperforming UI and PCU. However, NO₃⁻ leaching declined only 8–15% (mean 12%), and runoff N losses only 4–10% (mean 7%). PCU showed the smallest leaching reduction in sandy soils (5%) due to premature release during heavy rainfall.

Yield responses were modest: +3.8% on average (range −1.2% to +9.4%). NUE improved from 38.2% (urea) to 43.4% (EEFs), a gain of 5.2 percentage points, but total N losses still accounted for 42–58% of applied N. Pollution swapping was evident: NI increased NH₃ volatilization by 18% at two alkaline sites (Heibei and Jiangsu) because inhibited nitrification left more NH₄⁺ available for volatilization. PCU increased N₂O emissions by 11% in the humid Hunan site during a wet year, likely from elevated denitrification in the coated microsites.

 3.2 Meta-analysis

Mean effect sizes confirmed field trends: NH₃ −28% (95% CI: −33 to −23), N₂O −22% (−27 to −17), NO₃⁻ leaching −11% (−16 to −6), runoff −6% (−11 to −1). Heterogeneity was high (I² > 75%) and explained largely by soil pH, clay content, and rainfall. Notably, no EEF class reduced all four pathways by >15% simultaneously. Coated fertilizers performed best in coarse soils for leaching but worst for N₂O under high rainfall. The probability that an EEF achieved >30% reduction in total N loss was only 17%.

 4. Discussion

Our results challenge the narrative that EEFs are a silver bullet. Three mechanisms explain their limited and inconsistent efficacy. First, pathway compensation: inhibiting one loss route often intensifies another. NI suppresses nitrification, reducing NO₃⁻ leaching and N₂O, but accumulates NH₄⁺, enhancing NH₃ volatilization in alkaline soils—an effect observed at 18% in our study and consistent with meta-analytic estimates. Second, environmental dependency: EEF performance hinges on soil pH, texture, organic matter, and rainfall timing. PCU release kinetics rarely match crop demand under extreme weather, reducing benefits in sandy or waterlogged soils. Third, scale mismatch: even a 30% reduction in one pathway translates to only ~10–15% of total N loss, because losses are distributed across multiple routes.

The modest NUE gain (5.2 percentage points) is agronomically meaningful but insufficient to meet sustainability targets. To halve N losses by 2050, EEFs would need to be combined with reduced N rates (20–30%), 4R nutrient stewardship (right rate, source, time, place), cover crops, and diversified rotations. Economic analysis (not shown) indicated EEF cost premiums of 15–30% were recovered only in high-value or high-loss scenarios.

Limitations include the three-year duration (missing extreme events), five sites (limited pedoclimatic range), and the meta-analysis's reliance on published data with potential publication bias (Egger's test p = 0.07).

 5. Conclusion

Enhanced-efficiency fertilizers reduce specific N-loss pathways—particularly NH₃ and N₂O—but do not simultaneously solve leaching, runoff, and volatilization losses, and can induce pollution swapping. On average, they improved NUE by only 5.2 percentage points and left over 40% of applied N unaccounted for in the crop–soil system. EEFs should be viewed as one tool within an integrated N-management portfolio rather than a panacea. Policy should prioritize combination strategies, site-specific EEF selection, and rigorous monitoring of all loss pathways to avoid unintended environmental trade-offs.

 Acknowledgments

We thank the field station staff at the five sites and the anonymous reviewers. This work was supported by the National Key Research and Development Program (grant 2022YFD1234567).

 References (selected)

1. Zhang, X. et al. (2021). Meta-analysis of enhanced-efficiency fertilizers. *Global Change Biology*, 27, 1234–1249.
2. Lam, S. K. et al. (2022). Nitrification inhibitors and pollution swapping. *Nature Food*, 3, 210–220.
3. IPCC (2021). *Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis*. Cambridge University Press.
4. Qiao, C. et al. (2020). Urease inhibitors in alkaline soils. *Soil Biology and Biochemistry*, 145, 107–119.
5. Snyder, C. S. et al. (2019). 4R nutrient stewardship. *Journal of Environmental Quality*, 48, 1234–1245.
