title: Evaluation on antiviral activity of a novel arctigenin derivative against multiple rhabdoviruses in aquaculture
text:
Here is a 250-word abstract in SCI journal style:

Abstract

Rhabdoviruses pose a serious threat to global aquaculture, causing substantial economic losses in farmed fish populations. However, effective antiviral therapies remain scarce. In this study, we evaluated the antiviral activity of a novel arctigenin derivative (designated AD-1) against multiple rhabdoviruses affecting aquaculture, including infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus (IHNV), viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus (VHSV), and spring viremia of carp virus (SVCV). The cytotoxicity of AD-1 was first assessed in epithelioma papulosum cyprini (EPC) cells, yielding a 50% cytotoxic concentration (CC50) of 189.6 μM. Antiviral assays demonstrated that AD-1 significantly inhibited IHNV, VHSV, and SVCV replication in a dose-dependent manner, with 50% effective concentrations (EC50) of 3.42, 5.17, and 4.08 μM, respectively, and selectivity indices ranging from 37 to 55. Time-of-addition assays revealed that AD-1 exerted its antiviral effect primarily at the early stage of viral infection, suggesting interference with viral entry or early replication events. Furthermore, AD-1 markedly reduced viral-induced cytopathic effects and decreased viral titers by up to 3.5 log10 TCID50/mL. Mechanistic studies indicated that AD-1 did not directly inactivate viral particles but rather modulated host cellular responses, including suppression of reactive oxygen species production and inhibition of apoptosis. In vivo experiments using zebrafish (Danio rerio) infected with SVCV showed that AD-1 treatment improved survival rates by 40–55% compared with the untreated control group. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AD-1 possesses broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple aquacultural rhabdoviruses and may serve as a promising lead compound for the development of antiviral agents in aquaculture.

title: Characterisation of 2-HP-β-cyclodextrin-PLGA nanoparticle complexes for potential use as ocular drug delivery vehicles
text:
Characterisation of 2-HP-β-cyclodextrin-PLGA nanoparticle complexes for potential use as ocular drug delivery vehicles

Abstract

Ocular drug delivery remains a significant challenge due to the unique anatomical and physiological barriers of the eye, including tear turnover, corneal impermeability, and rapid nasolacrimal drainage. In this study, we developed and characterised a novel nanoparticle system composed of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) functionalised with 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (2-HP-β-CD) for potential ocular application. Nanoparticles were prepared using a modified emulsion-solvent evaporation method. The resulting 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles exhibited a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 187.4 ± 12.3 nm, a polydispersity index of 0.142 ± 0.021, and a zeta potential of −24.6 ± 3.1 mV. Entrapment efficiency and drug loading capacity, evaluated using a model hydrophobic drug (curcumin), reached 78.6 ± 4.2% and 9.3 ± 0.8%, respectively. In vitro release studies demonstrated a sustained release profile over 72 hours, with approximately 68% cumulative release. Mucoadhesive studies revealed a 2.4-fold increase in mucin adsorption compared to unmodified PLGA nanoparticles. Cytotoxicity assays using human corneal epithelial cells showed >85% cell viability at concentrations up to 500 µg/mL. These findings suggest that 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles possess favourable physicochemical and biological properties for ocular drug delivery, warranting further investigation.

Keywords: 2-HP-β-cyclodextrin; PLGA nanoparticles; ocular drug delivery; mucoadhesion; sustained release; corneal epithelium

1. Introduction

Ocular drug delivery is severely limited by the eye's protective mechanisms. Topical administration, the most common route, typically achieves less than 5% bioavailability due to precorneal loss factors such as tear dilution, reflex blinking, and corneal epithelial tight junctions (Gaudana et al., 2010). Consequently, frequent dosing is required, leading to poor patient compliance. To overcome these barriers, nanocarrier systems have emerged as promising strategies for enhancing drug retention, permeation, and controlled release.

Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) is a biodegradable and biocompatible copolymer approved by the FDA for various drug delivery applications. However, PLGA nanoparticles alone exhibit limited mucoadhesion and may be rapidly cleared from the ocular surface. Cyclodextrins, particularly 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (2-HP-β-CD), are cyclic oligosaccharides known for their ability to form inclusion complexes with hydrophobic drugs, thereby improving solubility and stability. Moreover, 2-HP-β-CD has demonstrated excellent tolerability in ocular formulations.

We hypothesised that conjugating 2-HP-β-CD onto PLGA nanoparticles would combine the sustained release properties of PLGA with the solubilising and mucoadhesive benefits of cyclodextrins, resulting in a superior ocular delivery vehicle. This study aimed to synthesise and characterise 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles, evaluating their physicochemical properties, drug release behaviour, mucoadhesive potential, and safety profile in vitro.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Materials

PLGA (50:50, MW 30–60 kDa), 2-HP-β-CD, curcumin, polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, MW 30–70 kDa), and mucin from porcine stomach were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Human corneal epithelial cells (HCECs) were obtained from ATCC. All other reagents were of analytical grade.

2.2 Synthesis of 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA conjugates

2-HP-β-CD was covalently linked to PLGA via carbodiimide chemistry. Briefly, PLGA (1 g) was dissolved in dimethylformamide (DMF, 10 mL), activated with N-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)-N′-ethylcarbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC, 0.2 g) and N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS, 0.1 g) for 2 hours at room temperature. 2-HP-β-CD (0.5 g) was then added, and the reaction proceeded for 24 hours under nitrogen. The conjugate was purified by dialysis (MWCO 3.5 kDa) against distilled water for 48 hours and lyophilised.

2.3 Preparation of nanoparticles

Nanoparticles were prepared by a modified emulsion-solvent evaporation method. Briefly, 50 mg of 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA conjugate and 5 mg curcumin were dissolved in 2 mL dichloromethane. This organic phase was emulsified with 10 mL of 1% (w/v) PVA aqueous solution using probe sonication (40% amplitude, 2 minutes). The emulsion was stirred overnight to evaporate the organic solvent. Nanoparticles were collected by centrifugation (15,000 × g, 30 minutes), washed three times, and lyophilised. Unmodified PLGA nanoparticles were prepared identically without the cyclodextrin conjugate.

2.4 Characterisation

Particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), and zeta potential were measured by dynamic light scattering (Zetasizer Nano ZS, Malvern). Morphology was examined by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Entrapment efficiency (EE) and drug loading (DL) were determined by UV-Vis spectrophotometry after disrupting nanoparticles in DMSO. In vitro release was performed in PBS (pH 7.4) containing 0.1% Tween 80 at 37°C using dialysis bags (MWCO 10 kDa). Mucoadhesion was assessed by incubating nanoparticles with mucin suspension and measuring the change in turbidity at 500 nm. Cytotoxicity was evaluated by MTT assay on HCECs after 24 hours of incubation.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Physicochemical properties

The 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles exhibited a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 187.4 ± 12.3 nm, which was slightly larger than unmodified PLGA nanoparticles (162.8 ± 9.7 nm). The PDI was 0.142 ± 0.021, indicating a narrow size distribution. Zeta potential was −24.6 ± 3.1 mV, sufficient to maintain colloidal stability. TEM images revealed spherical, smooth particles with uniform size (Figure 1, not shown). EE and DL for curcumin were 78.6 ± 4.2% and 9.3 ± 0.8%, respectively, significantly higher than unmodified PLGA nanoparticles (62.1 ± 5.3% EE, 6.7 ± 0.6% DL; p < 0.05).

3.2 In vitro drug release

The release profile of curcumin from 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles showed an initial burst release of 18.2 ± 2.1% within 2 hours, followed by sustained release up to 72 hours, reaching 68.4 ± 3.5% cumulative release. In contrast, free curcumin released >90% within 8 hours. Unmodified PLGA nanoparticles released 54.7 ± 4.1% over 72 hours. The release kinetics fitted the Korsmeyer-Peppas model (R² = 0.976), suggesting a diffusion-controlled mechanism with slight swelling.

3.3 Mucoadhesion

The mucin adsorption capacity of 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles was 2.4-fold higher than that of unmodified PLGA nanoparticles (p < 0.01), as indicated by increased turbidity. This enhancement is attributed to hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions between cyclodextrin moieties and mucin glycoproteins.

3.4 Cytotoxicity

MTT assay results showed that HCEC viability remained above 85% after 24-hour incubation with nanoparticle concentrations up to 500 µg/mL. At 1000 µg/mL, viability decreased to 72.3 ± 5.6%, indicating mild dose-dependent cytotoxicity. Unmodified PLGA nanoparticles showed similar biocompatibility. These results suggest that the 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles are safe for ocular use at therapeutic concentrations.

4. Discussion

The present study demonstrates that 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles possess advantageous characteristics for ocular drug delivery. The slightly increased particle size compared to unmodified PLGA nanoparticles is likely due to the grafted cyclodextrin moieties. The narrow PDI and negative zeta potential indicate good colloidal stability, which is essential for avoiding aggregation in tear fluid. The enhanced entrapment efficiency and drug loading can be explained by the formation of inclusion complexes between curcumin and 2-HP-β-CD, which improve drug solubilisation within the polymer matrix.

The sustained release profile is particularly relevant for ocular applications, as it could reduce dosing frequency and improve patient compliance. The initial burst release may be attributed to drug molecules loosely associated with the nanoparticle surface, while the subsequent slow release reflects diffusion through the PLGA matrix and cyclodextrin-controlled dissociation. The Korsmeyer-Peppas model suggests that release is governed by both diffusion and polymer relaxation.

Mucoadhesion is a critical factor for ocular retention. The 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles exhibited significantly higher mucin adsorption than unmodified PLGA nanoparticles. Cyclodextrins are known to interact with mucin via hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic effects, which can prolong precorneal residence time. This property could translate into improved drug bioavailability in vivo.

The cytotoxicity results are encouraging, as >85% cell viability at concentrations up to 500 µg/mL indicates good tolerability. The slight reduction at 1000 µg/mL may be due to excessive particle load or residual solvents, but such high concentrations are unlikely to be used clinically.

Limitations of this study include the use of curcumin as a model drug, which may not fully represent other ophthalmic drugs. Additionally, in vitro release and mucoadhesion assays do not fully replicate the dynamic ocular environment. Future studies should include ex vivo corneal permeation and in vivo pharmacokinetic evaluations.

5. Conclusion

In this study, 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles were successfully synthesised and characterised. The nanoparticles exhibited desirable size, narrow size distribution, negative zeta potential, high entrapment efficiency, and sustained release behaviour. The cyclodextrin functionalisation significantly enhanced mucoadhesion without compromising biocompatibility. These findings suggest that 2-HP-β-CD-PLGA nanoparticles are promising candidates for ocular drug delivery, offering potential advantages over conventional formulations. Further optimisation and in vivo studies are warranted to validate their clinical potential.

title: Who is a good neighbor? Analysis of frontrunner cities with comparative advantages in low-carbon development
text: Cities are pivotal to global decarbonization, yet they differ markedly in their capacity to advance low-carbon development. While national commitments dominate climate governance, urban-level action often determines whether targets translate into measurable outcomes. A growing body of research examines municipal climate performance, but comparatively little attention has been paid to the frontrunner cities that consistently outperform their peers. Understanding what distinguishes these leaders—and whether their advantages stem from structural endowments, policy entrepreneurship, or institutional capacity—remains an open question. This study addresses that gap by identifying frontrunner cities in low-carbon development and analyzing the comparative advantages that underpin their performance. Drawing on a multi-city dataset, we ask: Who is a good neighbor in the low-carbon transition, and why do some cities lead while others lag? By clarifying the sources of comparative advantage, this paper offers both a conceptual contribution to urban climate scholarship and practical insights for cities seeking to accelerate their own low-carbon trajectories.

title: Functional analysis of a dietary recombinant fatty acid binding protein 10 (FABP10) on the Epinephelus coioides in response to acute low temperature challenge
text:
Results and Discussion

Following a 12-h acute low-temperature challenge (18°C), recombinant FABP10 (rFABP10)-supplemented grouper exhibited a significantly higher survival rate (86.7%) than the control group (53.3%, *P* < 0.01). Serum cortisol and glucose levels in the rFABP10 group peaked at 6 h but were 31.5% and 24.8% lower, respectively, than those of controls (*P* < 0.05), indicating attenuated stress responses. Hepatic *fabp10* expression was upregulated 4.6-fold at 6 h and remained 2.9-fold higher at 12 h relative to the control (*P* < 0.01). Correspondingly, hepatic triglyceride content decreased by 38.2%, while serum non-esterified fatty acids increased by 42.6% (*P* < 0.01), suggesting that rFABP10 promoted lipid mobilization to meet cold-induced energy demands. Activities of antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutase and catalase) were elevated by 45.3% and 37.9%, whereas malondialdehyde content was reduced by 33.1% (*P* < 0.05), reflecting alleviated oxidative damage. Intestinal *occludin* and *zo-1* transcripts were 2.3- and 1.8-fold higher in the rFABP10 group (*P* < 0.05), indicating preserved barrier integrity. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that dietary rFABP10 enhances cold tolerance in *E. coioides* by modulating lipid metabolism, suppressing stress and oxidative responses, and maintaining intestinal barrier function, supporting its potential as a functional feed additive for overwintering aquaculture.

title: Effect of Long-Term Fertilization on Ammonia-Oxidizing Microorganisms and Nitrification in Brown Soil of Northeast China
text:
Effect of Long-Term Fertilization on Ammonia-Oxidizing Microorganisms and Nitrification in Brown Soil of Northeast China

Abstract

Long-term fertilization practices profoundly influence soil nitrogen cycling, yet the responses of ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms and nitrification potential in brown soils of Northeast China remain insufficiently quantified. This study investigated the effects of 12-year fertilization regimes on ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) abundance, community structure, and nitrification potential in a brown soil under a maize-soybean rotation. Four treatments were established: no fertilization (CK), inorganic nitrogen fertilizer alone (N), inorganic nitrogen plus phosphorus and potassium (NPK), and NPK combined with organic manure (NPKM). Real-time quantitative PCR and high-throughput sequencing of *amoA* genes were employed, alongside soil physicochemical analyses and potential nitrification rate (PNR) measurements. Results showed that long-term inorganic N application significantly decreased soil pH (from 6.42 to 5.58) and reduced AOA abundance by 38.5%, while AOB abundance increased by 2.1-fold relative to CK. The NPKM treatment maintained soil pH at 6.18, enhanced soil organic carbon and total nitrogen, and supported the highest AOB and AOA abundances and PNR. Community structure analysis revealed that long-term N fertilization shifted AOB communities toward *Nitrosospira*-dominated assemblages, whereas AOA communities remained relatively stable but declined in diversity under N alone. Redundancy analysis indicated that soil pH, available phosphorus, and organic carbon were the dominant drivers of ammonia-oxidizer community composition. Structural equation modeling suggested that AOB, rather than AOA, was the primary contributor to nitrification potential in this acidic brown soil. These findings demonstrate that organic amendment combined with balanced inorganic fertilization sustains ammonia-oxidizer abundance and nitrification capacity, whereas long-term sole inorganic N application impairs AOA and acidifies soil, with implications for nitrogen use efficiency and environmental sustainability in Northeast China.

Keywords: long-term fertilization; ammonia-oxidizing bacteria; ammonia-oxidizing archaea; nitrification; brown soil; Northeast China

1. Introduction

Nitrification, the microbial oxidation of ammonia to nitrate via nitrite, is a central process in the global nitrogen cycle and a key determinant of nitrogen availability, nitrate leaching, and greenhouse gas emissions in agricultural soils. The first and rate-limiting step is catalyzed by ammonia monooxygenase, encoded by the *amoA* gene, which is present in both ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA). Since the discovery of AOA, considerable debate has surrounded their relative contribution to nitrification in different soil ecosystems. In acidic and low-ammonium soils, AOA often dominate numerically and functionally, whereas AOB tend to respond more strongly to elevated ammonium inputs in neutral to alkaline soils.

The brown soils (cinnamon soils) of Northeast China constitute one of the country's most important grain-producing regions, supporting extensive maize and soybean cultivation. Intensive fertilization over recent decades has increased crop yields but has also led to soil acidification, organic matter decline, and altered microbial communities. Long-term fertilization experiments provide an invaluable platform for disentangling the cumulative effects of nutrient management on soil microbial processes. Previous studies in this region have largely focused on crop yield, soil organic carbon dynamics, and general microbial biomass, while the specific responses of AOA and AOB communities and their linkage to nitrification potential under contrasting fertilization regimes remain poorly resolved.

We hypothesized that (i) long-term inorganic nitrogen fertilization would acidify brown soil and differentially affect AOA and AOB abundance and community structure; (ii) combined organic and inorganic fertilization would mitigate acidification and sustain higher ammonia-oxidizer abundance and nitrification potential; and (iii) AOB would be the dominant driver of nitrification potential in this slightly acidic brown soil. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a 12-year field experiment with four fertilization treatments and integrated quantitative PCR, high-throughput sequencing, and soil biochemical measurements.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Site description and experimental design

The long-term fertilization experiment was located at the Agricultural Ecological Experimental Station in Gongzhuling, Jilin Province, Northeast China (43°30′N, 124°48′E). The soil is classified as a typical brown soil (Udic Argiboroll) with an initial pH of 6.42, organic carbon of 13.8 g kg⁻¹, total nitrogen of 1.32 g kg⁻¹, available phosphorus of 22.6 mg kg⁻¹, and available potassium of 118 mg kg⁻¹. The region has a temperate continental monsoon climate with a mean annual temperature of 5.6 °C and mean annual precipitation of 560 mm. The experiment was established in 2011 with a maize-soybean rotation and four treatments arranged in a randomized complete block design with three replicates: (1) CK, no fertilizer; (2) N, inorganic nitrogen only (urea, 150 kg N ha⁻¹); (3) NPK, inorganic nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (urea 150 kg N ha⁻¹, superphosphate 75 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹, potassium sulfate 75 kg K₂O ha⁻¹); (4) NPKM, NPK plus organic manure (composted cattle manure at 15 t ha⁻¹ fresh weight). Fertilizers were applied annually before sowing.

2.2 Soil sampling and physicochemical analysis

In October 2023, after maize harvest, bulk soil samples were collected from the 0–20 cm layer at five random points per plot and composited. Fresh soils were sieved (2 mm), divided into subsamples for molecular analysis (stored at −80 °C) and physicochemical analysis (air-dried). Soil pH was measured in a 1:2.5 soil:water suspension. Soil organic carbon (SOC) and total nitrogen (TN) were determined by dichromate oxidation and Kjeldahl digestion, respectively. Available phosphorus (AP) was extracted with 0.5 M NaHCO₃ (pH 8.5) and measured by molybdenum-blue colorimetry. Ammonium (NH₄⁺-N) and nitrate (NO₃⁻-N) were extracted with 2 M KCl and quantified by continuous-flow analysis.

2.3 Potential nitrification rate

Potential nitrification rate (PNR) was determined by the chlorate inhibition method. Briefly, 10 g of fresh soil was incubated with 100 mL of 1 mM (NH₄)₂SO₄ and 10 mM KClO₃ at 25 °C for 24 h. Nitrite accumulation was measured colorimetrically at 540 nm, and PNR was expressed as μg NO₂⁻-N g⁻¹ dry soil h⁻¹.

2.4 DNA extraction and quantitative PCR

Soil DNA was extracted using the FastDNA SPIN Kit for Soil. Abundance of AOA and AOB *amoA* genes was quantified by real-time quantitative PCR with primers Arch-amoAF/Arch-amoAR and amoA-1F/amoA-2R, respectively. Standard curves were constructed from cloned *amoA* genes, and amplification efficiencies ranged from 92% to 98%.

2.5 High-throughput sequencing and bioinformatics

The *amoA* genes were amplified and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform. Raw reads were quality-filtered, and operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were clustered at 97% similarity. Representative sequences were taxonomically assigned against the NCBI non-redundant database. Alpha diversity indices (Shannon, Chao1) were calculated.

2.6 Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Duncan's multiple range test (P < 0.05). Relationships between environmental variables and community composition were explored by redundancy analysis (RDA). Structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to evaluate direct and indirect effects on PNR. All analyses were performed in R 4.3.1.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Soil physicochemical properties

Long-term fertilization significantly altered soil properties (Table 1). Soil pH declined in the order NPKM (6.18) > NPK (5.86) > N (5.58) > CK (6.42), with the N treatment showing the lowest value. SOC and TN were highest under NPKM (16.9 g kg⁻¹ and 1.68 g kg⁻¹), followed by NPK and N, and lowest under CK. AP increased markedly with P fertilization, reaching 41.3 mg kg⁻¹ under NPKM. Soil NH₄⁺-N was highest under N and NPK, while NO₃⁻-N was highest under NPKM, reflecting enhanced nitrification and mineralization.

3.2 Abundance of AOA and AOB

AOA *amoA* gene copies ranged from 2.1 × 10⁷ to 5.8 × 10⁷ copies g⁻¹ dry soil, consistently exceeding AOB abundance (3.2 × 10⁶ to 1.4 × 10⁷ copies g⁻¹). Compared with CK, the N treatment reduced AOA abundance by 38.5% and increased AOB abundance by 2.1-fold. NPK showed intermediate values, whereas NPKM supported the highest abundances of both groups (AOA: 5.8 × 10⁷; AOB: 1.4 × 10⁷ copies g⁻¹). The AOA:AOB ratio decreased from 6.6 under CK to 2.0 under N, indicating a pronounced shift toward bacterial dominance under inorganic N input.

3.3 Community structure and diversity

AOB communities were dominated by *Nitrosospira* (cluster 3) across all treatments, but its relative abundance increased from 54.2% under CK to 78.6% under N. *Nitrosomonas* declined correspondingly. AOA communities were dominated by *Nitrososphaera* (group I.1b) and *Nitrosotalea* (group I.1a-associated). Shannon diversity of AOB decreased significantly under N and NPK compared with CK and NPKM, whereas AOA diversity was less responsive, with only a slight decline under N. RDA revealed that pH, AP, and SOC collectively explained 71.4% of the variation in ammonia-oxidizer community composition, with pH as the strongest single factor.

3.4 Potential nitrification rate

PNR ranged from 0.42 to 1.36 μg NO₂⁻-N g⁻¹ h⁻¹ and followed the order NPKM > NPK > N > CK. PNR was positively correlated with AOB abundance (r = 0.86, P < 0.01) and, to a lesser extent, with AOA abundance (r = 0.51, P < 0.05). SEM indicated that AOB abundance had a stronger direct effect on PNR (standardized coefficient = 0.62) than AOA (0.18), while pH exerted indirect effects via both groups.

4. Discussion

Our results demonstrate that long-term fertilization exerts contrasting effects on AOA and AOB in brown soil, with soil pH acting as the principal mediator. The significant decline in AOA abundance under sole inorganic N application is consistent with the acidophilic yet pH-sensitive nature of many *Nitrososphaera* and *Nitrosotalea* lineages. Although AOA are often considered favored in acidic soils, extreme acidification below pH 5.8, as observed in the N treatment, may exceed their tolerance and reduce substrate availability through altered ammonia speciation. In contrast, AOB, particularly *Nitrosospira* cluster 3, proliferated under high ammonium input, reflecting their copiotrophic strategy and greater affinity for elevated NH₃ concentrations.

The NPKM treatment sustained the highest abundances of both groups and the highest PNR, which can be attributed to multiple mechanisms. First, manure application buffered soil pH, maintaining it near the initial level and thereby providing a more favorable habitat for AOA. Second, organic amendment increased SOC and TN, supplying carbon and nitrogen substrates that support microbial growth and activity. Third, improved phosphorus availability may alleviate nutrient limitation on nitrifiers. These findings align with previous reports that integrated fertilization enhances soil microbial functional capacity relative to sole inorganic fertilization.

The dominance of AOB in driving PNR in this study contrasts with some reports from acidic forest and grassland soils where AOA dominate nitrification. This discrepancy may arise from the agricultural context, where repeated ammonium inputs select for AOB with high ammonia oxidation capacity. Nevertheless, the substantial AOA abundance suggests that archaeal nitrification is not negligible and may contribute to background nitrification, particularly under low-ammonium conditions. The shift in AOB community composition toward *Nitrosospira* under N fertilization further implies functional adaptation, as this genus includes taxa tolerant of low pH and high ammonium.

The reduction in AOB diversity under inorganic N treatments, despite increased abundance, indicates that long-term fertilization acts as a selective filter, favoring a few competitive taxa. Loss of diversity may reduce community resilience to environmental perturbation and could impair nitrification stability under future climate change. The maintenance of higher diversity under NPKM suggests that organic inputs preserve a more balanced ammonia-oxidizer community.

From an agronomic and environmental perspective, the enhanced nitrification under NPKM may increase the risk of nitrate leaching if not matched by crop demand, whereas the acidification and AOA decline under sole N application threaten long-term soil fertility. These results support the adoption of integrated nutrient management that combines organic amendments with balanced inorganic fertilizers to sustain soil health and nitrogen cycling in Northeast China's brown soil region.

5. Conclusion

This 12-year field study demonstrated that long-term fertilization significantly altered ammonia-oxidizing microbial communities and nitrification potential in brown soil of Northeast China. Sole inorganic nitrogen fertilization acidified the soil, reduced AOA abundance and AOB diversity, and shifted AOB communities toward *Nitrosospira*-dominated assemblages. In contrast, combined organic and inorganic fertilization maintained soil pH, enhanced SOC, TN, and AP, and supported the highest AOA and AOB abundances and potential nitrification rates. Soil pH, available phosphorus, and organic carbon were the key drivers of ammonia-oxidizer community composition. AOB, rather than AOA, was the primary contributor to nitrification potential in this agricultural soil. These findings indicate that balanced fertilization with organic amendments is essential for sustaining ammonia-oxidizer abundance, diversity, and nitrification function, thereby supporting nitrogen use efficiency and soil sustainability in the brown soil region of Northeast China.

title: Influence of drought stress on afalfa yields and nutritional composition
text:
Influence of Drought Stress on Alfalfa Yields and Nutritional Composition

 Abstract

Alfalfa (*Medicago sativa* L.) is among the most important forage legumes worldwide, yet its productivity is increasingly threatened by recurrent drought events. This study evaluated the effects of varying drought intensities on biomass yield and nutritional quality of alfalfa over two consecutive growing seasons (2022–2023). A randomized complete block design with four irrigation regimes—well-watered control (100% field capacity, FC), mild drought (70% FC), moderate drought (50% FC), and severe drought (30% FC)—was employed. Results demonstrated that drought stress significantly reduced dry matter yield, plant height, and stem number, with severe drought causing a 46.8% yield reduction relative to the control. Conversely, drought stress increased crude protein content (from 17.2% to 21.6%) and improved relative feed value, while simultaneously elevating acid detergent fiber and neutral detergent fiber concentrations. These findings indicate a yield–quality trade-off, wherein moderate drought may enhance certain nutritional attributes at the cost of biomass production. The results provide practical implications for irrigation scheduling and forage management in water-limited regions.

Keywords: alfalfa; drought stress; dry matter yield; crude protein; fiber content; forage quality; irrigation regimes

 Introduction

Alfalfa is widely cultivated as a high-protein forage crop, occupying over 30 million hectares globally (Zhang et al., 2021). Its deep root system confers moderate drought tolerance; however, prolonged water deficit markedly constrains productivity, particularly in semi-arid and arid regions where irrigation water is increasingly scarce (Liu et al., 2020). Drought affects plants through reduced cell turgor, impaired photosynthesis, and altered assimilate partitioning, ultimately influencing both biomass accumulation and nutritive value (Anjum et al., 2017).

While numerous studies have documented drought-induced yield losses in alfalfa, the concurrent effects on nutritional composition remain inconsistently reported. Some authors report increased crude protein (CP) under water stress due to concentration effects, whereas others describe reduced protein synthesis and elevated fiber fractions (Peterson et al., 1992; Halim et al., 1989). Understanding this yield–quality relationship is essential for optimizing forage utilization and livestock feeding strategies.

This study hypothesized that drought stress reduces alfalfa dry matter yield while differentially altering nutritional composition, with moderate stress potentially improving certain quality parameters. The objective was to quantify the influence of four irrigation regimes on alfalfa yield components and nutritional composition across two growing seasons.

 Materials and Methods

Site and Experimental Design. The experiment was conducted at the Agricultural Research Station (34°12′N, 108°52′E; elevation 410 m) during 2022 and 2023. The soil was a silt loam with pH 7.8, organic matter 1.4%, and available water capacity of 180 mm m⁻¹. The region has a semi-arid climate with mean annual precipitation of 520 mm. A randomized complete block design with four treatments and four replications was used. Plot size was 4 m × 5 m with 0.5 m row spacing.

Treatments. Irrigation regimes were imposed based on field capacity (FC): T1 = 100% FC (control), T2 = 70% FC (mild drought), T3 = 50% FC (moderate drought), and T4 = 30% FC (severe drought). Soil moisture was monitored weekly using a time-domain reflectometer (TDR) to a depth of 60 cm, and irrigation was applied accordingly via drip lines.

Crop Management. Alfalfa cultivar 'Zhongmu No. 1' was sown in September 2021 at 22 kg ha⁻¹. Phosphorus (P₂O₅, 90 kg ha⁻¹) and potassium (K₂O, 60 kg ha⁻¹) were applied pre-planting. Weeds were controlled manually. Plants were harvested at 10% bloom in three cuttings per season (June, August, October).

Measurements. At each harvest, plant height (cm) and stem number per plant were recorded from ten randomly selected plants per plot. Dry matter yield (DMY, t ha⁻¹) was determined by oven-drying subsamples at 65°C to constant weight. Nutritional composition was analyzed using near-infrared reflectance spectroscopy (NIRS), including crude protein (CP), acid detergent fiber (ADF), neutral detergent fiber (NDF), and relative feed value (RFV). All analyses were performed in triplicate.

Statistical Analysis. Data were subjected to analysis of variance (ANOVA) using SAS 9.4. Treatment means were compared using Duncan's multiple range test at P < 0.05. Year was treated as a random factor.

 Results

Yield Components. Drought stress significantly reduced plant height, stem number, and dry matter yield in both years (P < 0.05). Averaged across seasons, plant height declined from 78.4 cm (control) to 52.1 cm under severe drought. Stem number decreased from 42.6 to 27.3 per plant. Total annual DMY was 18.7, 16.2, 13.5, and 9.9 t ha⁻¹ for T1, T2, T3, and T4, respectively, representing yield reductions of 13.4%, 27.8%, and 46.8% relative to the control.

Nutritional Composition. In contrast to yield, CP content increased with drought severity, rising from 17.2% (T1) to 21.6% (T4). ADF and NDF also increased, from 28.4% and 41.2% in the control to 34.7% and 48.9% under severe drought, respectively. RFV declined from 152 (T1) to 128 (T4), indicating reduced digestibility. Moderate drought (T3) produced intermediate values, with CP of 19.8% and RFV of 139.

 Discussion

The observed yield reductions under drought align with previous findings attributing biomass loss to reduced cell expansion, stomatal closure, and diminished photosynthetic capacity (Anjum et al., 2017). The 46.8% yield decline under severe drought underscores alfalfa's sensitivity to prolonged water deficit despite its relatively deep root system.

The increase in CP concentration under drought likely reflects a concentration effect, as reduced biomass dilution elevates nitrogen-containing compounds per unit dry matter (Halim et al., 1989). However, elevated ADF and NDF indicate increased cell wall lignification and reduced cell soluble content, which negatively affect digestibility and intake potential (Peterson et al., 1992). The decline in RFV from 152 to 128 suggests that drought-stressed alfalfa, while higher in protein, may provide less energy to ruminants.

The trade-off between yield and quality has practical implications. Moderate drought (T3) maintained acceptable yield (13.5 t ha⁻¹) with improved CP (19.8%), suggesting that deficit irrigation strategies could balance productivity and quality under water scarcity. However, severe drought is clearly detrimental to both.

Limitations of this study include its two-year duration and single cultivar. Future research should evaluate multiple cultivars and incorporate physiological indicators such as water use efficiency and osmotic adjustment.

 Conclusion

Drought stress significantly reduced alfalfa dry matter yield while increasing crude protein and fiber concentrations and decreasing relative feed value. Severe drought caused the greatest yield penalty (46.8%), whereas moderate drought offered a potential compromise between yield and nutritional quality. These results highlight the importance of optimized irrigation management to sustain alfalfa production and forage quality in water-limited environments.

title: Relationship between FDI, fiscal expenditure and green total-factor productivity in China: From the perspective of spatial spillover
text: Abstract: This study investigates the spatial spillover effects of foreign direct investment (FDI) and fiscal expenditure on green total-factor productivity (GTFP) in China, using panel data of 30 provincial-level regions from 2004 to 2019. GTFP is measured by the Super-SBM model with undesirable outputs, and the spatial Durbin model is employed to capture both direct and indirect effects. The results show that GTFP exhibits significant positive spatial autocorrelation, indicating that green productivity in neighboring regions is closely interconnected. FDI exerts a negative direct effect but a positive spatial spillover effect on GTFP, suggesting that while foreign investment may suppress local green productivity, it can benefit neighboring regions through technology diffusion and knowledge transfer. Fiscal expenditure generates a positive direct effect on GTFP, whereas its spillover effect is significantly negative, implying that local government spending may crowd out green development in adjacent areas through resource competition. Moreover, the interaction between FDI and fiscal expenditure produces a notable positive spillover effect, indicating that well-designed fiscal policies can enhance the green spillover potential of FDI. Regional heterogeneity analysis reveals that these effects are more pronounced in eastern and central regions than in western regions. These findings suggest that policymakers should strengthen inter-regional coordination, optimize the structure of fiscal expenditure, and formulate differentiated FDI attraction policies to promote green total-factor productivity through spatial spillover channels.

title: Bioconversion of corncob acid hydrolysate into microbial oil by the oleaginous yeast Lipomyces starkeyi
text:
Bioconversion of corncob acid hydrolysate into microbial oil by the oleaginous yeast *Lipomyces starkeyi*

Abstract

Corncob is an abundant lignocellulosic agricultural residue that can be hydrolyzed into fermentable sugars for biotechnological applications. In this study, the oleaginous yeast *Lipomyces starkeyi* was evaluated for its ability to accumulate microbial oil using corncob acid hydrolysate as the sole carbon source. The hydrolysate was prepared by dilute sulfuric acid pretreatment and contained mainly xylose, glucose, and arabinose, with minor amounts of acetic acid, furfural, and 5-hydroxymethylfurfural. After detoxification with activated carbon and overliming, the hydrolysate supported robust yeast growth and lipid accumulation. Under optimized conditions (initial sugar concentration 60 g/L, pH 5.5, 28 °C, 180 rpm, 96 h), the lipid content reached 52.3% of dry cell weight, with a lipid concentration of 8.9 g/L and a lipid yield coefficient of 0.18 g/g sugar consumed. The extracted microbial oil was composed mainly of oleic acid (48.2%), palmitic acid (26.5%), stearic acid (12.1%), and linoleic acid (8.7%), resembling typical plant oils. These results demonstrate that *L. starkeyi* can efficiently convert corncob acid hydrolysate into microbial oil, offering a promising route for valorizing agricultural waste.

Keywords: *Lipomyces starkeyi*; corncob; acid hydrolysate; microbial oil; single cell oil; lignocellulose; oleaginous yeast

1. Introduction

The increasing global demand for edible and industrial oils, coupled with the limitations of conventional plant oil production, has stimulated interest in alternative lipid sources. Microbial oil, also known as single cell oil, produced by oleaginous microorganisms, has attracted considerable attention because of its similar fatty acid composition to plant oils and its potential for production from low-cost substrates (Ratledge and Cohen, 2008). Oleaginous yeasts are particularly promising due to their rapid growth, high lipid content, and ability to utilize a wide range of carbon sources.

Lignocellulosic biomass, especially agricultural residues, represents an abundant and renewable feedstock for microbial oil production. Corncob is a major byproduct of corn processing, with an annual production of millions of tons worldwide. It is rich in xylan and cellulose, which can be hydrolyzed into fermentable sugars. Dilute acid hydrolysis is an effective method for releasing xylose and other sugars from corncob hemicellulose, but it also generates inhibitory compounds such as furfural, 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), and acetic acid (Palmqvist and Hahn-Hägerdal, 2000). Therefore, detoxification is often required before fermentation.

*Lipomyces starkeyi* is a well-known oleaginous yeast capable of accumulating lipids up to 60% of its dry cell weight. It can utilize both hexoses and pentoses, making it suitable for lignocellulosic hydrolysates (Wild et al., 2010). However, its performance on corncob acid hydrolysate has not been fully optimized. In this study, we investigated the bioconversion of corncob acid hydrolysate into microbial oil by *L. starkeyi*, focusing on hydrolysate detoxification, fermentation conditions, and lipid characterization.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Materials

Corncobs were collected from a local farm in Shandong Province, China. They were dried, milled, and sieved to a particle size of 0.5–1.0 mm. All chemicals were of analytical grade. *Lipomyces starkeyi* AS 2.1560 was obtained from the China General Microbiological Culture Collection Center.

2.2. Preparation of corncob acid hydrolysate

Corncob powder was mixed with 1% (w/v) sulfuric acid at a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:10 and autoclaved at 121 °C for 60 min. The mixture was filtered, and the liquid fraction was collected as the hydrolysate. The hydrolysate was detoxified by adjusting the pH to 10.0 with Ca(OH)₂, heating at 60 °C for 30 min, and then filtering. The pH was readjusted to 5.5 with H₃PO₄. Activated carbon (2%, w/v) was added, and the mixture was shaken at 150 rpm for 60 min at 30 °C, followed by filtration. The detoxified hydrolysate was sterilized by autoclaving at 115 °C for 20 min.

2.3. Fermentation

*L. starkeyi* was maintained on yeast extract peptone dextrose (YPD) agar slants. Seed cultures were prepared in YPD broth at 28 °C and 180 rpm for 24 h. Fermentation was carried out in 250-mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing 50 mL of detoxified hydrolysate supplemented with 0.5 g/L yeast extract, 0.5 g/L (NH₄)₂SO₄, 0.1 g/L KH₂PO₄, and 0.05 g/L MgSO₄·7H₂O. The initial sugar concentration was adjusted to 60 g/L with sterile water. The flasks were inoculated with 10% (v/v) seed culture and incubated at 28 °C and 180 rpm for 96 h. Samples were taken periodically for analysis.

2.4. Analytical methods

Sugars (glucose, xylose, arabinose) and inhibitors (acetic acid, furfural, HMF) were quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using an Aminex HPX-87H column with 5 mM H₂SO₄ as the mobile phase at 65 °C. Cell dry weight (CDW) was determined by filtering the culture broth through a pre-weighed 0.45-μm membrane, washing with distilled water, and drying at 105 °C to constant weight. Lipid content was measured by the chloroform-methanol extraction method (Folch et al., 1957). Fatty acid composition was analyzed by gas chromatography after transesterification.

2.5. Calculations

Lipid yield coefficient (Y_L/S) was calculated as the amount of lipid produced per gram of sugar consumed. Lipid productivity was defined as lipid concentration divided by fermentation time.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1. Composition of corncob acid hydrolysate

The raw hydrolysate contained 28.5 g/L xylose, 8.2 g/L glucose, 3.1 g/L arabinose, 2.8 g/L acetic acid, 0.9 g/L furfural, and 0.6 g/L HMF. After detoxification, the sugar concentrations were slightly reduced (xylose 26.8 g/L, glucose 7.6 g/L, arabinose 2.8 g/L), while inhibitors were largely removed (acetic acid 0.3 g/L, furfural not detected, HMF 0.05 g/L). The detoxified hydrolysate was supplemented with nutrients and used for fermentation.

3.2. Time course of fermentation

*L. starkeyi* grew well on the detoxified hydrolysate. The sugar consumption, cell growth, and lipid accumulation profiles are shown in Table 1. Glucose was consumed rapidly within the first 24 h, while xylose utilization was slower and continued until 72 h. By 96 h, 94.2% of total sugars were consumed. CDW increased from 2.1 g/L at 12 h to 17.0 g/L at 96 h. Lipid content increased steadily, reaching 52.3% at 96 h, corresponding to a lipid concentration of 8.9 g/L. The lipid yield coefficient was 0.18 g/g sugar consumed, and lipid productivity was 0.093 g/L/h.

Table 1. Time course of sugar consumption, cell growth, and lipid accumulation by *L. starkeyi* on corncob acid hydrolysate.

| Time (h) | Residual sugars (g/L) | CDW (g/L) | Lipid content (%) | Lipid concentration (g/L) |
|----------|------------------------|-----------|--------------------|----------------------------|
| 0        | 60.0                   | 2.1       | 8.5                | 0.18                       |
| 12       | 52.3                   | 4.5       | 15.2               | 0.68                       |
| 24       | 38.6                   | 8.2       | 28.7               | 2.35                       |
| 48       | 22.4                   | 12.8      | 41.5               | 5.31                       |
| 72       | 9.1                    | 15.6      | 49.8               | 7.77                       |
| 96       | 3.5                    | 17.0      | 52.3               | 8.89                       |

3.3. Effect of initial sugar concentration

The effect of initial sugar concentration on lipid production was investigated (Table 2). The highest lipid content (52.3%) and lipid concentration (8.9 g/L) were obtained at 60 g/L sugars. At 80 g/L, although CDW increased to 19.2 g/L, lipid content decreased to 44.1%, likely due to substrate inhibition or osmotic stress. At 40 g/L, lipid content was 48.5%, but lipid concentration was lower (6.2 g/L) due to limited carbon availability.

Table 2. Effect of initial sugar concentration on lipid production by *L. starkeyi*.

|-----------------------|-----------|--------------------|----------------------------|

3.4. Fatty acid composition of microbial oil

The fatty acid profile of the lipid extracted from *L. starkeyi* grown on corncob hydrolysate is shown in Table 3. The major fatty acids were oleic acid (C18:1, 48.2%), palmitic acid (C16:0, 26.5%), stearic acid (C18:0, 12.1%), and linoleic acid (C18:2, 8.7%). The content of saturated fatty acids was 38.6%, and unsaturated fatty acids accounted for 56.9%. This composition is similar to that of palm oil and can be used for biodiesel production or as a cocoa butter substitute.

4. Discussion

The results demonstrate that *L. starkeyi* can efficiently utilize corncob acid hydrolysate for microbial oil production after appropriate detoxification. The detoxification process removed most of the inhibitors, which are known to inhibit yeast growth and lipid accumulation (Palmqvist and Hahn-Hägerdal, 2000). The remaining low levels of acetic acid (0.3 g/L) and HMF (0.05 g/L) did not significantly affect fermentation.

The lipid content (52.3%) and lipid concentration (8.9 g/L) obtained in this study are comparable to those reported for *L. starkeyi* grown on other lignocellulosic hydrolysates. For example, Wild et al. (2010) reported a lipid content of 50% on wheat straw hydrolysate. The lipid yield coefficient (0.18 g/g) is slightly lower than the theoretical maximum (0.32 g/g), likely due to energy maintenance and byproduct formation. The fatty acid composition, rich in oleic and palmitic acids, is suitable for biodiesel production with good cold-flow properties.

The use of corncob acid hydrolysate as a substrate offers several advantages: it is inexpensive, renewable, and does not compete with food supply. However, scale-up challenges remain, including the cost of detoxification and the need for efficient pentose utilization. Further optimization of fermentation conditions and genetic improvement of the yeast strain could enhance lipid productivity.

5. Conclusion

In this study, *Lipomyces starkeyi* was successfully cultivated on detoxified corncob acid hydrolysate for microbial oil production. Under optimized conditions, the yeast accumulated 52.3% lipid with a lipid concentration of 8.9 g/L and a lipid yield coefficient of 0.18 g/g. The microbial oil was rich in oleic acid (48.2%) and palmitic acid (26.5%), resembling plant oils. These findings suggest that corncob acid hydrolysate is a promising feedstock for microbial oil production by *L. starkeyi*, providing a sustainable route for valorizing agricultural residues.

title: The association between sociodemographic factors, frailty, and health-related quality of life in older inpatients: a cross-sectional study
text: The global population is ageing rapidly, and the demand for hospital care among older adults continues to rise. Older inpatients often present with complex health needs, including frailty, a syndrome of reduced physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors. Frailty is highly prevalent in hospital settings and is associated with adverse outcomes such as falls, disability, prolonged length of stay, and mortality. Beyond clinical consequences, frailty may substantially impair health-related quality of life (HRQoL), which reflects patients’ perceived physical, psychological, and social well-being. However, HRQoL is also shaped by sociodemographic factors, including age, sex, education, income, marital status, and living arrangements, which may influence access to care, social support, and coping resources. Despite growing interest in frailty and HRQoL, evidence from older inpatient populations remains limited, and the interplay between sociodemographic characteristics, frailty, and HRQoL is not fully understood. Most previous studies have been conducted in community-dwelling older adults or outpatient settings, with few focusing on hospitalized patients who are particularly vulnerable. Moreover, many studies have examined frailty or sociodemographic factors in isolation, without considering their combined associations with HRQoL. A better understanding of these relationships could inform targeted screening and interventions to improve inpatient care and discharge planning. Therefore, this cross-sectional study aimed to examine the association between sociodemographic factors, frailty, and HRQoL among older inpatients. We hypothesized that frailty would be independently associated with poorer HRQoL, and that sociodemographic factors would further modify or confound this relationship.

title: Evaluation on the risk controlling value of urban soil organic pollutants based on land-use planning in China
text:
Results and Discussion

The evaluation covered 126 planning units in a representative Chinese city, with 312 topsoil samples analyzed for 16 priority PAHs and 8 OCPs. Total PAH concentrations ranged from 82 to 4,760 μg/kg (mean 612 μg/kg), while OCPs ranged from 3.1 to 188 μg/kg (mean 24.6 μg/kg). Under the existing land-use plan, 23.8% of units exceeded the risk screening value for residential use, versus only 6.3% for industrial use, indicating that current zoning misallocates high-risk parcels to sensitive receptors. After applying the proposed risk-controlling framework, which integrates land-use classification with pollutant benchmarks, exceedance in residential units dropped to 9.5%, while 71% of contaminated parcels were reassigned to green space or commercial use. Incremental health risk fell from 3.2×10⁻⁵ to 1.1×10⁻⁵, below the acceptable threshold of 1×10⁻⁵ for carcinogenic risk in most units. Spatial analysis revealed that risk hotspots clustered near former industrial zones and arterial roads, consistent with emission sources and atmospheric deposition. These findings demonstrate that embedding soil pollutant risk into land-use planning can reduce remediation costs by an estimated 34% compared with end-of-pipe treatment, while safeguarding residents. However, the framework's effectiveness depends on accurate cadastral data and enforcement capacity, which vary across Chinese cities. Overall, the results support land-use planning as a proactive, cost-effective instrument for urban soil risk control.

title: Application of airborne ultrasound in the convective drying of fruits and vegetables: A review
text:
Application of Airborne Ultrasound in the Convective Drying of Fruits and Vegetables: A Review

Abstract

Convective drying is one of the most widely used methods for preserving fruits and vegetables; however, its high energy consumption and adverse effects on product quality remain significant challenges. Airborne ultrasound, as a non-contact and non-thermal physical field, has attracted increasing attention for its ability to enhance heat and mass transfer during convective drying. This review summarizes recent advances in the application of airborne ultrasound in the convective drying of fruits and vegetables, focusing on equipment configuration, process parameters, drying kinetics, quality attributes, and energy efficiency. Representative studies on apple, carrot, banana, strawberry, and mushroom are analyzed. Results indicate that airborne ultrasound at frequencies between 20 and 40 kHz and sound pressure levels of 130–160 dB can reduce drying time by 20–60% and improve rehydration capacity and color retention, while excessive acoustic intensity may cause cell damage and nutrient degradation. The review also discusses the underlying mechanisms, including acoustic streaming, cavitation-like effects, and surface vibration, as well as the limitations of current research. Future research should focus on standardized ultrasonic equipment, multi-physics modeling, and combined ultrasound-assisted technologies for industrial-scale applications.

Keywords: airborne ultrasound; convective drying; fruits and vegetables; mass transfer; drying kinetics; food quality

1. Introduction

Fruits and vegetables are rich in vitamins, minerals, dietary fiber, and bioactive compounds, but their high moisture content makes them highly perishable. Drying is one of the oldest and most effective preservation methods, reducing water activity and extending shelf life while lowering transportation and storage costs. Among drying technologies, convective hot-air drying is widely used in the food industry due to its simple operation, low equipment cost, and controllable conditions. Nevertheless, convective drying is energy-intensive and often leads to quality deterioration, including color browning, nutrient loss, shrinkage, and poor rehydration capacity (Mujumdar & Law, 2010).

In recent decades, several emerging technologies, such as microwave, infrared, radio frequency, and freeze drying, have been investigated to overcome these drawbacks. However, high equipment costs, non-uniform heating, and limited scalability still restrict their industrial application. Airborne ultrasound, defined as sound waves with frequencies above 20 kHz propagating through air, has emerged as a promising non-contact assistance technology for convective drying. Unlike contact ultrasound, airborne ultrasound does not require direct coupling between the transducer and the food material, avoiding contamination and mechanical damage (Gallego-Juárez et al., 2007).

The application of airborne ultrasound in drying is based on several physical mechanisms. First, high-intensity acoustic waves generate acoustic streaming, which reduces the thickness of the boundary layer at the product surface and enhances convective mass transfer. Second, ultrasonic vibration may induce rapid alternating compression and expansion within the product, promoting the migration of internal moisture to the surface. Third, acoustic energy can partially rupture cell walls, creating microchannels that facilitate water diffusion (Cárcel et al., 2007). These effects can significantly reduce drying time and improve energy efficiency without excessive heating.

Although numerous studies have examined ultrasound-assisted drying, most have focused on contact ultrasound or ultrasonic pretreatment. Airborne ultrasound, which is more suitable for continuous industrial drying systems, has received less systematic attention. This review aims to summarize the current state of knowledge on airborne ultrasound-assisted convective drying of fruits and vegetables, analyze the effects of key process parameters, evaluate drying kinetics and product quality, and identify research gaps and future directions.

2. Materials and Methods

This review was conducted based on a systematic literature search of peer-reviewed articles published between 2005 and 2023. The databases used included Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect. The search terms were combinations of “airborne ultrasound,” “ultrasonic drying,” “convective drying,” “fruits,” “vegetables,” and “mass transfer.” Only studies that applied airborne ultrasound during convective drying, rather than as a pretreatment or in contact mode, were included. A total of 42 relevant studies were selected for detailed analysis.

For the purpose of comparison, representative experimental data were extracted and, where necessary, average values were calculated from reported results. In addition, a set of simulated experiments was designed to illustrate typical trends, based on parameters commonly reported in the literature. These simulated data are clearly identified in the text and should be regarded as illustrative rather than original experimental results. The main parameters analyzed included ultrasonic frequency (20–40 kHz), sound pressure level (120–160 dB), air temperature (40–70 °C), air velocity (0.5–2.0 m/s), and sample thickness (3–10 mm). Drying time, effective moisture diffusivity, rehydration ratio, color difference (ΔE), and energy consumption were used as evaluation indicators.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Effect of airborne ultrasound on drying kinetics

Across the reviewed studies, airborne ultrasound consistently reduced drying time compared with conventional convective drying. For apple slices dried at 60 °C and 1.0 m/s, the application of airborne ultrasound at 20 kHz and 150 dB reduced drying time from 240 min to 150 min, a reduction of approximately 37.5%. Similar trends were observed for carrot, banana, and mushroom. In a simulated experiment based on average literature values, the effective moisture diffusivity of apple slices increased from 1.2 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s to 2.1 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s when ultrasound was applied. This increase is attributed to acoustic streaming and micro-vibration, which reduce external resistance and promote internal moisture migration.

The drying rate curves generally exhibited a falling-rate period, indicating that internal diffusion controlled the process. Airborne ultrasound was more effective in the early and intermediate stages of drying, when the product surface was still wet. As drying progressed and the surface became dry, the efficiency of ultrasound decreased, likely due to reduced acoustic transmission and increased attenuation.

3.2 Influence of process parameters

Ultrasonic frequency and sound pressure level were the most critical parameters. Lower frequencies (20–25 kHz) generally provided better penetration and higher drying enhancement than higher frequencies (35–40 kHz). For instance, in banana drying, increasing the sound pressure level from 130 dB to 155 dB at 21 kHz reduced drying time by an additional 18%. However, beyond 160 dB, further improvement was marginal, and quality deterioration became more pronounced.

Air temperature also interacted with ultrasound. At 50 °C, ultrasound reduced drying time by 28%, while at 70 °C, the reduction was only 15%, suggesting that ultrasound is more beneficial at lower temperatures where conventional drying is slower. This is practically important because lower temperatures help preserve heat-sensitive nutrients and color.

Air velocity had a less pronounced effect. Increasing velocity from 0.5 to 2.0 m/s improved drying rate in both conventional and ultrasound-assisted drying, but the relative advantage of ultrasound decreased at higher velocities, possibly because enhanced convection already reduced the boundary layer thickness.

3.3 Product quality attributes

Airborne ultrasound generally improved rehydration capacity and color retention. For strawberry drying at 50 °C, the rehydration ratio increased from 2.8 to 3.4 when ultrasound was applied. Color difference (ΔE) decreased from 12.5 to 8.7, indicating better preservation of natural pigments. These improvements are likely related to reduced thermal exposure and the formation of porous microstructures.

However, high-intensity ultrasound could negatively affect texture and nutrient content. In apple slices treated at 160 dB, vitamin C retention decreased by 12% compared with the control, possibly due to cell membrane disruption and oxidation. Therefore, an optimal acoustic intensity must be selected to balance drying efficiency and quality.

3.4 Energy consumption

Energy consumption is a key factor for industrial application. In the reviewed studies, airborne ultrasound-assisted convective drying reduced total energy consumption by 15–30% compared with conventional drying, mainly due to shorter drying time. However, the energy required to generate ultrasound must be considered. When the ultrasonic power was too high, the net energy saving decreased or even became negative. Thus, process optimization should consider both drying time and ultrasonic energy input.

4. Discussion

The mechanisms by which airborne ultrasound enhances convective drying can be summarized as follows. Acoustic streaming reduces the boundary layer thickness, increasing the convective mass transfer coefficient. Ultrasonic vibration creates alternating pressure gradients within the product, enhancing internal moisture diffusion. In addition, high-intensity ultrasound may cause cavitation-like effects near the surface, disrupting cell structures and creating microchannels for water transport.

However, the application of airborne ultrasound in food drying still faces several challenges. First, acoustic transmission in air is inefficient, and energy losses are significant, especially at high frequencies. Second, the acoustic field distribution in large-scale drying chambers is often non-uniform, leading to uneven drying. Third, most studies have been conducted at laboratory scale, and scaling up remains difficult. Fourth, the interaction between ultrasound and different food matrices is complex and not fully understood.

Compared with contact ultrasound, airborne ultrasound has the advantage of non-contact operation, which is more suitable for continuous production and avoids contamination. However, its energy efficiency is lower, and the required sound pressure levels are higher. Future research should focus on developing high-efficiency ultrasonic transducers, optimizing chamber design, and combining airborne ultrasound with other technologies such as microwave, infrared, or vacuum drying.

5. Conclusion

Airborne ultrasound is a promising non-contact technology for enhancing convective drying of fruits and vegetables. It can significantly reduce drying time, improve rehydration capacity and color retention, and lower energy consumption under optimized conditions. The effectiveness of ultrasound depends on frequency, sound pressure level, air temperature, air velocity, and product characteristics. Lower frequencies and moderate intensities are generally more effective, while excessive acoustic energy may cause quality degradation. Current research is still limited to laboratory scale, and industrial application requires further development of standardized equipment and multi-physics modeling. Future studies should also explore combined ultrasound-assisted drying systems and evaluate their economic feasibility. Overall, airborne ultrasound has the potential to contribute to more efficient and sustainable drying processes in the food industry.

title: Nitrous oxide emissions in Chinese vegetable systems: A meta-analysis
text:
Nitrous oxide emissions in Chinese vegetable systems: A meta-analysis

 Abstract

Vegetable production in China has expanded rapidly to meet rising demand, and these systems receive exceptionally high nitrogen (N) inputs. However, the magnitude and controls of nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions from Chinese vegetable systems remain poorly quantified. We conducted a meta-analysis of 87 field studies (312 observations) published between 2005 and 2023 to quantify direct N₂O emissions, emission factors (EFs), and yield-scaled emissions in open-field and greenhouse vegetable systems, and to identify the management and environmental factors that regulate them. Mean annual N₂O flux was 8.9 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ (95% CI: 7.6–10.3), approximately 3.4 times higher than the IPCC default estimate for croplands in the region. The mean EF was 1.42% (95% CI: 1.21–1.64%), substantially exceeding the IPCC Tier 1 default of 1.0%. Greenhouse systems emitted 42% more N₂O than open-field systems (11.1 vs. 7.8 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹). Emissions increased exponentially with N application rate above ~400 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹. Substituting 20–40% of synthetic N with manure-based amendments reduced N₂O emissions by 18% without yield penalties, whereas flooding irrigation and high basal-N proportions increased emissions. Yield-scaled emissions averaged 4.6 g N₂O–N kg⁻¹ vegetable. Our results indicate that current IPCC defaults underestimate N₂O emissions from Chinese vegetable systems and that improved N management, particularly reduced total N and optimized irrigation, could substantially mitigate emissions while maintaining productivity.

Keywords: nitrous oxide; vegetable production; emission factor; meta-analysis; nitrogen management; greenhouse; China

 Introduction

China produces over 50% of the world's vegetables on roughly 12% of its cropland, and vegetable cultivation area has grown from ~15 million ha in 2000 to ~22 million ha in 2022. Vegetable systems are characterized by intensive management, with annual N application rates frequently exceeding 600 kg N ha⁻¹—two to three times the rates used in cereal production. This excessive N input, combined with frequent irrigation and high soil temperatures, creates conditions highly favorable for microbial nitrification and denitrification, the primary pathways of N₂O production.

N₂O is a potent greenhouse gas with a 100-year global warming potential ~273 times that of CO₂, and it also contributes to stratospheric ozone depletion. Agriculture accounts for roughly 60% of global anthropogenic N₂O emissions, and vegetable systems are increasingly recognized as emission hotspots. However, national greenhouse gas inventories typically apply uniform IPCC emission factors (1.0% of applied N) across all croplands, which may substantially misestimate emissions from high-input vegetable systems.

Previous field studies in China have reported N₂O EFs ranging from 0.3% to over 4%, with considerable variability driven by climate, soil properties, irrigation regime, and fertilizer type. Individual studies, however, are limited in spatial and temporal scope, making it difficult to derive robust regional estimates or identify generalizable mitigation strategies. A quantitative synthesis is therefore needed to (i) establish a baseline emission estimate for Chinese vegetable systems, (ii) quantify the EF and its uncertainty, and (iii) identify management practices that reduce emissions without compromising yields. Here we present a meta-analysis addressing these objectives.

 Materials and Methods

 Data collection

We searched the Web of Science, CNKI, and Google Scholar databases for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2005 and December 2023 using combinations of the terms "nitrous oxide," "N₂O," "vegetable," "greenhouse," "emission factor," and "China." Studies were included if they: (1) reported direct N₂O fluxes measured by static chamber–gas chromatography or micrometeorological methods for at least one full growing season; (2) included a control or documented N application rate; (3) reported means and sample sizes (or standard errors); and (4) were conducted in China. A total of 87 studies with 312 treatment observations met these criteria (open-field: 198 observations; greenhouse: 114 observations).

 Data extraction and effect size

For each observation we extracted: N₂O flux (kg N ha⁻¹ season⁻¹ or yr⁻¹), N application rate, fertilizer type, irrigation method, cropping system, soil pH, soil organic carbon (SOC), mean annual temperature and precipitation, and vegetable yield. Emission factors were calculated as the difference in N₂O–N between fertilized and unfertilized treatments divided by the N application rate, where unfertilized controls were available (n = 121). Yield-scaled emissions (g N₂O–N kg⁻¹ yield) were computed for observations reporting marketable yield.

 Statistical analysis

We used a random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation in the `metafor` package (R 4.3.1). Effect sizes were log-transformed response ratios for comparisons of management practices. Heterogeneity was assessed with I² statistics, and publication bias was evaluated using Egger's regression and funnel plots. Mixed-effects models tested the influence of moderators (system type, N rate, irrigation, fertilizer type, soil and climate variables). Nonlinear relationships were examined using quadratic and exponential regression. All results are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

 Results

 Overall N₂O emissions and emission factors

Across all observations, mean annual N₂O flux was 8.9 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ (95% CI: 7.6–10.3), with a range of 1.1–34.7 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹. Greenhouse systems emitted significantly more than open-field systems (11.1 vs. 7.8 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹; P < 0.001). The overall mean EF was 1.42% (95% CI: 1.21–1.64%), with greenhouse EFs (1.71%) exceeding open-field EFs (1.28%). Both values exceeded the IPCC Tier 1 default of 1.0%. High heterogeneity was observed (I² = 78%), justifying the mixed-effects analysis. Egger's test indicated no significant publication bias (P = 0.21).

 Influence of nitrogen rate

Emissions increased with N application rate, but the relationship was nonlinear. Below ~400 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, N₂O flux increased approximately linearly (slope = 0.011 kg N₂O–N per kg N applied). Above this threshold, emissions rose exponentially, reaching 16.8 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ at rates exceeding 900 kg N ha⁻¹. The EF also increased with N rate, from 1.05% at <300 kg N ha⁻¹ to 1.88% at >700 kg N ha⁻¹.

 Management and environmental moderators

Fertilizer type significantly affected emissions. Compared with 100% synthetic N, substituting 20–40% of N with manure or compost reduced N₂O emissions by 18% (RR = 0.82; 95% CI: 0.74–0.91) with no significant yield reduction (P = 0.34). Substitution rates above 50% increased emissions, likely due to additional labile carbon. Application of nitrification inhibitors reduced emissions by 26% (RR = 0.74; 95% CI: 0.63–0.87).

Irrigation method was a strong moderator: flooding irrigation increased emissions by 31% relative to drip irrigation (RR = 1.31; 95% CI: 1.14–1.51). High basal-N proportions (>60% of total N applied before planting) increased emissions by 22% compared with split application. Soil pH was negatively correlated with N₂O flux (r = −0.34, P < 0.01), and SOC was positively correlated (r = 0.29, P < 0.01). Mean annual temperature explained 16% of the variance in emissions across sites.

 Yield-scaled emissions

Mean yield-scaled N₂O emissions were 4.6 g N₂O–N kg⁻¹ vegetable (95% CI: 3.9–5.3). Leafy vegetables had higher yield-scaled emissions (6.1 g N₂O–N kg⁻¹) than fruit vegetables (3.4 g N₂O–N kg⁻¹), reflecting lower biomass N-use efficiency and shallower rooting depth. Optimized treatments (reduced N + drip irrigation + partial manure substitution) lowered yield-scaled emissions to 2.8 g N₂O–N kg⁻¹ while maintaining yields within 5% of conventional practice.

 Discussion

Our synthesis demonstrates that Chinese vegetable systems are substantial N₂O sources, with mean emissions roughly 3.4 times the IPCC default estimate for the region and EFs 42% above the Tier 1 default. This discrepancy likely arises because IPCC defaults were derived largely from cereal systems with lower N inputs, less frequent irrigation, and shorter growing seasons. Vegetable systems receive more N, are irrigated more intensively, and often support multiple cropping cycles per year, all of which amplify N₂O production.

The exponential increase in emissions above ~400 kg N ha⁻¹ indicates that N inputs in many Chinese vegetable systems exceed the agronomic and environmental optimum. This threshold is consistent with the concept of "N surplus" driving gaseous losses once crop demand is saturated. The higher EFs in greenhouse systems reflect elevated soil temperatures, high humidity, and frequent irrigation, which accelerate both nitrification and denitrification.

The mitigating effect of partial manure substitution (20–40%) aligns with evidence that organic amendments can improve soil structure and synchronize N supply with crop demand, though high substitution rates may stimulate denitrification by supplying labile carbon. Nitrification inhibitors were effective, consistent with findings in other cropping systems, but their adoption in Chinese vegetable production remains limited by cost and farmer awareness.

Irrigation management emerged as a key lever: drip irrigation reduced emissions by nearly a third relative to flooding, mainly by reducing anaerobic microsites and leaching. The negative correlation between soil pH and N₂O flux suggests that acidification—common in long-term vegetable fields—may further increase emissions, creating a feedback loop that warrants attention.

Several limitations apply. Most studies were short-term (<2 years) and concentrated in eastern China, potentially underrepresenting northwestern and southwestern regions. Measurement methods varied, and few studies reported background emissions from unfertilized controls, limiting EF calculations. Nonetheless, the consistency of management effects across studies strengthens confidence in our conclusions.

For policy, our results suggest that revising national emission factors for vegetable systems, promoting partial organic substitution, and incentivizing drip irrigation and nitrification inhibitors could reduce N₂O emissions from Chinese vegetable production by an estimated 25–35% relative to current practice, while maintaining or improving yields.

 Conclusion

This meta-analysis shows that Chinese vegetable systems emit N₂O at rates substantially higher than IPCC defaults assume, with a mean EF of 1.42% and annual fluxes of 8.9 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹. Emissions are strongly modulated by N rate, irrigation method, fertilizer type, and system type, with greenhouse and high-N systems representing the greatest hotspots. Partial manure substitution (20–40%), nitrification inhibitors, drip irrigation, and split N application consistently reduce emissions without yield penalties. These findings highlight the need for vegetable-specific emission factors in national inventories and for targeted management interventions to reconcile vegetable productivity with climate mitigation goals.

 References (illustrative)

1. IPCC (2021). Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Cambridge University Press.
2. Zhang, Y. et al. (2019). N₂O emissions from vegetable fields in China. *Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment*, 273, 1–9.
3. Wang, X. et al. (2021). Meta-analysis of N₂O emission factors in Chinese croplands. *Global Change Biology*, 27, 1123–1137.
4. Liu, C. et al. (2020). Effects of irrigation on N₂O emissions in greenhouse vegetable systems. *Science of the Total Environment*, 715, 136912.
5. Chen, Z. et al. (2022). Organic substitution reduces N₂O emissions in intensive vegetable production. *Journal of Cleaner Production*, 340, 130781.

title: Identification and Validation of a Five-Gene Signature Associated With Overall Survival in Breast Cancer Patients
text: Breast cancer is a heterogeneous malignancy with highly variable clinical outcomes, underscoring the need for reliable prognostic biomarkers. In this study, we aimed to identify and validate a gene signature associated with overall survival (OS) in breast cancer patients. Differentially expressed genes were screened from public transcriptomic datasets, and a five-gene signature was constructed using univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses. The prognostic performance of the signature was evaluated by Kaplan–Meier survival analysis and time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves. Patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups based on the risk score, with the high-risk group exhibiting significantly poorer OS. Functional enrichment analyses suggested that the signature was involved in cell cycle regulation and immune-related pathways. The five-gene signature was further validated in an independent cohort, demonstrating robust predictive value. These findings indicate that the identified five-gene signature may serve as a promising prognostic tool and provide potential therapeutic targets for breast cancer.

title: PEPC of sugarcane regulated glutathione S-transferase and altered carbon-nitrogen metabolism under different N source concentrations in Oryza sativa
text:
PEPC of sugarcane regulated glutathione S-transferase and altered carbon-nitrogen metabolism under different N source concentrations in *Oryza sativa*

Abstract

Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) plays a central role in carbon and nitrogen interactions in plants. In this study, transgenic rice (*Oryza sativa* L. cv. Nipponbare) overexpressing sugarcane PEPC (SoPEPC) was cultivated under three nitrogen source concentrations (0.5, 2.0, and 8.0 mM NH₄NO₃) to investigate its effects on glutathione S-transferase (GST) activity and carbon-nitrogen metabolism. Results showed that SoPEPC overexpression significantly increased PEPC activity by 42.6–68.3% across all N levels. GST activity was elevated by 28.5%, 35.2%, and 21.7% under low, moderate, and high N conditions, respectively, compared with wild-type (WT). Soluble protein and free amino acid contents were consistently higher in transgenic lines, while nitrate reductase (NR) and glutamine synthetase (GS) activities were upregulated under low and moderate N but downregulated under high N. Soluble sugar and starch contents increased in transgenic plants, accompanied by reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulation.
