These findings suggest that SoPEPC enhances GST-mediated antioxidant defense and optimizes carbon-nitrogen balance in rice under varying nitrogen regimes.

Keywords: sugarcane PEPC; transgenic rice; glutathione S-transferase; carbon-nitrogen metabolism; nitrogen source concentration

1. Introduction

Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC, EC 4.1.1.31) catalyzes the irreversible β-carboxylation of phosphoenolpyruvate to oxaloacetate, a key anaplerotic reaction linking carbon and nitrogen metabolism. In C₄ and CAM plants, PEPC is essential for photosynthetic carbon fixation, while in C₃ plants it participates in replenishing tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, regulating pH, and supporting nitrogen assimilation. Sugarcane (*Saccharum* spp.), a C₄ crop, possesses a highly active PEPC isoform that has been used to engineer C₃ crops for improved photosynthetic efficiency and stress tolerance.

Glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) are multifunctional detoxification enzymes that conjugate reduced glutathione to xenobiotics and reactive oxygen species, thereby mitigating oxidative damage. GST activity is often modulated by carbon and nitrogen availability, as both carbon skeletons and amino acid precursors influence enzyme synthesis and substrate supply. However, how PEPC overexpression affects GST activity and carbon-nitrogen partitioning under different nitrogen source concentrations remains poorly understood.

Rice (*Oryza sativa*) is a staple C₃ cereal and a model for functional genomics. Nitrogen fertilization strongly affects rice growth, grain yield, and quality. Excessive or deficient nitrogen leads to metabolic imbalances and oxidative stress. We hypothesized that introducing sugarcane PEPC into rice would enhance carbon flow into organic acids and amino acids, thereby altering GST activity and carbon-nitrogen metabolism in an N-dependent manner. To test this, we generated transgenic rice overexpressing SoPEPC and evaluated physiological and biochemical parameters under three NH₄NO₃ concentrations.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Plant materials and growth conditions

Transgenic rice lines (T₃ generation) overexpressing sugarcane PEPC (SoPEPC) under the control of the maize ubiquitin promoter were generated via *Agrobacterium*-mediated transformation of *Oryza sativa* cv. Nipponbare. Wild-type (WT) and three independent transgenic lines (L1, L2, L3) were surface-sterilized and germinated on half-strength Murashige-Skoog medium. Seven-day-old seedlings were transferred to hydroponic solution containing 0.5 (low N, LN), 2.0 (moderate N, MN), and 8.0 mM (high N, HN) NH₄NO₃ as the sole nitrogen source. The nutrient solution was renewed every two days. Plants were grown in a growth chamber at 28/24 °C (day/night), 60% relative humidity, and 12 h photoperiod (400 μmol m⁻² s⁻¹). After 21 days, the third fully expanded leaves were harvested and immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen for biochemical assays.

2.2 Enzyme activity assays

PEPC activity was measured spectrophotometrically by monitoring NADH oxidation at 340 nm. GST activity was determined using 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene (CDNB) as substrate, and the increase in absorbance at 340 nm was recorded. NR activity was assayed by nitrite formation, and GS activity was measured by the synthetase reaction. All enzyme activities were expressed as U mg⁻¹ protein. Soluble protein content was determined by the Bradford method.

2.3 Metabolite measurements

Soluble sugar and starch contents were quantified by anthrone colorimetry. Free amino acids were determined by ninhydrin reagent. MDA content was measured by thiobarbituric acid reaction. Nitrate content was determined by salicylic acid method.

2.4 Statistical analysis

Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) of three biological replicates. One-way ANOVA followed by Duncan’s multiple range test (P < 0.05) was used to compare means among genotypes and N treatments.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 PEPC activity and GST activity

SoPEPC overexpression significantly increased leaf PEPC activity under all N conditions. Under MN, transgenic lines showed 68.3% higher PEPC activity than WT (P < 0.05), followed by LN (52.1%) and HN (42.6%). GST activity exhibited a similar trend: compared with WT, transgenic lines had 28.5%, 35.2%, and 21.7% higher GST activity under LN, MN, and HN, respectively. The highest GST activity was observed in L2 under MN.

3.2 Carbon and nitrogen metabolites

Soluble sugar content was elevated by 18.4–31.2% in transgenic lines across N treatments, with the greatest increase under MN. Starch content followed a comparable pattern, increasing by 22.7% under MN relative to WT. Free amino acid content was 15.6–27.9% higher in transgenic lines than in WT, particularly under LN and MN. Nitrate content was lower in transgenic lines under LN and MN but higher under HN.

3.3 Enzyme activities related to nitrogen assimilation

NR activity was significantly higher in transgenic lines under LN (34.8%) and MN (29.5%) but reduced by 18.2% under HN. GS activity showed a similar N-dependent response, with increases of 26.3% and 31.7% under LN and MN, respectively, and a decrease of 14.5% under HN.

3.4 Oxidative stress marker

MDA content was consistently lower in transgenic lines than in WT, with reductions of 19.8% (LN), 24.3% (MN), and 12.6% (HN). The lowest MDA level was recorded in L2 under MN, coinciding with peak GST activity.

4. Discussion

The present study demonstrates that sugarcane PEPC overexpression in rice coordinately regulates GST activity and carbon-nitrogen metabolism in a nitrogen-dependent manner. The enhanced PEPC activity likely increased the supply of oxaloacetate and malate, which can serve as carbon skeletons for amino acid biosynthesis and as substrates for antioxidant defense. The upregulation of GST activity under all N regimes, especially under moderate N, suggests that PEPC-derived metabolites may stimulate GST gene expression or provide precursors for glutathione synthesis. Glutathione, a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine, is closely linked to nitrogen and sulfur assimilation. Thus, increased carbon flow through PEPC may enhance glutathione availability and GST-mediated detoxification.

The N-dependent changes in NR and GS activities indicate that PEPC overexpression improves nitrogen assimilation under low and moderate N but may cause feedback inhibition under high N. Under HN, excessive ammonium can be toxic, and the downregulation of NR and GS in transgenic lines may reflect a metabolic adjustment to avoid ammonium accumulation. The lower nitrate content under LN and MN in transgenic lines suggests enhanced nitrate reduction and assimilation, consistent with higher NR activity.

The reduced MDA content in transgenic lines confirms alleviated oxidative stress, likely due to enhanced GST activity and improved carbon-nitrogen balance. Soluble sugar and starch accumulation in transgenic lines may result from increased photosynthetic carbon fixation or reduced carbon consumption for detoxification. These findings collectively suggest that SoPEPC acts as a metabolic regulator that fine-tunes carbon and nitrogen fluxes, thereby enhancing GST-mediated antioxidant capacity under varying nitrogen availability.

5. Conclusion

Overexpression of sugarcane PEPC in rice enhanced PEPC and GST activities, increased soluble sugar, starch, free amino acid, and soluble protein contents, and modulated NR and GS activities in an N-dependent manner. Transgenic lines exhibited lower MDA accumulation, indicating reduced oxidative stress. These results suggest that SoPEPC improves carbon-nitrogen metabolic coordination and strengthens GST-related antioxidant defense under different nitrogen source concentrations. This study provides a physiological basis for engineering C₃ crops with C₄ PEPC to improve nitrogen use efficiency and stress tolerance.

title: Genome-Wide Characterization of Salt-Responsive miRNAs, circRNAs and Associated ceRNA Networks in Tomatoes
text: Soil salinization is a major abiotic constraint on global crop production, and tomato (*Solanum lycopersicum*), one of the most widely cultivated vegetable crops, is moderately salt-sensitive and suffers substantial yield and quality losses under saline conditions. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying salt tolerance in tomato is therefore of both fundamental and applied importance. Beyond protein-coding genes, non-coding RNAs have emerged as key post-transcriptional regulators of stress responses. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) modulate the expression of target genes involved in ion homeostasis, reactive oxygen species scavenging and osmotic adjustment, while circular RNAs (circRNAs), a class of covalently closed non-coding RNAs, can act as miRNA sponges and thereby influence downstream gene expression. The competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) hypothesis posits that mRNAs, circRNAs and other transcripts compete for shared miRNA binding, forming complex regulatory networks that fine-tune stress responses. Although salt-responsive miRNAs and circRNAs have been documented individually in several plant species, genome-wide identification of these molecules and systematic construction of miRNA–circRNA–mRNA ceRNA networks under salt stress remain largely unexplored in tomato. In particular, how circRNAs participate in miRNA-mediated regulation of salt tolerance, and which core ceRNA modules govern the response, are still poorly understood. To address these gaps, we performed integrated transcriptome-wide analyses of miRNAs, circRNAs and mRNAs in tomato seedlings exposed to salt stress, using high-throughput sequencing combined with bioinformatics and experimental validation. We identified differentially expressed miRNAs and circRNAs, predicted their targets, and constructed salt-responsive ceRNA networks. Our results reveal candidate regulatory modules that may coordinate ion transport, antioxidant defense and hormone signaling under salinity, providing a valuable resource for functional studies and for molecular breeding of salt-tolerant tomato cultivars.

title: Margin purchases, short sales and stock return volatility in China: Evidence from the COVID-19 outbreak
text:
Results and Discussion

Table 2 reports the baseline difference-in-differences estimates. Consistent with our hypothesis, stocks with higher margin purchase intensity experienced a significant increase in return volatility following the COVID-19 outbreak. The coefficient on the interaction term (Margin × COVID) is 0.084 (t = 3.12, p < 0.01), indicating that a one-standard-deviation increase in margin trading activity raised daily return volatility by approximately 8.4% relative to the sample mean of 2.31%. In contrast, the coefficient on short selling (Short × COVID) is −0.047 (t = −2.28, p < 0.05), suggesting that short sales attenuated volatility by roughly 4.7%, consistent with the view that informed short sellers improve price efficiency during crises.

These effects are economically meaningful and robust to alternative specifications. Controlling for firm size, book-to-market ratio, turnover, and the market return, the margin effect remains positive and significant (β = 0.076, t = 2.87), while the short-selling effect remains negative (β = −0.041, t = −2.05). The results hold when we exclude firms in Hubei province (β = 0.081 and −0.044, respectively) and when we adopt an event window ending 30 trading days after the Wuhan lockdown.

The asymmetric pattern is plausible given China's retail-dominated investor base: margin traders amplify sentiment-driven buying, whereas short sellers—mostly institutional—help correct overpricing. Overall, our findings indicate that leverage availability and short-sale constraints jointly shape volatility during exogenous shocks, offering policy lessons for emerging markets.

title: The epigenetic mechanisms in Fusarium mycotoxins induced toxicities
text:
The epigenetic mechanisms in Fusarium mycotoxins induced toxicities

Abstract
Fusarium mycotoxins, such as deoxynivalenol (DON), zearalenone (ZEA), and fumonisin B1 (FB1), are common contaminants of cereal crops and pose significant health risks to humans and animals. While their classical toxicological effects are well documented, the epigenetic mechanisms underlying these toxicities have gained attention only recently. This study investigates the role of DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs in DON-, ZEA-, and FB1-induced toxicities using both in vitro (HepG2 cells) and in vivo (BALB/c mice) models. Our results show that DON (0.5–2 μM) significantly increased global DNA hypomethylation and reduced DNMT1 and DNMT3a expression, while ZEA (10–50 μM) induced histone H3K27me3 enrichment at the promoter of the tumor suppressor gene *PTEN*. FB1 (5–20 μM) upregulated miR-27b and miR-34a, leading to suppressed *PPARγ* and *Bcl-2* expression. In mice, dietary exposure to DON (2 mg/kg feed) for 4 weeks caused hepatic oxidative stress and altered methylation of *Nrf2*. These findings suggest that epigenetic dysregulation is a key event in Fusarium mycotoxin toxicity and may serve as a target for intervention.

Keywords: Fusarium mycotoxins; deoxynivalenol; zearalenone; fumonisin B1; epigenetics; DNA methylation; histone modification; microRNA

1. Introduction
Fusarium mycotoxins are secondary metabolites produced by *Fusarium* species that frequently contaminate maize, wheat, and barley. Among them, DON, ZEA, and FB1 are the most prevalent and cause a range of toxicities including hepatotoxicity, immunotoxicity, genotoxicity, and carcinogenicity (Pestka, 2010). Traditional toxicology has focused on direct cellular damage, but emerging evidence indicates that epigenetic alterations—heritable changes in gene expression without DNA sequence changes—play a critical role in mycotoxin-induced effects (Kouadio et al., 2005). DNA methylation, histone post-translational modifications, and microRNAs (miRNAs) are major epigenetic regulators. For instance, DON has been shown to alter global methylation in intestinal cells, while ZEA affects histone acetylation. FB1 disrupts sphingolipid metabolism, which can indirectly influence epigenetic enzymes. However, a comparative analysis of these three mycotoxins on multiple epigenetic layers is lacking. This study aims to elucidate the epigenetic mechanisms underlying their toxicities in hepatic and intestinal models.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Chemicals and reagents
DON, ZEA, and FB1 (purity >98%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Antibodies against DNMT1, DNMT3a, H3K27me3, and β-actin were from Abcam. miRNA mimics and inhibitors were from GenePharma.

2.2 Cell culture and treatment
HepG2 and Caco-2 cells were cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS. Cells were treated with DON (0.5, 1, 2 μM), ZEA (10, 25, 50 μM), or FB1 (5, 10, 20 μM) for 24 h. Controls received DMSO (0.1%).

2.3 Animals and exposure
Male BALB/c mice (6 weeks old, n=24) were randomly divided into four groups: control, DON (2 mg/kg feed), ZEA (10 mg/kg feed), and FB1 (20 mg/kg feed) for 4 weeks. Liver and colon tissues were collected.

2.4 Global DNA methylation and DNMT activity
Global 5-mC levels were measured using ELISA (Zymo Research). DNMT activity was assessed by colorimetric assay.

2.5 Histone modification analysis
Histone extracts were prepared and subjected to Western blot for H3K27me3, H3K9ac, and H3K4me3. ChIP-qPCR was performed for *PTEN* promoter using H3K27me3 antibody.

2.6 miRNA expression and target validation
Total RNA was extracted and miRNAs were quantified by qRT-PCR. miR-27b and miR-34a mimics were transfected into HepG2 cells, and *PPARγ* and *Bcl-2* 3'UTR luciferase reporters were used.

2.7 Statistical analysis
Data are expressed as mean ± SD. One-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post-hoc test was used; p<0.05 was considered significant.

3. Results and Analysis
3.1 DON induces global DNA hypomethylation
DON treatment (2 μM) reduced global 5-mC levels by 38% in HepG2 cells (p<0.01) and decreased DNMT1 and DNMT3a protein levels by 45% and 52%, respectively. In mice, hepatic 5-mC was reduced by 29% after DON exposure.

3.2 ZEA alters histone modifications at *PTEN* promoter
ZEA (50 μM) increased H3K27me3 at the *PTEN* promoter by 3.2-fold (p<0.001) and reduced *PTEN* mRNA by 60%. H3K9ac was decreased, while H3K4me3 showed no change. In ZEA-treated mice, colonic *PTEN* expression was downregulated.

3.3 FB1 upregulates oncogenic and apoptotic miRNAs
FB1 (20 μM) increased miR-27b and miR-34a levels by 2.8- and 3.5-fold in HepG2 cells. Luciferase assays confirmed that miR-27b targets *PPARγ* and miR-34a targets *Bcl-2*. FB1 reduced *PPARγ* and *Bcl-2* protein levels, and induced apoptosis (caspase-3 activity +2.4-fold).

3.4 Synergistic epigenetic effects
Co-treatment with DON+ZEA+FB1 at low doses (0.5, 10, 5 μM) caused greater reduction in global methylation and higher miR-34a than individual treatments, suggesting additive epigenetic toxicity.

4. Discussion
Our findings demonstrate that Fusarium mycotoxins disrupt multiple epigenetic layers. DON primarily affects DNA methylation machinery, consistent with its known inhibition of protein synthesis. ZEA’s effect on H3K27me3 at *PTEN* links endocrine disruption to epigenetic silencing of a tumor suppressor. FB1’s induction of miR-27b and miR-34a reveals a novel miRNA-mediated mechanism for its hepatotoxicity and apoptosis. The synergistic effects at low doses are particularly concerning for food safety, as real-world exposure involves mixtures. These epigenetic changes may persist after toxin removal, contributing to long-term health risks such as cancer and metabolic disorders. Limitations include the use of only two cell lines and a single animal dose. Future studies should examine dose-response and transgenerational effects.

5. Conclusion
Fusarium mycotoxins DON, ZEA, and FB1 induce toxicity through distinct but overlapping epigenetic mechanisms: DNA hypomethylation, histone methylation changes, and miRNA dysregulation. These epigenetic alterations may serve as early biomarkers and therapeutic targets for mycotoxin-induced diseases.

title: A review on Cadmium Exposure in the Population and Intervention Strategies Against Cadmium Toxicity
text:
A review on Cadmium Exposure in the Population and Intervention Strategies Against Cadmium Toxicity

 Abstract

Cadmium (Cd) is a ubiquitous environmental toxicant ranked among the top ten chemicals of major public health concern by the World Health Organization. Chronic exposure, primarily through contaminated food, water, tobacco smoke, and occupational settings, leads to progressive accumulation in the kidneys, liver, and bones, resulting in nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, osteotoxicity, and carcinogenesis. This review synthesizes current evidence on population-level cadmium exposure and evaluates intervention strategies against cadmium toxicity. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a systematic literature survey with a cross-sectional biomonitoring dataset of 1,842 participants recruited from three industrially distinct regions (an industrial zone, an urban center, and a rural agricultural area). Blood cadmium (BCd) and urinary cadmium (UCd) were measured alongside dietary and lifestyle questionnaires. Mean BCd and UCd concentrations were 1.42 µg/L and 2.18 µg/g creatinine, respectively, with the industrial zone showing significantly higher values (BCd: 2.11 µg/L; UCd: 3.46 µg/g creatinine) than urban (1.18 µg/L; 1.74 µg/g creatinine) and rural (0.97 µg/L; 1.34 µg/g creatinine) regions (p < 0.001). Smokers exhibited 2.3-fold higher BCd than non-smokers. Dietary interventions, including zinc and selenium supplementation, chelation therapy, and antioxidant-rich diets, demonstrated variable efficacy in reducing cadmium bioavailability and mitigating oxidative damage. The review concludes that integrated strategies combining exposure reduction, nutritional intervention, and biomonitoring are essential for protecting vulnerable populations.

Keywords: Cadmium toxicity, biomonitoring, oxidative stress, chelation therapy, selenium, zinc, nephrotoxicity, public health intervention

 Introduction

Cadmium is a non-essential heavy metal that occurs naturally in the Earth's crust and is released into the environment through anthropogenic activities such as mining, smelting, battery manufacturing, pigment production, and the application of phosphate fertilizers. Unlike many toxicants, cadmium has an exceptionally long biological half-life of 10–30 years in humans, leading to cumulative toxicity even at low-level chronic exposure (Järup & Åkesson, 2009). The primary route of exposure in the general population is dietary, with cereals, leafy vegetables, shellfish, and organ meats being major contributors. Tobacco smoking constitutes an additional significant source, as tobacco plants readily accumulate cadmium from soil.

The toxicological profile of cadmium is well documented. Once absorbed, cadmium is transported bound to metallothionein and accumulates predominantly in the proximal tubular cells of the kidney and in the liver. Renal tubular dysfunction, manifested as increased excretion of low-molecular-weight proteins such as β2-microglobulin, is considered the critical effect of chronic cadmium exposure. Cadmium also interferes with calcium and vitamin D metabolism, contributing to osteomalacia and osteoporosis, as famously observed in the Itai-itai disease outbreak in Japan. Furthermore, cadmium is classified as a Group 1 human carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, with associations reported for lung, prostate, and renal cancers.

Despite regulatory efforts, cadmium exposure remains a global public health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where industrial regulation is weak. Intervention strategies span primary prevention (reducing environmental emissions and dietary exposure), secondary prevention (biomonitoring and early detection), and tertiary measures (nutritional and pharmacological countermeasures). This review aims to (i) characterize cadmium exposure levels in a representative population sample, (ii) examine determinants of exposure, and (iii) critically evaluate intervention strategies against cadmium toxicity.

 Materials and Methods

 Study Design and Population

A cross-sectional biomonitoring study was conducted between January and December 2023 across three regions: an industrial zone (Region A), an urban center (Region B), and a rural agricultural area (Region C). A total of 1,842 participants aged 18–75 years were recruited using stratified random sampling. Exclusion criteria included known renal disease, pregnancy, and recent occupational exposure to other heavy metals.

 Sample Collection and Analysis

Fasting blood samples and spot urine samples were collected in acid-washed, metal-free polyethylene containers. BCd and UCd were quantified using graphite furnace atomic absorption spectrometry (GFAAS) with a detection limit of 0.05 µg/L. Urinary creatinine was measured to adjust for dilution. Quality control included certified reference materials (Seronorm Trace Elements) with recovery rates of 96–104%.

 Questionnaire and Dietary Assessment

A validated semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire assessed consumption of rice, leafy vegetables, shellfish, and offal. Lifestyle data on smoking, alcohol consumption, and residential history were recorded.

 Intervention Sub-Study

A subset of 180 participants with elevated UCd (>3 µg/g creatinine) was randomized into three intervention arms for 12 weeks: (1) zinc (30 mg/day) plus selenium (200 µg/day) supplementation; (2) antioxidant-rich dietary counseling (increased intake of fruits, cruciferous vegetables, and green tea); and (3) control (standard diet). Primary outcomes were changes in UCd, plasma malondialdehyde (MDA), and urinary β2-microglobulin.

 Statistical Analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS v27. Group comparisons used ANOVA and Kruskal–Wallis tests; associations were assessed by multiple linear regression. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

 Results

 Exposure Levels

The overall geometric mean BCd was 1.42 µg/L (95% CI: 1.36–1.48) and UCd was 2.18 µg/g creatinine (95% CI: 2.09–2.27). Regional stratification revealed a clear exposure gradient (Table 1). Region A had the highest concentrations (BCd: 2.11 µg/L; UCd: 3.46 µg/g creatinine), significantly exceeding Region B (1.18 µg/L; 1.74 µg/g creatinine) and Region C (0.97 µg/L; 1.34 µg/g creatinine) (p < 0.001 for both biomarkers).

Table 1. Cadmium biomarker concentrations by region (geometric means).

| Region | n | BCd (µg/L) | UCd (µg/g creatinine) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A (Industrial) | 604 | 2.11 | 3.46 |
| B (Urban) | 638 | 1.18 | 1.74 |
| C (Rural) | 600 | 0.97 | 1.34 |

 Determinants of Exposure

Smokers had 2.3-fold higher BCd (2.54 µg/L) than non-smokers (1.10 µg/L; p < 0.001). Rice consumption (>5 servings/week) was associated with a 0.42 µg/g creatinine increase in UCd (β = 0.42; p = 0.003), while shellfish consumption showed a weaker association (β = 0.21; p = 0.041). Age was positively correlated with UCd (r = 0.38; p < 0.001), consistent with cumulative lifetime exposure.

 Intervention Outcomes

After 12 weeks, the zinc + selenium group showed a 22% reduction in UCd (from 3.81 to 2.97 µg/g creatinine; p = 0.002) and a 31% decrease in plasma MDA (p < 0.001). The antioxidant diet group exhibited a 17% reduction in MDA (p = 0.008) but no significant change in UCd. Urinary β2-microglobulin decreased modestly in both intervention groups (12% and 9%, respectively) but did not reach statistical significance in the diet arm. The control group showed no significant changes.

 Discussion

The present findings confirm that cadmium exposure remains a significant public health concern, with pronounced regional disparities linked to industrial activity. The mean UCd in the industrial region exceeded the 3 µg/g creatinine threshold associated with early renal tubular damage proposed by EFSA, indicating that a substantial proportion of this population is at risk of cadmium-related nephrotoxicity. These results align with previous biomonitoring surveys in smelting-adjacent communities, which consistently report elevated body burdens relative to reference populations.

Smoking emerged as a major modifiable determinant, corroborating evidence that tobacco contributes up to 50% of cadmium intake in smokers. The strong association between rice consumption and UCd reflects the well-documented soil-to-plant transfer of cadmium in paddy fields, particularly in regions where irrigation water is contaminated by mining effluent.

The intervention sub-study provides encouraging evidence that nutritional strategies can mitigate cadmium toxicity. Zinc and selenium exert protective effects through multiple mechanisms: zinc induces metallothionein synthesis, sequestering cadmium and reducing its free ionic fraction; selenium enhances antioxidant enzyme activity (glutathione peroxidase) and forms inert cadmium–selenium complexes. The reduction in MDA indicates attenuation of cadmium-induced lipid peroxidation, a key pathway in renal and hepatic injury. However, the lack of significant UCd reduction in the antioxidant diet group suggests that dietary antioxidants primarily modulate oxidative damage rather than enhance cadmium excretion.

Chelation therapy, while effective in acute poisoning, has limited utility in chronic low-level exposure due to poor specificity, potential redistribution of cadmium to the kidney, and nephrotoxicity of chelating agents themselves. Consequently, primary prevention—emission control, soil remediation, and dietary diversification—remains the cornerstone of public health strategy. Secondary prevention through biomonitoring programs enables early identification of at-risk individuals before irreversible renal damage occurs.

This study has limitations. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Spot urine samples may not fully capture long-term exposure, though creatinine adjustment mitigates variability. The 12-week intervention period is relatively short; longer trials are needed to assess sustained benefits.

 Conclusion

Cadmium exposure in the studied population varies markedly by region, with industrial proximity, smoking, and rice consumption as principal determinants. Chronic exposure at the observed levels poses a tangible risk of renal tubular dysfunction and oxidative injury. Integrated intervention strategies are warranted: (1) stringent industrial emission controls and soil remediation in hotspot areas; (2) tobacco cessation programs; (3) dietary diversification to reduce reliance on high-cadmium staples; and (4) targeted zinc and selenium supplementation for high-risk groups. Continued biomonitoring and longitudinal intervention research are essential to translate these findings into policy and clinical practice.

 References (Selected)

1. Järup, L., & Åkesson, A. (2009). Current status of cadmium as an environmental health problem. *Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology*, 238(3), 201–208.
2. Satarug, S., et al. (2010). Cadmium, environmental exposure, and health outcomes. *Environmental Health Perspectives*, 118(2), 182–190.
3. EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain. (2012). Cadmium dietary exposure in the European population. *EFSA Journal*, 10(1), 2551.
4. Nordberg, G. F., et al. (2018). Metallothionein in cadmium toxicology. *Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology*, 360, 1–10.
5. IARC. (2012). Cadmium and cadmium compounds. *IARC Monographs*, 100C, 121–145.

title: Phenotypic Variability and Genetic Diversity in a Pinus koraiensis Clonal Trial in Northeastern China
text: Abstract: *Pinus koraiensis* Siebold & Zucc. is a economically and ecologically important conifer in northeastern China, yet the extent of phenotypic variability and genetic diversity within its breeding populations remains insufficiently characterized. In this study, we assessed 15 growth, form, and adaptive traits across 60 clones of *P. koraiensis* in a clonal trial established in northeastern China, and genotyped all clones using 20 polymorphic microsatellite (SSR) markers to quantify genetic diversity and population structure. Analysis of variance revealed highly significant clonal effects (*P* < 0.01) for all measured traits, with broad-sense heritability estimates ranging from 0.41 to 0.86, indicating substantial genetic control over phenotypic variation. Coefficients of phenotypic and genotypic variation varied from 8.7% to 32.4% and from 6.2% to 24.9%, respectively, with the highest variability observed for branch angle and stem straightness. The 20 SSR loci produced a total of 132 alleles, with a mean of 6.6 alleles per locus, mean observed heterozygosity of 0.612, mean expected heterozygosity of 0.674, and mean polymorphic information content of 0.643, reflecting moderate-to-high levels of genetic diversity. Genetic differentiation among clones was low (*F*ST = 0.041), and analysis of molecular variance attributed 95.9% of the total variation to within-clone variation. Principal coordinate analysis and UPGMA clustering based on Nei's genetic distance did not reveal clear grouping by geographic origin, suggesting extensive gene flow among source populations. Mantel tests indicated no significant correlation between phenotypic and genetic distances (*r* = 0.087, *P* = 0.213), implying that neutral molecular markers may not adequately capture adaptive trait variation. These findings demonstrate considerable phenotypic variability and ample genetic diversity in the *P. koraiensis* clonal trial, providing a valuable basis for clone selection, germplasm conservation, and the design of future breeding strategies for this species in northeastern China.

title: Effect of the addition of six antioxidants on sperm motility, membrane integrity and mitochondrial function in red seabream (Pagrus major) sperm cryopreservation
text:
Effect of the addition of six antioxidants on sperm motility, membrane integrity and mitochondrial function in red seabream (*Pagrus major*) sperm cryopreservation

Abstract

The present study evaluated the effects of six antioxidants—ascorbic acid (AA), α-tocopherol (VE), glutathione (GSH), catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and melatonin (MT)—on sperm quality in red seabream (*Pagrus major*) during cryopreservation. Semen samples were diluted with a basic extender containing 10% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and supplemented with each antioxidant at concentrations of 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0 mg/mL. Post-thaw sperm motility, membrane integrity, and mitochondrial function were assessed. The results showed that all antioxidants improved post-thaw sperm quality compared with the control, with MT and CAT exhibiting the strongest protective effects. At 0.5 mg/mL, MT significantly increased total motility (from 41.2% to 68.7%), membrane integrity (from 45.6% to 72.3%), and mitochondrial membrane potential (from 52.1% to 78.4%) (P < 0.05). CAT at 0.5 mg/mL also markedly improved these parameters (64.5%, 69.8%, and 74.1%, respectively). AA and VE showed moderate benefits, whereas GSH and SOD provided relatively weaker protection. These findings indicate that supplementation with MT or CAT at 0.5 mg/mL effectively alleviates cryodamage in red seabream sperm, likely by reducing oxidative stress and preserving mitochondrial function.

Keywords: *Pagrus major*; cryopreservation; antioxidant; sperm motility; membrane integrity; mitochondrial function

1. Introduction

Red seabream (*Pagrus major*) is an economically important marine fish in East Asia, and sperm cryopreservation is valuable for genetic improvement and aquaculture production. However, cryopreservation induces oxidative stress through excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to lipid peroxidation, membrane damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Antioxidants have been widely used to mitigate such damage in fish sperm. Nevertheless, comparative studies on different antioxidants in red seabream sperm are limited. This study examined six antioxidants for their ability to improve post-thaw sperm motility, membrane integrity, and mitochondrial function.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Semen collection

Mature male red seabream (body weight 1.2–1.8 kg) were maintained in aerated seawater at 20°C. Semen was collected by abdominal massage, excluding samples contaminated with urine or feces. Only samples with >85% initial motility were used.

2.2 Extender and cryopreservation

The basic extender consisted of 0.5 M glucose, 15% fetal bovine serum, and 10% DMSO. Six antioxidants were added individually at 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0 mg/mL: AA, VE, GSH, CAT, SOD, and MT. A control without antioxidant was also prepared. Semen was diluted 1:3 (v/v) with extender, equilibrated at 4°C for 15 min, loaded into 0.5-mL straws, and frozen in liquid nitrogen vapor for 10 min before plunging into liquid nitrogen. Thawing was performed in a 35°C water bath for 10 s.

2.3 Sperm quality assessment

Motility was assessed under a light microscope (×200) and expressed as total motile sperm (%). Membrane integrity was evaluated using the eosin–nigrosin staining method. Mitochondrial function was assessed using rhodamine 123 staining and flow cytometry, expressed as the percentage of sperm with high mitochondrial membrane potential.

2.4 Statistical analysis

Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. One-way ANOVA followed by Duncan’s multiple range test was used. P < 0.05 was considered significant.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Sperm motility

Post-thaw total motility in the control was 41.2 ± 3.5%. All antioxidants improved motility, but the effects were concentration-dependent. MT at 0.5 mg/mL yielded the highest motility (68.7 ± 4.1%), followed by CAT at 0.5 mg/mL (64.5 ± 3.8%). AA and VE reached maximum values of 57.3% and 55.9% at 0.5 mg/mL, respectively. GSH and SOD showed weaker improvements, with peak motilities of 52.4% and 50.8% at 0.5 mg/mL. At 1.0 mg/mL, motility declined for all groups, suggesting a pro-oxidant effect at higher concentrations.

3.2 Membrane integrity

Membrane integrity followed a similar trend. The control showed 45.6 ± 4.0%. MT (0.5 mg/mL) increased integrity to 72.3 ± 3.7%, and CAT (0.5 mg/mL) to 69.8 ± 4.2%. AA and VE resulted in 61.5% and 59.7%, respectively. GSH and SOD produced 56.2% and 54.9%. Again, 1.0 mg/mL reduced membrane integrity relative to 0.5 mg/mL.

3.3 Mitochondrial function

Mitochondrial membrane potential in the control was 52.1 ± 4.5%. MT (0.5 mg/mL) elevated this to 78.4 ± 3.9%, and CAT (0.5 mg/mL) to 74.1 ± 4.3%. AA and VE reached 65.8% and 63.4%. GSH and SOD showed 60.1% and 58.7%. The highest concentration (1.0 mg/mL) was less effective for all antioxidants.

4. Discussion

The results demonstrate that antioxidant supplementation mitigates cryodamage in red seabream sperm. MT and CAT were most effective, likely because MT directly scavenges ROS and protects mitochondrial membranes, while CAT decomposes hydrogen peroxide, a major ROS. The superior performance of MT may also relate to its ability to stabilize mitochondrial electron transport. AA and VE, as chain-breaking antioxidants, provided moderate protection. GSH and SOD were less effective, possibly due to limited membrane permeability or insufficient regeneration of reduced forms. The decline at 1.0 mg/mL suggests that excessive antioxidants can disturb redox balance and cause reductive stress. The parallel improvements in motility, membrane integrity, and mitochondrial function indicate that these parameters are closely linked and that mitochondrial protection is central to sperm cryosurvival.

5. Conclusion

Supplementation of the extender with MT or CAT at 0.5 mg/mL significantly improves post-thaw sperm motility, membrane integrity, and mitochondrial function in red seabream. These antioxidants are recommended for optimizing cryopreservation protocols. Further studies should examine combined antioxidant treatments and in vivo fertilization success.

title: Burden of injury along the development spectrum: associations between the Socio-demographic Index and disability-adjusted life year estimates from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017
text: Injuries remain a leading cause of premature death and long-term disability worldwide, yet their burden is unevenly distributed across populations at different levels of socioeconomic development. The Socio-demographic Index (SDI), a composite measure of income per capita, education, and fertility, provides a standardized framework for examining these disparities. However, comprehensive global assessments of how injury burden varies along the development spectrum remain limited. Using data from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017, this study examines associations between SDI and disability-adjusted life year (DALY) estimates for injuries across 195 countries and territories. We aim to quantify injury burden patterns by SDI quintile, identify leading injury causes at each development level, and explore sex-specific differences. These findings can inform targeted prevention strategies and resource allocation tailored to countries' developmental contexts, supporting progress toward global injury control and health equity.

title: Detection of Endogenous Iron Reduction during Hepatocarcinogenesis at Susceptibility-Weighted MR Imaging: Value for Characterization of Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Dysplastic Nodule in Cirrhotic Liver
text:
Results and Discussion

Of 87 cirrhotic patients enrolled, 112 focal lesions were confirmed histopathologically: 58 hepatocellular carcinomas (HCCs), 21 dysplastic nodules (DNs), and 33 regenerative nodules (RNs). Intratumoral susceptibility signal intensity (ITSS) on SWI was absent in 49/58 (84.5%) HCCs, 17/21 (81.0%) DNs, and 31/33 (93.9%) RNs. The mean ITSS score was significantly lower in HCCs (0.31 ± 0.54) and DNs (0.38 ± 0.67) than in RNs (0.91 ± 0.72; *P* < 0.001 and *P* = 0.004, respectively), but did not differ between HCCs and DNs (*P* = 0.612). Correspondingly, quantitative R2* values were elevated in HCCs (48.7 ± 12.3 s⁻¹) and DNs (45.2 ± 11.6 s⁻¹) relative to RNs (31.4 ± 9.8 s⁻¹; both *P* < 0.001), consistent with depleted storage iron. The sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of absent ITSS for discriminating HCC/DN from RN were 83.5%, 93.9%, and 86.6%, respectively.

These findings indicate that endogenous iron reduction occurs early during hepatocarcinogenesis, preceding overt malignant transformation, and is detectable noninvasively by SWI. Loss of ITSS likely reflects impaired iron uptake and storage within dysplastic and neoplastic hepatocytes. Importantly, SWI distinguished borderline lesions from benign regenerative nodules, a distinction that conventional imaging frequently fails to make. The inability of ITSS to separate HCC from DN suggests that iron depletion is an early, shared event rather than a marker of progression. Limitations include the single-center design, modest DN sample size, and potential susceptibility artifacts from prior locoregional therapy. Nevertheless, SWI may serve as a useful adjunct for characterizing nodules in the cirrhotic liver.

title: Improved chromosome-level genome assembly and annotation of the seagrass, Zostera marina (eelgrass)
text:
Improved chromosome-level genome assembly and annotation of the seagrass, *Zostera marina* (eelgrass)

Abstract

*Zostera marina* (eelgrass) is a foundational marine angiosperm that supports coastal ecosystem services worldwide. The original reference genome, published in 2016, was assembled primarily from short reads and contains thousands of fragmented scaffolds, limiting fine-scale comparative and functional genomic analyses. Here, we present an improved chromosome-level genome assembly and annotation for *Z. marina* using a combination of PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing, high-throughput chromatin conformation capture (Hi-C), and transcriptome-assisted gene prediction. The new assembly spans 1.32 Gb with a contig N50 of 8.7 Mb and a scaffold N50 of 62.4 Mb, with 96.8% of the assembly anchored onto the 12 expected chromosomes. BUSCO completeness reached 97.4% (embryophyta_odb10), and the consensus quality value was 42.6. We predicted 21,486 protein-coding genes, of which 93.1% were functionally annotated. Comparative analyses revealed improved resolution of tandem gene families, expanded hypoxia-responsive gene clusters, and a more complete reconstruction of the sulfated polysaccharide biosynthesis pathway. This chromosome-level resource provides a robust foundation for seagrass population genomics, adaptation studies, and conservation planning under climate change.

Keywords: *Zostera marina*; seagrass; chromosome-level assembly; HiFi sequencing; Hi-C; genome annotation; marine angiosperm

1. Introduction

Seagrasses are the only flowering plants that have successfully recolonized marine environments, and they form highly productive coastal ecosystems that sequester carbon, stabilize sediments, and provide nursery habitat for fisheries (Orth et al., 2006; Duarte et al., 2013). Among them, *Zostera marina* (eelgrass) is the most widely distributed and ecologically best-studied species in the northern hemisphere. Its evolutionary transition from terrestrial to fully submerged life involved profound adaptations in osmoregulation, gas exchange, light harvesting, and cell wall chemistry (Wissler et al., 2012; Olsen et al., 2016).

The first genome of *Z. marina* was released in 2016 and represented a landmark for marine plant biology (Olsen et al., 2016). However, that assembly was generated mainly from Illumina short reads, resulting in a fragmented draft with limited chromosome-scale contiguity. Such fragmentation hampers the analysis of structural variation, long-range linkage, repetitive element dynamics, and the physical clustering of gene families involved in stress responses. In addition, the original annotation likely missed or mis-joined genes embedded in repetitive regions, which are abundant in seagrass genomes.

Recent advances in long-read sequencing and chromatin conformation capture now allow chromosome-level assemblies even for large, repetitive plant genomes. Here, we report an improved chromosome-level genome assembly and annotation of *Z. marina* using PacBio HiFi, Hi-C, and RNA-seq data. Our objectives were to (i) produce a highly contiguous, chromosome-anchored assembly; (ii) improve gene annotation completeness; and (iii) evaluate biologically relevant improvements relative to the previous reference. The resulting resource is intended to support seagrass genomics, conservation, and restoration research.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Sample collection and sequencing

A single *Z. marina* individual was collected from a shallow subtidal meadow in Jiaozhou Bay, China (36.1°N, 120.3°E). Tissue was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. High-molecular-weight DNA was extracted from leaf tissue using a modified CTAB protocol. PacBio HiFi libraries were prepared and sequenced on the Sequel IIe platform, yielding 38.6 Gb of HiFi reads with an average length of 14.2 kb. For Hi-C, nuclei were cross-linked, digested with MboI, and sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000, producing 62.4 Gb of paired-end reads. RNA was extracted from roots, rhizomes, leaves, and reproductive shoots under ambient and low-light conditions, and sequenced on the same platform to support gene prediction.

2.2 Genome assembly

HiFi reads were assembled with hifiasm v0.19.5. Primary contigs were polished with the same HiFi data, and duplicates were removed with purge_dups. Hi-C reads were mapped to the draft assembly with BWA-MEM, and chromosome-scale scaffolding was performed using YaHS. Manual curation was conducted in Juicebox to correct mis-joins and orient contigs. Assembly quality was assessed using BUSCO v5.4.3 against embryophyta_odb10, Merqury for consensus quality, and LAI for repeat annotation quality.

2.3 Repeat annotation and gene prediction

Tandem repeats were identified with TRF and RepeatMasker. Transposable elements were annotated de novo using RepeatModeler2 and combined with the plant repeat database. Protein-coding genes were predicted with a hybrid pipeline integrating ab initio predictions (BRAKER2), transcript evidence (StringTie), and protein homology (GeMoMa). Functional annotation was performed against Swiss-Prot, KEGG, GO, and Pfam. Non-coding RNAs were annotated with Infernal and tRNAscan-SE.

2.4 Comparative and evolutionary analyses

We compared the new assembly with the 2016 reference using MUMmer and synteny plots generated with MCScanX. Gene family expansion was analyzed with OrthoFinder using five additional marine angiosperms and three terrestrial monocots. Positive selection was tested with PAML on single-copy orthologs. Gene clusters involved in hypoxia and sulfated polysaccharide biosynthesis were manually curated and validated by RT-qPCR.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Assembly statistics

The final assembly was 1.32 Gb, with contig N50 of 8.7 Mb, scaffold N50 of 62.4 Mb, and a maximum scaffold length of 101.3 Mb. A total of 96.8% of the assembly was anchored to 12 pseudochromosomes, consistent with the known karyotype of *Z. marina* (2n = 12). BUSCO completeness was 97.4%, with 1.2% fragmented and 1.4% missing. The consensus quality value was 42.6, and the LAI score was 18.9, indicating high repeat integrity. Compared with the 2016 assembly, scaffold N50 improved approximately 40-fold, and the number of unanchored scaffolds decreased from 5,842 to 214.

3.2 Repetitive elements and annotation

Repetitive sequences accounted for 61.3% of the genome, including 44.8% transposable elements and 7.9% tandem repeats. Long terminal repeat retrotransposons were the most abundant class. We predicted 21,486 protein-coding genes with an average transcript length of 3,142 bp and 5.2 exons per gene. BUSCO assessment of the proteome reached 96.1%. Among predicted genes, 93.1% had at least one functional annotation, and 78.4% were assigned GO terms. Non-coding RNA annotation identified 1,246 tRNAs, 312 rRNAs, and 894 lncRNAs.

3.3 Comparative genomics

Synteny analysis revealed strong collinearity with the 2016 reference, but the new assembly resolved 148 previously unplaced gene models and corrected 63 likely chimeric genes. OrthoFinder identified 18,742 orthogroups, of which 1,024 were lineage-specific to seagrasses. We detected significant expansion in gene families related to anaerobic metabolism, light signaling, and cell wall sulfation. In particular, a cluster of 14 hypoxia-responsive genes on chromosome 4 was collapsed into 6 fragments in the old assembly, whereas the new assembly resolved them as a tandem array. Similarly, the sulfotransferase family expanded to 42 genes, compared with 31 in the previous annotation.

3.4 Transcriptional validation

RT-qPCR confirmed low-oxygen induction of four hypoxia-responsive genes and light-dependent expression of two sulfotransferase genes. These results support the improved structural and functional accuracy of the new annotation.

4. Discussion

The improved assembly demonstrates the value of combining HiFi and Hi-C for repetitive marine plant genomes. The chromosome-level contiguity resolves regions that were previously inaccessible, especially around centromeric and transposable-element-rich domains. This is important because seagrass adaptation to submerged life likely involved repeated recruitment of stress-response genes and cell wall remodeling enzymes, many of which reside in repetitive regions.

The expansion of hypoxia-related and sulfotransferase gene families is consistent with the physiological demands of life in marine sediments, where oxygen availability fluctuates and sulfated polysaccharides contribute to cell wall integrity and ion regulation. The corrected tandem array on chromosome 4 suggests that the previous assembly underestimated the copy number of these genes, which may have biased expression and selection analyses.

Several limitations remain. First, the genome is still highly repetitive, and some centromeric regions are not fully resolved. Second, annotation of lncRNAs and alternative splicing remains incomplete. Third, our sample represents a single population, so structural variation within the species is not captured. Future work should integrate multiple populations and long-read transcriptomics to build a pan-genome.

Despite these limitations, the new resource substantially improves the foundation for seagrass genomics. It will facilitate genome-wide association studies, climate adaptation modeling, and restoration genetics, and it provides a benchmark for assembling other seagrass genomes.

5. Conclusion

We present a chromosome-level genome assembly and annotation of *Zostera marina* with markedly improved contiguity, completeness, and gene resolution compared with the previous reference. The assembly anchors 96.8% of the genome to 12 chromosomes, achieves 97.4% BUSCO completeness, and predicts 21,486 protein-coding genes. Comparative analyses reveal expanded hypoxia-responsive and sulfotransferase gene families and correct several chimeric models. This resource will support functional, evolutionary, and conservation studies of seagrasses and other marine angiosperms.

title: Metabolic Basis of Pathogenesis and Host Adaptation in Rice Blast
text:
Metabolic Basis of Pathogenesis and Host Adaptation in Rice Blast

 Abstract

Rice blast, caused by the filamentous fungus *Magnaporthe oryzae*, remains the most destructive disease of cultivated rice worldwide. Although the genetic and cytological basis of infection is well described, the metabolic reprogramming that underpins pathogenesis and host adaptation remains incompletely understood. In this study, we integrated untargeted metabolomics, isotope-assisted flux analysis, and targeted gene deletion to characterize the metabolic landscape of *M. oryzae* during infection of susceptible (Nipponbare) and resistant (IR64) rice cultivars. A total of 412 metabolites were differentially abundant across infection stages, with pronounced enrichment of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, amino acid biosynthesis, and lipid remodeling pathways. Flux analysis revealed that appressorial penetration is fueled primarily by glycogen-derived trehalose and β-oxidation of stored lipids, contributing up to 68.4% of the acetyl-CoA pool at 12 h post-inoculation (hpi). Deletion of the trehalose-6-phosphate synthase gene (*MoTPS1*) reduced appressorial turgor by 41.2% and attenuated virulence by 73.5%. Host-adapted isolates exhibited elevated secretion of mannitol and glycerol, which suppressed reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation in planta by 52.8%. Comparative metabolomics of resistant interactions revealed accumulation of salicylic acid, kaempferol derivatives, and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), correlating with restricted fungal biomass (0.31 mg/g versus 2.14 mg/g fresh weight in susceptible plants). Our findings define a metabolic framework in which carbon flux, osmolyte production, and redox buffering collectively determine pathogenic success and host range, offering new targets for durable blast control.

Keywords: *Magnaporthe oryzae*; metabolomics; appressorium; carbon flux; redox homeostasis; rice immunity; host adaptation

 Introduction

Rice (*Oryza sativa* L.) feeds more than half of the global population, and rice blast, caused by the ascomycete *Magnaporthe oryzae*, annually destroys 10–30% of the world harvest (Dean et al., 2012; Wilson & Talbot, 2009). The fungus deploys a specialized infection structure, the appressorium, which generates enormous turgor pressure to breach the host cuticle. This process is energetically expensive and depends on the mobilization of endogenous storage reserves, particularly glycogen and lipids. However, the precise metabolic routes that sustain penetration and subsequent biotrophic growth are still debated.

Host adaptation in *M. oryzae* is manifested as cultivar-specific virulence, governed by both fungal effectors and host metabolic responses. Resistant rice genotypes often mount rapid reprogramming of phenylpropanoid and phytohormone pathways, whereas susceptible hosts fail to restrict fungal colonization. Despite advances in transcriptomics, few studies have directly linked fungal metabolic flux to virulence outcomes across contrasting host genotypes.

We hypothesized that (i) appressorial penetration depends on a defined hierarchy of carbon sources, (ii) secreted polyols buffer host-derived ROS to promote compatibility, and (iii) resistant hosts impose metabolic constraints that starve the fungus of key intermediates. To test these hypotheses, we combined metabolomics, flux analysis, and reverse genetics using two rice cultivars differing in blast resistance.

 Materials and Methods

Fungal strains and culture. *M. oryzae* wild-type strain Guy11 and the field isolate FJ-08 were maintained on complete medium (CM) agar at 25 °C under continuous light. For liquid cultures, conidia were inoculated into minimal medium (MM) containing 1% glucose or 1% olive oil as the sole carbon source.

Plant material and infection assays. *O. sativa* cv. Nipponbare (susceptible) and IR64 (resistant) were grown in a controlled chamber (28/22 °C day/night, 12 h photoperiod). Six-week-old plants were spray-inoculated with conidial suspensions (1 × 10⁵ spores/mL) and sampled at 0, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hpi.

Metabolite extraction and LC-MS/MS. Metabolites were extracted in 80% methanol, and untargeted profiling was performed on a Vanquish UHPLC coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 240 mass spectrometer. Data were processed with Compound Discoverer 3.3 and normalized to internal standards.

Isotope flux analysis. Conidia were incubated with ¹³C-labeled glucose, acetate, or palmitate, and ¹³C enrichment in TCA intermediates was quantified by GC-MS. Flux ratios were calculated using the isotopomer distribution analysis (IDA) approach.

Gene deletion and complementation. *MoTPS1* (MGG_07460) and *MoMTL1* (mannitol dehydrogenase, MGG_04516) were deleted by homologous recombination using a split-marker strategy. Complementation was performed with the native gene under its endogenous promoter.

ROS and turgor measurements. ROS was quantified using 2′,7′-dichlorofluorescein diacetate. Appressorial turgor was estimated by incipient plasmolysis using polyethylene glycol solutions.

Statistical analysis. Data represent means ± SD of three biological replicates. Differences were assessed by ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test (P < 0.05).

 Results

Global metabolic reprogramming during infection. Untargeted metabolomics identified 412 differential metabolites (VIP > 1, FDR < 0.05) across infection stages. At 12 hpi, TCA cycle intermediates (citrate, malate, succinate) increased 2.1–3.4-fold, while free amino acids (glutamate, alanine, aspartate) rose 1.8–2.9-fold. Lipid-derived species, including oleic and linoleic acid, peaked at 24 hpi (4.2-fold). In resistant IR64, 87 metabolites were uniquely enriched, dominated by flavonoids and salicylic acid derivatives.

Carbon flux during appressorium formation. ¹³C tracing revealed that glycogen-derived trehalose contributed 44.6% of acetyl-CoA at 12 hpi, while β-oxidation of lipids supplied an additional 23.8%. Glucose oxidation via glycolysis contributed only 18.2%. Deletion of *MoTPS1* reduced trehalose content by 78.3%, appressorial turgor by 41.2% (from 5.8 MPa to 3.4 MPa), and lesion formation by 73.5% (P < 0.01). Complementation restored wild-type virulence (94.1% of wild-type).

Polyol secretion and ROS suppression. Isolates adapted to Nipponbare secreted mannitol (18.7 μg/mL) and glycerol (12.4 μg/mL) at 24 hpi. In Δ*MoMTL1* mutants, mannitol secretion dropped by 81.5%, and host ROS levels increased 2.3-fold. Fungal biomass in IR64 was significantly lower (0.31 mg/g FW) than in Nipponbare (2.14 mg/g FW), and this difference was amplified in the mutant (0.09 mg/g versus 1.02 mg/g FW).

Host metabolic resistance signatures. IR64 accumulated GABA (6.8-fold), kaempferol-3-O-glucoside (9.2-fold), and salicylic acid (5.4-fold) by 48 hpi. Exogenous GABA application to Nipponbare reduced fungal biomass by 46.7%, suggesting a direct antifungal role. Conversely, susceptible plants showed elevated sucrose and fructose, which correlated with increased fungal growth (r = 0.82, P < 0.01).

 Discussion

Our results define a metabolic model in which *M. oryzae* sequentially exploits trehalose, lipids, and amino acids to fuel appressorial penetration and early biotrophic growth. The dominance of trehalose-derived acetyl-CoA at 12 hpi is consistent with the classical view of glycogen catabolism but reveals a larger-than-expected contribution from β-oxidation (23.8%). This dual-fuel strategy may buffer the fungus against carbon source fluctuations in the phyllosphere.

Mannitol secretion appears central to host adaptation. By scavenging ROS, mannitol suppresses the oxidative burst that otherwise restricts fungal invasion. The increased ROS and reduced biomass in Δ*MoMTL1* mutants confirm that polyol metabolism is not merely a byproduct but a virulence determinant. This aligns with the concept of "metabolic compatibility," wherein the pathogen actively shapes the host redox environment.

The resistant cultivar IR64 imposes a metabolic blockade characterized by GABA, flavonoid, and salicylic acid accumulation. GABA's antifungal activity and its role in priming immunity suggest that it may act as a metabolic checkpoint. The inverse correlation between host sucrose and fungal biomass implies that sugar availability is a key determinant of susceptibility, consistent with the "sugar tug-of-war" hypothesis.

A limitation of this study is that flux analysis was performed in vitro; future work should validate these fluxes in planta using dynamic ¹³C labeling. Additionally, the role of the host microbiome in modulating these metabolic interactions remains unexplored.

 Conclusion

This study establishes a metabolic framework for rice blast pathogenesis, demonstrating that appressorial carbon flux, mannitol-mediated ROS buffering, and host-derived GABA and flavonoid accumulation collectively determine disease outcomes. *MoTPS1* and *MoMTL1* represent promising targets for chemical or genetic intervention. Moreover, the metabolic signatures identified here could inform breeding strategies for blast-resistant rice varieties with enhanced metabolic immunity.

 References (selected)

Dean, R., et al. (2012). The Top 10 fungal pathogens in molecular plant pathology. *Molecular Plant Pathology*, 13(4), 414–430.

Wilson, R. A., & Talbot, N. J. (2009). Under pressure: investigating the biology of plant infection by *Magnaporthe oryzae*. *Nature Reviews Microbiology*, 7(3), 185–195.

Fernandez, J., & Orth, K. (2018). Metabolic reprogramming in plant-pathogen interactions. *Cell Host & Microbe*, 24(2), 185–194.

*Note: All data presented are fabricated for illustrative purposes. This paper is a simulated research article and should not be cited as factual.*

title: Bacterial communities in the rhizosphere, phyllosphere and endosphere of tomato plants
text: Plant-associated microbiomes play essential roles in plant health and productivity. However, the composition and assembly of bacterial communities across different plant compartments remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the bacterial communities inhabiting the rhizosphere, phyllosphere and endosphere of tomato (*Solanum lycopersicum*) plants using high-throughput 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. Distinct bacterial community structures were observed among the three compartments, with the rhizosphere harboring the highest bacterial diversity and the endosphere the lowest. Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes were the dominant phyla across all compartments, while their relative abundances varied markedly. The rhizosphere was enriched with taxa such as *Acidobacteria* and *Gemmatimonadetes*, whereas the phyllosphere was dominated by *Proteobacteria*, including *Sphingomonas* and *Methylobacterium*. Endophytic communities were characterized by reduced diversity and selective enrichment of specific taxa, such as *Pseudomonas* and *Bacillus*. Principal coordinate analysis revealed that compartment type was the primary driver of community variation, explaining a larger proportion of variance than sampling site. Co-occurrence network analysis further indicated compartment-specific interactions among bacterial taxa. These findings provide a comprehensive overview of the spatial distribution of bacterial communities associated with tomato plants and offer a foundation for understanding plant–microbe interactions and for developing microbiome-based strategies to improve crop health and productivity.

title: Toward an adverse outcome pathway for impaired growth: Mitochondrial dysfunction impairs growth in early life stages of the fathead minnow (Pimephales promelas)
text:
Toward an adverse outcome pathway for impaired growth: Mitochondrial dysfunction impairs growth in early life stages of the fathead minnow (*Pimephales promelas*)

Abstract

Growth impairment in early life stages of fish is a sensitive endpoint for ecological risk assessment, yet the mechanistic linkages between subcellular perturbations and organism-level growth deficits remain poorly defined. Here, we propose and test a putative adverse outcome pathway (AOP) linking mitochondrial dysfunction to reduced growth in larval fathead minnow (*Pimephales promelas*). Larvae were exposed to a sublethal concentration of the mitochondrial complex I inhibitor rotenone (2 µg/L) from 1 to 14 days post-hatch (dph). We measured key events across three levels of biological organization: (i) mitochondrial function (ATP production, mitochondrial membrane potential, reactive oxygen species), (ii) cellular and physiological responses (citrate synthase activity, lipid peroxidation, routine oxygen consumption), and (iii) organismal growth (dry mass, standard length, and specific growth rate). Rotenone exposure significantly reduced mitochondrial ATP synthesis (48% of controls) and membrane potential (62% of controls) at 7 dph, with a concurrent 2.3-fold increase in ROS. These mitochondrial key events preceded significant reductions in organismal growth: at 14 dph, larval dry mass and standard length were 31% and 18% lower than controls, respectively. Routine oxygen consumption was reduced by 27% at 10 dph, and citrate synthase activity was elevated by 35%, suggesting compensatory mitochondrial biogenesis. Path analysis supported a causal chain in which mitochondrial dysfunction directly and indirectly (via reduced metabolic capacity) impairs growth. Our results provide empirical support for an AOP describing how mitochondrial dysfunction leads to impaired growth in early life stages of fish, with potential utility for regulatory decision-making.

Keywords: adverse outcome pathway; mitochondrial dysfunction; growth impairment; fathead minnow; rotenone; early life stages; bioenergetics

1. Introduction

Adverse outcome pathways (AOPs) are conceptual frameworks that describe the sequential chain of causally linked events spanning from a molecular initiating event (MIE) to an adverse outcome (AO) relevant to risk assessment (Ankley et al., 2010). For fish early life stages, growth impairment is a widely used apical endpoint in ecological risk assessment because it integrates multiple physiological processes and is strongly linked to survival and recruitment (Mebane et al., 2022). However, the mechanistic basis of chemically induced growth inhibition is often inferred rather than empirically demonstrated, limiting the predictive power of AOPs for regulatory applications.

Mitochondria are central to energy homeostasis, converting nutrients into ATP through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Mitochondrial dysfunction—whether caused by direct inhibition of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes, uncoupling, or oxidative damage—can reduce ATP availability and increase reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Murphy, 2009). In fish, ATP demand is particularly high during early life stages due to rapid cell proliferation, differentiation, and organogenesis (Finn and Kapoor, 2008). Consequently, mitochondrial perturbations are plausible drivers of impaired growth. Nevertheless, few studies have explicitly tested the causal sequence from mitochondrial dysfunction to reduced growth in fish, and most existing AOPs for growth impairment focus on endocrine or nutritional pathways rather than bioenergetics (Knapen et al., 2018).

Rotenone, a natural plant-derived compound, is a well-characterized inhibitor of mitochondrial complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase). It blocks electron transfer from iron-sulfur clusters to ubiquinone, reducing proton pumping and ATP synthesis, and promotes ROS generation at the flavin site (Li et al., 2003). Rotenone has been used as a reference chemical for mitochondrial dysfunction in mammalian and fish models, but its effects on fish early life stage growth and the associated AOP remain incompletely described.

The fathead minnow (*Pimephales promelas*) is a model species in aquatic toxicology, with well-documented early life stage development, genomic resources, and standardized test guidelines (OECD 210). Here, we hypothesized that sublethal exposure to rotenone would initiate a sequence of key events: (1) inhibition of mitochondrial complex I, (2) reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP synthesis, (3) increased ROS and oxidative stress, (4) reduced aerobic metabolic capacity, and ultimately (5) impaired growth (dry mass and length). We tested this putative AOP by measuring endpoints across molecular, cellular, physiological, and organismal levels in larval fathead minnows exposed from 1 to 14 days post-hatch (dph). Our specific objectives were to (i) quantify the temporal sequence of mitochondrial and growth responses, (ii) assess the magnitude and consistency of effects, and (iii) evaluate the plausibility of the proposed AOP using path analysis.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Fish culture and exposure

Fathead minnow embryos were obtained from an in-house culture at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee (approval no. IACUC 22-045). Embryos were incubated in reconstituted moderately hard water (MHW; 80–100 mg/L as CaCO₃, pH 7.8–8.2, 25 ± 1 °C) under a 16:8 h light:dark cycle. At 1 dph, larvae were randomly distributed into 2-L glass beakers (density: 50 larvae/L) and exposed to either MHW (control) or rotenone (2 µg/L; ≥98% purity, Sigma-Aldrich) dissolved in 0.01% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). The DMSO concentration was identical in all treatments, including controls. Exposure was static-renewal (80% volume exchange every 24 h) for 14 days. Water quality (dissolved oxygen, pH, temperature, ammonia) was monitored daily. Rotenone concentrations were verified by HPLC-MS at 0, 7, and 14 dph; measured values were 1.9 ± 0.2 µg/L (mean ± SD), with no detectable degradation products.

2.2. Sampling and endpoints

Larvae were sampled at 1, 3, 7, 10, and 14 dph. At each time point, 10 larvae per replicate (n = 4 replicates per treatment) were euthanized with tricaine methanesulfonate (300 mg/L, buffered), rinsed, and either processed immediately for mitochondrial assays or frozen in liquid nitrogen for biochemical analyses. Growth endpoints (dry mass, standard length) were measured on separate groups of 15 larvae per replicate at 1, 7, and 14 dph. Dry mass was determined after drying at 60 °C for 24 h to constant weight (µg per larva). Standard length was measured from digital images using ImageJ.

2.3. Mitochondrial function assays

Mitochondria were isolated from pooled larvae (n = 30 per replicate) by differential centrifugation as described by Ragan and Darley-Usmar (1987), with modifications. Briefly, larvae were homogenized in ice-cold isolation buffer (250 mM sucrose, 10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 7.4) and centrifuged at 600 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 15 min, and the pellet was resuspended in isolation buffer. Protein concentration was determined by Bradford assay.

ATP synthesis was measured using a luciferin-luciferase bioluminescence assay (ATP Determination Kit, Invitrogen) after incubating isolated mitochondria (50 µg protein) with 5 mM pyruvate/malate and 1 mM ADP for 10 min at 25 °C. Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) was assessed using the fluorescent dye JC-1 (5 µM) and quantified as the ratio of red (590 nm) to green (530 nm) fluorescence using a microplate reader. ROS production was measured using the fluorescent probe 2',7'-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (H₂DCFDA, 10 µM) after 30 min incubation, with fluorescence normalized to protein content.

2.4. Biochemical and physiological endpoints

Citrate synthase (CS) activity was measured spectrophotometrically at 412 nm using 5,5'-dithiobis-(2-nitrobenzoic acid) (DTNB) as described by Srere (1969). Lipid peroxidation was quantified as thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) using malondialdehyde (MDA) standards. Routine oxygen consumption (MO₂) was measured at 10 dph using closed respirometry chambers (1.5 mL) with fiber-optic oxygen sensors (PreSens) at 25 °C. Larvae were acclimated for 30 min, and MO₂ was calculated as µmol O₂ g⁻¹ h⁻¹ dry mass.

2.5. Statistical analysis

Data were checked for normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homogeneity of variance (Levene). Two-way ANOVA (treatment × time) followed by Tukey's HSD was used for multiple comparisons. When assumptions were violated, log or arcsine transformations were applied. Path analysis was conducted using structural equation modeling (SEM) in R (lavaan package) to test the hypothesized causal chain: rotenone → complex I inhibition (assumed) → ΔΨm reduction → ATP decline → ROS increase → reduced MO₂ → reduced growth. Model fit was assessed using χ², CFI (>0.95), and RMSEA (<0.08). Significance was set at α = 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1. Mitochondrial function

Exposure to 2 µg/L rotenone significantly inhibited mitochondrial function in larval fathead minnows. At 3 dph, ATP synthesis rates in rotenone-treated larvae were 72% of control values (p < 0.05), declining to 48% at 7 dph and 41% at 14 dph (p < 0.001; Fig. 1A). Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) followed a similar temporal pattern: no significant difference at 1 dph, but a 38% reduction at 7 dph and a 44% reduction at 14 dph relative to controls (p < 0.01; Fig. 1B). ROS production, measured as DCF fluorescence, increased significantly at 3 dph (1.8-fold), peaked at 7 dph (2.3-fold), and remained elevated at 14 dph (2.0-fold) (p < 0.001; Fig. 1C). These results indicate that rotenone-induced complex I inhibition led to progressive mitochondrial depolarization, ATP depletion, and oxidative stress.

3.2. Cellular and physiological responses

Citrate synthase (CS) activity, a marker of mitochondrial content, was significantly elevated in rotenone-treated larvae at 7 and 10 dph (35% and 42% above controls, respectively; p < 0.01; Fig. 2A), suggesting a compensatory increase in mitochondrial biogenesis. However, this response was insufficient to restore ATP levels. Lipid peroxidation (TBARS) was significantly higher in rotenone-treated larvae at 7 dph (2.1-fold) and 14 dph (1.9-fold) compared to controls (p < 0.001; Fig. 2B), consistent with ROS-mediated oxidative damage. Routine oxygen consumption (MO₂) at 10 dph was reduced by 27% in rotenone-treated larvae (p < 0.01; Fig. 2C), indicating a decline in aerobic metabolic capacity.

3.3. Growth impairment

Growth endpoints diverged between treatments after 7 dph. At 7 dph, dry mass and standard length did not differ significantly between treatments (p > 0.05). However, by 14 dph, rotenone-treated larvae exhibited 31% lower dry mass (p < 0.001; Fig. 3A) and 18% lower standard length (p < 0.01; Fig. 3B) compared to controls. Specific growth rate (SGR) calculated from 1 to 14 dph was 0.18 ± 0.02 day⁻¹ in controls versus 0.11 ± 0.02 day⁻¹ in rotenone-treated larvae (p < 0.001). The temporal sequence—mitochondrial dysfunction at 3–7 dph, physiological impairment at 7–10 dph, and growth reduction at 14 dph—supports the proposed AOP.

3.4. Path analysis

Structural equation modeling supported the hypothesized causal chain (χ² = 12.4, df = 8, p = 0.13; CFI = 0.97; RMSEA = 0.06). Rotenone exposure had a significant direct effect on ΔΨm (β = -0.62, p < 0.001) and ATP synthesis (β = -0.58, p < 0.001). ATP synthesis was positively associated with MO₂ (β = 0.54, p < 0.01), and MO₂ was positively associated with dry mass (β = 0.61, p < 0.001). ROS had a significant negative direct effect on growth (β = -0.34, p < 0.05), independent of ATP. The model explained 68% of the variance in dry mass. These results indicate that mitochondrial dysfunction impairs growth both directly (via oxidative stress) and indirectly (via reduced ATP and metabolic capacity).

4. Discussion

Our study provides empirical support for an AOP linking mitochondrial dysfunction to impaired growth in early life stages of fathead minnow. The proposed pathway begins with complex I inhibition by rotenone, leading to reduced ΔΨm and ATP synthesis, increased ROS production, oxidative damage, reduced aerobic metabolism, and ultimately diminished growth. The temporal sequence of key events—mitochondrial dysfunction preceding physiological impairment, which in turn preceded growth reduction—is consistent with the causal criteria for AOPs (Becker et al., 2015).

The observed 48–59% reduction in ATP synthesis is consistent with rotenone's known mechanism of action as a complex I inhibitor (Li et al., 2003). The concurrent increase in ROS (2.3-fold) likely reflects enhanced electron leakage at complex I due to impaired electron transfer. Mitochondrial depolarization (38–44% reduction in ΔΨm) further compromises ATP synthesis, as the proton motive force is essential for OXPHOS. These mitochondrial key events occurred as early as 3 dph, well before detectable growth effects at 14 dph, supporting their role as initiating events.

The elevation of citrate synthase activity (35–42%) suggests a compensatory increase in mitochondrial biogenesis, possibly mediated by PGC-1α signaling in response to energy deficit (LeMoine et al., 2010). However, this compensatory response was insufficient to maintain ATP levels or oxygen consumption, indicating that mitochondrial dysfunction overwhelmed adaptive capacity. Similar compensatory responses have been observed in fish exposed to other mitochondrial toxicants (e.g., 2,4-dinitrophenol; Best et al., 2018).

The reduction in routine oxygen consumption (27%) at 10 dph likely reflects both reduced mitochondrial ATP demand and impaired electron transport. Because aerobic metabolism provides the majority of ATP for growth processes (e.g., protein synthesis, cell division), a decline in MO₂ would directly constrain growth. Indeed, our path analysis showed that MO₂ was a strong predictor of dry mass (β = 0.61). The additional direct negative effect of ROS on growth (β = -0.34) suggests that oxidative damage to macromolecules (e.g., proteins, lipids) may further impair growth independently of ATP.

The growth impairment observed at 14 dph (31% reduction in dry mass, 18% reduction in length) is ecologically relevant. In natural populations, reduced larval growth can lead to increased predation risk, delayed metamorphosis, and reduced overwinter survival (Mebane et al., 2022). The AOP proposed here is potentially applicable to other mitochondrial toxicants (e.g., uncouplers, complex III inhibitors) and other fish species, though species-specific differences in mitochondrial sensitivity and compensatory capacity should be considered.

Several limitations of this study warrant mention. First, we did not directly measure complex I activity,

title: Exploring the Promiscuity of Phenol Hydroxylase from Pseudomonas stutzeri OX1 for the Biosynthesis of Phenolic Compounds
text: Phenol hydroxylase from *Pseudomonas stutzeri* OX1 (PHₒₓ₁) is a member of the diiron monooxygenase family and has attracted considerable attention for its ability to catalyze the hydroxylation of phenol and various substituted phenols. Unlike many related enzymes with narrow substrate ranges, PHₒₓ₁ exhibits remarkable substrate promiscuity, accepting a broad spectrum of phenolic compounds and even non-phenolic aromatics. This relaxed specificity makes it an attractive biocatalyst for the biosynthesis of valuable phenolic compounds, which are widely used as pharmaceuticals, antioxidants, and fine chemicals. However, the structural and mechanistic basis of this promiscuity remains incompletely understood, and its synthetic potential has not been systematically explored. In this study, we investigated the substrate scope of PHₒₓ₁ toward a diverse panel of phenolic substrates and evaluated its capacity for regioselective hydroxylation. Our results reveal that PHₒₓ₁ efficiently converts various mono- and di-substituted phenols into catechol derivatives with high conversion rates. These findings highlight PHₒₓ₁ as a versatile biocatalytic tool for phenolic compound synthesis and provide a foundation for future protein engineering efforts aimed at tailoring its activity.

title: The Association Between Traditional Chinese Medicine Body Constitution Deviation and Essential Hypertension: A Case-Control Study
text:
Results and Discussion
