Participants. We analyzed data from 412 healthy adults (mean age = 22.6 ± 3.4 years; 231 female) recruited across three sites as part of an ongoing imaging-genetics consortium. Exclusion criteria included psychiatric or neurological disorders, psychoactive medication use, and MRI contraindications. All participants provided written informed consent, and the protocol was approved by the institutional review boards of the participating sites.

Behavioral measure. Loneliness was assessed with the UCLA Loneliness Scale (Version 3), a 20-item self-report instrument (range 20–80). Mean score was 39.8 ± 9.6 (range 21–68), consistent with normative young-adult samples. Internal consistency was high (Cronbach's α = 0.92).

Image acquisition and preprocessing. Resting-state fMRI data were acquired on 3T scanners (TR = 2,000 ms, TE = 30 ms, 3 mm isotropic voxels, 240 volumes). Preprocessing followed a standard pipeline: slice-timing correction, motion realignment, normalization to MNI space, spatial smoothing (6 mm FWHM), band-pass filtering (0.01–0.1 Hz), and nuisance regression (24 motion parameters, white matter, CSF, and global signal). Participants with mean framewise displacement > 0.25 mm or > 20% volumes exceeding 0.5 mm were excluded.

Connectivity matrices. We parcellated the brain into 268 nodes (Shen atlas) and computed Pearson correlations between node time series, yielding 35,778 unique edges per participant. Correlations were Fisher z-transformed.

Connectome-based predictive modeling. We implemented CPM with 10-fold cross-validation. In each training fold, edges were correlated with loneliness scores; edges exceeding p < 0.01 (positive network) or p < 0.01 (negative network) were retained. Summary scores were computed as the mean edge strength within each network, and a linear model predicted loneliness from these scores. Predictions were generated for held-out participants. Model performance was indexed by Pearson correlation between predicted and observed scores and assessed with 5,000 permutations of the behavioral labels.

Control analyses. We tested robustness by (1) repeating CPM within each site, (2) regressing out age, sex, and mean framewise displacement from behavioral scores before modeling, and (3) using a stricter edge threshold (p < 0.005). Network contributions were quantified by assigning predictive edges to seven canonical networks.

 Results

Loneliness is predictable from functional connectivity. The positive-network model significantly predicted loneliness in held-out participants (r = 0.41, p < 0.001; permutation p = 0.002; Fig. 1A). The negative-network model was weaker and not significant (r = 0.14, p = 0.11). Combining networks did not improve performance (r = 0.38). Predicted scores explained approximately 17% of variance in observed loneliness.

Network contributions. Predictive edges were widely distributed but concentrated in specific systems. The largest proportion involved DMN–DMN connections (23.4%), followed by DMN–frontoparietal (16.1%), salience–salience (12.7%), and salience–frontoparietal (10.9%) connections. Hub regions included ventromedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, temporoparietal junction, and anterior insula. Higher loneliness was associated with stronger connectivity between DMN and salience nodes but weaker connectivity within frontoparietal control regions.

Robustness. Site-wise models yielded comparable predictions (Site A: r = 0.39; Site B: r = 0.36; Site C: r = 0.44). After regressing out age, sex, and motion, prediction remained significant (r = 0.37, p < 0.001). The stricter threshold produced similar performance (r = 0.35, p < 0.001), and results were stable across 100 random fold assignments (mean r = 0.40, SD = 0.03).

 Discussion

This study demonstrates that loneliness can be predicted from an individual's intrinsic functional connectome. The moderate but reliable effect size (r = 0.41) is comparable to CPM predictions of other complex phenotypes and supports the view that loneliness is a brain-encoded disposition rather than merely a situational response.

Predictive edges converged on DMN, salience, and frontoparietal systems. The DMN supports self-referential and social-cognitive processes, including mentalizing about others' evaluations—processes heightened in lonely individuals. Stronger DMN–salience coupling may reflect amplified vigilance to social threat, consistent with evolutionary models of loneliness as a signal prompting social reconnection. Weaker frontoparietal connectivity, in turn, may index reduced regulatory control over negative social expectations.

Our findings extend prior group-level work by showing that connectivity patterns carry individualized information. Clinically, connectome-based markers could complement self-report, which is susceptible to bias, and could identify individuals at risk before loneliness becomes chronic. Longitudinal designs are needed to determine whether connectivity predicts changes in loneliness or reflects its consequences.

Limitations. The sample comprised young, healthy adults, limiting generalization to older or clinical populations. Resting-state connectivity is sensitive to physiological noise, though control analyses mitigated this concern. Finally, prediction is correlational; causal manipulation of social experience is required to establish directionality.

 Conclusion

Loneliness is encoded in distributed patterns of intrinsic functional connectivity, particularly involving default mode, salience, and frontoparietal networks. Connectome-based modeling enables reliable individualized prediction, offering a neurobiological window onto a pressing public-health problem and a foundation for future predictive and interventional work.

title: Effect of exogenous ammonium gluconate on growth, ion flux and antioxidant enzymes of maize (Zea Mays L.) seedlings under NaCl stress
text: Abstract: Soil salinization severely limits crop productivity worldwide, and developing effective strategies to mitigate salt stress is of great agronomic importance. This study investigated the effects of exogenous ammonium gluconate (AG) on the growth, ion flux, and antioxidant enzyme activities of maize (*Zea mays* L.) seedlings under NaCl stress. Maize seedlings were subjected to 150 mM NaCl with or without the application of 0.5 mM AG. Salt stress markedly inhibited seedling growth, as evidenced by reduced shoot and root biomass, plant height, and leaf relative water content. NaCl stress also induced a significant influx of Na⁺ and efflux of K⁺ in root cells, leading to a drastic increase in the Na⁺/K⁺ ratio, along with overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and elevated membrane lipid peroxidation. Exogenous application of AG alleviated salt-induced growth inhibition and significantly improved biomass accumulation and water status. AG treatment reduced Na⁺ influx and promoted K⁺ retention in roots, thereby maintaining a lower Na⁺/K⁺ ratio. Furthermore, AG supplementation markedly enhanced the activities of antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxidase (POD), catalase (CAT), and ascorbate peroxidase (APX), which coincided with decreased malondialdehyde (MDA) content and ROS accumulation. These results indicate that exogenous AG mitigates NaCl-induced oxidative damage and ion imbalance by regulating ion homeostasis and strengthening the antioxidant defense system, thereby promoting maize seedling growth under saline conditions. This study provides a promising and eco-friendly approach for improving salt tolerance in maize and offers a theoretical basis for its application in saline agriculture.

title: How do farmland rental markets affect farmers' income? Evidence from a matched renting-in and renting-out household survey in Northeast China
text:
How do farmland rental markets affect farmers' income? Evidence from a matched renting-in and renting-out household survey in Northeast China

Abstract

Farmland rental markets are widely promoted as a mechanism to improve agricultural efficiency and rural livelihoods. However, whether participation in these markets—either by renting in or renting out land—translates into higher household income remains contested, particularly in China’s major grain-producing regions. Using a matched sample of 612 renting-in and renting-out farm households collected in Heilongjiang, Jilin, and Liaoning provinces in 2023, this study employs an endogenous switching regression (ESR) model to address selection bias and estimate the income effects of farmland rental market participation. Results show that renting-in households obtain significantly higher per capita net income than renting-out households, with an average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) of 4,217 RMB (14.6%). Renting-out households, by contrast, experience modest income gains only when non-farm employment opportunities are accessible; without such opportunities, rental income alone does not compensate for forgone agricultural earnings. Farmland rental intensity, contract duration, and access to agricultural credit significantly moderate the income effects. These findings suggest that farmland rental markets can raise rural incomes, but their distributional benefits depend critically on complementary non-farm labor markets and institutional safeguards.

Keywords: farmland rental market; farmer income; endogenous switching regression; Northeast China; land transfer; rural livelihoods

1. Introduction

Farmland rental markets have expanded rapidly in China since the 2000s, driven by rural labor migration, agricultural mechanization, and policy reforms that formalized land contracting rights. By 2023, approximately 36% of China’s cultivated land was transferred through rental arrangements, with the highest participation rates observed in the northeastern grain belt. The theoretical case for rental markets is straightforward: transferring land from less productive to more productive operators can improve allocative efficiency, facilitate scale economies, and allow renting-out households to reallocate labor to higher-return non-farm activities. Yet empirical evidence on whether these efficiency gains translate into higher household income—and for whom—remains mixed.

Three gaps motivate this study. First, most existing studies examine either renting-in or renting-out households in isolation, making it difficult to compare income outcomes across participation modes. Second, selection bias is pervasive: households that choose to rent in or rent out differ systematically in observable and unobservable characteristics, so naive comparisons of income are misleading. Third, the northeastern region, characterized by large farm sizes, high mechanization, and distinct land endowments, has received less attention than central or eastern China, despite its strategic importance for national food security.

This paper addresses these gaps by using a matched survey of renting-in and renting-out households in Northeast China and applying an endogenous switching regression model to estimate counterfactual income outcomes. We ask: (1) How do farmland rental markets affect household income for renting-in and renting-out participants? (2) What factors moderate these effects? (3) What are the policy implications for inclusive rural development?

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study area and data

The data were collected through a stratified random survey conducted between June and September 2023 in six counties across Heilongjiang, Jilin, and Liaoning provinces. These counties represent typical grain-producing landscapes dominated by maize, rice, and soybean. A two-stage sampling procedure was used: first, townships were randomly selected within each county; second, households were randomly sampled from village registration lists. A screening question identified whether the household had rented in or rented out farmland in the past two years. The final matched sample consists of 612 households: 318 renting-in households and 294 renting-out households. After data cleaning, 587 observations were retained for analysis.

2.2 Variables

The dependent variable is household per capita net income (RMB/year), calculated as total household income minus agricultural and non-farm production costs, divided by household size. Key explanatory variables include rental market participation mode (renting-in = 1, renting-out = 0), rented land area (mu), rental contract duration (years), and whether the household has access to formal agricultural credit. Control variables include household head age, education, off-farm employment ratio, household size, farm machinery value, land endowment, and county fixed effects.

2.3 Empirical strategy

Households self-select into renting-in or renting-out status, so ordinary least squares estimates may be biased by unobserved heterogeneity. We therefore employ an endogenous switching regression (ESR) model. The ESR model first estimates a probit selection equation for participation mode, then estimates separate income equations for renting-in and renting-out households, and finally computes counterfactual outcomes to derive average treatment effects. Identification requires at least one exclusion restriction; we use village-level rental market maturity (proportion of households participating in rental transactions) as an instrument, which affects participation but not household income directly.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Descriptive statistics

Renting-in households operate significantly larger farms (mean = 86.4 mu) than renting-out households (mean = 18.7 mu). Renting-in households also report higher per capita net income (mean = 32,480 RMB) compared with renting-out households (mean = 24,190 RMB). However, renting-out households have a higher off-farm employment ratio (0.61 vs. 0.34), suggesting that their income strategies rely more on wage employment. Rental income accounts for 18.3% of total income for renting-out households but only 2.1% for renting-in households, reflecting the latter’s greater reliance on agricultural production.

3.2 Determinants of participation

Probit estimates show that household head education, farm machinery value, and village rental market maturity significantly increase the probability of renting in. Conversely, off-farm employment ratio and proximity to urban centers increase the probability of renting out. These patterns confirm that participation is not random and justify the use of the ESR model.

3.3 Income effects of rental market participation

The ESR results reveal substantial heterogeneity. For renting-in households, the ATT is 4,217 RMB (14.6% of counterfactual income), significant at the 1% level. This gain is driven primarily by scale economies: larger operated area reduces per-unit machinery and labor costs. For renting-out households, the ATT is 1,346 RMB (5.8%), significant at the 5% level, but this effect is entirely concentrated among households with at least one member engaged in off-farm employment. For renting-out households without off-farm income, the ATT is statistically insignificant (−412 RMB, p = 0.31), implying that rental income alone does not offset reduced agricultural earnings.

3.4 Moderating factors

Interaction terms show that contract duration positively moderates income for renting-in households: each additional year of contract increases per capita income by 312 RMB. Access to formal credit raises the income effect by 1,840 RMB for renting-in households, consistent with the need for working capital to finance inputs and machinery. For renting-out households, the income effect is stronger where local non-farm job density is high, confirming the complementary role of labor markets.

4. Discussion

Our findings contribute to the debate on whether farmland rental markets are inclusive. On one hand, renting-in households clearly benefit through scale expansion and efficiency gains, supporting the productivity-enhancing narrative. On the other hand, renting-out households only benefit when non-farm employment is available. This challenges the assumption that rental income alone can serve as a poverty-reduction tool. In the absence of vibrant non-farm economies, renting out land may simply transfer agricultural income to others without compensating the transferring household.

These results align with studies in central China but differ in magnitude. The larger ATT for renting-in households in Northeast China likely reflects the region’s flatter topography, larger field sizes, and higher mechanization potential. The modest ATT for renting-out households is consistent with evidence that land rental income constitutes a small share of total income in most Chinese villages.

Policy implications are threefold. First, strengthening non-farm employment opportunities in rural areas is essential for renting-out households to realize income gains. Second, formalizing and extending rental contracts can enhance investment incentives and income stability for renting-in households. Third, expanding rural credit access can alleviate capital constraints that prevent productive renting-in households from fully realizing scale economies.

Several limitations should be noted. The cross-sectional design cannot fully capture dynamic income trajectories. The instrument, while statistically valid, may not be perfectly exogenous. Future research should employ panel data and experimental designs to identify causal mechanisms more convincingly.

5. Conclusion

This study uses a matched survey of renting-in and renting-out households in Northeast China and an endogenous switching regression model to estimate the income effects of farmland rental market participation. We find that renting-in households gain significantly—about 14.6% higher per capita income—through scale economies and mechanization. Renting-out households gain only modestly, and only when non-farm employment is accessible. Contract duration, credit access, and local labor market conditions are important moderators. These findings suggest that farmland rental markets are not a panacea for rural income growth. Their effectiveness depends on complementary policies that expand non-farm employment, strengthen contractual security, and improve rural financial services. Policymakers should therefore treat land rental reform as one component of a broader rural development strategy rather than a standalone income-boosting instrument.

title: Antibiotics and Food Safety in Aquaculture
text: The rapid expansion of aquaculture has made it the fastest-growing food-producing sector worldwide, supplying nearly half of the fish consumed by humans. However, intensification of production has been accompanied by the extensive use of antibiotics for disease prevention and growth promotion, raising serious concerns about food safety and public health. Residues of these compounds in aquaculture products can reach consumers through the food chain, potentially causing allergic reactions, disrupting gut microbiota, and promoting antimicrobial resistance. Moreover, the transfer of antibiotic resistance genes from aquatic environments to human pathogens represents a global health threat. Regulatory frameworks vary considerably across countries, and weak surveillance in some regions exacerbates the problem. This review examines the main antibiotics used in aquaculture, their residue dynamics in edible tissues, associated food safety risks, and current regulatory and monitoring strategies. It also highlights the need for integrated approaches, including alternative disease control measures and international harmonization of standards, to ensure the safety of aquaculture products.

title: Triacylglycerol biosynthesis in shaded seeds of tung tree (Vernicia fordii) is regulated in part by Homeodomain Leucine Zipper 21
text:
Results and Discussion

Shading significantly altered lipid accumulation in developing tung seeds. Seeds from 70% shade-treated trees accumulated 38.2 ± 2.1% total lipids (dry weight basis) compared to 52.6 ± 1.8% in full-light controls, a 27.4% reduction (P < 0.01). Triacylglycerol (TAG) content followed a similar trend, declining from 44.9 ± 2.3 mg g⁻¹ to 29.7 ± 1.9 mg g⁻¹ fresh weight, while free fatty acid levels increased 1.8-fold, suggesting impaired acyl flux into storage lipids. Notably, the proportion of α-eleostearic acid (18:3Δ9cis,11trans,13trans), the predominant tung oil fatty acid, decreased from 71.3% to 62.5% of total fatty acids under shade.

Transcriptomic profiling of seeds collected 25 days after pollination revealed 1,247 differentially expressed genes, including 14 transcription factors. Among these, *VfHDZ21*, encoding a Homeodomain Leucine Zipper (HD-Zip) class I protein, was downregulated 4.6-fold under shade (log₂FC = −2.2, FDR < 0.001) and positively correlated with TAG content across developmental stages (r = 0.87, P < 0.001). Subcellular localization confirmed VfHDZ21-GFP fusion in the nucleus, consistent with its predicted role as a transcriptional regulator.

Yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase assays demonstrated that VfHDZ21 binds the promoter of *VfDGAT2* (diacylglycerol acyltransferase 2), a rate-limiting enzyme in TAG assembly, and activates its expression 3.4-fold. Transient overexpression of *VfHDZ21* in tung cotyledons increased *VfDGAT2* transcript levels 2.9-fold and TAG content by 21.6%, whereas RNAi-mediated silencing reduced TAG by 18.3%. These findings indicate that shade suppresses TAG biosynthesis in tung seeds partly through downregulation of *VfHDZ21*, which in turn diminishes *VfDGAT2*-mediated flux into storage lipids.

title: Next-Gen Approaches to Flavor-Related Metabolism
text:
Next-Gen Approaches to Flavor-Related Metabolism

Abstract
Flavor formation in fermented and plant-based foods is governed by complex metabolic networks that remain difficult to engineer with traditional breeding or single-strain fermentation. This study integrates genome-scale metabolic modeling, transient CRISPR interference (CRISPRi), and untargeted volatile metabolomics to dissect and redirect flavor-related metabolism in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* and *Lactiplantibacillus plantarum*. A constraint-based model (iFLV2024) was reconstructed, encompassing 2,847 reactions and 1,936 metabolites, with 214 reactions annotated as flavor-associated. Model-guided CRISPRi targeting of *BAT1*, *ARO10*, and *PDC5* produced predictable shifts in higher alcohols and esters, with a mean absolute prediction error of 11.4% for ester titers. Parallel adaptive laboratory evolution under valine supplementation yielded a *L. plantarum* variant with a 2.3-fold increase in 3-methylbutanal and a 1.8-fold increase in diacetyl, accompanied by a 34% reduction in acetate. Co-culture experiments revealed that lactate cross-feeding between the two organisms increased total ester production by 41% relative to monocultures. These findings demonstrate that next-generation metabolic approaches can deliver rational, multi-target flavor engineering and provide a scalable framework for precision fermentation.

Keywords: flavor metabolism; genome-scale metabolic model; CRISPRi; volatile organic compounds; adaptive laboratory evolution; co-culture; precision fermentation

1. Introduction
Flavor is a primary determinant of consumer acceptance in fermented foods, yet its molecular basis remains only partially understood. Flavor-related metabolism comprises pathways for amino acid catabolism (Ehrlich pathway), fatty acid β-oxidation, ester biosynthesis, and terpene modification, all of which intersect central carbon metabolism. Traditional strain improvement relies on random mutagenesis and screening, which is laborious and often pleiotropic. Recent advances in systems biology, genome editing, and machine learning offer an opportunity to move from empirical to predictive flavor engineering.

Three gaps motivate this work. First, most metabolic models treat flavor compounds as secondary outputs rather than explicit objectives. Second, single-target gene edits frequently fail to produce the desired sensory profile because of pathway redundancy and feedback regulation. Third, microbial communities, rather than single strains, dominate real fermentation systems, yet metabolic interactions underlying community-level flavor generation are rarely quantified.

Here we address these gaps by combining (i) a flavor-annotated genome-scale model, (ii) multiplex CRISPRi to test model predictions, (iii) adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) to relieve metabolic constraints, and (iv) a two-species co-culture to examine cross-feeding. We hypothesized that model-guided, multi-target perturbation would improve flavor compound titers more effectively than single-gene approaches, and that cross-species metabolite exchange would further expand the accessible flavor space.

2. Materials and Methods
*2.1 Strains and cultivation.* *S. cerevisiae* CEN.PK113-5D and *L. plantarum* WCFS1 were used. Yeast was cultivated in synthetic defined medium with 20 g/L glucose at 30 °C, 180 rpm. *L. plantarum* was grown in MRS medium at 37 °C under static conditions. For co-culture, yeast was pre-grown to mid-exponential phase, washed, and inoculated into MRS-glucose medium at an initial ratio of 1:10 (yeast:bacteria).

*2.2 Model reconstruction.* The iFLV2024 model was constructed by merging Yeast8 and a manually curated lactic acid bacteria model, followed by gap-filling with flavor compound exchange reactions. Flavor-associated reactions were annotated using KEGG, MetaCyc, and a curated volatile database. Flux balance analysis (FBA) and minimization of metabolic adjustment (MOMA) were performed in Python 3.11 using COBRApy 0.29.

*2.3 CRISPRi design.* Single-guide RNAs targeting *BAT1*, *ARO10*, *PDC5*, *ATF1*, and *EHT1* were cloned into a dCas9-Mxi1 vector. Multiplex constructs were assembled by Golden Gate. Knockdown efficiency was assessed by RT-qPCR, and off-target effects were checked by whole-genome sequencing.

*2.4 Adaptive laboratory evolution.* *L. plantarum* was serially passaged for 60 days in MRS containing 10 g/L valine with increasing valine concentrations (up to 30 g/L). Evolved clones were isolated and whole-genome sequenced.

*2.5 Metabolomics.* Volatile organic compounds were quantified by headspace solid-phase microextraction coupled to gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (HS-SPME-GC-MS). Organic acids and sugars were measured by HPLC. All measurements were performed in biological triplicate.

*2.6 Statistical analysis.* Data were analyzed by ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test. Model predictions were evaluated by mean absolute percentage error (MAPE).

3. Results and Analysis
*3.1 Model structure and flavor annotation.* iFLV2024 contained 2,847 reactions, 1,936 metabolites, and 214 flavor-associated reactions, including 38 esterases, 27 alcohol dehydrogenases, and 19 amino acid transaminases. Flux variability analysis identified 46 reactions with high flexibility, suggesting potential targets for redirection.

*3.2 CRISPRi validation.* Single knockdowns of *BAT1* and *ARO10* reduced isoamyl alcohol and 2-phenylethanol by 28% and 41%, respectively. Multiplex knockdown of *BAT1*, *ARO10*, and *PDC5* increased ethyl acetate by 1.9-fold and isoamyl acetate by 2.4-fold. Model predictions correlated well with measured ester titers (R² = 0.87; MAPE = 11.4%). Unexpectedly, *EHT1* knockdown increased ethyl hexanoate by 22%, likely due to reduced competitive inhibition.

*3.3 Adaptive evolution.* After 60 days, evolved *L. plantarum* showed a 2.3-fold increase in 3-methylbutanal and a 1.8-fold increase in diacetyl. Acetate decreased by 34%, and lactate production increased by 19%. Genome sequencing revealed mutations in *alsS*, *aldC*, and a putative *ldh* promoter region.

*3.4 Co-culture.* In co-culture, yeast consumed glucose and produced ethanol and higher alcohols, while *L. plantarum* utilized residual sugars and lactate. Total ester production increased by 41% compared with monocultures. Lactate cross-feeding was confirmed by ¹³C-labeling, with 18% of yeast-derived carbon incorporated into bacterial biomass.

4. Discussion
The results support the hypothesis that model-guided multi-target engineering outperforms single-gene edits. The iFLV2024 model successfully predicted ester shifts, although discrepancies for *EHT1* indicate gaps in our understanding of esterase competition. The ALE experiment demonstrated that relieving valine catabolism constraints can substantially increase aldehyde precursors, but the acetate reduction suggests a trade-off with central carbon flux.

Co-culture emerged as a powerful strategy for expanding flavor complexity. The 41% increase in esters likely arises from complementary precursor supply: yeast provides alcohols, while *L. plantarum* provides acetyl-CoA and lactate-derived pyruvate. This mutualistic interaction mirrors natural fermentation consortia and offers a route to engineer community-level flavor.

Several limitations remain. First, the model lacks dynamic regulation and enzyme kinetics. Second, flavor perception is not equivalent to volatile concentration; sensory validation is needed. Third, long-term stability of co-culture and evolved strains under industrial conditions requires further testing. Future work should integrate machine learning for retrosynthetic flavor design and microfluidic screening for high-throughput selection.

5. Conclusion
This study presents an integrated next-generation framework for flavor-related metabolism, combining genome-scale modeling, CRISPRi, adaptive evolution, and co-culture. The approach enabled predictable increases in esters and aldehydes and revealed cross-feeding as a key driver of flavor diversity. These findings provide a rational foundation for precision fermentation and suggest that future flavor engineering should target not only single pathways but also microbial interactions and metabolic trade-offs. The iFLV2024 model and associated datasets are available for community use.

title: Driver's mental workload prediction model based on physiological indices
text:
Driver's Mental Workload Prediction Model Based on Physiological Indices

 Abstract

Driver mental workload is a critical determinant of traffic safety, as both underload and overload can impair driving performance. This study aimed to develop and validate a predictive model of driver mental workload based on physiological indices. Thirty-six licensed drivers (22 males, 14 females; mean age = 34.2 ± 8.7 years) completed a simulated driving task under three workload conditions: low (highway driving), medium (urban driving), and high (urban driving with a secondary cognitive task). Physiological signals—heart rate variability (HRV), skin conductance level (SCL), pupil diameter, and electroencephalographic (EEG) theta-to-alpha ratio—were continuously recorded. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX, and performance was measured via lane-keeping error and reaction time. A random forest regression model was trained to predict NASA-TLX scores from physiological features. Results showed that all physiological indices differed significantly across workload conditions (p < .001), with EEG theta/alpha ratio and pupil diameter exhibiting the strongest correlations with subjective workload (r = 0.71 and r = 0.66, respectively). The prediction model achieved a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.83 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 5.42 NASA-TLX points in cross-validation. These findings suggest that multimodal physiological monitoring can reliably estimate driver mental workload in real time, with potential applications in adaptive vehicle safety systems.

Keywords: mental workload; driver monitoring; heart rate variability; pupil diameter; EEG; machine learning; traffic safety

 1. Introduction

Mental workload refers to the proportion of attentional resources required to perform a task relative to the operator's available capacity (Young et al., 2015). In driving, mental workload fluctuates dynamically in response to traffic density, road complexity, and secondary tasks such as phone conversations. When workload exceeds capacity, drivers may fail to detect hazards; conversely, underload can induce vigilance decrements and mind-wandering. Both states are associated with elevated crash risk (Heikoop et al., 2017).

Traditional workload assessment relies on subjective self-reports (e.g., NASA-TLX) and performance measures. However, self-reports are retrospective and intrusive, while performance measures often lack sensitivity until performance degrades substantially. Physiological indices offer a continuous, objective alternative. Heart rate variability (HRV) reflects autonomic balance and typically decreases under cognitive demand (Thayer et al., 2012). Skin conductance level (SCL) indexes sympathetic arousal. Pupil diameter increases with cognitive load due to LC-NE system activation (Beatty, 1982). EEG theta-to-alpha ratio has been linked to attentional resource allocation (Klimesch, 1999).

Despite extensive research, few studies have integrated these indices into a single predictive model validated across multiple workload levels. The present study addresses this gap by (1) quantifying physiological responses to three experimentally controlled workload conditions and (2) developing a machine learning model to predict subjective workload from physiological features.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Participants

Thirty-six licensed drivers (22 males, 14 females) aged 22–55 years (M = 34.2, SD = 8.7) with at least two years of driving experience participated. Exclusion criteria included cardiovascular disease, psychiatric disorders, use of psychoactive medication, and corrected visual acuity below 20/40. All participants provided written informed consent, and the study was approved by the institutional ethics committee.

 2.2 Apparatus and Driving Scenarios

A fixed-base driving simulator (STISIM Drive, version 3.0) with a 135° field-of-view projection system was used. Three 10-minute scenarios were designed:

- Low workload: monotonous highway driving with minimal traffic.
- Medium workload: urban driving with moderate traffic, intersections, and pedestrians.
- High workload: urban driving combined with an auditory n-back task (1-back), requiring verbal responses to letters presented every 3 seconds.

Scenario order was counterbalanced across participants.

 2.3 Physiological Measurements

A Biopac MP160 system recorded electrocardiography (ECG; 1000 Hz), electrodermal activity (EDA; 100 Hz), and EEG (500 Hz, 8-channel). Pupil diameter was recorded at 60 Hz using an SMI eye tracker. Data were segmented into 60-second epochs, yielding 30 epochs per participant across conditions.

Feature extraction: From ECG, R-peaks were detected and RR intervals computed; HRV features included RMSSD, SDNN, and low-to-high frequency ratio (LF/HF). SCL was averaged per epoch. EEG was band-pass filtered, and the theta (4–8 Hz) to alpha (8–12 Hz) ratio was computed at frontal sites (Fz, F3, F4). Mean pupil diameter was extracted after blink removal.

 2.4 Subjective and Performance Measures

After each scenario, participants completed the NASA-TLX. Lane-keeping error (standard deviation of lateral position) and reaction time to peripheral events were recorded as performance indices.

 2.5 Data Analysis

Repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition effects on each measure. Pearson correlations assessed relationships between physiological features and NASA-TLX scores. A random forest regression model (500 trees, maximum depth = 10) was trained using 70% of epochs and validated on the remaining 30% via 10-fold cross-validation. Feature importance was computed using permutation importance.

 3. Results

 3.1 Workload Manipulation Check

NASA-TLX scores increased significantly across conditions: low (M = 28.4, SD = 9.1), medium (M = 51.7, SD = 10.3), and high (M = 74.2, SD = 11.6), F(2, 70) = 187.4, p < .001, η² = 0.84. Lane-keeping error also increased (low: 0.21 m; medium: 0.34 m; high: 0.49 m), F(2, 70) = 42.8, p < .001.

 3.2 Physiological Responses

All physiological indices showed significant condition effects (Table 1). RMSSD decreased from 42.6 ms (low) to 28.1 ms (high). SCL increased from 6.2 µS to 11.8 µS. Pupil diameter increased from 3.4 mm to 4.6 mm. Theta/alpha ratio increased from 1.12 to 2.03.

Table 1. Physiological indices across workload conditions (mean ± SD).

| Index | Low | Medium | High | F(2,70) | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RMSSD (ms) | 42.6 ± 8.3 | 34.9 ± 7.1 | 28.1 ± 6.4 | 38.2 | <.001 |
| LF/HF ratio | 1.8 ± 0.6 | 2.6 ± 0.8 | 3.7 ± 1.1 | 44.1 | <.001 |
| SCL (µS) | 6.2 ± 2.1 | 8.9 ± 2.7 | 11.8 ± 3.4 | 51.6 | <.001 |
| Pupil diameter (mm) | 3.4 ± 0.4 | 4.0 ± 0.5 | 4.6 ± 0.6 | 62.9 | <.001 |
| Theta/alpha ratio | 1.12 ± 0.21 | 1.54 ± 0.28 | 2.03 ± 0.37 | 78.4 | <.001 |

 3.3 Correlations with Subjective Workload

Theta/alpha ratio showed the strongest correlation with NASA-TLX (r = 0.71, p < .001), followed by pupil diameter (r = 0.66), SCL (r = 0.58), LF/HF (r = 0.52), and RMSSD (r = −0.49).

 3.4 Prediction Model Performance

The random forest model predicted NASA-TLX scores with R² = 0.83 and RMSE = 5.42 in cross-validation. Permutation importance ranked theta/alpha ratio (0.28), pupil diameter (0.24), SCL (0.19), LF/HF (0.16), and RMSSD (0.13) as the most influential features. A simplified model using only the top three features achieved R² = 0.79, RMSE = 5.98.

 4. Discussion

This study demonstrates that driver mental workload can be predicted with high accuracy from multimodal physiological indices. Consistent with prior work, cognitive demand elicited sympathetic activation (increased SCL, LF/HF) and parasympathetic withdrawal (decreased RMSSD), alongside increased pupil diameter and frontal theta/alpha ratio (Beatty, 1982; Klimesch, 1999; Thayer et al., 2012).

The superior predictive contribution of EEG theta/alpha ratio and pupil diameter aligns with their direct linkage to attentional resource allocation. Notably, combining autonomic and central measures improved prediction beyond any single modality, supporting a multimodal approach.

The model's R² = 0.83 compares favorably with earlier efforts. For instance, Wang et al. (2021) reported R² = 0.72 using HRV alone, while Solovey et al. (2011) achieved 75% classification accuracy across two workload levels. Our continuous prediction across three levels represents a methodological advance.

 4.1 Practical Implications

Real-time workload estimation could inform adaptive automation—for example, suppressing non-critical notifications during high-load periods or triggering alerts during underload. With miniaturized sensors, such systems could be integrated into steering wheels or seatbelts.

 4.2 Limitations

First, the simulated environment may not fully capture real-world stress. Second, the sample was relatively young and healthy, limiting generalizability. Third, individual differences in physiological baselines were not fully modeled; personalized normalization may improve accuracy. Fourth, the n-back task may not represent naturalistic secondary tasks.

 4.3 Future Directions

Future work should validate the model in on-road studies, incorporate individual baseline calibration, and explore deep learning architectures for temporal dynamics. Longitudinal data could also capture fatigue-related workload changes.

 5. Conclusion

This study developed a random forest model predicting driver mental workload from HRV, SCL, pupil diameter, and EEG theta/alpha ratio, achieving R² = 0.83 across three workload conditions. Theta/alpha ratio and pupil diameter were the strongest predictors, and multimodal integration outperformed single-modality approaches. These findings support the feasibility of continuous, objective workload monitoring for adaptive vehicle safety systems. With further validation in naturalistic settings, such models could contribute meaningfully to reducing workload-related crash risk.

 References

Beatty, J. (1982). Task-evoked pupillary responses, processing load, and the structure of processing resources. *Psychological Bulletin, 91*(2), 276–292.

Heikoop, D. D., de Winter, J. C. F., van Arem, B., & Stanton, N. A. (2017). Effects of mental workload and fatigue on the lateral position. *Transportation Research Part F, 45*, 44–56.

Klimesch, W. (1999). EEG alpha and theta oscillations reflect cognitive and memory performance. *Brain Research Reviews, 29*(2–3), 169–195.

Solovey, E. T., Schermerhorn, P., Scheutz, M., Sassaroli, A., Fantini, S., & Jacob, R. J. K. (2011). Brainput: Enhancing interactive systems with streaming fNIRS brain input. *Proceedings of CHI 2011*, 2193–2202.

Thayer, J. F., Åhs, F., Fredrikson, M., Sollers, J. J., & Wager, T. D. (2012). A meta-analysis of heart rate variability and neuroimaging studies. *Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 36*(2), 747–756.

Wang, Y., Zhang, L., & Chen, F. (2021). Heart rate variability-based mental workload estimation in simulated driving. *Applied Ergonomics, 92*, 103341.

Young, M. S., Brookhuis, K. A., Wickens, C. D., & Hancock, P. A. (2015). State of science: Mental workload in ergonomics. *Ergonomics, 58*(1), 1–17.

title: Morphology, Phylogeny, and Pathogenicity of Pestalotioid Species on Camellia oleifera in China
text: Pestalotioid fungi are a diverse group of asexual ascomycetes that include important plant pathogens, endophytes, and saprobes. Species of *Camellia oleifera*, an economically important woody oil crop widely cultivated in China, are frequently affected by pestalotioid diseases, yet their diversity and pathogenicity remain poorly understood. In this study, diseased leaf and fruit samples of *C. oleifera* were collected from major cultivation regions in China, and 68 pestalotioid isolates were obtained. Based on morphological characterization and multi-locus phylogenetic analyses of the internal transcribed spacer (ITS), β-tubulin (*tub2*), and translation elongation factor 1-alpha (*tef1*) regions, these isolates were identified as belonging to five species within three genera: *Neopestalotiopsis clavispora*, *Neopestalotiopsis cubana*, *Pestalotiopsis chamaeropis*, *Pestalotiopsis rhodomyrtus*, and *Pseudopestalotiopsis camelliae-sinensis*. Among them, *P. rhodomyrtus* and *N. cubana* represent new host records for *C. oleifera*. Pathogenicity tests on detached leaves and fruits, as well as on potted seedlings, revealed that all five species were pathogenic to *C. oleifera*, with *Pseudopestalotiopsis camelliae-sinensis* and *Neopestalotiopsis clavispora* exhibiting the highest virulence. Significant variation in lesion size was observed among species and inoculation methods. This study provides the first comprehensive account of pestalotioid species associated with *C. oleifera* in China, clarifies their phylogenetic relationships and morphological delimitation, and identifies the principal pathogenic agents responsible for leaf blight and fruit rot. These findings offer a foundation for disease diagnosis, quarantine, and the development of effective management strategies for pestalotioid diseases in *C. oleifera* plantations.

title: Molecular response and evolution of plant anion transport systems to abiotic stress
text:
Molecular response and evolution of plant anion transport systems to abiotic stress

Abstract

Anion transport systems are essential for maintaining cellular ion homeostasis, pH regulation, and osmotic balance in plants. While cation transport under abiotic stress has been extensively studied, the molecular response and evolutionary dynamics of anion transporters remain comparatively less understood. In this study, we performed a genome-wide identification and expression analysis of anion transporter gene families—including chloride channels (CLCs), aluminum-activated malate transporters (ALMTs), and slow anion channels (SLACs)—across six plant species representing distinct evolutionary lineages. Using simulated transcriptomic and physiological data under salt, drought, and cold stress, we found that anion transporter genes exhibit lineage-specific expansion, with ALMT and CLC families showing the most significant copy number variation. Expression profiling revealed that 68% of anion transporter genes were differentially expressed under at least one abiotic stress condition, with OsCLC1, AtALMT9, and ZmSLAC1 showing >5-fold upregulation under salt and drought stress. Co-expression network analysis identified 14 hub genes linked to abscisic acid signaling and reactive oxygen species scavenging. Evolutionary analysis indicated that purifying selection dominated anion transporter evolution, though positive selection signatures were detected in ALMT subfamilies of halophytic species. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how anion transport systems contribute to plant stress adaptation and offer potential targets for crop improvement.

Keywords: anion transporters; abiotic stress; CLC; ALMT; SLAC; gene family evolution; transcriptomics

1. Introduction

Abiotic stresses such as salinity, drought, and extreme temperatures severely limit global crop productivity, causing estimated annual losses exceeding $170 billion worldwide (fictional estimate). Plants respond to these stresses through complex molecular networks involving ion transport, osmotic adjustment, and hormonal signaling. While cation transporters (e.g., NHX, SOS1, HKT) have been well characterized, anion transport systems—which mediate the flux of chloride (Cl⁻), nitrate (NO₃⁻), malate, and other anions—remain comparatively understudied despite their critical roles in stomatal movement, pH homeostasis, and heavy metal detoxification.

Anion transport in plants is mediated by several gene families: chloride channels (CLCs), aluminum-activated malate transporters (ALMTs), slow anion channels (SLACs), and nitrate transporters (NRTs). The CLC family regulates Cl⁻ homeostasis and vacuolar acidification; ALMTs facilitate malate efflux in response to aluminum toxicity and stomatal closure; SLACs are central to guard cell anion efflux during drought-induced stomatal closure. Despite their physiological importance, the evolutionary conservation and stress-responsive expression patterns of these families across diverse plant species have not been systematically compared.

This study aims to: (1) identify anion transporter genes across six representative plant species; (2) profile their expression under salt, drought, and cold stress; (3) construct co-expression networks to identify regulatory hubs; and (4) analyze selection pressures acting on these gene families. We hypothesize that anion transporter families exhibit lineage-specific expansion and that stress-responsive members are conserved across angiosperms.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Data sources and gene identification

Genome and proteome data were retrieved from public databases for *Arabidopsis thaliana*, *Oryza sativa*, *Zea mays*, *Glycine max*, *Sorghum bicolor*, and *Suaeda salsa* (a halophyte). Anion transporter genes were identified using HMMER 3.3 with Pfam domains PF00654 (CLC), PF11744 (ALMT), and PF04515 (SLAC). Sequences with E-value < 1e-5 were retained and manually curated.

2.2 Phylogenetic and selection analysis

Multiple sequence alignments were performed using MAFFT v7.4, and phylogenetic trees were constructed with IQ-TREE using the LG+G model and 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Ka/Ks ratios were calculated using the Yang-Nielsen method implemented in PAML 4.9. Positively selected sites were identified using site models (M1a vs. M2a, M7 vs. M8) with likelihood ratio tests.

2.3 Stress treatment and expression profiling

Simulated expression data were generated based on previously published transcriptomic patterns (fictional dataset). Briefly, 14-day-old seedlings were subjected to 200 mM NaCl (salt), 20% PEG-6000 (drought), or 4°C (cold) for 0, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were defined as |log₂FC| > 1 and adjusted *P* < 0.05. Co-expression networks were constructed using WGCNA with a soft-thresholding power of 12.

2.4 Physiological validation

Stomatal conductance, malate content, and Cl⁻ accumulation were measured using simulated datasets calibrated to published physiological ranges. All experiments were performed with three biological replicates.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Gene family identification and expansion

A total of 187 anion transporter genes were identified across the six species: 34 CLCs, 89 ALMTs, and 64 SLACs. *Glycine max* possessed the highest number (48 genes), consistent with its paleopolyploid genome, while *Arabidopsis* had the fewest (21 genes). Phylogenetic analysis clustered CLCs into three clades (Clade I–III), with Clade II containing the highest proportion of stress-responsive members. ALMTs formed five subfamilies (ALMT1–5), with ALMT1 and ALMT2 showing lineage-specific expansion in *S. salsa* and *G. max*.

3.2 Expression profiling under abiotic stress

Under salt stress, 72% of CLC genes, 65% of ALMT genes, and 58% of SLAC genes were differentially expressed at ≥6 h. Notably, *OsCLC1* and *AtCLCc* were upregulated 6.2-fold and 4.8-fold, respectively, at 12 h. Under drought stress, *AtALMT9* and *ZmSLAC1* showed the strongest induction (7.1-fold and 5.9-fold). Cold stress elicited milder responses, with only 31% of genes differentially expressed. Hierarchical clustering revealed that salt and drought responses shared 44% overlap in DEGs, suggesting partially conserved signaling pathways.

3.3 Co-expression networks and hub genes

WGCNA identified two stress-related modules (turquoise and blue). The turquoise module (r = 0.82 with salt tolerance) contained 14 hub genes, including *CLC1*, *ALMT9*, *SLAC1*, and *SnRK2.6* (an ABA signaling kinase). The blue module (r = 0.76 with drought tolerance) was enriched for ROS scavenging genes (*CAT1*, *SOD2*). Hub genes exhibited high connectivity (kME > 0.85) and were predominantly localized to the plasma membrane and tonoplast.

3.4 Selection pressure analysis

Global Ka/Ks ratios for CLC, ALMT, and SLAC families were 0.21, 0.34, and 0.18, respectively, indicating strong purifying selection. However, site model analysis identified 12 positively selected sites in ALMT subfamilies of *S. salsa* (ω = 2.4, *P* < 0.01), primarily located in the transmembrane domain. In contrast, no positively selected sites were detected in CLCs or SLACs.

4. Discussion

Our results demonstrate that anion transport systems are deeply integrated into plant abiotic stress responses, with CLCs and ALMTs playing particularly prominent roles. The lineage-specific expansion of ALMTs in *S. salsa* and *G. max* suggests that gene duplication has contributed to stress adaptation, consistent with the "expansion–neofunctionalization" model. The strong induction of *OsCLC1* and *AtALMT9* under salt and drought stress aligns with their known functions in vacuolar Cl⁻ sequestration and malate-mediated stomatal closure, respectively.

The co-expression network identified *SnRK2.6* as a central hub connecting anion transporters to ABA signaling. This is consistent with the established role of SnRK2 kinases in phosphorylating SLAC1 and ALMT channels during stomatal closure. The enrichment of ROS scavenging genes in the drought module suggests that anion transport may indirectly mitigate oxidative damage by maintaining pH and ion balance.

Evolutionary analysis revealed that purifying selection dominates anion transporter evolution, likely due to their essential housekeeping functions. However, the positively selected sites in halophytic ALMTs indicate that specific residues may confer enhanced malate efflux capacity under saline conditions. These sites warrant functional validation via site-directed mutagenesis.

Several limitations should be noted. First, our expression data are simulated and require experimental validation. Second, post-translational regulation (e.g., phosphorylation, ubiquitination) was not modeled. Third, the role of anion transporters in cold stress appears minor, but this may reflect tissue-specific or temporal dynamics not captured here.

5. Conclusion

This study provides a comprehensive analysis of anion transport systems across six plant species, revealing conserved and lineage-specific molecular responses to abiotic stress. CLC and ALMT families are the most stress-responsive, with hub genes linked to ABA signaling and ROS homeostasis. Evolutionary analysis indicates that purifying selection predominates, though positive selection in halophytic ALMTs suggests adaptive potential. These findings establish a foundation for functional characterization of anion transporters and identify promising targets—particularly *CLC1*, *ALMT9*, and *SLAC1*—for engineering stress-tolerant crops. Future work should integrate proteomic and electrophysiological approaches to validate these predictions.

title: Agent-based model with asymmetric trading and herding for complex financial systems
text:
1. Introduction

Complex financial systems are characterized by non-trivial stylized facts, such as fat-tailed return distributions, long-range volatility correlations, and clustered trading activity, which challenge the efficient-market paradigm. Agent-based models have emerged as powerful tools for reproducing these empirical regularities from microscopic interactions among heterogeneous traders. However, most existing models assume symmetric trading behavior or treat herding as a homogeneous tendency, neglecting the fact that real investors differ systematically in their propensity to follow the crowd and in their buy–sell asymmetry. In this paper, we propose an agent-based model that incorporates asymmetric trading and heterogeneous herding to investigate how these two features jointly shape market dynamics. Through extensive simulations, we examine the resulting return distributions, volatility clustering, and long-memory effects, and compare them with empirical data from Chinese stock markets. Our results highlight the essential role of behavioral asymmetry in generating realistic financial fluctuations.

title: A double built-in containment strategy for production of recombinant proteins in transgenic rice
text:
Results and Discussion

Transgenic rice lines expressing the model recombinant protein were successfully generated and characterized. PCR and Southern blot analyses confirmed stable integration of the transgene in 18 of 24 independent T₀ lines. Protein expression levels in mature seeds, quantified by ELISA, ranged from 0.8 to 4.6 μg/g dry seed weight, with line L12 showing the highest accumulation (4.6 ± 0.4 μg/g).

The double built-in containment strategy combined cleistogamy with seed-specific transgene expression. Cleistogamy reduced outcrossing to 0.02% under field conditions, compared with 1.35% in the non-cleistogamous control—a 67-fold reduction. Furthermore, no transgene-derived protein was detected in pollen, leaf, or root tissues (below the 0.01 μg/g detection limit), restricting expression exclusively to the endosperm.

Glasshouse trials across two generations showed no significant fitness penalty: mean plant height (98.2 ± 4.1 cm vs. 100.5 ± 3.8 cm) and grain yield (28.4 ± 2.2 g vs. 29.1 ± 2.0 g per plant) did not differ significantly from wild-type controls (p > 0.05). These results demonstrate that combining cleistogamy with tissue-specific expression provides robust, dual-layer containment without compromising agronomic performance, offering a practical framework for biosafe molecular farming in rice.

title: Machine learning risk prediction model for acute coronary syndrome and death from use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in administrative data
text:
Machine Learning Risk Prediction Model for Acute Coronary Syndrome and Death from Use of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs in Administrative Data

Abstract

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are widely prescribed, yet their cardiovascular safety profile remains a major concern, particularly regarding acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and death. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning (ML) risk prediction model for ACS and all-cause death within 90 days of NSAID initiation using routinely collected administrative health data. We constructed a retrospective cohort of 184,562 adult patients who initiated NSAIDs between January 2018 and December 2022 from a regional administrative claims database. Candidate predictors included demographics, comorbidities, concomitant medications, prior healthcare utilization, and NSAID type/dose. The primary composite outcome was hospitalization for ACS or all-cause death within 90 days. We compared logistic regression with three ML algorithms: random forest, gradient boosting machine (GBM), and deep neural network. The GBM model achieved the best discrimination (AUROC 0.812, 95% CI 0.798–0.826) and calibration (Brier score 0.072) in the hold-out test set, outperforming logistic regression (AUROC 0.764). The most influential predictors were prior ACS, chronic kidney disease, age, heart failure, and concurrent use of anticoagulants or corticosteroids. We deployed the model as a web-based calculator. In conclusion, an ML model using administrative data can accurately stratify short-term ACS and death risk after NSAID initiation, potentially supporting safer prescribing decisions.

Keywords: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; acute coronary syndrome; machine learning; risk prediction; administrative data; pharmacoepidemiology

1. Introduction

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are among the most commonly used medications worldwide for pain and inflammation. Despite their efficacy, NSAIDs are associated with an increased risk of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and cardiovascular death, particularly in patients with underlying cardiovascular disease or renal impairment. Regulatory agencies have issued warnings, and clinical guidelines recommend cautious use in high-risk populations. However, risk assessment in routine practice remains challenging because individual risk varies substantially based on comorbidity burden, concomitant medications, and NSAID selectivity.

Traditional risk prediction models for NSAID-related cardiovascular events have relied on logistic regression with a limited number of predictors. These models often suffer from modest discrimination and may not capture complex nonlinear interactions among risk factors. Machine learning (ML) offers a promising alternative by automatically learning high-order interactions and handling large numbers of predictors. Administrative health data, such as claims and electronic health records, provide rich longitudinal information on diagnoses, procedures, and prescriptions, making them ideal for developing ML models. Nevertheless, few studies have applied ML to predict short-term ACS and death after NSAID initiation using administrative data.

This study aimed to: (1) develop and internally validate ML models for predicting ACS or all-cause death within 90 days of NSAID initiation; (2) compare ML models with traditional logistic regression; and (3) identify key predictors to inform clinical decision-making. We hypothesized that ML models would achieve superior discrimination and calibration compared with logistic regression.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Data Source and Study Population

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using a de-identified administrative claims database from a regional health insurer covering approximately 3.2 million adults. The database contains inpatient and outpatient diagnoses (ICD-10 codes), procedures, pharmacy dispensing records, and demographic information. Eligible patients were adults aged ≥18 years who filled at least one prescription for a non-aspirin NSAID (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, celecoxib, meloxicam, etoricoxib, or indomethacin) between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2022. The date of the first NSAID dispensing was defined as the index date. We excluded patients with less than 12 months of continuous enrollment before the index date, those with a prior ACS hospitalization within 30 days, and those with missing key covariates. The final cohort comprised 184,562 patients.

2.2 Outcome Definition

The primary composite outcome was hospitalization for ACS (ICD-10 codes I20.x, I21.x, I22.x) or all-cause death within 90 days after the index date. ACS events were identified from inpatient claims with a primary discharge diagnosis of ACS. Deaths were ascertained from the database’s vital status file linked to national death registry. Patients were followed from the index date until the earliest of outcome, disenrollment, or 90 days.

2.3 Candidate Predictors

We extracted 68 candidate predictors from the 12 months before the index date, including: demographics (age, sex, region, insurance type); comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, prior ACS, prior stroke, peripheral artery disease, atrial fibrillation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, gastrointestinal ulcer, anemia, cancer); medication use (antihypertensives, statins, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, proton pump inhibitors, opioids); healthcare utilization (number of hospitalizations, emergency department visits, outpatient visits, number of distinct medications); and NSAID characteristics (type, dose, duration of action, selectivity). Missing values for continuous variables were imputed using median, and categorical variables were assigned a missing indicator.

2.4 Model Development and Validation

The cohort was randomly split into a training set (70%, n=129,193) and a hold-out test set (30%, n=55,369) stratified by outcome. We developed four models: (1) logistic regression with LASSO regularization; (2) random forest; (3) gradient boosting machine (GBM); and (4) deep neural network (DNN) with three hidden layers. Hyperparameters were tuned using 5-fold cross-validation on the training set. Class imbalance was addressed using class weights. Model performance was evaluated on the test set using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), Brier score, and calibration plots. We also calculated sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value at the optimal threshold determined by Youden’s index. Feature importance was assessed using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values for the best model.

2.5 Statistical Analysis

Continuous variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range), and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between patients with and without the outcome were performed using t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, or chi-square tests as appropriate. A two-sided p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were conducted in Python 3.9 using scikit-learn, XGBoost, and TensorFlow.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Cohort Characteristics

Among 184,562 NSAID initiators, the mean age was 58.3 ± 14.2 years, and 54.1% were female. The most commonly prescribed NSAIDs were ibuprofen (38.2%), naproxen (24.5%), diclofenac (15.1%), celecoxib (12.3%), and meloxicam (9.9%). During the 90-day follow-up, 2,847 patients (1.54%) experienced the composite outcome: 1,932 ACS hospitalizations and 1,215 deaths (some patients had both). Patients with the outcome were older (67.8 vs. 57.9 years), more likely to be male (58.3% vs. 45.7%), and had higher prevalence of prior ACS (18.4% vs. 4.2%), heart failure (22.1% vs. 6.8%), chronic kidney disease (19.7% vs. 5.1%), and diabetes (34.6% vs. 18.9%). They also used more concomitant medications, including anticoagulants (12.3% vs. 3.1%) and corticosteroids (15.8% vs. 7.2%).

3.2 Model Performance

Table 1 summarizes the performance of the four models on the test set. The GBM model achieved the highest AUROC (0.812, 95% CI 0.798–0.826), followed by DNN (0.803), random forest (0.789), and logistic regression (0.764). The AUPRC was also highest for GBM (0.421 vs. 0.312 for logistic regression). The Brier score for GBM was 0.072, indicating good calibration, compared with 0.089 for logistic regression. Calibration plots showed that GBM predictions closely followed the observed outcome rates across deciles of predicted risk, whereas logistic regression tended to overestimate risk in the highest decile.

At the optimal threshold (predicted risk ≥2.1%), GBM achieved sensitivity 76.4%, specificity 78.9%, positive predictive value 8.9%, and negative predictive value 99.3%. The number needed to evaluate to prevent one additional event was 12.4.

3.3 Feature Importance

SHAP analysis identified the top 15 predictors for the GBM model. The strongest predictor was prior ACS hospitalization (mean |SHAP| = 0.342), followed by chronic kidney disease (0.287), age (0.265), heart failure (0.241), and concurrent anticoagulant use (0.218). Other important predictors included diabetes (0.192), corticosteroid use (0.178), prior stroke (0.165), NSAID type (diclofenac and celecoxib had higher risk than naproxen; 0.154), and high-dose NSAID (0.142). Interestingly, the model captured a nonlinear interaction between age and chronic kidney disease: the risk increased sharply for patients ≥75 years with eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73m².

3.4 Subgroup Analysis

The GBM model performed consistently across subgroups defined by sex, age group, and NSAID type. AUROC ranged from 0.798 to 0.821. However, discrimination was slightly lower in patients without prior cardiovascular disease (AUROC 0.781) compared with those with prior ACS (AUROC 0.834). The model also showed good calibration in the subgroup of patients using celecoxib (Brier score 0.068).

4. Discussion

In this large retrospective cohort, we developed and validated an ML model that predicts 90-day ACS or death after NSAID initiation using administrative data. The GBM model demonstrated good discrimination (AUROC 0.812) and calibration, outperforming traditional logistic regression. To our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to apply ML to NSAID-related cardiovascular risk prediction in a real-world administrative dataset.

The superior performance of GBM likely stems from its ability to capture nonlinear relationships and interactions among predictors. For example, the combined effect of advanced age and renal impairment on NSAID risk is well recognized but not easily modeled with linear terms. Our SHAP analysis confirmed that prior ACS, chronic kidney disease, and heart failure were dominant predictors, consistent with previous pharmacoepidemiological studies. The finding that diclofenac and celecoxib carried higher risk than naproxen aligns with regulatory warnings and meta-analyses.

From a clinical perspective, our model could be integrated into electronic prescribing systems to provide real-time risk scores at the point of NSAID initiation. A threshold of 2.1% identified 76% of events while maintaining 79% specificity. Given the low absolute risk (1.54%), the positive predictive value was modest (8.9%), but the negative predictive value was excellent (99.3%), meaning the model is particularly useful for ruling out low-risk patients who can safely use NSAIDs. For high-risk patients, clinicians might consider alternative analgesics, lower NSAID doses, or gastroprotective and cardiovascular protective strategies.

Strengths of this study include the large sample size, use of routinely collected data, and rigorous ML validation. However, several limitations warrant mention. First, administrative data may contain coding errors and lack clinical detail such as blood pressure, lipid levels, or smoking status. Second, over-the-counter NSAID use is not captured, potentially leading to exposure misclassification. Third, the model was internally validated only; external validation in different healthcare systems is needed. Fourth, although we included many predictors, residual confounding by indication cannot be excluded. Fifth, the outcome definition relied on ICD codes, which may have imperfect sensitivity and specificity.

Future work should incorporate laboratory values and vital signs from electronic health records to improve prediction. Prospective validation and impact studies are also necessary to determine whether model-guided prescribing reduces cardiovascular events without compromising pain control. Additionally, fairness audits across racial and socioeconomic groups should be conducted to ensure equitable performance.

5. Conclusion

We developed a gradient boosting machine learning model that accurately predicts 90-day acute coronary syndrome or death following NSAID initiation using administrative data. The model outperformed logistic regression and identified key risk factors including prior ACS, chronic kidney disease, age, heart failure, and anticoagulant use. With an AUROC of 0.812 and excellent negative predictive value, this model holds promise as a clinical decision support tool to stratify patients and guide safer NSAID prescribing. External validation and prospective impact evaluation are warranted before widespread implementation.

title: A machine learning framework to determine geolocations from metagenomic profiling
text:
Here is a complete research paper on the requested topic, written in a formal academic style with realistic, invented data.

---

 A machine learning framework to determine geolocations from metagenomic profiling

Abstract
The human microbiome is a complex ecosystem that is influenced by a multitude of factors, including host genetics, diet, lifestyle, and environment. This environmental influence imparts a unique, location-specific signature on an individual's microbiome, offering a novel avenue for forensic and epidemiological applications. This study presents a machine learning framework designed to predict an individual's geographic origin based on their metagenomic profile. We utilized a synthetic dataset of 1,200 human gut microbiome samples, simulated to represent six distinct global regions (North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Oceania), each with unique taxonomic compositions. Our framework employed a two-stage approach: feature selection using a Random Forest classifier to identify the most discriminative microbial taxa, followed by geolocation prediction using a Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM). The model achieved an overall accuracy of 87.5% in predicting the correct region of origin. The most informative features included the relative abundances of *Prevotella copri*, *Bacteroides vulgatus*, and *Akkermansia muciniphila*, which varied significantly across the simulated populations. This research demonstrates the potential of machine learning in microbial forensics and highlights the strong link between geolocation and the human microbiome. While our results are based on simulated data, they provide a robust proof-of-concept for developing tools that could have significant implications for public health, anthropology, and forensic science.

Keywords
Metagenomics, Machine Learning, Geolocation, Microbiome, Forensic Science, Gradient Boosting, Random Forest

1. Introduction
The human body harbors trillions of microorganisms, collectively known as the microbiome, which play a critical role in human health and disease. The composition of these microbial communities, particularly in the gut, is shaped by a complex interplay of factors. While host genetics and age contribute to this variation, environmental factors such as diet, geography, and lifestyle are increasingly recognized as dominant forces [1]. This has led to the concept of a "geographic signature" within the microbiome, where individuals from different parts of the world can be distinguished by the unique taxonomic and functional profiles of their microbial communities [2].

The ability to determine an individual's geographic origin from biological samples has profound implications in various fields. In forensic science, it could provide crucial evidence in identifying unknown individuals or tracing the origin of biological materials. In epidemiology, understanding the geographic distribution of specific microbial strains can help track the spread of infectious diseases and inform public health interventions. Furthermore, in anthropology, it can offer insights into human migration patterns and population history.

Traditional methods for geolocation, such as analyzing human DNA markers (e.g., single nucleotide polymorphisms), are well-established. However, the microbiome presents a complementary and potentially more dynamic source of information, as it reflects not only ancestry but also recent environmental exposures. The challenge lies in developing robust computational methods capable of deciphering this complex microbial signature.

Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have provided powerful tools for analyzing high-dimensional biological data like metagenomic profiles [3]. Algorithms such as Random Forest and Gradient Boosting Machines can identify complex, non-linear patterns and interactions within microbial community data that are not easily discernible through traditional statistical methods.

In this study, we propose and evaluate a machine learning framework to predict an individual's geolocation based on their gut metagenomic profile. We hypothesized that a sufficiently trained ML model could accurately classify samples into their region of origin by learning the specific microbial taxa associated with each location. Using a large, simulated dataset, we aimed to: (1) develop a robust classification pipeline, (2) identify the key microbial taxa that serve as geographic indicators, and (3) assess the overall accuracy and potential limitations of this approach.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Dataset Generation
For this proof-of-concept study, we generated a synthetic dataset comprising 1,200 human gut metagenomic profiles. These profiles were simulated to represent six distinct geographic regions: North America (NA), South America (SA), Europe (EU), Africa (AF), Asia (AS), and Oceania (OC), with 200 samples per region. The simulation was designed to mimic real-world microbial distributions based on published literature [2, 4].

For each region, we defined a unique set of mean relative abundances for 50 common gut genera. For instance, samples from Africa and South America were simulated to have a high mean relative abundance of *Prevotella* (e.g., 25-30%), while samples from North America and Europe were simulated with a higher abundance of *Bacteroides* (e.g., 30-35%) and lower *Prevotella* (<5%). To introduce realistic variability, the relative abundance of each genus for each sample was drawn from a Dirichlet distribution, parameterized by the region-specific mean abundances. This process created a dataset where each sample had a unique taxonomic profile, with a strong but not absolute correlation to its region of origin. The final dataset was a matrix of 1,200 samples by 50 genera, with corresponding region labels.

2.2. Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering
The raw relative abundance data was first normalized using a centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation to account for the compositional nature of metagenomic data [5]. This transformation converts the data from a simplex space to a real Euclidean space, making it suitable for use with standard machine learning algorithms.

To reduce dimensionality and focus on the most informative features, we employed a two-stage feature selection process. First, we calculated the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for all genera to remove features with high multicollinearity (VIF > 5.0). Second, we used a Random Forest classifier to rank the remaining features by their Gini importance. The top 20 genera were selected as the final feature set for the geolocation model.

2.3. Machine Learning Framework
Our predictive framework was a Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) classifier, implemented using the XGBoost library in Python. GBM is an ensemble technique that builds a series of weak prediction models (decision trees) sequentially, with each new tree correcting the errors of the previous ones. It is known for its high performance on tabular data and its ability to handle complex interactions.

The dataset was split into a training set (80%, n=960) and a testing set (20%, n=240) using stratified sampling to ensure equal representation of all six regions in both sets. The model was trained on the training set using 5-fold cross-validation to tune hyperparameters, including learning rate, maximum tree depth, and the number of estimators. The final model's performance was evaluated on the held-out testing set.

2.4. Model Evaluation
The performance of the model was assessed using several metrics: overall accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score for each region. A confusion matrix was generated to visualize the classification performance and identify patterns of misclassification between regions.

3. Results

3.1. Feature Selection
The initial feature selection process reduced the 50 genera to the 20 most informative ones. The Random Forest importance ranking identified *Prevotella copri*, *Bacteroides vulgatus*, *Akkermansia muciniphila*, *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*, and *Eubacterium rectale* as the top five most discriminative taxa. The relative abundance of *P. copri* was a particularly strong indicator, with high abundances strongly associated with samples from Africa and South America, and low abundances with North America and Europe.

3.2. Model Performance
The trained GBM model demonstrated high predictive accuracy on the held-out test set. The overall accuracy was 87.5% (210 out of 240 samples correctly classified). The model's performance varied across regions, with the highest accuracy for Africa (95%) and the lowest for Europe (82%).

Table 1: Classification Performance Metrics by Region

| Region | Precision | Recall | F1-Score | Support |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| North America | 0.89 | 0.85 | 0.87 | 40 |
| South America | 0.86 | 0.90 | 0.88 | 40 |
| Europe | 0.84 | 0.82 | 0.83 | 40 |
| Africa | 0.95 | 0.95 | 0.95 | 40 |
| Asia | 0.85 | 0.88 | 0.86 | 40 |
| Oceania | 0.85 | 0.85 | 0.85 | 40 |
| Overall | 0.87 | 0.88 | 0.87 | 240 |

The confusion matrix (Figure 1) revealed specific patterns of misclassification. The most common error was misclassifying European samples as North American (5 out of 40 samples). Similarly, some North American samples were misclassified as European (4 out of 40). Misclassifications were also observed between Asian and Oceanian samples, suggesting some overlap in their simulated microbial profiles.

4. Discussion
This study successfully demonstrates that a machine learning framework can accurately predict the geographic origin of an individual from their gut metagenomic profile. Our GBM model achieved an overall accuracy of 87.5% on a simulated dataset, confirming the hypothesis that geolocation leaves a strong, learnable signature on the human microbiome. The high predictive power, particularly for regions like Africa, underscores the potential of this approach.

The feature importance analysis provided biological insights into our model's decision-making process.
