The prominence of *Prevotella copri* as a key feature aligns with existing literature, which has repeatedly shown its association with non-Westernized, high-fiber diets typical of many African and South American populations [4]. Conversely, the association of *Bacteroides* species with Westernized diets in North America and Europe was also captured by the model. This consistency with established microbiome science lends credibility to our framework, even when applied to simulated data.

The misclassifications observed, such as between Europe and North America, are also biologically plausible. These regions share similar dietary habits and lifestyles, which can lead to more similar microbiome compositions compared to, for example, Europe and Africa. This suggests that the model is learning subtle differences and that its errors are not random but reflect the underlying biological reality.

4.1. Limitations and Future Directions
The primary limitation of this study is its reliance on simulated data. While our simulation was designed to be realistic, it cannot capture the full complexity and noise of real-world metagenomic data. Factors such as technical variation from sequencing platforms, the influence of transient microbes, and the impact of individual health status were not fully modeled. Therefore, the 87.5% accuracy should be considered an upper bound of what might be achievable with real data.

Future work must focus on validating this framework using large, diverse, and well-curated real-world datasets, such as those from the American Gut Project or the MetaSUB Consortium [6]. Applying the model to real data will require more sophisticated preprocessing to handle batch effects and other technical artifacts. Furthermore, expanding the framework to predict location at a finer resolution (e.g., city-level) and incorporating functional gene profiles in addition to taxonomic data could further enhance its predictive power. The development of interpretability techniques, such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), would also be valuable to provide more detailed insights into the specific microbial drivers of geolocation.

5. Conclusion
In conclusion, this research presents a robust machine learning framework for determining geolocation from metagenomic profiles. By leveraging a Gradient Boosting Machine and a careful feature selection process, we achieved high accuracy in classifying samples into their region of origin. Our findings, while based on simulated data, provide a strong proof-of-concept and highlight the potential of microbial forensics. With further validation on real-world data, this approach could evolve into a powerful tool for forensic science, epidemiology, and anthropological research, offering a new lens through which to view the intricate relationship between humans and their microbial counterparts.

References
[1] Rothschild, D., et al. (2018). Environment dominates over host genetics in shaping human gut microbiota. *Nature*, 555(7695), 210-215.
[2] Yatsunenko, T., et al. (2012). Human gut microbiome viewed across age and geography. *Nature*, 486(7402), 222-227.
[3] Pasolli, E., et al. (2019). Extensive unexplored human microbiome diversity revealed by over 150,000 genomes from metagenomes spanning age, geography, and lifestyle. *Cell*, 176(3), 649-662.
[4] De Filippo, C., et al. (2010). Impact of diet in shaping gut microbiota revealed by a comparative study in children from Europe and rural Africa. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 107(33), 14691-14696.
[5] Gloor, G. B., et al. (2017). Microbiome datasets are compositional: and this is not optional. *Frontiers in Microbiology*, 8, 2224.
[6] Thompson, L. R., et al. (2017). A communal catalogue reveals Earth's multiscale microbial diversity. *Nature*, 551(7681), 457-463.

title: Effectiveness of traditional Chinese medicine in treating gastrointestinal dysfunction in patients with acute stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials
text: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in treating gastrointestinal dysfunction in patients with acute stroke. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple electronic databases from inception to the present. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing TCM (alone or combined with conventional therapy) versus conventional therapy alone in acute stroke patients with gastrointestinal dysfunction were included. Sixteen RCTs involving a total of 1,362 participants met the inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan software, with pooled effect estimates expressed as risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The results demonstrated that TCM significantly improved clinical effectiveness (RR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.15–1.32, P < 0.001), reduced the incidence of constipation (RR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.35–0.63, P < 0.001), and shortened the time to first defecation (MD = −12.36 hours, 95% CI: −16.21 to −8.51, P < 0.001) compared with conventional therapy alone. Additionally, TCM markedly elevated serum motilin levels (MD = 38.72 pg/mL, 95% CI: 25.14–52.30, P < 0.001) and reduced adverse events. In conclusion, TCM appears to be effective and safe in alleviating gastrointestinal dysfunction in acute stroke patients. However, due to heterogeneity and limited methodological quality of included studies, larger, well-designed RCTs are warranted to confirm these findings.

title: Determinants of compassion satisfaction, compassion fatigue and burn out in nursing: A correlative meta-analysis
text:
Determinants of Compassion Satisfaction, Compassion Fatigue and Burnout in Nursing: A Correlative Meta-Analysis

Abstract

Background: Compassion satisfaction (CS), compassion fatigue (CF), and burnout (BO) are three interrelated professional quality of life outcomes in nursing. Although individual studies have identified potential determinants, the correlative strength and consistency of these factors across settings remain unclear.

Objective: This meta-analysis aimed to synthesize correlational evidence on determinants of CS, CF, and BO among nurses.

Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science was conducted for studies published between January 2010 and December 2024. Studies reporting correlation coefficients between antecedent variables and CS, CF, or BO were included. Random-effects models were used to pool Fisher’s z-transformed correlations. Heterogeneity was assessed using I² and Q statistics. Moderator analyses examined sample size, region, and clinical setting.

Results: Forty-two studies comprising 18,736 nurses were included. Work environment (r = 0.41 for CS; r = -0.38 for BO), social support (r = 0.36 for CS; r = -0.31 for CF), and resilience (r = 0.44 for CS; r = -0.35 for BO) were significant determinants. Emotional exhaustion was strongly associated with CF (r = 0.52) and BO (r = 0.58). Age and years of experience showed weak negative correlations with BO (r = -0.12 and -0.15, respectively). Heterogeneity was moderate to high (I² = 58%–79%). Region and clinical setting significantly moderated several relationships.

Conclusion: Modifiable factors, particularly work environment, social support, and resilience, are robust determinants of nurses’ professional quality of life. Interventions targeting these factors may simultaneously enhance CS and reduce CF and BO.

Keywords: compassion satisfaction; compassion fatigue; burnout; nursing; meta-analysis; determinants

---

1. Introduction

The professional quality of life of nurses has attracted increasing attention because of its implications for workforce retention, patient safety, and healthcare quality. Three constructs are central to this literature: compassion satisfaction (CS), compassion fatigue (CF), and burnout (BO). CS refers to the pleasure derived from helping others and feeling effective in one’s caregiving role. CF encompasses secondary traumatic stress and emotional exhaustion resulting from prolonged exposure to patient suffering. BO is characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment.

Although these constructs are conceptually distinct, empirical evidence suggests they are correlated and share common determinants. Studies have reported that supportive work environments, adequate staffing, and strong social support enhance CS while mitigating CF and BO. Conversely, high workload, moral distress, and workplace violence are associated with adverse outcomes. However, individual studies are often limited by small samples, single-site designs, and inconsistent measurement tools.

A correlative meta-analysis can overcome these limitations by pooling correlation coefficients across studies, thereby providing more precise estimates of association strength and identifying sources of heterogeneity. Previous meta-analyses have focused primarily on BO or CF alone, with less attention to CS as a positive outcome. Moreover, few have simultaneously examined multiple determinants across all three constructs.

This study aimed to: (1) synthesize correlational evidence on determinants of CS, CF, and BO in nursing; (2) compare the strength of associations across determinant domains; and (3) examine moderating effects of region, clinical setting, and sample characteristics.

---

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Search Strategy

A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science for studies published from January 2010 to December 2024. Search terms included combinations of “compassion satisfaction,” “compassion fatigue,” “burnout,” “nurse,” “nursing,” “determinants,” “correlates,” “predictors,” and “professional quality of life.” Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched.

2.2 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Studies were included if they: (1) sampled registered nurses or nursing students in clinical placements; (2) reported Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients between at least one determinant and CS, CF, or BO; (3) used validated instruments such as the Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL) or Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI); and (4) were published in English. Studies were excluded if they were qualitative, interventional, case reports, or lacked sufficient correlational data.

2.3 Data Extraction and Quality Assessment

Two reviewers independently extracted data on author, year, country, sample size, clinical setting, instruments, and correlation coefficients. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale adapted for cross-sectional studies. Scores ≥7 were considered high quality.

2.4 Statistical Analysis

Correlation coefficients were converted to Fisher’s z for pooling and back-transformed for presentation. Random-effects models were used because of expected heterogeneity. Heterogeneity was quantified using I² and Cochran’s Q. Subgroup analyses examined region (Asia, Europe, North America, others), clinical setting (critical care, oncology, general wards, mixed), and sample size. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger’s test. Analyses were performed in R 4.3.1 with the metafor package.

---

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Study Characteristics

A total of 42 studies met inclusion criteria, comprising 18,736 nurses. Sample sizes ranged from 98 to 2,145. Studies were conducted in Asia (n = 18), Europe (n = 10), North America (n = 9), and other regions (n = 5). Clinical settings included critical care (n = 12), oncology (n = 8), general wards (n = 10), and mixed settings (n = 12). Most studies used the ProQOL (n = 31) or MBI (n = 11). Quality scores ranged from 7 to 9, indicating acceptable methodological rigor.

3.2 Determinants of Compassion Satisfaction

Work environment was the strongest determinant of CS (r = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.34–0.48). Social support (r = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.29–0.43) and resilience (r = 0.44, 95% CI: 0.37–0.51) were also positively associated with CS. Age (r = 0.11, 95% CI: 0.05–0.17) and years of experience (r = 0.13, 95% CI: 0.07–0.19) showed weak positive correlations. Emotional exhaustion was negatively associated with CS (r = -0.32, 95% CI: -0.39 to -0.25).

3.3 Determinants of Compassion Fatigue

Emotional exhaustion showed the strongest positive association with CF (r = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.45–0.59). Workload (r = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.31–0.45) and exposure to patient suffering (r = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.27–0.41) were also significant. Social support (r = -0.31, 95% CI: -0.38 to -0.24) and resilience (r = -0.29, 95% CI: -0.36 to -0.22) were protective. Age and experience were weakly negatively correlated with CF (r = -0.09 and -0.11, respectively).

3.4 Determinants of Burnout

Emotional exhaustion was strongly associated with BO (r = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.51–0.65). Work environment (r = -0.38, 95% CI: -0.45 to -0.31), social support (r = -0.31, 95% CI: -0.38 to -0.24), and resilience (r = -0.35, 95% CI: -0.42 to -0.28) were significant negative determinants. Workload (r = 0.42, 95% CI: 0.35–0.49) and moral distress (r = 0.39, 95% CI: 0.32–0.46) were positive determinants. Age (r = -0.12, 95% CI: -0.18 to -0.06) and years of experience (r = -0.15, 95% CI: -0.21 to -0.09) showed weak negative associations.

3.5 Heterogeneity and Moderator Analyses

Heterogeneity was moderate to high (I² = 58%–79%). Region significantly moderated the relationship between work environment and BO (Q = 8.42, p = 0.038), with stronger associations in Asia than in Europe or North America. Clinical setting moderated the association between emotional exhaustion and CF (Q = 7.91, p = 0.048), with critical care showing stronger effects. Sample size did not significantly moderate any relationship. Funnel plots and Egger’s tests suggested no significant publication bias (p > 0.05).

---

4. Discussion

This meta-analysis provides robust evidence that modifiable factors—work environment, social support, resilience, workload, and moral distress—are consistent determinants of CS, CF, and BO in nursing. The findings align with the Job Demands-Resources model, which posits that job resources enhance engagement and satisfaction while buffering the impact of demands. Work environment and social support emerged as key resources, whereas emotional exhaustion and workload functioned as demands.

The strong association between emotional exhaustion and both CF and BO suggests overlapping affective processes. However, CF also includes secondary traumatic stress, which is more specifically linked to exposure to patient suffering. This distinction is important for intervention design: BO may respond to workload reduction and organizational support, whereas CF may require targeted psychological support and trauma-informed care training.

Resilience was consistently protective across all three outcomes. This finding supports resilience training as a potentially effective strategy, although structural interventions should not be neglected. The weak negative correlations of age and experience with BO and CF suggest that older, more experienced nurses may develop coping mechanisms, but the effect sizes are small and should not substitute for systemic change.

Moderator analyses revealed regional and setting-specific variations. Stronger associations in Asia may reflect differences in staffing ratios, hierarchical work cultures, or social support structures. Critical care settings showed stronger links between emotional exhaustion and CF, likely due to repeated exposure to high-acuity suffering and death.

Limitations: Most included studies were cross-sectional, limiting causal inference. Self-report measures may introduce common method bias. Heterogeneity remained substantial despite subgroup analyses. Finally, publication bias cannot be entirely excluded, although statistical tests were non-significant.

Implications: Healthcare organizations should prioritize supportive work environments, adequate staffing, and peer support programs. Resilience training and mental health resources should be integrated into nursing education and continuing professional development. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and objective measures to clarify causal pathways.

---

5. Conclusion

CS, CF, and BO in nursing are shaped by a common set of modifiable determinants, particularly work environment, social support, resilience, workload, and moral distress. Emotional exhaustion is a central mechanism linking demands to adverse outcomes. Interventions that simultaneously enhance resources and reduce demands are likely to improve nurses’ professional quality of life. Regional and clinical setting differences warrant tailored approaches. Longitudinal and interventional studies are needed to confirm causality and evaluate effectiveness.

title: Limited aerenchyma reduces oxygen diffusion and methane emission in paddy
text:
Rice paddies are a major anthropogenic source of atmospheric methane (CH₄), contributing approximately 10% of global CH₄ emissions. Methane is produced by methanogens in anaerobic paddy soils and is subsequently transported to the atmosphere through three principal pathways: molecular diffusion, ebullition, and plant-mediated transport. Among these, plant-mediated transport through the aerenchyma—a specialized gas-space tissue that connects roots to shoots—dominates CH₄ emission in vegetated paddies, accounting for up to 90% of total flux. The same aerenchyma network also supplies oxygen (O₂) from the atmosphere to the rhizosphere, thereby regulating root respiration, radial O₂ loss, and the activity of methanotrophs that oxidize CH₄ before it escapes.

Because aerenchyma simultaneously governs O₂ influx and CH₄ efflux, its structural and functional traits are expected to exert a first-order control on paddy CH₄ emission. However, the two processes are not symmetric: O₂ and CH₄ diffuse along opposite gradients through the same gas spaces, and their transport efficiencies depend on tissue porosity, cell-wall resistance, and the continuity of gas channels. Consequently, a reduction in aerenchyma formation could suppress CH₄ emission either by limiting the physical conduit for CH₄ escape or by restricting O₂ supply and thereby altering belowground CH₄ production and oxidation. The relative importance of these mechanisms remains poorly quantified, particularly across rice genotypes that differ intrinsically in aerenchyma development.

Here we test the hypothesis that limited aerenchyma reduces both O₂ diffusion into the rhizosphere and CH₄ emission from paddy soils. Using a combination of genotype screening, anatomical quantification, gas-diffusion measurements, and field flux monitoring, we examined how variation in aerenchyma traits modulates O₂ availability and CH₄ dynamics. Our results aim to clarify the mechanistic linkage between root gas-space architecture and CH₄ flux, and to assess whether aerenchyma limitation can serve as a viable breeding target for low-emission rice paddies without compromising yield.

title: Stochastic configuration network ensembles with selective base models
text:
Results and Discussion

Table 2 summarizes the performance of the proposed selective ensemble (SCN-SE) against a single stochastic configuration network (SCN), a full ensemble (SCN-FE), and three mainstream baselines across six regression datasets. SCN-SE achieved the lowest average RMSE on five of six datasets, with a mean rank of 1.33 versus 2.50 (SCN-FE), 3.17 (SCN), and 4.00 or worse for the baselines. On the largest dataset (Airfoil, N = 1503), SCN-SE reduced RMSE from 0.0842 (SCN) and 0.0791 (SCN-FE) to 0.0734, a 12.9% and 7.2% improvement, respectively.

The gains are attributable to selective pruning: retaining only the top 40% of base models by validation error removed redundant, correlated learners while preserving diversity. Ensemble size dropped from 50 to 20, cutting training time by 58% (from 41.6 s to 17.5 s) and testing time by 61%. Notably, SCN-SE's advantage widened as noise increased; on the noisy Concrete dataset it outperformed SCN-FE by 9.8%, indicating that selection acts as an implicit regularizer. A limitation is that selection relies on a validation split, which may be costly for very small samples. Overall, the results confirm that selective ensembling yields more accurate and efficient SCNs than naive averaging.

title: Synthesis of attapulgite/N-isopropylacrylamide and its use in drug release
text:
Synthesis of attapulgite/N-isopropylacrylamide and its use in drug release

Abstract
In this study, a novel organic–inorganic hybrid material based on attapulgite (ATP) and poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) was synthesized via in-situ radical polymerization. The resulting ATP/PNIPAM composite was characterized by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The composite exhibited a temperature-responsive phase transition with a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) of approximately 32.5 °C. Using ibuprofen as a model drug, the drug loading efficiency and in-vitro release behavior were investigated. The ATP/PNIPAM composite achieved a drug loading efficiency of 28.6% and demonstrated sustained release over 12 h. The release rate was markedly higher at 37 °C (above LCST) than at 25 °C (below LCST), indicating a thermosensitive “on–off” release mechanism. These results suggest that ATP/PNIPAM is a promising carrier for controlled drug delivery.

Keywords: attapulgite; N-isopropylacrylamide; thermosensitive; composite; drug release

1. Introduction
Controlled drug delivery systems have attracted considerable attention because they can maintain therapeutic drug concentrations, reduce administration frequency, and minimize side effects. Among various stimuli-responsive carriers, thermosensitive polymers such as poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) are particularly attractive due to their reversible phase transition near physiological temperature. PNIPAM exhibits a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) around 32 °C; below LCST it is hydrophilic and swollen, while above LCST it becomes hydrophobic and collapses.

However, pure PNIPAM hydrogels often suffer from poor mechanical strength and rapid drug leakage. To overcome these limitations, inorganic nanofillers such as attapulgite (ATP) have been introduced. ATP is a natural hydrated magnesium aluminum silicate with a fibrous morphology, high specific surface area, and abundant surface hydroxyl groups. These features enable strong interfacial interactions with polymers and provide additional adsorption sites for drug molecules.

In this work, ATP/PNIPAM composites were prepared by in-situ polymerization. The structure, thermal properties, and temperature-responsive drug release behavior were systematically evaluated using ibuprofen as a model drug. The objective was to develop a hybrid carrier that combines the mechanical reinforcement of ATP with the thermosensitivity of PNIPAM.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Materials
Attapulgite (ATP, purity > 95%) was obtained from Xuyi, Jiangsu, China. N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM, 98%) was recrystallized from n-hexane before use. N,N′-methylenebisacrylamide (MBA), ammonium persulfate (APS), and ibuprofen were of analytical grade. Deionized water was used throughout.

2.2 Synthesis of ATP/PNIPAM composite
ATP (1.0 g) was dispersed in 50 mL deionized water and sonicated for 30 min. NIPAM (2.0 g) and MBA (0.05 g) were added, and the mixture was purged with nitrogen for 20 min. APS (0.04 g) dissolved in 5 mL water was then injected to initiate polymerization. The reaction proceeded at 70 °C for 6 h under nitrogen. The product was washed repeatedly with deionized water and ethanol, then dried at 50 °C under vacuum.

2.3 Characterization
FTIR spectra were recorded on a Nicolet 6700 spectrometer. XRD patterns were obtained using a Rigaku D/max-2500 diffractometer. SEM images were taken on a Hitachi S-4800 microscope. TGA was performed on a Netzsch STA 449C at a heating rate of 10 °C/min under nitrogen. The LCST was determined by cloud point measurement at 550 nm.

2.4 Drug loading and release
Ibuprofen (0.1 g) and composite (0.2 g) were dispersed in 20 mL phosphate buffer saline (PBS, pH 7.4) and stirred for 24 h at 25 °C. The loaded composite was separated by centrifugation and dried. Drug loading efficiency (DLE) was calculated as: DLE (%) = (mass of loaded drug / mass of composite) × 100%.

In-vitro release was performed in PBS at 25 °C and 37 °C. At predetermined intervals, 3 mL aliquots were withdrawn and replaced with fresh PBS. Ibuprofen concentration was measured by UV–vis spectrophotometry at 264 nm.

3. Results and Analysis
3.1 FTIR analysis
The FTIR spectrum of ATP showed characteristic peaks at 3615 cm⁻¹ (OH stretching), 1030 cm⁻¹ (Si–O–Si), and 470 cm⁻¹ (Si–O bending). In ATP/PNIPAM, new peaks appeared at 1650 cm⁻¹ (amide I, C=O) and 1540 cm⁻¹ (amide II, N–H), confirming successful polymerization of NIPAM. The broadened OH peak at 3400 cm⁻¹ indicated hydrogen bonding between ATP silanol groups and PNIPAM amide groups.

3.2 XRD and SEM
XRD of ATP exhibited typical reflections at 2θ = 8.4° (110), 19.8° (040), and 27.5° (400). In the composite, the intensity of these peaks decreased, suggesting partial exfoliation or coating of ATP by PNIPAM. SEM images showed that pure ATP had a fibrous morphology, while the composite displayed a rough, aggregated structure with polymer layers covering the fibers.

3.3 Thermal properties
TGA showed that ATP had a weight loss of 12.5% up to 600 °C, mainly due to dehydration. The composite exhibited a two-step degradation: 8.2% below 200 °C (moisture) and 42.3% between 300 and 450 °C, attributed to PNIPAM decomposition. The residual mass at 600 °C was 49.5%, consistent with the ATP content.

3.4 LCST and drug release
The LCST of ATP/PNIPAM was 32.5 °C, slightly higher than pure PNIPAM (31.8 °C) due to hydrophilic ATP interactions. The DLE was 28.6%. Release profiles showed that at 25 °C, cumulative release reached 45.2% after 12 h, whereas at 37 °C it reached 78.9%. The initial burst release at 37 °C was 32.1% within 2 h, compared to 18.4% at 25 °C.

4. Discussion
The incorporation of ATP into PNIPAM networks improved the structural stability and provided additional adsorption sites. The FTIR and XRD results confirmed that ATP was well dispersed and interacted with the polymer through hydrogen bonding. The slight increase in LCST can be explained by the hydrophilic nature of ATP, which disrupts hydrophobic aggregation of PNIPAM chains.

The thermosensitive release behavior is attributed to the phase transition of PNIPAM. Below LCST, the polymer chains are extended and hydrophilic, forming a swollen network that restricts drug diffusion. Above LCST, the chains collapse, expelling water and creating channels for drug release. The higher release at 37 °C indicates that the composite can release drug preferentially at body temperature, which is advantageous for fever-related or tumor-site targeting.

Compared with pure PNIPAM, the ATP/PNIPAM composite showed a more sustained release without a large initial burst, likely due to the tortuous diffusion path created by ATP fibers. The DLE of 28.6% is moderate and could be further improved by optimizing ATP content or drug loading conditions.

5. Conclusion
A thermosensitive ATP/PNIPAM composite was successfully synthesized by in-situ radical polymerization. The composite exhibited an LCST of 32.5 °C and achieved a drug loading efficiency of 28.6% for ibuprofen. In-vitro release was significantly faster at 37 °C than at 25 °C, demonstrating a temperature-controlled “on–off” release mechanism. The hybrid material shows potential as a smart carrier for controlled drug delivery. Future work will focus on cytotoxicity evaluation and in-vivo studies.

title: Does the adaptation of climate-smart agricultural practices increase farmers' resilience to climate change?
text:
Does the Adaptation of Climate-Smart Agricultural Practices Increase Farmers' Resilience to Climate Change?

 Abstract

Climate change poses a significant threat to agricultural systems worldwide, particularly in developing countries where smallholder farmers depend on rain-fed agriculture. Climate-smart agricultural (CSA) practices have been promoted as a strategy to enhance farmers' resilience to climate-related shocks. This study investigates whether the adaptation of CSA practices increases farmers' resilience to climate change in the Upper East Region of Ghana. Using a cross-sectional survey of 420 farming households, we employed a multinomial endogenous switching regression model to account for selection bias and estimate the impact of CSA adoption on resilience. Resilience was measured using a composite index comprising adaptive capacity, absorptive capacity, and transformative capacity. Results indicate that adopting multiple CSA practices significantly increases farmers' resilience index by 0.187 to 0.312 standard deviations compared to non-adopters. Specifically, farmers who adopted a combination of drought-tolerant varieties, soil and water conservation techniques, and crop diversification experienced the highest resilience gains. The findings suggest that promoting integrated CSA packages rather than single practices could substantially enhance farmer resilience. Policy implications include strengthening extension services, improving access to climate information, and providing targeted credit facilities to facilitate CSA adoption.

Keywords: Climate-smart agriculture, resilience, climate change adaptation, smallholder farmers, Ghana, endogenous switching regression

 1. Introduction

Climate change is increasingly recognized as one of the most pressing challenges facing global agriculture in the twenty-first century. Rising temperatures, erratic rainfall patterns, and increased frequency of extreme weather events such as droughts and floods have significantly affected agricultural productivity and rural livelihoods (IPCC, 2022). Smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa are particularly vulnerable due to their heavy reliance on rain-fed agriculture, limited access to modern inputs, and constrained adaptive capacity (Morton, 2007).

In response to these challenges, climate-smart agriculture (CSA) has emerged as a promising approach to sustainably increase productivity, enhance resilience, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions where possible (Lipper et al., 2014). CSA encompasses a range of practices including drought-tolerant crop varieties, soil and water conservation techniques, agroforestry, crop diversification, and improved livestock management. These practices are designed to help farmers cope with climate variability while maintaining or improving agricultural productivity.

Despite the growing body of literature on CSA adoption, there remains limited empirical evidence on whether these practices actually increase farmers' resilience to climate change, particularly in West African contexts. Most existing studies focus on adoption determinants or productivity impacts rather than resilience outcomes (Aryal et al., 2018). Furthermore, few studies have examined the differential effects of adopting single versus multiple CSA practices.

This study addresses these gaps by examining the impact of CSA adoption on farmers' resilience in the Upper East Region of Ghana, an area characterized by high climate vulnerability, erratic rainfall, and widespread poverty. Specifically, we address two research questions: (1) Does the adoption of CSA practices increase farmers' resilience to climate change? (2) Do farmers who adopt multiple CSA practices exhibit higher resilience than those adopting single practices?

We contribute to the literature by constructing a multidimensional resilience index and employing a robust econometric approach that accounts for potential selection bias in CSA adoption. Our findings provide empirical evidence to inform policies aimed at enhancing climate resilience among smallholder farmers.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Study Area

The study was conducted in the Upper East Region of Ghana, located in the Sudan Savannah agro-ecological zone. The region experiences a unimodal rainfall pattern with an average annual precipitation of 800-1,100 mm, characterized by high inter-annual variability. The predominant farming system is smallholder rain-fed agriculture, with major crops including millet, sorghum, maize, groundnuts, and cowpea. The region has been identified as one of the most climate-vulnerable areas in Ghana, experiencing recurrent droughts and floods.

 2.2 Sampling and Data Collection

A multistage sampling procedure was employed. First, three districts (Bongo, Kassena-Nankana East, and Talensi) were purposively selected based on their exposure to climate shocks and prevalence of CSA promotion programs. Second, five communities were randomly selected from each district. Third, farming households were randomly selected from household lists provided by community leaders. A total of 420 farming households were surveyed between March and June 2023.

Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered by trained enumerators. The questionnaire captured information on household demographics, farm characteristics, climate shock experiences, CSA adoption, access to extension services, credit access, and various indicators of resilience. Focus group discussions and key informant interviews supplemented the quantitative data.

 2.3 Measuring Resilience

We constructed a composite Resilience Index (RI) based on the three-dimensional framework proposed by Bahadur et al. (2015), comprising:

Absorptive capacity: Ability to absorb shocks without significant loss of function. Indicators included household asset ownership, savings, food stock, and access to remittances.

Adaptive capacity: Ability to adjust to changing conditions. Indicators included education level, access to climate information, membership in farmer groups, and use of improved inputs.

Transformative capacity: Ability to create fundamental changes in livelihood systems. Indicators included income diversification, access to markets, and engagement in non-farm activities.

Each indicator was normalized using min-max scaling, and the composite index was calculated as the weighted average of the three dimensions, with weights derived from principal component analysis. The resulting index ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater resilience.

 2.4 CSA Practices

We focused on five CSA practices promoted in the study area:
1. Drought-tolerant crop varieties
2. Soil and water conservation techniques (e.g., contour bunding, mulching)
3. Crop diversification
4. Agroforestry
5. Improved livestock management

Farmers were categorized into four groups based on adoption status: non-adopters (0 practices), low adopters (1 practice), medium adopters (2-3 practices), and high adopters (4-5 practices).

 2.5 Empirical Strategy

To estimate the impact of CSA adoption on resilience while accounting for potential selection bias, we employed a multinomial endogenous switching regression (MESR) model. This approach is appropriate when farmers self-select into multiple adoption categories and unobserved factors may affect both adoption decisions and resilience outcomes.

The MESR model proceeds in two stages. In the first stage, a multinomial logit model estimates the probability of adopting different combinations of CSA practices. In the second stage, separate ordinary least squares regressions are estimated for each adoption category, incorporating inverse Mills ratios derived from the first stage to correct for selection bias. Counterfactual scenarios are then constructed to estimate average treatment effects.

Control variables included age, gender, education, household size, farm size, land tenure, access to extension, credit access, distance to market, and climate shock experience.

 3. Results

 3.1 Descriptive Statistics

Table 1 presents summary statistics for the sample. The average age of household heads was 47.3 years, and 68.6% were male. Mean household size was 6.2 persons, and average farm size was 2.4 hectares. Approximately 42% of respondents had no formal education. Access to extension services was reported by 38.1% of farmers, while only 22.4% had access to credit.

Regarding CSA adoption, 18.3% of farmers were non-adopters, 31.2% were low adopters, 35.7% were medium adopters, and 14.8% were high adopters. The most commonly adopted practice was crop diversification (67.4%), followed by soil and water conservation (52.1%), drought-tolerant varieties (44.3%), agroforestry (28.6%), and improved livestock management (21.9%).

 3.2 Determinants of CSA Adoption

Results from the multinomial logit model (Table 2) show that education, access to extension services, credit access, and climate shock experience significantly influenced CSA adoption. Farmers with at least primary education were 1.8 times more likely to be high adopters compared to those without formal education. Access to extension services increased the probability of being a medium or high adopter by 12.4 and 8.7 percentage points, respectively. Farmers who had experienced climate shocks in the past five years were more likely to adopt multiple CSA practices.

 3.3 Impact of CSA on Resilience

Table 3 presents the average treatment effects estimated from the MESR model. The results indicate that CSA adoption significantly increases farmers' resilience index. Compared to non-adopters, low adopters had a resilience index 0.187 standard deviations higher, medium adopters 0.254 standard deviations higher, and high adopters 0.312 standard deviations higher. All effects were statistically significant at the 1% level.

Disaggregating by resilience dimensions, we found that CSA adoption had the strongest impact on adaptive capacity (0.341 SD for high adopters), followed by absorptive capacity (0.278 SD) and transformative capacity (0.219 SD). This suggests that CSA practices primarily enhance farmers' ability to adjust to changing conditions rather than fundamentally transforming their livelihood systems.

 3.4 Heterogeneous Effects

We examined heterogeneous effects across different farmer characteristics. The resilience gains from CSA adoption were larger for farmers with smaller landholdings (<2 hectares) compared to larger farms, suggesting that CSA may be particularly beneficial for resource-poor farmers. Similarly, female-headed households experienced greater resilience gains from CSA adoption than male-headed households, though the difference was only marginally significant (p<0.10).

 4. Discussion

This study provides empirical evidence that the adaptation of climate-smart agricultural practices significantly increases farmers' resilience to climate change in the Upper East Region of Ghana. Our findings align with previous research suggesting that CSA can enhance adaptive capacity and reduce vulnerability (Aryal et al., 2018; Mwungu et al., 2020).

The finding that multiple CSA practices generate greater resilience benefits than single practices is particularly important. This suggests synergistic effects, where combining practices such as drought-tolerant varieties with soil and water conservation creates more robust farming systems than any single intervention. This supports the argument for promoting integrated CSA packages rather than isolated technologies (Lipper et al., 2014).

The stronger impact of CSA on adaptive capacity compared to transformative capacity highlights both the potential and limitations of CSA. While CSA helps farmers adjust to changing conditions, it may not fundamentally alter the structural constraints that keep smallholders vulnerable, such as limited market access, weak institutions, and poverty. Complementary interventions beyond farm-level practices may be needed to achieve transformative resilience.

The heterogeneous effects observed suggest that CSA may be particularly beneficial for resource-poor and female-headed households, who are often the most vulnerable to climate change. This has important equity implications, suggesting that CSA promotion could contribute to reducing vulnerability gaps if targeted appropriately.

However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, our cross-sectional design limits causal inference, although the MESR model addresses selection bias to some extent. Second, resilience is a multidimensional concept that is challenging to measure, and our index, while comprehensive, may not capture all relevant dimensions. Third, the study is limited to one region of Ghana, and findings may not be generalizable to other contexts.

 5. Conclusion

This study examined whether the adaptation of climate-smart agricultural practices increases farmers' resilience to climate change in the Upper East Region of Ghana. Using a multinomial endogenous switching regression model and a composite resilience index, we found that CSA adoption significantly enhances farmers' resilience, with the greatest benefits accruing to those who adopt multiple practices.

Our findings have important policy implications. First, efforts to promote CSA should emphasize integrated packages rather than single practices to maximize resilience benefits. Second, strengthening extension services and improving access to climate information are crucial for facilitating CSA adoption. Third, targeted support for resource-poor and female-headed households could help ensure that CSA contributes to equitable resilience building.

Future research should employ longitudinal designs to better establish causality and examine the long-term resilience impacts of CSA adoption. Additionally, research should explore how contextual factors such as market access, institutional support, and social networks mediate the relationship between CSA and resilience.

In conclusion, climate-smart agriculture represents a promising pathway for enhancing smallholder farmers' resilience to climate change. However, realizing this potential requires supportive policies, institutional arrangements, and investments that enable farmers to adopt and sustain these practices over time.

 References

Aryal, J. P., Jat, M. L., Sapkota, T. B., Khatri-Chhetri, A., Kassie, M., Rahut, D. B., & Maharjan, S. (2018). Adoption of multiple climate-smart agricultural practices in the Gangetic plains of Bihar, India. *International Journal of Climate Change Strategies and Management*, 10(3), 407-427.

Bahadur, A. V., Peters, K., Wilkinson, E., Pichon, F., Gray, K., & Tanner, T. (2015). The 3As: Tracking resilience across BRACED. *BRACED Working Paper*.

IPCC. (2022). Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. *Contribution of Working Group II to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change*. Cambridge University Press.

Lipper, L., Thornton, P., Campbell, B. M., Baedeker, T., Braimoh, A., Bwalya, M., ... & Hottle, R. (2014). Climate-smart agriculture for food security. *Nature Climate Change*, 4(12), 1068-1072.

Morton, J. F. (2007). The impact of climate change on smallholder and subsistence agriculture. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 104(50), 19680-19685.

Mwungu, C. M., Mwongera, C., Shikuku, K. M., Acosta, M., & Läderach, P. (2020). Determinants of adoption of climate-smart agriculture technologies at farm plot level: An assessment from southern Tanzania. *Sustainability*, 12(2), 520.

title: Microbial carbon source utilization in rice rhizosphere soil with different tillage practice in a double cropping rice field
text: Abstract: Soil microorganisms play a pivotal role in carbon (C) cycling and nutrient turnover in paddy ecosystems; however, how long-term tillage practices regulate microbial C source utilization in the rhizosphere of double cropping rice remains poorly understood. Here, rhizosphere soils were collected from a long-term tillage experiment in a double cropping rice field, comprising conventional tillage with residue removal (CT), rotary tillage with residue retention (RT), and no-tillage with residue retention (NT). Microbial C source utilization patterns were characterized using Biolog EcoPlate analysis, and soil physicochemical properties and enzyme activities were determined to elucidate the underlying drivers. Results showed that tillage practice significantly altered the average well color development (AWCD) and Shannon–Wiener and McIntosh indices, with NT and RT exhibiting higher overall C source utilization and functional diversity than CT in both early and late rice seasons. Among the six C source categories, carbohydrates, carboxylic acids, and amino acids were preferentially utilized, whereas polymers and amines were less utilized. Principal component analysis and redundancy analysis indicated that microbial C source utilization was primarily driven by soil organic carbon, total nitrogen, available phosphorus, and dissolved organic carbon, which were higher under NT and RT. Partial least squares path modeling further revealed that tillage-induced changes in soil nutrient status indirectly regulated microbial C metabolism by shaping the composition and activity of the microbial community. Notably, the response of rhizosphere microorganisms to tillage was season-dependent, with stronger treatment effects observed in the late rice season. These findings demonstrate that no-tillage and rotary tillage with residue retention enhance the functional diversity of rhizosphere microbial communities and their capacity to utilize labile C sources, thereby favoring soil C sequestration and nutrient supply in double cropping rice systems. The results provide a microbiological basis for optimizing tillage management to sustain soil health and productivity in intensive paddy agriculture.

title: A multimodal deep learning framework for predicting drug-drug interaction events
text:
A multimodal deep learning framework for predicting drug-drug interaction events

Abstract
Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are a major cause of adverse clinical outcomes, yet preclinical detection remains incomplete because pharmacological, structural, and textual evidence are rarely integrated in a unified model. This study proposes a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts specific DDI event types by jointly encoding drug molecular graphs, target-binding profiles, and biomedical literature semantics. The model combines a graph convolutional network for chemical structure, a sparse autoencoder for protein-target signatures, and a domain-adapted language model for literature-derived embeddings. Using a curated dataset of 1,842 approved drugs and 191,953 pairwise instances covering 64 DDI event categories, the framework achieved a macro-F1 of 0.812 and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.947 under five-fold cross-validation, outperforming single-modality and concatenation-based baselines. Ablation analysis indicated that target and literature modalities contributed complementary gains, especially for rare metabolic and cardiovascular events. These results suggest that multimodal fusion offers a practical route to mechanism-aware DDI event prediction and may support pharmacovigilance prioritization.

Keywords: drug-drug interaction; multimodal learning; graph neural network; pharmacovigilance; event prediction; deep learning

1. Introduction
Combination pharmacotherapy is common in chronic disease management, but co-administered drugs may interact through pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic mechanisms, producing bleeding, arrhythmia, hepatotoxicity, or reduced efficacy. Traditional DDI screening relies on spontaneous reporting systems, clinical trials, and rule-based databases. Although these resources are valuable, they suffer from under-reporting, delayed curation, and limited coverage of rare or newly approved agents. Computational prediction has therefore attracted increasing attention, with early methods using chemical similarity, target overlap, or matrix factorization. More recent approaches employ deep neural networks on molecular fingerprints or knowledge graph embeddings. However, most existing models treat DDI prediction as binary classification and ignore event specificity, although clinical management depends on whether an interaction causes QT prolongation, hyperkalemia, or another distinct outcome. Moreover, single-modality models cannot capture the fact that DDI mechanisms emerge from chemical structure, biological target context, and accumulated biomedical evidence. To address these gaps, this study develops a multimodal deep learning framework for multi-class DDI event prediction. The contributions are threefold: (i) a fusion architecture integrating molecular graphs, target profiles, and literature embeddings; (ii) systematic evaluation across 64 event categories; and (iii) interpretability analysis linking model attention to known pharmacological mechanisms.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Data collection and preprocessing. Drug entities were obtained from a simulated integrated resource combining DrugBank-like identifiers, PubChem-like structures, and literature abstracts. After filtering, 1,842 drugs were retained. Pairwise DDI events were generated from a curated interaction table, yielding 191,953 positive instances across 64 event labels. Negative instances were sampled at a 1:2 ratio using drugs with no recorded interaction and were verified against structured contraindication fields. Molecular graphs were constructed with atoms as nodes and bonds as edges; atomic features included element type, degree, formal charge, aromaticity, and hybridization. Target profiles were represented as 2,048-dimensional binary vectors from 1,536 protein targets. Literature embeddings were generated by a biomedical language model fine-tuned on 1.2 million PubMed-like abstracts, producing 768-dimensional vectors for each drug.

2.2 Model architecture. The framework contains three encoders. The chemical encoder is a four-layer graph convolutional network with mean pooling and batch normalization. The target encoder is a sparse autoencoder with a 512-unit bottleneck, intended to denoise incomplete binding annotations. The text encoder applies a transformer layer followed by attention pooling. Drug-level representations from the three branches are concatenated and passed through a gated fusion module, which learns modality weights for each drug pair. The fused pair representation is formed by element-wise product and absolute difference, then classified by a two-layer multilayer perceptron with dropout (0.3) and softmax output over 64 event classes.

2.3 Training and evaluation. The model was trained with categorical cross-entropy and the Adam optimizer (learning rate 1e-4, batch size 128, early stopping patience 10). Five-fold cross-validation was used, with splits at the drug-pair level to avoid leakage. Performance was measured by macro-F1, micro-F1, area under the curve (AUC), and precision at top 10%. Baselines included logistic regression on fingerprints, random forest on target overlap, a graph-only network, a target-only network, a text-only network, and a concatenation model without gating.

3. Results and Analysis
The proposed framework achieved a macro-F1 of 0.812, micro-F1 of 0.847, and AUC of 0.947. The graph-only, target-only, and text-only models reached macro-F1 scores of 0.703, 0.681, and 0.724, respectively. The concatenation baseline improved to 0.769, while gated fusion produced the best result, indicating that adaptive modality weighting is beneficial. For frequent event categories such as bleeding risk and QT prolongation, F1 exceeded 0.86. Performance was lower for rare events such as serotonin syndrome (F1 = 0.714) and rhabdomyolysis (F1 = 0.698), likely due to limited positive examples. Ablation showed that removing the literature branch reduced macro-F1 by 6.1%, removing targets reduced it by 5.4%, and removing chemical graphs reduced it by 8.7%. When all three modalities were retained, precision at top 10% reached 0.901, suggesting utility for screening. Error analysis revealed that confusions often occurred between mechanistically related events, such as hyperkalemia and renal impairment, implying partial biological overlap rather than random misclassification.

4. Discussion
The results support the hypothesis that DDI event prediction benefits from multimodal evidence. Chemical structure captures intrinsic reactivity and transporter affinity; target profiles reflect shared pathways; literature embeddings encode human-curated clinical observations. The gated fusion module allowed the model to emphasize different modalities depending on drug class. For example, predictions for anticoagulant-antiplatelet pairs relied more on target features, whereas hepatotoxicity predictions for antifungal agents benefited from literature signals. Interpretability analysis using attention weights showed enrichment for known cytochrome P450 and hERG-related targets, providing preliminary mechanistic plausibility. Nevertheless, several limitations remain. First, the dataset is simulated and may not fully represent clinical heterogeneity. Second, negative sampling may introduce false negatives. Third, the model predicts associations rather than causal mechanisms, and temporal effects such as dose dependency are not modeled. Future work should incorporate electronic health records, pharmacokinetic parameters, and prospective validation.

5. Conclusion
This study presents a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates molecular graphs, target-binding profiles, and biomedical literature for DDI event prediction. The model outperformed single-modality and simple fusion baselines, achieving a macro-F1 of 0.812 and AUC of 0.947 across 64 event categories. The findings indicate that mechanism-aware, multi-source representation learning can improve DDI risk stratification and may assist pharmacovigilance and clinical decision support. Further validation with real-world clinical data is warranted.

title: CsBRC1 inhibits axillary bud outgrowth by directly repressing the auxin efflux carrier CsPIN3 in cucumber
text:
Cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.) is an economically important vegetable crop worldwide, and plant architecture, particularly the pattern of lateral branching, directly affects its cultivation density, light interception, and fruit yield. Axillary bud outgrowth determines the number of lateral branches and is tightly regulated by a complex network involving phytohormones, transcription factors, and environmental signals. Among these regulators, strigolactones (SLs) and auxin play central roles in suppressing bud activation, while cytokinins promote bud outgrowth. However, the molecular mechanisms by which these signals are integrated to control bud dormancy in cucumber remain largely unknown.

BRC1 (BRANCHED1), a TCP-family transcription factor, is a conserved key integrator of branching signals in diverse plant species. It is preferentially expressed in axillary buds and acts as a negative regulator of bud outgrowth downstream of SLs and auxin. Despite its evolutionary conservation, the downstream targets of BRC1 and the precise mechanism by which it represses bud outgrowth are still poorly understood, especially in cucurbit crops. Auxin efflux carriers of the PIN family mediate polar auxin transport and are essential for establishing auxin maxima that influence bud activity. Whether BRC1 directly regulates PIN genes to modulate bud outgrowth has not been demonstrated in cucumber.

Here, we identify CsBRC1 as a negative regulator of axillary bud outgrowth in cucumber. We show that CsBRC1 is highly expressed in dormant axillary buds and that its expression is induced by auxin and SL treatment. Using biochemical and genetic approaches, we demonstrate that CsBRC1 directly binds to the promoter of CsPIN3, an auxin efflux carrier gene, and represses its transcription. This repression reduces auxin transport from the bud, leading to auxin accumulation and inhibition of bud outgrowth. Our findings reveal a novel BRC1–PIN3 regulatory module that links strigolactone and auxin signaling to bud dormancy, providing new insights into the molecular control of plant architecture in cucumber.

title: ACC Deaminase from Lysobacter gummosus OH17 Can Promote Root Growth in Oryza sativa Nipponbare Plants
text:
Results and Discussion

*L. gummosus* OH17 grown in DF minimal medium with 5 mM ACC as sole nitrogen source reached an OD₆₀₀ of 1.42 ± 0.08 after 48 h, while no growth occurred in nitrogen-free controls, confirming ACC-dependent growth. ACC deaminase activity in cell-free extracts peaked during late exponential phase at 412 ± 27 nmol α-ketobutyrate mg⁻¹ protein h⁻¹, approximately 6-fold higher than the activity measured in the reference strain *P. putida* UW4 (68 ± 9 nmol mg⁻¹ h⁻¹) under identical conditions. The corresponding *acdS* gene was amplified and sequenced (1,017 bp; 98.7% identity to *L. gummosus* 3.1.6), and its product contains the conserved KXSC motif required for catalytic activity.

Inoculation of *O. sativa* Nipponbare seedlings with OH17 significantly promoted root development. After 14 days in gnotobiotic culture, root length increased from 8.9 ± 0.7 cm (uninoculated control) to 12.4 ± 0.9 cm (+39%), and lateral root number rose from 6.2 ± 1.1 to 10.8 ± 1.4 per plant (+74%) (P < 0.01, n = 20). Fresh root biomass increased by 46% (from 38 ± 4 to 55 ± 6 mg plant⁻¹). An *acdS* deletion mutant (ΔacdS) abolished these effects; root length (9.3 ± 0.8 cm) did not differ significantly from the control, and complementation with wild-type *acdS* restored the phenotype (11.9 ± 1.0 cm). These results demonstrate that ACC deaminase is the principal mediator of root growth promotion by strain OH17, likely by lowering root ethylene levels and thereby relieving ethylene-mediated inhibition of root elongation.

title: Marker-assisted selection of YY supermales from a genetically improved farmed tilapia-derived strain
text:
Marker-assisted selection of YY supermales from a genetically improved farmed tilapia-derived strain

Abstract

The production of all-male Nile tilapia (*Oreochromis niloticus*) populations is a cornerstone of commercial aquaculture because males grow faster and reduce uncontrolled reproduction in ponds. YY supermale technology offers a genetic alternative to hormone-based sex reversal, but its efficiency depends on the accurate identification of sex-determining genotypes. In this study, we developed and applied a marker-assisted selection (MAS) pipeline to identify YY supermales from a genetically improved farmed tilapia (GIFT)-derived strain. A male-specific marker tightly linked to the sex-determining region was screened across 480 candidate fish. Putative YY males were first identified by testcrosses and then confirmed by marker genotyping and progeny sex-ratio analysis. Among 36 candidate males, 5 were diagnosed as YY supermales. Crossing these supermales with normal XX females produced 98.7–100% male progeny in experimental tanks, with an overall male proportion of 99.2%. Growth performance of the all-male progeny was superior to that of mixed-sex controls, with a 17.8% increase in average body weight after 120 days. The results demonstrate that MAS combined with testcross validation can efficiently recover YY supermales from a GIFT-derived population and support the large-scale production of genetically male tilapia without hormonal treatment.

Keywords: Nile tilapia; YY supermale; marker-assisted selection; sex determination; GIFT strain; all-male population

1. Introduction

Nile tilapia (*Oreochromis niloticus*) is one of the most widely cultured freshwater fish species worldwide. Its rapid growth, tolerance to diverse environmental conditions, and acceptance by consumers have made it a major protein source in many tropical and subtropical regions. In tilapia farming, mixed-sex populations often lead to excessive reproduction, stunted growth, and variable harvest sizes. Therefore, the production of all-male populations is highly desirable because males generally grow faster than females and because a male-only population prevents uncontrolled recruitment in production ponds.

Traditionally, all-male tilapia has been produced by dietary administration of androgens, most commonly 17α-methyltestosterone, during early gonadal differentiation. Although effective, hormone-based sex reversal raises concerns regarding food safety, environmental release, and consumer acceptance. As a result, genetic approaches to male production have attracted increasing attention. Among these, the YY supermale technology is particularly promising. In the XX/XY sex-determination system of Nile tilapia, normal males are XY and normal females are XX. A YY individual, although rare, is genetically male and, when crossed with an XX female, produces exclusively XY male offspring. Thus, YY supermales provide a sustainable genetic route to all-male production.

The practical bottleneck in YY supermale technology is the reliable identification of YY individuals. Because YY and XY males are phenotypically similar, progeny testing has traditionally been required. However, progeny testing is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and dependent on successful spawning. Marker-assisted selection (MAS) can accelerate this process by genotyping candidate males at sex-linked molecular markers before or in parallel with testcrosses. The genetically improved farmed tilapia (GIFT) strain, developed through selective breeding for growth, provides an excellent genetic background for combining improved growth with YY-based male production. Nevertheless, the recovery of YY supermales from GIFT-derived populations requires a validated MAS workflow.

In this study, we aimed to establish a marker-assisted selection pipeline for identifying YY supermales from a GIFT-derived strain of Nile tilapia. The specific objectives were to screen candidate males with a male-specific marker, confirm putative YY genotypes by testcrosses, evaluate progeny sex ratios, and assess the growth performance of all-male offspring. The results are expected to provide a practical framework for genetic male tilapia production.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Fish materials and rearing conditions

The base population was derived from a GIFT strain maintained at an experimental aquaculture station. A total of 480 fish, including 240 presumed males and 240 presumed females, were used for initial marker screening. Fish were reared in 1.5 m³ circular tanks with recirculating freshwater at 26–28 °C, dissolved oxygen above 5 mg/L, and pH 7.0–8.0. Fish were fed a commercial diet containing 32% crude protein twice daily at 3–5% body weight. All procedures followed institutional animal care guidelines.

2.2 Marker screening

Fin clips were collected from all 480 fish and preserved in 95% ethanol. Genomic DNA was extracted using a standard salt-extraction protocol. A male-specific sequence-characterized amplified region (SCAR) marker, designated MsT-1, was used for sex genotyping. The marker was previously reported to be tightly linked to the sex-determining region in Nile tilapia. PCR reactions were performed in 20 μL volumes containing 50 ng DNA, 1× PCR buffer, 2.0 mM MgCl₂, 0.2 mM dNTPs, 0.4 μM each primer, and 1 U Taq polymerase. Amplification conditions were 94 °C for 4 min; 35 cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 58 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 45 s; and a final extension at 72 °C for 7 min. Products were resolved on 1.5% agarose gels. Males were expected to show a 520 bp band, whereas females were expected to lack this band.

2.3 Identification of putative YY males

Males positive for MsT-1 were selected as candidate XY or YY individuals. Because the marker cannot distinguish XY from YY males, all marker-positive males were subjected to testcrosses with known XX females. A total of 36 candidate males were used in testcrosses. Each male was mated with two to three virgin XX females in separate haploid breeding hapas. After spawning, eggs were collected, incubated, and reared separately by family. Progeny were raised to 60 days post-hatch, and sex was determined by gonadal inspection and marker genotyping.

2.4 Progeny sex ratio and growth evaluation

For each testcross family, at least 80 progeny were sexed. Families producing 100% male progeny were considered to be derived from YY sires. Confirmed YY supermales were then crossed with XX females to produce experimental all-male populations. A mixed-sex control group was produced from XY male × XX female crosses. Both groups were reared in triplicate tanks for 120 days. Body weight, body length, and survival were recorded at 0, 60, and 120 days. Growth data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA, and sex ratios were tested against expected ratios using chi-square analysis.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Marker amplification and initial screening

The MsT-1 marker produced a clear 520 bp band in 236 of 240 presumed males and in none of the 240 presumed females. The remaining four presumed males failed to amplify and were excluded from further analysis. The marker therefore showed 98.3% concordance with phenotypic sex in the sampled population. Among the 236 marker-positive males, 36 were randomly selected for testcross evaluation based on body size and sexual maturity.

3.2 Testcross identification of YY supermales

Of the 36 candidate males, 31 produced progeny with sex ratios consistent with normal XY males. Their male proportions ranged from 48.9% to 55.2%, with an overall male ratio of 51.6% (χ² = 0.87, P > 0.05), which did not deviate significantly from the expected 1:1 ratio. The remaining five males produced progeny with male proportions of 98.7%, 99.1%, 99.4%, 100%, and 100%, respectively. These five males were diagnosed as YY supermales. The overall male proportion among their progeny was 99.2% (1,984 males out of 2,000 progeny), which was significantly different from 1:1 (χ² = 1,936.5, P < 0.001). The five YY supermales were designated YY-1 to YY-5.

3.3 Progeny performance of YY supermales

Crosses between confirmed YY supermales and XX females produced all-male or nearly all-male progeny. In the experimental production trial, the male proportion was 99.4% for YY-1, 99.0% for YY-2, 99.6% for YY-3, 100% for YY-4, and 100% for YY-5. No significant differences in fertilization rate or hatching rate were observed between YY crosses and control XY crosses (P > 0.05). Survival at 120 days was 91.2% in the all-male group and 89.7% in the mixed-sex control, with no significant difference (P > 0.05).

3.4 Growth performance

At 120 days, the all-male group had an average body weight of 286.4 ± 18.7 g, whereas the mixed-sex control had an average body weight of 243.1 ± 21.5 g. The all-male group showed a 17.8% increase in body weight compared with the control (P < 0.01). Average body length was 22.6 ± 0.9 cm in the all-male group and 21.1 ± 1.1 cm in the control (P < 0.05). The coefficient of variation for body weight was lower in the all-male group (6.5%) than in the mixed-sex control (8.8%), indicating more uniform growth. Feed conversion ratio was 1.42 in the all-male group and 1.55 in the control.

4. Discussion

The present study demonstrates that marker-assisted selection can efficiently identify YY supermales from a GIFT-derived Nile tilapia population. The MsT-1 marker showed high concordance with phenotypic sex and allowed the preselection of male candidates before testcrossing. This is important because testcrossing alone requires substantial tank space, mature females, and several months of progeny rearing. By reducing the number of candidates requiring testcrosses, MAS improved the efficiency of YY recovery.

The frequency of YY supermales in the candidate group was 13.9% (5 out of 36), which is higher than expected under a simple XX/XY model unless YY individuals were already present at low frequency in the founder population. This finding suggests that the GIFT-derived strain used here may carry segregating YY genotypes or that the sex-determining region has a more complex architecture than the classical single-locus model. Similar observations have been reported in other tilapia populations, where sex determination can be influenced by minor autosomal loci or environmental factors. Nevertheless, the near-100% male progeny produced by the five confirmed supermales supports their YY genotype.

The growth advantage of all-male progeny is consistent with previous studies. Males grow faster and more uniformly, which is advantageous for market-sized production. In this trial, the all-male group showed a 17.8% weight advantage at 120 days and a lower coefficient of variation. This is economically relevant because uniform size reduces grading costs and improves market value. The absence of significant differences in survival and fertilization rate also indicates that YY supermales do not suffer obvious reproductive penalties under the tested conditions.

From a practical perspective, the MAS pipeline described here can be integrated into existing GIFT breeding programs. Once YY supermales are identified, they can be maintained and crossed with selected XX females to produce all-male fingerlings. However, several limitations should be noted. First, the marker used here is linked to, but not necessarily within, the sex-determining locus; recombination could produce false positives or false negatives. Second, the number of YY supermales recovered was small, and their long-term reproductive performance and genetic diversity need further evaluation. Third, the influence of temperature or other environmental factors on sex ratio was not examined in this study.

Future work should focus on developing more tightly linked or functional markers for the sex-determining region, validating the MAS pipeline across multiple GIFT families, and assessing the growth and disease resistance of all-male populations under commercial pond conditions. Incorporating genomic selection for growth alongside MAS for sex genotype could further enhance the value of YY supermale technology.

5. Conclusion

This study established a marker-assisted selection workflow for identifying YY supermales from a GIFT-derived Nile tilapia strain. The male-specific marker MsT-1 enabled efficient preselection of male candidates, and testcross validation confirmed five YY supermales among 36 candidates. Crosses between these supermales and XX females produced 98.7–100% male progeny, with an overall male proportion of 99.2%. The all-male progeny showed a 17.8% growth advantage over mixed-sex controls at 120 days. These results indicate that MAS is a practical and effective approach for recovering YY supermales and for supporting genetically male tilapia production without hormonal treatment.

title: Solid lipid nanoparticles for enhanced oral absorption: A review
text:
Solid Lipid Nanoparticles for Enhanced Oral Absorption: A Review

 Abstract

The oral route remains the most preferred route of drug administration due to its convenience, patient compliance, and cost-effectiveness. However, approximately 40% of marketed drugs and up to 90% of drugs in development exhibit poor aqueous solubility, resulting in limited oral bioavailability. Solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) have emerged as promising colloidal drug delivery systems capable of enhancing the oral absorption of poorly soluble drugs. This review examines the mechanisms, formulation strategies, and performance of SLNs in improving oral drug absorption. A systematic analysis of 47 studies published between 2015 and 2024 was conducted, focusing on physicochemical characterization and pharmacokinetic outcomes. Our analysis revealed that SLN formulations increased oral bioavailability by an average of 3.2-fold (range: 1.4–8.7-fold) compared to conventional formulations. The mean particle size of analyzed SLNs was 187 ± 62 nm, with entrapment efficiency averaging 78.4 ± 11.3%. Key mechanisms facilitating enhanced absorption include lymphatic transport, P-glycoprotein inhibition, and improved dissolution kinetics. This review provides comprehensive insights into SLN design considerations and identifies critical formulation parameters governing oral absorption enhancement.

Keywords: Solid lipid nanoparticles, oral bioavailability, lymphatic transport, P-glycoprotein, colloidal drug delivery, lipid-based formulations

 1. Introduction

The oral route of drug administration accounts for approximately 80% of all pharmaceutical products due to its non-invasive nature, ease of self-administration, and favorable safety profile (Smith et al., 2019). Despite these advantages, poor oral bioavailability remains a significant challenge, particularly for Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) Class II and IV compounds. The primary barriers include limited aqueous solubility, poor membrane permeability, extensive first-pass metabolism, and efflux transporter activity (Johnson & Lee, 2020).

Over the past two decades, lipid-based nanocarriers have gained considerable attention as vehicles for enhancing oral drug absorption. Among these, solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) represent a particularly promising approach. SLNs are colloidal particles with diameters typically ranging from 50 to 1000 nm, composed of solid lipids at room and body temperature, stabilized by surfactants (Müller et al., 2000). Unlike emulsion-based systems, SLNs offer the advantage of controlled drug release, enhanced physical stability, and the ability to incorporate both lipophilic and hydrophilic compounds.

The mechanisms by which SLNs enhance oral absorption are multifaceted. These include increased surface area for dissolution, improved solubilization capacity, lymphatic transport bypassing first-pass metabolism, and inhibition of efflux transporters such as P-glycoprotein (P-gp) (Chen et al., 2021). Additionally, the lipid matrix may facilitate transcellular and paracellular transport across the intestinal epithelium.

This review aims to systematically evaluate the current evidence on SLNs for oral absorption enhancement, analyze formulation parameters influencing performance, and identify knowledge gaps for future research directions.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Literature Search Strategy

A comprehensive literature search was conducted using PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science databases. Search terms included combinations of "solid lipid nanoparticles," "oral bioavailability," "oral absorption," "pharmacokinetics," and "intestinal transport." The search was limited to articles published in English between January 2015 and December 2024.

 2.2 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Studies were included if they: (1) utilized SLN formulations for oral administration; (2) reported pharmacokinetic parameters including AUC, Cmax, or relative bioavailability; (3) provided physicochemical characterization data; and (4) employed in vivo animal models or human subjects. Studies were excluded if they involved other nanocarrier types, lacked quantitative pharmacokinetic data, or were review articles.

 2.3 Data Extraction and Analysis

Data were extracted using a standardized form capturing formulation composition, lipid type, surfactant, particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, entrapment efficiency, drug loading, and pharmacokinetic parameters. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 26.0, with results expressed as mean ± standard deviation.

 3. Results

 3.1 Study Characteristics

Of 312 initially identified articles, 47 met the inclusion criteria. These studies investigated 52 distinct SLN formulations incorporating 38 different drugs. The most commonly studied drug categories were anticancer agents (28.8%), anti-inflammatory drugs (19.2%), and antihypertensive agents (15.4%).

 3.2 Physicochemical Characterization

The mean particle size across all formulations was 187 ± 62 nm (range: 85–412 nm). Formulations with particle sizes below 200 nm demonstrated superior absorption enhancement compared to larger particles (p < 0.05). The polydispersity index averaged 0.21 ± 0.08, indicating narrow size distributions. Zeta potential values ranged from -42.3 mV to +28.7 mV, with most formulations (71.2%) exhibiting negative surface charge.

Entrapment efficiency averaged 78.4 ± 11.3%, with lipophilic drugs showing higher encapsulation (84.2 ± 9.1%) compared to amphiphilic compounds (68.7 ± 12.4%). Drug loading ranged from 1.2% to 24.6%, with a mean of 9.8 ± 5.2%.

Common lipid matrices included stearic acid (23.1%), glyceryl monostearate (19.2%), Compritol 888 ATO (17.3%), and Precirol ATO 5 (13.5%). Poloxamer 188 (26.9%) and Tween 80 (21.2%) were the most frequently employed surfactants.

 3.3 Pharmacokinetic Enhancement

SLN formulations significantly enhanced oral bioavailability compared to conventional formulations. The mean relative bioavailability was 3.2-fold (range: 1.4–8.7-fold). Cmax increased by an average of 2.8-fold, while Tmax was prolonged from 1.2 ± 0.4 h to 3.6 ± 1.8 h, suggesting sustained release characteristics.

Subgroup analysis revealed that particle size significantly influenced bioavailability enhancement. Formulations with particle sizes <150 nm achieved 4.1-fold enhancement, compared to 2.6-fold for particles >250 nm (p < 0.01). Similarly, formulations incorporating P-gp inhibiting surfactants (e.g., Tween 80, Cremophor EL) showed greater enhancement (3.9-fold) than those with non-inhibiting surfactants (2.4-fold).

 3.4 Mechanisms of Absorption Enhancement

Lymphatic transport was identified as a major absorption pathway, with chylomicron association demonstrated in 68% of studies employing triglyceride-based lipids. P-gp inhibition contributed to enhanced absorption in formulations containing Tween 80 or Pluronic block copolymers. Additionally, 82% of studies reported improved dissolution profiles for SLN-encapsulated drugs compared to crystalline drug suspensions.

 4. Discussion

The findings of this review demonstrate that SLNs represent an effective strategy for enhancing oral drug absorption. The 3.2-fold average bioavailability enhancement is consistent with previous meta-analyses of lipid-based nanocarriers (Zhang et al., 2022). However, considerable variability exists across studies, reflecting differences in drug properties, formulation parameters, and experimental conditions.

Particle size emerged as a critical determinant of absorption enhancement. Smaller particles provide greater surface area for dissolution and are more efficiently transported across the intestinal epithelium via endocytic pathways. Furthermore, particles below 200 nm may avoid rapid clearance by the mononuclear phagocyte system, prolonging residence time in the gastrointestinal tract.

The lipid matrix composition significantly influences absorption mechanisms. Long-chain triglycerides promote lymphatic transport by stimulating chylomicron formation, thereby bypassing hepatic first-pass metabolism. This mechanism is particularly advantageous for drugs with extensive hepatic extraction. Medium-chain triglycerides, while less effective for lymphatic targeting, may enhance cellular uptake through alternative pathways.

Surfactant selection plays a dual role in SLN performance.
