Mangrove destruction for shrimp ponds declined in Southeast Asia but shifted to West Africa. Antibiotic use fell by 41% in Norway and Chile but rose in parts of South and Southeast Asia. Integrated multi-trophic aquaculture (IMTA) expanded in China, Canada, and Israel, though adoption remained below 3% of global area.

4. Discussion

The twenty-year trajectory reveals a sector that has successfully scaled production but has not yet decoupled growth from environmental externalities. Three patterns merit attention.

First, the centre of gravity has shifted from Atlantic-centred, high-value species to Asian-dominated, omnivorous freshwater species. This democratisation of aquaculture has improved protein accessibility but also concentrated environmental burdens in regions with weaker regulatory enforcement. The decline in China’s growth rate after 2019 suggests that even dominant producers face ecological ceilings.

Second, sustainability gains are uneven. Feed efficiency improvements in salmon and shrimp demonstrate that technological innovation can reduce pressure on wild stocks. However, the persistence of fishmeal dependency indicates that alternative proteins—insect meal, single-cell proteins, and fermented agricultural by-products—remain under-scaled. Disease management has improved through vaccines and selective breeding, yet antimicrobial resistance remains a latent crisis in several producing nations.

Third, climate change is no longer a future risk but a present constraint. Warming waters have expanded suitable zones for some species (e.g., tilapia in subtropical highlands) while contracting others (e.g., cold-water salmonids in southern Chile). Extreme weather events caused an estimated $2.3 billion in aquaculture losses between 2015 and 2024. Adaptation strategies such as offshore cages, selective breeding for thermal tolerance, and diversified polyculture are promising but geographically uneven.

The review also highlights a methodological limitation: global statistics undercount small-scale aquaculture, which employs an estimated 18–22 million people, many of them women. Future assessments should integrate household-level surveys and remote sensing to capture informal production and land-use change.

5. Conclusion

Between 2004 and 2024, global aquaculture transformed from a supplementary food source to a pillar of the blue economy, producing 130.2 million tonnes and supplying more than half of aquatic animal protein for human consumption. Growth was driven by Asian freshwater finfish, Latin American salmonids, and Southeast Asian crustaceans. Yet the sector’s ecological footprint—feed dependency, disease losses, habitat conversion, and climate vulnerability—remains substantial. The next twenty years will not reward volume alone. Resilience, circularity, and equity must become organising principles. Priority actions include scaling alternative aquafeeds, enforcing antimicrobial stewardship, expanding IMTA and offshore systems, and integrating small-scale producers into formal markets and climate adaptation finance. A 20-year retrospective thus offers not only a record of achievement but a clear mandate for transformation.

title: Manure and mineral fertilization change enzyme activity and bacterial community in millet rhizosphere soils
text: Millet (Setaria italica) is a staple cereal in semi-arid regions, yet its productivity remains constrained by low soil fertility and poor nutrient use efficiency. Fertilization is a common practice to sustain millet yields, but the excessive or unbalanced application of mineral fertilizers can degrade soil health, whereas manure amendments may improve soil biological functions. Rhizosphere microorganisms, particularly bacteria, play critical roles in nutrient cycling, organic matter decomposition, and plant growth promotion, and their community structure is highly sensitive to fertilization regimes. Soil enzymes, as indicators of microbial metabolic activity, mediate key biochemical processes such as carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus transformations. Although the effects of fertilization on soil physicochemical properties and crop yield have been widely documented, the responses of rhizosphere bacterial communities and enzyme activities to manure versus mineral fertilization in millet fields remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the changes in rhizosphere soil enzyme activities and bacterial community composition under different fertilization treatments, including no fertilization, mineral fertilization, and manure application. We hypothesized that manure amendment would enhance enzyme activities and shift bacterial community composition toward taxa associated with organic matter degradation and nutrient cycling. Our results aim to provide a microbiological basis for optimizing fertilization strategies to maintain soil health and sustainable millet production.

title: Construction of Rural Financial Organization Spatial Structure and Service Management Model Based on Deep Convolutional Neural Network
text:
Results and Discussion

The proposed DCNN-based model was evaluated against logistic regression (LR) and backpropagation neural network (BPNN) baselines across 1,200 rural credit cooperatives in six provinces. The DCNN achieved 94.7% classification accuracy for spatial structure optimization, outperforming LR (81.3%) and BPNN (88.5%). Service matching efficiency improved by 23.6%, reducing average loan approval time from 5.8 to 3.1 days. Spatial coverage of financial services expanded from 72.4% to 89.2% of surveyed townships. Ablation tests confirmed that the multi-scale convolution module contributed 6.2 percentage points to overall accuracy. These findings indicate that deep convolutional architectures effectively capture nonlinear spatial dependencies among rural branches, though performance declined slightly (91.4%) in mountainous regions with sparse data, suggesting future work should integrate transfer learning for data-scarce areas.

title: Evaluation of the uptake capacities of heavy metals in Chinese cabbage
text:
Evaluation of the uptake capacities of heavy metals in Chinese cabbage

Abstract

Heavy metal contamination in agricultural soils poses a serious threat to food safety and human health. Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa L. ssp. pekinensis) is one of the most widely consumed leafy vegetables in East Asia, yet its differential uptake capacities for individual heavy metals remain insufficiently quantified under controlled conditions. In this study, a pot experiment was conducted to evaluate the uptake, accumulation, and translocation characteristics of cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), and nickel (Ni) in Chinese cabbage grown in soils spiked with graded concentrations of these metals (0, 5, 10, 20, and 40 mg kg⁻¹). After a 60-day growth period, root and shoot biomass, metal concentrations in roots and edible leaves, bioconcentration factors (BCF), and translocation factors (TF) were determined. Results showed that Cd exhibited the highest bioconcentration factor (BCF = 1.87–3.42), followed by Zn (1.12–2.05), Cu (0.68–1.24), Ni (0.41–0.93), and Pb (0.09–0.27). Shoot biomass declined significantly (p < 0.05) when soil Cd exceeded 10 mg kg⁻¹ and when Pb exceeded 20 mg kg⁻¹. Translocation factors followed the order Cd > Zn > Ni > Cu > Pb, indicating that Cd and Zn were readily transported from roots to edible leaves, whereas Pb was largely retained in roots. The results demonstrate that Chinese cabbage is a strong accumulator of Cd and Zn, a moderate accumulator of Cu and Ni, and a weak accumulator of Pb. These findings provide a quantitative basis for risk assessment and safe production of Chinese cabbage in mildly contaminated soils.

Keywords: Chinese cabbage; heavy metals; bioconcentration factor; translocation factor; cadmium; food safety

1. Introduction

Soil contamination by heavy metals has become a global environmental concern due to rapid industrialization, mining activities, excessive application of chemical fertilizers, and irrigation with wastewater. Unlike organic pollutants, heavy metals are non-biodegradable and can persist in soils for decades or centuries, accumulating in crops and eventually entering the human food chain (Alloway, 2013). Long-term dietary exposure to heavy metals such as cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), and nickel (Ni) has been associated with renal dysfunction, skeletal damage, neurotoxicity, and carcinogenesis (Järup, 2003). Among agricultural products, leafy vegetables are particularly vulnerable because their edible parts are directly exposed to soil and atmospheric deposition, and they generally exhibit higher metal accumulation than cereals or fruits (Alexander et al., 2006).

Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa L. ssp. pekinensis) is a cruciferous leafy vegetable cultivated extensively in China, Korea, Japan, and Southeast Asia. It accounts for a substantial proportion of daily vegetable intake in these regions and is often consumed fresh, pickled, or fermented. Because of its large leaf area, shallow root system, and high water content, Chinese cabbage may readily absorb heavy metals from contaminated soils. Several studies have reported that Brassica species can accumulate Cd and Zn to concentrations exceeding soil levels (Xiong et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016). However, most previous investigations focused on a single metal or on field surveys with confounding factors, and comparative data on the relative uptake capacities of multiple metals under identical experimental conditions are still limited.

Understanding the differential uptake and translocation capacities of heavy metals in Chinese cabbage is essential for (i) predicting the transfer of contaminants from soil to the edible portion, (ii) establishing soil threshold values for safe cultivation, and (iii) selecting appropriate remediation or management strategies. The objectives of this study were therefore to: (1) quantify the accumulation of Cd, Pb, Zn, Cu, and Ni in roots and edible leaves of Chinese cabbage under controlled pot conditions; (2) calculate bioconcentration factors (BCF) and translocation factors (TF) for each metal; and (3) assess the effects of metal stress on plant biomass. The results are expected to provide a comparative ranking of metal uptake capacities and to support risk assessment for Chinese cabbage production.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Soil preparation and experimental design

Surface soil (0–20 cm) was collected from an uncontaminated agricultural field in the suburbs of Nanjing, China. The soil was air-dried, sieved through a 2-mm mesh, and analyzed for basic physicochemical properties: pH 6.8, organic matter 24.3 g kg⁻¹, cation exchange capacity 18.6 cmol kg⁻¹, and background concentrations of Cd 0.08, Pb 12.4, Zn 56.7, Cu 18.2, and Ni 14.5 mg kg⁻¹. All background values were below the national soil environmental quality standards.

The experiment was arranged in a completely randomized design with five metal treatments (Cd, Pb, Zn, Cu, Ni) and five concentration levels (0, 5, 10, 20, and 40 mg kg⁻¹), each with four replicates. Metals were applied as analytical-grade CdCl₂·2.5H₂O, Pb(NO₃)₂, ZnSO₄·7H₂O, CuSO₄·5H₂O, and NiCl₂·6H₂O dissolved in deionized water. The spiked soils were thoroughly mixed, equilibrated for 30 days at 25 °C and 60% water-holding capacity, and then placed in plastic pots (25 cm diameter, 20 cm height) containing 5 kg soil each.

2.2 Plant cultivation and sampling

Seeds of Chinese cabbage (cv. ‘Beijing New No. 3’) were surface-sterilized with 2% NaClO for 10 min, rinsed with deionized water, and germinated on moist filter paper. Ten uniform seedlings were transplanted into each pot and thinned to four plants per pot after one week. Plants were grown in a greenhouse under natural light (12–14 h photoperiod), 22–28 °C, and 60–75% relative humidity. Deionized water was supplied daily to maintain 65% water-holding capacity. No fertilizers or pesticides were applied.

After 60 days, plants were harvested. Roots were carefully separated from soil, washed with tap water and then with deionized water, and shoots were divided into outer leaves (edible portion) and inner leaves. Fresh biomass of roots and edible leaves was recorded. Samples were oven-dried at 70 °C to constant weight, ground, and stored for analysis.

2.3 Heavy metal analysis

Dried plant samples (0.5 g) were digested with a mixture of HNO₃ and HClO₄ (4:1, v/v) at 180 °C until clear. The digests were filtered and diluted to 25 mL with deionized water. Concentrations of Cd, Pb, Zn, Cu, and Ni were determined by flame atomic absorption spectrometry (FAAS, Shimadzu AA-7000) or graphite furnace atomic absorption spectrometry (GFAAS) for Cd and Pb when concentrations were low. Certified reference material (GBW10015, spinach) and blanks were used for quality control; recovery rates ranged from 92% to 106%.

2.4 Data calculation and statistical analysis

The bioconcentration factor (BCF) was calculated as the ratio of metal concentration in edible leaves (mg kg⁻¹ dry weight) to that in soil (mg kg⁻¹). The translocation factor (TF) was calculated as the ratio of metal concentration in edible leaves to that in roots. Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Duncan’s multiple range test at p < 0.05 using SPSS 22.0. Figures were plotted with Origin 9.0.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Biomass response

Root and shoot biomass of Chinese cabbage decreased with increasing metal concentrations, but the degree of inhibition varied among metals (Table 1). At 5 mg kg⁻¹, no significant difference in biomass was observed for any metal compared with the control. At 10 mg kg⁻¹, shoot dry weight was significantly reduced by Cd (28.4%) and Zn (18.7%), while Pb, Cu, and Ni caused less than 10% reduction. At 40 mg kg⁻¹, shoot biomass reductions were 62.3% for Cd, 48.5% for Zn, 31.2% for Cu, 27.8% for Ni, and 22.1% for Pb. Root biomass followed a similar trend but was generally less affected than shoot biomass, except under Cd treatment. These results indicate that Cd and Zn exerted the strongest phytotoxic effects on Chinese cabbage.

3.2 Metal concentrations in roots and edible leaves

The concentrations of all five metals in roots and edible leaves increased with increasing soil spiking levels (Table 2). Cd accumulated to the highest concentrations in both tissues. At 40 mg kg⁻¹ soil Cd, root and leaf Cd concentrations reached 38.6 and 21.4 mg kg⁻¹, respectively. Zn was the second most accumulated metal, with root and leaf concentrations of 112.5 and 86.3 mg kg⁻¹ at the highest treatment. Cu and Ni showed moderate accumulation, while Pb exhibited the lowest accumulation, with leaf concentrations never exceeding 6.8 mg kg⁻¹ even at 40 mg kg⁻¹ soil Pb.

3.3 Bioconcentration factors

The BCF values for edible leaves differed markedly among metals (Fig. 1). Cd had the highest BCF, ranging from 1.87 to 3.42 across treatments, followed by Zn (1.12–2.05), Cu (0.68–1.24), Ni (0.41–0.93), and Pb (0.09–0.27). For Cd and Zn, BCF values greater than 1 indicate that Chinese cabbage can accumulate these metals in edible tissues at concentrations exceeding those in soil. In contrast, BCF values for Pb were consistently below 0.3, suggesting a strong restriction on Pb uptake. The BCF of Cd tended to decrease at the highest soil concentration (40 mg kg⁻¹), possibly due to saturation of transport sites or root damage.

3.4 Translocation factors

Translocation factors from roots to edible leaves followed the order Cd (0.55–0.72) > Zn (0.48–0.65) > Ni (0.32–0.45) > Cu (0.28–0.39) > Pb (0.08–0.15) (Fig. 2). The relatively high TF for Cd and Zn indicates efficient root-to-shoot transport, whereas the low TF for Pb suggests that Pb is largely immobilized in root cell walls and vacuoles. The TF for Cd increased slightly with soil Cd up to 20 mg kg⁻¹ and then declined, while Zn TF remained relatively stable across treatments.

4. Discussion

The present study provides a comparative evaluation of the uptake capacities of five heavy metals in Chinese cabbage under identical experimental conditions. The results clearly demonstrate that Cd and Zn are the most readily accumulated metals, while Pb is the least accumulated. This ranking is consistent with previous reports on Brassica species and other leafy vegetables (Xiong et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016). The high BCF and TF of Cd can be attributed to its chemical similarity to Zn, which allows Cd to be transported across the plasma membrane via Zn transporters such as ZIP and NRAMP families (Clemens, 2006). Once inside the root, Cd is loaded into the xylem and translocated to shoots, where it can bind to phytochelatins and accumulate in leaf vacuoles.

Zn is an essential micronutrient, and its high accumulation in Chinese cabbage reflects active uptake mechanisms mediated by Zn-regulated transporters. However, excessive Zn can interfere with photosynthesis and enzyme activities, as indicated by the significant biomass reduction at 20 and 40 mg kg⁻¹. Cu and Ni are also essential micronutrients but were accumulated to a lesser extent, likely because their uptake is tightly regulated and their translocation is restricted under excess conditions. Pb, a non-essential metal, showed very low BCF and TF values, which is consistent with its strong adsorption to soil particles, low solubility, and sequestration in root cell walls and vacuoles (Pourrut et al., 2011).

The differential uptake capacities have important implications for food safety. The Codex Alimentarius Commission has set maximum levels for Cd in leafy vegetables at 0.2 mg kg⁻¹ fresh weight and for Pb at 0.3 mg kg⁻¹ fresh weight. In our study, leaf Cd concentrations at soil Cd ≥ 10 mg kg⁻¹ exceeded these limits when converted to fresh weight (assuming 90% moisture), whereas leaf Pb concentrations remained below the limit even at 40 mg kg⁻¹ soil Pb. This suggests that Cd is the priority metal of concern for Chinese cabbage cultivation in contaminated soils. The high TF of Cd also implies that soil-to-leaf transfer is efficient, and soil remediation or cultivar selection should target Cd specifically.

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the pot experiment used spiked soils, which may not fully represent field conditions where metals age and speciation changes over time. Second, only one cultivar was tested; genetic variation in metal uptake among Chinese cabbage cultivars may be substantial. Third, interactions among metals were not examined, although in real contaminated soils multiple metals often coexist and may compete for transporters. Future studies should incorporate field validation, multi-cultivar screening, and binary or multi-metal treatments to refine the risk assessment.

5. Conclusion

This study evaluated the uptake capacities of Cd, Pb, Zn, Cu, and Ni in Chinese cabbage under controlled pot conditions. The results showed that Chinese cabbage is a strong accumulator of Cd and Zn, a moderate accumulator of Cu and Ni, and a weak accumulator of Pb. Cadmium exhibited the highest bioconcentration factor (up to 3.42) and translocation factor (up to 0.72), indicating efficient soil-to-leaf transfer and a high potential health risk. Lead was largely retained in roots, with BCF and TF values below 0.3 and 0.15, respectively. Shoot biomass was most severely reduced by Cd and Zn, followed by Cu, Ni, and Pb. These findings suggest that Cd is the most critical heavy metal for food safety in Chinese cabbage production, and that soil Cd thresholds should be strictly enforced. The quantitative ranking of metal uptake capacities provided here can support site-specific risk assessment, safe vegetable production, and the development of mitigation strategies such as soil amendment, phytoextraction, and cultivar selection.

title: Restoring fresh texture in cooked aged rice with reducing agents
text:
Title: Restoring Fresh Texture in Cooked Aged Rice with Reducing Agents

Abstract
Aged rice, commonly stored for over a year, develops an undesirable hard, less sticky texture upon cooking, primarily due to protein disulfide cross-linking and lipid oxidation. This study investigated the efficacy of reducing agents—L-cysteine, dithiothreitol (DTT), and sodium metabisulfite (SMB)—in restoring the fresh-like texture of cooked aged rice. Aged rice samples (Indica, 18 months old) were cooked with varying concentrations (0.1–1.0% w/w) of each agent. Texture profile analysis (TPA) revealed that 0.5% DTT and 0.75% SMB significantly reduced hardness by 42% and 38%, respectively, while increasing adhesiveness by 55% compared to the control (p < 0.05). Scanning electron microscopy showed a looser starch granule network in treated samples. Sensory evaluation indicated that 0.5% DTT-treated rice scored closest to freshly harvested rice in tenderness and overall acceptability. However, higher concentrations (>0.75%) imparted off-flavors. We conclude that mild reducing agents can partially restore fresh texture in aged rice, offering a practical intervention for post-harvest quality management.

Keywords: aged rice, reducing agents, texture restoration, dithiothreitol, protein disulfide bonds, cooked rice quality

1. Introduction
Rice (Oryza sativa L.) undergoes significant physicochemical changes during prolonged storage, a phenomenon known as aging. Aged rice typically exhibits increased kernel hardness, reduced stickiness, and lower water absorption during cooking, leading to a firm, dry, and less palatable cooked product (Zhou et al., 2010). These changes are attributed to oxidation of lipids, formation of protein disulfide bonds, and increased rigidity of the starch-protein matrix (Chrastil, 1990). While aging can be desirable for certain traditional dishes, it is a major quality defect for consumers and the food industry. Current mitigation strategies include enzymatic treatment or blending with fresh rice, but these have limitations. Reducing agents can cleave disulfide bonds, potentially reversing protein cross-linking. This study hypothesizes that reducing agents can restore fresh-like texture in cooked aged rice. We systematically evaluated three reducing agents—L-cysteine, DTT, and sodium metabisulfite—on texture, microstructure, and sensory attributes.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Materials. Aged Indica rice (cv. IR64, 18 months old, moisture 13.5%) and fresh rice (0 months, moisture 14.0%) were obtained from a local warehouse. L-cysteine, DTT, and SMB (analytical grade) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich.
2.2 Cooking treatment. Rice (50 g) was rinsed and cooked in 100 mL distilled water containing reducing agent at 0.1%, 0.25%, 0.5%, 0.75%, or 1.0% (w/w rice basis). Control used water only. Cooking was in a rice cooker (1:2 rice:water ratio) for 30 min, followed by 10 min resting.
2.3 Texture profile analysis (TPA). Cooked rice (3 kernels) was compressed twice (75% strain) using a TA.XTplus texture analyzer. Hardness, adhesiveness, and springiness were recorded.
2.4 Microstructure. Cooked rice was freeze-dried, sputter-coated, and viewed under a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi SU3500) at 500× magnification.
2.5 Sensory evaluation. A trained panel (n=12) scored tenderness, stickiness, and overall acceptability on a 9-point hedonic scale, with fresh rice as reference.
2.6 Statistical analysis. Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test (p < 0.05). Values are means ± SD (triplicate).

3. Results
3.1 Texture. Table 1 shows TPA results. Control aged rice had hardness of 2450 ± 120 g, adhesiveness of -12.5 ± 1.2 g·s, and springiness of 0.78 ± 0.03. Fresh rice showed hardness 1580 ± 90 g, adhesiveness -28.4 ± 2.1 g·s, and springiness 0.86 ± 0.02. All reducing agents reduced hardness in a dose-dependent manner. DTT at 0.5% reduced hardness to 1420 ± 110 g (42% reduction vs. control, p < 0.05), close to fresh rice. SMB at 0.75% reduced hardness to 1520 ± 130 g (38% reduction). L-cysteine was least effective (25% reduction at 1.0%). Adhesiveness increased significantly with DTT and SMB: 0.5% DTT gave -29.2 ± 2.5 g·s (near fresh rice). Springiness improved modestly.

Table 1. Texture of cooked rice (mean ± SD).
| Sample | Hardness (g) | Adhesiveness (g·s) | Springiness |
|--------|--------------|---------------------|-------------|
| Fresh rice | 1580 ± 90 | -28.4 ± 2.1 | 0.86 ± 0.02 |
| Aged control | 2450 ± 120 | -12.5 ± 1.2 | 0.78 ± 0.03 |
| 0.5% DTT | 1420 ± 110* | -29.2 ± 2.5* | 0.85 ± 0.02 |
| 0.75% SMB | 1520 ± 130* | -26.8 ± 2.0* | 0.83 ± 0.03 |
| 1.0% L-cysteine | 1840 ± 140* | -19.5 ± 1.8* | 0.80 ± 0.03 |
*Significantly different from control (p < 0.05).

3.2 Microstructure. SEM images (not shown) revealed that control aged rice had a dense, compact starch granule structure with numerous protein deposits. In contrast, 0.5% DTT-treated rice showed a looser, more open network, resembling fresh rice. SMB showed similar but slightly less pronounced effects.

3.3 Sensory. Panel scores (9-point scale) for tenderness: fresh = 8.2, control = 4.1, 0.5% DTT = 7.5, 0.75% SMB = 7.0, 1.0% L-cysteine = 5.8. Overall acceptability: fresh = 8.0, control = 4.5, 0.5% DTT = 7.2. Off-flavors were noted at ≥0.75% DTT and ≥1.0% SMB (sulfurous note).

4. Discussion
The results support the hypothesis that reducing agents can restore fresh texture in cooked aged rice. The mechanism likely involves cleavage of disulfide bonds formed between rice proteins (glutelin and prolamin) during aging, which otherwise entrap starch granules and limit swelling (Chrastil, 1990). DTT, a strong disulfide reductant, was most effective at 0.5%, reducing hardness to fresh levels. SMB, a food-grade alternative, was also effective but required a slightly higher concentration and introduced off-flavors at elevated doses. L-cysteine was less potent, possibly due to its lower redox potential and partial degradation during cooking. The SEM results corroborate that a looser microstructure allows greater water penetration and starch swelling, improving tenderness and adhesiveness. However, excessive reduction (>0.75%) likely over-softens the matrix and releases sulfurous volatiles. Practical application must balance efficacy with sensory acceptability. A 0.5% DTT treatment is not food-approved for direct addition; thus, SMB (0.5–0.75%) or cysteine (0.5%) with flavor masking may be more viable. Future studies should explore synergistic combinations with mild heating or ultrasound.

5. Conclusion
Reducing agents, particularly DTT and sodium metabisulfite, significantly restore fresh-like texture in cooked aged rice by disrupting protein disulfide cross-links and loosening the starch-protein matrix. A 0.5% DTT or 0.75% SMB treatment reduced hardness by 38–42% and increased adhesiveness by over 50%, closely matching fresh rice. However, off-flavors limit higher concentrations. This approach offers a promising post-harvest intervention to improve the palatability of aged rice, though food-grade optimization and sensory masking remain necessary for commercial adoption.

References (invented)
- Chrastil, J. (1990). *J. Agric. Food Chem.*, 38, 351–355.
- Zhou, Z., et al. (2010). *Food Chem.*, 120, 1120–1125.

title: Macro-Nutritional Adaptive Strategies of Moose (Alces alces) Related to Population Density
text: Abstract: Understanding how large herbivores adapt their foraging strategies to changing population densities is crucial for wildlife management. We investigated macro-nutritional adaptation in moose (*Alces alces*) across a gradient of population densities in Fennoscandia. Using fecal near-infrared reflectance spectroscopy and seasonal browse surveys, we quantified dietary intake of protein, carbohydrates, and lipids relative to available forage. At high population densities, moose exhibited increased consumption of browse rich in non-structural carbohydrates and lipids, while protein intake remained relatively stable, suggesting compensatory selection for energy-dense resources under intraspecific competition. Conversely, at low densities, diets reflected greater reliance on protein-rich forage. These shifts indicate density-dependent plasticity in macro-nutritional selection, likely mediated by declining per-capita forage availability and altered plant chemistry from browsing pressure. Our findings demonstrate that moose adjust nutritional strategies to mitigate competition, with implications for habitat carrying capacity, population dynamics, and forest regeneration. This study highlights the importance of integrating nutritional ecology into density-dependent management frameworks for boreal ungulates.

title: Comparison of attitudes toward disability and people with disability among caregivers, the public, and people with disability: findings from a cross-sectional survey
text:
Comparison of attitudes toward disability and people with disability among caregivers, the public, and people with disability: findings from a cross-sectional survey

Abstract

Attitudes toward disability shape social participation, service access, and the well-being of people with disability. This study compared attitudes toward disability and people with disability among three key groups: caregivers, the general public, and people with disability themselves. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 1,248 participants (caregivers, n = 386; public, n = 512; people with disability, n = 350). Attitudes were measured using the Attitudes to Disability Scale (ADS), which includes dimensions of inclusion, discrimination, gains, and prospects. Results indicated that people with disability reported the most positive attitudes overall, followed by caregivers, while the general public showed the least positive attitudes. Significant differences were found across all four ADS subscales (p < .01). Caregivers scored higher than the public on inclusion and gains but lower than people with disability on prospects and discrimination. Educational level, contact frequency, and disability type were significant predictors of attitudes. The findings suggest that targeted anti-stigma education and increased intergroup contact are needed, particularly for the general public, to foster more inclusive communities.

Keywords: disability attitudes; caregivers; general public; people with disability; cross-sectional survey; inclusion

1. Introduction

Attitudes toward disability are powerful determinants of social inclusion and quality of life for people with disability. Negative attitudes can lead to discrimination, limited employment opportunities, and reduced access to healthcare and education (World Health Organization, 2011). Conversely, positive attitudes promote empowerment, community participation, and psychological well-being. Understanding how different groups perceive disability is essential for designing effective interventions.

Three groups are particularly important in the disability context: people with disability themselves, their caregivers, and the general public. People with disability experience disability directly and may internalize or resist societal stigma. Caregivers, often family members, provide daily support and may develop unique insights but also experience burden that could influence their attitudes. The general public, lacking direct experience, often relies on stereotypes and media representations.

Previous research has compared attitudes between two groups, such as public versus professionals or caregivers versus people with disability. However, few studies have simultaneously compared all three groups using a validated multidimensional instrument. Moreover, most studies have been conducted in Western countries, with limited evidence from Asian or mixed cultural settings. This study aims to fill that gap by comparing attitudes toward disability among caregivers, the general public, and people with disability in a cross-sectional survey. The research questions are: (1) Are there significant differences in attitudes across the three groups? (2) Which demographic and contact-related variables predict more positive attitudes?

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Design and Participants

A cross-sectional survey was conducted between March and July 2024 in three urban districts of a mid-sized city. Participants were recruited through community centers, disability service organizations, and online platforms. Inclusion criteria were: age 18–75 years; ability to read and complete the questionnaire; and self-identification as a caregiver, a member of the general public, or a person with disability. Caregivers were defined as individuals providing unpaid or paid support to a family member or friend with disability for at least six months. People with disability included those with physical, sensory, or intellectual disabilities. The general public included individuals with no caregiving role and no disability.

A total of 1,350 questionnaires were distributed, and 1,248 valid responses were returned (response rate 92.4%). The final sample comprised 386 caregivers (30.9%), 512 general public (41.0%), and 350 people with disability (28.1%). Ethical approval was obtained from the institutional review board. Written informed consent was provided by all participants.

2.2 Measures

The Attitudes to Disability Scale (ADS) was used. The ADS contains 16 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). It yields four subscales: Inclusion (e.g., “People with disability should be included in mainstream education”), Discrimination (e.g., “People with disability face discrimination in employment”), Gains (e.g., “People with disability can contribute meaningfully to society”), and Prospects (e.g., “People with disability have a positive future”). Higher scores indicate more positive attitudes. The ADS has demonstrated good reliability in previous studies. In this sample, Cronbach’s alpha was .87 for the total scale and .72–.84 for subscales.

Demographic variables included age, gender, education level, income, and frequency of contact with people with disability (none, occasional, frequent). Disability type was recorded for participants with disability and caregivers.

2.3 Data Analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0. Descriptive statistics summarized sample characteristics. One-way ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey tests compared ADS scores across the three groups. Multiple linear regression examined predictors of total ADS scores. Statistical significance was set at p < .05.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Sample Characteristics

The mean age was 42.3 years (SD = 12.6). Females comprised 58.2% of the sample. Education levels varied: 28.5% had high school or below, 44.1% had college/university, and 27.4% had postgraduate degrees. Among caregivers, 62.4% cared for a family member with physical disability, 21.8% for intellectual disability, and 15.8% for sensory disability. Among people with disability, 54.3% had physical disability, 23.1% sensory, and 22.6% intellectual or developmental disability.

3.2 Group Differences in Attitudes

Table 1 presents mean ADS scores by group. People with disability reported the highest total ADS score (M = 3.92, SD = 0.58), followed by caregivers (M = 3.61, SD = 0.62), and the general public (M = 3.24, SD = 0.67). One-way ANOVA revealed significant group differences, F(2, 1245) = 48.72, p < .001, η² = .073.

On the Inclusion subscale, people with disability (M = 4.12) and caregivers (M = 3.98) scored higher than the public (M = 3.45), F(2, 1245) = 36.14, p < .001. On Discrimination, people with disability (M = 4.05) scored highest, followed by caregivers (M = 3.72) and public (M = 3.31), F(2, 1245) = 29.88, p < .001. On Gains, caregivers (M = 3.65) and people with disability (M = 3.78) scored higher than public (M = 3.12), F(2, 1245) = 33.21, p < .001. On Prospects, people with disability (M = 3.73) scored significantly higher than caregivers (M = 3.09) and public (M = 3.08), F(2, 1245) = 41.56, p < .001. Post-hoc tests confirmed all pairwise differences were significant except between caregivers and public on Prospects.

3.3 Predictors of Attitudes

Multiple linear regression with total ADS score as the dependent variable showed that group membership (β = .28, p < .001), education level (β = .19, p < .01), and frequent contact (β = .22, p < .001) were significant predictors. Age, gender, and income were not significant. Among caregivers, caring for a person with intellectual disability was associated with lower Prospects scores (β = -.17, p < .05). Among people with disability, those with intellectual disability reported lower Inclusion scores than those with physical disability (β = -.21, p < .01).

4. Discussion

This study found significant differences in attitudes toward disability among caregivers, the general public, and people with disability. People with disability held the most positive attitudes, particularly regarding prospects and discrimination. This may reflect their lived experience, resilience, and advocacy. Caregivers showed moderately positive attitudes, likely due to direct contact and emotional investment, but their lower Prospects scores suggest they may worry about the future of those they care for. The general public demonstrated the least positive attitudes, consistent with previous research showing that lack of contact perpetuates stereotypes.

The finding that education and frequent contact predicted more positive attitudes aligns with intergroup contact theory. Contact reduces anxiety and enhances empathy. Caregivers, by definition, have frequent contact, which explains their higher scores than the public on inclusion and gains. However, caregivers’ lower prospects scores may stem from burnout or realistic concerns about long-term support.

Disability type mattered: intellectual disability was associated with less positive attitudes, especially among caregivers and people with disability themselves. This may reflect greater stigma and fewer perceived opportunities for people with intellectual disability. Anti-stigma interventions should therefore be tailored to disability type.

Implications for policy and practice include: (1) public awareness campaigns featuring direct contact with people with disability; (2) support services for caregivers to address future-oriented anxiety; (3) empowerment programs for people with disability to maintain positive self-perceptions; and (4) education curricula that include disability studies.

Limitations include the cross-sectional design, which cannot establish causality. The sample was drawn from urban areas, limiting generalizability. Self-report measures may be subject to social desirability bias. Future research should use longitudinal designs and include rural populations.

5. Conclusion

Attitudes toward disability differ significantly among caregivers, the general public, and people with disability. People with disability report the most positive attitudes, followed by caregivers, while the general public holds the least positive attitudes. Education, frequent contact, and disability type are key predictors. To promote inclusive societies, interventions should target the general public through contact-based education, support caregivers’ emotional needs, and empower people with disability. Reducing stigma requires multisectoral efforts that recognize the unique perspectives of each group.

title: Genome-wide transcriptome analysis of microspore abortion initiation in radish (Raphanus sativus L.)
text: Radish (Raphanus sativus L.) is an important root vegetable crop worldwide, and the utilization of heterosis through male sterility has become a cornerstone of commercial hybrid seed production. Microspore abortion, which leads to male sterility, is a complex developmental process governed by precisely coordinated gene expression networks. Although several male-sterile lines have been characterized in radish, the molecular mechanisms underlying the initiation of microspore abortion remain largely elusive. Elucidating the earliest events that commit microspores to abort is therefore essential for understanding male sterility and for efficient breeding applications. In this study, we performed genome-wide transcriptome analysis of floral buds at the critical stage of microspore abortion initiation in a male-sterile radish line and its fertile near-isogenic counterpart. Differentially expressed genes were identified and functionally annotated, revealing candidates associated with tapetum development, pollen wall formation, hormone signaling, and programmed cell death. Our results provide a comprehensive transcriptional framework for the initiation of microspore abortion and offer valuable genetic resources for hybrid breeding in radish.

title: Physical properties of mucilage polysaccharides from Dioscorea opposita Thunb
text:
Results and Discussion

The mucilage polysaccharides from *Dioscorea opposita* Thunb. (DOP) were extracted with a yield of 8.42 ± 0.31% (w/w) based on dry tuber weight. The crude extract appeared as a fluffy, off-white powder with a moisture content of 6.75 ± 0.18% and total ash of 3.12 ± 0.09%, indicating a relatively low inorganic fraction. The total carbohydrate content was 82.6 ± 1.4%, with uronic acid accounting for 21.3 ± 0.7%, suggesting the presence of acidic polysaccharides. Monosaccharide composition analysis revealed mannose (42.8 mol%), glucose (23.5 mol%), galactose (14.2 mol%), arabinose (9.6 mol%), rhamnose (5.4 mol%), and galacturonic acid (4.5 mol%), indicating a heteropolysaccharide nature.

The weight-average molecular weight (Mw) of DOP was 3.24 × 10⁵ Da with a polydispersity index of 1.68, determined by HPSEC-MALLS. The intrinsic viscosity [η] in deionized water at 25 °C was 2.87 dL/g, consistent with a semi-flexible chain conformation. Rheological measurements showed shear-thinning behavior at concentrations above 0.5% (w/v), with apparent viscosity decreasing from 128 mPa·s at 0.1 s⁻¹ to 14 mPa·s at 100 s⁻¹ for a 1.0% solution. The storage modulus (G′) exceeded the loss modulus (G″) at frequencies above 1.2 rad/s, indicating weak gel-like behavior. Thermal analysis by TGA showed a major degradation stage between 240 and 340 °C, with a peak decomposition temperature of 298 °C and 62.4% mass loss, reflecting moderate thermal stability.

These physicochemical properties suggest that DOP possesses favorable thickening and gelling capacities, supporting its potential application as a natural hydrocolloid in food and pharmaceutical formulations. The high mannose content and acidic nature likely contribute to its chain rigidity and functional performance.

title: Students' mental health clinical placements, clinical confidence and stigma surrounding mental illness: A correlational study
text:
Students' mental health clinical placements, clinical confidence and stigma surrounding mental illness: A correlational study

Abstract

Mental health clinical placements are widely regarded as a cornerstone of nursing education, yet their relationship with students' clinical confidence and stigmatising attitudes remains insufficiently understood. This study examined the correlations among the quality of mental health clinical placement experiences, self-reported clinical confidence, and stigma surrounding mental illness among nursing students. A cross-sectional correlational design was employed. A total of 246 undergraduate nursing students from three universities in eastern China who had completed at least four weeks of mental health clinical placement were recruited through convenience sampling. Data were collected using the Clinical Placement Experience Scale (CPES), the Mental Health Clinical Confidence Scale (MHCCS), and the Opening Minds Stigma Scale for Health Care Providers (OMS-HC). Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression analyses were conducted. The results showed that placement experience quality was positively correlated with clinical confidence (r = 0.52, p < 0.01) and negatively correlated with stigma (r = −0.41, p < 0.01). Clinical confidence was negatively correlated with stigma (r = −0.37, p < 0.01). Regression analysis indicated that placement experience quality and clinical confidence together explained 34.6% of the variance in stigma. The findings suggest that well-structured, supportive mental health placements may simultaneously enhance clinical confidence and reduce stigmatising attitudes, highlighting the need for deliberate pedagogical design in clinical mental health education.

Keywords: mental health nursing; clinical placement; clinical confidence; stigma; nursing students; correlational study

1. Introduction

The global burden of mental illness continues to rise, and the demand for a competent, compassionate mental health workforce has never been greater. Nursing students are future frontline providers, yet many enter mental health settings with limited prior exposure and considerable apprehension. Clinical placements are therefore expected to serve as a transformative learning experience, shaping not only psychomotor and assessment skills but also professional attitudes.

Two outcomes of placement have attracted particular attention: clinical confidence and stigma. Clinical confidence refers to students' perceived ability to perform mental health assessments, communicate therapeutically, and manage challenging situations. Stigma, by contrast, refers to negative stereotypes, prejudice, and discriminatory inclinations towards people with mental illness. These constructs are theoretically linked: students who feel more competent may interact more openly with service users, while stigmatising beliefs may erode confidence and therapeutic engagement. However, empirical evidence on the interrelationships among placement experience, confidence, and stigma is fragmented, with most studies examining only one or two of these variables.

Furthermore, the direction of influence remains debated. Some scholars argue that confidence reduces stigma through increased contact and familiarity; others contend that reduced stigma is a prerequisite for confidence development. Understanding these associations is essential for designing placements that produce both skilled and non-stigmatising practitioners. Accordingly, this study addressed three research questions: (1) Is the quality of mental health clinical placement experience correlated with clinical confidence? (2) Is placement quality correlated with stigma? (3) Is clinical confidence correlated with stigma, and to what extent do placement quality and confidence jointly predict stigma?

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Design and Participants

A cross-sectional, correlational design was adopted. Participants were undergraduate nursing students recruited from three universities in eastern China between March and June 2024. Inclusion criteria were: (a) enrolment in a four-year bachelor of nursing programme; (b) completion of at least four weeks of mental health clinical placement; and (c) willingness to participate. Students with prior paid employment in mental health settings were excluded to reduce confounding. Of 280 distributed questionnaires, 246 valid responses were returned (response rate 87.9%). The sample was predominantly female (n = 201, 81.7%), with a mean age of 21.4 years (SD = 1.3). Most participants (n = 158, 64.2%) reported no previous personal or family contact with mental health services.

2.2 Instruments

The Clinical Placement Experience Scale (CPES) is a 20-item instrument measuring perceived supervision quality, learning opportunities, team atmosphere, and service-user contact. Items are rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree), with higher scores indicating more positive placement experiences. Cronbach's α in this study was 0.89.

The Mental Health Clinical Confidence Scale (MHCCS) comprises 16 items assessing confidence in assessment, communication, risk management, and therapeutic intervention. Responses range from 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (extremely confident). Cronbach's α was 0.91.

The Opening Minds Stigma Scale for Health Care Providers (OMS-HC) contains 15 items measuring attitudes, disclosure, and behaviour intentions towards people with mental illness. Items are scored on a five-point scale, with higher scores indicating greater stigma. Cronbach's α was 0.84.

2.3 Data Collection and Analysis

Questionnaires were administered online via a secure platform after informed consent was obtained. Ethical approval was granted by the institutional review board of the lead university. Data were analysed using SPSS 26.0. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation coefficients, and hierarchical multiple regression were computed. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Descriptive Statistics

The mean CPES score was 3.68 (SD = 0.61), indicating moderately positive placement experiences. The mean MHCCS score was 3.42 (SD = 0.58), reflecting moderate clinical confidence. The mean OMS-HC score was 2.71 (SD = 0.49), suggesting moderate levels of stigma.

3.2 Correlation Analysis

Placement experience quality was significantly and positively correlated with clinical confidence (r = 0.52, p < 0.01) and significantly and negatively correlated with stigma (r = −0.41, p < 0.01). Clinical confidence was also negatively correlated with stigma (r = −0.37, p < 0.01). These associations remained significant after controlling for age, gender, and prior contact with mental health services.

3.3 Regression Analysis

Hierarchical regression was performed with stigma as the dependent variable. In Step 1, control variables (age, gender, prior contact) explained 4.2% of the variance. In Step 2, placement experience quality added significant explanatory power (ΔR² = 0.21, p < 0.001). In Step 3, clinical confidence added a further 9.4% (ΔR² = 0.094, p < 0.001), yielding a final model explaining 34.6% of the variance in stigma. Placement quality (β = −0.29, p < 0.001) and clinical confidence (β = −0.34, p < 0.001) were both independent negative predictors of stigma.

4. Discussion

This study provides empirical support for the interconnectedness of placement experience, clinical confidence, and stigma. The positive correlation between placement quality and confidence aligns with previous findings that supportive supervision and meaningful service-user contact foster self-efficacy. Students who perceived their placements as well organised and emotionally safe were more likely to report confidence in core mental health skills.

More importantly, the negative association between placement quality and stigma suggests that structured exposure can challenge stereotypes. This is consistent with the contact hypothesis, which posits that intergroup contact under favourable conditions reduces prejudice. Placements offering collaborative, recovery-oriented interactions may humanise mental illness and diminish social distance.

The negative correlation between confidence and stigma is particularly noteworthy. One interpretation is that as students gain competence, they feel less threatened by mental illness and therefore endorse fewer stigmatising beliefs. Alternatively, lower stigma may facilitate engagement, which in turn builds confidence, suggesting a reciprocal relationship. The regression results indicate that both variables contribute independently to stigma, underscoring the value of targeting both in educational interventions.

These findings have practical implications. Nurse educators should prioritise placement quality through robust supervision, reflective debriefing, and deliberate exposure to recovery narratives. Simulation and contact-based education may complement clinical placement, especially for students with limited prior exposure. Future research should employ longitudinal designs to clarify causal directions and include objective competence measures alongside self-report scales.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Convenience sampling from three universities limits generalisability. Self-report measures may be subject to social desirability bias, particularly regarding stigma. Future studies should incorporate multi-site probability sampling and mixed methods.

5. Conclusion

Among nursing students, higher-quality mental health clinical placements are associated with greater clinical confidence and lower stigma towards mental illness. Clinical confidence is also negatively associated with stigma, and both placement quality and confidence independently predict stigmatising attitudes. These findings suggest that investments in placement quality and confidence-building may yield dual benefits: a more skilled and a less stigmatising mental health workforce. Curricular and clinical partnerships should therefore be designed intentionally to foster supportive learning environments that promote both competence and compassion.

title: Components of A Successful Peritoneal Dialysis Program
text:
Components of A Successful Peritoneal Dialysis Program

 Abstract

Background: Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a cost-effective, home-based renal replacement therapy, yet its utilization varies widely across dialysis programs. Identifying the components associated with successful PD programs is essential for improving patient outcomes and therapy uptake.

Methods: This retrospective observational study analyzed data from 12 dialysis centers over a five-year period (2019–2023), involving 1,248 patients initiated on PD. Program success was defined by a composite metric: PD utilization rate >25%, technique survival >80% at two years, peritonitis rate <0.5 episodes per patient-year, and patient satisfaction scores >85%. Centers were categorized as high-performing (n=5) and low-performing (n=7). Structural, process, and outcome variables were compared.

Results: High-performing centers demonstrated significantly higher rates of pre-dialysis education (92% vs. 61%, p<0.001), dedicated PD nurse staffing ratios (1:18 vs. 1:42, p<0.001), and structured training programs exceeding 25 hours (p=0.002). Peritonitis rates were 0.31 vs. 0.68 episodes/patient-year (p<0.001), and two-year technique survival was 86% vs. 68% (p<0.001). Multivariate analysis identified dedicated PD coordinators (OR 3.42, 95% CI 2.11–5.54), standardized protocols (OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.76–4.68), and home visits (OR 2.15, 95% CI 1.32–3.50) as independent predictors of program success.

Conclusion: Successful PD programs are characterized by multidisciplinary staffing, comprehensive patient education, standardized protocols, and robust infection control. These components should guide program development and quality improvement initiatives.

Keywords: Peritoneal dialysis, program development, peritonitis, technique survival, patient education, dialysis outcomes

 Introduction

Peritoneal dialysis offers significant advantages over hemodialysis, including greater patient autonomy, preserved residual renal function, reduced hemodynamic instability, and lower healthcare costs. Despite these benefits, PD remains underutilized globally, accounting for only 11% of dialysis patients worldwide. The disparity in PD uptake and outcomes suggests that program-level factors substantially influence success.

A successful PD program requires more than clinical competence; it demands coordinated infrastructure, patient-centered education, infection surveillance, and continuous quality improvement. Previous studies have examined individual factors affecting PD outcomes, but few have comprehensively evaluated the structural and process components distinguishing high-performing from low-performing programs.

This study aimed to identify the key components of successful PD programs by comparing structural characteristics, clinical processes, and patient outcomes across dialysis centers with varying performance levels. We hypothesized that dedicated staffing, structured education, standardized protocols, and proactive infection control would be independently associated with program success.

 Materials and Methods

 Study Design and Setting

This retrospective observational study was conducted across 12 dialysis centers in a multicenter renal network between January 2019 and December 2023. Institutional ethics approval was obtained, and patient data were anonymized.

 Participants

All adult patients (≥18 years) initiated on PD during the study period were included. Exclusion criteria were: PD duration <90 days, transfer from another center, and incomplete records. A total of 1,248 patients met inclusion criteria (mean age 56.4 ± 14.2 years; 52.3% male; 38.7% diabetic).

 Data Collection

Data were extracted from electronic medical records, program registries, and administrative databases. Variables included:
- Structural: PD nurse-to-patient ratio, presence of dedicated PD coordinator, training duration, home visit availability, protocol standardization.
- Process: Pre-dialysis education rate, modality selection process, peritonitis surveillance, retraining frequency.
- Outcomes: Peritonitis rate, technique survival, patient satisfaction (validated 10-point Likert survey), hospitalization rates.

 Program Classification

Centers were classified as high-performing if they met all four criteria: PD utilization >25%, two-year technique survival >80%, peritonitis rate <0.5 episodes/patient-year, and satisfaction score >85%. Five centers met these criteria; seven did not.

 Statistical Analysis

Continuous variables were compared using t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests; categorical variables using chi-square tests. Multivariate logistic regression identified independent predictors of program success. A p-value <0.05 was considered significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS version 28.

 Results

 Structural Characteristics

High-performing centers had significantly lower PD nurse-to-patient ratios (1:18 vs. 1:42, p<0.001) and were more likely to employ dedicated PD coordinators (100% vs. 28.6%, p<0.001). Structured training programs exceeding 25 hours were present in all high-performing centers versus 42.9% of low-performing centers (p=0.002). Home visit programs were available in 80% of high-performing versus 28.6% of low-performing centers (p=0.014).

 Process Measures

Pre-dialysis education was delivered to 92% of patients in high-performing centers compared to 61% in low-performing centers (p<0.001). Standardized peritonitis protocols were implemented in 100% versus 57.1% of centers (p=0.021). Routine retraining every six months was practiced in 80% versus 28.6% (p=0.014).

 Clinical Outcomes

Peritonitis rates were 0.31 ± 0.08 episodes/patient-year in high-performing centers versus 0.68 ± 0.15 in low-performing centers (p<0.001). Two-year technique survival was 86.2% versus 68.4% (p<0.001). Patient satisfaction scores averaged 91.3 ± 3.2 versus 76.8 ± 5.7 (p<0.001). Hospitalization rates were 0.42 versus 0.79 admissions/patient-year (p=0.003).

 Multivariate Analysis

Independent predictors of program success included: dedicated PD coordinator (OR 3.42, 95% CI 2.11–5.54, p<0.001), standardized protocols (OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.76–4.68, p<0.001), home visits (OR 2.15, 95% CI 1.32–3.50, p=0.002), and pre-dialysis education (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.18–3.19, p=0.009).

 Discussion

This study identified several interdependent components characterizing successful PD programs. The strongest predictor was the presence of a dedicated PD coordinator, consistent with findings that specialized nursing leadership improves patient selection, training quality, and complication management. Dedicated coordinators facilitate continuity of care and serve as advocates for PD within multidisciplinary teams.

Structured training exceeding 25 hours was associated with superior outcomes, supporting evidence that comprehensive education reduces peritonitis risk. The International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis recommends structured curricula, yet implementation varies widely. Our findings reinforce that training duration and standardization are modifiable factors directly impacting technique survival.

Standardized protocols and routine retraining emerged as critical process components. High-performing centers employed systematic peritonitis surveillance and root-cause analysis, enabling rapid identification of trends and targeted interventions. This proactive approach likely explains the observed 54% reduction in peritonitis rates.

Home visits, though resource-intensive, independently predicted success. Home environment assessment identifies barriers to technique adherence and allows personalized problem-solving. This patient-centered approach may improve satisfaction and reduce technique failure.

Pre-dialysis education was strongly associated with program success. Comprehensive education enables informed modality selection, reducing late referrals and urgent starts—factors known to compromise PD outcomes. High-performing centers integrated education early in chronic kidney disease management.

Our findings align with the "PD First" philosophy and the concept that program success is multifactorial, requiring alignment of structure, process, and outcomes. Limitations include the retrospective design, potential selection bias, and lack of randomization. Residual confounding cannot be excluded. Additionally, satisfaction measures may be influenced by cultural factors.

Future research should prospectively evaluate interventions targeting these components, including cost-effectiveness analyses of dedicated coordinators and home visit programs. Quality improvement collaboratives could disseminate best practices across centers.

 Conclusion

Successful PD programs share identifiable structural and process components: dedicated PD coordinators, adequate nurse staffing, comprehensive pre-dialysis education, structured training exceeding 25 hours, standardized protocols, routine retraining, and home visit programs. These elements independently predict lower peritonitis rates, superior technique survival, reduced hospitalization, and higher patient satisfaction. Healthcare systems should prioritize investment in these components to optimize PD utilization and outcomes. Program leaders can use these findings to benchmark performance and guide quality improvement initiatives, ultimately expanding access to this patient-centered, cost-effective therapy.

title: Effects of the addition of waxy and normal hull-less barley flours on the farinograph and pasting properties of composite flours and on the nutritional value, textural qualities, and in vitro digestibility of resultant breads
text: Abstract: This study investigated the effects of substituting wheat flour with waxy (W) and normal (N) hull-less barley flours at different levels (0–40%, w/w) on the farinograph and pasting properties of composite flours, as well as on the nutritional value, textural qualities, and in vitro starch digestibility of the resultant breads. Increasing the substitution level of either barley flour decreased water absorption, development time, and stability of the composite dough, while pasting viscosity, breakdown, and setback values were also reduced, with waxy barley flour exerting more pronounced effects than normal barley flour at the same substitution level. Breads containing barley flour exhibited lower specific volume and darker crumb color, but higher dietary fiber, β-glucan, and total phenolic contents compared with the control. Texture profile analysis showed that barley incorporation increased crumb hardness and chewiness and decreased springiness and cohesiveness, with waxy barley flour resulting in softer crumbs than normal barley flour at equivalent levels. In vitro digestion revealed that both barley flours significantly reduced the rapidly digestible starch content and the predicted glycemic index (pGI) of breads, while increasing the slowly digestible starch and resistant starch fractions; the waxy genotype was more effective in lowering pGI, which decreased from 88.6 in the control to 71.4 and 74.8 in breads with 40% waxy and normal barley flour, respectively. Correlation analysis indicated that β-glucan and phenolic contents were negatively correlated with pGI and crumb hardness. Overall, partial substitution with hull-less barley flour, particularly the waxy type, improved the nutritional and functional properties of bread, although it compromised dough handling and bread volume at high substitution levels. These findings provide a theoretical basis for developing barley-enriched bakery products with enhanced health benefits.

title: An efficient, green and sustainable potassium hydroxide activated magnetic corn cob biochar for imidacloprid removal
text:
An efficient, green and sustainable potassium hydroxide activated magnetic corn cob biochar for imidacloprid removal

Abstract

Imidacloprid, a widely used neonicotinoid insecticide, poses persistent threats to aquatic ecosystems and human health due to its high water solubility and resistance to conventional degradation. In this study, a novel magnetic biochar derived from agricultural waste corn cob was synthesized via a green potassium hydroxide (KOH) activation route and evaluated for imidacloprid removal from aqueous solution. The optimized material, designated as K-MCB-700 (pyrolysis at 700 °C, KOH:biomass mass ratio of 1:1, Fe₃O₄ loading of 15 wt%), exhibited a high specific surface area of 892.6 m² g⁻¹, a total pore volume of 0.48 cm³ g⁻¹, and a saturation magnetization of 12.4 emu g⁻¹, enabling rapid magnetic separation. Batch adsorption experiments revealed a maximum Langmuir adsorption capacity of 312.5 mg g⁻¹ for imidacloprid at 298 K and pH 6.0. The adsorption kinetics followed a pseudo-second-order model (R² > 0.99), and thermodynamics indicated a spontaneous and endothermic process. The removal efficiency remained above 88% after five consecutive regeneration cycles, demonstrating excellent reusability. Mechanistic analysis suggested that pore filling, π–π electron donor–acceptor interactions, hydrogen bonding, and electrostatic attraction collectively governed the adsorption. This work presents a sustainable, low-cost, and easily recoverable biochar adsorbent for efficient removal of neonicotinoid pollutants from contaminated water.

Keywords: Corn cob biochar; Potassium hydroxide activation; Magnetic separation; Imidacloprid; Adsorption; Sustainable remediation

1. Introduction

Neonicotinoid insecticides, particularly imidacloprid (1-(6-chloro-3-pyridylmethyl)-N-nitroimidazolidin-2-ylideneamine), have become the most extensively applied class of insecticides worldwide owing to their high efficacy against sucking pests and low mammalian toxicity. However, their widespread use has led to ubiquitous environmental contamination. Imidacloprid is highly soluble in water (610 mg L⁻¹ at 20 °C), moderately persistent in soil (half-life 40–120 days), and mobile in aquatic environments. It is toxic to non-target organisms such as bees, aquatic invertebrates, and birds, and has been detected in surface water, groundwater, and even drinking water sources at concentrations ranging from ng L⁻¹ to μg L⁻¹. Chronic exposure to imidacloprid has been associated with neurotoxicity, oxidative stress, and potential endocrine disruption in humans. Therefore, developing efficient, affordable, and environmentally friendly technologies for imidacloprid removal from water is urgently needed.

Among various remediation techniques—including advanced oxidation, photocatalysis, membrane filtration, and microbial degradation—adsorption is widely regarded as one of the most promising due to its simplicity, low energy consumption, and absence of toxic by-products. Activated carbon is a conventional adsorbent, but its high production cost and difficulty in regeneration limit its large-scale application. In recent years, biochar derived from agricultural and forestry wastes has emerged as a cost-effective and sustainable alternative. Biochar possesses abundant surface functional groups, high porosity, and good chemical stability. Nevertheless, pristine biochar often suffers from limited adsorption capacity toward hydrophilic pollutants like imidacloprid due to insufficient porosity and lack of specific binding sites.

Chemical activation with potassium hydroxide (KOH) is a well-established green method to enhance biochar porosity and surface reactivity. KOH reacts with carbonaceous materials to generate micro- and mesopores, increase surface area, and introduce oxygen-containing functional groups. Unlike ZnCl₂ or H₃PO₄, KOH avoids heavy metal contamination and corrosive residues, aligning with green chemistry principles. Furthermore, endowing biochar with magnetic properties via Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles facilitates easy separation and recovery, preventing secondary pollution and reducing operational costs.

Corn cob, an abundant agricultural residue generated worldwide (over 200 million tons annually), is rich in cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, making it an ideal precursor for porous carbon. To date, few studies have systematically optimized KOH-activated magnetic corn cob biochar for imidacloprid removal, and the underlying adsorption mechanisms remain insufficiently elucidated.

In this study, we synthesized a magnetic KOH-activated corn cob biochar (K-MCB) through a simple co-precipitation method. The objectives were to: (1) optimize pyrolysis temperature, KOH ratio, and Fe₃O₄ loading; (2) characterize the physicochemical properties of the optimized material; (3) evaluate adsorption performance under varying pH, contact time, initial concentration, and temperature; (4) assess reusability and magnetic recovery; and (5) propose adsorption mechanisms. This work aims to provide a green, efficient, and sustainable strategy for neonicotinoid pesticide remediation.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Materials

Corn cobs were collected from a local farm in Henan Province, China. They were washed, dried at 80 °C for 24 h, crushed, and sieved to 60–80 mesh. Imidacloprid (purity ≥ 98%) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. KOH, FeCl₃·6H₂O, FeSO₄·7H₂O, NH₃·H₂O, HCl, and NaOH were of analytical grade and used without further purification. Deionized water (18.2 MΩ cm) was used throughout.

2.2 Synthesis of K-MCB

Raw corn cob powder was impregnated with KOH solution at mass ratios of 0.5:1, 1:1, and 2:1 (KOH:biomass). The mixtures were stirred for 2 h, dried at 105 °C overnight, and then pyrolyzed in a tube furnace under N₂ flow (100 mL min⁻¹) at 500, 600, 700, and 800 °C for 2 h (heating rate 5 °C min⁻¹). The resulting biochars were washed with 1 M HCl and hot deionized water until neutral pH, then dried at 80 °C. The optimized KOH-activated biochar (KCB-700) was selected for magnetic modification. Fe₃O₄ loading was achieved by co-precipitating Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ (molar ratio 1:2) in the presence of KCB-700 under N₂ atmosphere, adjusting pH to 10 with NH₃·H₂O, and stirring at 60 °C for 1 h. The final product (K-MCB-700) was magnetically separated, washed, and dried. Fe₃O₄ content was determined by thermogravimetric analysis.

2.3 Characterization

Surface morphology was observed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi SU8000). Specific surface area and pore size distribution were measured by N₂ adsorption–desorption at 77 K (Micromeritics ASAP 2020). Surface functional groups were analyzed by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR, Thermo Nicolet iS50). Crystal structure was examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance). Magnetic properties were measured by vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM, Lake Shore 7404). Zeta potential was determined using a Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS.

2.4 Adsorption experiments

Batch adsorption experiments were conducted in 100 mL conical flasks containing 50 mL imidacloprid solution of desired concentration and 10 mg adsorbent. The flasks were shaken at 150 rpm in a thermostatic shaker. Parameters investigated included: pH (2–10, adjusted with 0.1 M HCl/NaOH), contact time (0–240 min), initial concentration (10–500 mg L⁻¹), and temperature (288, 298, 308 K). After adsorption, the adsorbent was separated by a magnet, and residual imidacloprid concentration was measured by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, Agilent 1260) with a C18 column (4.6 × 150 mm, 5 μm) and UV detector at 270 nm. The mobile phase was methanol/water (60:40, v/v) at a flow rate of 1.0 mL min⁻¹. Adsorption capacity (qₑ, mg g⁻¹) and removal efficiency (%) were calculated using standard equations.

2.5 Regeneration

Spent K-MCB-700 was regenerated by washing with 0.1 M NaOH followed by deionized water, then dried at 60 °C. Five consecutive adsorption–desorption cycles were performed.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Optimization of synthesis conditions

The yield and adsorption capacity of biochars varied with pyrolysis temperature and KOH ratio. At 700 °C with KOH:biomass = 1:1, the biochar exhibited the highest imidacloprid adsorption capacity (298.4 mg g⁻¹) and reasonable yield (32.5%). Lower temperatures (500–600 °C) resulted in incomplete carbonization and lower porosity, while higher temperature (800 °C) caused pore collapse and reduced surface functional groups. A higher KOH ratio (2:1) over-activated the carbon, decreasing yield and mechanical stability. Fe₃O₄ loading of 15 wt% provided sufficient magnetic response without significantly blocking pores.

3.2 Characterization

SEM images showed that K-MCB-700 possessed a rough, porous surface with abundant cavities, and spherical Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles (20–40 nm) were uniformly dispersed. The specific surface area and total pore volume were 892.6 m² g⁻¹ and 0.48 cm³ g⁻¹, respectively, much higher than those of unactivated biochar (126.3 m² g⁻¹, 0.11 cm³ g⁻¹). Micropores (<2 nm) accounted for 68% of the pore volume, with mesopores contributing 27%. FTIR spectra displayed characteristic peaks at 3420 cm⁻¹ (–OH), 1580 cm⁻¹ (aromatic C=C), 1120 cm⁻¹ (C–O), and 580 cm⁻¹ (Fe–O). XRD patterns confirmed the presence of Fe₃O₄ (JCPDS 19-0629) with a spinel structure. VSM analysis showed a saturation magnetization of 12.4 emu g⁻¹, with negligible coercivity, indicating superparamagnetic behavior. Zeta potential measurements revealed an isoelectric point at pH 4.2; the surface was negatively charged at pH > 4.2.

3.3 Adsorption performance

Effect of pH: Imidacloprid removal increased from 45.2% at pH 2.0 to a maximum of 96.8% at pH 6.0, then declined to 72.1% at pH 10.0. The optimal pH 6.0 was close to the pKa of imidacloprid (1.6 for the pyridine nitrogen and 11.1 for the imidazolidine nitrogen), favoring neutral species and π–π interactions.

Kinetics: Adsorption reached equilibrium within 120 min. The pseudo-second-order model fitted the data best (R² = 0.998), suggesting chemisorption as the rate-limiting step. The intraparticle diffusion model indicated that both film diffusion and pore diffusion contributed.

Isotherms: The Langmuir model (R² = 0.995) described the isotherm better than the Freundlich model, indicating monolayer adsorption. The maximum adsorption capacities at 288, 298, and 308 K were 278.6, 312.5, and 341.2 mg g⁻¹, respectively. The Freundlich constant n was 3.21, suggesting favorable adsorption.

Thermodynamics: The negative ΔG° values (–18.6 to –22.4 kJ mol⁻¹) confirmed spontaneity. Positive ΔH° (24.7 kJ mol⁻¹) and ΔS° (0.15 kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) indicated an endothermic and entropy-driven process.

3.4 Reusability and magnetic recovery

After five cycles, the adsorption capacity of K-MCB-700 decreased from 312.5 to 275.6 mg g⁻¹, with a removal efficiency of 88.2%. The slight loss was attributed to pore blockage and minor Fe₃O₄ leaching (<2%). The adsorbent was rapidly separated (<30 s) under an external magnet, demonstrating excellent operational convenience.

4. Discussion

The superior adsorption performance of K-MCB-700 can be attributed to multiple synergistic mechanisms. First, the high specific surface area and micro/mesoporous structure provided abundant active sites for pore filling, which is particularly effective for small imidacloprid molecules (molecular dimensions ~1.2 × 0.5 nm). Second, KOH activation introduced oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., –OH, –COOH) that can form hydrogen bonds with the nitro and imidazolidine groups of imidacloprid. Third, the graphitic domains in biochar acted as π-electron donors, while the electron-deficient pyridine ring of imidacloprid served as a π-electron acceptor, facilitating π–π electron donor–acceptor interactions. Fourth, electrostatic attraction occurred between the negatively charged biochar surface (at pH 6.0) and the partially protonated imidacloprid species. Fifth, Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles not only enabled magnetic separation but also contributed to adsorption via surface complexation with the nitro group.

The endothermic nature suggests that higher temperatures promote adsorption, likely due to increased molecular mobility and enhanced diffusion. The good reusability indicates that NaOH effectively desorbed imidacloprid by deprotonating surface groups and disrupting π–π interactions.

Compared with other reported adsorbents (e.g., commercial activated carbon: 180–220 mg g⁻¹; graphene oxide: 250–300 mg g⁻¹; modified clays: 80–150 mg g⁻¹), K-MCB-700 exhibits competitive or superior capacity, while offering the advantages of low cost, green synthesis, and easy magnetic recovery. The use of agricultural waste corn cob aligns with circular economy principles, and KOH activation avoids toxic reagents. The magnetic property prevents secondary pollution and reduces separation costs. However, long-term stability and Fe₃O₄ leaching under acidic conditions warrant further investigation. Future work should also evaluate the adsorption performance in real water matrices containing competing ions and natural organic matter.

5. Conclusion

In this study, a green and sustainable magnetic biochar (K-MCB-700) was successfully synthesized from corn cob via KOH activation and Fe₃O₄ co-precipitation. The material exhibited a high surface area (892.6 m² g⁻¹), good magnetic responsiveness (12.4 emu g⁻¹), and excellent imidacloprid adsorption capacity (312.5 mg g⁻¹ at 298 K). Adsorption followed pseudo-second-order kinetics and Langmuir isotherm, and was spontaneous and endothermic. The removal efficiency remained above 88% after five regeneration cycles. Mechanisms involved pore filling, π–π interactions, hydrogen bonding, and electrostatic attraction. This work provides a promising, low-cost, and environmentally friendly adsorbent for neonicotinoid pesticide removal, contributing to sustainable water remediation and agricultural waste valorization.

title: Impact of manure on soil biochemical properties: A global synthesis
text:
Manure application is a longstanding agricultural practice used to sustain soil fertility and crop productivity. As global demand for food increases, livestock production has expanded, generating substantial quantities of manure that are increasingly recycled into croplands as organic amendments. Compared with synthetic fertilizers, manure supplies not only nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium but also organic carbon and diverse microbial communities, which may broadly influence soil biochemical functioning. Understanding these effects is essential for evaluating manure as a strategy for soil health and climate mitigation.

Soil biochemical properties, including enzyme activities, microbial biomass, respiration, and organic matter fractions, are sensitive indicators of soil quality and nutrient cycling.
