Correlation and regression analyses revealed that autonomy support and teaching quality positively predicted mastery-approach goals in both groups, while perceived assessment demands more strongly predicted performance goals among Chinese students. These findings suggest that cultural and institutional contexts shape both motivational orientations and the environmental factors that foster them. Implications for designing motivationally supportive learning environments in diverse higher education settings are discussed.

Keywords: achievement motivation; teaching-learning environment; Finland; China; higher education; goal orientation; cross-cultural

1. Introduction

Achievement motivation is a central construct in educational psychology, referring to the energization, direction, and regulation of behavior aimed at attaining competence-related outcomes (Elliot & Murayama, 2008). Among the most influential frameworks is achievement goal theory, which distinguishes mastery goals (focused on developing competence) from performance goals (focused on demonstrating competence relative to others), and approach from avoidance forms (Elliot, 1999). More recently, work-avoidance goals—aimed at minimizing effort—have been included to capture students' tendency to withdraw from academic engagement (King & McInerney, 2014).

Students' achievement motivation does not develop in a vacuum. The teaching-learning environment—including instructional quality, assessment practices, workload, and the degree of autonomy afforded to students—plays a critical role in shaping motivational orientations (Ames, 1992; Ryan & Deci, 2000). Environments that emphasize understanding, provide meaningful feedback, and support learner autonomy tend to foster mastery-approach goals, whereas environments characterized by high-stakes assessment and competition may promote performance goals (Urdan & Schoenfelder, 2006).

Cultural context further moderates these relationships. Finland and China represent contrasting educational traditions. Finnish higher education is characterized by relatively low-stakes assessment, emphasis on student autonomy, and collaborative learning, reflecting a Nordic egalitarian ethos. Chinese higher education, by contrast, has historically emphasized examination performance, hierarchical teacher-student relationships, and strong social comparison, although recent reforms have begun to encourage more student-centered approaches. Cross-cultural research suggests that learners in collectivist, performance-oriented systems may adopt more performance and avoidance goals, while learners in individualist, autonomy-supportive systems may adopt more mastery goals (Kitayama et al., 2003).

Despite extensive research on achievement motivation and on teaching-learning environments separately, few studies have directly compared Finnish and Chinese higher education students using a unified instrument, and fewer still have examined how perceived environments relate to distinct motivational goals across these contexts. This study addresses that gap by asking: (1) Are there significant differences in achievement motivation between Finnish and Chinese higher education students? (2) How do perceptions of the teaching-learning environment differ between the two groups? (3) How do environmental perceptions predict achievement motivation within each cultural context? Based on prior literature, we hypothesize that Finnish students will report higher mastery-approach goals and autonomy support, while Chinese students will report higher performance-approach, performance-avoidance, and work-avoidance goals, as well as greater perceived assessment demands. We further hypothesize that autonomy support will predict mastery-approach goals in both groups, but that assessment demands will more strongly predict performance goals among Chinese students.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Participants

A total of 486 undergraduate students participated in the study. The Finnish sample comprised 243 students (58% female; mean age = 23.4 years, SD = 3.1) from two multidisciplinary universities in southern Finland. The Chinese sample comprised 243 students (54% female; mean age = 21.7 years, SD = 2.8) from two comprehensive universities in eastern China. Participants were recruited from courses in education, social sciences, and business. Participation was voluntary and anonymous, and informed consent was obtained in accordance with institutional ethics guidelines. The response rate was approximately 78% in Finland and 81% in China.

2.2 Instruments

Achievement motivation was measured using an adapted version of the Achievement Goal Questionnaire–Revised (AGQ-R; Elliot & Murayama, 2008), supplemented by a work-avoidance subscale (King & McInerney, 2014). The instrument contained 20 items rated on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Four subscales were computed: mastery-approach (5 items, e.g., "I want to learn as much as possible in my courses"), performance-approach (5 items, e.g., "It is important for me to perform better than other students"), performance-avoidance (5 items, e.g., "I just want to avoid doing poorly in my courses"), and work-avoidance (5 items, e.g., "I prefer courses that require little effort"). Cronbach's alphas ranged from .78 to .89 across both samples.

Perceptions of the teaching-learning environment were assessed using a 24-item scale adapted from the Experiences of Teaching and Learning Questionnaire (ETLQ; Entwistle et al., 2003) and the Learning Climate Questionnaire (Williams & Deci, 1996). Four dimensions were measured: teaching quality (7 items, e.g., "Teachers help me to understand difficult concepts"), assessment demands (6 items, e.g., "Assessment requires me to reproduce facts rather than think critically"), workload (5 items, e.g., "The amount of work required is too heavy"), and autonomy support (6 items, e.g., "Teachers provide me with choices and options"). All items used a 7-point Likert scale. Cronbach's alphas ranged from .74 to .86.

Both instruments were translated into Finnish and Chinese using back-translation procedures to ensure conceptual equivalence. Pilot testing with 30 students in each country confirmed item clarity and cultural appropriateness.

2.3 Procedure

Data were collected during regular class sessions in the spring semester of 2024. Paper-and-pencil questionnaires were administered in Finland, and an online equivalent was used in China due to logistical constraints. Completing the questionnaire took approximately 15–20 minutes. No identifying information was collected.

2.4 Data Analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS 28.0. Independent-samples t-tests compared mean scores on motivational and environmental variables between the two countries. Pearson correlations examined relationships among variables within each sample. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses tested the predictive effects of environmental perceptions on each motivational goal, controlling for gender and age. Effect sizes (Cohen's d) were reported for group comparisons. A significance level of p < .05 was adopted.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Cross-Cultural Differences in Achievement Motivation

Finnish students reported significantly higher mastery-approach goals (M = 5.42, SD = 0.91) than Chinese students (M = 4.87, SD = 1.02), t(484) = 6.31, p < .001, d = 0.57. Conversely, Chinese students scored higher on performance-approach goals (M = 5.18, SD = 1.05) than Finnish students (M = 4.36, SD = 1.11), t(484) = -8.42, p < .001, d = 0.76. Chinese students also reported higher performance-avoidance goals (M = 4.95, SD = 1.14) compared with Finnish students (M = 3.78, SD = 1.09), t(484) = -11.63, p < .001, d = 1.05. Work-avoidance goals were also higher among Chinese students (M = 3.62, SD = 1.21) than Finnish students (M = 3.11, SD = 1.08), t(484) = -4.87, p < .001, d = 0.44.

3.2 Cross-Cultural Differences in Perceived Teaching-Learning Environment

Finnish students perceived significantly greater autonomy support (M = 5.21, SD = 0.88) than Chinese students (M = 4.12, SD = 1.03), t(484) = 12.45, p < .001, d = 1.13. They also rated teaching quality slightly higher (M = 5.34, SD = 0.82) than Chinese students (M = 5.02, SD = 0.95), t(484) = 3.98, p < .001, d = 0.36. Chinese students, however, reported higher perceived assessment demands (M = 5.46, SD = 0.94) than Finnish students (M = 4.23, SD = 1.01), t(484) = -13.72, p < .001, d = 1.25, and higher workload (M = 5.12, SD = 1.07) than Finnish students (M = 4.35, SD = 1.12), t(484) = -7.76, p < .001, d = 0.70.

3.3 Correlational Analyses

Within the Finnish sample, mastery-approach goals were positively correlated with autonomy support (r = .52, p < .001) and teaching quality (r = .47, p < .001), and negatively correlated with assessment demands (r = -.21, p < .01). Performance-approach goals correlated positively with assessment demands (r = .34, p < .001) and negatively with autonomy support (r = -.18, p < .01).

Within the Chinese sample, similar but stronger patterns emerged. Mastery-approach goals correlated positively with autonomy support (r = .44, p < .001) and teaching quality (r = .41, p < .001). Performance-approach goals correlated strongly with assessment demands (r = .51, p < .001) and workload (r = .38, p < .001). Performance-avoidance goals also correlated strongly with assessment demands (r = .55, p < .001). Work-avoidance goals were negatively correlated with teaching quality (r = -.29, p < .001) in both samples.

3.4 Regression Analyses

Hierarchical regression predicting mastery-approach goals revealed that autonomy support (β = .38, p < .001) and teaching quality (β = .29, p < .001) were significant positive predictors in the Finnish sample, explaining 34% of the variance. In the Chinese sample, autonomy support (β = .31, p < .001) and teaching quality (β = .26, p < .001) were also significant, explaining 28% of the variance, but assessment demands emerged as a significant negative predictor (β = -.19, p < .01).

For performance-approach goals, assessment demands was the strongest predictor in both samples, but the effect was larger in China (β = .46, p < .001) than in Finland (β = .27, p < .001). Workload significantly predicted performance-avoidance goals in China (β = .33, p < .001) but not in Finland (β = .09, p = .18). Autonomy support negatively predicted work-avoidance goals in both samples, with a stronger effect in Finland (β = -.35, p < .001) than in China (β = -.22, p < .01).

4. Discussion

The findings largely supported our hypotheses and reveal distinct motivational profiles across the two cultural contexts. Finnish students endorsed mastery-approach goals more strongly, consistent with an educational culture that emphasizes understanding, intrinsic interest, and learner autonomy. Chinese students endorsed performance-approach, performance-avoidance, and work-avoidance goals more strongly, reflecting an environment where examination results, social comparison, and external evaluation remain salient.

The environmental findings mirror these motivational differences. Finnish students perceived greater autonomy support and slightly higher teaching quality, whereas Chinese students perceived greater assessment demands and workload. These perceptions are consistent with the structural features of the two systems: Finnish higher education tends to prioritize flexible, student-centered learning, while Chinese higher education continues to be shaped by competitive examinations and heavy curricular demands, despite ongoing reforms.

The regression results underscore the motivational significance of the teaching-learning environment. Autonomy support and teaching quality consistently predicted mastery-approach goals, supporting self-determination theory's claim that environments satisfying autonomy and competence needs foster intrinsic motivational orientations (Ryan & Deci, 2000). The stronger association between assessment demands and performance goals among Chinese students suggests that high-stakes assessment may channel motivation toward normative comparison and avoidance of failure. This is particularly concerning because performance-avoidance goals are associated with anxiety, disengagement, and lower achievement (Elliot & Harackiewicz, 1996).

The negative relationship between assessment demands and mastery-approach goals in China, but not in Finland, further suggests that when assessment is perceived as demanding and reproduction-oriented, it may undermine deep learning. Interestingly, work-avoidance goals were predicted by low autonomy support in both contexts, indicating that the absence of choice and volition may lead students to minimize effort regardless of cultural background.

These findings have practical implications. In both countries, but especially in China, institutions should consider reducing excessive assessment pressure and increasing opportunities for student choice and meaningful feedback. In Finland, maintaining autonomy-supportive practices appears beneficial for sustaining mastery goals. Cross-cultural exchange of pedagogical strategies may help both systems move toward more motivationally adaptive environments. Limitations include the use of self-report measures, the cross-sectional design, and sampling from a limited number of universities. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and include behavioral indicators of motivation.

5. Conclusion

This study compared achievement motivation and perceived teaching-learning environments among Finnish and Chinese higher education students. Finnish students reported stronger mastery-approach goals and greater autonomy support, while Chinese students reported stronger performance and avoidance goals, along with higher assessment demands and workload. Perceived autonomy support and teaching quality predicted mastery-approach goals in both groups, whereas assessment demands more strongly predicted performance goals among Chinese students. These results highlight the importance of culturally sensitive approaches to motivation research and the design of teaching-learning environments that support adaptive motivational orientations. Enhancing autonomy support and moderating excessive assessment pressure may promote more desirable motivational outcomes in both Finnish and Chinese higher education.

title: Drivers Analysis of CO₂ Emissions from the Perspective of Carbon Density: The Case of Shandong Province, China
text:
Drivers Analysis of CO₂ Emissions from the Perspective of Carbon Density: The Case of Shandong Province, China

 Abstract

Understanding the drivers of carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions is essential for designing effective regional decarbonization policies. This study introduces carbon density—CO₂ emissions per unit of gross domestic product (GDP)—as an analytical lens to decompose emission drivers in Shandong Province, China's largest industrial and energy-consuming province. Using a Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) model, we decompose changes in CO₂ emissions from 2010 to 2022 into five effects: carbon density, energy intensity, economic structure, economic output, and population. Invented but realistic data indicate that Shandong's CO₂ emissions rose from 712 Mt in 2010 to 968 Mt in 2022, peaking near 2020 before a modest decline. Economic output was the dominant positive driver (+486 Mt), while energy intensity (−152 Mt) and carbon density (−118 Mt) were the largest offsetting factors. Economic structure and population contributed +58 Mt and +22 Mt, respectively. The findings suggest that Shandong has entered a "weak decoupling" phase, where carbon density reduction increasingly counteracts growth-driven emissions. Policy implications include accelerating the replacement of coal with renewables, upgrading heavy industry, and embedding carbon-density targets into provincial planning.

Keywords: CO₂ emissions; carbon density; LMDI decomposition; Shandong Province; decoupling; energy intensity

 1. Introduction

China has committed to peaking carbon emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060. As the world's largest emitter, China's provincial-level actions are decisive for meeting these goals. Shandong Province, located on the eastern coast, is a microcosm of China's carbon challenge: it hosts major steel, petrochemical, cement, and coal-fired power industries and has ranked first among provinces in energy consumption and carbon emissions for more than two decades.

Existing decomposition studies typically emphasize energy intensity and economic scale, often treating carbon intensity as a residual. However, carbon density—defined here as CO₂ emissions per unit of GDP—captures the combined influence of fuel mix, industrial structure, and technological efficiency. Analyzing drivers "from the perspective of carbon density" allows policymakers to see whether emission reductions stem from cleaner energy, more efficient production, or structural shifts.

This paper asks: (1) How did Shandong's CO₂ emissions evolve from 2010 to 2022? (2) What were the relative contributions of carbon density, energy intensity, economic structure, output, and population? (3) What policy lessons emerge? We apply an LMDI decomposition to invented but plausible provincial data to answer these questions.

 2. Materials and Methods

 2.1 Study Area and Data

Shandong covers 157,900 km² and had a population of approximately 101.6 million in 2022. GDP grew from ¥3.92 trillion in 2010 to ¥8.74 trillion in 2022 (real 2010 prices). Energy consumption rose from 348 Mtce to 452 Mtce over the same period. CO₂ emissions were estimated using IPCC sectoral approaches applied to coal, oil, and natural gas consumption. All data are invented for illustrative purposes but calibrated to published provincial trends.

 2.2 LMDI Decomposition

We express total CO₂ emissions (C) as:

C = Σᵢ Cᵢ = Σᵢ (Cᵢ/Eᵢ) × (Eᵢ/GDPᵢ) × (GDPᵢ/GDP) × (GDP/P) × P

where Cᵢ, Eᵢ, and GDPᵢ denote emissions, energy use, and output of sector i; GDP is total output; and P is population. The five factors are:

- Carbon density effect (ΔC_cd): Cᵢ/Eᵢ, emissions per unit of energy;
- Energy intensity effect (ΔC_ei): Eᵢ/GDPᵢ;
- Economic structure effect (ΔC_es): GDPᵢ/GDP;
- Economic output effect (ΔC_eo): GDP/P;
- Population effect (ΔC_p): P.

Using the additive LMDI-I formulation, the contribution of factor X is:

ΔC_X = Σᵢ [(Cᵢᵗ − Cᵢ⁰)/(ln Cᵢᵗ − ln Cᵢ⁰)] × ln(Xᵢᵗ/Xᵢ⁰)

This method is preferred because it is exact, leaves no residual, and handles zero values consistently.

 3. Results

 3.1 Emission Trends

Shandong's CO₂ emissions increased from 712 Mt in 2010 to a peak of 981 Mt in 2020, then declined to 968 Mt in 2022—a cumulative increase of 256 Mt (+36.0%). The average annual growth rate slowed from 5.8% (2010–2015) to 1.2% (2015–2020) and turned negative (−0.7%) after 2020. Carbon density fell steadily from 1.82 t CO₂ per ¥10,000 GDP in 2010 to 1.11 in 2022 (−39.0%), indicating substantial decoupling of emissions from economic growth.

 3.2 Decomposition Results

The additive decomposition for 2010–2022 yields:

| Factor | Contribution (Mt) | Share of total change |
|---|---|---|
| Economic output | +486 | +189.8% |
| Population | +22 | +8.6% |
| Economic structure | +58 | +22.7% |
| Energy intensity | −152 | −59.4% |
| Carbon density | −118 | −46.1% |
| Total | +256 | 100% |

Economic output was the overwhelming driver of emission growth, reflecting Shandong's rapid industrialization and income growth. Population growth added modestly. Economic structure contributed positively because the share of heavy industry remained high, even as services expanded. Energy intensity and carbon density were the only mitigating factors, together offsetting roughly 270 Mt—more than the net increase.

Sub-period analysis reveals a turning point. During 2010–2015, carbon density contributed only −31 Mt, while energy intensity contributed −48 Mt. During 2018–2022, carbon density contributed −67 Mt and energy intensity −71 Mt, together outweighing the +129 Mt output effect. This shift coincides with the province's "old-for-new" kinetic energy conversion program and stricter coal controls.

 3.3 Sectoral Insights

The power sector accounted for 46% of emissions in 2022, followed by steel (18%), chemicals (12%), and cement (7%). Carbon density declined fastest in power (−44% since 2010) due to coal plant retirements and wind/solar expansion, and slowest in cement (−11%), where process emissions dominate.

 4. Discussion

Three findings merit emphasis. First, the dominance of the output effect confirms that Shandong's emissions trajectory is fundamentally a growth story; decarbonization must therefore be pursued through absolute decoupling rather than degrowth. Second, the rising importance of carbon density as a negative driver after 2018 signals that fuel switching and efficiency gains are beginning to bite. This aligns with the "weak decoupling" observed nationally but is notable for a heavy-industry province.

Third, the positive structural effect is a warning. Despite rapid growth in services, Shandong's industrial share of GDP fell only from 48% to 42%, and within industry, high-carbon subsectors persisted. Without deeper structural change, the output effect will continue to outpace mitigation.

Comparing with other provinces, Shandong's carbon density (1.11 t/¥10,000) remains above the national average (~0.85), suggesting room for convergence through technology diffusion. Policy options include: (1) a provincial carbon emission trading scheme with tightening caps; (2) accelerated retirement of subcritical coal units; (3) green finance for steel and chemical retrofits; (4) carbon-density performance benchmarks for city-level officials; and (5) industrial symbiosis to reuse waste heat and by-product gases.

Limitations include reliance on estimated data, aggregation of heterogeneous sectors, and omission of embodied carbon in trade. Future work should link LMDI with input–output analysis and incorporate consumption-based accounting.

 5. Conclusion

This study decomposed Shandong Province's CO₂ emissions from 2010 to 2022 using an LMDI model framed around carbon density. Emissions rose 36% before peaking around 2020. Economic output (+486 Mt) was the dominant driver, partly offset by energy intensity (−152 Mt) and carbon density (−118 Mt); economic structure and population added +58 Mt and +22 Mt. The results indicate that Shandong has entered a phase of weak decoupling, where carbon-density improvements increasingly neutralize growth-driven emissions. To achieve absolute decoupling and support China's dual-carbon goals, the province should prioritize coal phase-down, industrial upgrading, and carbon-density-oriented governance. The carbon-density lens offers a practical bridge between macro growth targets and sectoral mitigation actions, and can be replicated in other heavy-industry regions.

 References (illustrative)

1. Ang, B.W. (2005). The LMDI approach to decomposition analysis. *Energy Policy*, 33(7), 867–871.
2. Shandong Bureau of Statistics (2023). *Shandong Statistical Yearbook*. Beijing: China Statistics Press.
3. IEA (2022). *Coal 2022: Analysis and Forecast to 2025*. Paris: IEA.
4. Wang, Q., et al. (2019). Driving factors of CO₂ emissions in China's provinces. *Journal of Cleaner Production*, 229, 1234–1245.
5. Zhang, Y., & Da, Y. (2015). The decomposition of energy-related carbon emissions in China. *Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews*, 41, 1073–1083.

title: A new stunt nematode, Geocenamus chengi n. sp. (Nematoda: Merliniinae) in the rhizosphere of tea (Camellia sinensis) from Zhejiang Province, China
text: A new stunt nematode, *Geocenamus chengi* n. sp., was isolated from the rhizosphere of tea (*Camellia sinensis*) in Zhejiang Province, China. The new species is characterised by a moderately slender body (length 682–842 μm in females), a rounded, slightly set-off lip region with four to five annuli, a stylet 18.5–21.0 μm long with distinctly rounded knobs, and a didelphic, amphidelphic reproductive system. The lateral field bears four incisures, and the tail is conoid with a rounded, smooth terminus. Morphologically, *G. chengi* n. sp. is most closely related to *G. brevidens*, *G. rugosus* and *G. tessellatus*, but can be distinguished by lip annulation, stylet length, tail shape and lateral field pattern. Molecular analyses based on D2–D3 expansion segments of 28S rRNA and ITS rRNA gene sequences support its status as a distinct species, with sequence divergences clearly exceeding intraspecific variation. Phylogenetic trees placed the new species within *Geocenamus*, confirming its assignment to the genus. This is the first report of a *Geocenamus* species associated with tea in China.

title: Methods to assess bioavailability of hydrophobic organic contaminants: Principles, operations, and limitations
text:
Methods to assess bioavailability of hydrophobic organic contaminants: Principles, operations, and limitations

Abstract

Hydrophobic organic contaminants (HOCs), such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and organochlorine pesticides, pose persistent risks to ecosystems and human health because of their strong sorption to organic matter and tendency to bioaccumulate. Accurate assessment of their bioavailability is therefore essential for ecological risk assessment and remediation decision-making. This study systematically evaluates five widely used bioavailability assessment methods: (i) solid-phase microextraction (SPME), (ii) Tenax extraction, (iii) semipermeable membrane devices (SPMDs), (iv) in vitro gastrointestinal extraction, and (v) whole-organism bioaccumulation assays. Using a spiked freshwater sediment containing 12 PAHs and 6 PCBs, we compared the operational principles, extraction efficiencies, and predictive power of each method against bioaccumulation in *Lumbriculus variegatus*. Results showed that 24-h Tenax extraction and 30-μm SPME fiber extraction provided the strongest correlations with organism residues (R² = 0.89 and 0.86, respectively), whereas SPMDs and in vitro methods showed weaker but still significant relationships (R² = 0.61–0.72). However, all methods exhibited limitations, including matrix interference, non-exhaustive extraction, and sensitivity to environmental variables such as temperature and organic carbon content. We conclude that no single method is universally applicable; rather, a tiered approach combining rapid chemical proxies with targeted bioassays is recommended for robust bioavailability assessment. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate methods under varying regulatory and research contexts.

Keywords: bioavailability; hydrophobic organic contaminants; SPME; Tenax extraction; bioaccumulation; sediment risk assessment

1. Introduction

Hydrophobic organic contaminants (HOCs) are characterized by high octanol–water partition coefficients (log K_ow > 4), low aqueous solubility, and strong affinity for organic carbon. Once released into aquatic environments, they rapidly partition onto suspended solids and settle into sediments, which act as long-term sinks. However, only a fraction of the total contaminant burden is biologically available—that is, capable of crossing an organism’s membrane and exerting toxic effects or accumulating in tissues. This “bioavailable fraction” is often orders of magnitude smaller than the total extractable concentration, leading to risk assessments that either overestimate hazards or misguide remediation targets.

Over the past three decades, numerous methods have been developed to operationally define and quantify HOC bioavailability. These range from passive sampling techniques that mimic diffusive uptake, to mild solvent extractions that target the rapidly desorbing fraction, to biological assays that directly measure accumulation or effects. Each method rests on distinct principles and carries inherent operational constraints. For example, solid-phase microextraction (SPME) measures freely dissolved concentrations (C_free), which drive diffusive uptake, but its performance depends on fiber coating, equilibration time, and matrix agitation. Tenax extraction, by contrast, depletes the aqueous phase and promotes desorption from labile sites, yet it is non-exhaustive and may not capture strongly bound residues. Semipermeable membrane devices (SPMDs) accumulate HOCs via passive diffusion but require long deployment times and are sensitive to biofouling. In vitro gastrointestinal extraction simulates digestive processes for human or wildlife receptors but varies widely in protocol. Finally, whole-organism bioaccumulation assays provide direct evidence but are costly, time-consuming, and ethically constrained.

Despite this methodological diversity, a comparative synthesis under controlled conditions is lacking. The objective of this study is to evaluate five representative methods—SPME, Tenax extraction, SPMD, in vitro gastrointestinal extraction, and whole-organism bioaccumulation—using a single spiked sediment and a standard test organism (*Lumbriculus variegatus*). We hypothesize that (1) methods measuring the rapidly desorbing or freely dissolved fraction will correlate better with bioaccumulation than total solvent extraction, and (2) each method will exhibit distinct limitations that necessitate a tiered assessment framework. The results are intended to guide researchers and regulators in selecting fit-for-purpose bioavailability methods.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Sediment preparation and spiking

A pristine freshwater sediment (organic carbon content = 2.8%, particle size: 45% sand, 40% silt, 15% clay) was collected from a reference site. After sieving (2 mm) and homogenization, the sediment was spiked with a mixture of 12 PAHs (naphthalene, acenaphthylene, acenaphthene, fluorene, phenanthrene, anthracene, fluoranthene, pyrene, benz[a]anthracene, chrysene, benzo[b]fluoranthene, benzo[a]pyrene) and 6 PCBs (congeners 28, 52, 101, 118, 138, 153) in acetone. The solvent was evaporated under a fume hood for 48 h, and the spiked sediment was aged for 28 days at 4°C in the dark to simulate field weathering. Nominal total HOC concentration was 10 mg kg⁻¹ dry weight for each compound. Actual concentrations were verified by accelerated solvent extraction (ASE) followed by GC–MS analysis.

2.2 Bioaccumulation assay with *Lumbriculus variegatus*

Twenty-four-hour bioaccumulation tests were conducted in 1-L glass beakers containing 100 g wet sediment and 600 mL overlying water (hardness 180 mg L⁻¹ as CaCO₃, pH 7.4 ± 0.2, dissolved oxygen > 6 mg L⁻¹). Fifty adult *L. variegatus* worms were added per beaker. Three replicate beakers were used. After 24 h, worms were retrieved, rinsed, depurated for 6 h in clean water, freeze-dried, and extracted for HOC analysis. Lipid content was determined gravimetrically. Bioaccumulation factors (BAFs) were calculated as the ratio of lipid-normalized worm concentration to total sediment concentration.

2.3 SPME extraction

Commercially available 30-μm polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) fibers were conditioned and used. For each sample, 2 g wet sediment and 40 mL Milli-Q water were placed in a 50-mL amber vial. Fibers were exposed to the slurry for 24 h at 20 ± 1°C with constant stirring (300 rpm). After exposure, fibers were removed, wiped clean, and desorbed in 200 μL of hexane for GC–MS analysis. C_free was calculated using pre-determined partition coefficients (K_f). Three replicates were performed.

2.4 Tenax extraction

Tenax TA (60–80 mesh) was pre-cleaned with acetone and hexane. For each sample, 1 g wet sediment and 0.5 g Tenax were shaken in 40 mL of water at 20°C. At 6, 12, 24, and 48 h, Tenax was replaced with fresh sorbent. The 24-h fraction was used for comparison. Tenax was extracted with hexane:acetone (1:1) and analyzed by GC–MS. The rapidly desorbing fraction (F_rapid) was estimated using a three-compartment first-order desorption model.

2.5 SPMD deployment

Standard SPMDs (91.4 cm × 2.5 cm, 70% triolein) were pre-dialyzed in hexane. Each SPMD was placed in a stainless-steel cage and exposed to 2 L of sediment slurry (1:4 sediment:water) for 14 days at 20°C with gentle agitation. After retrieval, SPMDs were cleaned, dialyzed twice in hexane, and concentrated for GC–MS. Uptake was expressed as ng SPMD⁻¹.

2.6 In vitro gastrointestinal extraction

A simplified three-step method simulating human digestion was used. Briefly, 1 g sediment was sequentially extracted with (i) saliva (pH 6.5, 37°C, 30 min), (ii) gastric fluid (pepsin, pH 1.8, 37°C, 2 h), and (iii) intestinal fluid (pancreatin, bile salts, pH 7.5, 37°C, 4 h). After centrifugation, supernatants were combined and extracted with hexane for GC–MS. Results were expressed as bioaccessible fraction (%). 

2.7 Chemical analysis and quality control

All HOC analyses were performed on an Agilent 7890B GC coupled to a 5977A MSD. Quantification was by internal standard calibration. Method detection limits ranged from 0.5 to 2.0 ng g⁻¹. Recovery of surrogate standards (d10-phenanthrene, PCB-209) was 85–112%. All glassware was baked at 450°C for 4 h.

2.8 Data analysis

Correlations between method-derived metrics and lipid-normalized worm concentrations were assessed using linear regression. Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05. All analyses were performed in R 4.2.1.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Total extraction and bioaccumulation

Total solvent-extractable HOC concentrations in aged sediment ranged from 7.2 to 9.8 mg kg⁻¹ dry weight, representing 72–98% of nominal values. After 24 h, *L. variegatus* accumulated all 18 compounds, with lipid-normalized concentrations ranging from 12.4 to 187.6 μg g⁻¹ lipid. BAFs varied by compound: higher for low-K_ow PAHs (e.g., phenanthrene, log K_ow = 4.5; BAF = 2.8) and lower for high-K_ow compounds (e.g., benzo[a]pyrene, log K_ow = 6.0; BAF = 0.9), consistent with steric hindrance and reduced desorption.

3.2 SPME and Tenax extraction

SPME-derived C_free values ranged from 0.08 to 3.2 ng L⁻¹. The correlation between C_free and worm residues was strong for PAHs (R² = 0.88) but weaker for PCBs (R² = 0.72), likely due to slower mass transfer of planar congeners. Tenax 24-h extraction yielded F_rapid values between 18% and 64% of total HOCs. The relationship between F_rapid and bioaccumulation was the strongest overall (R² = 0.89 across all compounds), indicating that the rapidly desorbing fraction best predicts short-term uptake.

3.3 SPMD and in vitro methods

SPMD uptake after 14 days ranged from 45 to 620 ng per device. Correlation with worm residues was moderate (R² = 0.61), probably because SPMDs integrate over longer periods and may not reflect short-term desorption kinetics. In vitro gastrointestinal extraction gave bioaccessible fractions of 12–48% for PAHs and 8–32% for PCBs. Correlation with bioaccumulation was R² = 0.72, better than SPMD but inferior to Tenax and SPME. The method overestimated bioaccessibility for high-K_ow compounds, possibly due to bile salt enhancement of desorption.

3.4 Comparative performance

When all methods were compared using the same sediment, the ranking of predictive power was: Tenax 24-h > SPME 24-h > in vitro gastrointestinal > SPMD > total solvent extraction (R² = 0.42). This confirms that operationally defined labile fractions outperform total concentrations. However, no method was free of outliers: SPME underpredicted naphthalene (volatilization loss), Tenax overpredicted fluoranthene (matrix effects), and SPMD underpredicted PCB-153 (slow uptake).

4. Discussion

The results support the hypothesis that methods targeting the rapidly desorbing or freely dissolved fraction provide superior predictions of short-term bioaccumulation. Tenax extraction, which depletes the aqueous phase and drives desorption from labile sites, emerged as the most robust proxy. This is consistent with the concept that desorption kinetics, not thermodynamic partitioning alone, govern bioavailability over ecologically relevant time scales. SPME, while theoretically elegant, requires careful calibration of K_f values and is sensitive to dissolved organic carbon (DOC) competition, which may explain its slight underperformance for PCBs.

The moderate performance of SPMDs and in vitro methods highlights their context-specific utility. SPMDs are better suited for long-term integrative monitoring of hydrophobic compounds in water rather than sediment bioavailability. In vitro gastrointestinal extraction is valuable for human health risk assessment but suffers from poor standardization and overestimation for highly hydrophobic compounds. Whole-organism assays remain the gold standard but are impractical for routine screening.

Limitations of this study include the use of a single sediment type and one test organism. Bioavailability is species-dependent and influenced by factors such as feeding strategy, lipid composition, and gut surfactants. Aging time (28 days) may not represent field-aged sediments where sequestration can be more pronounced. Furthermore, our spiked sediment may not capture the heterogeneity of native HOC mixtures.

A tiered framework is therefore recommended. Tier 1: rapid screening using Tenax or SPME to estimate labile fractions. Tier 2: confirmatory bioaccumulation assays with representative benthic organisms. Tier 3: site-specific in vitro or SPMD methods when regulatory endpoints require human or wildlife receptor assessment. This approach balances cost, speed, and ecological relevance.

5. Conclusion

This study compared five methods for assessing HOC bioavailability in a controlled sediment system. Tenax 24-h extraction and SPME provided the strongest correlations with bioaccumulation in *Lumbriculus variegatus*, while SPMD and in vitro gastrointestinal extraction showed moderate predictive power. Total solvent extraction was a poor surrogate. Each method has distinct principles, operational requirements, and limitations: SPME is sensitive to DOC and volatilization; Tenax is non-exhaustive and matrix-sensitive; SPMDs require long deployment; in vitro methods lack standardization. No single method is universally superior. A tiered, fit-for-purpose strategy combining chemical proxies with targeted bioassays is recommended for regulatory and research applications. Future work should validate these findings across diverse sediments, organisms, and field-contaminated sites.

title: A large-scale genomic association analysis identifies the candidate causal genes conferring stripe rust resistance under multiple field environments
text: Stripe rust, caused by *Puccinia striiformis* f. sp. *tritici*, is one of the most destructive diseases of wheat worldwide, causing substantial yield losses under epidemic conditions. Deployment of resistant cultivars is the most economical and environmentally sustainable strategy for disease control. However, resistance frequently breaks down due to the rapid evolution of pathogen races, and many resistance loci remain uncharacterized at the gene level. Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) combined with multi-environment field phenotyping provide a powerful approach to dissect the genetic architecture of quantitative disease resistance and to prioritize candidate causal genes. Here, we conducted a large-scale genomic association analysis of stripe rust resistance evaluated across multiple field environments. We identified stable quantitative trait loci and resolved several candidate causal genes underlying field resistance. These findings advance our understanding of the genetic basis of durable stripe rust resistance and provide valuable targets for marker-assisted breeding in wheat.

title: Enhanced Treatment Effects of Tilmicosin Against Staphylococcus aureus Cow Mastitis by Self-Assembly Sodium Alginate-Chitosan Nanogel
text:
Results and Discussion

The tilmicosin-loaded sodium alginate-chitosan nanogel (TMS-ACN) exhibited a uniform spherical morphology with a mean particle size of 186.3 ± 4.7 nm, a PDI of 0.21, and a zeta potential of +28.6 mV. The encapsulation efficiency and drug loading capacity were 82.4 ± 2.1% and 18.7 ± 0.9%, respectively. In vitro release studies showed a sustained profile, with 64.2% of tilmicosin released from TMS-ACN over 72 h versus 91.5% from free tilmicosin within 12 h. In a murine model of *S. aureus*-induced mastitis, TMS-ACN reduced bacterial counts in mammary tissue to 2.31 ± 0.28 log₁₀ CFU/g, significantly lower (P < 0.01) than free tilmicosin (4.12 ± 0.35 log₁₀ CFU/g) and saline control (6.54 ± 0.41 log₁₀ CFU/g). Histopathology revealed minimal neutrophil infiltration and preserved glandular architecture in the TMS-ACN group. The enhanced efficacy is attributed to chitosan-mediated mucoadhesion, prolonged drug retention in the mammary gland, and improved intracellular delivery to infected epithelial cells. These findings suggest that the self-assembled nanogel is a promising strategy for treating bovine mastitis.

title: Epidemiology of injuries from fire, heat and hot substances: global, regional and national morbidity and mortality estimates from the Global Burden of Disease 2017 study
text:
Epidemiology of injuries from fire, heat and hot substances: global, regional and national morbidity and mortality estimates from the Global Burden of Disease 2017 study

Abstract

Background: Injuries from fire, heat and hot substances remain a significant global public health challenge, yet comprehensive estimates of their burden across regions and nations are limited. This study aims to provide global, regional and national estimates of morbidity and mortality attributable to fire, heat and hot substance injuries from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2017 study.

Methods: Using the GBD 2017 framework, we analysed data on incidence, prevalence, years lived with disability (YLDs), years of life lost (YLLs), disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and deaths due to fire, heat and hot substances. Estimates were stratified by age, sex, year, and Socio-demographic Index (SDI) quintiles across 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2017. Age-standardised rates were calculated per 100,000 population with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs).

Results: In 2017, fire, heat and hot substances caused an estimated 8.6 million (95% UI: 7.9–9.4) new injuries, 120,600 deaths (95% UI: 108,300–134,700), and 4.9 million DALYs (95% UI: 4.4–5.5) globally. The age-standardised mortality rate declined by 32.4% from 1990 to 2017, while the age-standardised DALY rate decreased by 28.7%. Low-SDI and low-middle-SDI regions bore disproportionate burdens, with sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia accounting for 61.3% of global deaths. Children under five and older adults exhibited the highest mortality rates. Males had higher age-standardised rates than females across most regions. Falls, contact with hot liquids, and residential fires were the leading mechanisms.

Conclusions: Despite substantial declines in age-standardised rates over nearly three decades, the absolute burden of fire, heat and hot substance injuries remains high, particularly in low-income settings. Targeted prevention strategies—including safe cooking practices, smoke alarms, and burn care capacity strengthening—are urgently needed to reduce this preventable burden.

Keywords: burns; fire; hot substances; global burden of disease; epidemiology; disability-adjusted life years; injury prevention

1. Introduction

Injuries resulting from exposure to fire, heat and hot substances—commonly encompassing flame burns, scalds, contact burns and inhalation injury—represent a major but often neglected component of the global injury burden. Unlike many infectious and chronic diseases, these injuries are largely preventable and disproportionately affect vulnerable populations, including young children, the elderly, and those living in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

The World Health Organization has estimated that burns alone account for hundreds of thousands of deaths annually, with the vast majority occurring in LMICs. Survivors frequently endure prolonged hospitalisation, disfigurement, disability, psychosocial sequelae and catastrophic health expenditure. Despite this, burn and fire-related injuries have received comparatively less attention in global health agendas than road traffic injuries or violence.

The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study provides a systematic, comparative framework to quantify health loss from diseases and injuries across populations and time. The GBD 2017 iteration incorporated updated data sources, refined modelling strategies, and expanded geographical coverage, enabling more granular estimates of morbidity and mortality.

This study aims to: (1) describe global, regional and national levels and trends of morbidity and mortality from fire, heat and hot substances between 1990 and 2017; (2) examine patterns by age, sex and Socio-demographic Index (SDI); and (3) identify priority regions and populations for prevention and health system strengthening. We hypothesise that although age-standardised rates have declined globally, absolute numbers remain stable or increasing in low-SDI regions due to population growth and limited prevention infrastructure.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study design and data sources

We conducted a secondary analysis of GBD 2017 estimates for injuries due to fire, heat and hot substances. The GBD 2017 study collated data from vital registration systems, verbal autopsy studies, hospital records, surveys and published literature. Injury causes were classified according to the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) codes X00–X19 (exposure to smoke, fire and flames), X10–X19 (contact with heat and hot substances), and related sequelae.

2.2 Case definitions

Fire, heat and hot substance injuries included: burns from flames, hot liquids, steam, hot objects, and chemical or electrical burns where heat was the primary mechanism. Inhalation injury and smoke inhalation were included when coded as part of fire-related events. Intentional self-harm by fire was excluded from the main analysis and treated separately to avoid confounding.

2.3 Statistical modelling

Estimates were generated using DisMod-MR 2.1, a Bayesian meta-regression tool, to model incidence, prevalence and remission. Mortality estimates were derived from cause-of-death ensemble models. YLDs were calculated as prevalence multiplied by disability weights. YLLs were computed using standard GBD life expectancy tables. DALYs were the sum of YLLs and YLDs. All rates were age-standardised to the GBD world population.

2.4 Stratification and uncertainty

Estimates were stratified by 21 GBD regions, 195 countries, 5-year age groups, sex, and SDI quintiles. Uncertainty intervals (UIs) were generated from 1,000 draws of the posterior distribution and reported as 95% UIs. Trends were assessed as percentage change in age-standardised rates between 1990 and 2017.

2.5 Ethical considerations

This study used publicly available, de-identified aggregate data; therefore, ethical approval was not required.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Global burden in 2017

In 2017, fire, heat and hot substances resulted in an estimated 8.6 million (95% UI: 7.9–9.4) incident cases, 120,600 deaths (95% UI: 108,300–134,700), and 4.9 million DALYs (95% UI: 4.4–5.5). The global age-standardised mortality rate was 1.6 per 100,000 (95% UI: 1.4–1.8), and the age-standardised DALY rate was 63.2 per 100,000 (95% UI: 56.8–70.1). YLLs accounted for 88.4% of total DALYs, reflecting the high case fatality and premature mortality associated with severe burns.

3.2 Trends from 1990 to 2017

Between 1990 and 2017, the age-standardised mortality rate declined by 32.4% (from 2.4 to 1.6 per 100,000), and the age-standardised DALY rate declined by 28.7% (from 88.6 to 63.2 per 100,000). However, due to population growth and ageing, the absolute number of deaths increased slightly in low-SDI regions. The global number of incident cases rose by 11.2%, from 7.7 million to 8.6 million.

3.3 Regional distribution

The burden was highly uneven. Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia together accounted for 61.3% of global deaths in 2017. The highest age-standardised mortality rates were observed in low-SDI (3.1 per 100,000) and low-middle-SDI (2.2 per 100,000) regions, compared with 0.6 per 100,000 in high-SDI regions. Central sub-Saharan Africa had the highest regional rate (4.8 per 100,000), while Australasia had the lowest (0.3 per 100,000).

3.4 Age and sex patterns

Children under five years had the highest mortality rate (4.2 per 100,000), followed by adults aged 70 years and older (3.8 per 100,000). Among children, scalds from hot liquids and contact with hot surfaces predominated. Among older adults, residential fires and flame burns were more common. Males had higher age-standardised mortality rates than females in nearly all regions, with a global male-to-female ratio of 1.4:1. This disparity was widest in Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

3.5 Mechanisms and settings

Based on available data, the leading mechanisms were: residential fires (34.2% of deaths), contact with hot liquids and steam (27.8%), contact with hot objects (16.5%), and chemical or electrical burns (8.9%). Occupational exposures accounted for an estimated 12.6% of cases, disproportionately affecting young adult males in construction, manufacturing and informal sectors.

3.6 SDI gradients

There was a strong inverse gradient between SDI and age-standardised DALY rates. For every 0.1 increase in SDI, the age-standardised DALY rate decreased by an average of 9.4% (95% CI: 7.8–11.0). This gradient was consistent across sexes and age groups, though the magnitude was greatest among children under five.

4. Discussion

This study provides comprehensive estimates of the global burden of fire, heat and hot substance injuries from GBD 2017. Three principal findings emerge. First, although age-standardised rates have declined substantially since 1990, the absolute burden remains enormous, with over 120,000 deaths and 4.9 million DALYs in 2017. Second, the burden is disproportionately concentrated in low-SDI and low-middle-SDI regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Third, children under five and older adults bear the highest mortality rates, with males at elevated risk across most settings.

The decline in age-standardised rates likely reflects improvements in fire safety regulations, building codes, smoke alarm use, safer cooking technologies, and burn care in many high- and middle-income countries. However, these gains have not been equitably distributed. In low-SDI regions, rapid urbanisation, reliance on open fires and kerosene for cooking, overcrowded housing, and limited access to acute burn care perpetuate high mortality.

The male predominance observed in our analysis is consistent with occupational and behavioural exposures, including firefighting, industrial work, and risk-taking behaviours. The elevated risk among older adults may reflect reduced mobility, sensory impairment, and frailty, which impair escape from fires and increase susceptibility to severe burns.

Our findings align with previous GBD analyses and WHO estimates, though differences in case definitions and modelling approaches exist. The inclusion of hot substance injuries beyond flame burns is a strength, as scalds are a leading mechanism in children. However, several limitations warrant consideration. First, data from low-SDI regions rely heavily on verbal autopsy and may be subject to misclassification. Second, disability weights for disfigurement and psychosocial sequelae may underestimate true morbidity. Third, GBD excludes intentional self-harm by fire and some occupational exposures, potentially underestimating the full burden. Fourth, uncertainty intervals are wide in data-sparse regions.

Implications for policy and practice are clear. First, governments should enforce and expand fire safety legislation, including smoke alarms, fire-retardant materials, and safe cooking appliances. Second, community-based prevention programmes should target caregivers of young children, promoting safe storage of hot liquids and supervision. Third, health systems in low-SDI regions require strengthened burn care capacity, including specialised units, skin grafting supplies, and rehabilitation services. Fourth, surveillance systems must be improved to capture mechanism, setting and outcome data to inform targeted interventions. Fifth, global health financing should prioritise injury prevention as part of universal health coverage.

Future research should focus on implementation science, evaluating the effectiveness of prevention programmes in low-resource settings, and on longitudinal studies of burn survivors to quantify long-term disability and economic impact.

5. Conclusion

Fire, heat and hot substance injuries remain a major cause of preventable morbidity and mortality worldwide. Although age-standardised rates declined by approximately one-third between 1990 and 2017, the absolute burden remains high, with 120,600 deaths and 4.9 million DALYs in 2017. The burden is heavily concentrated in low-SDI and low-middle-SDI regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and disproportionately affects children under five and older adults. Males experience higher rates than females across most regions. Scaling up evidence-based prevention—including safe cooking practices, smoke alarms, fire safety regulations, and improved burn care—is essential to reduce this preventable burden and achieve health equity.

title: Progress in Tissue Culture and Genetic Transformation of Oil Palm: An Overview
text:
Progress in Tissue Culture and Genetic Transformation of Oil Palm: An Overview

 Abstract

Oil palm (*Elaeis guineensis* Jacq.) is the world's most productive oilseed crop, yet its improvement through conventional breeding is constrained by a long generation cycle and limited genetic variability. This paper reviews advances in tissue culture and genetic transformation technologies developed for oil palm, drawing on a synthesis of published protocols and illustrative experimental data. Using zygotic embryos and immature inflorescences as explants, we established embryogenic callus cultures with initiation frequencies of 68.4% and 41.2%, respectively. Regeneration efficiency reached 74.6% for somatic embryos matured on medium supplemented with 0.5 mg/L abscisic acid. *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*-mediated transformation of embryogenic callus using strain EHA105 harbouring pCAMBIA1301 yielded 12.3% transient GUS expression and 3.8% stable transformation, confirmed by PCR and Southern blot analysis. Particle bombardment produced higher transient expression (21.7%) but lower stable integration (1.9%). Key limitations include somaclonal variation, low transformation frequency, and genotype dependence. Emerging tools such as CRISPR/Cas9 and minimal-growth conservation offer promising avenues for accelerating oil palm genetic improvement.

Keywords: *Elaeis guineensis*; somatic embryogenesis; *Agrobacterium*; particle bombardment; somaclonal variation; genetic improvement

 Introduction

Oil palm (*Elaeis guineensis* Jacq.) accounts for approximately 40% of global vegetable oil production on less than 6% of oilseed-crop land, making it the most efficient oil-producing crop worldwide. Major breeding objectives include increased mesocarp oil content, improved fatty acid composition, dwarf stature, and resistance to *Ganoderma boninense*, the causal agent of basal stem rot. Conventional breeding, however, requires 10–15 years per generation, and the crop's narrow genetic base limits progress.

Tissue culture, particularly somatic embryogenesis, enables clonal propagation of elite palms and provides the totipotent material essential for genetic transformation. Since the first successful oil palm tissue culture in the 1970s, protocols have improved substantially, although somaclonal variation—especially the "mantled" flowering abnormality—remains problematic. Genetic transformation offers a complementary route for introducing desirable traits, but oil palm is notoriously recalcitrant, with reported stable transformation frequencies generally below 5%.

This paper provides an overview of progress in oil palm tissue culture and transformation, presenting representative data from our laboratory alongside a critical appraisal of current bottlenecks and future prospects.

 Materials and Methods

Plant material. Zygotic embryos and immature inflorescences were excised from *E. guineensis* var. *tenera* (Deli × Yangambi) palms aged 8–10 years at a commercial plantation.

Callus induction. Explants were cultured on MS medium supplemented with 2,4-D (100–450 µM), 3% sucrose, and 0.3% Gelrite at pH 5.7, incubated in darkness at 27 ± 1 °C. Callus initiation was scored after 12 weeks.

Somatic embryogenesis and regeneration. Embryogenic calli were transferred to medium containing 2,4-D (10–50 µM) and ABA (0–2 mg/L). Mature somatic embryos were germinated on hormone-free MS medium under a 16/8 h photoperiod.

Transformation. Embryogenic calli were co-cultivated with *A. tumefaciens* EHA105 carrying pCAMBIA1301 (hptII, *uidA*) for 3 days, then selected on hygromycin (20–40 mg/L). Particle bombardment used 1.0 µm gold particles at 1,100 psi. GUS expression was assayed histochemically; stable integration was verified by PCR and Southern blotting.

Experimental design. Each treatment comprised three replicates of 60 explants; data were analysed by ANOVA (P < 0.05).

 Results

Callus induction and regeneration. Zygotic embryos produced embryogenic callus at 68.4 ± 4.1%, significantly higher than immature inflorescences (41.2 ± 3.7%) (Table 1). Optimal 2,4-D concentration was 350 µM for embryos and 450 µM for inflorescences. Addition of 0.5 mg/L ABA increased somatic embryo maturation to 74.6 ± 3.2%, compared with 52.1 ± 4.8% in controls. Germination of mature embryos averaged 61.3%.

Table 1. Callus induction and regeneration from two explant types (mean ± SD, n = 3).

| Explant | Callus induction (%) | Embryogenic callus (%) | Regeneration (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zygotic embryo | 68.4 ± 4.1 | 44.7 ± 3.5 | 74.6 ± 3.2 |
| Immature inflorescence | 41.2 ± 3.7 | 22.9 ± 2.8 | 58.4 ± 4.5 |

Transformation. *Agrobacterium*-mediated transformation gave 12.3 ± 1.8% transient GUS expression and 3.8 ± 0.6% stable transformation. Particle bombardment yielded higher transient expression (21.7 ± 2.4%) but lower stable transformation (1.9 ± 0.4%). Southern analysis of ten putative transgenic lines confirmed single- or low-copy integration in six lines. Regenerated transformants showed normal phenotype in the nursery, though 8% exhibited abnormal frond morphology.

 Discussion

The present data confirm that zygotic embryos remain the most responsive explant for oil palm embryogenesis, consistent with earlier reports. The stimulatory effect of ABA on somatic embryo maturation likely reflects its role in desiccation tolerance and storage reserve accumulation. Nonetheless, regeneration efficiency remains genotype-dependent, and the mantled abnormality—affecting up to 5% of regenerants in some studies—continues to limit commercial exploitation of clonal propagation.

Transformation frequencies obtained here (1.9–3.8%) fall within the range reported internationally (0.5–5%). *Agrobacterium*-mediated methods generally produce cleaner integration events with fewer transgene copies than bombardment, but both suffer from low efficiency and prolonged selection periods (6–9 months). Improvements in selectable markers, such as the use of phosphomannose isomerase, and the incorporation of surfactants or sonication during co-cultivation have raised efficiencies modestly in other laboratories.

Emerging technologies promise to transform the field. CRISPR/Cas9 has been applied in oil palm protoplasts and embryogenic calli, targeting the *EgFAD2* gene, with editing efficiencies of 5–15% reported. However, regeneration of edited plants remains the principal bottleneck. Minimal-growth conservation and cryopreservation of embryogenic lines could safeguard elite genotypes and reduce somaclonal variation during long culture cycles.

 Conclusion

Oil palm tissue culture is now sufficiently mature to support clonal propagation of elite palms, with embryogenic callus induction exceeding 68% and regeneration approaching 75% under optimised conditions. Genetic transformation, while demonstrated, remains inefficient, with stable frequencies below 4%. Future progress will depend on integrating improved regeneration systems with precise genome-editing tools, reducing somaclonal variation, and developing genotype-independent protocols. Such advances are essential if biotechnology is to contribute meaningfully to sustainable oil palm improvement.

 References (illustrative)

1. Corley, R.H.V. & Tinker, P.B. (2016). *The Oil Palm*, 5th edn. Wiley-Blackwell.
2. Parveez, G.K.A. et al. (2015). *Plant Cell Reports*, 34, 1123–1136.
3. Masani, M.Y.A. et al. (2014). *Plant Cell, Tissue and Organ Culture*, 118, 1–13.
4. Yeap, W.C. et al. (2021). *Frontiers in Plant Science*, 12, 687–701.

title: Causation mechanism analysis for haze pollution related to vehicle emission in Guangzhou, China by employing the fault tree approach
text:
Haze pollution has become a major environmental concern in rapidly urbanizing megacities, and vehicle emission is widely recognized as a critical contributor. However, the causal relationships among the multiple interacting factors that drive vehicle-emission-related haze remain insufficiently quantified, which hinders the formulation of effective mitigation policies. This study develops a fault tree approach to systematically analyze the causation mechanism of haze pollution related to vehicle emission in Guangzhou, China. A fault tree model is constructed with "haze pollution related to vehicle emission" as the top event, and the causal factors are decomposed into multiple intermediate and basic events covering vehicle characteristics, fuel quality, traffic conditions, meteorological factors, and road infrastructure. Boolean logic and minimal cut set analysis are employed to identify the critical causal pathways, and the importance of each basic event is evaluated through structural importance and probability importance analysis. The results reveal that the most probable causal paths are associated with high vehicle density, frequent traffic congestion, low fuel quality, and adverse meteorological conditions such as low wind speed and high humidity, which jointly promote the accumulation and secondary formation of fine particulate matter. Among the basic events, inadequate emission control technology, poor maintenance of in-use vehicles, and insufficient traffic management are identified as the dominant contributors, while meteorological factors act as important amplifying conditions. The findings indicate that haze pollution related to vehicle emission in Guangzhou is not attributable to a single factor but results from the coupling of technical, managerial, and meteorological causes. Accordingly, integrated control strategies are proposed, including strengthening emission standards and in-use vehicle inspection, promoting clean fuels and new energy vehicles, optimizing traffic organization, and enhancing regional joint prevention and control. This study demonstrates that the fault tree approach is an effective tool for revealing the causation mechanism of complex urban haze pollution and can provide a scientific basis for decision-making on vehicle emission reduction and air quality improvement in megacities.

Keywords: haze pollution; vehicle emission; fault tree analysis; causation mechanism; minimal cut set; Guangzhou

title: Better understanding of homologous recombination through a 12-week laboratory course for undergraduates majoring in biotechnology
text:
Better understanding of homologous recombination through a 12-week laboratory course for undergraduates majoring in biotechnology

Abstract

Homologous recombination (HR) is a central concept in molecular genetics and biotechnology, yet undergraduate students often struggle to connect its mechanistic details with experimental practice. This study reports the design, implementation, and evaluation of a 12-week laboratory course for biotechnology majors aimed at deepening understanding of HR through a coherent sequence of wet-lab experiments and data analysis. The course integrated gene knockout construction in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, double-strand break repair assays, PCR-based verification, and quantitative analysis of recombination efficiency. A total of 48 third-year undergraduates participated across two semesters. Learning outcomes were assessed using pre- and post-course concept inventories, experimental reports, and a final practical examination. Results showed a significant increase in conceptual scores from 42.3 ± 11.7 to 78.6 ± 9.4 (p < 0.001), with the largest gains in mechanisms of strand invasion and resolution. Students also demonstrated improved experimental design and troubleshooting skills. Questionnaire responses indicated high satisfaction, particularly with the continuity of the project and the emphasis on data interpretation. These findings suggest that a long-term, inquiry-based laboratory course can effectively bridge theoretical knowledge and practical skills in HR teaching.

Keywords: homologous recombination; laboratory course; undergraduate biotechnology; gene knockout; inquiry-based learning; molecular genetics education

1. Introduction

Homologous recombination is a fundamental biological process that enables accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), promotes genetic diversity during meiosis, and underpins many biotechnological applications such as gene targeting, CRISPR-assisted knock-in, and synthetic biology (Krogh & Symington, 2004; Jasin & Rothstein, 2013). For undergraduates majoring in biotechnology, a robust understanding of HR is essential not only for advanced courses in molecular biology and genetic engineering but also for laboratory work involving gene editing, vector construction, and strain improvement.

However, teaching HR effectively remains challenging. Traditional lecture-based instruction often presents HR as a series of abstract steps—resection, strand invasion, D-loop formation, and resolution—without allowing students to observe or manipulate the process (Newman et al., 2018). As a result, students may memorize terminology but fail to apply it to experimental scenarios. Laboratory courses can address this gap, but short, disconnected practicals frequently reduce complex phenomena to recipe-following exercises (Hofstein & Lunetta, 2004). There is thus a need for integrated laboratory curricula that allow students to investigate HR over an extended period, generate meaningful data, and reflect on mechanistic models.

In this study, we designed and evaluated a 12-week laboratory course specifically focused on HR. The course used the budding yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* as a model organism because of its efficient HR machinery and ease of genetic manipulation. Students constructed a gene deletion strain, measured HR efficiency using a reporter assay, and analyzed recombination outcomes by PCR and sequencing. We hypothesized that this sustained, inquiry-based approach would improve both conceptual understanding and practical competence. The following sections describe the course design, assessment methods, results, and implications for biotechnology education.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Course design and participants

The course was offered to third-year undergraduates majoring in biotechnology at a comprehensive university. A total of 48 students (26 female, 22 male) enrolled across two consecutive semesters. All students had completed prerequisite courses in genetics, molecular biology, and basic microbiology. The course ran for 12 weeks, with one 4-hour laboratory session and one 1-hour tutorial per week.

The course was organized around a central project: constructing a *rad52* deletion strain of *S. cerevisiae* and characterizing its HR deficiency. *RAD52* encodes a key recombination mediator, and its deletion reduces HR efficiency. Each week built on the previous one, moving from strain maintenance to transformation, selection, verification, and quantitative assays.

2.2 Week-by-week experimental workflow

Weeks 1–2 introduced yeast culture, transformation, and the concept of DSB repair. Students learned aseptic technique and prepared competent cells. In week 3, they performed lithium acetate transformation with a *rad52::KanMX* deletion cassette flanked by homology arms. Weeks 4–5 involved selection on YPD+G418 plates and colony PCR to confirm integration. Weeks 6–7 focused on PCR verification of the deletion junction and sequencing of the homology arm. In week 8, students set up a plasmid-based HR reporter assay using a split-lacZ construct with an I-SceI-induced DSB. Weeks 9–10 involved measuring β-galactosidase activity and calculating recombination efficiency. Week 11 was dedicated to data analysis, statistical testing, and troubleshooting. Week 12 comprised a final practical examination and poster presentation.

2.3 Assessment instruments

Conceptual understanding was measured using a 20-item multiple-choice concept inventory developed from previously validated instruments on DNA repair and recombination (Bowling et al., 2008). The inventory was administered in week 1 (pre-test) and week 12 (post-test). Experimental skills were assessed through weekly lab notebooks, two formal lab reports, and a final practical exam. A 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire evaluated student perceptions of the course. Statistical analysis used paired t-tests and Cohen’s d for effect size.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Conceptual gains

The pre-test mean score was 42.3 ± 11.7 (out of 100), indicating limited prior understanding. The post-test mean increased to 78.6 ± 9.4, a statistically significant improvement (t(47) = 18.42, p < 0.001, d = 2.31). Item-level analysis showed the greatest gains for questions on strand invasion (from 31% to 84% correct), D-loop resolution (from 28% to 79%), and the role of RAD52 (from 35% to 88%). Smaller but significant gains were observed for questions on non-homologous end joining and crossover versus non-crossover outcomes.

3.2 Experimental performance

All 48 students successfully generated the *rad52* deletion strain, although 7 students required troubleshooting due to weak PCR bands. Colony PCR confirmed correct integration in 41 of 48 strains on the first attempt; the remaining 7 were corrected after repeating transformation. In the HR reporter assay, the wild-type strain showed a mean recombination efficiency of 8.7 ± 1.2 × 10⁻³, while the *rad52* mutant showed 1.4 ± 0.5 × 10⁻³, representing an 84% reduction. Students’ calculated values were consistent with instructor reference data (within 15% error). Lab report scores averaged 82.4 ± 6.8, with the highest marks for data presentation and interpretation.

3.3 Student perceptions

Questionnaire results indicated strong satisfaction. 91% of students agreed that the 12-week structure helped them understand HR as a process rather than a set of facts. 87% reported increased confidence in designing genetic experiments. Open-ended comments highlighted the value of “seeing the deletion work” and “connecting PCR results to recombination mechanisms.” The most common suggestion was to allocate more time for sequencing analysis.

4. Discussion

The results support the hypothesis that a sustained, project-based laboratory course can significantly improve undergraduate learning of homologous recombination. The large conceptual gains (d = 2.31) exceed typical effect sizes reported for short laboratory modules (Springer et al., 1999), likely because students repeatedly encountered HR concepts in different experimental contexts over 12 weeks. This aligns with constructivist theories of learning, which emphasize iterative, situated practice (Kolb, 1984).

The hands-on construction of a *rad52* mutant was particularly effective. Students directly observed the phenotypic consequence of HR deficiency, which made the abstract role of RAD52 tangible. The reporter assay further allowed quantitative reasoning about recombination efficiency, bridging molecular mechanisms and statistical analysis. This integration of wet-lab and dry-lab work reflects best practices in biotechnology education (Wei & Woodin, 2011).

Several limitations should be noted. First, the study lacked a control group receiving traditional instruction, so causal claims are tempered. Second, the concept inventory, while validated, may not capture all dimensions of HR understanding. Third, the 48-student sample from one institution limits generalizability. Future iterations could include multi-institutional trials and delayed post-tests to assess retention.

Pedagogically, the course demonstrates the value of “vertical” laboratory curricula that build skills and concepts incrementally. Instead of isolated practicals on DNA extraction or PCR, students engaged in a coherent investigation. This approach also mirrors real research, where recombination analysis requires iterative troubleshooting. For biotechnology majors, such experience is directly relevant to careers in gene editing, biopharmaceutical development, and molecular diagnostics.

5. Conclusion

This 12-week laboratory course successfully improved undergraduate biotechnology students’ understanding of homologous recombination and their experimental competence. By integrating gene knockout construction, HR reporter assays, and data analysis into a single project, the course transformed HR from an abstract lecture topic into a tangible, investigatable phenomenon. Significant gains in concept inventory scores and high satisfaction ratings support the effectiveness of the design. We recommend that biotechnology programs consider adopting similar long-term, inquiry-based laboratory courses to strengthen molecular genetics education. Future work should examine long-term retention and transfer to novel gene-editing tasks.

title: Evolving population distribution in China's border regions: Spatial differences, driving forces and policy implications
text: China’s border regions are vast, strategically significant, and home to diverse ethnic groups, yet they have experienced dramatic demographic shifts amid rapid urbanization, market reforms, and changing geopolitical priorities. Understanding how population distribution has evolved in these peripheries is crucial for territorial governance, national security, and equitable development. Existing studies often focus on coastal or interior regions, leaving border areas underexamined, particularly regarding spatial heterogeneity and underlying drivers. This paper analyzes the evolving population distribution across China’s border counties from 2000 to 2020, identifies spatial differences using geographic information systems and spatial statistical methods, and explores driving forces through econometric modeling. It further discusses policy implications for population stabilization, border security, and regional revitalization. The findings aim to inform balanced development strategies and contribute to international debates on peripheral regions in transitional economies.

title: 3-Dimensional simulations and student learning in orthodontic education
text:
Results and Discussion

Students in the 3D simulation group (n = 48) outperformed the traditional mannequin group (n = 47) on the post-test (mean 84.6 ± 6.2 vs. 76.3 ± 7.8; p < 0.001, d = 1.18). The 3D group also completed bracket-placement tasks faster (12.4 ± 2.1 min vs. 16.8 ± 2.9 min; p < 0.001) with fewer positioning errors (2.3 ± 1.1 vs. 4.6 ± 1.7; p < 0.001). Satisfaction scores were higher in the 3D group (4.5 ± 0.5 vs. 3.9 ± 0.7 on a 5-point scale; p < 0.001). These findings suggest that 3D simulation enhances both skill acquisition and efficiency, likely by providing immediate visual feedback and unlimited repetition. However, the modest sample and single-institution design limit generalizability, and long-term retention of skills remains untested.

title: Sonication enhances polyphenolic compounds, sugars, carotenoids and mineral elements of apple juice
text:
Sonication enhances polyphenolic compounds, sugars, carotenoids and mineral elements of apple juice

Abstract

Ultrasound-assisted processing has emerged as a promising non-thermal technology for preserving and improving the nutritional quality of fruit juices. This study investigated the effects of sonication on the bioactive compounds and mineral profile of freshly pressed apple juice. Apple juice samples were subjected to ultrasonic treatment at a frequency of 20 kHz with varying amplitudes (40%, 60%, and 80%) and treatment times (5, 10, and 15 min). Results showed that sonication significantly increased the total phenolic content (from 312.5 to 478.3 mg GAE/L), total flavonoids (from 98.7 to 156.2 mg CE/L), and individual phenolic acids such as chlorogenic acid and caffeic acid. Total soluble sugars increased by up to 18.6%, while carotenoid content improved from 1.24 to 2.07 mg β-carotene/L. Mineral elements including potassium, calcium, magnesium, and iron also showed significant increases after sonication. The maximum enhancement was generally observed at 60% amplitude for 10 min. These findings suggest that sonication is an effective technique for enhancing the nutritional value of apple juice without compromising its safety.

Keywords: sonication; apple juice; polyphenols; carotenoids; sugars; mineral elements

1. Introduction

Apple juice is one of the most widely consumed fruit juices globally, valued for its pleasant taste and rich content of bioactive compounds. It contains significant amounts of polyphenols, dietary fibers, vitamins, and essential minerals that contribute to human health. Regular consumption of apple juice has been associated with reduced risk of chronic diseases such as cardiovascular disorders, diabetes, and certain types of cancer, largely due to its antioxidant properties (Boyer & Liu, 2004).

Traditional thermal processing, while effective in microbial inactivation and enzyme stabilization, often leads to degradation of heat-sensitive bioactive compounds, loss of volatile aroma, and undesirable changes in color and nutritional quality. Consequently, non-thermal technologies such as high-pressure processing, pulsed electric fields, and ultrasound have gained considerable attention as alternatives to conventional thermal treatment.

Sonication, or ultrasound processing, involves the application of high-frequency sound waves (typically 20–100 kHz) to a liquid medium. The acoustic cavitation generated by ultrasound creates localized high pressure and temperature zones, leading to cell wall disruption and enhanced mass transfer. This mechanism can facilitate the release of intracellular bioactive compounds into the juice matrix, thereby improving nutritional quality. Previous studies have reported that sonication can increase the extractability of polyphenols in various fruit juices, including grape, orange, and pomegranate. However, comprehensive studies examining the simultaneous effects of sonication on multiple nutrient categories in apple juice remain limited.
